This decision of ours corresponds most exactly to the doctrine concerning the providence of God. For although of all things, as also of all afflictions falling under the providence of God, some necessity is given and conceded: a necessity, namely, ex hypothesi: yet this itself does not depend on the perpetual and immutable nexus of secondary causes, and an implicit series, but on the infallible certainty of divine providence and foreknowledge. For in the same way that things happen: in that same way they were already foreseen and provided for by God from all eternity: so that divine providence is never deceived, since it depends on the infallible omniscience of God's foreknowledge, and on that divine order (τάξει) of all human things and events, subservient to a certain end, the glory of God, and the benefit of the Church: but not on the indissoluble connection of causes, about which the Stoics, and Boethius following their opinion, babble.

III. Not much different from the Stoics are the Calvinist Doctors, who contend that salvation, and damnation, and good and evil, and the means and causes leading to those ends, depend not on the faith, or infidelity, or impiety of men: but on the absolute, immutable good pleasure and decree of God, which precedes all causes: which can be demonstrated to the eye from their own doctrine concerning the providence and predestination of God, indeed it has already been demonstrated by us in the exposition of those Articles. To whose impiety we oppose the same oracles and foundations of Scripture that we oppose to the Stoics.

IV. There are certain astrologers (for not all approve of judicial astrology in all things) who refer all events of all actions, counsels, and studies immutably to the position of the stars, to conjunctions, oppositions, and other aspects of the planets, and, speaking summarily, to the influences of the stars on these lower things. Whence was born that judicial astrology, by which some dare to predict what is going to happen of good or evil, not only to each private individual whose hour of birth they know exactly: but also what fate individual empires, duchies, academies, and republics are to experience. Which judicial astrology, indeed, as the primary predecessors of astronomers themselves admit, fights diametrically against the most noble art of astronomy, and its own proper and genuine end, both by reason of its precepts and by reason of its use and end: thus it collapses by its own vanity and futility, and deserves no suffrage or applause in the sacred Scriptures, nor in Orthodox Antiquity, and the writings of approved Authors.

And that much-talked-of passage of Jeremiah ch. 10, 2 is well known: Do not be afraid of the signs of heaven, which the nations fear. And that calamities are sent by GOD himself, no less than that all other things are governed by him, is also proven by that passage of Amos ch. 3, 6: Shall there be evil in a city, which the Lord has not done? Whence our Author Philip also, in his discussion of these articles, expressly denies that the causes of calamities are to be sought or established in the stars. Nor do we meanwhile deny (what is falsely imputed to us by calumny) that GOD, in inflicting punishments, as in the rest of the government of the universe, uses what they call secondary causes as instruments or means. For we willingly grant this very thing, as having been taught it by the Holy Spirit himself. For according to the Prophet Isaiah, when GOD wishes to punish men with war or the sword, he often summons enemies from far-off places with a hiss, like flies or bees; and he uses them as a hired razor, Isa. 5, 26 and ch. 7, 18 and 20. Thus the cause of famine is for the most part the barrenness of the earth: of barrenness, harmful weather: of weather, there is also some cause in the motion and position of the stars. Nor are there lacking natural causes by which beasts are said to be made fierce against men. Just as certain causes of pestilences can also be assigned from Nature itself. But it is fitting to consider such causes, in whatever way they inhere in Nature, so that we do not reduce to order the divine providence which uses them most freely as it wills: nor should we fear more from them than from GOD himself. Which circumspection some today from the crowd of Astrologers and Calendar-makers are accustomed to apply themselves in their predictions,

V. There are certain Diviners who assign calamities, especially public ones, such as the ruins and changes of Empires, the dissipations of Republics, and more solemn confusions of this kind, to certain and clearly fatal periods of specific years. Whence some have progressed so far that they would not shrink from writing books of Divinations and prescribing this art of divining to the youth. Although we do not deny that books of this kind perhaps deserve the testimony of some not-vulgar erudition: yet we maintain that the end itself which they look to is impious: which can be demonstrated to the eye by those arguments by which we have already refuted the madness of the Stoics above. It is added that these very Diviners are not sufficiently consistent with themselves in defining those certain periods of kingdoms and Empires. For some establish the fatal term as the 250th year, others the 700th, others another cycle of years. Now if you accommodate these very periods of years to the more notable changes of Monarchies, kingdoms, and Republics, you will discover that they nowhere fit or correspond to the event. The first Babylonian Monarchy certainly had a period of one thousand six hundred and forty-six years. For it lasted for that many years. The Monarchy of the Persians expired in the 207th year of its duration. The Monarchy of the Greeks, in the 300th year. The Monarchy of Alexander the Great, in the twelfth year of his reign, was split and torn into four parts. The Kingdom of the Vandals in Africa, certainly most powerful, suffered ruin in the 96th year of its duration. Therefore, as many fatal periods, or Climacteric years of Empires, will have to be established as the number of years each of these is found to have stood. Whence the uncertainty and vanity of this profane art is willingly clear.

VI. There are, as our Author notes, certain Philosophers who seek the cause of calamities and changes in matter, which they say rushes with eternal impulse to other forms and seeks changes. Hence Aristotle built up that dogma of his concerning privation in matter: although we do not entirely reject this opinion, especially if you consider those evils which, by natural constitution, are subject to motion, generation, and corruption: yet it does not define or explain the true and primary cause: which will become plain from what follows.

VII. Therefore, that we may finally open up the true causes of human afflictions: we distinguish them into General or Common, and into Special, proper partly to the pious, partly to the impious.

The general [cause], and the fountain and origin of all evil, is the fall of our first parents, and the most sad defection of the whole human race from GOD resulting thence through sin. For through sin Death entered into the world, and death passed through to all men; even to those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression. Rom. 5, 12 and 14. Whence Augustine writes learnedly in Sermon 4 on the words of the apostle: It passed through, it passed through, attend to the Word: Consider what you have heard: Do you see what 'passed through' is? Thence even the infant is guilty: he did not commit sin, but he contracted it: For that sin did not remain in the fountain: but it passed through: not into him as into him: but it passed through to all men. Thence all men are subject to death, diseases, and other calamities, which our nature itself drags with it as inseparable companions, as the Poet truly said.

At birth we die, and the end hangs from the beginning.

And Hippocrates: ἄνθρωπος ὅλος νόσος δοσογένητης. And the Apostle Rom. 8, 10. The body is destined for death because of sin.

A SECOND general cause is the Justice of GOD, declaring His wrath against sin: so that the distinction between well-doing and evil-doing may be more illustriously perceived in the punishments. For even the godly, although regenerated and reconciled to GOD by faith, often sin gravely: and by their own sins they deserve punishments. Whence GOD himself Jerem. 30, 11. I will chasten you in judgment, that you may not seem innocent to yourself. Mich. 7, 9. I will bear the indignation of the Lord, because I have sinned against him. Isa. 64, 5. & 6. Behold you are angry, and we have sinned, and we have been in sins for a long time, and at length we have been delivered: We have fallen as a leaf, and our iniquities like the wind have carried us away.

THE THIRD General and common cause is the Mercy of GOD, which, as it does at other times by various kinds of benefits, so not rarely by public calamities also, recalls both the ungodly and the godly, who have fallen into sins, to Repentance. In which manner they are like warnings, admonishing of a future judgment at some time, and of the eternal punishments of those who do not repent before death. David acknowledged this in Psalm 119, 71. Saying, It is good for me, O LORD, that you have humbled me, that I might learn your statutes. Isa. 28, 19. Vexation gives understanding. Isa. 26, 16. LORD, in distress they have sought you: the distress, in which they cry out, is discipline to them, Hebr. 12, 6. The LORD scourges every son whom he receives.

THE FOURTH and last General or common cause is, that by the spectacles of horrible punishments others may be deterred, and with greater circumspection and care may avoid the offenses by which such atrocious punishments are drawn on; But especially, that the faithful may become wiser, that is, may progress more and more in the knowledge and fear of GOD, that they may love his Word, fear his judgments, and beware of similar sins, especially those which are committed against conscience. The Apostle treats of this cause expressly, and handles it as a whole common place, showing in what manner the punishments of the Israelites, which they suffered most atrociously, ought to be an example to the Corinthians, so that they do not commit the same crimes and outrages that they did. 1 Cor. 10, 6. up to 13. And David concerning himself, Psal. 119, 120. You cause, that as dross all the wicked of the earth cease: therefore I love your testimonies: My flesh shudders for fear of you, and I am afraid of your judgments.

Latin:

DE hac quæstione non unum, idemq; videtur omnibus. Proinde ut veritatem rectiùs investigemus, κατ᾽ ἄρσιν καὶ θέσιν per remotionem fallarum opinionum, ad positionem veræ doctrinæ paulatim progrediemur.

Ac initiò quidem reperti jam olim fuerunt Epicuræi, hodieq; reperiuntur ἐμπαĩκται, irrisores, & Epicuri de grege porci, qui cœco casui, & cuidam volubilitati Fortunæ, uti cætera universa, sic afflictiones quoque adscribebant, ἀπὸ τῆς ἐνοικόσης ἀυτῆς ἀθεότητος, per inhabitantem quandam impietatem, ut ait Basilius. Verùm istorum furori magis, quàm errori, suprà in dexodo Articuli de Providentia DEI, justam & accuratam Refutationem opposuimus. Hoc loco illud sufficiat, quòd Scriptura Sacra singula & universa, quæ sub Sole sunt, fiunt, & geruntur, ad DEI providentiam expressè refert: adeò, ut ne gressus quidem hominum, volatus passerum, lapsus capillorum, imò ne sortes quidem ab eâ eximi debeant: Jerem. 10. v. 23. Proverb. 5. v. 21. & cap. 16. v. 1, 2. & 9. & 33. Matth. 10. v. 29. & 30. Coloss. 1. v. 17. Hebr. 1. v. 3. Salomon certè rex sapientissimus, felicem ac prosperum regni statum, fecundosq; rerum gerendarum successus, à solo DEO sperandos & petendos esse, disertè docet 1. Reg. 3. v. 9. Propheta Amos, nullum in civitate malum sive pœnam esse scribit, quod non fecerit DOMINUS cap. 3. v. 6. Jeremias in threnis cap. 3. v. 37. Quis est iste, inquit, qui dicere ausit, fieri aliquid DOMINO non jubente? ex ore altissimi non egredi vel bona, vel mala: mala scilicet pœnarum & afflictionum. Facessat ergò istorum prophanitas.

II. Sunt deinde & alii, qui Fato omnia fieri dictitabant, & sempiternam quandam seriem nectebant causarum immutabilium, in ipsa rerum natura, atque mundo inclusarum. Quem errorem jam olim in Stoicis notavit Augustinus, Fatalia, inquiens: appellant isti, quæ præter DEI & hominum voluntatem, Ordinis alicujus necessitate contingunt. lib. 5. de civit. DEI. cap. 1. Nam si ipsam DEI voluntatem, & potentiam, absque omni tamen coactione, & violentia Stoica consideratam, per Fatum intelligerent: Sententiam utique tenere, linguam vero corrigere deberent: uti eodem loco recte subjicit Augustinus. Jam vero quid per Fatum illi intellexerint: inde patet: 1. quod distinxerunt Fatum a Deo: & eidem non voluntatem tantum hominum, sed DEUM etiam ipsum subesse contenderunt. 2. Causis secundis naturæ infixis eam vim tribuerunt, qua agere ex seipsis, & suis viribus quoslibet effectus producere possent. 3. Seriem istarum causarum statuerunt absolute immutabilem, ac proinde omnia absoluta & simplici necessitate fieri ac evenire, opinati sunt, uti refert Augustinus, lib. 5. de civit. DEI. cap. 8. 9. 10. Tale igitur Fatum stupenda prophanitate laborat: Ita, ut haud male censuerit Augustinus, nunquam Stoicos tale fatum credituros fuisse, nisi cor ipsorum fuisset fatuum. Opponimus autem prophanitati huic initio illa ipsa Scripturæ testimonia, quibus Epicuræorum insaniam modo protrivimus. Deinde prædictiones Propheticas pœnarum: ut & eventus prædictionibus examussim respondentes. Exempli gratia: Jerobeam primus rex Israelis, cum duos vitulos aureos idololatricos extrueret: non modo eversio illius Idololatriæ, a Propheta ex tribu Juda prædicitur; sed etiam Rex Josias nominatur, trecentis amplius ante, quam nasceretur, annis 1. Reg. 13. v. 2. 2. Reg. 23. v. 15. Et Jesaias cap. 44. v. 28. & cap. 45. v. 1. non modo liberationem populi Judaici ex Babylonica captivitate, ducentis ferme annis post futuram, prædicit: Sed Regem etiam Persicum Cyrum nominat, qui Judæis reditum in patriam concessurus erat. Jeremias item non modo certum annorum constituit numerum, quibus duratura esset captivitas Babylonica, Jerem. 25. v. 12. & cap. 29. v. 10. sed etiam, quot Reges captivitatis tempore regnaturi sint, expresse prædicit, Jerem. 27. v. 7. Et Daniel non tantum concionatur de venturo Messia, & ejus beneficiis: sed etiam septuaginta annorum hebdomades constituit, intra quas venturus esset Christus, cap. 9. v. 24. Nulla profecto hic fatalis causarum series, nulla absoluta necessitas dari aut monstrari potest. Facesfat ergo hæc Stoicorum impietas; Cui rectissime etiam opponitur tertio loco Conditio illa cominationibus pœnarum Propheticis adjecta. Si pœnitentiam egerit gens a malo suo, contra quam locutus sum: agam & ego pœnitentiam super malo, quod cogitavi, ut facerem ei. Jerem. 18. v. 18.

id quod exemplo Ninevitarum, pœnitentiam agentium ad prædicationem Jonæ, evidentissime demonstratur. Congruit hæc nostra decisio exactissime ad doctrinam de Providentia DEI. Etsi enim rerum omnium, ut & afflictionum omnium, sub DEI providentiam cadentium, aliqua datur, & conceditur necessitas: necessitas nimirum ἐξ ὑποθέσεως: hæc ipsa tamen non dependet a causarum secundarum perpetuo, & immutabili nexu, & implicita quadam serie, sed a Providentiæ & præscientiæ divinæ certitudine infallibili. Quo enim modo res eveniunt: eodem a DEO etiam jam inde ab omni æternitate fuerunt præscitæ & provisæ: ita ut nunquam fallatur divina providentia, quippe quæ dependet a præscientijs DEI infallibili Omniscientia, & a ταξει sive ordinatione illa divina, rerum & eventuum humanorum omnium, ad certum quendam finem, gloriæ DEI, & Ecclesiæ commodo subservientem: non vero ab indissolubili causarum connexione, de qua Stoici, & ex istorum sententia Boëtius nugantur.

III. Stoicis non multum dissimiles sunt Doctores Calviniani, qui & salutem, & damnationem, & bonum & malum, & media ac causas, ad fines istos perducentes, non ab hominum vel fide, vel infidelitate, vel impietate: sed ab absoluto, immutabili, omnesq; causas antegrediente Dei beneplacito ac decreto dependere contendunt: id quod ex ipsorum doctrina de Providentia & Prædestinatione DEI, ad oculum demonstrari potest, imo jam a nobis in istorum Articulorum diexodo demonstratum fuit. Quorum impietati eadem, quæ Stoicis opponimus Scripturæ oracula & fundamenta.

IV. Sunt Astrologi quidam, (non enim omnes judiciariam Astrologiam per omnia probant) qui ad positionem siderum, ad conjunctiones, oppositiones, aliosque aspectus Planetarum, & summatim loquendo, ad influentias astrorum in hæc in feriora omnes omnium actionum, consiliorum, studiorum eventus immutabiliter referunt. Unde nata Astrologia illa judiciaria, qua nonnulli prædicere audent, quid non modo unicuique privato, cujus quidem Nativitatis horam exacte noverunt, sit vel boni, vel mali eventurum: sed & quam sortem, singula imperia, ducatus, Academiæ, Respublicæ sint experturæ. Quæ sane Astrologia judiciaria, fatentibus hoc ipsum primariis Astronomorum antecessoribus, uti cum nobilissima arte Astronomica, ejusdemque proprio ac genuino fine, tum ratione præceptorum, tum ratione usus ac finis, e diametro pugnat: ita propria vanitate ac futilitate concidit, & neque in Scripturis sacris, neque in Orthodoxa Antiquitate, & probatorum Autorum Scriptis, ullam suffragium aut applausum meretur.

Et notum est illud πολυθρύλλητον Jeremiae cap. 10, 2. A fignis cœli nolite timere, quæ timent gentes. Et a DEO ipso calamitates immitti, non minùs; quâm cætera universa ab eo gubernari, vel illud Amosi cap, 3, 6. comprobat: An erit malum in civitate, quod non fecerit Dominus? Unde Autor etiam noster Philippus in articulis hujus pertractatione, Cealamitatu causas in astris quærendas, aut constituendas esse, exprefsé negat. Neque tamen interim negamus (quod per calumniam nobis affingitur,) DEUM in pœnis infligendis, ut & in reliquâ gubernatione universi, Caufis quas secundas appellant, tanquam instrumentis aut medijs uti. Hoc ipsum enim ultrò largimur, sic ac à Spiritu Sancto ipso edocti. Nam secundum Prophetam Jesaiam, quando bello sive gladio punire homines vult DEUS; hostes sibilo, tanquam muscas, aut apes, ex longinquis sæpè locis evocat: ijsq́; tanquàm novaculâ con ducta utitur, Iesa. 5, 26. & cap. 7, 18. & 20. Ita Famis causa plerumq; Sterilitas terræ est: Sterilitatis tempestates noxiæ: Tempestatum etiam nonnulla in motu ac positu siderum causa est, Neque desunt naturales causæ, quibus bestiæ contra homines efferarari dicuntur. Quemadmodum & Pestilentiæ certæ quædam causæ, ex ipsâ Natura possunt assignari, Verum hujusmodi causas, quovis modo in Naturâ hærentes, ita confiderare decet, ne divinam providentiam liberrime eis, prout vult, utentem in ordinem redigamus: neque ab eis plus, quàm à DEO ipso metuamus. Quam circumspectionem nonnulli hodiè ex turbâ Astrologorum, & Calendariographorum, ipsi in prædictionibus suis adhibere solent,

V. Sunt Divinatores quidam, qui Calamitates, præsertim publicas, ut ruinas & mutationes Imperiorum, dissipationes Rerumpublicarum, & hujus generis solenniores confusiones, certis quibusdam, & planè fatalibus adsignant certorum annorum periodis. Unde aliqui eò progressi sunt, ut libros Divinationum conscribere, & hanc divinandi artem juventuti præscribere non exhorrescerent. Quanquam verò hujusmodi libros, non vulgaris alicujus eruditionis testimonium forte mereri non negamus: finem tamen ipsum, quem spectant, impium esse statuimus: id quod illis argumentis ad oculum demonstrari potest, quibus Stoicorum vesaniam jam supra refutavimus. Accedit, quòd hi ipsi Divinatores in definiendis certis illis regnorum, Imperiorumque periodis, sibi non satis constant. Alij enim terminum fatalem constituunt annum 250. alij 700. alij alium annorum circulum. Jam si has ipsas annorum periodos, ad insigniores Monarchiarum, regnorum, & Reumpublicarum mutationes accommodes, nuspiam eas quadrare, aut evenrui respondere, deprehendes. Monarchia certè prima Babylonica periodum habuit annorum mille, sexcentorum, quadraginta sex. Tot enim annis duravit. Monarchia Persarum expiravit anno durationis 207. Monarchia Græcorum, anno 300. Alexandri M. Monarchia, anni regni duodecimo, in quatuor partes scissa fuit, ac divulsa. Regnum Vandalorum in Africâ certè potentissimum, ruinam passum est, anno durationis 96. Tot ergò constituendæ erunt poriodi fatales, sive anni ClimactericiImperiorum: quot annis quodlibet istorum stetisse deprehenditur. Unde incertitudo & vanitas istius prophanæ artis ultrò liquet

VI. Sunt, annotante Autore nostro, quidam Philosophi, qui Calamitatum & mutationum causam quærunt in materia, quam ajunt ruere æterno impetu ad alias formas, ac appetere vices. Hinc extruxit Aristoteles suum illud dogma, de privatione in materiâ: Quanquam verò ex omni parte sententiæ huic non relectamur, præsertim si ea mala consideres, quæ ex naturali constitutione motui, generationi & corruptioni subjacent: nondum tamen veram ac principem causam ea definit aut explicat: id quod ex sequentibus planum fiet

VII. Ergò, ut veras tandem afflictionum humanarum causas aperiamus: distinguimus eas in Generales sive Communes & in Spetales, partim pijs, partim impijs proprias.

Generalis, & fons atque origo omnis mali est lapsus primorum parentum, & in de resultans tristissima universi generis humani, à DEO per peccatum defectio. per peccatum enim Mors intravit in mundum, & in omnes homines mors pertransijt; etiam in eos, qui non peccaverunt in similitudinem transgressionis Adam. Rom. 5, 12. & 14. Unde scitè Augustinus Serm 4. de verbis apostoli scribit: Pertransijt, pertransijt, Verbum attendite: Quod audivistis, considerate: Videtis quid est pertransijt? Inde est & parvulus reus: peccatum non fecit, sed traxit: Etenim peccatum illud non in fonte mansit: sed pertransijt: non in illum, ut in illum:: sed in omnes homines pertransijt. Inde omnes homines morti, morbis, alijsque calamitatibus, quas natura ipsa nostra secum, ceu individuos comites trahit, sunt obnoxij, ut verè dixerit Poëta.

Nascentes morimur, finisque ab origine pendet.

Et Hippocrates: ἄνθρωπος ὅλος νόσος δοσογένητης. Et Apostolus Rom. 8. 10. Corpus morti destinatum est propter peccatum.

ALTERA causa Generalis, est Iustitia DEI, iram suam declarans adversus peccatum: ut discrimen benè & male factorum, in pœnis illustrius conspiciatur. Nam & Pij, licèt regenerati, & fide reconciliati DEO, graviter sæpè peccant: suisque peccatis pœnas promerentur. Unde DEUS ipse Jerem. 30, 11. Castigabo te in judicio, ut non videaris tibi innocens. Mich. 7, 9. Iram Domini portabo, quia peccavi ei. Jes. 64, 5. & 6. Ecce tu iratus es, & peccavimus, ac diu in peccatis fuimus, & tandem liberati sumus: Cecidimus quasi folium, & iniquitates nostræ quasi venti dissipaverunt nos.

TERTIA causa Generalis & communis est Misericordia DEI, quæ ut aliàs varijs beneficiorum generibus, ita non rarò publicis etiam calamitatibus, tàm impios, quàm pios, in peccata prolapsos, ad Pœnitentiam revocat. Quo pacto Commonefactionum instar sunt, admonentes de futuro aliquando judicio, & æternis supplicijs eorum, qui ante mortem non agunt pœnitentiam. Agnovit hoc David Psalmo 119, 71. Bonum, inquiens, est mihi DOMINE, quòd humiliasti me, ut discerem justificationes tuas. Jesa. 28, 19. Vexatio dat intellectum. Jesa. 26, 16. DOMINE in angustiâ quæsiverunt te: angustia, in quâ clamant, disciplina est eis, Hebr. 12, 6. Flagellat DOMINUS omnem filium, quem recipit.

QUARTA & postrema causa Generalis sive communis est, ut spectaculis horribilium pœnarum alij deterriti, majore circumspectione & curâ vitent delicta, quibus ejusmodi atroces pœnæ attrahuntur; Cumprimis autem, ut fideles evadant sapientiores, hoc est, magis magisque proficiant in agnitione & timore DEI, ut Verbum ejus diligant, ab ejus judicijs timeant, & à consimilibus peccatis, illis præsertim, quæ contra conscientiam designantur, sibi caveant. De hac causâ ex professo differit Apostolus, & integrum quasi locum communem pertractat, ostendens, quo pacto Israëlitarum pœnæ quas perpessi sunt atrocissimas, Corinthijs exemplo esse debeant, ne eadem scelera atque flagitia, quæ illi, designent. 1. Cor. 10, 6. usq; ad 13. Et David de seipso, Psal. 119, 120. Facis, ut tanquam scoria cessent omnes improbi terræ: ideo diligo testimonia tua: Horret pavore tui caro mea, adeò à judiciis tuis timeo.


### Chapter I. On the Nature, genera and causes of human afflictions: The special causes of the punishments which are sent upon the ungodly are chiefly these

The special causes of the punishments which are sent upon the ungodly are chiefly these:

I. That GOD may declare the glory of his Justice and power in destroying them, Rom. 11, 22. Behold the severity of GOD towards those who fell. Rom. 9, 17. For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you: and that my name might be announced in all the earth Exod 9, 16.

II That from the punishments of the ungodly, the Elect and faithful may not only learn to be wise, but also may rejoice in those most just judgments of the Lord, by which he punishes and breaks the malice of his enemies. Concerning which matter David Psal. 52. 7. & following: Therefore GOD will destroy you forever, he will pluck you up, and he

he shall remove thee out of thy tabernacle, and root thee out of the land of the living: The righteous also shall see, and fear, and shall laugh at him: And shall say, Lo, this is the man that made not GOD his strength; but trusted in the abundance of his riches, and strengthened himself in his wickedness. Psal. 64. almost entire. Psal. 68, 3 & 4. As smoke is driven away, so drive them away: as wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of GOD: But let the righteous be glad; let them rejoice before GOD: yea, let them exceedingly rejoice. Psal 91, 7. & 8. A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee. Only with thine eyes shalt thou behold and see the reward of the wicked with pleasure. Hence Solomon constructed a Theological Aphorism, Prov. 11, 10. when the wicked perish, there is shouting.

Moreover, this exultation of the godly in the destruction of the ungodly is not to be defined by ἐπιχαιρεκακίαν [rejoicing in evil], who with some carnal affection insult the ungodly in their tribulation: For this would fight against the rule of Charity, which ought to love even an enemy: But it ought to be defined by an admiration of the judgments of GOD, by which we both acknowledge and proclaim the justice of GOD vindicating the malice of the ungodly, and we conceive an undoubted hope of his mercy towards us, and in it we rejoice, and glory, And hence now emerges the cause.

III. That, namely, from the punishments of the ungodly the Elect may seek firm matter for consolation, by which they are certain that they are a care to GOD, and will certainly be delivered from the snares and persecutions of the ungodly Psal. 58, 11. & 12. The righteous will rejoice, when he sees the vengeance: he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner, and will say: Truly there is fruit for the righteous: truly GOD is judging in the earth. Psalm 119, 52: I remembered your judgments of old O LORD: and I was comforted.

IV. That the truth of divine threats may be established most exactly, and that they may not be held as empty rattles, or thunderbolts from a chamber pot: but that it may be true, which the LORD said in Ezekiel 6:10: They shall know and experience that I the LORD have not spoken in vain, that I would do this evil unto them.

V. That the distinction between the pious and the impious may appear, and the world, or at least the Church, may be purged of such cancers: that a limit may be set to the malice of the impious, so that even against their will they may find it necessary to acknowledge GOD as the most just judge and avenger, according to that of Psalm 59:13: Consume them in wrath, consume them, that they may not be any more: and let them know that GOD ruleth in Jacob unto the ends of the earth.

VI. And the last: That they may be a testimony of the final judgment that will one day come, even against those who had gone away unpunished in this world. For it is a righteous thing with GOD to ἀνταποδοῦναι, to recompense tribulation to them that trouble you: And to you who are troubled, rest. 2 Thess. 1:6 & 7. And for this very reason GOD does not punish all the impious in this life, so that even from this we may take a firm and evident argument that there remains

The resurrection of the dead and another Judgment, by which GOD is to render to each one according to his works, good or evil, which he did in this world. Rom. 2, 5. & 6. & seqq.

The special causes of the punishments by which the pious and the Elect are exercised in this life are given in the Scriptures in great number: but the principal ones are the following.

I. That they may from time to time be reminded of the corruption of their inner Nature, of the impurity and ἀταξίας (disorder) of the affections, which clings even to the Reborn themselves as long as they live: for which cause GOD Himself says through the Prophet: I will chasten you in judgment, that you may not seem innocent to yourself. Jerem. 46, 28.

II. Lest, with favorable things flowing according to their will, they become inflated and fall into carnal security, or give free rein to the lusts of the flesh, and deviate from the way of the commandments of GOD. 1 Pet. 4, 1. & 2. He who suffers in the flesh ceases from sin, that he may live the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for the desires of men but for the will of GOD. Paul acknowledged this, confessing ingenuously that, lest he be exalted above measure by the excellence of the heavenly revelations, a σκόλοπα (thorn) was given to his flesh, and an angel of Satan, by whom he might be buffeted. 1 Cor. 12, 7. Therefore it would not be right to make a judgment about the truth or falsity of religion itself from the diseases, poverty, persecutions, prisons, exiles, and other afflictions of the pious: especially since GOD is accustomed to chasten His Elect in this life almost more and more severely than the impious. For whom He loves, He chastens. Hebr. 12, 6. And again in verse 10, GOD chastens us for our benefit, that we may be partakers of His holiness. And Isa. 26, 9. When You have executed Your judgments on the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness.

III. That the Fear of GOD, Faith, Invocation, Patience, Confession, and the other virtues of the pious may be explored, exercised, and confirmed. 2 Chron. 20, 12. Since we do not know what we ought to do, we have this only remaining, that we direct our eyes to You. Isa. 26, 16. LORD, in distress they sought You; in tribulation, a secret meditation was for them. Isa. 28, 10. Vexation gives understanding. Rom. 5, 3. & 4. We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience: and patience, probation: and probation, hope. 1 Pet. 1, 7. It is necessary to be grieved for a little while now in various temptations, that the proof of your faith may be found much more precious than gold.

IV. That the examples of these very virtues may be in the sight of others, and be useful for imitation: Psal. 22, 5. In You our fathers trusted: they trusted, and You delivered them; they cried to You, and were saved: in You they trusted and were not confounded: Therefore You will not forsake me either, as I cry out. Psalm 34, 6. This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him; and saved him out of all his tribulations. Therefore I also will seek the LORD, and He will hear me, verse 5.

V. That these and similar calamities may excite in us a desire for another life, and produce a contempt for this life: and that we may not, as if attached to earthly goods, despise and contemn heavenly and eternal things: and that we may always think about our mortality, Psal. 90, 12. Teach us, O Lord, to number our days, that we may apply our heart to wisdom.

VI. That, kept within the bounds and limits of true piety, we may not depart into the way of the impious, to our eternal destruction. 1 Cor. 11, 32. While we are judged by the LORD, we are chastened, that we may not be condemned with the world.

VII. Many pious people are also afflicted for the sake of illustrating the glory of GOD: and that heavenly doctrine may be confirmed by their testimony: as is said concerning the man born blind, John 9, 3, and concerning Peter, John 21, 19.

VIII. That at length the Pious and Elect may through afflictions become conformed to the image of the Son of GOD, whom it also behooved to enter into His glory through passion: Luke 24, 26. Rom. 8, 29.

IX. That it may appear that the Church is gathered, defended, and preserved not by human counsels and supports, but by the Son of God Himself, the head and leader of the Church, by divine power: and thus in the midst of our afflictions the presence and power of our Immanuel may be seen, defending us against the Devil and the furies of tyrants: according to the clear promise of Isaiah 46:3 and 4: Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, which are borne by me from the belly, which are carried from the womb: And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you.

X. And finally, as to that singular species of afflictions which we call Martyrdom, it is that ornament and glory of the Church. For through it the Church acquires for itself a most celebrated name, and receives great increase. Whence Tertullian did not hesitate to write that the Church of Christ is watered by the blood of the Martyrs. Hence also were born those well-worn verses:

The Church was founded in blood: in blood it began: in blood it grew: in blood shall be its end.

For it cannot be but that the remaining faithful and Elect, seeing the constancy and patience of the Martyrs, are wonderfully confirmed in the truth acknowledged: that thence they may take true consolation, and an example of patience and perseverance, that they may trust in GOD alone, and place all their hope in the coming of the great GOD, of ours, and in the liberation of the children of GOD, they place them with great spirit for eternal salvation. On which matter see 2 Cor. 1:4 up to 8; 2 Tim. 2:10. Ecclesiastical history also testifies that the more numerous and severe the persecutions were with which tyrants raged against the Church, the more they were increased, and the more glorious it emerged. Therefore, let us not be broken in spirit if the whole world seems to have conspired today for the destruction of our Church: for it is certain, and will always be, what the Apostle long ago revealed in Philip. 1:12. I want you to know that all things have happened to me for the progress of the Gospel. And in verse 19. I know that this will turn out for my salvation.

Against this purer doctrine of ours concerning the causes, ends, and effects of the afflictions of the pious, the Romanists set up obelisks on the side where they contend that the afflictions of the Saints are before GOD satisfactions for the guilt of temporal punishment, which would otherwise have to be inflicted for their sins; indeed, that they have the power of satisfying divine justice condignly: so much so that the virtue and efficacy of this satisfaction redounds to the benefit not only of the suffering person himself, but also of other men: as Bellarmine writes in his treatise on Indulgences, book 1, chapters 2, 3, and 9.

To which assertion, the more we are unable to support it, the more very grave reasons stand in the way. For 1. The satisfaction of Christ is a most absolute and most sufficient λύτρον, not only for guilt but also for the punishment owed for our sins. And there does not occur in the whole Scripture a single testimony that affirms that Christ satisfied most fully for guilt only, but not for punishment, and that this remains for us to expiate by our own sufferings, as the Romanists wish. Scripture expressly testifies to the contrary, and clearly confirms that punishment also has been expiated and removed by Christ: As Coloss. 1:13 and 14. Christ forgives us all offenses, blotting out the handwriting that was against us, which was contrary to us through decrees, and he took it out of the way, having nailed it to the cross, and having despoiled principalities and powers, he showed them openly, triumphing over them by himself. And Isaiah 53:5. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed: Therefore not by our stripe. Is. 63:3. I have trodden the winepress ALONE, and of the nations there was no man with me. Heb. 10:14. By one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified: Therefore there is no need for a double offering, or satisfaction: For if one makes us perfect, there is no need for another. 2. The most exact rule of divine justice does not admit such a partition. For it is eternal and infinite: nor does it suffer itself to be satisfied, either in respect to punishment or in respect to guilt, except through an equivalent infinite and eternal price. Now, however, the calamities of the Elect, individually and collectively, cannot by any means or degree rise to the perfection of divine justice: since between the temporal, or momentary, and the eternal, between the finite and the infinite, there is no proportion. 3. These very afflictions of the pious are in all ways imperfect: they are mixed with the perpetual infirmities of the flesh; so that it always lusts and murmurs against the Spirit, Galat. 5:17. And even the most holy have need to pray: Enter not, O Lord, into judgment with your servant: For if you observe iniquities, O LORD, who shall stand, Psalm 130:3, and Psalm 143:2.

But the Romanists object to that Apostolic passage Coloss. 1:24. Where Paul affirms that he in his flesh fills up those things which are lacking in the sufferings of Christ in his own sufferings. But a gross ἄγνοια ἐλέγχυ is committed, while it is not attended to which sufferings of Christ the Apostle is speaking about as being filled up. Now, however, just as Christ is described in the Scriptures not only as Mediator and Redeemer, but also as the head of the Church: so the sufferings of Christ are also not of one and the same kind. For some are the sufferings which Christ endures as Mediator and Redeemer of the human race: but others are those which, as Head of the Church, he endures daily in his members, namely in the faithful and the elect, and will endure until the end of the age. Those former ones belong to Christ the Savior ALONE and uniquely, so that he admitted no companion in filling them up, just as he has the work of our Mediation and Redemption in common with no mortal, either in whole or even in any part. And an end was imposed on these sufferings on the Cross, so that the Savior himself cried out: It is finished. If it is finished, nothing at all remains to be filled up regarding our redemption and the expiation of our sins, both as to punishment and as to guilt: much less did Paul, or any other of the Saints, arrogate to himself the filling up of those sufferings. But as for the latter sufferings, they concern the lot and condition of the Church militant on this earth. This is indeed the mystical Body of Christ, whose members are the faithful and the Elect. This Body in its members is always exposed, and will be until the end of the age, to perpetual persecutions: so that these sufferings are not to be filled up before this state and condition of the Church has clearly and fully ceased on the last day. As long, therefore, as the Church is subject to the cross and calamities: as long as the Saints and Elect endure persecutions in this world: so long something is still lacking in the sufferings of CHRIST, which he himself, as Head of the Church, suffers in his Saints. These sufferings, therefore, Paul, Peter, and of the Elect each one fulfills according to his own allotted portion: not, however, for that end which the Romanists invent of their own, that they might obtain the remission of punishments, whether temporal or eternal, either for themselves or for others: For those former passions of the Body of Christ most fully and most sufficiently obtained this: but that they might declare their faith, that they might bear witness to the truth, that they might incite the remaining faithful to constancy and patience, that finally they might in this way be rendered conformable to the image of the Son of GOD, in this, that just as He, so also they themselves through many tribulations might enter into the heavenly glory. Which very Conformity itself also shows not a cause or merit, but only the manner which GOD is accustomed to observe in his elect, in promoting them to the possession of eternal glory: as has been shown elsewhere. The sense, therefore, of the words of the Apostle emerges as this: I rejoice in my afflictions for you, because I see the time of my liberation and death approaching, by which I will fulfill those passions which GOD himself, in my flesh, for the benefit of the Church, and for my part, willed and decreed to fulfill.

Latin:

Causæ speciales pœnarum, quæ impijs immittuntur, sunt potissimùm hæ:

I. Ut Justitiæ & potentiæ suæ gloriam DEUS in illis delendis declaret, Rom. 11, 22. Vide severitatem DEI in eos, qui ceciderunt. Rom. 9, 17. In hoc ipsum excitavi te, ut ostenderem in te virtutem meam: & ut annunciaretur nomen meum in universâ terrâ Exod 9, 16.

II Ut ex impiorum pœnis, Electi ac fideles non modò sapere discant, sed & lætentur in justissimis illis judicijs Domini, quibus hostium malitiam punit & infringit. Quâ de re Davidi Psal. 52. 7. & sequentibus: Propterea DEUS destruet te in finem, evellet te, & e-

migrabit de tabernaculo tuo, & radicem tuam de terra viventium : Videbunt justi, & timebunt, & super eum ridebunt: & dicent: Ecce homo, qui non posuit DEVM adjutorem suum: sed speravit in multitudine divitiarum suarum: & prævaluit in vanitate sua. Psal. 64. ferme integro. Psal. 68, 3 & 4. Sicut deficit fumus, deficiant: sicut fluit cera a facie ignis, sic pereant peccatores a facie DEI: Et justi gaudeant & exultent in conspectu DEI, & delectentur in lætitia. Psal 91, 7. & 8. Cadent a latere tuo mille, & decem millia a dextris tuis, ad te autem non appropinquabit : sed oculis tuis considerabis, & retributionem impiorum videbis cum voluptate. Hinc Aphorismum Theologicum extruxit Salomon, Prov. 11, 10. in perditione impiorum erit jubilatio.

Cæterum hæc piorum exultatio in interitu impiorum non est definienda per Ἐπιχαιρεκακίαν, qui excarnali quopiam affectu impijs insultent in tribulatione ipsorum : Hoc enim pugnaret cum regula Charitatis, quæ hostem etiam diligere debet : Sed definiri debet per admirationem judiciorum DEI qua & DEI justitiam vindicantem impiorum malitiam agnoscimus & prædicamus, & de ipsius misericordia erga nos spem indubiam concipimus, inqs eâ lætamur, & gloriamur, Et hinc jam emergit causa.

III. Ut nimirum ex pœnis impiorum firmam consolationis materiam petant Electi, qua certi sunt, se DEO curæ esse, & ab impiorum insidijs & persecutionibus certò liberatum iri Psal. 58, 11. & 12. Lætabitur justus, cùm viderit vindictam: manus suas lavabit in sanguine peccatoris, & dicet: Vtique est fructus justo: utique DEVS est judicans in terra. Psalm. 119, 52: Memor fui judiciorum tuorum a seculo DOMINE : & consolatus sum.

IV. Ut de veritate comminationum divinarum exactissimè constet, neque eæ habeantur pro inanibus crepitaculis, aut fulminibus, e pelvi: sed verum sit, quod dixit DOMINUS Ezech. 6. 10. Scient & experientur, quia ego DOMINUS non frustra locutus sum, ut facerem eis malum hoc.

V. Ut appareat discrimen inter pios & impios, & purgetur mundus, vel saltem Ecclesia ab ejusmodi carcinomatis: ut modus statuatur malitiæ impiorum, ut vel inviti DEUM justissimum judicem ac vindicem agnoscere necesse habeant, secundum illud Psalmi 59, 14. Consume impios in ira, consume, ut non sint amplius: & scient, quia DEVS dominatur Iacob, & finibus terræ.

VI. Et postrema : Ut sint testimonium futuri aliquando judicij ultimi, in eos etiam, qui hoc in mundo impune abierant. Iustum enim est apud DEVM ἀνταποδῦναι vicissim reddere afflictionem ijs, qui vos affligunt: Vobis verò, qui premimini, relaxationem. 2. Thess. 1, 6. & 7. Et hanc ipsam ob causam DEUS in hac vita non omnes impios punit, ut vel inde firmum & evidens argumentum capiamus, restare

Resurrectionem mortuorum & Judicium aliud, quo DEUS unicuique sit retributurus secundum opera sua, bona, vel mala, quæ fecit in hoc mundo. Rom. 2, 5. & 6. & seqq.

Cause speciales pœnarum, quibus pij & Electi hac in vitâ exercentur, dantur in Scripturis benè multo : præcipuæ autem sunt hæ sequentes.

I. Ut subinde recordentur interioris Naturæ corruptionis, inmunditiei. & ἀταξίας affectum, in ipsis etiam Renatis, quamdiu vivunt, hærentis : de quâ causâ DEUS ipse apud Prophetam: Castigabo te in judicio, ne tibi innocens videaris. Jerem. 46, 28.

II. Ne rebus secundis ad voluntatem fluentibus inflati, in carnalem securitatem incidant, aut carnis concupiscentijs frenum taxent, & à viâ mandatorum DEI exorbitent. 1. Pet. 4, 1. & 2. Qui patitur in carne, desinit peccare, ut non ampliůs cupiditatibus hominum sed voluntati DEI, quod in carne reliquum est temporis, vivat. Agnovit hoc Paulus, ingenuè confesus, ne revelationum cœlestium excellentiâ supra modum efferretur, datum σκόλοπα carni suæ, & angelum Satanam, à quo colaphis cæderetur. 1. Cor. 12. 7. Haud ergò fas fuerit, ex morbis, penurijs, persecutionibus. carceribus, exilijs alijsq; afflictionibus piorum de ipsius religionis veritate aut falsitate judicium facere: præsertim cùm DEUS hæc in vitâ suos Electos plus fermè & gravius plærunq; castigare soleat, quám impios Quos enim diligit, hos castigat Hebr. 12, 6. Et rursus versu 10 DEUS nos castigat ad commodum nostrum, ut participes simus sanctimoniæ ipsius. Et Jes. 26, 9. Cùm feceris judicia, tua in terra justitiam discunt habitatores orbis.

III. Ut Timor DEI, Fides. Invocatio Patientia. Confessio. & cæteræ virtutes piorum explorentur, exerceantur, & confirmentur. 2. Paralip. 20, 12. Cum ignoremus, quid agere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te. Esai. 26, 16. DOMINE in angustiâ requisiverunt te, in tribulatione afflictiœnu medicatio ipsis est da. Jes. 28, 10. Vexatio dat intellectum. Rom. 5, 3. & 4. Gloriamur in tribulationibus, scientes, quod tribulatio patientiam operatur : patientia autem probationem : probatio verò spem. 1. Pet. 1, 7. Oportet modicum nunc contristari in varijs tentationibus, ut probatio vestra fidei multò preciosior auro inveniatur.

IV. Vt harum ipsarum virtutum exempla alijs in conspectu sint, & ad imitationem prosint: Psal. 22, 5. In te speraverunt patres nostri:speraverunt, & liberasti eos; ad te clamaverunt, & salvi facti sunt: in te speraverunt non sunt confusi: Ergò & me ad declamantem non derelinques. Psalm 34, 6. Iste pauper clamavit, & Dominus exaudivit eum; & de omnibus tribulationibus ejus salvavit eum Ergò & ego exquiram DOMINUM, & ipse exaudiet me, versu. 5.

V. Ut hæ & similes calamitates desiderium in nobis excitent alterius vitæ, & hujus vitæ contemtum pariant: nevè terrenis bonis quasi affixi cœlestia & æterna aspernemur & contemnamus: & ut semper cogitemus de mortalitate nostra, Psal. 90, 12. Doce nos Domine numerare dies nostros, ut applicemus cor ad sapientiam.

VI. Ut intra cancellos ac limites veræ pietatis retenti, in viam impiorum, ad æternam nostram perniciem, non abeamus. 1. Cor. 11, 32. Dum judicamur à DOMINO, corripimur, ne cum mundo condemnemur.

VII. Multi etiam pij affliguntur, propter illustrandam gloriam DEI: & ut doctrina cœlestis ipsorum testimonio confirmetur: sicut de cæco nato Ioh. 9, 3. & de Petro, Ioh. 21, 19. dicitur.

VIII. Ut tandem Pij & Electi per afflictiones fiant conformes imagini Filij DEI, quem ipsum quoque per passionem intrare oportuit in gloriam suam: Luc. 24, 26. Rom. 8, 29.

IX. Ut appareat, Ecclesiam non humanis consilijs & præsidijs: Sed ab ipso Filio DEI, capite ac duce Ecclesiæ, divinâ potentiâ colligi, defendi, servari: & sic in mediis nostris afflictionibus conspiciatur præsentia & potentia Immanuelis nostri, propugnantis nos adversus Diabolum, & Tyrannorum furores: secundum luculentam promissionem Jesai. 46, 3. & 4. Audite me domus Iacob, & omne residuum domus Israel, quia portamini à meo utero, qui gestamini à meâ vulvâ: Usque ad senectam ego ipse & usque ad canos ego portabo, ego faciam, & ego feram, ego portabo, & salvabo.

X. Et postremò, quo ad singularem illam afflictionum speciem, quam Martyrium appellamus, est illud ornamentum & gloria Ecclesiæ. Per illud enim Ecclesia celeberrimum sibi nomen acquirit, & magnum incrementum accipit. Unde Tertullianus scribere non dubitavit, sanguine Martyrum irrigari Ecclesiam Christi. Hinc nati sunt etiam triti illi versiculi:

Sanguine fundata est Ecclesia: sanguine cepit: Sanguine fuccrevit: Sanguine finis erit.

Fieri enim nequit, quin reliqui fideles ac Electi, videntes constantiam & patientiam Martyrum, mirificè in veritate agnitâ confirmentur: ut inde veram consolationem, & exemplum patientiæ, ac perseverantiæ capiant, ut in solo DEO confidant, & spem omnem in adventu magni DEI, nostri, inque liberatione filiorum DEI plenaria ad æternam salutem magno spiritu collocent. Quâ de re videatur in 2. Cor. 1, 4. usque ad 8, 2. Tim. 2, 10. Testatur etiam historia Ecclesiastica, quò pluribus & gravioribus persecutionibus sævitum fuit in Ecclesiam à Tyrannis: eò magis illas fuisse auctas, & gloriosiores emersisse. Proinde non animo frangamur, si in Ecclesiæ nostræ interitum totus mundus hodieque conspirasse videtur: Certum enim est, & erit semper, quod jam olim prodidit Apostolus Philip. 1, 12. Volo vos scire, quod omnia ad profectum Evangelij mihi evenerunt. Et versu 19. Novi quòd hoc mihi cedet ad salutem.

Puriori huic doctrinæ nostræ de causis, finibus & effectis afflictionum piorum, obeliscos ex eâ parte fingunt Romanenses, quà contendunt, Afflictiones Sanctorum esse coram DEO satisfactiones pro reatu pœnæ temporalis, quæ peccatis ipsorum alias esset infligenda; imò habere eas vim satisfaciendi justitiæ divinæ ex condigno: usque adeò, ut virtus & efficacia hujus satisfactionis cedat in emolumentum non modò ipsius personæ patientis; sed & aliorum hominum: uti scribit Bellarminus tractatu de Indulgentijs, lib. 1. cap. 2. 3. & 9.

Cui assertioni quò minus suffragari possimus, obstant gravissimæ rationes. Nam 1. Satisfactio Christi est λύτρον absolutissimum, & sufficientissimum, non modò pro culpâ sed & pro pœnâ, peccatis nostris debitâ. Et non occurrit in universa Scripturâ unicum testimonium, quod affirmet, Christum pro culpâ tantùm, non autem pro pœna plenissimè satisfecisse, & hanc nobis restare expiandam nostris passionibus, uti volunt Romanenses. Contrarium Scriptura expressè testatur, & Pœnam quoque à Christo expiatam & sublatam esse, liquidò confirmat: Ut Coloss. 1, 13. & 14. Condonat nobis Christus omnia delicta, delens quod adversum nos erat Chirographum, quod erat contrarium nobis per decreta, & illud sustulit è medio, affixum cruci, expoliatosque principatus ac potestates ostentavit palàm triumphans de illis per semetipsum. Et Jesa. 53, 5. Disciplina pacis nostræ super eum, & livor ejus sanati sumus: Ergò non nostro livore. Jes. 63, 3. Torcular SOLVS ego calcavi, & de gentibus non erat vir mecum. Hebr. 10, 14. Vnicâ oblatione profectos fecit in perpetuum eos, qui sanctificantur: Ergo gemina oblatione, sive Satisfactione opus non est: Si enim unica perfectos nos facit, nil opus est alterâ. 2. Justitiæ divinæ exactissima regula talem partitionem non admittit. Est enim ea æterna, & infinita: neque patitur sibi vel respectu pœnæ, vel respectu culpæ, satisfieri, nisi per equivalens infinitum & æternum pretium. Jam verò Calamitates Electorum singulæ & universæ, nullo prorsus pacto, vel gradu ad perfectionem justitiæ divinæ possunt assurgere: siquidem inter temporaneum, sive momentaneum, & æternum, inter finitum & infinitum nulla est proportio. 3. Hæ ipsæ afflictiones piorum sunt modis omnibus imperfectæ: sunt mixtæ cum perpetuis infirmitatibus carnis; ut hæc semper concupiscat, & murmuret adversus Spiritum, Galat. 5, 17. & Sanctissimi etiam orare necesse habeant: Ne intres Domine in judicium cum servo tuo: Nam si iniquitates observaveris, DOMINE quis sustinebit, Psal. 130, 3. & Psal. 143. 2.

Sed objiciunt Romanenses locum illum Apostolicum Coloss. 1, 24. Ubi affirmat Paulus, se in carne passionibus suis adimplere ea quæ desunt passionibus Christi. Verùm crassa committitur ἄγνοια ἐλέγχυ, dum, de quibus passionibus Christi adimplendis sermo sit Apostolo, non attenditur. Jam verò, uti Christus in Sacris non tantùm ut Mediator & Redemtor: sed & ut caput Ecclesiæ describitur: ita passiones etiam Christi non unius ejusdemque sunt generis. Aliæ enim sunt passiones, quas Christus perfert, ut Mediator, & Redemtor generis humani: Aliæ verò sunt, quas ut Caput Ecclesiæ, in membris suis, nempè in fidelibus & electis quotidiè sustinet, & sustinebit ad finem usq; seculi. Priores illæ ita Christo Servatori SOLI atq; uni competunt, ut haud magis in illis adimplendis Socium aliquem admiserit, atque ipsum Mediationis & Redemtionis nostræ opus, cum nemine mortalium vel ex toto, vel ex parte saltem aliquâ commune habet. Et his passionibus ita in Cruce finis est impositus, ut Servator ipse exclamârit: Iam consummatum est. Si consummatum est, nihil utique ampliùs, quoad redemtionem nostram, & expiationem peccatorum nostrorum, quâ pœnam, quâ culpam, adimplendum restat: multò minùs vel Paulus, vel alius aliquis Sanctorum, istarum passionum adimpletionem sibi arrogavit. Cæterùm quoad posteriores passiones, respiciunt eæ sortem atquæ conditionem Ecclesiæ hac in terra militantis. Est verò hæc Corpus Christi mysticum, cujus membra sunt fideles & Electi. Hoc Corpus in membris suis semper expositum est, & erit ad finem usquæ seculi, perpetuis persecutionibus: ita ut hæ passiones haud prius sint adimplendæ, quàm status iste, & conditio Ecclesiæ, in die novissimo, planè ac plenè cessaverit. Quamdiu ergo Ecclesiæ cruci & calamitatibus est subjecta: quamdiu Sancti & Electi persecutiones in hoc mundo sustinent: tamdiu aliquid adhuc deest passionibus CHRISTI, quas ipse, quippe Caput Ecclesiæ, in Sanctis suis patitur. Has ergò passiones, Paulus, Petrus, & Electorum quisque, pro ratâ sibi portione adimplet: non autem eo fine, quem Romanenses de suo comminiscuntur, ut vel sibi, vel aliis impetent remissionem pœnarum, vel temporalium, vel æternarum: Hanc enim priores illæ passiones Corporis Christi plenissimè, sufficientissiméq; impetrarunt: sed ut fidem suam declarent, ut veritati testimonium perhibeant, ut reliquos fideles ad constantiam & patientiam incitent, ut denique conformes hoc pacto reddantur imagini filij DEI, in eo, ut quemadmodum ille, sic & ipsi per multas tribulationes intrent in gloriam cœlestem. Quæ ipsa quoque Conformitas, non causam, aut meritum: sed modum tantùm monstrat, quem DEUS in electis suis, ad possessionem æternæ gloriæ promovendis, observare soleat: uti alibi ostensum. Sensus ergo verborum Apostoli emergit iste: Gaudeo in afflictionibus meis pro vobis, quia ego video instare tempus liberationis & mortis meæ, qua adimplebo eas passiones, quas DEVS ipse, in carne mea, pro emolumento Ecclesiæ, & pro mea parte adimplere voluit, & decrevit.


### Chapter Two. Concerning Christian Consolation, both general and special, in any afflictions whatsoever

Just as a sick person eagerly seeks and inquires after a Physician and Medicine: so in afflictions a pious mind is always anxious and solicitous concerning true consolations by which it may be able to raise and sustain itself. For Consolation is a means prescribed by GOD, which powerfully strengthens and sustains us against tribulations and the sadness conceived from them, by opposing some good to any affliction, whether present or future, by the faithful contemplation and tireless meditation of which we mitigate pain and anguish, and, as Scripture speaks, possess our souls through patience in silence and hope. However, in this regard, for minds terrified by the sense of divine wrath, Philosophical consolations cannot suffice: Such as are: 1. Immutable necessity, according to that common saying: Bear what you cannot change, do not blame it.

Then a Good Conscience, which for the most part among the unregenerate, or even those who, although they may be regenerate, nevertheless weigh the causes of afflictions outside of the Word of GOD,

is accustomed to be the mother of impatience and murmuring against GOD: while it inquires and is tormented. Why is it well for the wicked, and ill for the good? by the example of Asaph writing of himself in Psalm 73, 2 and following: But my feet were almost moved, and my steps were almost poured out: Because I envied the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners, etc.

Thirdly, the examples of others, who have suffered either similar evils or ones greater than these.

Fourthly: Doubtful and uncertain hope:

Fifthly: The glory and immortality of a name, as a subsequent reward for the fortitude of the mind in bearing calamities.

Sixthly: A comparison of events: and if any consolations similar to these are brought forward by philosophers, they are too diluted and weak. These, therefore, having been relegated to the Schools of the Gentile philosophers, we must look to others much firmer. Where indeed that Theological practice is to be observed, without which the Christian soldier will never fight successfully under the banner of the cross of Christ. Now it is indeed true, and most rightly asserted by our Blessed LUTHER, that every true Christian Consolation ought to consist of a Syllogism: Whose major Proposition opposes the help of GOD, promised in His Word, to the evil by which we are afflicted: But the minor, or Assumption, applies that very promise to itself by true faith: Whence the Conclusion finally evidently and certainly gathers that the evil by which we are pressed must be borne patiently and bravely: since the help of GOD is at hand and will undoubtedly be present for us. But the whole Logic of Aristotle and other Gentiles is ignorant of this Spiritual Topic, nor will any place of Invention ever show a means of concluding. Whence Asaph himself confesses that he could in no way extricate himself by the benefit of Reason, what the cause is why the impious are happy, but the pious are scourged all the day long: but that he finally learned this in the Sanctuary of GOD: I labored, he says, to know this: and it was a labor before me: until I entered into the Sanctuary of GOD, etc. Psalm 73, 16 and 17. The Davidic practice in the Psalms shows us such Syllogisms excellently: as in Psalm 25, 2 and 3.

To you, O LORD, I have lifted up my soul: O my GOD, in you I trust, let me not be put to shame: For all who wait for you shall not be put to shame. From this, this syllogism arises:

All who hope in you, O LORD, are not put to shame.

I hope in you, and I lift up my soul to you.

Therefore I shall not be put to shame.

And in the verse immediately following, the fourth, David argues thus against his enemies and persecutors:

All who deal treacherously without cause shall be put to shame.

But my enemies deal treacherously without cause.

Therefore they shall be put to shame, and they shall not triumph over me.

But they deal treacherously without cause who do not in the goodness of the cause, do not in GOD'S help: but they trust in their power & strength: or even in their hypocritical holiness.

Every one of the godly can, nay ought to, imitate this Davidic practice in their own tribulations, by concluding thus:

GOD hears those who hope in Him. Therefore He will also hear me, because I hope in Him. And again.

All who insult the godly without cause, GOD confounds.

Therefore He will certainly confound my enemies too, because they afflict me without merit.

The same David shows another practice, in Psalm 27, 1. The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life, of whom shall I be afraid? This practical syllogism emerges:

Whoever have the LORD GOD as their Light and salvation: they ought to fear no one.

But the Lord is my light and salvation: Therefore I shall fear no one, I shall dread no one.

And again: Whoever has the Lord as light and salvation, his enemies must necessarily stumble and fall: even if whole camps rise up against him. Therefore my adversaries also will stumble and fall, whatever their power may be.

David shows the same practice, and a far more evident one, in the same Psalm 27, 8, saying: My heart has said to Thee: Seek my face: Therefore, O Lord, I seek Thy face: Do not turn Thy face from me, and do not repel Thy servant in anger. Whence such a complete practical syllogism emerges:

GOD has promised to those who call upon Him, and who seek His face, that He is willing to hear them, and to rescue them from tribulation and distress.

But my heart says and proposes this very promise of Thine to Thee, O GOD: Nay, I for this very reason, in my tribulation, seek Thy face.

Therefore it is just and right, nay even necessary, that you hear me.

Tertullian, weighing this practice of Christians, says: This, he says, is pleasing to GOD: for God is not so disposed as men, who bear it impatiently to be reminded of their promises, and therefore consider it an imputation of lying when someone, asking for a benefit, even modestly reminds them that this had been promised to him at some time: but GOD has so bound Himself to us by the Word of His promise, that He desires nothing more than to be reminded of His promise through faithful prayer. Tertull. on the prayers of Christians.

The practice of these arguments is very easy as long as we are situated outside the heat of affliction and dangers, and it is still engaged in mere contemplation, or θεωρίᾳ: but in temptations it is by far the most difficult of all, especially in that more serious struggle of Flesh and Spirit: where sometimes the Major of these syllogisms seems to be weaker: sometimes, however, regarding the assumption, or application to our individual selves, much doubt creeps in: so that the tempted and afflicted man either completely loses his confidence toward GOD, or feels it to be sufficiently languid. Therefore this is the work, this is the labor, that the certainty of both premises be known and perceived by us as immovable and infallible. But the foundations of that certainty are to be sought in GOD Himself: according to that of Isaiah 51:12. I, I am Jehovah, I myself will comfort you: Who are you, that you should fear from mortal man, and from the son of man, who withers like grass? But then at last are firm arguments of consolation sought and found in GOD, if we enter the Sanctuary of GOD, and in it learn what GOD has revealed in His Word concerning the afflictions of the pious: which it is pleasing to set forth according to the distinct attributes of GOD.

The FIRST argument of Consolation in general against any afflictions whatsoever, as much internal as external, must be sought from the providence of GOD. For although afflictions seem to proceed from secondary causes: yet they do not happen to the pious fortuitously, nor rashly, nor casually; but with GOD knowing, nay, so willing and permitting. Hence therefore the pious mind, amidst the storms of adversities, concludes thus: If it is GOD who strikes and afflicts, and indeed that GOD who does not permit evil unless He knows how to elicit from it a good and desired end; I shall safely and patiently bear whatever His fatherly will commands me to suffer.

The reason for the connection must be sought from the most evident nature of divine Providence. For this not only permits evils to happen to the pious: but also prescribes certain limits, which secondary causes cannot transgress, nay, beyond which not even the Devil himself, with all the powers of the underworld, can rage. Hence it is that not only does GOD Himself profess to be the author of all calamities by which the pious are pressed, Deut. 32:39, Job 2:4, Isa. 45:5, 7, Amos 3:6, Lam. 3:38. But also the Saints, groaning under their cross, have repeatedly looked to GOD who strikes, Ruth 1:13, 20, 21, 1 Sam. 2:6 & 7, Job 1:21. Hence the Savior Himself constructs a general practical aphorism, Matt. 10:29 & 30. GOD Himself testifies to this, Deut. 32:39, saying: See that I alone am, and there is no other GOD besides me: I will kill, and I will make to live: I will strike and I will heal: and there is no one who can snatch from my hand. That pious woman Ruth acknowledged this, who, weaving a catalog of her miseries, finally bursts into these words: To me, to me it is much more bitter than to you: for the hand of Jehovah has gone out against me, Ruth 1:13. And a little later in verse 20 and 21: Do not call me Naomi (that is, beautiful) but call me Mara (that is, bitter) because the LORD has afflicted me with bitterness greatly. Thus Hannah, the mother of Samuel, in her hymn: The Lord, she says, kills and makes alive, brings down to the underworld and brings back: The Lord makes poor and makes rich, humbles and lifts up, 1 Samuel 2:6 & 7. Job acknowledged this very thing, 1:21. Jehovah gave, Jehovah has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD. And GOD Himself to Satan, the tormentor of Job: Behold I have given him into thy hand: nevertheless spare his life Job 2, 4. And Isa. 45, 7. I the LORD creating light, and making darkness, making peace, and creating evil. Amos 3, 6. Is there evil in a city, which the LORD hath not done? Lam. 3, 38. Who is he, that saith, out of the mouth of the most High proceedeth not good and evil? Hence the Saviour Matt. 10, 29. & 30. infers a general Aphorism: Are not, he says, two sparrows sold for a farthing, and one of them does not fall upon the ground, without the will of your heavenly father: But all the hairs of your head are numbered, and one of them does not fall upon the ground without the will of your heavenly father: Fear not therefore, you are better than many sparrows.

Latin:

QUemadmodum ægrotus Medicum & Medicinam avidè expetit, & inquirit: ita in afflictionibus mens pia, de veris consolationibus, quibus se erigere, & sustentare queat, semper est anxia & sollicita. Est enim Consolatio, medium à DEO præscriptum, quod adversus tribulationes & tristitiam ex illis conceptam, nos potenter corroborat & sustentat, cuilibet afflictioni vel præsenti, vel futuræ bonum aliquod opponendo, cujus fideli intuitu, & indefessâ meditatione, dolorem & angustiam mitigemus, & ut Scriptura loquitur, animas nostras per patientiam in silentio & spe possideamus. Hac autem in parte mentibus sensu iræ divinæ perterrefactis, Philosophicæ consolationes sufficere non possunt: Quales sunt: 1. Necessitas immutabilis, secundum illud vulgatum Feras, non culpes, quod mutare non potes.

Deinde Bona Conscientia, quæ plerumque apud non Renatos, vel eos etjam, qui licèt Renati sint, tamen extra DEI Verbum, afflictionum causas expendunt,

Impatientiæ & murmurationis contra DEUM mater esse solet: dum inquirit, & angitur. Cur malu bene, bonis male sit? exemplo AsaphiPsalmo 73, 2. & seqq. de seipso scribentis: Mei autem pedes penè moti sunt, & penè effusi sunt gressus mei: Quia Zelavi super iniquos, pacem peccatorum videns &c.

Tertiò exempla aliorum, qui vel similia mala, vel his majora passi sunt.

Quartò: Spes dubia & incerta:

Quintò: Gloria & immortalitas nominis, animi fortitudinem in ferendis calamitatibus, ceu præmium subsequens.

Sextò: Collatio eventuum: & si quæ his similes à philosophis proferuntur consolationes, dilutæ nimis. & infirmæ, His ergo ad Philosophorum gentilium Scholas relegatis, de alijs multò firmioribus nobis dispiciendum fuerit. Ubi profectò ea praxis Theologica observanda, sine quâ miles Christianus, sub vexillo crucis Christi nunquam feliciter pugnabit. Jam verum quidem est, & à B. LUTHERO nostro rectissimè assertum, Quòd omnis vera Consolatio Christiana constare debeat Syllogismo: Cujus major Propositio auxilium DEI, in Verbo ipsius promissum, opponat malo, quo affligimur: Minor autem sive Assumtio, illam ipsam promissionem verâ fidei sibi applicet: Unde Conclusio tandem evidenter & certò colligat, Malum, quo premimur, patienter & fortiter ferendum esse: siquidem auxilium DEI præstò nobis sit indubitatò adfuturum. Verùm hanc Topicam Spiritualem, universa Logica Aristotelis, & aliorum Gentilium ignorat, neque medium concludendi, ullus Inventionis locus unquàm monstrabit. Unde Asaphus ipse fatetur, se Rationis beneficio extricare nullo modo se potuisse, Quid causæ sit, quòd impij felices sint, pij verò totâ die flagellentur: sed id tandem in Sanctuario DEI didicisse: Laborabam, inquid ut cognoscerem hoc: & labor erat ante me: donec intravi in Sanctuarium DEI &c Psal 73, 16. & 17. Tales Syllogismos praxis Davidica in Psalmis egregiè nobis monstrat: ut Psalmo 25, 2, & 3.

Ad te DOMINE levavi animam meam: DEVS meus in te confido, non confundar: Etenim universi, qui expectant te, non confundentur. Unde Sylogismus iste enascitur:

Omnes sperantes in te DOMINE, non confunduntur.

Ego spero in te, & elevo animam meam ad te.

Ergo no confundar.

Et versu statim subsequente quarto contra hostes & persecutores suos sic subsumit David:

Omnes sine causâ prævaricatores confundentur.

Atqui inimici mei sine causâ prævaricantur.

Ergo confundentur, & non insultabunt mihi

Prævaricantur autem sine causâ, qui non in causæ bonitate, non in DEI auxilio: sed in potentiâ & viribus: vel etiam Sanctitate suâ hypocriticâ confidunt.

Hanc praxin Davidicam piorum quisque in suis tribulationibus imitari potest, imò deber, sic colligendo:

DEVS exaudit Sperantes in ipsum. Ergo & me exaudiet, Quia spero in ipsum. Et rursus.

Omnes, qui pijs sine causâ insultant, confundit DEVS.

Ergo & meos hostes idem certò confundet, quia præter meritum me affligunt.

Aliam praxin monstrat idem David, Psalmo 27, 1. Dominus lux & salus mea, quem timebo? Dominus protector vitæ meæ, à quo trepidabo? Syllogismus practicus emergit iste:

Quicunque DOMINVM DEVM suum pro Luce & salute habent: illi neminem debent extimescere.

At Dominus est lux & salus mea: Ergo à nemine timebo, neminem reformidabo.

Et rursus: Cuicunq; Dominus lux & salus est, ejus hostes necesse est impingere & concidere: & si maximè castra tota in surgant adversus ipsum. Ergo & mei adversarij impingent, cadentq; quantacunq; etiam ipsorum sit potentia

Eandem praxin, & longè evidentissimam monstrat David eodem Psalmo 27, 8. in quiens: Tibi dixit Cor meum: Quærite faciem meam: Faciem ergo tuam Domine, requiro: Ne avertas faciem tuam à me, & non repellas in irâ servum tuum. Unde syllogismus integer practicus talis emergit:

DEVS promisit invocantibus se, & quærentibus faciem suam, quòd velit eos exaudire, & eripere ex tribulatione, & angustiâ.

Atqui hoc ipsum tuum promissum, Tibi, ô DEVS, dicit & proponit Cor meum: Imò Ego hanc ipsam ob causam, in tribulatione meâ quæro faciem tuam.

Ergo justum ac dignum, imò necessarium est, ut me exaudias.

Hanc praxin Christianorum expendens Tertullianus: Hæc vu inquit, DEO grata est: neq; enim ita animatus est Deus, ut Homines, qui impatiencer ferunt, se suarum promissionum admoneri, adeòq; mendacium sibi imputari arbitrantur, cùm quis beneficium postulans, vel modeste etiam ad monet, sibi hoc aliquando fuisse promissum: DEVS autem ita sese Verbo promissionis suæ nobis obstrinxit, ut nihil magis cupiat, quàm promissionis per fidelem præcationem admoneri. Tertull. de precibus Christianorum.

Horum argumentorum praxis perfacilis est, quandiu extra afflictionis, & periculorum æstum sumus constituti, & ea adhuc in nudâ comtemplatione, sive θεωρίᾳ versatur: In tentationibus verò longè omnium est difficillima, præsertim in lucta illa graviore Carnis & Spiritus: Ubi interdū Major horum Syllogismorum infirmior esse videtur: interdum verò circa affumtionem, sive applicationem ad nostra individua, dubitationis plurimum obrepit: ut homo tentatus & afflictus fiduciam erga DEUM vel plane amittat, rat, vel satis languidam sentiat. Ergo hoc opus, hic labor fuerit, ut utriusque præmissarum certitudo immota ac infallibilis nobis sit cognita & perspecta. Istius autem certitudinis fundamenta non nisi in ipso DEO sunt quærenda: secundum illud Jesai. 51, 12. Ego Iehova, Ego ipse consolabor vos: Quis tu, ut timeres ab homine mortali, & à filio hominis, qui ut fœnum arescit? Cæterùm tùm demùm in DEO consolationum argumenta firma & quærunntur, & in veniuntur, si ingrediamur Sanctuarium DEI, & in eo discamus, qualem se DEUS quod afflictiones piorum, in Verbo suo revelaverit: id quod secundnm distincta DEI attributa expedire placet.

PRIMUM ergo Consolationis argumentum in genere contra quasvis afflictiones tàm internas, quàm externas; peti debet à DEI providentiâ. Quanquam enim afflictiones à causis secundis proficisci videntur: non tamen proptereà fortuitò, non temerè, non casualiter; sed, DEO sciente, imò sic volente & permittente, mala pijs eveniunt. Hinc ergo mens pia sub medijs adversitatum procellis, sic colligit: Si DEVS est, qui percutit, & affligit, & DEVS quidem ille, qui malum non permittit, nisi ex quo finem bonum & optatum novit elicere;tutique patienter feram, quicquid me paterna ipsius pati jubet voluntas.

Ratio connexi ex Providentiæ divinæ naturâ peti debet evidentissima. Hæc enim non tantùm mala pijs evenire permittit: sed & certas metas præscribit, quas causæ secundæ transgredi non possunt, imò ultra quas ne Diabolus quidem ipse, cum omnibus inferorum potestatibus sævire queat. Hinc est, quod non modò DEUS ipse autorem se pro fitetur omnium calamitatum, quibus pij premuntur Deut. 32, 39. Iob. 2, 4. Iesa. 45, 45.7. Amos 3.6. Thren. 3, 38. Sed & Sancti suo cruce ingemiscentes subinde ad DEVM percutientem respexerunt, Ruth. 1, 13, 20. 21. 1. Sam. 2, 6. & 7. Job. 1, 21. Hinc Servator ipse generalem extruit aphorismum practicum Matth. 10, 29. & 30. Testatur hoc DEUS ipse Deut. 32, 39. Videte, inquiens, quòd ego sim solus, & non sit alius DEVS præter me: ego occidam, & ego vivere faciam: ego percutiam & sanabo: & non est, qui è manu mea eripiat. Agnovit hoc pia illa fœmina Ruth, quæ miseriarum suarum Catalogū texens, in hæc tandem verba erumpit: Mihi, mihi multò amarius est, quàm vobis: nam manus Iehovæ exiit se contra me, Ruth. 1, 13. Et paulò pòst versu 20. ac 21 Non vocetu me Nahomin (id est pulcram) sed vocate me Maran (id est amaram) quia amaritudine me affecit DOMINUS valde. Sic Hanna mater Samuelis in suo hymno: Dominus, inquit, mortificat, & vivificat, deducit ad inferos, & reducit: Dominus pauperem facit & ditat, humiliat & sublevat, 1. Samuel. 2, 6. & 7. Agnovit hoc ipsum Job. 1. 21. Iehova dedit, Iehova abstulit. Sit nomen DOMINI benedictum. Et DEUS ipse ad Satanam persossorem Jobis: Ecce dedi eum in manu tuâ: veruntamen vitam ejus serva Job. 2, 4. Et Esa. 45, 7. Ego DEVS creans lucem, & faciens tenebras, faciens pacem, & creans malum. Amos 3, 6. Non est malum in civitate, quod non fecerit DOMINVS. Thren. 3, 38. Quis est, qui dicat, ex ore altissimi non egredi bona, & mala. Hinc Servator Matth. 10, 29. & 30. generalem infert Aphorismum: Nonne inquiens, duo passeres asse veneunt, & unus ex illis non cadit super terram, sine voluntate patris cœlestis: Omnes autem capilli capitis vestri numerati sunt, & unus ex illis non cadit super terram sine voluntate patris vestri cœlestis: Ne igitur timeatis, multis passeribus meliores estis.


### Chapter Two. Concerning Christian Consolation, both general and special, in any afflictions whatsoever (continued)

This first foundation of Consolation, although it does not complete the entire Consolation, nevertheless shows such a practical Syllogism, the use of which can be very great: so that a pious mind may thus conclude: It is GOD alone who sends afflictions upon the pious, and without whose will not even a hair can fall from our head to the ground, nay not even a little sparrow. But this same GOD is supremely good: Therefore he will not permit me to be afflicted beyond my strength, but will give with the temptation a salutary outcome. That same GOD is supremely wise: Therefore he himself knows what can be for my salvation: He is our father: Therefore not with a hostile, but with a fatherly love and affection, he also chastises me as a son, lest I be condemned with the impious.

Finally that same GOD is supremely merciful: Therefore he will also look upon me with the eyes of his mercy, and will not give affliction to the just forever. And thus consequently by proceeding through the remaining attributes of GOD, both individual and universal, a pious mind can raise and sustain itself in any adversities whatsoever: which will become more manifest from the following.

A SECOND foundation of Consolation therefore can and ought to be sought from the immutable justice of GOD, which renders to each his own. When therefore the pious in this life are pressed and afflicted by Tyrants and other impious men: GOD wills these very afflictions to be an ἐνδειγμα of his future just judgment, in which he is also to liberate the pious who are afflicted from all evils: and to take due punishments from the impious who afflict us. The Apostle shows this foundation, 2 Thess. 1, 4, 5. & 6. We glory in the Church of GOD for your patience, and faith in all your persecutions, and tribulations, which you sustain, an example of the just judgment of GOD, that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of GOD, for which you also suffer. Since it is just with GOD ἀνταποδοῦναι a retribution of afflictions to those who afflict you: but to you who are afflicted, relaxation with us. From there emerges that practical Syllogism:

The glory of GOD is to be preferred to all vows, and desires, and the dearest things of this world, nay even to this mortal life itself.

Now indeed GOD declares the glory of his justice in my afflictions, which I suffer beyond merit from Tyrants and this world. Why therefore should I not prefer it to all the most precious things in this life? Why should I not acquiesce in the will of GOD? Why should I not serve his Counsels with a cheerful and humble mind.

A THIRD foundation of Consolation ought to be sought from the Omnipresence of GOD. For GOD, who is Father, is present with us truly present by his essence. Nor does he only see as if from afar, the adversities that happen to us: but he himself being most present, and nearest to all, is the primary cause of afflictions. David used this kind of consolation, Ps. 23, 4. If I shall walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will not fear evils, because thou O GOD art with me. And Elisha 2 Kings 6, 16. to the boy saying: Do not fear: for there are more with us, than with them. Which very presence of his GOD promised to his faithful, Ps. 91, 15. I am with him in tribulation: I will deliver him, and glorify him Isa. 43, 2. When thou shalt pass through the waters, I will be with thee, and the rivers shall not cover thee: when thou shalt walk through the fire, thou shalt not be burned, nor shall the flame burn in thee: Because I the Lord thy GOD, the Holy One of Israel thy Saviour. Deut. 31, 6. & 8. I will not desert thee, nor forsake thee. Heb. 13, 5. He himself said: I will not desert thee nor forsake thee. Hence in the minds of the pious such a practical collection emerges: GOD is present with me, in the midst of my afflictions: For this he promised: and not this alone, but also help, defense, and liberation. Why therefore should I rage against the LORD?
