Why should I despair, or be broken in spirit in my tribulation: but rather, the greater it is, the more illustrious will be the presence of GOD, and my liberation. For he is truthful, and knows not how to lie.

A FOURTH ought to be sought from the omnipotence of GOD. For this has a wonderful force, and efficacy, to strengthen and sustain the faith of the pious in divine promises: so that we may not doubt anything at all concerning the promised liberation and salvation. For a pious mind constructs such a practical Syllogism from it: GOD is omnipotent: for he can do what he wills: but he wills what he has promised: and he has promised eternal life to those believing in Christ: he has promised a salutary outcome from all tribulations. How therefore can I doubt, but that in reality he can also perform for me, nay in the very act will perform, what GOD has promised. To this pertains that of the Saviour, John 10, 29. No one shall snatch my sheep from the hand of my Father: because the Father is greater (that is, more powerful) than all: But I and the Father are one. And indeed this Consolation produces a singular fortitude of mind, and confidence against all enemies and temptations or afflictions whatsoever; so that the Pious, whatever may happen, fear nothing except their GOD. For those who are persuaded that this GOD is so powerful, that all creatures in heaven and on earth are compelled to serve him: and they certainly know, this GOD is their omnipotent Father: how, I ask, can or should they fear from any creature for themselves? For if GOD is for us, who is against us? Rom 8.31. But in this place, this also must be well observed, that even secondary causes, which GOD is usually wont to use in afflicting us, do not act out of absolute necessity, but are referred to GOD himself, as to the primary cause. For GOD is the Lord of all nature, and thus the most free ruler and moderator of all secondary causes. When, therefore, we see that even all secondary causes are contrary to us: let us know, however, that our spirit must not be cast down, as much in those things which pertain to the body as in those which pertain to the soul. An example of this thing may be seen in Abraham, who was old and as if dead: and in the sterility of his spouse Sarah: who, although they saw all natural secondary causes opposing them, which were necessary for the procreation of children: yet they did not cast down their spirit: but believed in hope against hope, especially Abraham. Wherefore? Because he had known the power of GOD: namely, that He who had promised the seed was able to perform the promise even without natural means. Rom. 4, 19. & 20. Hebr. 11, 11. An illustrious example may likewise be seen in the Israelite people in Isaiah chapter 12, 1 & 2, who break forth into these words: I will confess to thee, O LORD, because thou wast angry with me: thy fury is turned away, and thou hast comforted me: Behold GOD is my Saviour: I will act confidently, and will not fear: because the LORD is my strength and my praise. The Israelite people were established in the most grievous afflictions: but they boast that they act confidently and fear nothing. But how so? For in order that one may fear nothing, it is necessary that one rely upon a certain protection: Unless this is present, all confidence is foolish and pernicious vanity. Therefore, after they said that they act confidently and fear nothing, they immediately subjoin the reason for this confidence and ἀφοβίας: Because Jehovah is my strength. All the pious will imitate this practice of the Israelite people in any tribulations whatsoever, so that they may say: We will confess to thee, O LORD, because thou wast angry with us: but behold we will act confidently and will not fear: Because thou, O LORD, art our praise and our strength. We can do nothing without thee, John 15, 5, but we can do all things through Christ, who strengthens us, Phil. 4, 13, and whose power is perfected through our infirmity: 2 Cor. 12, 9. Who commands us to trust, because He himself has conquered the world for us. John 16, 33. Who causes that we also may conquer the world, through faith in Him. 1 John 5, 4, through which faith He who is more powerful than he who dwells in the world dwells in our hearts. Ephes. 1, 20. 1 John 4, 4. From Him, therefore, is defense, from Him is strength for warring, from Him is the armor of GOD, clothed with which we can resist in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. Ephes. 6, 13. From Him is our victory, 1 Cor. 15, 57, etc.

THE FIFTH foundation of consolation must be sought from the immense mercy of GOD, and from the infallible certainty and truth of the divine promises which depends upon this. Psalm 34, 19. The Lord is near to those who are of a troubled heart. Isaiah 54, 7. For a small moment I have forsaken thee, and with great mercies I will gather thee: In a moment of indignation I hid my face for a little while from thee, and in everlasting mercy I have had mercy on thee: said thy Redeemer the LORD: and in verse 10, The mountains shall be moved, and the hills shall tremble: but my mercy shall not depart from thee, and the covenant of my peace shall not be made void: said thy merciful Lord. Jerem. 31, 20. Is not Ephraim a most dear son to me? is not this my delight? I remember what I have spoken concerning him: Therefore my bowels are troubled for him: I will surely have mercy on him, says the LORD. Which passage our blessed LUTHER expressed in words that are very pathetic and that approach most closely to the Hebrew truth: Is Ephraim not my faithful son, and my dear child? For I still think well upon what I have said to him, therefore my heart breaks for him, so that I must have mercy on him, says the LORD. And Hosea 2, 19. I will betroth thee to me forever: and I will betroth thee to me in justice and judgment: in mercy, and in compassions. I will betroth thee to me in faith, that thou mayest know that I am the LORD.

But now GOD is faithful, and what He has once promised to the pious, He keeps most constantly: For He cannot deny Himself: and all His promises are in Christ Jesus, Yes and Amen. 2 Cor. 1, 20. Whence the pious mind infers such a practical syllogism: Whatever GOD has promised, that He wills to perform: but what He wills, that He performs in reality. But He has promised the liberation of the pious from all troubles. Therefore He wills to perform the same: and because He wills it, He will perform it in reality. The examples of the pious, whom GOD has miraculously snatched from evils, pertain here: and He has most powerfully repressed and crushed the attempts of enemies. And the reason for the consequence which the pious connect in this kind of consolation is most firm: For the same GOD is today who was present to the pious, equally always merciful toward all who trust in Him: equally just, equally truthful, equally powerful. The affliction is the same on both sides: the reason for the enemies is the same, who, by persecuting the pious, strive to heap reproach upon GOD himself: The end is the same on both sides, from our liberation and the destruction of the enemies, it redounds to the glory of GOD. Therefore, just as GOD has never failed to snatch the pious, so He will also snatch us who hope in Him: And underlying this argument is that most certain hypothesis, which is sought from the immutability of the divine will concerning the promises: according to that of Isaiah 14, 27.

When Jehovah of hosts has decreed, who shall make it void? And who shall turn back his outstretched hand? For the will of God in this kind of promise is never changed: The reason is: Because it is founded not on our dignity, or merits, but on the sole mercy of GOD, which always remains consistent with itself, and is never changed. Much less does he ever repent of this counsel, once made, to help, deliver, and glorify the pious and the elect: nor can anything better be shown or suggested to him, which he might prefer to his own counsel and decree: nor does he suffer himself to be led away from his righteousness, goodness, mercy, justice, and wisdom by the prayers, or persuasion, or exhortation, or fear, or thanks of anyone. Whence Malachi 3:6 says: I am GOD, and I am not changed. And Num. 23:19: GOD is not as man, that he should lie: nor as the son of man, that he should be changed. Isaiah 40:8: The word of the LORD our GOD remains forever. And Rom. 11:29. GOD never repents of his gifts. Since therefore this will of his, declared in his promises, is immovable, and perpetually consistent with itself, and cannot be hindered by anyone, it necessarily follows that what once pleased him, pleased him from eternity, and will please him to eternity. And what he testifies that he wills once, and has promised that he will do, nay rather, has confirmed with an oath, signs, and most evident examples: surely no one of the pious today should have even the slightest doubt concerning this promise and will of his. The heathens themselves also acknowledged that they owed this piety to their fictitious Gods: so that that Persian in Herodotus, book 9, confesses, that it is impossible for a man to avert what is destined to happen from God.

The SIXTH foundation of consolation must be sought from the incomparable benefit and emolument, which certainly redounds to the pious and the Elect from such tribulations, both in this life and in the other; so that the Apostle truly wrote in Rom. 8:18: I reckon that the sufferings of this time are nothing to the glory which shall at some time be revealed in us: And that the momentary affliction of this world produces an eternal weight of glory. 2 Cor. 4:17. For, says the same Apostle, to those who love GOD all things work together for good, Rom. 8:28, and consequently also Calamity: Since affliction produces patience: patience, probation: probation, hope: hope does not put to shame. To which pertain those practical Syllogisms, which the Apostle himself wished to form for the pious and faithful by his own example in this manner:

I. God did not spare his own son, but delivered him up for us all. Therefore in him, and with him, he has given us all things, which can promote the temporal and eternal salvation of the pious, Rom. 8:32.

II. It is God who justifies the pious and the elect: Therefore no one can or ought to take upon himself any right of accusing the pious and the elect. verse 33.

III. Christ died for us, nay rather he was also raised, sits at the right hand of God, and intercedes for us. Who therefore is he that condemns us? Rom. 8:34.

Nay, from these three arguments premised, the Apostle infers this conclusion with great Spirit, in verse 35 and following. Therefore neither affliction, nor distress, nor persecution, nor famine, nor nakedness, nor peril, nor sword can separate us from the love of Christ. And although we are killed all the day long, and are accounted as sheep of the slaughter: yet in all these things we are more than conquerors, through him who loved us. For it is certain that neither death, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, or depth, or any other creature can separate us from the love of GOD, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

The Apostles held this practice, who, having been beaten with rods and scourges, departed from the council rejoicing and exulting that they were counted worthy to suffer something for the name of Christ: Where indeed they were not conquered by the persecutors, but emerged as victors because they not only bore the scourges patiently: but from this they conceived an even greater ardor for preaching the Gospel, Acts 5:41. Job observed this practice, saying: Even if he should kill me, yet I will hope in him, Job 13:15. And David Ps. 46:2 and following: Our God is a refuge and strength: a strong helper in tribulations, which have seized us: Therefore we will not fear, even if the earth be moved, and the mountains cast themselves into the heart of the sea: God is in the midst of us: The Lord of hosts is with us: the God of Jacob is an insuperable fortification for us.

Our B. LUTHER held the same practice, who had a raging Pope, a roaring Emperor, and the whole world storming against him: but he was so far from being broken in spirit that he rather rejoiced greatly on this account, and congratulated himself vehemently.

But the goods and emoluments, which redound to the Elect from afflictions, both in this life and in the future, we touched upon above in chapter 1, where we explained the final causes for which GOD sends afflictions upon the pious. Let it suffice now to reduce all those things into a kind of summary. The cross or affliction of the pious therefore promotes the glory of GOD: produces patience, James 1:2 and 3: is a testimony of the love of GOD toward us. Heb. 12:6, 1 Pet. 2:19, 20: proves our faith, James 1:12, 1 Pet. 1:6 and 7: is the way through which one must enter into the kingdom of heaven. Acts 14:22: renders us conformed to the image of the son of GOD. Rom. 8:28, 1 Pet. 4:13: ensures that we are not condemned with this world. 1 Cor. 11:32: produces an eternal weight of glory, 2 Cor. 4:17: admonishes us of the corruption of our nature, of our weakness and fragility. Micah 7:9, Ps. 119:25 and 137. Jer. 3:39 and 40: mortifies and crucifies our flesh with its lusts and desires, confirms our hope, Rom. 5:4 and 5.

it educates and instructs us unto righteousness and obedience owed to GOD: Ps. 116:67. Heb. 12:11. It begets contempt and loathing of the world and of this life: and invites to the meditation of the future life: by the example of Elijah: 1 Kings 19:4. Finally, it delivers us from every evil. Ps. 34:23.

but that we may suffer as Christians, let us not be ashamed, nay rather let us glorify GOD. 1 Pet. 4:15 & 16. To which consolation corresponds also a certain trust in the healing of a wounded conscience, through faith in Christ, of which it is said in 1 John 2:1: If anyone has sinned, we have an advocate with God, Jesus Christ, the righteous: Who is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world.

THE SEVENTH foundation of consolation must be sought from the Example of CHRIST, and of all the Saints. Christ is certainly the most absolute exemplar of Christian patience, to whose image we are rendered conformable in this respect, if we imitate his example. For when we consider more accurately in our mind how many contradictions, how many persecutions, reproaches, curses, and finally death itself he sustained for us: why should it not behoove us also to labor toward a part of that tolerance? For is the disciple not above the Master? Much less, therefore, is it fitting that servants should be of a better condition than their Lord. John 15:20. For which very reason the Savior gravely warns that we should studiously imitate this example of his: Luke 14:26. If anyone wishes to be my disciple, let him take up his cross, and follow me. And Peter in chapter 2, v. 21. In this you were called, because Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps: And the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 12, 2. Looking unto the author and finisher of faith, Jesus, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame.

Latin:

Primum hoc Consolationis fundamentum, licet integram Consolationem non absolvat, talem tamen monstrat Syllogismum practicum, cujus usus queat esse longè maximus: ut mens pia sic colligere possit: Solus DEVS est, qui piis afflictiones immittit, & sine cujus voluntate ne capillus quidem de capite nostro, imo nec passerculus in terram cadere potest. Atqui hic ipse DEVS summè bonus est: Ergo non permittet supra vires me affligi, sed dabit cum tentatione salutarem exitum. Idem ille DEVS summe sapiens est: Ergo ipse novit, quid ex salute meâ esse possit: Ipse pater noster est: Ergo non hostili, sed paterno amore ac affectu, me quoq; ut filium castigat, ne cum impio condemner.

Tandem idem ille DEVS summè misericors est: Ergo me quoque oculis misericordiæ suæ respiciet, neque dabit in æternum afflictionem justo. Et sic consequenter per reliqua attributa DEI singula & universa progrediendo, mens pia in quibusvis adversitatibus se erigere, & sustentare potest: id quod ex sequentibus evadet manifestius

ALTERVM ergò Consolationis fundamentum peti potest & debet ex immutabili DEI justitia, quæ suum cuique tribuit. Quando ergò pij hac in vitâ à Tyrannis alijsq; impijs hominibus premuntur & affliguntur: vult DEUS has ipsas afflictiones esse ἐνδειγ μα justi sui futuri judicij, in quo & pios afflictos liberaturus sit ab omnibus malis: & de impijs nos affligentibus debitas sumturus pœnas. Fundamentum hoc monstrat Apostolus, 2. Thess. 1, 4, 5. & 6. Nos gloriamur in Ecclesiâ DEI pro patientiâ vestrâ, & fide in omnibus persecutionibus vestris, & tribulationibus, quas sustinetis, exemplum justi judicij DEI, ut digni habeamini regno DEI, pro quo & patimini. Siquidem justum est apud DEVM ἀνταποδῦναι retributionem afflictionum iis, qui vos affligunt: vobis autem, qui affligimini, relaxationem nobiscum. Emer git inde iste Sillogismus practicus:

Gloria DEI præferenda omnibus votis, & desideriis, & rebus charissimis hujus mundi, imò ipsi etiam vitæ huic mortali.

Iam verò DEVs gloriam justitiæ suæ declarat in afflictionibus meis, quas prater meritum è Tyrannis & mundo isto patior Cur ergo non eam práferam omnibus hac in vita pretiosissimis? Cur non acquiescam in voluntate DEI? Cur non ipsius Consiliis hilari & humili animo inserviam.

TERTIUM Consolationis fundamentum peti debet à DEI Omniprásentiâ. DEUS enim, qui Pater est, adest nobis verè prásens suâ essentiâ. Nec solùm quasi è longinquo videt, quæ nobis contingunt adversa : sed ipse prásentissimus , & omnium proximus, primaria est causa afflictionum. Hoc consolationis genere usus David, Psal. 23, 4. Si ambulavero in medio umbræ mortis, non timebo mala, quoniam tu DEUS mecum es. Et Elisæus 2. Reg. 6, 16. ad puerum dicentem : Noli timere : plures enim nobiscum sunt, quam cum illis. Quam ipsam præsentiam suam DEUS fidelibus suis promisit, Psal. 91, 15. Cum ipso sum in tribulatione : eripiam eum, & glorificabo eum Jesa. 43, 2. Cum transieris per aquas, tecum ero, & flumina non operient te : cùm ambulaveris per ignem, non comburêris, nec flamma ardebit in te : Quia ego Dominus DEUS tuus, Sanctus Israel Salvator tuus. Deut. 31, 6. & 8. Non ego te deseram, neque derelinquam. Hebr. 13, 5. Ipse dixit : Non te deseram neque derelinquam. Hinc in animis piorum talis emergit collectio practica : DEUS præsto mihi adest, in medijs meis afflictionibus : Hoc enim promisit : nec hoc solum, sed & auxilium, defensionem, & liberationem. Cur ergò fremam adversus DOMINUM? Cur desperem, aut frangar animo in tribulatione mea : quin potiùs, quo major ea est eo illustrior erit DEI præsentia, meáq; liberatio. Verax enim est, & mentiri nescit.

QUARTUM peti debet ab omnipotentiâ DEI. Hæc enim mirèm vim, & efficaciam habet, ad fidem piorum in promissionibus divinis firmandam, & sustentandam : ut de liberatione & salute promissâ nihil quicquam dubitemus. Talem enim Syllogismum practicum mens pia inde extruit : DEVS est omnipotens : potest enim, quæ vult : vult autem, quæ promisit : promisit verò vitam æternam credentibus in Christum:promisit salutarem exitum ex omnibus tribulationibus. Qui possim ergo dubitare, quin reipsà mihi quoque præstare possit, imo ipso actu præstiturus sit DEVS, quæ promisit. Huc pertinet illud Servatoris, Johan. 10, 29. Nemo rapiet oves meas de manu Patris mei : quia Pater major ( id est, potentior ) est omnibus : Ego autem & Pater unum sumus. Et sanè hæc Consolatio singularem parit animi fortitudinem, & confidentiam adversus omnes hostes & tentationes sive afflictiones quaslibet ; ita ut Pij, quicquid etiam eveniat, nihil præter DEUM suum metuant. Qui enim persuasi sunt, hunc DEUM tàm potentem esse, ut ipsi servire cogantur omnes creaturæ in cœlo & in terrâ: & certô noverunt, hunc DEUM omnipotentem suum esse patrem: quomodo quæso ab ullâ creaturâ sibi possint aut debeant metuere? Si enim DEUS pro nobis, quis contra nos? Rom 8.31. Est verò hoc loco & illud probè observandum, quòd causæ etiam secundæ, quibus DEUs in nobis affligendis plerumque uti solet, non ex necessitate absolutâ agant, sed in DEUm ipsum, tanquam in primam causam, referantur. est enim DEUS Dominus totius naturæ, & sic causarum omnium secundarum rector & moderator liberrimus. Cùm ergo videmus, omnes etiam causas secundas nobis esse contrarias: sciamus tamen, non despondendum esse animum, tàm in ijs, quæ ad corpus, quàm in ijs, quæ ad animam pertinent. Exemplum hujus rei videre licet in Abrahamo sene, & quasi emortuto: & in sterilitate conjugis Saræ: qui licet omnes causas secundas naturales sibi adversari viderent, ad liberorum procreationem necessarias: animum tamen non desponderunt: sed in spem contra spem crediderunt, præsertim Abraham. Quamobrem? Quoniam noverat potentiam DEI: posse scilicet illum, qui promiserat semen, etiam sine medijs naturalibus promifsionem præstare. Rom. 4, 19. & 20. Hebr. 11, 11. Illustre item exemplum videre licet in populo Israelitico apud Jesaiam cap. 12. 1. & 2. qui in hæc verba eurumpit Confitebor tibi DOMINE, quoniam iratus es mihi: conversus est furor tuus, & consolatus es me: Ecce DEUS Salvator meus: Fiducialiter agam, & non timebo: quoniam Fortitudo & laus mea DOMINVS. In afflictionibus longè gravissimis constitutus erat populus Israeliticus: sed gloriatur, se fiducialiter agere, & nihil timere. Quî sic verò: nam ut nihil metuat, præsidio certo nitatur necesse est: Hoc nisi ad sit, fiducia omnis est stulta & perniciosa vanitas. Ergò postquàm se fiducialiter agere, nihilq; metuere dixit, statim rationem hujus confidentiæ & ἀφοβίας subjicit: Quia Jehovah est fortitudo mea. Hanc praxin populi Israelitici imitabuntur pij quique in quibusvis tribulationibus, ut dicant: Confitebimur tibi DOMINE, quoniam iratus es nobis: sed ecce fiducialiter agemus & nihil timebimus: Quia tu DOMINE laus & fortitudo nostra. Nos sine te nihil possumus, Joh. 15, 5. sed omnia possumus per Christum, qui nos corroborat Phil. 4. 13. & cujus potentia per infirmitatem nostram perficitur: 2. Cor. 12, 9. Qui confidere nos jubet, quia ipse pro nobis vicerit mundum. Iohan. 16, 33. Qui facit, ut & nos vincamus mundum, per fidem in ipsum. 1. Iohan. 5, 4. per quam fidem in cordibus nostris habitat is, qui potentior est, quàm ille, qui in mundo habitat. Ephes. 1, 20. 1. Iohan. 4, 4. Ab illo igitur est defensio, ab illo est robur ad militandum, ab illo est armatura DEI, quâ induti possumus resistere tempore malo, & omnibus confectis stare. Ephes. 6, 13. Ab illo est victoria nostra, 1. Cor. 15, 57. &c.

QVINTVM Consolationis fundamentum peti debet ab immensa DEI misericordia, & ab hoc dependente infallibili promissionum divinarum certitudine & veritate. Psalm. 34, 19. Prope est Dominus his, qui tribulato sunt corde. Jesai. 54, 7. Ad punctum in modico dereliqui te, & in miserationibus magnis congregabo te: In momento indignationis abscondi faciem meam parumper a te & in misericordia sempiterna misertus sum tui: dixit Redemtor tuus DOMINVS: & versu, 10, Montes commovebuntur, & colles contremiscent: misericordia autem mea non recedet a te, & fœdus pacis meæ non fiet irritum: dixit miserator tuus Dominus. Jerem. 31, 20. Nonne Ephraim est mihi filius charissimus? nonne in hoc filio sunt delitiæ meæ; Recordor, quid locutus sim de eo: Ideo conturbata sunt viscera mea super eum: miserans miserebor ejus dicit DOMINVS. Quem locum verbis admodum patheticis & ad Hebræam veritatem maximè accedentibus verbis expressit B. LVTHERVS noster: Ist nicht Ephraim mein trewer Sohn/ vnd mein trawtes Kind? Denn ich dencke noch wol daran/ was ich jhm geredt habe/ darumb bricht mir mein Hertz gegen jhm daß ich mich sein erbarmen muß/ spricht der HERR. Et hoseæ 2, 19. Desponsabo te mihi in sempiternum: & desponsabo te mihi in justitia & judicio: in misericordia, & in miserationibus Desponsabo te mihi in fide, ut scias, quod ego sim DOMINVS.

Jam verò fidelis est DEUS, & quod semel promisit pijs, constantissime servat: Seipsum enim negare non potest: & omnes promissiones ipsius sunt in Christo Jesu Et. iam & Amen. 2. Cor. 1, 20. Unde mens pia talem infert syllogismum practicum: Quicquid DEUS promisit, illud vult præstare: quod autem vult, illud reipsa præstat. Atqui promisit liberationem piorum ex omnibus ærumnis. Ergo eandem vult præstare: & quia vult, reipsa præstabit. Pertinent huc exempla piorum, quos DEUS e malis mirabiliter eripuit: & hostium conatus potentissimè repressit & elisit. Et firmissima est Consequentiæ ratio, quam in hoc consolationis genere nectunt pij: Nam idem DEUS hodie est, qui pijs adfuit, æquè semper misericors erga omnes, qui confidunt in ipsum: æquè justus, æquè verax, æquè potens. Eadem est utrobiq; afflictio: eadem ratio hostium, qui pios persequendo, DEUM ipsum contumelia afficere student: Idem utrobique finis, ex liberatione nostra, & interitu hostium, ad gloriam DEI redundat. Ergo quemadmodum DEUS nunquam non eripuit pios, ita nos quoque sperantes in ipsum eripiet: Et subest argumento huic certissima illa hypothesis, quæ ab immutabilitate voluntatis divinæ circa promissiones petitur: secundum illud Esa. 14, 27.

Cum Jehovah exercituum decrevit, quis irritum faciet? & manum ejus extentam quis avertet? Dei enim voluntas in hoc promissionu genere nunquàm mutatur: Ratio est: Quia ea fundata est non in nostrâ dignitate, aut meritis, sed in solâ DEI misericordiâ, quæ semper sibi constat, & nunquàm mutatur. Multò minùs ipsum pœnitet unquam hujus consilii, de juvandis, liberandis, glorificandis piis & electis semel facti: neque melius aliquid ipsi monstrari aut suggeripotest, quod suo consilio & decreto præferat: neque cujusquam precibus, aut suasu, aut hortatu, aut metu, aut gratiâ patitur se à rectitudine, bonitate, misericordiâ, justiciâ, & sapientiâ suâ abduci. Unde Malach. 3. v. 6. dicit: DEUS sum ego, & non mutor. Et Num. 23. v. 19. Non est DEUS quasi homo, ut mentiatur: nec ut filius hominis, ut mutetur. Jesa. 40. v. 8. Verbum DOMINI DEI nostri manet in æternum. Et Rom. 11. v. 29. DEUM donorum suorum nunquam pœnitet. Cùm ergo hæc ipsius voluntas, in promissionibus declarata sit immota, & perpetuò sibi constet, neque à quoquam impediri possit, necessariò consequitur, quod semel placuit ei, ab æterno placuisse, & in æternum ei placiturum esse. Et quod velle se semel testatur est, ac se facturum promisit, quin imò juramento, signis & exemplis evidentissimis confirmavit: utiq; nulli piorum hodiéq; de hac ipsius promissione, & voluntate vel tantillum dubitandum fuerit. Agnoverunt ipsi quoque Ethnici, se hanc pietatem debere Diis suis fictitiis: ita ut Persa ille apud Herodotum lib. 9. fatetur, ὅτι δεῖ γενέσθαι ἐκ τῶ θεῶ ἀμήχανον ἀποτρέψαι ἀνθρώπω.

SEXTUM Consolationis fundamentum peti debet ab incomparabili commodo & emolumento, quod ex ejusmodi tribulationibus, tùm in hac, tùm in alterâ vitâ ad pios & Electos certò redundat; ita ut verè scripserit Apostolus Rom 8. v. 18. Statuo, quòd temporis hujus passiones nihil sunt ad gloriam, quæ aliquando in nobis revelabitur: Et quòd momentanea hujus mundi afflictio pariat æternum gloriæ pondus. 2. Cor. 4. v. 17. Nam, inquit idem Apostolus, diligentibus DEUM omnia cooperantur in bonum, Rom. 8. 28. & per consequens etiam Calamitas: Siquidem afflictio parit patientiam: patientia probationem: probatio spem: spes non confundit. Quò pertinent Syllogismi illi practici, quos ipse Apostolus suo exemplo piis & fidelibus hunc in modum formare voluit:

I. Deus proprio filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit ipsum. Ergo in ipso, & cum ipso dedit nobis omnia, quæ temporalem, & æternam salutem piorum promovere possunt, Rom. 8. v. 32.

II. Deus est, qui justificat pios & electos: Ergo nemo sibi jus aliquod accusandi pios & electos sumere vel potest, vel debet. verf. 33.

III. Christus mortuus est pro nobis, imò verò etiam excitatus, consedis ad dextram Dei, intercedit pro nobis. Quis ergò est, qui condemnet nos? Rom. 8. v. 34.

Imò ex præmissis istis tribus argumentis, magno Spiritu conclusionem hanc infert Apostolus, verf. 35. & sequentibus. Ergo neq; afflictio, neq; angustia, neq; persecutio, neq; fames, neq; nuditas, neq; periculum, neq; gladius separare nos potest à dilectione Christi. Et quanquam tota die occidimur, & reputamur tanquam oves mactationis: tamen in his omnibus plus quàm victores sumus, per eum, qui dilexit nos. Certum enim est, quòd neque mors, neq; angeli, neq; principatus, neq; virtutes, neque præsentia, neq; futura, neq; altitudo, aut profunditas, aut ulla creatura alia possit nos separare à dilectione DEI, quæ est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro.

Praxin hanc tenueruut Apostoli, qui virgis & flagris cæsi, lætantes ovantesq; à senatu abjerunt, quòd digni essent habiti, qui aliquid pro nomine Christi paterentur: Ubi sanè non victi fuerunt à persecutoribus, sed victores evaserunt quia non patienter tantùm flagra pertulerunt: sed hinc ardorem etiam majorem prædicandi Evangelii conceperunt, Act. 5. verf. 4. Praxin hanc observavit Job, dicens: Etiamsi occiderit me, tamen sperabo in ipso, Job. 13. v. 15. Et David Psal. 46, 2. & seqq. Deus noster, refugium & virtus: adjutor fortis in tribulationibus, quæ corripuerunt nos: Propterea non timebimus, etsi terra moveatur, & montes se projiciant in Cor maris: Deus in medio nostri: Dominus exercituum nobiscum: insuperabilis munitio est nobis Deus Jacob.

Praxin eandem tenuit B. LUTHERUS noster, qui furentem Papam, frementem Imperatorem; sævientem totum mundum habuit: sed usq; adeò animo non fractus fuit, ut potiùs hoc nomine plurimùm gauderet, sibique vehementer gratularetur.

Bona verò atque emolumenta, quæ ex afflictionibus ad Electos, tùm hac in vitâ, tùm in futurâ redundant, suprà cap. 1. perstrinximus, ubi causas finales, ob quas DEUS piis afflictiones immittat, expedivimus. Sisticiat jam in compendium quasi quoddam, omnia illa redigere. Crux ergo sive afflictio piorum promovet gloriam DEI: parit patientiam, Jacob. 1. v. 2. & 3. est testimonium amoris DEI in nos. Hebr. 12. v. 6. 1. Pet. 2. v. 19. 20. probat fidem nostram, Jacob. 1. verf. 12. 1. Petr. 1. v. 6. & 7. est via, per quam ingrediendum in regnum cœlorum. Act. 14. v. 22. reddit nos conformes imagini filii DEI. Rom. 8. v 28. 1. Pet. 4. v 13. præstat, ut non condemnemur cũ hoc mundo. 1. Cor. 11. v. 32. parit æternum gloriæ pondus, 2. Cor. 4. v. 17. admonet nos de naturæ nostræ corruptione, de imbecillitate & fragilitate nostrâ. Mich. 7. v. 9. Ps. 119. v. 25. & 137. Ier. 3. v 39 & 40. mortificat, & crucifigit carnem nostram cum concupiscentiis ac desideriis suis, confirmat spem nostram, Rom. 5. v. 4. & 5.

erudit & instruit nos ad justitiam & obedientiam DEO debitam: Psal. 116.v.67. Hebr.12.v.11. gignit contemtum & fastidium mundi ac vitæ hujus: & invitat ad futuræ vitæ meditatione: exemplo Eliæ: 1. Reg. 19. v. 4. liberat tandem nos ab omni malo. Psal. 34. v. 23.

sed ut Christiani patiamur, ne pudeffamus imò glorificemus DEUM. 1. Petr. 4. v. 15. & 16. Cui consolationi æquipollet etiam certa fiducia sanationis vulneratæ conscientiæ, per fidem in Christum, de quâ 1. Joh.2.v.1. dicitur: Sic quis peccaverit, advocatum babemus apud Deum, Jesum Christum, justum: Qui est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, non pro nostris autem tantum sed pro totius mundi peccatis.

SEPTIMUM Consolationis fundamentum peti debet ab Exemplo CHRISTI, & Sanctorum omnium. Christus certè absolutissimum est exemplar patientiæ Christianæ, cujus imagini hac in parte conformes reddimur, si exemplum ejus imitemur. Quando enim apud animum accuratius consideramus, quantas ipse contradictiones, quantas persecutiones, opprobria, maledicta, ipsam denique mortem pro nobis sustinuerit: quid ni nos quoque ad partem tolerantiam elaborare deceat: Neque enim discipulus est supra Magistrum? Multò ergò minùs convenit, ut servi melioris sint conditionis, quàm Dominus. Johan. 15. v. 20. Quam ipsam ob causam Servator graviter monet, ut hoc suum exemplum studiosè imitemur: Luc. 14. vers. 26. Si quis voluerit meus esse discipulus, tollat crucem suam, & sequatur me. Et Petrus in 1 cap. 2. v. rf. 21. In hoc vocati estis, quia Christus passus est pro nobis, relinquens vobis exemplum, ut sequamini vestigia ejus: Et autor Epistolæ ad Hebræos cap. 12, 2. Respiciten autorem fidei, & consummatorem Jesum, qui proposito sibi gaudio sustinuit crucem, confusione contemta.


### Chapter Two. Concerning Christian Consolation, both general and special, in any…: On the Leagues of Christians

AMONG other questions which are wont to be debated concerning the matter of human afflictions, this one holds a place that is by no means the last: Whether it is permitted for Christians and believers to use certain means and remedies, by which they might either entirely remove, or at least in some way mitigate, the force of calamities that are imminent or even already incumbent? And indeed, it is most rightly answered in the Affirmative: but generally. For just as illicit means, such as the responses of devils, pythons, enchanters, magicians, and poisoners, are by no means to be used, since GOD forbids it in Deut. 18:11, so there are certain means which it is entirely permitted to use: yet so that we do not rely upon them too much: or where they fail us, despair of the Grace of GOD and a salutary outcome. Thus it is permitted to use war and arms against enemies unjustly inflicting force, and to repel unjust force: unless the LORD expressly forbids it: just as Zedekiah the Jewish King was commanded not to resist, but to surrender himself to the Babylonian enemy. Thus it is also permitted to use treaties and auxiliary guards of neighbors and friends. Thus in diseases it is permitted to use medicine: which is, as the physicians themselves confess, nothing other than the very hand of GOD. Thus in time of Pestilence, when Physicians prescribe a change of air: it will be permitted to use that also: yet so that neither the necessary duties of one's calling, nor the due offices of mutual charity are meanwhile neglected by anyone. But above all, when such private or public calamities are impending, one must flee to the LORD who strikes us, through serious repentance. Nay, even public exercises of Repentance: such as fasts, prayers, and supplications, can be instituted by the example of the ancient Church, provided that it be done without superstition: that is, let there be no opinion of merit, worship, and absolute necessity. Thus in other external calamities, it is by no means prohibited to apply appropriate means and remedies: provided that it be done in due order and for a due end. And thus far indeed proceeds the general Response of most Theologians.

But the examples of the Saints also provide consolation in adversities: according to that of Peter, 1 Pet. 5:9. Resist the Devil, strong in faith: knowing that the same suffering is being accomplished in your brotherhood that is in the world: For there was never any of the Saints whom the LORD did not wish to drink his own, as it were, measured and better portion from the cup of affliction. Since, therefore, we are surrounded by such a cloud, by such a multitude of believers, why should we despise so venerable a society? Why should we hope for a better lot in this world? Christ himself showed his disciples a practical argument taken from this example, saying: Blessed are you, when they shall cast reproaches upon you, and shall say all manner of evil word against you: Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven: For so they persecuted the Prophets of old, who were before you. Matt. 5:11 & 12. Just as therefore Moses chose the reproaches and hardships of the people of GOD, and preferred them to all the treasures of the Egyptians: So let us also, with pious emulation, not refuse to be inscribed in this most beautiful and most holy society of the elect, who are warring under the Cross in this life.

THE EIGHTH and last foundation of consolation can also be sought from the testimony of a good conscience: that we are not as murderers, thieves, criminals, or busybodies in other men's matters,

However, at this point a question is raised, both in theory and in theological practice, which is indeed quite intricate, but most necessary to know: namely, whether, when the more serious machinations and efforts of our enemies are looming, against which we alone are unable to be a match, it is permitted to join treaties or enter into unions with the impious and with men of a different religion? For example: If the Papists wish to wage war upon the Lutherans and utterly exterminate them, but the latter alone are unable to resist such great forces of the enemies: or even if allies of the same confession bring force upon us by land and sea, prohibit free trade, and rashly violate promises and agreements sacredly confirmed on both sides, against all right and merit: and we, however, are unable to repress the attack of these men alone; the question is: In such a case, can and ought the Lutherans, with a good conscience, to enter into a treaty with men of a different religion, such as the Calvinists, and thus either assert the Orthodox religion safe and sound, or liberate their own life and fortunes and those of their subjects from unjust force and tyranny, and vindicate them into their former liberty? The decision of which question is so much the more difficult and intricate as the opinions of theologians are more divergent: most of whom descend into the negative, because God Himself has everywhere in His Word most severely prohibited that a treaty be joined with the impious.

And indeed, for the defense of the negative, those testimonies are first brought forward which seriously warn that the treaties of the impious are to be avoided: such as are: Exod. 23. 32. 34. 12. & 15. Beware that you never join friendships with the inhabitants of that land (who, by the testimony of the preceding verse 11, were the Amorites, Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites), which may be a ruin to you. The same thing is repeated in Deut. 7. 2. & 3. Judg. 2. 1. & 2. I have promised you that I would not make my covenant void with you forever: only so that a treaty should not be struck with the inhabitants of this land. Next, the punishments of those who struck a treaty with the impious are exaggerated: As 2 Chron. 20. 37. Because you, King Jehoshaphat, had a treaty with Ahaziah, the Lord has struck your works, and the ships were broken, and they could not go to Tarshish. 1 Kings 20. 34. & 42. Ahab, King of Israel, having struck a treaty with Benhadad, King of Syria, is forced to hear a sufficiently sharp threat from the Prophet: Because you have let go a man worthy of death from your hand, your soul shall be for his soul, and your people for his people. Isaiah 30. 2. Woe to you who walk to go down to Egypt, and have not asked my mouth, hoping for help in the strength of Pharaoh, and having trust in the shadow of Egypt. Verse 3. And the strength of Pharaoh shall be to your confusion, and the trust of the shadow of Egypt to your ignominy. Hosea 12. 1. Ephraim feeds on wind, and follows the heat: all day he multiplies lies and desolation: and he made a treaty with the Assyrians, and carried oil into Egypt.

But there are others who hold the affirmative, relying on the authority both of the Scriptures and of the examples of the holy Patriarchs and Kings, who did not hesitate to join treaties with impious kings and peoples. On both sides, therefore, reasons not entirely light are warring, which make the whole question concerning treaties more intricate. We shall therefore offer our examination of it: but in such a way that we do not wish it to be authoritative, or to yield to anyone to their prejudice: but rather that, having broken the ice, others may be able to navigate more safely, and to arrive more correctly at the port of unmoved certainty, and perhaps show more correct things to us who are hallucinating.

Latin:

INter quæstiones alias, quæ circa materiam afflictionum humanarum agitari solent, locum minimè postremum sortitur ista hæc: An Christianis & fidelibus licitum sit uti certis mediis ac remedijs, quibus imminentium, vel etiam jam incumbentium calamitatum vim, aut planè tollere, aut saltem quodammodo mitigare queant? Et sanè in Affirmantem rectissimè respondetur: sed generaliter. Quemadmodum enim inconceffis medijs, ut responsis Diabolorum, Pythonum, incantatorum, Magorum, veneficorum, nullo modo est utendum, si prohibente DEO Deut. 18. 11. ita quædam sunt media, quibus omninò uti licet: sic tamen ne illis nimiùm innitamur: aut ubi nos ea destituunt, de Gratia DEI, & salutari exitu desperemus. Ita bello & armis uti licet contra hostes vim injustè inferentes, & injustam vim depellere: nisi DOMINUS exprefsè illud vetet: quemadmodum Zepekias Rex Judaicus jubebatur non repugnare, sed hosti Babylonio se dedere. Sic licet etiam uti fœderibus & præsidiis auxiliaribus vicinorum & amicorum. Sic in morbis licet uti medicina: quæ est, ut ipsi fatentur medici, nihil aliud, quàm ipsa manus DEI. Sic Pestilentiæ tempore, quando aëris murationem præcipiunt Medici: eâ quoque uti licebit: Sic tamen, ne vel neceffaria vocationis munera, vel debita mutuæ charitatis officia interim à quoquam negligantur. Ante omnia verò, ingruentibus talibus sive privatis calamitatibus, ad percutientem nos DoMINUM, per seriam pœnitentiam est confugiendum. Quin publica etiam Pœnitentiæ exercitia: ut jejunia, preces, & supplicationes, exemplo veteris Ecclesiæ institui possunt, modò sine superstitione id fiat: hoc est, absit opinio meriti, cultus, & necessitatis absolutæ. Sic in aliis calamitatibus externis, appropriata media & remedia adhibere, minimè est prohibitum: modò debito ordine, ac fine illud fiat. Et hucusque quidem generalis plerorumque Theologorum procedit Responsio.

Sed Sanctorum etiam exempla, Consolationem in adversis subministrant: secundum illud Petri 1. cap. 5. v 9. Resistite Diabolo fortes in fide: scientes eandem passionem vestra etiam fraternitati, quæ in mundo est fieri: Nullus enim Sanctorum fuit unquam, quem non DOMINUS suum veluti dimensum, & κάλλιον μέρος, ex calice afflictionis haurire voluerit. Cum igitur tanta nube, tanta multitudine fidelium septi simus, cur nos tam venerandam societatem aspernemur? cur meliorém sortem hoc in mundo experamus! Argumentum practicum ab exemplo isto petitum monstravit suis discipulis Christus ipse, inquiens: Beati estis, cùm probra jecerint in vos, & dixerint omne malum Verbum adversum vos: Gaudete & exultate, quoniam merces vestra magna est in cœlis: Sic enim persecuti sunt olim Prophetas, qui fuerunt ante vos. Matth. 5. v. 11. & 12. Quemadmodum ergò Moses elegit opprobria, & ærumnas populi DEI, easque anteposuit cunctis Ægyptiorum thesauris: Sic & nos, pia æmulatione non recusemus adscribi pulcherrimæ huic & sanctissimæ societati electorum, sub Cruce hac in vitâ militantium.

OCTAVUM & postremum Consolationis fundamentum peti etiam potest ex testimonio bonæ conscientiæ: quòd non ut homicidæ, fur res, facinorosi, aut curiosi alienarum rerum,

Movetur autem hoc loco in specie Quæstio, quâ Theoriam, quâ praxin Theologica satis quidem intricata, sed cognitu maximè necessaria, An nimirùm ingruentibus gravioribus hostium nostrorum machinationibus & conatibus, quibus avertendis nos soli pares esse nequeamg, liceat fœdera jungere, sive Uniones inire cum impiis, & diversæ Religionis hominibus? Exempli gratiâ: Si Pontificij Lutheranis bellum inferre, & penitùs eos excindere velint, hi verò soli, tantis hostium viribus resistere haud valeant: vel etiam, si ejusdem confessionis socij, terra marique vim nobis inferant, libera commercia prohibeant, & promissa ac conventa utrinq; sanctè confirmata, temerè præter omne fas ac meritum violent: Nos verò soli istorum impetum reprimere haud valeamus; Quæritur: An tali casu Lutherani bonâ conscientiâ cum diversæ Religionis hominibus, utpotè cum Calvinianis fœdus inire, & sic vel Religionem Orthodoxam sartam tectam asserere: vel suam, suorumq; subditorum vitam fortunasq; ab injustâ vi ac tyrannide liberare, inq; pristinam libertatem vindicare possint & debeant? Cujus quæstionis decisio tantò est difficilior, & intricatior: quantò discrepantiores Theologorum sunt sententiæ: quorum plerique in Negantem descendunt, eò quòd DEUS ipse passim in Verbo suo, ne fœdus cum impiis jungatur, severissimè prohibuerit.

Et quidem pro defensione Negativæ primùm ea proferuntur testimonia, quæ impiorum fœdera fugienda esse, seriò monent: qualia sunt: Exod 23. 32. 34. 12. & 15. Cave, ne unquam cum habitatoribus terræ illius (qui teste vers. præcedente 11. erant Amorrhæi, Chananæi, Hethæi, Pherezæi, Hevæi, Jebusæi) jungas amicitias, quæ sint tibi in ruinam. Quod ipsum repetitur Deut. 7. 2. & 3. Judic. 2. 1. & 2. Pollicitus sum vobis, ut non facerem irritum meum pactum vobiscum in sempiternum: ità duntaxat, ut non feriretur fœdus cum habitatoribus terræ hujus. Deinde exagerantur pœnæ eorum, qui fœdus cum impiis percusserunt: Ut 2. Paral. 20. 37. Quia tu Rex Josaphat habuisti fœdus cum Ochozia, percussit DOMINUS opera tua, contritæq; sunt naves, nec potuerunt ire in Tharsis. 1. Reg. 20. 34. & 42. Achab Rex Israël per cusso fœdere cum Benhadad rege Syriæ, comminationem satis acrem à Propheta audire cogitur: Quia dimisisti virum dignum morte de manu tuâ, erit anima tua pro animâ ipsius, & populus tuus pro populo ipsius. Jesa. 30. 2. Væ vobis, qui ambulatis, ut descendatis in Ægyptum, & os meum non interrogastis, sperantes auxilium in fortitudine Pharaonis, & habentes fiduciam in umbrâ Ægypti. versu 3. Et erit vobis fortitudo Pharaonis in confusionem, & fiducia umbræ Ægypti in ignominiam. Osææ 12 1. Ephraim pascit ventum, & sequitur æstum: tota die mendacium & vastitatem multiplicat: & fœdus cum Assyriis iniit, & oleum in Ægyptum ferebat.

Sed sunt alij, qui Affirmativam tenent, freti autoritate tùm Scripturarum, tùm exemplorum Sanctorum Patriarcharum & Regum, qui cum Regibus ac populis impiis fœdera jungere non dubitarunt. Utrinque ergo militant rationes non planè leves, quæ totam Quæstionem de fœderibus intricatiorem reddunt. Nostram ergo de eâ ἐπίσκεψιν feremus quidem: sed ita, ut eam nolimus esse prætoriam, vel cuiquam in præjudicium cedere: sed potius, ut fractâ glacie alij tutiùs navigare, & ad portum immotæ certitudinis rectiùs appellere, & nobis fortasse hallucinantibus rectiora monstrare possint.


### Chapter Two. Concerning Christian Consolation, both general and special, in any…: Concerning the Treaties of Christians

CONCERNING THE TREATIES of Christians.

In the beginning, however, it does not come under the question at this point: What is to be thought of those treaties which peoples who are clearly impious and exiles from the Church are accustomed to strike among themselves: such as are the treaties of the Turks with the Tartars and Muscovites, etc. For whichever cause you look at, whether efficient, or material, or formal, or final, it is manifest that they are impious and blasphemous. For the persons themselves are an abomination to God: the matter itself of the treaties consists of robberies and unjust oppressions of others: the form which gives being to the thing is most insulting to God, since it consists of the invocation of fictitious gods, nay, of the Devil himself, whom historians report the Tartars worship as God. Finally, no end is seen other than the destruction of the Christian name, nay, of Christ Himself, and the total destruction of the Roman Empire. Therefore, that such treaties of the impious among themselves are by their nature impious and to be abhorred, can be a doubt to no pious person. Therefore, to treat of these at greater length is of no use.

But the question concerns Christian covenants: where three distinct members come under consideration: 1. with whom: 2. about what matters: 3. For what end covenants can and ought, or ought not, to be instituted.

Regarding the first member of the question, the subjects between whom covenants can be contracted are, on one side, the Orthodox; on the other side, others. And these again are twofold. For they are either impious and infidels κατ’ ἐξοχὴν so called, who indeed dwell outside the boundaries of the Church and are ignorant of the true GOD, and like those ancient Athenians worship an UNKNOWN GOD. Or they are Sectarians, Schismatics, or heretics, who are also themselves called infidels, not because they utterly abhor the faith of Christ, but because, having been imbued with false dogmas within the Church itself, they have made a sufficiently dangerous shipwreck of the faith. Hence, therefore, regarding the first member of the question, the κρινόμενον arises: Whether Christians, when some necessity urges, can with a good conscience enter into a covenant with peoples who are plainly impious and infidel, or the Orthodox with heretics and Schismatics?

The decision of this question is not rightly informed by a simple affirmative or negative: but there will be need of distinctions, which an accurate consideration of the remaining two members provides.

Regarding, therefore, the second member of the proposed Question: Concerning what matters, indeed, and to what end, may treaties be entered into by Christians with others, whether impious men or men of a different religion? We answer that, according to the diversity of the Objects, three distinct kinds of treaties can exist. The FIRST we can name an Ecclesiastical or Religious Treaty, which concerns the defense and propagation of the Church and of the purer religion, and is either offensive or defensive. It is offensive when, with combined forces, war is moved against the enemies of the Orthodox religion, to the end that heretics may be fully and plainly cut off: It is defensive when men of a different religion join their forces, to the sole end that if any violence is brought upon them by others, they may be able to repel and avert it so much the more conveniently. The SECOND kind of treaty is merely Political, regarding only public and common Peace: Where pacts, promises, and agreements have a place concerning the avoidance of injuries and offenses on both sides: concerning the protection of borders by land and sea: concerning the security of possessions, contracts, navigations, and journeys: concerning certain pensions, pastures, hunts, fishings, wood-cuttings, and similar duties of public peace, to be performed mutually to that end, so that public peace and the safety of citizens may be asserted and promoted on both sides. The THIRD kind of treaty is mixed, regarding partly the assertion of Religion and partly that of public peace. These things having been observed and premised, the Response to the proposed question must now be set forth distinctly according to the distinct kinds of treaties: lest confusion beget error and obscurity.

First, therefore, regarding Ecclesiastical Treaties, and those undertaken for the sake of Religion, we answer that it is by no means permitted for Christians or believers, and especially for the Orthodox, that for the sake of asserting or defending their Religion, they should in any way seek help from the impious or from men of a different Religion, or procure for themselves their love and favor to this end. The reason for this decision is this: Whatever GOD does not wish to be done, that it is not permitted to promise or to covenant. But GOD does not wish that heavenly truth be asserted or propagated by the impious or by men of a different religion. Therefore, it is not permitted to covenant with the impious and men of a different religion for this end. The truth and certainty of the assumption is evident from the whole of Holy Scripture, which clearly testifies that GOD has always claimed the defense of His word as so proper to Himself, that He has protected His Church only by Himself, either immediately or mediately through the Orthodox alone and brothers in Religion, and, beyond all hope and expectation of men, has very often miraculously defeated enemies through very few. Furthermore, it is evident from the most unhappy outcome which such treaties usually meet. Certainly, Judas Maccabaeus, as long as he relies on divine help and, trusting in the help of his brothers, fights most happily for worship and the true religion, emerges victorious. But after he is somewhat broken and dismayed by the power of the enemies, and doubts about obtaining victory thereafter against the persecutors of the Church, and joins treaties with the impious and infidels, and seeks auxiliary troops from the Romans, 1 Macc. 8. 1, he falls miserably in battle shortly after. The very same thing happened also to his brother Jonathan, when he was covenanting with the Romans and Spartans, 1 Macc. 12. 1 and 5. Thirdly, GOD Himself several times most severely rebukes such treaties entered into with the impious and men of a different religion for the sake of asserting Religion: as in Ezek. 16. 26 and the following three, the treaty of the Jews with the Egyptians, Assyrians, and Chaldeans, peoples impious and infidel, is named fornication against God, for the reason that the trust which was to be placed in GOD alone was transferred from Him to neighbors and confederates. Such an impious treaty was rebuked in Jehoshaphat, King of Judah, contracting a treaty with Ahab, a King of a different Religion: concerning whom God Himself says through the Prophet: You give help to the impious, and you are joined in friendship with those who hate the LORD: therefore you have deserved the wrath of the LORD. 2 Chron. 19. 2. Such was the treaty of Zedekiah with the Egyptians, which displeased the Lord so much that each of the confederates experienced the avenging hand of GOD: and all the hope which Zedekiah had conceived concerning the help of the Egyptians came to nothing, as the saying goes. Jer. 37. 6. Behold, says the Lord, the army of Pharaoh, which has gone out to you for help, will return to its own land to Egypt, and the Chaldeans will return and will fight against this city, and will take it, and will burn it with fire. How this was fulfilled in fact, one may read, 2 Kings 25. 6 and 7, Jer. 39. 5. Fourthly: Such treaties result in the insult of GOD, the ignominy of heavenly doctrine, the reproach of the Church, a snare to the Orthodox, and finally a scandal to the enemies themselves. For 1. the glory of GOD is obscured when the impious and men of a different Religion, called to help in this case, boast that our Church and Religion could not have subsisted or been kept safe and sound without their protection. 2. The praise of victory, due to GOD alone, is transferred to the confederates, and thus to men. 3. The impious and heretics are confirmed in their impiety and error. 4. The weaker among our own are offended, and are gradually inflamed toward the idolatry or heresy of the enemies. For when they are joined by federal love and strive to gratify one another, it can easily happen, indeed it happens very often, that as a sign of benevolence they become more indulgent and favorable to the heresy of their confederates, and thus at length wish that the same religion be among them. In this way, the Orthodox involve themselves in the guilt of others, and derive upon themselves a portion of the punishments decreed by GOD for the impious and the followers of a false religion, 6. and finally, by this pact, the Orthodox commit themselves and their Church to the most imminent danger. For because men of a different religion, in one and the same action, never look to one and the same end—but the Orthodox look to one, and the confederates, who are themselves mortal enemies of our religion, look to another—certainly such conspiracies easily and suddenly fall apart, and are changed into mutual and mortal enmities and assaults. Twice impious, therefore, are those who contract such leagues; more impious are those who trust in them.

But someone might say: If there is such a great abundance, force, and power of enemies attacking our Religion, that we are unequal in all ways to repelling them. What then is to be done in this case: Is it not more prudent to use the counsel and help of others, and of men of a different religion, than to permit the Church to be devastated and plundered by enemies? I answer 1. He who planted the Church, and has hitherto asserted and preserved the same safe against the furies of the world and the Devil: the same will not fail in his duty hereafter: Since the Religion and Doctrine, which is sought, is his, not ours. Indeed, he promised this very thing; namely, that he would so assert the doctrine of his word, that not even the gates of hell would prevail against it: Matt. 16. 18. Then, one must not sleep on both ears, as the saying goes: but the means must be seized which are shown in the Word of GOD: such as Serious Repentance, and Conversion to GOD, by which we render him propitious to us: but hostile to our enemies: Then prayers and supplications, by which, following the example of King Hezekiah, we cry to the LORD: This day is a day of trouble, and of rebuke, and of blasphemy: for the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth: O LORD of hosts, GOD of Israel, who dwellest between the Cherubim: thou art the GOD, even thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth, thou hast made heaven and earth: Incline thine ear, O LORD, and hear: open thine eyes, O LORD, and see, and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he hath sent to reproach the living GOD: Now therefore, O LORD, save us from his hand: that all the kingdoms of the earth may know, that thou art the LORD, even thou only, Isaiah 37. 3. 16. and following to 21. Judas Maccabeus used this means. and he departed a victor 1. Maccab. 4. 8. and following: Do not, he says, fear their multitude, and do not dread their attack: Remember how our Fathers were delivered and saved in the Red Sea: Let us therefore cry to heaven: and the LORD will have mercy on us, and will be mindful of the covenant made with our Fathers, and will crush this army before our face this day: and all nations shall know, that it is he alone who redeems and delivers Israel, etc. And from the preceding chapter 3. 18. It is easy to conclude many into the hand of a few: and there is no difference in the sight of the GOD of heaven, to deliver either by many, or by few: For victory in war is not in the multitude of an army, but strength is from heaven. And from book 2. Maccab. chap. 8. 18. They indeed trust in arms, and at the same time in audacity: but we trust in the Almighty LORD, who can destroy both those coming against us, and the whole world, with one nod.

Latin:

DE FOEDERIBUS Christianorum.

INitiò autem sub Quæstionem hoc loco non venit: Quid sentiendum sit de illis fœderibus, quæ populi planè, impij & extorres ab Ecclesiâ, inter se ferire solent: qualia sunt fœdera Turcarum cum Tartaris & Moschovitis &c. Namquamcunque causam, sive efficientem, sive materialem, sive formalem, sive finale spectes, manifestum sit, ea esse impia, & blasphema. Nam ipsæ personæ DEO sunt abominatio: materia ipsa fœderum constat latrocinijs, & injustis oppressionibus aliorum: Forma quæ dat esse rei maximè est contumeliosa in DEUM, quippe quæ constat invocatione Deorum fictitiorum, imò ipsius Diaboli, quem Tartaros pro DEO colere, historici referunt. Finis denique spectatur nullus alius, quàm excidium Christiani nominis, imò ipsius Chri sti, & totius imperij Romani πανολεθρία. Quin ergo naturâ suâ hujusmodi fœdera impiorum inter se sint impia, & abominanda, nemini pio potest esse dubium. De his ergo, ut prolixiùs agamus, nihil attinet.

Verùm de Christianorū fœderibus est quæstio: ubi tria distincta membra sub considerationem veniunt: 1. cum quibus: 2. de quibus rebus: 3. Quo fine fœdera institui possint & debeant, vel non debeant.

Quoad primū quæsiti mēbrū,subjecta,inter quæ fœdera cō trahi possunt, sunt ex unâ parte Orthodoxi:ex altera parte alij. Et hi rursῦ sunt duplices.vel enim sūt impij&infideles κατ’ ἐξοχὴν sic dicti, qui nimirùm extra Ecclesiæ pomeria versantur, & verum DEUM ignorant, cumque veteribus illis Atheniensibus IGNOTHM DEUM colunt. Vel sunt Sectarij, Schismatici, aut hæretici, qui & ipsi infideles dicuntur,non quòd à fide Christi planè abhorreant, sed quod intta ipsam Ecclesiam falsis dogmatis imbuti, periculosum satis fidei naufragium fecerunt. Hinc ergo quoad Primum Quæstionis membrum oritur κρινόμενον, An vel Christiani cum populis planè impiis ac infidelibus: vel Orthodoxi cum hæreticis ac Schismaticis,urgente necessitate aliquâ, fœdus bonâ conscientiâ inire possint?

Cujus Quæstionis decisio, simplici neque affirmativâ, neq; negativâ rectè informatur: sed distinctionibus opus fuerit, quas reliquorum duorum membrorum accurata consideratio subministrat.

Quoad secundum ergo Quaestionis propositae membrum: De quibus nimirum rebus, & quo fine foedera a Christianis cum aliis vel impiis, vel diversae religionis hominibus, iniri possint? Respondemus secundum diversitatem Objectorum, tria distincta Foederum genera dari posse. PRIMUM nominare possumus Foedus Ecclesiasticum sive Religionis, quod Ecclesiae & Religionis purioris defensionem & propagationem concernit, & est vel offensivum, vel defensivum. Offensivum est, quando conjunctis viribus bellum movetur in hostes religionis Orthodoxae, eo fine, ut haeretici plene ac plane exscindantur: Defensivum est, quando diversae religionis homines vires suas conjungunt, eo tantum fine, ut si vis aliqua ipsis ab aliis inferatur, tanto commodius propulsare eam, & avertere queant. ALTERUM genus foederum est mere Politicum, respiciens tantum Pacem publicam & communem: Ubi locum habent pacta promissa & conventa de vitandis utrinque injuriis & offensionibus: de tuendis finibus terra marique: de securitate possessionum, contractuum, navigationum, itinerum: de certis pensionibus, pascuis, venationibus, piscationibus, lignationibus, & similibus officiis pacis publicae, eo fine invicem praestandis, ut pax publica, & civium incolumitas utrinque asseratur, & promoveatur. TERTIUM genus foederum est mixtum, partim Religionis, partim pacis publicae assertionem respiciens. His observatis & praemissis, Responsio jam ad propositam quaestionem secundum distincta foederum genera, distincte etiam expediri debet: ne confusio errorem, & obscuritatem pariat.

Primum ergo Quoad Foedera Ecclesiastica, & Religionis causa suscepta, Respondemus, Christianis sive fidelibus, ac cumprimis Orthodoxis nullatenus licere, ut Religionis suae afferendae aut defendendae gratia, vel ab impiis, vel a diversae Religionis hominibus quovis modo auxilium petant, vel eorum amorem, ac favorem hoc fine sibi concilient. Ratio decisionis haec est: Quiquid DEUS fieri non vult: illud promittere aut pacisci non licet. Atqui DEUS non vult, ut vel ab impiis, vel a diversae religionis hominibus veritas coelestis asseratur, aut propagetur. Ergo nec, hoc fine cum impiis & diversae religionis hominibus pacisci licet. Assumtionis veritas & certitudo patet ex universa Scriptura sacra, quae liquido testatur, DEUM defensionem verbi sui, sibi ita propriam vendicasse semper, ut non nisi ipse solus vel immediate, vel mediate per solos orthodoxos ac in Religione fratres, Ecclesiam suam tutatus sit, & praeter omnem spem ac opinionem hominum, per paucissimos saepius miraculose hostes devicerit. Deinde patet illud ex infelicissimo eventu, quem ejusmodi foedera plerumque fortiuntur. Certe Judas Machabaeus, quamdiu nititur auxilio divino, & fretus auxilio fratrum, pro cultu & religione vera felicissime pugnat, & victor evadit. Postquam autem hostium potentia nonnihil fractus & consternatus, de victoria deinceps contra persecutores Ecclesiae obtinenda dubitat, & cum impiis ac infidelibus foedera jungit, ac a Romanis, 1. Mach. 8. 1. auxiliares copias quaerit, paulo post misere in praelio occumbit. Quod ipsum accidit etiam fratri ejus Jonathae, cum Romanis, & Spartanispaciscenti, 1. Mach. 12. 1. & 5. Tertio DEUS ipse hujusmodi foedera, Religionis afferendae causa, cum impiis, & diversae religionis hominibus inita, severissime per Prophetas aliquoties reprehendit: ut Jezech. 16. 26. & sequentibus tribus, foedus Judaeorum cum Aegyptiis, Assyriis, & Chaldaeis, populis impiis & infidelibus initu, nominatur fornicatio contra Deum, eo quod fiducia, quae in solum DEUM collocanda erat, in vicinos & confoederatos, ab illis transferebatur. Tale foedus impium reprehendebatur in Josaphato Rege Juda foedo contrahente cum diversae Religionis Rege Achabo: de quo Deus ipse per Prophetam: Impio praebes auxilium, & his, qui oderunt DOMINUM, amicitia jungeris: iccirco iram DOMINI promeristi. 2. Par. 19. 2. Tale erat foedus Zedechiae cum Aegyptiis, quod usque adeo displicuit Domino, ut uterque confoederatorum manum DEI vindicem expertus: & spes omnis quam de Aegyptiorum auxiliis Zedechias conceperat, in spongiam, quod dicitur, incubuerit. Jer. 37. 6. Ecce dicit Dominus, exercitus Pharaonis, qui egressus est vobis in auxilium, revertetur in terram suam in Aegyptum, & revertentur Chaldaei, & bellabunt contra civitatem hanc, & capient eam, & succendent eam igni. Quod quomodo ipso facto impletum fuerit, legere licet, 2. Reg. 25. 6. & 7. Jer. 39. 5. Quarto: Ejusmodi foedera cedunt in contumeliam DEI ignominiam doctrinae coelestis: opprobrium Ecclesiae: laqueum Orthodoxis scandalum denique ipsis hostibus. Nam 1. obscuratur gloria DEI, quando impij, & diversae Religionis homines, hoc casu in auxilium vocati, gloriantur, Ecclesiam & Religionem nostram non potuisse subsistere, aut sartam tecta conservari, sine ipsorum praesidio. 2. Laus victoriae soli DEO debita, transfertur in confoederatos, & sic in homines. 3. Confirmantur impij & haeretici in sua impietate & errore. 4. Offenduntur infirmiores ex nostris, & ad hostium sive idololatriam, sive haeresin paulatim inflammantur. Quando enim amore foederali conjuncti, sibi mutuo gratificari student, facile fieri potest, imo fit saepissime; ut in signu benevolentiae, confoederatorum haeresi indices reddantur aequiores, faventioresque, & sic tandem eandem inter ipsos religione esse velint. 5. Involvunt se hoc pacto Orthodoxi alieno reatu, & poenarum impiis ac falsae religionis asseclis a DEO decretarum partem, in se derivant, 6.& postremo, committuntur hoc pacto Orthodoxi se, suamque Ecclesiam praesentissimo periculo. Quia enim diversae religionis homines, in una eademque actione, finem unu eundemque nunquam respiciunt: sed alium Orthodoxi, alium confoederati, qui & ipsi nostrae religionis hostes sunt capitales: certe ejusmodi conspirationes facile ac subito dissiliut, inque inimicitias & oppugnationes mutuas & capitales mutantur. Bis ergo impij sunt, qui talia foedera contrahunt: magis impij, qui illis confidunt.

Sed dicat aliquis: Si hostium, nostram Religionem oppugnantium, tanta sit copia, vis & potentia, ut illis propulsandis modis omnibus simus impares. Quid nam hoc casu faciendu: Annon consultius, aliorum, & diversæ religionis hominum consilio, & auxilio uti, quàm Ecclesiam hostibus devastandam, diripiendamq́; permittere? Respondeo 1. Qui Ecclesiam plantavit, eandemque hactenus contra furores mundi & Diaboli tutam asseruit, & conservavit: idem deinceps quoque suo officio non deerit : Siquidem Religio & Doctrina, quæ petitur, ipsius est, non nostra est. Quin hoc ipsum promisit; Se nimirùm ita doctrinam verbi sui asserturum, ut ne portæ quidem inferorum adversus eam sint prævalituræ: Matth. 16. 18. Deinde non in utramque, quod dicitur, aurem indormiendum: sed media arripienda ea, quæ in Verbo DEI mõstrãtur: qualia sunt Seria Pœnitentia, & Conversio ad DEUM, qua ipsum nobis reddimus propitium: hostibus autem nostris inimicum: Deinde preces & supplicationes, quibus exemplo regis Ezechiæ, clamemus ad DOMINUM: Dies tribulationis & correptionis, & blasphemiæ dies hæc: quia venerunt filijusq́; ad partum, & virtus non est pariendi: DOMINE exercituum, DEUS Israel qui sedes super Cherubim: tu es DEUS solus omniũ regnorum terræ, tu fecisti cœlum & terram: Inclina Domine aurem tuam, & audi: aperi DOMINE oculos tuos, & vide, & audi omnia verba Senacherib, quæ misit ad blasphemandum DEUM viventem: Nunc ergo DOMINE salva nos de manu ejus: & cognoscant omnia regna terræ, quia tu es Dominus solus, Jesaiæ 37. 3. 16. & sequentibus ad 21. usq́;. Hoc medio usus est Judas Machabæus. & victor abiit 1. Macchab. 4. 8. & sequentibus: Nolite inqui ens, timere multitudinem eorum, & impetum eorũ ne formidetis: Mementote, quomodo liberati, & salvati sint Patres nostri in mari rubro: Clamemus ergo in cœlum: & miserebitur nostri DOMINUS, & memor erit fœderis cum Patribus nostris initi, & cõteret exercitum istum ante faciem nostram hodie: & scient omnes gentes, quòd ipse solus est, qui redimat, & liberet Israel &c. Et ex capite præced 3 18. Facile est concludi multos in manu paucorum: & non est differentia in conspectu DEI cœli, liberare vel in multis, vel in paucis : Quoniam non in multitudine exercitus victoria belli, sed de cœlo est fortitudo nostra. Et ex lib. 2. Macchab. cap. 8. 18. Illi quidem armis confidunt, simul & audacia: nos autẽ in Omnipotente DOMINO, qui potest & venientes adversum nos, & universum mundum & uno nutu delere, confidimus.


### Chapter Two. Concerning Christian Consolation, both general and special, in any…: Concerning the Treaties of Christians (continued)

If such faith, hope, and trust were also firm in us, and we did not trust more in men than in GOD, we would certainly never commit the cause of the Church and Religion to be defended by those who are manifestly impious, or by men of a different religion. The third means, with the two preceding ones having been premised, is entirely left to us, that if necessity itself demands it, either alone, or with brothers in Religion called upon, without foreign help, we may fight bravely and with an intrepid spirit with joined forces against those who, through force and tyranny, attempt to snatch from us the liberty of Religion, against all laws, sacred and profane, which we have acquired by the grace of God through honest means, and have hitherto asserted by legitimate means. In which case it would not be illicit to implore the help of brothers. Where indeed those who are of the same mind as our Religion will never show themselves difficult: For to consider the dangers of brothers as one's own is demanded by brotherly duty, and the rule of Charity, expressed by Christ himself: What you wish that men should do to you, do the same to them. Such was the covenant of Joab with his brother Abishai: 2. Sam. 10. 11 & 12. If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt be an help to me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will come and help thee. Be of good courage, and let us fight for our people, and for the cities of our GOD: and the LORD do that which seemeth him good. And such mutual help of brothers is so pleasing to GOD, that he not only accuses the Ephraimites of treachery, but also permits them to be slaughtered, because they had deserted Jephthah fighting against the Ammonites, Judg. 12. 2. 4. and following. Thus the men of Jabesh are punished with destruction, because they had deserted Israel in such a covenant against the Benjamites. Judg. 21. 8. & 10. Fourthly, Stratagems in this case (provided it be done without violation of pacts, if any have intervened) are not prohibited: as if by chance enemies can be set against each other by some honest reason, and divided into mutual battles, that should not be omitted: For thus either both, or certainly one party can be more easily conquered and overcome. For such Stratagems are nothing other than means, which God himself shows for the benefit of his Church, and are a part of civil prudence.

Now indeed, Christian faith and political Prudence do not destroy each other, much less do they harm the Conscience of the faithful. But there is need of great caution and circumspection in such alliances, entered into between brothers, and those of the same mind in Religion. 1. Indeed, that a brother should not promise help and defense to a brother too generally, and without any exception in any cases whatsoever: but the condition of just, and especially most necessary wars, should be expressed and kept. 2. That it should not be done with blind impulse and rashly: but that all things should be done with sound and shared counsel. For which matter, there is need of both Theological and Civil prudence. 3. That in those alliances, contracted between brothers and associates in Religion, we should not trust, but hope for and seek help from the LORD alone, no less than if no external defenses at all were prepared for us. 4. That we should only remain within defensive terms, and not out of curiosity and rashness move an unnecessary war against the enemies of our religion, even the most hostile ones. 5. That alliances entered into with even our own brothers should be strengthened on both sides by certain and just conditions, so that afterwards (which happens very often) we need not fear new danger and inconvenience from the mutability and inconstancy of the confederates. Looking to which, the never sufficiently praised Elector of Saxony, FREDERICK, surnamed the Wise, when solicited by other Princes, associates and brothers in Religion, to join their alliances, is read to have replied: Treaties are indeed good, but woe to those who keep them: implying that such is often the infirmity of the pious, such the variety, mutability, and dissimilarity of characters, wills, and counsels, that for the most part even the best Union and confederation degenerates into a lion's society: the other party being either deserted beyond expectation, or entangled in many difficulties, or plainly oppressed. 6. And finally: That under no pretext should any place be left for the Impious, and those addicted to a different Religion, in this first kind of treaties. Otherwise, no other end and Catastrophe of various parties and confederations is to be expected than that which is described quite graphically under the confederation of the Jews with the Egyptians: Isaiah 31, from verse 1 to 4: Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help, and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD! Yet he also is wise, and will bring evil, and will not call back his words: but will arise against the house of the evildoers, and against the help of them that work iniquity. Now the Egyptians are men, and not GOD; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. And when the LORD shall stretch out his hand, both he that helpeth shall fall, and he that is holpen shall fall down, and they all shall fail together. But let these things suffice concerning this first kind of treaties.

of navigation, of travel, and of similar things pertaining to the preservation of civil society, contracted, are nothing other than the nerves and bonds of public Peace. Therefore, the Apostle approves even treaties of this kind by his own reckoning: so that he does not even wish evil to be returned for evil to our enemies, namely by private daring and whim: or by some blind impulse, or foolish rashness, in the same chapter 12.17. To which also pertains the admonition of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 12.14. Follow peace with all men. Nor indeed does this first proof lack nerve and evidence because the Apostles wrote these things to private individuals. For it is certain that the precepts and rules of Christian Charity pertain not only to certain specific individuals, but to the whole race of the faithful or Christians. And indeed the Apostle wishes this pursuit of Peace towards all to be most highly commended to Christians, so that they may design nothing whatsoever against it: which that double προσδιορισμὸς proves: εἰ δυνατὸν, if it be possible, and if you can obtain peace from the infidels. 2. τὸ ἐξ ὑμῶν As much as lies in you.

Next, the examples of the Saints confirm our Affirmative, who thus, with necessity urging, struck treaties with infidels and men of a different Religion. Abraham certainly, that father of the faithful, entered into a treaty with the Amorite or Canaanite, namely with Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner against the Eastern Kings, or Persians, who had waged war on the Sodomites and had carried off Lot with his family captive. Gen. 14.13. Although indeed there are not lacking, especially among more recent interpreters, those who refuse to add their reckoning to those treaties contracted with infidels, and contend that the Example of Abraham has nothing to do with the matter, for the reason that those men, or Princes of the Sodomites, Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner, had first become believers and had joined themselves to the religion of Abraham before they were admitted into the society of the treaty: Yet what those men say, they do not prove, nor will they ever prove from sacred or profane histories: But rather the circumstances of the Mosaic text hint not obscurely that Abraham was asked and invited by the inhabitants of that place, infidel men, to the pact of a treaty: to which Abraham, notwithstanding the diversity of Religion, consented, partly lest he himself also be held for an enemy, partly indeed that he might so much the more easily liberate Lot, who had already been led away captive, who otherwise with his own household would not suffice alone to overthrow the tyranny of the Eastern kings. But if it were even granted that which they except in this place, there are nevertheless many far more evident examples of this matter in readiness.

We said above that the OTHER Kind of treaties is merely Political, and in the place of an Object looks only to public peace and civil tranquility. Concerning this it is asked: Can Christians, with necessity so urging, whether with the impious and plainly infidels, or with men of a different Religion, enter into Treaties of Peace (not of Religion, but of public and civil matters) with a safe Conscience? We, relying on the authority of both the Scriptures and the Holy Patriarchs and Kings, answer in the affirmative: and we prove it thus:

1. Whatever it is permitted to perform with a safe Conscience, and without the loss of Religion: that certainly it is also permitted to covenant by means of a treaty transaction. But the faithful ought to perform and cultivate public and common peace with all men: and it is the duty of pious Magistrates above all to assert the rights and privileges of subjects in such a way that Civil society, and what are the bonds and nerves of this, contracts, navigations, commerce, and other things of that kind, can be exercised freely and safely. Therefore, this very thing, even by means of a treaty transaction, it is permitted to covenant with all men.

I prove the assumption from chapter 12.18 to the Romans: If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. The Roman faithful certainly lived among the Gentiles at the time of the Apostle Paul: This notwithstanding, the Apostle wishes peace to be cultivated with these also. Now treaties of this kind concerning the protection of borders by land and sea, concerning the security of possessions, of contracts,

The same Abraham certainly, dwelling in Palestine and greatly increased in wealth, when with Abimelech, king of the Gerarites, a man certainly infidel, and with Phicol the commander-in-chief, or, as others would have it, the Chancellor of the same king, he made a covenant, with an oath interposed, that they would not harm one another. The end, therefore, of this covenant was common and public peace. Gen. 21. 22. 27 & 32.
