Ordines autê Evangelicos intelligo eos, qui immediate sub jacent Romano Imperio, & ejus sunt certa membra: ita ut cùm istorum, quàm Pontificiorũ voto ac consensu, omnia deliberari, & decerni in Imperio debeant. Aliud judicium ferendum de illis, qui Imperatori subsunt non tantùm quà Imperator : sed & ut Domino hæreditario: de quo alibi. David certè non Israelitis modò in Religione ὁμοψήφοις sed & Philistæis, Moabitis, Ammonitis, Syris, Damascenis, diversissimarum religionum populis imperasse, & in regno quidem Juda purioris religionis cultum adseruisse : reliquos verò populos ad eandé amplexandam bello armisq; coegisse, vel in ipsorũ conscientias quicquam sibi dominij arrogaffe nuspiam legitur. 2. Sam. 8. 1. & sequentibus. Salomon Regum omnium sapientissimus, & potentissimus regnasse legitur à flumine terræ Philistæorum, usq; ad terminum Ægypti: in horum autem fidem & religionem vi armisq; sæviisse, vel hoc nomine fœdera & pacta cum illis inita rupisse, nuspiam legitur: Quin Scriptura potius testis est, ipsum contentum tributis & pensionibus, quas in Signum subjectionis numerare cogebantur, libertatem ipsis suæ Religionis exercendæ concessisse. 1. Reg. 4. 21. Sic Nabuchodonosor Rex & Monarcha primus Babylonius, conversus ad DEUM Israelis, non statim omnes subjectas provincias, ad eam fidẽ externâ vi adegit : sed hoc proclamari curavit, ut ne cuipiam fas esset, DEUM Israelis blasphemiâ afficere. Sic enim habebat Edicti formula: A me positum est hoc decretum, ut omnis populus, tribus & lingua, quæcunq; locuta fuerit blasphemiã cõtra Deum Sidrach, Mefach, & Abednago, dispereat, & domꝰ ej9 vastetur. Qui tamẽ Zelo cõtra blasphemos, apud Põtificios, Judæos in suis ditionib6, Romæ præsertim ferentes, planè exulat. Cyr9 prim9 Persarũ Monarcha, Judæis libertatem suæ exercendæ religionis permisit, licet ipse Judæorum fidei non esset addictus Esdræ. 1. 2. & sequentib. Quam permissionem ratam etiam habuit Rex Persarum Darius: ita, ut licèt Artaxerxes quorundam aulicorum consiliis circumventus, de supprimendâ Judæorum religione, mandatum promulgasset, Esdræ. 4. 21. Darius tamen de prima illâ Sanctione Cyri edoctus, ratam omninò eam haberi voluerit gravissima adjecta comminatione hâc: Quicunq; legem hanc mutaverit, tollatur lignum de domo ejus, & erigatur, & configatur in eo, domus autem ipsius publicetur: Esdræ. 6. 6. & 11. Regum & Monarcharum istorum religione ductus Christianissimus Imperator MAXIMILIANUS II. præclarè æmulatus est, ita ut nonnullis flabellis, ipsum ad profundendum Lutheranum sanguinem instigantibus, magno animo aliquando responderet: Nullum peccatum gravius est, quàm Conscientiis dominari velle: DEO enim ipsi se opponunt, qui Conscientiis in causâ Religionis dominari volunt. Crato in orat. fun.

IV. Imperatorem à juramento confœderatis cujuscunque Religionis dato, fideliter servando, nemo mortalium, ne quidem Pontifex solvere potest: quin illud religiosè præstare ac servare tenetur. Neque enim verisimile est, Imperatorem de rebus impiis, atq; naturâ suâ illicitis, fidem cuiq; suam adstringere: Ubi Absolutio talis locum haberet. Contendunt quidem Monachi Lojolani, Pontificem posse tum Imperatorem, tùm reliquos Imperij Ordines Pontificios, à fidelitatis Juramento, Hæretico dato, plenissimè absolvere, ut nulla prorsus perjurij pœna ipsos maneat.

Hoccine verò non dico Theologicum, sed humanum saltem est dictum, factum, aut cogitatum? Quid enim? Anne potestas solventium clavium, eum in finem concessa Ecclesiæ, ut earum usu, Juramentum legitimè præstitum fiat elusorium? ut obligatio mutua, cum religiosa diviniNuminis attestatione pacta & confirmata (quam DEUS in verbo suo indissolubilem esse voluit) reddatur vana & irrita? Increpet te DEUS Satan, & sub pedibus suis conterat cito: Fiat, fiat. Materia sive Objectum absolutionis Evangelicæ proprium, non est Fides in politicis vel DEO, vel hominibus debita: quam nulla clavis sive in Cœlo, sive in terrâ, solvere aut tollere potest: Sed tantùm Peccatorum, quibus contrà DEI præcepta delinquimus, reatus. Quid? quòd vis absolvtoria non dependet vel â Magicâ, quâdam, sive arcanâ verborum, quæ pronunciantur, virtute: vel à dignitate aut intentione personæ vel absolventis, vel absolvendæ: sed tantùm à voluntate atq; ordinatione ejus, qui Clavis istius potestate Ecclesiarn instruxit: CHRISTI nimirùm Servatoris, cui cum perfidia atque perjurio haud magis convenit, quàm Luci cum tenebris, aut veritati cum mendacio. Et quàm vana, frivola, atque nugatoria talis sit hoc casu Pontificia Absolutio, vel solus ille tragicus exitus Vladislai Hungariæ & Poloniæ Regis, satis luculenter comprobat & evincit. Ubi tanta vis fuit Pontificiæ hujus Absolutionis, ut Rex ipse miserabiliter trucidatus: Cardinalis Cæsarinus in fugâ cæsus: Christianorum denique triginta millia perierint: teste Jovio in Amurathe II. Væ ergò illis Imperatoribus ac Principibus Catholicis, qui hac in parte à Pontifice sibi imponi patiuntur. Contrà verò perpetuis laudibus celebranda eorum magnanimitas, fides & Constantia, qui ad frangendam pactionem fœderalem, cum Lutheranis religiosè semel decretam & confirmatam, nullis verborum ac rationum lenociniis se moveri passi sunt. Inter quos primas facilè tenet CAROLUS V. Imperator invictissimus, qui cùm à quibusdam Pontificiis flabellis ac furiis, in Comitiis Wormatiensibus instigaretur, ut ne fidem LUTHERO datam servaret, propterea quôd secundum decretum Concilij Constantiensis, Hæretico non sit servanda fides; animosè respondit: Fidem rerum promissarum, & toto mundo exulet, apud Imperatorem tamen consistere oportere. Guliel. Zenocartis in vitâ Caroli. Quam heroicam animi magnitudinem æmulatus est FERDINANDUS Imp. qui usque aded Pacificationis cum Lutheranis semel confirmatæ studiosus & observans fuisse legitur: ut ante obitum singulari perfusus lætitia, sæpiùs in hæc verba erumperet: Inter summa, quæ DEUS in gubernatione Imperij mihi concessit, PRIMUM atque MAXIMUM verò animi judicio hoc duco, quòd ad sedandas discordias publicas animum adjeci, & Tolerantiæ in Religione Formulam DEUS mihi in mentem dedit. Vide Epistolam præliminarem Cratonis à Crafftheim, in histor. Bohem. Dubravij: Quem eundem pium generosissimumque animum hodieque esse Invictissimo Imp. Matthiæ nullatenus dubitamus: DEUM venerati supplices, ut majores & prædecessores suos nùquàm satis laudatos egregiè æmulatus, aliorum Papæ mancipiorum sive Esawitarum, sive insulatorum quorundam vafris consiliis, in transversum se abripi nunquàm patiatur.

Ex præmissis istis hypothesibus, pro decisivâ sententiâ propositæ quæstionis, evidenter & irrefragabiliter colligimus: 1. Non nos, sed Pontificios perfidiæ, & fractæ pacis culpam sustinere. 2. Causam violati fœderis Passaviensis nullam esse aliam, quàm dominandi libidinem, quam Antichristus Romanus sibi arrogat, & postliminiò quasi in Germaniâ stabilire rursum & confirmare studet. 3. Tyrannidem in Ordines Evangelicos contrà jura omnia sacra & profana exerceri ab illis sive Principibus, sive Episcopis Pontificiis, qui eos denuò jugo Idolomaniæ Pontificiæ, & quidem vi, armisque implicare satagunt. 4. Controverti hodie inter Ordines Evangelicos, & Pontificios, primò ac principaliter propter Religionem : sed ex horum quidem parte pro asserendo Dominatu Pontificis Romani : dum per indirectum quasi Romanenses Jus sibi aliquod & imperium in Lutheranorum privilegia, dignitates & Regalia, uti vocant, Ecclesiastica, sibi arrogant : hoc est, Jurisdictionem Episcopalem Romanam in nostras Ecclesias exercere student: Ex nostra verò parte pugnari itidem non pro Religione in se & per se considerata : sed pro ea Libertate, quam circa Religionis exercitium, honestis mediis, & interventu sacratissimarum sanctionum fœderalium obtinuimus: Item pro asserenda pace publica & civili, quam Romanenses per vim ac Tyrannidem nobis eripere, & nos in tristissimam servitutem redigere conantur. Licet Ergo Religionis respectus aliquis sub istis turbis omninò ab utraq; parte spectetur: non tamen ille est simplex & absolutus, sed accidentalis.

Quibus ita constitutis Quæstio Principalis eò redit: Utrum Lutherani Pontificiis fœdera, pacta & conventa, religioso etiam Juramento confirmata temere & præter jus ac æquum frangentibus, & vi ac armis omnia tentantibus, resistere, & pro asserenda libertate, in quam justo titulo venerunt, quamq; vi pactorum fœderalium possident, pugnare, & auxiliares manus, interventu unionis legitimæ, à diversæ Religionis hominibus petere, sibiq; jungere bonâ conscientiâ possint? Ubi Affirmatè Respondeo, iisdem fretus rationibus & argumentis, quæ jam suprà ex Scripturis Sacris produximus, ubi de secundo Fœderum genere disseruimus. Nam utrobique una eademque est ratio, unus idemque finis & scopus: Una ergo utrobique etiam Veritas. Proinde licèt cum diversæ Religionis hominibus, in casu Religionis simplici & absoluto, fœdera jungere & pacisci in sacris prohibitum sit: siquidem Religionis fœdus cum talibus iniri non potest, nisi fidei, sive Religionis concordia præcedat, quæ est vinculum & fundamentum religiosi fœderis. Jam verò in Religionis negocio nulla potest esse conventio Christi cum Belial: nulla pars fideli & infideli: nulla participatio justitiæ cum injustitia: nulla societas luci ad tenebras, 2. Cor. 6. 15. ac proinde fraternitatis dextera rectè hactenùs Calvinianis, hoc casu, negata sit, ac deinceps negari debeat: nihil tamen obstat, quò minùs in civilibus, libertatem, jura, privilegia, vitam, fortunasq; nostras concernentibus, Humanitatis dextras illis porrigamus, & vicissim ab ipsis accipiamus: quas neque B. LUTHERUM Zwinglio, neque Orthodoxos Bezæ Mompelgarti negasse novimus.

Cæterùm ne modus hac in parte vel in excessu, vel in defectu excedatur, sequentes cautiones probè observandæ sunt :

grustans, inutile, & puriori Religioni multis modis noxium.

2. Nihil quicquam per seditionem aut conspirationem contra Imperatorem, quippe summum Ordinarium Magistratum, vel decernatur, vel suscipiatur.

3. Mala impendentia, & consilia callida & crudelia, vel Imperatori, vel aliis Ordinibus Imperij, per Esawitas & Pontificis flabella, insidiosè suggesta, precibus ad DEUM, seriâ vitæ emendatione, supplicationibus humillimis, obsecrationibus & admonitionibus, consiliisq; sanioribus, neque cædem, neque sanguinem spirantibus, quantum fieri potest, avertantur.

4. Si frustrà, & irrito conatu tententur omnia, & vis nobis, nostrisq; inferatur, utiq; vim vi repellere licebit, in subsidium etiam vocatis confœderatis, sed ut intra terminos defensivos nos contineamus; neque belli successu efferamur, eoq; ad Tyrannidem aut crudelitatem ullam abutamur.

5. Conditiones in Transactione Passaviensi, aliisque Recessibus Imperij, unanimi Ordinum omnium consensu approbatæ & confirmatæ, nullo pacto à nobis (si fieri queat) violentur: sed ita gerantur omnia, ut non Regionem quæ sivisse, sed justitiam, pacem publicam, libertatem asseruisse, etiam hostibus ipsis videri queamus: idque unicum spectasse, ut sit pax in turribus, & salus in palatiis nostris.

6. Fiducia planè nulla in ejusmodi fœdera collocetur, sed habeantur tantùm pro mediis, concessiis, per quæ solus DEUS, non verò externa munitio nos salvare ac tueri queat.

7. Absit inter confœderatos ipsos omnis πλεονεξία, dolus, ambitio, infidelitas, & vitia consimilia: quorum si unum aut plura adsint, mox ipsa fœdera sua sponte dissilient, & infelicem sortientur exitum.

8. Inter ipsas bellorum (si ita necessitas ferat) expeditiones, non quidem offensivas, sed defensivas, semper cogitetur de mediis & consiliis pacis, quibus hostes mitigari, nobisque reconciliari queant.

9. Tandem si necesse sit, pugnetur fortiter, & piis precibus eventus DEO soli commendetur, qui nostra est victoria, & tam potest salvare per paucos, quàm per multos, 1. Sam 14. 6. adhibitâ tamen circumspectione & prudentiâ debitâ, ne nostra consilia hosti citiùs, quàm nobis ipsis innotescant: Unde omnia rerum gerendarum momenta impediuntur. Nam, ut August. inquit, lib. 6. quæstionum super Josuam, quæst. 10. cùm quis justum bellum susceperit, utrum apertâ pugnâ, an insidiis vincat, ad justitiam nihil interest, cùm DEUS ipse etiam insidias quandoque præcepisse legatur, ut in Josua videre est c. 8. Ubi locum habet tritum adagium: ὅπω μὴ ἡ λέαινα ἰσχύει, παρέςχειν τὴν ἀλώπεκα. Verùm de his & similibus præceptis viderint Politici.

Et haec de foederibus, tanquam medio, quo in publicis calamitatibus uti licet, dixisse sufficiat. Superest alterum, nempe BELLUM ipsum, quod num pro medio ad reprimendas tribulationes utendum sit, & quomodo, paucis dispiciemus.


### Chapter Two. Concerning Christian Consolation, both general and special, in any…: Of War

OF WAR.

About to speak of War, we shall consider only those things which pertain to the Schools of Theologians: committing the rest to Politicians.

Since war, whether said so antiphrastically, or rather so called from beasts [belluis], has both a foul origin of its notion, and presents such a horrendous appearance of things that at its mere mention the pious shudder: it will certainly be worth knowing and necessary [to determine] what the pious ought to think about war.

Now, however, we shall not concern ourselves with that ancient Church of the Jews: Was it permitted for them to handle arms and wage wars? For sacred history confirms the affirmative: And the examples of the Saints, which carry the appearance of law, and the commands of GOD also, are more illustrious in the Old Testament than can be called into doubt by anyone. But this is the Question: Is it permitted for the Evangelical people in any way to rage with arms and to invade other men in war?

Authors not to be despised have followed the negative side in this question, although they relied on reasons not sufficiently firm, yet not entirely null either: And indeed not only manifest heretics of old held the negative, such as the Marcionites and Manichaeans: and in this our century the Catabaptists: But also grave and Orthodox authors, such as Tertullian was in the primitive Church, who in his writings takes away the use of the sword from Christians entirely: Whom in the memory of our fathers Erasmus of Rotterdam followed, a grave and witty writer, although not sufficiently Orthodox. The principal arguments are these: 1. That it was indeed permitted for the Jews to handle arms, because their polity was ruder and almost carnal: which now under the New Testament, for the Evangelical people or Christians, ought to be more perfect and, as they say, clearly spiritual. The other, depending on the former, is taken from the fact that the use of wars and arms is clearly contrary to the very profession of the Christian faith. For since the most powerful matter of Evangelical virtues is situated in the exercise of patience, which has to do only with injuries: they maintain that one falls from the faith if an Evangelical man proceeds with arms to avenge injuries.

But these reasons notwithstanding, it is established by firmer reasons that the use of arms and warring is permitted to Christians, which we shall comprise in a few hypotheses, in which the hinge of this business seems to be placed.

1. Polities have not been abrogated by the Gospel, but the worship of GOD has been especially refined. Since its perfection can consist while the Polity still stands, and these differ among themselves in their very genus: that change is by no means to be drawn outside its genus: that is, the Gospel and the Polity are not to be opposed as contraries. This hypothesis completely overturns the first reason of the adversaries. For the genus of things which came under amendment in the New Testament concerns not Politics, but Ecclesiastical matters.

2. The Gospel expressly instructs the Magistrate also with the sword, and substitutes him as a vicar for GOD in its legitimate use. Rom. 13. 4. This being posited, although the vengeance of injuries is by no means granted to any private person: yet it is by no means prohibited to the magistrate to pursue with public vengeance what each private person had to endure from the Christian faith. By this theorem the second reason is weakened. And no reason can be given why anyone should think it a crime for the Magistrate to undertake against a crowd of many wicked men what he may lawfully decree separately against individuals or a few.

3. Those things which are proper to the Law of Nature do not admit a condition or exception of time: but are established in perpetual force. Now wars and the use of arms pertain to natural Law. For that the wicked should be punished and the good defended is of natural and perpetual right. Therefore it ought not to be assigned to any certain time as its own and peculiar [property].

Since these theorems are firm, although they abundantly declare what is at issue in the controversy, they nevertheless receive a greater force of certainty from the authority of the Scriptures and from the matter itself as judged. Scripture makes mention of soldiers, whom their way of life did not exclude from the profession of the Evangelical faith, neither with the Apostles as censors, nor with Christ himself as judge. Acts 10. Matt. 8.

When soldiers consult John the Baptist about a salutary way of life, they receive an answer concerning the abuse of military service, not that military service itself is to be avoided. John 4. Luke 3. Which one point alone is abundantly sufficient to obtain what we desire.

Meanwhile, lest the abuse of a matter, in itself sufficiently unfortunate, appear to be approved, a definition of the thing must be kept before the eyes: War, therefore, is called a lawful defense, by which a Magistrate, having taken up arms for just and necessary causes, for the sake of protecting the public peace and honesty, repels the crimes and injuries of the wicked from the innocent.

Therefore, in order for any war whatsoever to come under the category of lawful things, three requirements must be noted: 1. That war be undertaken only by the public authority of the Magistrate. For a private person can no more move wars, or wage them once moved, than he can usurp the office of Magistrate: which is sufficiently conspicuous to be a crime by the law itself.

II. That there may be a just cause for war, which if it be absent, it deserves to be called not war, but robbery. A cause will be just, however, when it is inevitable. Whence Livy, dec. 1, lib. 9, wrote not altogether ineptly: A just war is that which is necessary: and those arms are pious, for which no hope is left except in arms.

III. Let the end and purpose of wars be the procuring of peace and the assertion of public honesty. For if either plunder or the slaughter of men alone be proposed, it will be more correctly called either robbery or butchery than war.

There are those who demand more requirements in war, such as: That arms should serve not by initiating, but only by repelling war. And as it seems to some, wars are indeed lawful for Christians, but only against infidels. But both are weakened and excluded by our definition, nay, they collapse by their very nature. Certainly, it is fitting for a wise man to try everything before arms, so that this should be the last degree of defense: Now, however, if a magistrate cannot otherwise protect peace than by arms, it makes no difference to Justice whether arms are taken up or opposed when taken up, since their force lies not in the time, but in the author, the cause, and the manner. Experience itself testifies that no one fights more keenly and successfully than he who is dragged into the fight unwilling and against his will. The reason is plain: Because then the cause is just: but in a just cause the spirit is always most brave: ἐν τῷ δικαίῳ μέγα ἔξεστι φρονεῖν. But on the contrary: Fear always torments the wicked, as the Law of GOD stands, and no one is so bold whom a bad Conscience does not make most timid, Pythagoras used to say.

But to the point: If Christians can wage war against no one, one of two things will be necessary: either that Christians cannot disturb peace and commit injuries, or that even those doing such things are not to be restrained by Magistrates. Since neither is the case, but there is an ambiguity in the word itself, this knot is untied in such a way that it may be said: if they are Christians, they will either not disturb the peace, and thus a just cause for war will cease; or if they do disturb the peace, this name does not apply to them, and thus the reasoning by which it was denied that war could be justly waged against them will expire; that is, the condition which they require in this matter will either be entirely superfluous or certainly useless.

It is asked, however, in this place, Why did the New Testament prescribe nothing concerning Wars? I answer, that two causes for the fact can be given. 1. It would have been superfluous, because everything had already been prescribed in the Old Testament. 2. It was also not convenient, because Christians were then destitute of their own Magistrates. But this pertains to public law. Therefore, Christ took upon Himself the task of forming the morals of private men more.

It remains that we answer the Anabaptists: who, in order to forbid the use of wars to Christians simply, bring forward that passage in Matt. 5. 39: I say to you, do not resist evil: If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also. To which it is answered variously by various people: Augustine, against Faustus the Manichaean, lib. 22, c. 29, refers this to the preparation of the mind. Others understand it comparatively from the subject matter; Rather than that you should repay evil with evil, you should bear or do any adversities. B. LUTHER looks to that time, establishing that this was said to the pious then, when they had Magistrates alien to the Christian Religion, Tom 7, page 86. Which individual responses, when joined together, satisfy the saying of Christ. But in this place, it must be added that the saying of Christ and the responses already given are outside the state of the present question: Because there it is only a matter of private persons. The same response is given to the remaining places of Scripture also, which are brought forward by the Anabaptists: Such as: Rom. 12, 17. 1 Pet. 3, 9. Rendering to no one evil for evil. Matt. 26, 52. He who takes the sword will perish by the sword. 2 Cor. 10, 4. The weapons of our warfare are not carnal. Prov. 20, 22. Rom. 12, 9. Vengeance is mine, I will repay.

But they bring forward, and urge, the prophecies of the Prophets: Isa. 2, 4. They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks, nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore: Which is repeated in Micah 4, 3, and elsewhere. I answer: This is to be referred to the doctrine of Christ: for such is it, that if one were to live exactly according to it, that which was predicted by the Prophets would also come to pass: which is manifest to be done among the pious indeed. Now, however, the Church has never been so purified that it is lived perfectly even among those who have given their names to the Gospel. Therefore, there is need of magistrates. Furthermore, many things have been predicted, the beginnings and inception of which we see in this world in the Church: the consummation in the other life.

But let these things suffice concerning Wars. It remains that we also say something about that Means, which Nature itself suggests in private and public calamities, namely FLIGHT.

Latin:

DE BELLO.

DE Bello dicturi, ea tantùm pensi habebimus, quae ad Scholas Theologorum pertinent: Reliqua Politicis committentes.

BELLUM cùm vel ἀντιφραστικῶς sic dictum, vel à belluis potiùs sic appellatum, & foedam habeat notionis suae originem, & tam horrendam prae se ferat speciem rerum, ut ad solam ejus mentionem pij cohorrescant: scitu sanè dignum & necessarium fuerit, quid de bello piis sit sentiendum.

Jam verò non curabimus veterem illam Judaeorum Ecclesiam: An arma tractare, & belta gerere ipsis fuerit licitum? Nam Affirmativam sacra confirmat historia: Et Sanctorum exempla, quae juris speciem prae se ferunt, & DEI quoque jussa illustriora sunt in Veteri Testamento, quàm quae in dubium vocari à quoquam possint. Verùm hoc Quaestionis est: Num populo Evangelico armis saevire, bello grassari in homines alios ullâ ratione liceat?

Partem negantem in hac quaestione, Autores non contemnendi sunt secuti, quamvis non satis firmis, non tamen planè etiam nullis rationibus niterentur: Et quidem non haeretici tantùm manifesti olim negantem tenuerunt, ut Marcionitae & Manichaei: & nostro hoc seculo Catabaptistae: Sed autores etiam graves & Orthodoxi, qualis in primitiva Ecclesia fuit Tertullianus, qui in scriptis suis usum gladii, Christianis prorsus adimit: Quem patrum nostrorum memoriâ secutus est Erasmo Roterodamus, scriptor gravis & argutus, quamvis non satis Orthodoxus. Argumenta praecipua sunt haec: 1. Judaeis quidem licuisse arma tractare, eò quòd rudior, & propemodum carnalis ipsorum fuerit politia: quae jam sub Novo Testamento, populo Evangelico sive Christianis perfectior, & planè, quod inquiunt, spiritualis esse debeat. Alterum à priore dependens sumitur ex eo, quòd ipsi professioni fidei Christianae, bellorum armorumq; usus planè sit contrarius. Cùm enim in exercitio patientiae, cui cum injuriis duntaxat est res, potissima virtutum Evangelicarum sita sit materia: à fide defici statuunt, si ad vindicandas injurias armis homo Evangelicus procedat.

Caeterùm rationibus his non obstantibus, licitum esse Christianis armorum & bellandi usum, firmioribus constat rationibus, quas paucis hypothesibus complectemur, in quibus negocii hujus cardo positus esse videtur.

1. Evangelio non sunt abrogatæ politiæ, sed cultus DEI potissimùm expolitus. Cui cùm sua constare perfectio possit, stante etiam Politiâ, & genere ipso hæc inter sese differant: extra genus suum mutatio ista minimè est trahenda: hoc est, Evangelium & Politia, ut contraria, non sunt opponenda. Hæc hypothesis primam rationem adversariorum penitus evertit. Genus enim rerum, quæ in Novo Testamento sub emendationem venerant, concernit, non Politica, sed Ecclesiastica.

2. Evangelium expressè gladio etiam Magistratum instruit, & in hujus legitimo usu DEO illum vicarium substituit. Rom. 13. 4. Hoc posito, quamvis privato cuiq; injuriarum vindicta minimè est concessa: magistratui tamen minimè est prohibitum, quod privatim cuiq; ex fide Christianâ ferendum erat, vindictâ publicâ prosequi. Hoc theoremate Secunda ratio infirmatur. Et nulla potest dari ratio, cur, quod seorsim in singulos aut paucos licitè statuir Magistratus, adversus turbam multorum sceleratorum suscipere, nefas esse quisquam existimet.

3. Quæ Legis Naturæ propria sunt, conditionem sive exceptionem temporis non admittunt: sed in perpetuo vigore constitutæ sunt. Bella autem, atque armorum usus, ad Legem naturalem pertinent. Nam ut plectantur mali, defendantur boni: juris est naturalis & perpetui. Non debet ergò certo cuidam tempori tanquam proprium ac peculiare illud adsignari.

Hæc theoremata cùm firma sint, quamvis abundè declarent, quod in Controversiâ versatur: tamen ex Scripturarum autoritate, & re ipsâ judicatâ majorem suæ certitudinis vim accipiunt. Facit Scriptura militum mentionem, quos vitæ genus à professione fidei Evangelicæ, neque Apostolis censoribus, neque Christo ipso judice, exclusit. Actor. 10. Matth. 8.

Cùm de salutari vitæ instituto Johannem Baptistam milites consulunt: de abusu militiæ, non militia ipsa fugienda responsum accipiunt Joh. 4. Luc. 3. Quod vel unum, ad obtinendum quod volumus, abundè sufficit.

Interim ne abusus rei, per se satis infaustæ, approbari videatur: Definitio rei ob oculos est habenda: Bellum igitur legitima vocatur defensio, quâ Magistratus justas & necessarias ob causas sumtis armis, pacis & honestatis publicæ tutandæ gratia, scelera atque injurias improborum ab insontibus propulsat.

Ut ergo sub censum rerum licitarum bellum quodcunque veniat, tria requisita notanda sunt: 1. Ut non nisi publica Magistratus autoritate bellum suscipiatur. Bella namq; movere, aut mota gerere privatus nihilo magis potest, quam Magistratum usurpare: quod jure ipso nefas esse satis est conspicuum.

II. Ut justa belli causa sit, quæ si absit, non bellum: sed latrocinium appellari meretur. Justa autem fuerit causa tùm, quando est inevitabilis. Unde Livius dec. 1. lib. 9. non planè ineptè scripsit: Bellum justum est, quod necessarium est: & arma sunt pia, quibus nulla, nisi in armis spes relinquitur.

III. Finis & propositum bellorum sit pacis parandæ, & honestatis publicæ assertio. Nam si vel rapinæ, vel internecio hominum sola sit proposita, rectiùs vel latrocinium, vel carnificina, quàm bellum appellabitur.

Sunt, qui plura in bello requisita flagitant, qualia sunt, Ut non movendo, sed propulsando tantùm bello, arma serviant. Et ut quibusdam videtur, Christianis quidem licita sunt bella: sed non nisi adversus infideles. Sed utrumq; definitio ne nostra infirmatur atque excluditur, imò suâ etiam naturâ concidit. Sanè quidem omnia priùs experiri sapientem, quàm armis decet, ut extremus hic esse defensionis gradus debeat: Jam verò, si aliter quàm armis pacem tueri nequeat magistratus: ad Justitiam nihil interest, sive sumantur, sive sumtis opponantur arma, quippe quorum vis non in tempore, sed autore, causa, & modo omne sitú est. Experientia ipsa testatur, quòd nemo acriùs & feliciùs pugnet, quàm qui nolens & invitus ad pugnam pertrahitur. Ratio plana est: Quia tùm causa justa est: In causa autem justa animus semper est fortissimus: ἐν τῷ δικαίῳ μέγα ἔξεστι φρονεῖν. Contrà verò: Lege DEUM stabili semper metus angit iniquos, Et nemo tàm audax est, quem mala Conscientia non faciat timidissimum, dicebat Pythagoras.

Sed ad rem: Si Christiano nemini bellum inferre Christiani possunt: duorum alterū erit necessarium: aut non posse Christianos pacem turbare atq; injurias facere: aut ista etiam facientes, à Magistratibus non coercendos esse. Quorum cùm neutrum sit, insit autem in vocabulo ipso ambiguitas: sic nodus iste solvitur, ut dicatur, si Christiani sint, aut pacem non esse turbaturos: & sic justa belli causa cessabit: aut si pacem turberit, nomen hoc ipsis non competere: & sic ratio expirabit, qua ipsis bellum justè inferri posse negatum fuit, hoc est, aut planè supervacanea erit conditio, aut inutilis certè, quam isti in hac materia requirunt.

Quæritur autem hoc loco, Cur Novum Testamentum nihil præceperit de Bellis? Respondeo, duas facti causas dari posse. 1. Supervacaneum id fuerat, quia jam præscripta erant omnia in Veteri Testamento. 2. Non etiam commodum, quia Christiani tùm destituebantur Magistratibus propriis. Pertinet autem hoc ad jus publicum. Proinde privatorum hominum mores magis formandos sibi sumsit Christus.

Superest ut Anabaptistis respondeamus: qui ut bellorum usu Christianis simpliciter interdicant, proferunt illud Matt. 5. 39. Ego dico vobis, ne resistite malo: Si quis te percusserit sua co per dextram maxillam, præbe illi & alteram. Ad quod variè à variis respondetur: Augustinus contra Faustum Manichæum, lib. 22. c. 29. ad præparationem animi hoc refert. Alii comparativè intelligunt ex materia subjectâ; Potiùs, quàm ut malum malo rependas, quævis adversa feras aut facias. B. LUTHERUS tempus illud respicit, statuens hoc dictum fuisse, piis tùm, cùm Magistratus haberent à Religione Christiana alienos Tom 7. pag. 86. Quæ responsiones singulæ conjunctæ, dicto Christi satisfaciunt. Sed hoc loco addendum est illud, Dictum Christi, & responsionis jam datas, extra statum præsentis quæstionis versari: Quia ibi de privatis tantùm agitur. Quæ ipsa responsio datur ad reliqua etiam Scripturæ loca, quæ ab Anabaptistis proferuntur: Qualia sunt: Rom. 12, 17. 1 Petr 3, 9. Nulli malum pro malo reddentes. Matt. 26, 52. Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit. 2 Cor 10, 4. Arma militiæ nostræ non sunt carnalia, Proverb. 20, 22. Rom. 12, 9. Mihi vindicta, ego ulciscam.

Sed proferunt illi, & urgent vaticinia Prophetarum: Esa. 2, 4. Conflabunt gladios suos in vomeres, & lanceas suas in falces, non levabit gens contra gentem gladium, nec exercebuntur ultrà ad prælium: Quod repetitur Micheæ 4, 3. & alibi. Respondeo: Hoc ad doctrinam Christi referri: talis enim est, ut si secundum eam exactè viveretur, id etiam futurum esset quod à Prophetis prædictum: id quod inter pios sanè fieri manifestum est. Jam verò Ecclesia nunquàm ita purgata est, ut perfectè vivatur inter eos etiam, qui Evangelio sua dederunt nomina. Ergo opus est magistratibus. Deinde multa prædicta sunt, quorum initia tantùm & inchoationem videmus in hoc mundo in Ecclesia: Consumationem in altera vita.

Sed de Bellis isthæc sufficiant. Superest, ut de illo etiam Medio, quod Natura ipsa in privatis ac publicis calamitatibus suadet, nempede FUGA aliquid dicamus.


### Chapter Two. Concerning Christian Consolation, both general and special, in any…: On Flight, Whether It Be Lawful for Christians

Among the remaining afflictions, which seem able to be either entirely removed or at least mitigated by flight, pestilence and persecution easily hold the first place. It is asked, therefore, whether a pious person, with these two afflictions encroaching, can with a good conscience seek safety for himself and his own by flight? Concerning each separately.

And at the beginning indeed, regarding the pestilence, two things are asked: 1. Whether it is contagious: 2. Whether it is permitted to flee from it. Regarding the former question, although it is more physical and medical than theological: nevertheless, these two things can be answered about it by a theologian. First indeed, that one must not protest against the public experience of all times, which testifies with great consensus that such diseases spread through contagion. But a second point must be added immediately, that that very contagion has no power without the providence of God, and therefore by no means are duties

Latin:

INter reliquas Afflictiones, quæ fuga vel planè tolli, vel saltem mitigari posse videntur, primas facilè tenent, Pestilentia & Persecutio. Quæritur ergò, Utrum bonâ Conscientiâ Pius, ingruentibus istis duabus afflictiontbus, Fugâ salutem sibi, suisq; quærere possit? De utraque seorsim.

Ac initiô quidem, quoad Pestilentiam, duô quæruntur: 1. An ea sit contagiosa: 2. An fugere eam liceat. Quoad Priorem quæstionem, quanquam Physica magis ea est, & Medica, quàm Theologica: duô tamen isthæc de ea responderi possunt à Theologo. Primùm quidem, non esse reclamandum publicæ omnium temporum experientiæ, quæ magno consensu testatur, tales morbos per contagium serpere. Sed addendum mox est alterum, Illud ipsum contagium vires nullas habere sine Providentiâ DEI, & propterea nequaquam Officia


### Chapter Two. Concerning Christian Consolation, both general and special, in any…: Whether the plague is to be fled

of one's calling, or of charity, to be interrupted for fear of contagion. Where it will be profitable to have in view from time to time the sweetest promises, which show us that we are in the care of GOD even in the danger of contagion, and convince us that nothing can happen to anyone without the good pleasure of the heavenly Father: Jonah 4:11. I, says the LORD, should I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which are more than twelve myriads of men, who do not know the difference between good and evil, or between the right hand and the left? Psalm 36:7. You, O LORD, will save men and beasts. Matthew 10:29. Are not two little sparrows sold, and not one of them falls to the ground without the will of the heavenly Father? But the very hairs of your head are all numbered: Do not fear therefore: you are better than many sparrows. But if indeed anyone objects that experience itself often contradicts this promise: The answer is that all bodily promises are to be understood with the exception of chastisement and the cross. Wherefore, even if in such cases that promise does not seem to be fulfilled, yet another equivalent, nay, more excellent promise is fulfilled, namely that even in the very calamity and disease, such persons are still in the care of GOD, and through death itself are finally transferred to the eternal fatherland and the long-hoped-for inheritance. Meanwhile, as long as we must run in the stadium of this life, we ought deservedly to acknowledge that these promises are most often fulfilled in each of us, and while others suffer, we by divine benefit are kept safe for so long, until it seems good to the LORD to call us also from this station.

Regarding the latter question about the Plague, it is asked, whether it is permitted to avert and flee it, and how, and to what extent, by a change of place? Where theologians depart into different opinions. For there are those who simply deny that the plague is to be fled, moved especially by these reasons: 1. that the Pestilence is not a contagious disease, but a scourge of GOD sent immediately from heaven. 2. that the divine Providence, which is the mover and ruler of the Pestilence, is by no means to be resisted in this way: for HE has in numbered detail most accurately those who and how many men ought to perish by this evil. 3. that Christian charity does not permit one to desert either one's own, or certainly one's neighbor struggling with this evil.

But there are others on the contrary who hold the Affirmative, and contend that flight in the time of a raging plague is not illicit, provided that it is done in a legitimate manner, and that the duties of neither one's calling nor of Charity are simply neglected by us.

And indeed, regarding the three proposed reasons, they are not of such weight or moment that they can entirely invalidate the Affirmative. For regarding the First, that the Pestilence is truly contagious, besides the reasons by which physicians prove it, experience itself, the teacher of fools, confirms it too certainly. And the proof which is brought to the contrary is weak. For there is also Leprosy: there is Elephantiasis, as there are other diseases that are a scourge of GOD: nevertheless, Scripture itself commands one to flee Leprosy and similar contagious diseases. But the judgment is the same concerning similar ones. Therefore, if it is permitted to flee leprosy, it will certainly be permitted to flee the plague.

For the providence of GOD is indeed the first cause of those things which happen in the world: but it does not remove secondary causes. Otherwise, neither would leprosy be to be fled. Then there is no nerve of consequence in: GOD has in numbered detail those whom and how many HE wishes to be extinguished by this disease. Therefore the pestilence is not to be fled. For from the universal foreknowledge of GOD to the negation of the means granted by GOD himself, the consequence is not valid. What? That this would be nothing else than to tempt GOD: and by foolish rashness to involve ourselves in dangers which we could avoid. Where that saying has place: He who loves danger will perish in it. Which itself depends on the Providence of GOD. Let it be therefore: The foreknowledge of GOD is certain and infallible: yet it is not fatal. HE sees indeed whether you are about to rashly expose yourself to danger, and to perish in it: and because HE infallibly sees and knows, therefore it is rightly said that HE has in numbered detail all those who are to be extinguished by the plague. But if, having cast aside all rashness, you had not tempted GOD with a foolish impulse and daring, you would neither have perished by that evil, nor would GOD have foreseen that you were to perish by this evil.

Providence therefore does not prevent you from consulting for the safety of yourself, and of your own, and of the whole Republic by flight for a time: provided that it can be done legitimately, and with a good conscience, and without injury and harm to anyone. Furthermore, the futility of this argument is evident if it is applied to other calamities. Certainly, divine providence has in numbered detail those whom and how many it wishes to take away, either by famine or by war. Is it therefore not permitted to flee famine and wars? Did not the Patriarch Jacob flee famine even into Egypt? Did not the Savior himself prescribe this rule: If they have persecuted you from one city, flee into another. Will it not be permitted to others to repel the injuries of both famine and wars by means? It remains therefore settled and firm that GOD does not forbid flight in the time of plague, provided (as has been said several times) it is done legitimately: that is, that the duties of your calling permit you to flee: and that nothing is neglected by you of those things which pertain to the care of our own, or of our neighbor, in this necessity.

The third reason likewise does not militate. For if it has been provided for the ill-affected by the care and benefit of the Ordinary Magistrate, so that in terms of medicines and necessary sustenance nothing is lacking to them, if you also, according to the measure of your means, assist them with counsel and help; certainly nothing prevents you from consulting for yourself and your own by flight and change of place, with that caution applied, about which it has already been spoken. For here that trite saying holds: Charity is ordered, and begins from itself. What? That account must be taken of the Church and the Republic. For what, I ask, would this charity be, if the Ministers of the Church were to rashly expose themselves to this evil? Will not the whole Church soon be deprived of its Ministry? Thus, what use would redound to the Republic if those who preside over public offices were to destroy both themselves and their own by foolish rashness? The Apostolic saying has place here rather: He who does not have care of his own, and especially of those of his household, has denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel. 1 Timothy 5:8. And it is the command of GOD: You shall not kill.

The conditions, however, which must be observed by those fleeing the plague, are chiefly these:

1. That serious repentance and conversion to God should come first.

2. That we commend ourselves and our own to the divine will with pious and ardent prayers, and that we instantly invoke God for the mitigation, or rather the total removal, of this evil.

3. That we omit nothing in performing the duties of our calling, nor depart from our post before either the superior Magistrate commands it, or total dispersion makes it advisable.

4. That we assist our fellow citizens who are oppressed by this evil, in whatever way possible, both those absent and those present, with help and counsel.

5. That we remember that we are fleeing not death, but the plague: that is, to use at least that means by which, if it so pleases the Lord, we may be safe from contagion: but not that we should think we can avoid death, which can attack us in every place and at every time.

6. And lastly: That when freed from this evil and returned to our own, we give thanks to God, publicly and privately: and that we allow this chastisement to be a παιδευτήριον, so that henceforth we may more rightly order the ways of our life and morals according to the will of God, lest worse things happen to us.

The second question, which is debated concerning flight, concerns the time of persecution: Can the pious avoid it by flight? To which I answer affirmatively, but again with certain conditions observed. Certainly, in Matt. 2:15, when the Pharisees were laying snares for Christ and were taking counsel about destroying him, he himself fled. He did the very same thing also in John 7:1 and 8:59. Indeed, he commanded his disciples to do the same, in Matt. 10:23: When they persecute you in this city, flee to another. Observing this command, the Apostle, having taken to flight, avoids the persecution intended for him at Damascus by the Jews, Acts 9:23 and 25.

In the Old Testament, Moses fled: Exod. 2:15. Elijah, 1 Kings 19:3. Indeed, David also commemorates his flights to God: Ps. 56:8.

It must be noted, however, in this place, the distinction between the universal persecution of an entire Church and the particular persecution of this or that Doctor, of this or that pious and faithful Christian.

That former flight admits no middle ground, according to the Doctors of the Church. For where the whole Church is in danger, there is the greatest need for the work and protection of Pastors and Doctors, and he is not a pastor, but a hireling, who in this case deserts the sheep of the Church. It must be decided otherwise if the enemies of the truth are, in appearance, only one or several ministers. For then it is permitted to flee: indeed, the hearers of the word themselves will take pains that they may reach a safer place, until a calmer breeze shines upon the Church. The zeal of the disciples ought to be an example, who by common effort let Paul down in a basket through the wall of Damascus, so that he might escape safe and sound. This very course of action pious and faithful people can take with a clear conscience: nor will they think that on this account they will incur the charge of having denied the truth. For they flee for this very reason, so that it may be clear to the enemies in part that they do not wish to depart from the truth, but that they have consulted their own interests by flight for this reason, that they may be able to confess the acknowledged truth all the more freely.

Furthermore, one must flee in such a way that, if necessity requires, we are prepared to bear witness to the truth even by the shedding of blood, committing the outcome to God with prayers, certain that His right hand can change all things, Psalm 77, v. 11. Or even, where no means appear, to help and deliver us by other wondrous methods if He wills. Wherefore let us cast all our care upon Him, who will certainly be with us even in the midst of tribulations: Psalm 91, v. 15. Isaiah 43, v. 1 & 2. To whom be glory and adoration for infinite ages, AMEN.

Latin:

vel Vocationis, vel Charitatis intermittenda esse, metu contagii. Ubi proderit subindè in conspectu habere dulcissimas promissiones, quæ nos & in contagii periculo DEO curæ esse ostendunt, & convincunt, nihil cuiquam posse accidere, sine beneplacito Patris cœlestis: Jonæ 4, 11. Ego, inquit DOMINUS, non misererer Niniue civitatis magnæ, in qua sunt plures, quàm duodecim myriades hominum, nescientium discrimen inter bonum & malum, sive inter dextrã & sinistram? Psal. 36, 7. Homines & jumenta DOMINE salvabis. Matth 10, 29. Nonne passcrculi duo esse veneunt, & unus ex illis non cadit in terrã, sine voluntate Patris cœlestis; Vestri autem capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt: Nolite ergo timere: multis passeribus meliores estis vos. Quòd si verò aliquis objiciat, Promissioni huic ipsam sæpè repugnare experientiam: Respondetur, Promissiones omnes corporales intelligendas esse cum exceptione castigationis & crucis. Quapropter etsi in talibus ista promissio non videtur impleri: impletur tamen alia ei æquivalens, imò excellentior promissio, quod in ipsa quoque calamitate & morbo, tales tamé sunt DEO curæ, & per ipsam tandem mortem ad æternam patriam & hæreditatem diu speratam transferuntur. Interim quamdiu in stadio vitæ hujus currendũ nobis est, meritò debemus agnoscere, in unoquoque nostrūm sæpissimè impleri has promissiones, & dum alii patiuntur, nos divino beneficio tamdiu incolumes servari, donec DOMINO videatur, nos quoque ex hac statione evocare.

Quoàd posteriorem de Peste Quæstionem, quæritur, An eam, & quomodo, ac quatenus, mutatione loci avertere & fugere liceat? Ubi in diversas sententias abeunt Theologi. Sunt enim qui pestem fugiendam esse simpliciter negant, his potissimùm moti rationibus: 1. quòd Pestilentia non sit morbus contagiosus: sed flagellum DEI immediatè è cœlo immissum. 2. quòd Providentia divina, quæ Pestilentiæ motrix & rectrix sit, nullo pacto sic resistendum: Illâ verò in numerato accuratissimè habere, qui & quot homines hoc malo perire debeant. 3. quòd Charitas Christiana non permittat, ut vel suos, vel certè proximum cum hoc malo conflictantem deserat.

Sunt verò contrà alii, qui Affirmativam tenent, & tempore grassantis pestilentiæ fugam non illicitam esse contendant, modò id fiat legitima ratione, & neq; vocationis, neque Charitatis officia simpliciter à nobis negligantur.

Et quidem quoad tres rationes propositas, eæ tanti non sunt ponderis aut momenti, ut Affirmativam penitùs infirmare possint. Nam quoad Primam, Pestilentiam vere contagiosam esse, præter rationes quibus Medici id probant, experientia ipsa Stultorum magistra, nimis certò confirmat. Et elumbis est probatio, quæ in contrarium adducitur. Est enim & Lepra: est Elephantiasis, sut & alii morbi flagellum DEI: nihilominus Scriptura ipsa, Lepram & similes morbos contagiosos fugere jubet. De similibus autem idem est judicium. Ergo si lepram, utique & pestem fugere licebit.

tia enim DEI, causa quidem est prima eorum, quæ in mundo fiunt: sed non tollit ea causas secundas. Aliàs neque lepra fugienda esset. Deinde nullus nervus consequentiæ, DEUS in numerato habet, quos & quot velit hoc morbo extinctos. Ergo pestilentia non est fugienda. Nam à præscientia DEI universali, ad negationem mediorum ab ipso DEO concessorum, non valet consequentia. Quid? quòd hoc nihil foret aliud, quàm tentare Deum: & stulta temeritate nos ipsos involvere periculis, quæ evitare possemus. Ubi locum habet illud: Qui amat periculum, peribit in eo. Quod ipsum à Providentia DEI dependet. Esto ergò: Certa & infallibilis sit præscientia DEI: tamen ea non est fatalis. Videt quidem, utrum te temerè sis periculo objecturus, inque eo peritutus: & quia infallibiliter videt & novit, ideò rectè dicitur, quòd in numerato habeat omnes, peste extinguendos. Si verò abjecta temeritate omni, stulto impetu & ausu DEUM non tentasses, neque malo illo periisses, neque DEUS præscivisset te hoc malo periturum.

Providentia ergò non prohibet, quo minùs & tuæ, & tuorum, & totius Reipubl. saluti per fugam ad tempus consulas: dummodò id legitimè, & bona conscientia, & sine ullius injuria ac damno fieri possit. Deinde patet futilitas hujus argumenti, si ad alias calamitates id accommodetur. Certè divina providentia in numerato habet, quos & quot, vel fame, vel bello velit tollere. Anne ergò famem & bella fugere non licebit? Annon Jacobus Patriarcha famem fugit in Ægyptum usque? An non Servator ipse regulam hanc præscripsit: Si persecuti vos fuerint ex civitate una, fugite in aliam. Annon aliis medius & famis, & bellorum injurias propulsare licebit; Ratum ergo firmúmque manet, quòd DEUS neq; tempore pestis fuga prohibeat, modò (ut aliquoties est dictum) id fiat legitimè: hoc est, ut vocationis offica te fugere permittant: & ut per te nihil negligatur eorum, quæ vel ad nostrorum, vel proximi curam, hac in necessitate pertinent.

Tertia ratio itidem non militat. Si enim vel Magistratus Ordinarii curâ ac beneficio ita prospectum est malè affectis, ut qua medicamenta, quâ sustentationem necessariam, nihil ipfis desit, si tu etiam pro facultatum tuarum ratione, consilio & auxilio ipsis adsis; nihil certè prohibet, quò minus fuga & loci mutatione tibi tuisq; consulas, ea adhibita cautione, de quâ jam dictum. Hic enim valet illud tritum: Charitas est ordinata, & à seipsa incipit. Quid? quod Ecclesiæ & Reipub. habenda ratio. Quæ enim quæso hæc foret charitas, Si Ministri Ecclesiæ temerè se huic malo objicere velint? Annon mox tota Ecclesia suo privabitur Ministerio? Sic quis usus redundaret ad Rempubl. si qui publicis præsunt muneribus, stulta temeritate & seipsos, & suos perderent? Locum hîc potius habet illud Apostolicum: Qui suorum, ac præsertim domesticorum curam non habet, fidem negavit, & infideli est deterior. 1. Timoth. 5, 8. Et mandatum DEI est: Non occides.

Conditiones autem, quæ pestem fugientibus observangæ, præcipuè sunt hæ:

1. Ut præcedat seria pœnitentia, & ad Deum conversio.

2. Ut nos, nostrosq́; voluntati divinæ, piis & ardentibus precibus commendemus, & pro mitigatione, imò omnimoda ablatione mali hujus instanter Deum invocemus.

3. Ut in obeundis vocationis nostræ officiis nihil prætermittamus, neq; priùs cedamus loco, quàm vel superior Magistratus illud mandet, vel dispersio totalis id suadeat.

4. Ut concives nostros, malo hoc pressos, qua fieri queat ratione, tam absentes, quàm præsentes, auxilio & consilio juvemus.

5. Ut meminerimus, nos non mortem, sed pestem fugere: hoc est, eo saltem uti medio, quo si ita placeat Domino, à contagio tuti esse possimus: non verò ut mortem, quæ nos omni loco ac tempore invadere potest, evitare nos posse, existimemus.

6. Et postremò: Ut à malo isto libertati, & ad nostros reversi, devotas Deo agamus gratias, publicè, privatimque: & castigationem hanc παιδευτήριον esse sinamus, ut deinceps rectiùs vitæ, morumq́; nostrorum rationes ad voluntatem Dei instituamus, ne pejora nobis eveniant.

Quæstio altera, quæ de Fuga agitatur, concernit Tempus persecutionis, An eam fugâ declinare pii possint? Ubi affirmatè quidem respondeo sed rursus observatis certis conditionibus. Certè Matth. 2. v. 15. cùm Pharisæi insidias struerent Christo, déque ipso perdendo consilia agitarent: ipse aufugit. Quod ipsum fecit etiam Joh. 7. v. 1. & c. 8. v. 59. Quin ut idem facerent discipuli, præcepit, Matth. 10. v. 23. Cùm persecuti vos fuerint in civitate istâ: fugite in aliam. Quod præceptum observans Apostolus, fugâ arrepta declinat persecutionem sibi Damasci, per Judæos intentatam Act. 9. v. 23. & 25.

In Veteri Testamento fugit Moses: Exod. 2. v. 15. Elias, 1. Reg. 19. v. 3. Quin & David fugas suas Deo commemorat: Psal. 56. v. 10.

Notandum verò hoc loco discrimen inter Persecutionem universalem totius alicujus Ecclesiæ: & inter persecutionem particularem hujus vel illius Doctoris, hujus vel illius pii ac fidelis Christiani.

Prior illa fuga medium non admittit, quoad Doctores Ecclesiæ. Nam ubi tota periclitatur Ecclesia, ibi vel maximè Pastorum ac Doctorum opera ac præsidio opus est, Et non pastor, sed mercenarius, qui hoc casu Ecclesiæ oves deserit. Secus statuendum, si hostes veritatis in specie, unum vel plures tantùm ministros. Tùm enim fugere licet: imò ut in tutiorem locum perveniant, dabunt operam ipsi quoq; Auditores verbi, donec serenior aura Ecclesiæ affulgeat. Exemplo debet esse studium discipulorum, qui Paulum communi opera in sporta demittunt per murum Damasci, ut evadat salvus & incolumis. Quam ipsam rationem inire possunt salva conscientia pii & fideles quique: neque existimabunt, hoc nomine se incursuros in crimen abnegatæ veritatis. Nam vel hanc ipsam ob causam fugiunt, ut partim hostibus constet, se à veritate nolle discedere, sed ideò fuga sibi consuluisse, ut tantò liberius veritatem agnitam confiteri possint.

Deinde verò ita fugiendum est, ut si necessitas ferat, parati simus etiam sanguinis profusione veritati perhibere testimonium, precibus Deo eventum committentes, certi, quòd ipsius dextera omnia possit mutare, Psal. 77. v. 11. Vel etiam, ubi nulla apparent media, rationibus aliis mirandis nos juvare & eruere si velit. Quare curam omnem in ipsum conjiciamus, qui in mediis etiam tribulationibus certò nobis aderit: Psalm. 91. v. 15. Jesa. 43. v. 1. & 2. Cui sit gloria & adoratio seculis infinitis, AMEN.


## 33 On the Worship and Invocation of GOD

The treatment of the Invocation of GOD follows the place concerning the cross and afflictions in a most correct order. For just as the pious, established in straits, seek the LORD, Isaiah 26, v. 16, so no more effective consolation can be obtained by them than that which comes from the Invocation of GOD, and the most certain hearing of prayers, according to that of David: Unless thy Law, O LORD, had been my consolation, I would have perished in my affliction. Psalm 119, verse 92. Which is the very reason, without doubt, that our Author wished to treat this Place both more lengthily and more accurately.

For first he discourses both on the greatest use of right invocation, and on the twofold distinction which exists between the invocation of Christians and of the Gentiles, while, namely, the latter are partly ignorant of what kind of GOD has revealed Himself according to His essence: and partly, indeed, they know nothing at all about the Will of GOD toward sinners, revealed in the Gospel.

Then he disputes concerning the Object, the matter, and the impulsive causes of Invocation. He constitutes GOD alone as the Object: the matter, bodily and spiritual goods: the impulsive causes, three: the command of GOD: the promises concerning being heard: Faith, and its πληροφορίαν, resting in the promises.

Thirdly, he prescribes certain formulas of Praying: and explains the Lord's Prayer accurately according to its individual precepts.

Fourthly and lastly, he discusses the invocation of saints against the Romanists: and at the same time inveighs against the astonishing ingratitude of men toward God: by certain prescribed formulas of thanksgiving. And indeed, the entire Philippean treatise consists of and is completed by these four parts.

We, partly following the same footsteps, but partly considering more closely the controversies of the present age, and especially the theology of the Esauites, in this place, establish two general chapters of our treatise: The former, indeed, the positive, will propose the purer teaching concerning the right invocation of God: the latter, however, the antithetical, will explain the refutation or exposure of the most crass errors, by which both other heretics, and especially the Esauites, have most foully defiled the orthodoxy of this article, and do defile it today.

CHAPTER I. Concerning the true invocation of God, of positive doctrine.

The invocation of God is sometimes named prayer in the Scriptures, sometimes the worship of God. Prayer, indeed, with respect to the instrument by which it is generally performed, which is the mouth of the body. Worship, however, with respect to God, to whom invocation or prayer is uniquely directed. For this word is equivalent to the Greek word latreia, which signifies religious veneration. In this respect, a certain homonymy is discovered in the term invocation: so that sometimes it is taken strictly only for worship, or the religious adoration of God: sometimes, however, it denotes loosely any imploring of aid, which is also done by men still living. For Scripture testifies not obscurely in many places that the imploring of aid can also be directed to creatures, not indeed those devoid of reason, whether they be animals or inanimate things: such as the stars and that kind of natural things. For besides the fact that it would be foolish and insane to invoke such creatures as are endowed with neither intellect, nor will, nor strength to help: in the very Word of God, such invocation, among the Gentiles, is condemned as execrable idolatry: which can be seen from the sermons of the prophets and chapter 1 to the Romans. But that the imploring of aid can be directed to rational creatures, that is, to living men, in external and bodily matters, is manifest from the Scriptures. James certainly, chapter 5, verse 14,

commands that if anyone is sick, he should summon the elders, who should pray over him: Where, indeed, to summon the elders is nothing other than to demand their prayers and intercessions to God. Thus the Apostle commands that one should pray for another: indeed, he very often commends himself to the prayers of the Church.

Thus Sirach commands, chapter 38, verse 1 and following, that those struggling with diseases should call physicians to their aid. And Scripture warns everywhere that in private and public calamities we should implore the aid of others, and help one another. However, we do not have a dissertation in this place properly about this general species of invocation: but only about that by which we religiously and with true confidence in all necessities invoke God, as the one and primary author and director of all aids.

This religious invocation is either internal or external. Internal, which is done only by the mind, or by the internal groans and sighs of the mind: External, which is done at the same time with heart and mouth, and external gestures: by voice or song: of which more must be said below in its place. Both of these are either serious or hypocritical. About the serious, we shall have a discussion expressly hereafter. Hypocritical is that which gives sound without a mind, that is, it invokes God indeed with external lips: but it does not proceed from the heart: much less from a certain confidence in God, or from charity toward one's neighbor.

The Apostle establishes four species of serious invocation of God: 1. deēsis, supplication or petition, which we direct to God for ourselves, that He may either clearly forgive us the punishments we have deserved: or mitigate and take away those already sent, according to the good pleasure of His will, and for the benefit of our salvation. 2. enteuxis, intercession, by which we intercede for others before God, that He may either impart to them some good, whether bodily or spiritual: or avert some evil from them. 3. proseuchē, prayer, by which we ask of God that goods, whether spiritual or bodily, be conferred upon us: with that distinction observed which will be shown below. 4. eucharistia, thanksgiving for the beneficence of God, bestowed either upon ourselves or upon others. 1 Tim. 2, verse 1. Although indeed these four species differ somewhat by reason of their end: yet they share in object and causes in such a way that in every serious and perfect prayer they always concur and exist together: especially if our prayers are composed (which ought by all means to be done) according to the formula of the Lord's Prayer.

Concerning this serious and true invocation of God, therefore, and what its proper nature and affection is, we must next examine more accurately. Scarcely, however, will a more convenient method of treatment be shown than if the primary questions, which indeed [arise] concerning invocation We shall explain in order those things that deserve the observation of GOD. Of these, eight occur primarily. I. is: Is it a matter of some necessity to call upon GOD? II. Is it GOD alone? III. Through Whom? IV. How? V. Where and When? VI. In what language? VII. For whom? VIII. And lastly, with what certainty of being heard ought GOD to be called upon? Concerning each of these, it will be profitable to observe those things whose use in the following dispute against the Romanists may be of the greatest importance.

Latin:

LOcum de cruce & afflictionibus, rectissimo ordine excipit tractatio de Invocatione DEI. Quemadmodum enim pii in angustiis constituti requirunt DOMINUM, Jesa. 26. v. 16. ita efficacior consolatio nulla iisdem obtingere potest, quàm quæ ex Invocatione DEI, certissimaqve precum exauditione, secundum illud Davidis: Nisi Lex tua DOMIN E mea fuisset consolatio, periissem in afflictione mea. Psalm. 119. vers. 92. Quæ ipsa causa sine dubio fuit, quòd Autor noster Locum hunc & prolixiùs & accuratiùs pertractare voluit.

Nam primùm disserit tùm de usu maximo rectæ invocationis: tùm de gemino discrimine, quod Christianorum & gentilium invocationi invicem intercedit, dum nimirùm hi partim ignorant, qualem se DEUS secundum essentiam suam patefecerit: partim verò de Voluntate DEI erga peccatores, in Evangelio revelata, nihil quicquam noverunt.

Deinde disputat de Objecto, materia, & causis impulsivis Invocationis. Objectum constituit solum DEUM: Materiam, bona Corporalia & Spiritualia: Causas impulsivas tres: mandatum DEI: promissiones de exauditione: Fidem, ejusq; πληροφορίαν, in promissionibus acquiescentem.

Tertiò præscribit certas quasdam Orandi formulas: & Orationem Dominicam accuratè secundùm singula præcepta explicat.

Quartò & postremò disputat de Invocatione Sanctorum contra Romanenses: simulque invehitur in stupendam hominum ἀχαριστίαν erga Deum : certis quibusdam præscriptis Gratiarum actionum formulis. Et his quidem quatuor partibus constat ac absolvitur universa Tractatio Philippea.

Nos iisdem partim insistentes vestigiis: partim verò præsentis seculi controversias, & Esawitarum potissimùm Theologiam, hoc loco, pressiùs considerantes, duo constituimus Tractationis nostræ capita generalia : Prius quidem θετικὸν, puriorem διδασκαλίαν de Rectâ invocatione DEI proponet : Posterius autem ἀντιθετικὸν, expediet ἔλεγχον sive refutationem crassissimorum errorum, quibus tùm Hæretici alii, tùm imprimis Esawitæ, ὀρθοδοξίας hujus Articuli fœdissimè conspurcârunt, hodieq; consparcant.

CAPVT I. De Invocatione DEI vera, doctrinæ θετικῆς.

INvocatio DEI in Scripturis interdum nominatur Oratio, interdum cultus DEI. Oratio quidem, respectu Instrumenti. quò plerumque peragitur, quod est Os corporis. Cultus verò respectu DEI, ad quem Invocatio sive Oratio unicè dirigitur. Æquipollet enim hæc vox Græco vocabulo λατρείας, quod religiosam venerationem significat. Hoc respectu, Invocationis termino aliquam ὁμωνυμίαν inesse deprehenditur: ita ut interdum strictè tantùm pro cultu, sive religiosa adoratione DEI accipiatur: interdum verò laxè quamlibet implorationem auxilii, quæ etiam fit ab hominibus viventibus adhuc: notet. Scriptura enim haud obscurè multis in locis testatur, implorationem auxilii dirigi etiam posse ad Creaturas, non quidem rationis expertes, sive sint animalia, sive sint inanima: ut astra, & id genus Φυσικὰ. Nam præterquàm quod stultum & insanum foret, ejusmodi creaturas invocare, quæ nec intellectu, nec voluntate, nec viribus ad juvandum præditæ sunt: in ipso certè DEI Verbo, talis invocatio, in Gentilibus, tanquam execranda Idololatria damnatur: id quod ex Prophetarum concionibus cap. 1. ad Romanos videre est. Verùm ad Creaturas rationales, hoc est, ad homines viventes, in externis & corporalibus implorationem auxilii dirigi posse, ex Scripturis manifestum est. Jacobus certè cap. 5. v. 14.

mandat, ut si quis aegrotet, accersat Presbyteros, qui orent super eum: Ubi sanè, accersere Presbyteros nihil est aliud, quàm ipsorum preces ac intercessiones ad Deum efflagitare. Sic Apostolus praecipit, ut alter pro altero oret: imò semetipsum saepissimè commendat precibus Ecclesiae.

Sic praecipit Siracides, cap. 38. v. 1. & seqq. ut conflictantes cum morbis, in auxilium vocemus Medicos. Et Scriptura passim monet, ut in calamitatibus privatis ac publicis, auxilia aliorum imploremus, nosque invicem juvemus. Caeterùm de hac generali invocationis specie hoc loco nobis non est propriè dissertatio: sed de ea tantùm, qua religiosè & vera cum fiducia in omnibus necessitatibus, invocamus Deum, tanquàm Unum ac primum omnium auxiliorum autorem, & directorem.

Haec Invocatio religiosa est vel Interna, vel Externa. Interna, quae fit tantùm mente, sive internis mentis gemitibus ac suspiriis: Externa, quae simul fit corde & ore, ac externis gestibus: voce sive cantu: de qua infrà suo loco dicendum erit. Utraque haec, vel Seria est, vel Hypocritica. De seria ex professo nobis deinceps futura disputatio. Hypocritica est, quae dat fine mente sonum, hoc est, Deum quidem externis labiis invocat: sed non ex corde: multò minùs ex certa fiducia in Deum, aut ex charitate proximi proficiscitur.

Seriae Invocationis DEI, Apostolus quatuor constituit species: 1. δέησιν precationem sive petitionem, quam dirigimus ad Deum pro nobis ipsis, ut vel poenas promeritas planè nobis condonet: vel jam immissas mitiget & auferat, pro beneplacito voluntatis suae, & salutis nostrae emolumento. 2. ἔντευξιν Intercessionem, qua pro aliis apud Deum intercedimus, ut vel bonum aliquod sive corporale, sive spirituale illis impertiat: vel malum aliquod ab ipsis avertat. 3. προσευχὴν Orationem, qua à DEO petimus, nobis conferri bona vel spiritualia, vel corporalia: eo observato discrimine, quòd infrà monstrabitur. 4. εὐχαριστίαν Gratiarum actionem pro DEI beneficentia, vel nobis ipsis, vel aliis praestita. 1 Tim. 2. v. 1. Quanquam verò quatuor hae species ratione finis nonnihil differunt: Objecto tamen & causis ita communicant, ut in omni Oratione seria & perfecta semper concurrant, & simul sint: praesertim si ad formulam Orationis Dominicae, preces nostrae, (id quod fieri omninò debet) componantur.

De hac ergo seria & vera Invocatione DEI, & quae propria ipsius sit natura atq; affectio, nobis deinceps accuratiùs dispiciendum. Vix autem commodior Tractationis Methodus monstrabitur, quàm si primarias Quaestiones, que quidem circa Invocationem DEI observationem merentur, ordine explicaverimus. Earum verò octo potissimùm occurrunt. I. est: An neßitatis alicujus sit Invocare DEVM? II. An solus DEVS? III. per Quem? IV. Quomodo? V. Vbi & Quando? VI. Quâ linguâ? VII. Pro quibus ? IIX. & postremò, Quâ exauditionis certitudine DEVS invocari debeat? De quibus singulis ea observare proderit, quorum usus insubsequenti disputatione contra Romanenses possit esse maximus.


### Whether God is to be invoked

The observation of this question is most necessary, partly against Epicureans and profane men, but partly against the Sacramentarians. For the former dream that it is absurd if it be posited that GOD is moved by human prayers; indeed, that there is no need for prayers at all, because GOD no longer takes care of us, or certainly, being good and beneficent by his own nature, he confers necessary goods upon us if he wills; but if he does not will it, he is wearied in vain by our prayers. The latter, however, namely the Sacramentarians, utterly remove every necessity of praying from the midst, as long as they persist in fighting for an absolute decree of GOD, preceding all causes, regarding our salvation and reprobation. For that which is absolute does not admit of intermediate causes, and, by the admission of the Calvinists themselves, not even faith in Christ. Therefore, with such an absolute decree of both Salvation and Reprobation standing: I would have called upon GOD in vain, whether for the granting of eternal salvation to me: or for the averting of eternal damnation likewise. For if I am chosen for the former, or destined for the latter by the immutable and absolute will of GOD from eternity, it is necessary that either one or the other must necessarily and immutably befall me. This is, of course, to uproot all piety and to eliminate the pursuit of all prayers from the Church of GOD: or certainly to concede prayers only as some mark and token of the Elect, or as a fruit of absolute Election; but meanwhile to simply deny and overturn all their power regarding the promoting and preserving of our salvation, as well as for the averting of eternal damnation.

Therefore, our Churches, making a divorce from these impieties, posit and teach that the Invocation of GOD is not ἀδιάφορον, free or indifferent, and placed in our own judgment: but simply and absolutely necessary, for the following five causes.

I. The cause is the Command of GOD, who seriously seeks this worship from us: Psalm 27:8. My heart thinks of your word: Seek my face: Therefore I seek your face.

Psalm 50:15. Call upon me in the day of trouble and I will deliver you: and you shall glorify me. Isaiah 55:6. Seek the LORD, while he can be found: call upon him, while he is near. Matthew 7:7. Ask, and it shall be given to you: Seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you. 1 Timothy 2:1. I exhort, that before all things supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men.

Our Reason objects two things primarily to this first cause. For first, it concludes thus: GOD is omniscient, and takes care of us; therefore it is not necessary that he be brought to mind by prayers as to what things we are in need of. The antecedent is evident from Scripture itself: Hebrews 4:13. All things are naked and open to his eyes. Psalm 121:4. Behold, he who keeps Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep: Matthew 6:31 and 32. Do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or what shall we wear? The Gentiles seek all these things: For your Father knows that you need all these things.

Then, however, Reason clamors in this manner: GOD bestows all things, even without our prayers, just as he lets his Sun rise without our prayers. Isaiah 65:24. Before they call, I will answer. Psalm 21:4. You have prevented him with blessings of goodness. Matthew 6:8. That Father of yours knows what you have need of, before you ask him. Therefore, Prayers, or the Invocation of GOD, is not necessary.

And such was the force of these arguments, that as Clement of Alexandria testifies in book 7 of the Stromata, already long ago, soon after the times of the Apostles, there were heretics who contended that neither prayers nor sacrifices ought to be offered to GOD, for the reason that GOD takes no pleasure in these.

But the most vain vanity of both cavils is manifest in itself. For the antecedent of the former is destitute of any refutation: and a gross Sophism of a faulty consequent is committed, nay, a most shameful begging of the Principle. For it does not follow: GOD knows all things. Therefore He ought not to be invoked. For this very thing is in question, whether GOD ought to be invoked for the reason that He knows all things? Where we hold the affirmative, and maintain that GOD ought to be invoked precisely because He has all our tears and sighs numbered, and commands that help be sought from Him.

The latter cavil also labors under this same twin Sophistication. For the consequent does not follow from the antecedent. Because the argument is again inverted, and we infer: For this very reason GOD ought to be invoked more ardently. For if GOD grants all things even without our prayers: Therefore, much more, He will grant many more and more excellent things, when invoked by us: not indeed because of the dignity of our prayers, but because of the immovable certainty of His promises. Therefore, the Sophistication of Begging the Principle emerges from this as well. For this very thing would have to be proven, that GOD ought not to be invoked for the reason that He grants all things to the pious without our prayers.

The second impulsive cause of prayer is the certainty and infallibility of divine promises. For GOD, when invoked through and on account of Christ the Mediator, has so holily pledged that He will hear our vows and prayers, that unless He were willing to deny Himself, or rather to cease to be and remain GOD, He must needs be affected by our necessities and bring aid to them: according to the sweetest promises: Ps. 145, 18 & 19. The LORD is near to all who call upon Him: to all who call upon Him in truth: He will fulfill the desire of those who fear Him, and will hear their supplication, and will save them.

Isa. 65, 24. And it shall come to pass, that before they call, I will answer: while they are yet speaking, I will hear.

Matt. 7, 7 & 8. Everyone who asks, receives: he who seeks, finds: and to him who knocks, it will be opened.

Matt. 11, 28. Come to me all you who labor, and are burdened: I will refresh you.

John 14, 13 & 14. Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son: If you ask anything in my name: I will do it.

John 16, 23. Amen, amen I say to you, if you ask anything of the Father in my name, He will give it to you.

James 5, 15. The prayer of faith will heal the sick, and the LORD will raise him up, and if he be in sins, it will be forgiven him.

The Jesuitical race strives in a wonderful manner to corrupt, obscure, and turn into a snare of desperation these sweetest promises concerning the most certain hearing of the prayers of the faithful: relying on these little arguments.

I. Promises are of benefit to those who keep the law: But those who pray from faith alone, and are destitute of good works and their own merits, do not keep the law. Therefore, the promises concerning the certainty of being heard are of no benefit to them.

II. A conditional promise renders no one certain. But the promise concerning being heard and aid has an annexed condition of the divine will. Therefore, it does not render us certain of being heard and of aid.

III. Many who even invoke GOD, oppressed by calamities, succumb and are not heard: Therefore, the certainty of being heard does not depend on the promises of aid.

IV. King Hezekiah, calling upon the LORD in his distress, does not recall to God those promises, but rather his own merits, saying: Remember, O LORD, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in thy sight. 2 Kings 20:3. Therefore, in prayer, one must rely rather on our merits than on bare promises.

V. Thus David, Psalm 7:9 and elsewhere throughout, asks to be heard on account of his own righteousness, saying: Judge me, O GOD, according to my righteousness, and according to mine integrity. Therefore, where there is not properly righteousness and holiness, promises concerning the hearing of prayers are of no avail.

But the impiety of those arguments is revealed of its own accord if they are examined according to the analogy of faith, as an infallible Cynosure of Truth.

THE FIRST, therefore, fails by a base Sophism

ὁμωνυμίας ἑτεροζητήσεως. For there are two kinds of divine promises. For some are Legal: but others are Evangelical. The argument therefore concludes truly indeed concerning legal promises, the utility of which is nothing unless the fulfillment of the law through our good works and merits is added: but it concludes falsely concerning Evangelical promises, which, by reason of us, are purely gratuitous. Now, promises concerning the hearing of prayers are Evangelical, being founded solely in the mercy of GOD through and on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith: without any regard to our dignity, works, or merits: Just as Daniel by his example taught us to pray, chapter 9:18. Incline, O my GOD, thine ear, and hear: open thine eyes, and behold our desolations, and the City, upon which thy name is called: for we do not present our supplications before thy face for our righteousnesses: but for thy great mercies. Hear, O LORD; O LORD, forgive; hearken and do; defer not, FOR THINE OWN SAKE, O my GOD, etc. Taught by this example and the practice of all the pious, in our prayers we rely not on legal promises, which place the fulfillment of the Law and the merits of Works as the foundation of being heard: but on Evangelical promises, which do not demand the fulfillment of the Law from us: but are founded solely in the mercy of GOD on account of the merit of Christ: and are therefore far most certain.

THE SECOND Argument labors under the same faults, and is true only concerning legal promises, the condition of which can render no one certain of being heard, because no one performs to the Law the perfect obedience which GOD in the Law demands from the followers of the law: but it is most false concerning Evangelical promises, which do not bind the will of GOD concerning helping and hearing us to any condition of our dignity: but entirely to the merciful will of GOD, by which He wills to hear all who call upon Him through Christ.

THE THIRD Argument fails by the Sophism ὧδε τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον, καὶ τὸ πῆ καὶ παρεξ ἁπλῶς. For 1. Promises concerning being heard, in corporal matters, always have the exception of the Cross annexed: Where GOD, who is supremely good, knows it to be for our salvation that He does not always hear us according to our pleasure. But from this, the Consequence does not hold for overturning the common rule concerning the certainty of promises. For the reasons are constant with GOD, for which He does not always hear us in corporal matters: and because we submit ourselves and all that is ours to His will in this kind of goods, GOD surely hears us even then, when He denies what we ask: as will be shown below concerning Being Heard.
