For the former, indeed, that GOD may be willing to grant them a sounder mind and lead them to repentance: Matt. 5:44. but for the latter, that GOD may be willing to perfect and consummate that good work which He began in them; and that He may be willing to deliver them, and especially the Church, from all evil. And such assiduous prayer of the righteous avails much before GOD, as James testifies, ch. 5:16. Isa. 1:15, When you spread out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you: and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear: for your hands are full of blood. Acts 10:4, The prayers of Cornelius are read to have ascended into the sight of the LORD, because they were joined with alms.

3. Assiduity, Constancy, and perseverance in praying. For every remission, languor, and sloth argues a defect of faith: And again, the more excellent the faith is, the more ardent the zeal, and the more fervent the Spirit, entices and inflames a man to pray repeatedly. Hence that saying of the Savior, and Luke 18:1, It is necessary to pray always, and not to faint: And the Apostle 1 Thess. 5:17, Pray without ceasing. This note, however, is not to be taken in the sense in which the Hermits of old, and the Monks and Nuns of today, take it, as if one must be so vacant for the study of prayers that it is not even permitted to perform the duties of a legitimate vocation, nor to carry out other things pertaining to civil society with a good and uninjured conscience—even neglecting and interrupting the exercises of prayer for some time—nay, it is hardly permitted to sleep. Whence in the Papacy the custom has grown that even at night at certain hours one must rise from sleep and be vacant for prayers. But this whole religion of the Romanists and Hermits is impious and superstitious, since it is defiled by the opinion of merit and of some singular holiness: and therefore hateful and abominable to GOD. Furthermore, it does not attain the genuine mind and sense of Scripture. For the Savior and the Apostle do not look to the perpetuity of the act of praying, but rather to the affection and the fervor of the Spirit, which, even if it is occupied with civil, or economic, or natural, or other legitimate matters, nevertheless always and everywhere proclaims the goodness of GOD in its heart, and groans that He may further do us good. For this is the nature of true faith, that it never rests, but always burns in our heart, although in the second act it does not always erupt into voices and external gestures. And in this respect, the faithful are said to pray always and incessantly, and never to faint, or as the Savior speaks, to cry out day and night: insofar as they are governed and burn with a perpetual affection of piety and fear toward GOD, and an incessant desire for their own salvation and that of their neighbor, even amidst the very works of their vocation.

4. True purity of Heart. For although the Renewal and Sanctification of our mind, in this life, is never perfect or absolute in all respects, without some infirmity and sin occasionally creeping in even among the pious and the elect: and therefore every most holy person has need to pray for the remission of sins, Ps. 32:6. Yet the reborn strive that they may not have the will and desire to sin, nor loosen the reins to the depraved concupiscences of the flesh, and thus rush into crimes and wicked deeds against their conscience: but rather they crucify the flesh with all its concupiscences, Gal. 5:24, Rom. 6:6, lest sin reign in their mortal body, that they should obey its concupiscences: nor do they present their members as weapons of injustice to sin: but they present themselves to GOD, as living from the dead, and their members as weapons of justice to GOD: as the Apostle speaks, Rom. 6:12 & 13. And this is to lift up pure hands to GOD, without wrath and disputing, 1 Tim. 2:8. And to worship the Father in Spirit and Truth, John 4:23, that is, sincerely and without hypocrisy. For if, says Ambrose on this passage, we conduct ourselves rightly, the Holy Spirit remains in us, and what we ask, we are able to obtain: This, therefore, is to pray always in the Spirit, to direct prayers to GOD with a clean conscience and integral faith. For he prays in the Flesh who prays with a polluted mind.

5. Undoubted hope of being heard, and patiently acquiescing in the will of GOD: By the example of the Saints, and especially of David, Ps. 40:2 & 3, Waiting I waited for the LORD, and He inclined Himself to me, and heard my prayers: and Ps. 130:5 & 6, My soul has waited in His Word: and my soul has hoped in the LORD, from the morning watch even to the night, let Israel hope in the LORD. Likewise by the example of Job crying out, ch. 13:15, Even if the LORD should kill me, yet I will hope in Him: And He Himself shall be my Savior.

Therefore, let not the delay of being heard break off the study and fervor of praying. For this would be nothing else than to tempt GOD, and out of impatience to murmur against Him: which is what GOD is accustomed to punish gravely: as can be seen in Saul, who, when he did not immediately receive an answer from GOD, decided that GOD was no longer to be consulted: and by this pact he not only suffered the loss of being heard, but also exposed himself to punishments both temporal and eternal. 1 Sam. 14:20, and in the whole history of Saul.

6. Right information of prayers, both regarding the internal gestures of the mind and the external gestures of the Body. Of the internal, it has been spoken thus far. If these are present, it cannot be but that the external gestures, expressing such an affection of the mind, will follow. But external gestures are partly privative, partly positive. The privative ones remove those vices which violate and defile the correct form of praying: such as: Βαττολογία, that is, the empty murmuring of long and many prayers, without a serious movement and affection of the heart, and also without faith. This is vicious. 1. Because it is condemned by Christ the Savior, Matt. 6, v. 7. When you pray, do not be talkative. 2. Because it is proper to the Gentiles, whose worship and religion does not befit Christians, Matt. 6, v. 7 & 8. 3. Because God is worshipped in vain by the external movement of the lips, but without a faithful affection of the heart: Isa. 29, v. 13. Matt. 15, v. 8. And therefore it is frustrated of all hope of being heard. Isa. 1, v. 15. Matt. 6, v. 7. But just as such an empty murmuring of long and many prayers, made without faith and Spirit, is deservedly condemned among the Papists and other fanatics: so a long prayer ought not to be judged as such, which proceeds from true faith, however much it may consist of a prolixity of words and phrases, and even the frequent repetition of the same petition. For this is, as it were, the peculiar passion of the pious and the Elect groaning under the Cross, that they, as it were, stumble and fluctuate in prayer, and repeat the same things again and again: and the more ardently they pray, the more frequently they inculcate to God the truth of his promises and his mercy: which can be seen especially from the Psalms of David. And it is too ignorantly objected in this place, that saying of Ecclesiasticus 7, 15. In prayer do not repeat your petition: Since it is clear by itself that this must be understood of empty and superstitious garrulity and Βαττολογία at least: unless perhaps we wish to condemn the prayers of all the Saints, especially David and Daniel, which were sufficiently prolix and consisted of the frequent petition of the same benefit.

The second vice results from the former, and is Ambition, by which one strives to hunt for a singular appearance of holiness and an aura of glory among men from the murmuring of long and many prayers: which is the property of all hypocrites, and especially in our time of the Capuchins and Esauites. This vice is condemned in express words by Christ the Savior. Matt. 6, v. 5.

The third vice is the petition for another's property, which proceeds from avarice. Now just as avarice is the root of all evils, 1 Tim. 6, v. 10. So it is accustomed to be the mother of every divine curse: so far is it from the case that such a prayer obtains anything from God.

Finally, let every anger and desire for revenge also be avoided, by which we wish evil and pray against those to whom we are hostile. For such an imprecation, for the most part by the just judgment of God, falls back upon the head of him who prays in this way. Whence the Apostle wishes us to pray without anger and disputation: 1 Tim. 2, v. 8.

Positive external gestures can scarcely be defined exactly: since the internal affection of the mind for the most part moves and rules them. And although GOD does not properly and principally look upon such gestures, but requires a right heart and wishes to be worshipped in Spirit and in truth: yet because the body is moved by the mind, it cannot be but that just as the mind is affected, so also the body is moved externally: and therefore such gestures also, proceeding from a right and pure heart, please GOD: especially those which breathe and reflect the internal humility of the mind. Scripture notes such gestures in the Saints: the beating of the breast, the spreading of the hands, the uncovering of the head, the lifting of the eyes to heaven, the lowering of the same to the earth, tears, crying out, but especially kneeling, which the Evangelical history testifies that the Savior also used in the garden, and that he fell down even to the ground. But if any opinion of worship, or merit, or dignity, or holiness is attached to such external gestures: we determine that this is idolatrous, superstitious, and hateful to God. For which reason we deservedly reject and condemn as idolatrous both the ancient practice of the Baalitic priests, lacerating themselves with small swords and spears until the blood flowed, and the sacks, ashes, sleeping on the ground, flagellations, and similar gestures of the modern Romanists.

And thus we have so far explained the principal matters which are required in the Person of the one praying. It follows that we show what Conditions are to be observed concerning the object of Prayer.

At the beginning, however, it is confessed among all the pious that nothing at all is to be sought from GOD which is not contained in the Scriptures, either explicitly or implicitly, by way of either a commandment or a promise. For such a prayer would be nothing other than a presumptuous rashness, by which a man might wish to tempt GOD, to see whether He himself could be swayed by prayers to grant those things which simply conflict with the will of GOD, or are clearly contrary to the order of nature.

Furthermore, the object of things to be sought is handed down in the Scriptures as twofold: one of spiritual things, and those looking toward our salvation; the other of corporal things, concerning the sustenance of this life, society, and political peace, and the remaining goods of fortune and the body. Concerning both being sought from GOD, we have in the Scriptures commandments and promises that are by far most clear: with the observation of this diversity, however, that we always seek corporal goods with this condition, if indeed the will of GOD so carries it, if it makes for the promoting of the glory of GOD, and also our own salvation and that of our neighbor: by the example of Christ praying: Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.

Matth. 26. v. 39. But spiritual things are without any condition or exception, since they depend solely upon the revealed will of GOD concerning our salvation. For whoever would frame prayers conditionally in this kind of things to be requested: he would either be ignorant of, or call into doubt, the universal will of GOD and the ardent desire of GOD concerning the salvation of the whole human race: the former of which would be of stupendous negligence, but the latter of prodigious blasphemy and impiety. Let the Calvinists see to it, however, in this place, whether they themselves dare to ask of GOD, and hope for, without condition, those things which make for their own eternal salvation. For whoever, according to the doctrine of the Calvinists, believes and maintains: that GOD from eternity made a certain absolute decree concerning a few certain persons to be absolutely saved, and to be endowed with persevering faith: he is certainly destitute of all πληροφορία [full assurance], which he ought to have had in that universal and revealed will of GOD concerning all men being endowed with faith and eternally saved, unless they themselves contemptuously reject and despise this purpose of GOD. But where such πληροφορία [full assurance] is exiled: there doubt and disputation reign. Now, however, he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, which is driven and tossed by the winds: let not such a man, therefore, think that he will receive anything from GOD. James 1. v. 6. & 7. And this is the confidence, says John, that we have toward GOD: That whatever we ask according to his will, he hears us: And we know that he hears us, whatever we ask, we know that we have the petitions which we request from him. 1. John 5. v. 14. & 15.

Latin:

Utraque hæc in verâ in vocatione DEI maximè requiritur: siquidem Finis legis & præceptorum DEI est Charitas de corde puro, & conscientiâ bonâ, & fide non fictâ: 1. Tim. 1. 5. Quòd si ergò sine Charitate hæc, nullum DEI præceptum verè servari poterit: utique sine eâ neq; illud servabitur, quod est de rectè invocando DEO. Hinc in sacris, omnis eorum, qui charitate hæc destituebantur, cultus, quantumvis sanctus, religiosus & splendidus, DEO abominatio fuisse legitur: Ut Proverb. 12. v. 13. Qui obturat aurem suam ad clamorem pauperis, & ipse clamabit, sed non exaudietur. Et hinc est, quòd Veri adoratores, non pro suis tantùm, & nostrorum necessitatibus: sed & pro aliis, & quidem tàm pro inimicis & hostibus, quàm pro fratribus & amicis nostris. Pro illis quidem, ut DEUS saniorem largiri ipsis mentem, & ad pœnitentiam adducere velit: Matth. 5. v. 44. pro his verò, ut DEUS bonum illud opus, quod in ipsis cœpit, perficere & consummare: eosq; & cum primis Ecclesiam ab omni malo liberare velit. Et talis Oratio justi assidua multùm valet apud DEUM, teste Jacobo, cap. 5. v. 16. Jes. 1. v. 15. Cùm extenderitis manus vestras, avertam oculos meos à vobis: & cùm multiplicaveritis orationem, non exaudiam: Manus enim vestræ sanguine plenæ sunt. Actor. 10 v. 4. Orationes Cornelii in conspectum DOMINI ascendisse leguntur, eò quòd cum eleemosynis conjunctæ erant.

3. Assiduitas, Constantia & perseverantia in precando. Omnis enim remissio, languor & socordia arguit defectum fidei: Et rursus, Quò excellentior est fides, eò ardentius studium, & ferventior Spiritus ad precandum subindè hominem allicit & inflammat. Hinc illud Servatoris, & Luc. 18. v. 1. Oportet semper orare, & non deficere: Et Apostolus 1. Thess 5. 17. Sine intermissione orate. Est verò nota hæc non eo accipienda sensu, quo olim Eremitæ, & hodie Monachi, & Montales eam accipiunt, ac si ita precum studio sit vacandum, ut ne quidem legitimæ vocationis munera obire, neque alia ad civilem societatem spectantia, bonâ atque illæsâ conscientiâ, neglectis etiam ac interruptis aliquamdiu precum exercitiis, peragere, imò vix dormire liceat. Unde in Papatu Consuetudo inolevit, ut noctu etiam certis horis è somno sit surgendum, & precibus vacandum. Verùm tota hæc Romanensium & Eremitarum Religio est impia & superstitiosa, quippe opinione meriti, & singularis alicujus sanctitatis, conspurcata: ac proinde DEO exosa & abominabilis. Deinde mentem & sensum Scripturæ genuinum non assequitur. Servator enim & Apostolus non actus precandi perpetuitatem, sed affectus potiùs, & Spiritus fervorem respiciunt, qui si maximè vel civilibus, vel Oeconomicis, vel naturalibus, vel rebus aliis legitimis sit occupatus, semper tamen & ubique in corde suo DEI bonitatem prædicat, & ut porrò nobis benefaciat, ingemiscit. Hæc enim veræ fidei est natura, ut nunquàm quiescat, sed semper ardeat in Corde nostro, licet actu secundo non semper in voces & gestus externos erumpat. Et hoc respectu dicuntur fideles semper & indefinenter orare, & nunquàm deficere, vel ut Servator loquitur, die ac nocte clamare: quatenus perpetuo pietatis, & timoris affectu erga DEUM, & indefinenti desiderio salutis & suæ & proximi, inter ipsa etiam vocationis opera, reguntur & ardent.

4. Vera Cordis puritas Etsi enim Renovatio & Sanctificatio mentis nostræ, hac quidem in vita, nunquam est perfecta, aut omnibus numeris absoluta, quin infirmitatis & peccati aliquid subinde in piis etiam & electis obrepat: ac proinde sanctissimus quisque pro Peccatorum remissione orare necesse habeat, Psal.32.v.6. Operam tamen dant renati, ut voluntatem & desiderium peccandi non habeant, neque frena laxent pravis concupiscentiis carnis, & sic in scelera & flagitia ruant contra conscientiam: sed crucifigunt potiùs carnem cum omnibus suis concupiscentiis Gal. 5. v. 24. Rom.6.v.6. ne regnet peccatum in mortali ipsorum corpore, ut obediant concupiscentiis ejus: nec exhibeant membra sua arma injustitiæ peccato: sed exhibeant se DEO, tanquam ex mortuis viventes, & membra sua arma justitiæ DEO: ut loquitur Apostolus, Rom. 6. v. 12. & 13. Et hoc est, puras levare manus ad DEUM, sine irâ & disceptatione, 1. Tim. 2. v. 8. Et adorare Patrem in Spiritu & Veritate, Joh.4.v.23. hoc est, sincerè, ac sine hypocrisi. Si enim, inquit, Ambrosius super hunc locum, rectè conversemur, Spiritus Sanctus manet in nobis, & quod postulamus, possumus impetrare: Hoc est ergò in Spiritu semper orare, mundâ conscientiâ & fide integrâ preces ad DEUM dirigere. In Carne enim orat, qui pollutâ mente precatur.

5. Spes indubia de exauditione, & patienter acquiescens in voluntate DEI: Exemplo Sanctorum, & præcipuè Davidis, Psal. 40. v. 2. & 3. Expectans expectavi DOMINUM, & inclinavit se ad me, & exaudivit preces meas: & Psal 130. 5. & 6. Sustinuit anima mea in Verbo ejus: & speravit anima mea in DOMINO, à custodiâ matutinâ usq; ad noctem, speret Israel in DOMINO. Exemplo item Jobis exclamantis cap. 13.v.15. Etiamsi occiderit me DOMINUS; tamen sperabo in ipsum: Et ipse erit Salvator meus.

Non ergò exauditionis mora abrumpat studium & fervorem precandi. Hoc enim nihil esset aliud, quàm tentare DEUM, & ex impatientiâ murmurare contra ipsum: id quod DEUS graviter punire solet: uti videre est in Saule, qui cùm non illicò responsum à DEO acciperet, statuit DEUM non amplius esse consulendum: & hoc pacto non modò exauditionis jacturam fecit:sed & pœnis tum temporalibus, tum æternis seipsum objecit. 1. Sam. 14. v. 20. & in totâ historiâ Saulis.

6. Recta precum informatio, tum quoad internos animi, tùm quoad externos Corporis gestus. De internis hactenus dictum. Hi si adsint, fieri nequit, quin etiam externi gestus, talem animi affectum exprimentes consequantur. Sunt verò externi gestus partim privativi: partim positivi. Privativi tollunt ea vitia, quæ rectam precandi formam violant & conspurcant: Qualia sunt: Βαττολογία, hoc est, inanis, & sine serio cordis motu & affectu, ut & sine fide effusa longarum multarumque precum demurmuratio. Hæc vitiosa est. 1. Quia à Christo Servatore damnata, Matth. 6. v. 7. Cùm oratis, ne sitis multiloqui. 2. Quia Ethnicorum est propria, quorum cultus & religio Christianis non convenit, Matth. 6. v. 7. & 8. 3. Quia frustrà colitur Deus externo labiorum motu, sine verò & fideli cordis affectu: Jesa. 29. v. 13. Matth. 15. v. 8. Ac proinde omni exauditionis spe frustratur. Jesa. 1. v. 15. Matth. 6. v. 7. Quemadmodum verò talis inanis longarum, multarumq; precum, sine fide, & Spiritu facta demurmuratio, in Pontificiis, aliisq; Sanctulis meritò damnatur: Ita longa Oratio censeri non debet, quæ ex fide verâ proficiscitur, quantumvis etiam ea verborum ac phraseωn prolixitate, ejusdemq; etiam petitionis crebrâ repetitione constet. Hoc enim piorum & Electorum sub Cruce gementium ἴδιον quasi παθος est, ut in Oratione quasi cespitent & fluctuent, eademque subinde repetant: & quò ardentius orant, eò crebrius Deo subinde veritatem promissionum ipsius, & misericordiam inculcent: id quod ex Psalmis Davidis cumprimis videre licet. Et inscitè nimis hoc loco objicitur illud Ecclesiastici 7, 15. In Oratione ne reiteres petitionem tuam: Siquidem de inani saltem & superstitiosâ garrulitate & Βαττολογία illud intelligendum esse, per se liquet: nisi fortassis omnium Sanctorum, Davidis cumprimis, & Danielis precationes, satis & prolixas, & crebrâ ejusdem beneficii petitione constantes, damnare velimus.

Alterum vitium ex priore resultat, & est Ambitio, quâ quis ex longarum, multarumq; precum demurmuratione, singularem Sanctitatis speciem, & gloriosæ auram apud homines aucupari studet: id quod hypocritaru omnium, & nostro cumprimis tempore Cappuzianorum ac Esavitarum est proprium. Damnatur hoc vitiu expressis verbis à Christo Servatore. Matth. 6. v. 5.

Tertium vitium est, alienæ rei petitio, quæ ex avaritiâ proficiscitur. Jam sicut avaritia radix est omnium malorum, 1. Timoth. 6. v. 10. Ita omnis etiam maledictionis divinæ mater esse consuevit: tantum abest, ut talis oratio quicquam à Deo impetret.

Tandem caveatur etiam omnis ira, vindictæ cupiditas, quâ malè ominamur & precamur iis, quibus infensi sumus. Talis enim imprecatio, plerumq; justo Dei judicio, in caput illius recidit, qui sic orat. Unde Apostolus vult nos orare sine ira & disceptatione: 1. Timoth. 2. v. 8.

Gestus externi positivi vix exactè definiri possunt : Siquidem hos internus animi affectus utplurimùm movet & regit. Et quanquam DEUS tales gestus propriè & principaliter non respicit : sed Cor rectum requirit, & adorari vult in Spiritu & veritate : quia tamen Corpus movetur ab animo, fieri nequit, quin sicut affectus est animus, sic etiam externè moveatur corpus : ac proinde hujusmodi etiam gestus ex corde recto & puro provenientes, DEO placeant : præsertim qui internam animi humilitatem spirant & referunt. Tales gestus in Sanctis notat Scriptura, Pectoris contusionem, manuum expansionem, denudationem capitis, oculorum elevationem ad cælum, eorundem depressionem ad terram, lachrymas, clamorem, cumprimis autem genuflexionem, quâ etiam Servatorem in horto usum, & in terram usque procubuisse, historia Evangelica testatur. Verùm si externis hujusmodi gestibus ulla affingatur opinio vel cultus, vel meriti, vel dignitatis, vel Sanctitatis: id Idololatricum, Superstitiosum, Deoque exosum esse statuimus. Quo etiam nomine tùm Veterem Baaliticorum Sacerdotum, gladiolis & spiculis ad sanguinis usque profluvium sese lacerantium: tum modernorum Romanensium saccos, cineres, chamæunias, flagellationes, & similes gestus, tanquam Idololatricos meritò rejicimus & damnamus.

Et sic hactenus præcipua προκείμενα, quæ in orantis Personâ requiruntur, expedivimus. Sequitur, ut quæ Conditiones circa Orationis objectum observandæ sint, ostendamus.

Initio autem apud pios omnes in confesso est, nihil quicquam à DEO esse petendum, cujus non vel præceptum, vel promissio in Sacris, sive explicitè sive implicitè contineatur. Talis enim Oratio nihil esset aliud, quàm præsumtuosa temeritas, qua homo tentare velit DEUM, an flecti ipse precibus possit ad præstanda ea, quæ cum voluntate DEI simpliciter pugnent, vel ordini naturæ planè sint contraria.

Deinde verò rerum petendarum Objectum in Scripturis traditur geminum : Unum rerum Spiritualium, & ad salutem nostram spectantium : Alterum rerum Corporalium, vitæ hujus sustentationem, societatem, & pacem politicam, reliquaq́; fortunarum & corporis bona concernentium. De utroq́; à DEO petendo & præcepta, & promissiones in Sacris habemus longè luculentissimas : sub eâ tamen diversitatis observatione, ut corporalia bona semper cum conditione hac petamus, si nimirum sic DEI ferat voluntas, si faciat ad promovendam DEI gloriam, nostram quoque & proximi salutem : exemplo Christi precantis : Pater, si fieri potest, transeat à me calix iste : Verùm non mea sed tua fiat voluntas.

Matth. 26. v. 39. Spiritualia verò sine ullâ vel conditione, vel exceptione, qvippe qvæ à revelatâ DEI voluntate de salute nostrâ unicè dependet. Qvi enim in hoc rerum petendarum genere preces conditionaliter informaret: is vel universalem DEI voluntatem & ardens DEI desiderium, de totius generis humani salute ignoraret, vel in dubium vocaret: quorum istud stupendæ foret oscitantiæ, hoc verò prodigiosæ blasphemiæ & impietatis. Viderint autem hoc loco Calviniani, num & ipsi sine conditione à DEO petere, & sperare ausint ea, qvæ ad salutem ipsorum æternam faciunt. Quicunqve enim secundum Calvinianorum doctrinam credit & statuit: DEUM ab æterno fecisse absolutum quoddam decretum, de paucis quibusdam iisdem absolutè salvandis, & fide perseverante donandis: is certè destituitur omni πληροφορία, quam in universali, & revelatâ illâ DEI voluntate, de omnibus hominibus fide donandis, & æternùm salvandis, nisi ipsimet hoc DEI propositum contemtim abjiciant & contemnant, habere debebat. Ubi verò talis exulat πληροφορία: ibi dubitatio & disceptatio regnat. Jam verò qui dubitat, similis est fluctui maris, qui ventis agitatur & jactatur: non ergo existimet talis homo, quòd à DEO aliquid sit accepturus. Jacob. 1. v. 6. & 7. Et hæc est fiducia, inquit Johannes, quam habemus ad DEUM: Quia quodcunq; petierimus secundum voluntatem ejus, audit nos: Et scimus, quia audit nos, quicquid petierimus scimus, quoniam habemus petitiones, quas postulamus ab eo. 1. Joh. 5. v. 14. & 15.


### Question V. Where to Pray, & When

Although in the Old Testament the invocation of GOD was as it were restricted and bound to a certain place, namely to the Mercy Seat, which was upon the ark of the covenant in the Tabernacle: and that for this reason, that thus through a certain illustrious Type, Christ might be shadowed forth, the promised Messiah of the world, that true and only propitiator of both Testaments, in whom, through whom, and for whose sake alone, GOD willed to be invoked: yet in the New Testament, after the Messiah of the World has now been exhibited, the invocation and prayers of Christians are not so superstitiously bound to a certain place or time: but rather it is permitted to lift up suppliant hands to GOD in every place, and always: Christ the Savior thus defining it, John 4. v. 21. 22. & 23. Believe me woman, the hour is coming, when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain, nor in Jerusalem: You worship what you do not know: We worship what we know: But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshipers will worship the Father in Spirit and Truth. For which very reason our same Savior, when the disciples asked to be instructed concerning the right form and manner of praying, prescribes no certain place or time: but leaving these to their own discretion. He prescribes how and what they ought to pray: When, saying, you wish to pray, say, Our Father, who art in heaven, &c. Matth. 6. v. 9. Luke 11. v. 2. What? that he does not want us to be so restricted to some public solemn place, that he rather asserts in express words that prayers poured out in some private place, whether a study or a bedroom, do not displease him, and prefers such prayers in every way to the public solemnities of Hypocrites: But you, he says, when you pray, enter into your room, and having closed the door, pray to your Father in secret: and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you: Matth. 6, 6. Thus the Apostle 1. Tim. 2, 8. I desire, he says, that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands.

And this is what Malachi once predicted, chap. 1. v. 11. From the rising of the Sun even to its setting, great is the name of GOD among the nations, and in every place a pure offering is sacrificed and offered to him.

Hence Augustine excellently: Why do you seek a suitable and holy place when about to supplicate GOD? Cleanse your inner parts, and having repelled every evil desire from there, prepare for yourself a secret place in the peace of your heart: Wishing to pray in a temple, pray in yourself, and act always so that you may be the temple of God: For God hears where he dwells.

Moreover, concerning this decision, two precipices of errors must be well avoided: One of the Enthusiasts, who, under the pretext of the sayings of Scripture already produced, simply disapprove and reject public and solemn prayers, which are made in temples by the whole people. For refuting which impiety, that one distinction suffices, by which some prayers are said to be private, and of any private men whatsoever: but others public, and of the whole Church. We readily concede that the former are not to be restricted by any determination of place or time: but that the latter cannot or ought not to be performed in some certain public place, hardly anyone would affirm, unless he who would dare to accuse GOD himself of impiety: who clearly declared concerning the Jerusalem temple: My house shall be called a house of prayer: Isa. 56. v. 7. Nay, the profanity of these fanatics proceeds even so far, that it presumes to rebuke Christ the Savior, because He did not hesitate to accommodate this prophetic [passage] to the time of the New Testament: Matt. 21. v. 13. John 2. v. 16. And what, I pray, will these men answer to the Apostles Peter and John, who are read to have gone up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer: Acts 3. v. 1. and to Paul, who is reported to have entered the temple also for the sake of performing the same worship: Acts 21, v. 26. But let these fanatics begone.

A SECOND precipice of error is objected in this place by the Romanists, who indeed stir up no dispute with us concerning private prayers: but in the question of public prayers, they corrupt both the words of the Savior, John 4. v. 21. etc. and of the Apostle, 1. Tim. 2. 8. with such a gloss: that GOD can indeed be invoked in every place: but in every place chosen, dedicated, and legitimately consecrated for this purpose: as a certain Jesuit of Dillingen did not hesitate to write in his assertions on this epistle of Paul.

He understands this Dedication, however, to be about that Consecration which is performed by a Bishop or suffragan through holy water, through feigned and counterfeit relics of the Saints, through votive offerings, and other superstitious rites which are accustomed to be used in the dedications of temples among the Papists. Against these superstitions the purer Church protests first as being manifestly impious: and on this account it accuses the Papal Church of impiety. Then it warns that one must carefully distinguish between times. For if they are tranquil and peaceful, so that prayers and supplications can and ought to be made by the whole Church in public temples, none of us has ever opposed this. But if the Church is pressed by persecution or other calamities: we maintain that public prayers can be piously made in every place, even one not yet chosen or dedicated; being thus taught by the Holy Spirit, Ps. 24, 1. The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof. Tit. 1, 15. To the pure all things are pure. Now foods also are sanctified through the word of GOD and prayer. 1 Tim. 4, 5. Why not also the earth, the sea, the woods, the mountains, the valleys, etc.? And let the Romanists remember that in this part they judaize. Since it is manifest that by Isaiah ch. 66, 1, and by Stephen the protomartyr, Acts 7, 48, the Jews were sharply rebuked because they imagined that GOD dwelt in temples made with hands, and was enclosed as it were by the walls of temples.

A difficult Question is raised at this point: Whether one should pray with any Church whatsoever, and thus with the Calvinist and Papal Church. For example: If some huge calamity should arise, and the Roman Pontiff should order public supplications to be made to God at certain hours, and should command the Lutherans to attend the same prayers, under threat of confiscation of goods or even the danger of life itself: Whether the Lutherans can, in this part, join themselves to the worship of the Papists with a good Conscience, or even attend under any pretext? The handle and occasion for this Question was provided by that Synod of the Jesuits and the counsel of certain mad-headed Romanist Bishops, by which in previous years they were the authors and persuaders to the Emperor and the Archdukes of Austria, that while the Turk was then raging more vehemently through Hungary, public Prayers and supplications, continued for forty whole hours, should be instituted in an Idolatrous or Papal temple, and that each and every Viennese subject of lower Austria should be forced to attend them. Where indeed a solid and Orthodox decision of this Question was desired by many: Which, although it is not without every danger, is nevertheless held and defended by us simply as Negative, for the following far most evident causes and reasons.

I. Prayer or Invocation is the chief part of divine worship. Therefore, such as the worship of GOD is among the Papists, such is their public Prayer. The reason for the connection is that worship ought to be estimated and defined by nothing other than the quality of the faith and Religion which publicly obtains in the Church of the Romanists. Now if that worship is by its nature impious and Idolatrous: it is necessary that their Prayer itself be of the same condition: especially since it is placed beyond all doubt that the Papists, according to the tenor of their Region, invoke 1. not only the One GOD, but also Mary the Mother of God, ever virgin, and other Saints. 2. They do not invoke GOD through Christ alone and his merit: but also through the works of supererogation of the Saints, Monks, and Nuns. Therefore, he who does not wish to participate in this Idolatry will never communicate in the Prayer of the Romanists with a good conscience. With this decision standing, it is clear that no orthodox person can pray with the Church of the Turks: because no communion of religion, faith, and worship exists for him with them. If a true Christian cannot pour out and join his prayers with the Synagogue of the Jews, because of the contrariety of faith, religion, and worship. Which same thing must be determined also concerning the conventicles of the Heathens.

Nor does it stand in the way that Turks, Jews, and Gentiles are outside the Church of GOD: but Papists and Calvinists and other modern heretics have fixed their seat within the very boundaries of the Church. For external society and communion of the Church does not produce a consonance of faith and worship. Therefore, in whatever assembly manifest blasphemy, idolatry, superstition, false dogmas, and those overturning the foundation of faith obtain, there true faith is exiled, and consequently true worship of GOD as well. But where there is a disparity of faith and divine worship, there society and communion of Prayer and supplications cannot have a place: For whatever does not proceed from true faith cannot please God. Rom. 14, 23. Heb. 11, 6. And to this, in its own way, that Apostolic passage can be rightly referred, 2 Cor. 6, verse 14 and following up to the end: Do not be yoked together with unbelievers. For what participation has righteousness with iniquity? And what fellowship has light with darkness? And what concord has Christ with Belial? What part has a believer with an unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols? You are the temple of the living God: as God says: For I will dwell in them, and walk among them: and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Wherefore come out from among them, and be separate, says the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing: and I will receive you, etc.

2. Orthodox people in such a state of affairs are in a case of having to make a Confession: Where indeed one must abstain entirely from every appearance of evil and collusion with heretics. 1 Thess. 5, 22. For if they join themselves to them, they certainly communicate in the sins and impieties of others: which is nothing else than denying Christ before men. Therefore, the Son of man will also deny such Hypocrites at the last day, Matt. 10, v. 33.

Latin:

QUanquam in Veteri Testamento ad certum locum, nempe ad Propitiatorium, qvod erat super arcam fœderis in Tabernaculo, Invocatio DEI erat quasi adstricta & alligata: idqve proptereà, ut sic per illustrem quendam Typum adumbraretur Christus, promissus mundi Messias, verus & unicus ille, utriusqve Testamenti propitiator, in quo, per & propter quem solum, DEUS invocari voluit: in Novo tamen Testamento, post exhibitum jam Mundi Messiam, non usque adeò superstitiosè Invocatio & preces Christianorum ad certum vel locum, vel tempus sunt alligatæ: quin in omni loco, & semper supplices ad DEUM manus elevare licèt: sic definiente Christo Servatore, Johan. 4. v. 21. 22. & 23. Crede mihi mulier, venit hora, quando neque in monte hoc, neque Hierosolymis adorabitis Patrem: Vos adoratis, quod nescitis: Nos adoramus, quod scimus: Sed venit hora, & nunc est, quando veri adoratores adorabunt Patrem in Spiritu & Veritate. Quam ipsam ob causam idem Servator noster, discipulis de rectâ precandi formâ & ratione instrui petentibus, nullum certum vel locum, vel tempus præscribit: sed hæc in ipsorum arbitrio relinquens. Quomodo, & quid precari debeant, præscribit : Quando, inquiens, vultis orare, dicite, Pater noster, qui es in cælis, &c. Matth. 6. v. 9. Luc. 11. v. 2. Quid? quòd usq; adeò ad locum aliquem publicum solennem nos non vult esse adstrictos, ut potiùs preces in privato aliquo sive musæo, sive cubili fusas, sibi non displicere disertis verbis asserat, & tales preces publicis Hypocritarum solennitatibus modis omnibus præferat : Tu verò, inquiens, cùm oraveris, intra in cubiculum tuum, & clauso ostio ora Patrem tuum in abscondito: & Pater tuus, qui videt in abscondito, reddet tibi: Matth. 6, 6. Sic Apostolus 1. Tim. 2, 8. Volo, inquit, viros orare qvovis loco, levantes puras manus.

Et hoc est, quod olim prædixit Malachias cap. 1. v. 11. Ab ortu Solis usq; ad occasum, magnum est nomen DEI in gentibus, & in omni loco sacrificatur, & offertur illi oblatio munda.

Hinc præclarè Augustinus: Quid supplicaturus DEO, locum aptum & sanctum requiris? Interiora tua emunda, & omni inde malâ cupiditate repulsâ, præpara tibi in cordu tui pace secretum: Volens in templo orare, in te ora, & ita age semper, ut Dei templum sis: Ibin. Deus exaudit, ubi habitat.

Cæterùm circa decisionem hanc duo errorum præcipitia probè sunt cavenda: Unum Enthusiastarum, qui prætextu dictorum Scripturæ jam productorum preces publicas & solennes, quæ in templis ab universo fiunt populo, simpliciter improbant & rejiciunt. Pro quâ refutanda impietate, unica illa distinctio sufficit, quâ preces aliæ dicuntur esse privatæ, & privatorum quorumlibet hominum: aliæ verò publicæ, & totius Ecclesiæ. Priores illas nullius vel loci, vel temporis determinatione adstringendas esse, ultrò concedimus: posteriores verò has in publico aliquo certo loco ex pediri non posse, aut debere, vix quisquam affirmaverit, nisi qui DEUM ipsum impietatis insimulare ausit: quide templo Hierosolymitano clarè edixit: Domus mea, domus orationis vocabitur: Jesa. 56. v. 7. Imò eò usq; fanaticorum istorum prophanitas progreditur, ut Christum Servatorem reprehendere præsumat, quod propheticum hoc ad tempus Novi Testamenti accommodare non dubitavit: Matth. 21. v. 13. Joh. 2. v. 16. Et quid quæso respondebunt isti Apostolis Petro & Johanni, qui horâ Orationis nonâ in templum ascendisse leguntur: Act. 3. v. 1. & Paulo, qui ejusdem cultus peragendi gratiâ, templum etiam ingressus fuisse perhibetur: Act. 21, v. 26. Sed facessant isti fanatici.

ALTERUM erroris præcipitium hoc loco à Romanensibus objicitur, qui de privatis quidem precibus litem nobis nullam movent: sed in quæstione publicarum precum, tali gloffemate tum verba Servatoris, Joh. 4. v. 21. &c. tùm Apostoli, 1. Tim. 2. 8. depravant : DEUM invocari quidem posse in omni loco: sed in omni loco, hunc in finem delecto, dedicato, & legitimè consecrato: uti Jesuita quidam Dillinganus, in suis assertionibus ad hanc Pauli epistolam scribere non dubitavit.

Intelligit verò Dedicationem hanc, de eâ Confecratione, quæ ab Episcopo vel suffraganeo fiat, per aquã benedictam, per fictas & ementitas Sančtorum reliquias, per donaria, ritusq; alios superstitiosos, qui in templorum dedication bus apud Pontificios solent adhiberi. Contra has superstitiones Ecclesia purior primùm tanqvàm manifestè impias protestatur: & hoc nomine Ecclesiam Pontificiam impietatis arguit. Deindè inter tempora accuratè distinguendum esse monet. Nam si tranquilla & pacata ea sint, quin in templis publicis, preces & supplicationes à tota Ecclesia fieri possint, & debeant, nemo nostrum repugnavit unquàm. Sin persecutione aut aliis calamitatibus prematur Ecclesia: publicas preces in omni loco, etiam adhuc non delečto aut dedicato, piè fieri posse, statuimus; sic edocti à Spiritu Sancto, Psal. 24, 1. Domini est terra, & omnis plenitudo ejus. Tit. 1, 15. Omnia munda sunt mundis. Jam cibi qvoq; sanctificantur per sermonem DEI & precationem. 1. Tim. 4, 5. quidnî terra etiam, mare, sylvæ, montes, valles &c. Et meminerint Romanenses, quòd hac in parte judaizent. Siquidem manifestum est, ab Esaia cap. 66, 1. & à Stephano protomartyre, Act. 7, 48. Judæos acriter reprehensos fuisse, eò quôd DEUM in templis manufactis habitare, & velut parietibus templorum includi opinarentur.

Difficilis hoc loco movetur Quæstio: An cum qualibet Ecclesia, & sic cum Ecclesiâ Calvinianâ & Pontificiâ sit orandum. Exempli gratia: Si ingens aliqua ingruat calamitas, & Pontifex Romanus certis horis publicas ad Deum suppli cationes fieri jubeat, & Lutheranos iisdem precibus, sub interminatione confiscationis bonorum, vel ipsius etiam vitæ periculo interesse mandet: An Lutherani Pontificiorum cultui hac in parte, bonâ Conscientiâ se aggregare, vel quavis etiam specie intere se possint? Quæstioni huic ansam & occasionem præbuit Sinômum illud Esawitarum, & maleferratorum quorundam Episcoporum Romanensium consilium, quo superioribus annis Imperatori & Archiducibus Austriæ autores, suasoresque fuerunt, ut Turcâ tum vehementiùs per Hungariam sæviente, Preces & supplicationes publicæ, per quadraginta horas integras continuatæ, in templo Idololatrico sive Pontificio instituerentur, iisǻ; singuli & universi subditi Viennenses inferioris Austriæ interesse cogerentur. Ubi sanè Quæstionis hujus decisio solida & Orthodoxa à multis desiderabatur: Quæ licèt non omni careat periculo, Negativa tamen à nobis simpliciter tenetur & defenditur, ob causas & rationis sequentes longè evidentissimas.

I. Oratio sive Invocatio est pars cultus divini præcipua. Qualis ergò est cultus DEI apud Pontificios, talis est eorundem Oratio publica. Ratio connexi est, quia cultus æstimari ac definiri debet, non nisi ex qualitate fidei, & Religionis, quæ in Ecclesiâ Romanensium publicè obtinet. Jam si cultus iste natu, râ suâ sit impiùs ac Idololatricus : ejusdem etiam conditionis ipsa eorundem Oratio sit necesse est : præsertim cùm extra omnem dubitationis aleam sit positum, Pontificios secundum suæ Regionis tenorem, invocare 1. non solum & Unum DEUM, sed & Mariam Deiparam semper virginem, & Sanctos alios. 2. DEUM non invocare per solum Christum, ejusdemq; meritum: sed & per opera supererogationis Sanctorum, Monachorum & Monialium. De hac ergò Idolomaniâ qui participare nolit, is nec de Oratione Romanensium bonâ conscientiâ communicabit unquàm. Stante hac decisione, patet, quòd orthodoxus nemo, cum Turcarum Ecclesia orare possit : quia cum religione, fide ac cultu illorum nihil communionis ipsi intercedit. Si cum Judæorum Synagoga preces suas fundere & jungere verus Christianus non potest, propter fidei, ac religionis, & cultuum contrarietatem. Quod ipsum de Ethnicorum etiam conventiculis est statuendum.

Neq; obstat, quòd Turcæ, Judæi ac Gentiles sunt extra Ecclesiam DEI : Pontificii verò & Calviniani, aliiq; moderni hæretici intra ipsa Ecclesiæ pomeria sedem suam fixerunt. Nam externa Ecclesiæ societas & communio non parit consonantiam fidei & cultus. In quocunq; ergò cœtu manifesta obtinet blasphemia, idolomania, superstitio, dogmata falsa, & fundamentum fidei evertentia, ibi exulat vera fides, & consequenter verus etiam DEI cultus, Ubi verò est disparitas fidei & cultus divini, ibi Orationis & precum societas & communio locum habere nequit : Quicquid enim non ex verâ fide procedit, DEo placere nequit. Rom. 14, 23. Hebr. 11, 6. Et huc suo modo rectè referri potest illud Apostolicum, 2. Corinth. 6. vers. 14. & seqq. usque ad finem : Nolite jugum ducere cum infidelibus. Quæ enim participatio justitiæ cum ini quitate? quæ societas luci ad tenebras? Quæ conventio Christi ad Belial? Quæ pars fideli cum infideli? Quis consensus templo Dei cum idolis? Vos estis templū Dei vivi: sicut dicit Deus: Quoniam inhabitabo in illis, & inambulabo:& ero ipsorum Deus, & ipsi mihi erunt populus. Propter quod exite de medio eorum, & separamini, dicit Dominus, & immundū ne tetigeritis: & ego recipiā vos &c.

2. Orthodoxi tali rerum statu versantur in casu edendæ Confessionis : Ubi profectò ab omni specie mali & collusionis cum hæreticis omninò est abstinendum. 1. Thess. 5, 22. Si enim se illis conjungant, utiq; alienis peccatis & impietatibus communicant: id quod nihil est aliud, quàm negare Christum coram hominibus. Tales ergò Hypocritas aliquando in die novissimo negabit etiam filius hominis, Matth. 10. v. 33.


### Question V. Where to Pray, & When (continued)

3. The Papists, not primarily for the averting of impending evils, but rather for the solemn and public confirmation of their Idolatry, and especially of that truly abominable Mass-sacrifice, through those prayers of forty hours, they sought with a truly cunning plan. For with this end, not only while those prayers lasted did they repeat the celebration of this Sacrifice several times: but also by Imperial mandate this clause was inserted, that near the fortieth or last hour it was permitted to no one at all, of whatever Religion he might be, to be absent: but each and all were to accompany the Sacrament (that fictitious one, and falsely so called) to be carried to its place: Or as the formal words of the Mandate had it: In the last hour, and at the conclusion of the Common Prayer, everyone shall come together to accompany the (supposed) Sacrament back to its place. Therefore, the more atrocious the impiety of this Sacrifice is, the more studiously ought every pious person to beware, so that in no way or under any pretext does he participate in it.

4. By this cunning invention, the Jesuits sought to cast shackles upon the Evangelicals or Lutherans, and either to recall the unwary under the most wretched yoke of Papal servitude, or if they persisted in resisting the mandate, to precipitate them into danger of life and fortune.

5. To public prayers of this kind was attached an opinion of merit, as if God were bound in turn to hear them out of condignity, or at least out of congruity. Whoever approves of this one impiety, he is to be judged as approving of the entire religion, or more truly, the Papal abomination.

But it is asked at this point: What if the Magistrate by external force and tyranny compels you to attend such prayers and Papal rites? I answer that two means remain: One, which is of most humble supplication, by which you explain that you are prepared to perform any services whatsoever that can indeed be performed with an uninjured conscience, and therefore that you will certainly continue to offer even more ardent prayers and sighs at home with your own people, without intermission, to God for the mitigation of the evils and punishments that are looming. But that you are prevented from attending the rites of the Papists by the diversity of Religion and by conscience. If, however, this means is attempted in vain, the other is left, shown by Christ the Savior himself, Matt. 10:23. When they have persecuted you from one city, flee to another. And even if the loss of all goods of body and fortune must be made, that incomparable treasure nevertheless cannot be snatched away: namely, Faith in Christ, a good conscience, and the unfading crown of glory, with the Savior himself thus promising: Matt. 5:10. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven: And Matt. 19:29. Everyone who has left house, or brothers or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name's sake: shall receive a hundredfold, and shall possess eternal life.

The example of Naaman the Syrian is objected at this point, who asked that, if he should perform external service to his King in the idolatrous temple of Rimmon, and at the same time adore the Lord there, this might not be imputed to him as a sin:

Elisha answered, Go in peace, and thus by this act of his approved it by his own judgment. 2 Kings 5:18 and 19. The resolution of this knot has indeed twisted interpreters so that they went off into clearly different opinions. There are some who maintain that the Prophet, in that singular case, and indeed not without a peculiar divine revelation, granted a dispensation. While we willingly allow them to abound in their own sense, we cannot agree with them. For 1. concerning any divine revelation, not a single word appears in the whole text, nay, not even any suspicion or conjecture of it. 2. Naaman himself confesses that if he adores GOD in the idolatrous temple of Rimmon, he will sin gravely against GOD, and will accumulate grave punishments for himself. Who, therefore, will ever maintain that the Prophet dispensed in any way in a matter that is in itself impious? No dispensation, in truth, has ever had a place, or can have, in a matter prohibited by GOD himself in express words, and directly inflicting insult upon the true worship of GOD. Concerning the dispensation of GOD regarding the polygamy of the Patriarchs, whether such a thing can be clearly and evidently demonstrated from the Scriptures, we shall not now dispute: but we only answer that it was of a very different kind and condition: for it was not held as a sin by those most pious Patriarchs. 2. Most useful ends were looked to, namely, the multiplication of the human race: the desire for the promised Seed, and the like. 3. Polygamy did not directly attack the worship of God. Since the deed of Naaman is destitute of these conditions, and he values private advantage more than the offense of GOD, a singular Prophetic dispensation certainly cannot and ought not to be admitted regarding it: especially since it is in itself idolatrous, and can be painted or palliated by no excuse.

There are, moreover, some among the interpreters who presume to excuse the action of Naaman, on the grounds that he had been recently converted, and was still weak regarding the Jewish faith in Tyre, and not yet so confirmed that he could determine that his own affairs and himself must be denied for the sake of GOD, that is, for the confession of the truth: but he opined that the profession of the Jewish Religion and that service and worship of GOD in an idolatrous temple could stand together without prejudice to the profession. Others add: For this very reason the Prophet Elisha did not wish to rebuke this action or practice of Naaman, or to inform him more correctly: because he understood that he, being indeed weak, was not capable of a just rebuke, and therefore a smoking flax was not to be entirely extinguished: but that it was to be granted to him which, in the case of one confirmed, could by no means be granted. Furthermore, there are others who write that the Prophet at least tolerated the action of Naaman, but did not approve of it: and they claim that the knot can be untied in this way. But we cannot subscribe to the opinions of these either. For what practice ought to be observed regarding the instruction of the weak is clearly evident from the Scriptures. Now, indeed, nothing can or ought to be indulged or granted to the weak in faith, except what is by its nature indifferent, and neither commanded nor prohibited by GOD. In those things, however, which are directly and openly opposed to the word of GOD, and therefore are truly and by their nature sins, nothing at all can or ought to be dispensed or indulged, even to the weak. Next, the infirmity of Naaman was not so great that he did not know whom he ought to invoke, and where he ought to invoke him? For in the same chapter 5, verse 17, in express words offer burnt offering or sacrifice to strange gods, but to Jehovah alone. 2. He had not been ignorant that he would sin against GOD if, prostrating himself in the temple of Rimmon before an idol, he should worship. Elisha therefore understood that Naaman was in need not of better information, but rather of consolation, so that, if by chance he should fall into that sin, he might not despair of its forgiveness: as will be shown a little later. Finally, that distinction between tolerance and approval is too diluted and trivial. For it will never be proven that such a great prophet tolerated that which he knew to be a sin in itself and by its nature.

These things being thus removed, we maintain that the proposed argument can be solidly refuted and explained: if we examine more accurately, partly the petition of Naaman, and partly the response of the Prophet.

I. The petition of Naaman is as follows, according to the Hebrew version: In this matter may Jehovah pardon thy servant, when my lord shall enter the house of Rimmon, to worship there, and he shall lean upon my hand, and I shall bow myself in the house of Rimmon, in this my bowing in the house of Rimmon, may Jehovah pardon I pray thy servant in this matter. 2 Kings 5, verse 18. The sum of the petition is that Naaman asks to be pardoned by GOD if, while the king is worshipping in the temple of Rimmon, he himself, as the reason of his office requires, is compelled to enter the temple, to support the king with his shoulders or right hand, and thus also to prostrate himself before the idol of Rimmon, and to bow himself. Where four things deserve observation: 1. That Naaman does not say that he will do this by design, and will worship his GOD in the temple of Rimmon: but if such a thing should happen, and he is compelled by the reason of his office to perform service to the King, and together with him to prostrate himself before the idol. Therefore no support redounds from there to those Neutrals and Nicodemites who, by set purpose, accommodate themselves to all religions, and are accustomed to attend idolatrous rites, such as the Papal Mass. Naaman the Syrian would never have done such a thing if he could have used his own right. 2. It is to be noted that Naaman does not say that he will worship GOD before the idol of Rimmon: as the Latin Vulgate version has it: but, if the King leans upon his hand, that he himself also has need to bow himself: so that this external bowing may not be imputed to him by GOD. For although the Hebrew word בְּהִשְׁתַּחֲוָיָתִי, that is, in my bowing, according to the condition of the subject matter, sometimes denotes the external gesture of adoration, namely bowing, and sometimes indeed the adoration itself: yet the thing itself speaks, in this place, that it is a matter only of the external posture of bowing, which Naaman thought to be vicious, because it would be done before an idol, and in an idolatrous temple. For if the discourse had been about adoration itself for Naaman, he would not have used a phrase and words denoting contingency and a fortuitous event: since he knew that the adoration of God is not an arbitrary, not a contingent, but a necessary worship of God, and one to be performed incessantly. Now because he expresses a mode of contingency, it is evidently gathered from there that Naaman was not constrained and obligated to perform this kind of duty in an idolatrous temple to the King of Syria, but only posits that case, if by chance it should happen that he has need to perform it, so that God might not impute this to him. Which observation again cuts off every excuse for Hypocrites and Neutrals. 3. It is to be noted that Naaman himself acknowledged that sin was involved in this act: Whence a double ἔλεγχος (reproof) is sought: the former regarding Naaman himself, namely that he was something human, and preferred to undergo some injury to his conscience rather than to lose all favor and dignity with the King of Syria: which in him ought in no way to be praised. For if he had simply resigned his office and duty, no danger of a fall or sting of conscience would have been to be feared. Therefore (regarding the latter ἔλεγχον) those Neutrals try in vain to pretend this act of Naaman, as a thing done well and laudably, to color their own simulation. 4. And finally it is to be noted that in the entire sacred history there is nothing from which it can be gathered, even in appearance, at least probably, that Naaman ever did what he feared might happen to him. Therefore no argument can be sought from this passage by Neutrals and hypocrites. And such indeed was the petition of Naaman.

II. Now regarding the response of the Prophet, it is as follows: Go in peace. Where it deserves observation at the beginning that the Prophet did not say: Go and do so, the Lord will be propitious to you in this act: which would imply the consent and approval of the Prophet: but he only says: Go in peace: Which phrase has a double respect, both consolatory and prophetic. Consolatory indeed in that he wished to raise and confirm Naaman, who was anxious about a fall that might happen by chance, and about the offense of God, namely that even if it should happen that such a fall should befall him out of some infirmity, he should not however despair of the help and mercy of God, by which He is about to forgive that sin to him who freely confesses and acknowledges it. In which part he also wishes to help him with his own prayers.

But this response has a prophetic respect, in that Elisha, foreseeing the future events of things, predicted to Naaman that there was no need for this fear and for that anxiety: since divine help would never be lacking to him, but rather would keep him immune from such a fall and such a sin. The sense therefore of these words is: Go in peace: As if the Prophet had said: My Naaman, there is no reason for you to be anguished in mind on account of some such fall that might happen to you: There is no need for this worry, be content, God will surely keep you from such a fall.

For I predict to you that it will never happen that you fall into that sin. For I will be present with you through my prayers in such a way that God may guard you from it and confirm you more and more in the true faith, so that at length, confirmed in the Lord, you may be about to renounce both yourself and your honors for the glory of God.

Latin:

3. Pontificii non principaliter ingruentium malorum aversionem, sed potiùs Idolomaniæ suæ, & cumprimis Sacrificii illius Missatici verè abominandi solennem & publicam confirmationem per preces illas quadraginta horarum, astuto sanè consilio quærebant. Hoc enim fine non tantùm durantibus istis precibus, celebrationem hujus Sacrificii aliquoties repetebant: sed & mandato Imperatorio hæc inserta erat clausula, ut sub horam quadragesimam sive ultimam nemini prorsus, cujuscunque esset Religionis, liceret abesse: sed singuli & universi comitarentur Sacramentum (fictitium illud, & falsò sic dictum) in suum locum deportandum: Vel uti verba formalia Mandati habebant: Das in der lezten Stund / vnd zum beschluß des Gemeinen Gebets / jederman solle zusammen kommen / das (vermeinte) Sacrament widerumb an seinen Ort zu begleiten. Quò atrocior ergò est Sacrificii hujus impietas: eò studiosius sibi cavere debet pius quisque, ut nullo pacto aut præxtu de eâ participet.

4. Callido hoc invento, Esawitæ Evangelicis sive Lutheranis compedes injicere, & vel sub tristissimum servitutis Pontificię jugum incautos revocare, vel si mandato repugnare pergant, in discrimen capitis & fortunarum præcipitare studebant.

5. Precibus hujusmodi publicis affingebatur opinio meriti, quasi de condigno, vel saltem de congruo Deus vicissim teneatur eas exaudire. Quam vel unam impietatem qui probat, is universam religionem, abominationem veriùs Pontificiam probare censendus est.

Sed quæritur hoc loco: Quid si Magistratus externâ vi & tyrannide, ejusmodi precibus, & sacris Pontificiis te interesse cogat? Respondeo duo superesse media: Unum, quod est humilimæ supplicationis, quâ exponas Te paratum esse ad quævis præstanda servitia, quæ quidem illæsâ conscientiâ præstari queant, ac proinde tantò ardentiores etiam preces & suspiria domi tuæ cum tuis, sine intermissione ad Deum pro mitigatione malorum & pœnarum ingruentium certò facturum. Quo minus autem Pontificiorum sacris interfis, Religionis diversitate & conscientiâ te prohiberi. Sin frustrà medium istud tentetur, alterum est relictum ab ipso Christo Servatore monstratum, Matth. 10. v. 23. Cùm persecuti vos fuerint ex civitate unâ, fugite in aliam. Et si maximè jactura bonorum omnium Corporis & fortunæ sit facienda, incomparabilis tamen ille thesaurus eripi haud potest: nempe Fides in Christum, bona conscientia, & immarcescibilis gloriæ corona, sic promittente ipso Servatore: Matth. 5. v. 10. Beati, qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cælorum: Et Matth. 19. v. 29. Omnis qui reliquerit domum, vel fratres aut sorores, aut patrem, aut matrem, aut uxorem, aut filios, aut agros propter nomen meum: centuplum accipiet, & vitam æternam possidebit.

Objicitur hoc loco exemplum Naamani Syri, cui petenti, ut, si in templo Idololatrico Remmon non modò Regi suo externum servitium præstet, & simul ibi adoret Dominum, hoc ipsi in peccatum non imputetur:

responderit Elisaeus, Abi in pace, & sic factu hoc suo calculo approbarit. 2. Reg. 5. v. 18. & 19. Torsit sane nodi hujus dissolutio ita interpretes, ut in diversas plane abirent sententias. Sunt nonnulli, qui statuunt, Prophetam in casu isto singulari, & quidem non sine peculiari revelatione divina, dispensasse. Quos sane uti suo sensu libenter abundare patimur: ita suffragari illis non possumus. Nam 1. de revelatione aliqua divina, in toto textu nullum apparet verbulum, imo ne ulla quidem ejus suspicio aut conjectura. 2. Fatetur Naaman ipse, si in templo Idololatrico Remmon adoret DEUM, se graviter in DEUM peccaturum, gravesq; sibi poenas accumulaturum. Quis ergo unquam statuet, Prophetam in re per se impia ullo pacto dispensasse? Nulla profecto dispensatio locum habuit unquam, aut habere potest, in re a DEO ipso disertis verbis prohibita: & directe verum DEI cultum contumelia afficiente. De dispensatio ne quidem DEI circa polygamiam Patriarcharu, utrum talis e Scripturis liquido & evidenter demonstrari possit, jam non disputabimus: sed tantum diversissimi eam fuisse generis & conditionis respondemus: quippe quae a Patriarchis illis longe piissimis pro peccato non habebatur. 2. Fines spectabantur utilissimi, nempe multiplicatio generis humani: Seminis promissi desiderium, & similes. 3. Non directe cultum Dei impugnabat Polygamia. Qvibus conditionibus cum factum Naamani destituatur, & privatum commodum pluris aestimet, quam DEI offensionem, utiqve singularis dispensatio Prophetica admitti circa illud nec potest, nec debet: praesertim cum in se illud sit idololatricum, & nullo suco pingi aut palliari queat.

Sunt deinde ex interpretibus alii, qui factum Naamani excusare praesumunt, eo quod recens fuerit conversus, & adhuc circa fidem Judaicam Tyro infirmus, ac nondum ita confirmatus, ut sua, & seipsum DEI causa, hoc est, pro confessione veritatis abnegandum esse statueret: sed salva professioffe Religionis Judaicae servitium illud, & cultum DEI in templo idololatrico simul stare posse, opinaretur. Subjiciunt alii: Ob hanc ipsam causam Prophetam Elisæum noluisse factu hoc, sive institutum Naamani reprehendere, rectiusq; informare: quia intelligeret ipsum, qvippe infirmum, justae reprehensionis non esse capacem, ac propterea linum fumigans non plane esse extingvendum: sed concedendu ipfi esse, quod circa confirmato concedi nulla ratione poterat. Sunt porro alii, qvi Prophetam Naamani factum tolerasse saltem, sed non probasse, scriptitant: & hoc pacto nodum solvi posse autumant. Verum neq; istorum sententiis subscribere possumus. Nam quae praxis circa erudiendos infirmos observanda sit, ex Sacris liquido patet. Jam vero infirmis in fide nihil indulgeri, nihilq; concedi potest, aut debet, nisi qvod natura sua est ἀδιάφορον, & a DEO neque pra̧eceptum, neq; prohibitum. In iis autem, quæ verbo DEI directè & palam adverfantur, ac proindè verè ac naturâ suâ peccata sunt, nihil quicquam vel dispenfari, vel indulgeri etiam infirmis potest aut debet. Deinde infirmitas Naamanis non erat tanta, ut ignoraret, quis invocari, & ubi invocari debeat? Nam eodem cap. 5. v. 17. disertis verbis protestatus fuerat, se non ultra holocaustum aut sacrificium facturum diis alienis, sed soli Jehove. 2. Non ignoraverat, se peccaturum contra DEUM, si in templo Rimmon coram Idolo procumbens adoret. Intellexit ergò Elisæus, Naamanum non rectiore informatione, sed Consolatione potiùs indigere, ut, si forte in peccatum istud prolaberetur, de ejus condonatione non desperaret: ut paulò pòst ostendetur. Tandem distinctio illa inter tolerantiam & approbationem, nimis est diluta & nugatoria. Nam talem & tantùm Prophetam tolerasse id, quod in se, & naturâ suâ peccatum esse noverat, nunquam probabitur.

His ita remotis, propositum argumentum solidè refutari & explicari posse statuimus: si partim Naamanis petitionem: partim verò responsum Prophetæ accuratiùs excutiamus.

I. Petitio Naamanis sic habet, secundum versionem Hebræam: Hac in re parcat Jehova servo tuo, quando ingredietur Dominus meus ædem Rimmon, ut adoret ibi, & ipse innixus fuerit super manum meam, & incurvavero me in æde Rimmon, in hac incurvatione meâ in æde Rimmon, ignoscat quæso Jehovah servo tuo hac in re. 2. Reg. 5. v. 18. Summa petitionis est, quod petit Naaman sibi ignosci à DEO, si adorante rege in templo Rimmón, ipse, sic exigente officii ratione, simul templum ingredi, regem humeris vel dextrâ sustinere, & sic quoque coram Idolo Rimmón procumbere, seq; incurvare necesse sum habeat. Ubi quatuor observationem merentur: 1. Quòd Naaman non dicit, se studio hoc facturum, & adoraturum DEUM suum in templo Rimmón: sed si tale quid eveniat, & pro officii ratione Regi servitium præstare, & unà cum ipso coram idolo procumbere cogatur. Ergò nihil quicqvam inde præsidii redundat ad Neutrales & Nicodemitas illos, qui destinato consilio ad omnes se Religiones accommodant, & sacris idolatricis, ut Missæ Pontificiæ interesse solent. Tale quid Naaman Syrus nunquam fecisset, si jure suo uti potuisset. 2. Notandum, quòd Naaman non dicit, se adoraturum DEUM coram idolo Rimmón: uti vulgata latina habet versio: sed, si Rex innixus super manum suam, ut ipse qvoqve curvare se necesse habeat: ut hæc externa incurvatio ipsi à DEO non imputetur. Etsi enim verbum Hebræum בְּהִשְׁתַּחֲוָיָתִי hoc est, in incurvatione mea pro conditione subjectæ materiæ interdum externum adorationis gestum, nempe incurvationem, interdum verò adorationem ipsam notat: res ipsa tamen loquitur, hoc loco, de externo tantùm incurvationis situ agi, quem vitiosum esse putabat Naaman, quia fieret coram idolo, & in templo idololatrico. Nam si de adoratione ipsâ sermo fuisset Naamani, non usus fuisset phrasi & verbis contingentiam & casum fortuitum notantibus : siqvidem adorationem Dei noverat esse cultum Dei non arbitrarium, non contingentem, sed necessarium, & indesinenter præstandum. Jam quia contingentiæ modum exprimit, evidenter inde colligitur, Naamanem ad præstandum hoc officii genus in templo Idololatrico, Regi Syriæ non fuisse adstrictum & obligatum, sed tantùm casum istum ponere, si forte eveniat, ut illud præstare necesse habeat, ne Deus hoc ipsi imputet. Qvæ observatio rursum Hypocritis & Neutralibus omnem excusationem præcidit. 3. Notandum, qvòd Naaman ipse facto huic peccatum subesse agnovit: Unde duplex ἔλεγχος petitur: prior qvoad Naamanem ipsum, nempe humani aliquid ipsum esse, & maluisse subire læsionem aliqvam Conscientiæ, qvàm gratiâ & dignitate omni apud Regem Syriæ excidere : id qvod in ipso laudari nullo modo debet. Nam si munus & officium suum simpliciter resignasset, nullum periculum lapsus, aut morsus conscientiæ extimescendum fuisset. Proinde (qvoad posteriorem ἔλεγχον) Neutrales illi factum hoc Naamani, tanqvam bene ac laudabiliter factum, Simulationi suæ fucandæ frustrà prætendere student. 4. Ac postremò notandum, in nniversâ historiâ sacrâ nihil haberi, ex qvo vel in speciem saltem probabiliter colligi queat, qvòd Naaman unqvàm fecerit, qvod sibi evenire posse metuebat. Nullum ergô argumentum ex loco isto, à Neutralibus &c hypocritis peti potest. Et talis quidem fuit Naamans petitio.

II. Jam qvoad responsum Prophetæ, illud sic habet: Vade in pace. Ubi illud initiò observationem meretur, qvod Prophetá non dixit: Abi & sic agito, Dominus tibi infacto isto propitius erit: id qvod consensum & approbationem Prophetæ innueret: sed tantùm inquit. Vade in pace: Quæ phrasis geminum respectum habet, & consolatorium & Propheticum. Consolatorium qvidem in eò, qvòd Naamanum de lapsu forte eventuro, deq; offensione Dei solicitum, erigere & confirmare voluit, nempe si maximè eveniat, ut ex infirmitate aliqva talis ipsi lapsus obveniat, non tamen desperet de auxilio & misericordia Dei, quâ ipsi peccatum sponte fatenti & agnoscenti, illud condonaturus sit. Quâ in parte suis qvoqve precibus ipsum juvare velit.

Propheticum verò respectum habet hoc responsum, qvòd Elisæus futuros rerum eventus prævidens, prædixit Naamani, non opus esse hoc timore, & sollicitudine ista: siquidem divinum auxilium ipsi nunquàm sit defuturum, sed potiùs à tali lapsu, tamoq; peccato ipsam immunem præstiturum. Sensus ergo verborum istorum est: Vade in pace: Quasi dixerit Prophetæ: Mi Naaman, non est, ut ob talem aliqvem lapsum, qui tibi evenire queat, angaris animo: Es bedarff dieser sorge nicht/ gib dich zufrieden/ Gott wird dich vor solchem Fall wol behuͤten:

Praedico enim tibi, nunquam futurum, ut in peccatum istud prolabaris. Nam precibus meis tibi ita adero, ut Deus te ab eo custodiat, & in vera fide magis magisq; confirmet: ut tandem in Domino confirmatus, & te, & honores tuos, pro gloria Dei sis abnegaturus.


### Question VI. In which language ought prayer to be?

To this simple question we give this affirmative answer: namely, that one must pray in that language which is rightly and in all respects understood both by ourselves and by those who hear us. And we understand this not only of private prayers, but also of public ones, so that ecclesiastical supplications, which are commonly called Collects, should both be recited and sung in the vernacular language. For nothing is more vain than to speak in such a way that, like a flute, you give forth a sound without a mind, which neither you nor others understand. And although God has no need of this or that language, indeed He is the author and bestower of all languages, the Most Greatest, knows them most exactly; nay, He looks into the inner chambers of our hearts and knows most perfectly what we wish to ask and what things we are in need of; yet because He wills that invocation be made in spirit and in truth, and that others also be incited by us to the pursuit of the same; because He also wills that in our tribulation our distresses and calamities, by which we are pressed, be enumerated in detail; because, finally, public prayers especially ought to be like a confession, by which we acknowledge our unworthiness with true humility of heart and rest solely in the merit of Christ: certainly they sin gravely against this institution of God, and indeed convert the entire act of invocation into a certain theatrical and almost histrionic gesticulation, who in pouring forth prayers use that language more often which not even the priests themselves understand sufficiently well, let alone the hearers.

The Apostle deals expressly with this matter and demonstrates that from such preaching, and consequently from the invocation of God which is performed in an unknown and foreign language, no use or fruit at all redounds to the Church; and thus those praying are like those who speak into the air; and finally he concludes with this epiphonema, as it were: Unless I understand the force of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to him who speaks, and he who speaks will be a barbarian to me, verse 11.

Let the Romanist mass-priests therefore see what they will one day answer to the Apostle, who perform all sacred rites in such a way that, neglecting the vernacular language and that which is intelligible to all, they use only the Latin language, which not even they themselves can often read quite correctly, let alone the hearers understand.

Moreover, this decision of ours suffers and admits its limitations, which the Apostle himself, in the place already cited, expresses quite clearly.

For 1. if any private person pours forth prayers to GOD alone at his own home, whether he be most skilled in Latin, or Greek, or Hebrew, or French, or some other language, nothing at all prevents him from framing his prayers in such a language. For the Apostle only wishes this, that everyone should understand those things which he speaks to GOD.

Next, one must distinguish between ecclesiastical assemblies which consist either of persons who are purely ignorant and illiterate: where indeed no other language than the vernacular alone is to be used in divine worship. Nor is it fitting to observe anything different in this regard for the sake of one or two learned men. Or they consist for the most part of learned men, and those clear in the knowledge of both Latin and other languages: such as is the condition of courts and more celebrated republics, and especially of Academies, in which nothing prohibits prayers and certain Latin hymns from being retained and exercised, especially on more solemn feast days. For 1. there occurs no passage in the entire Scripture which—I do not say in the interpretation of Scripture or the celebration of the Sacraments (for these must always be done in a language intelligible to all)—but in prayers and singing, prohibits the use of the Latin language simply, and thus even with respect to the learned; for it cannot be affirmed of these that they do not understand what is either recited or sung. 2. These Latin psalmodies and figured chants serve to instruct the Scholastic youth, whose studies and progress, as in the chapters of the Christian religion, so also in the most noble and truly divine art of Music, can and indeed ought to be explored and promoted not only in schools but also in temples. 3. These very Latin songs, the use of which prevails in our Churches, such as the Introit, Kyrie, Gradual, and the like, are a clear and notable testimony that GOD, even under those densest shadows of the Papal kingdom, preserved for Himself some Church, which, insisting upon the footsteps of Orthodox Antiquity, would celebrate even in those songs the most illustrious benefits of GOD concerning the redemption of the human race, and concerning our gratuitous justification before GOD through Christ, and would in this very way apply them to itself: a fact which no one will deny was accomplished especially through the hymns and Collects, as they call them, appointed for individual feast days and Sundays, unless he should dare to deny that the Sun itself shines at midday.

We therefore execrate the insane μωρεσοφίαν of the Calvinist race, which, just as it wages an ἄσπονδον πόλεμον against the entire order of Ecclesiastical ceremonies introduced by salutary counsel out of Christian Liberty, so it has always studied to banish Latin, figured, and Organ music simply from the Church, and studies to do so today, such that you may find among that sort of men those who declare themselves to be prohibited by Conscience from even entering the temples of the Lutherans, in which there are Musical organs.

But these people flee in vain to the authority of the Apostle, and indeed to the first verses of chapter 14 of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, in this matter. For a gross and childish fallacy of ἑτεροζητήσεως is committed: while they adapt what the Apostle restricts specifically to Prophecy, that is, the interpretation of Scripture, to the entire genus of all those things which are done in the Church: and they distort it indefinitely to any ecclesiastical assembly whatsoever. Certainly, as regards the interpretation of Scripture, we readily concede that it ought to be done in the vernacular language, and in one intelligible to all equally in any assembly of the Church. Which same thing we also establish entirely concerning the celebration of the Sacraments, against the madness of the Papists. But from that, the consequence does not hold for any prayers, any songs, or even any assembly whatsoever. Hence the Apostle does not simply exterminate the use of foreign languages from the Church: but only in a qualified sense, namely in comparison to Prophecy or the interpretation of Scripture: as is especially clear from verse 6. Then the same Apostle in verses 7 and 8 adds a sufficiently illustrious commendation of music, both figural and instrumental, to be retained in the Church: Just as, he says, it is not enough to blow a flute, or to strike a lyre with an uncertain noise of fingers: but it is necessary that it be done harmoniously and according to art: so he who speaks in the Church, but in such a way that he cannot be understood, beats the air, and ought to be considered a barbarian. Such praises of both kinds of music are contained elsewhere in the Scriptures: as in Num. 10. 2 and 3, where by the very institution of GOD a signal had to be given with silver trumpets when the people were to gather to the tabernacle of the Lord. Thus in speaking praises to GOD, and celebrating his benefits, according to the arrangement of Moses, Exod. 15. v. 1 and 20, the people of GOD used music both instrumental and vocal. Which same thing is sufficiently clearly evident concerning David and Asaph, both from the Psalms and from 1 Chron. 23. v. 5 and 25. 1. Whence David wishes GOD to be praised in the sound of the trumpet, in the psaltery and lyre, in the timbrel and dance, in strings and organ, in well-sounding cymbals, in cymbals of jubilation, Psal. 150. Furthermore, Scripture is a witness that both kinds of music possess a certain peculiar and, as it were, secret power in refreshing the minds of men, and in driving away the melancholic spirit, which is the father of all sadness. 1 Sam. 16. v. 16 and 23, 2 Kings 3. v. 15, Eccles. 32. v. 7 and 8. Finally, since in the other life the chief duty of the blessed will be to sing in turn with the whole heavenly host that τρισάγιον to GOD: Holy, Holy, Holy Lord GOD of Sabaoth, Isa. 6, it is not wrongly gathered from that, that hymns and songs in praise of GOD, instituted both with voice and musical instruments, are a certain kind of prelude to that eternal and heavenly harmony; to which we all rightly aspire with desire. Away, therefore, with that gloomy spirit of the Calvinists, to whom the lowing of an ox or the barking of dogs is more pleasing than harmonic concert in praise of GOD, whether instituted publicly or privately.

But that same Spirit objects to us, 1 Cor. 14, that the mind does not always respond to the singing: but that more often than not a sound is given without the mind.
