But this is the sophistry of an accident. Let this vice therefore be removed, and let the lethargy be shaken off, then the singing will be right, and will correspond to the mouth. What, since with this reasoning standing, all singing whatsoever, even that conceived in the vernacular language, nay even prayers recited in the most common language, and one intelligible to all, would have to be utterly abrogated: to each of which, from the vice of the hearers, it is wont to happen ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ. Here therefore that much-repeated saying, which the Calvinists always have in their mouths, has its place:

Not the voice: but the vow: not the musical string: but the heart: Not the one crying, but the one loving, sings in the ear of GOD.

Then they object the authority of the Holy Fathers, especially the Blessed Jerome, who wrote in his Commentary on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Ephesians: We ought to sing, and play the psaltery, and praise the Lord more with the mind than with the voice. But a gross ἄγνοια ἐλέγχου is committed. For he does not say that we ought not to praise the Lord with the voice at all: but that it ought to be done more with the mind than with the voice: thus implying that true praise of the LORD does not consist in the singing of the voice alone: but especially in the devotion of the mind, which ought to be added to the external voice. Which same thing we also establish. In which sentiment the Divine Augustine wrote excellently in book 10 of his Confessions, chapter 33: When I fluctuate between the danger of pleasure and the experience of healthfulness, I am more led to approve the custom of singing in the Church, so that through the delights of the ears, the weaker mind may rise to the affection of piety.

Finally they object that figural and organic singing was not used in the apostolic Church.

We answer that although this cannot be denied by us, yet in the meantime nothing is lost to our opinion. For the reason for a Church finally being planted is one thing, and that of a Church already planted is another. The former had need to accommodate itself in ceremonies to the state of the time and the condition of the people. But the latter, now brought as it were fully into the state of its liberty, can according to the precept of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 14. last, ordain in ceremonies those things which make for τάξιν καὶ εὐσχημοσύνην. Then, although the use of figural and organic music does not reach the age of the Apostles: yet it is sufficiently certain that it is very ancient. Marianus Scotus reports that in the year of the Lord 756, organic instruments, never before seen in the West, were sent by Constantine Copronymus to King Pepin in France. Whence it is easy to gather that their use in the East was more ancient.

But let it suffice to have said these things in this place concerning Latin prayers and songs.

Latin:

AD quaestionem hanc simplicem hanc danus affirmativam: nempe orandum esse ea lingua, quae & a nobis ipsis, & ab iis, qui nos audiunt, recte & per omnia intelligatur. Neque de privatis tantum, sed & publicis precibus illud intelligimus, ut lingua vernacula Ecclesiasticae supplicationes, quas vulgo Collectas vocant, & recitentur & cantentur. Nihil enim vanius, quam ita loqui, ut instar tibiae des sine mente sonum, quem neque tu, neque alii intelligant. Et quanquam Deus non opus habet vel hac, vel illa lingua, quin omnes linguas, quippe earum autor & largitor Opt. Max. exactissime callet, imo cordium nostrorum penetralia introspicit, & quid petere velimus, quibusve rebus indigeamus, perfectissime novit, quia tamen Invocationem in Spiritu & veritate fieri vult, & ad ejusdem studium per nos incitari quoque alios: quia etiam in tribulatione nostra, aerumnas & calamitates, quibus premimur, in specie enumerari vult: quia denique preces cumprimis publicae, debent esse instar confessionis alicujus, qua vera cordis humilitate indignitatem nostram agnoscimus, & in merito Christi unice acquiescimus: certe contra hanc Dei institutionem graviter peccant, imo universum Invocationis actum in Scenicam quandam, & ferme histrionicam gesticulationem convertunt, qui in fundendis precibus ea saepius lingua utuntur, quam nec ipsi Sacerdotes satis dextre nedum Auditores intelligunt.

Qua de re Apostolus ex professo agit, & demonstrat ex tali praedicatione, & consequenter invocatione Dei quae lingua ignota & peregrina peragatur, nullum prorsus usum aut fructum ad Ecclesiam redundare; sicq; orantes similes esse illis qui in aërem loquuntur: & tandem hoc quasi epiphonemate concludit: Nisi intellexero vim vocis, ero ei, qui loquitur, barbarus: & is, qui loquitur, apud me erit barbarus, versu 11.

Viderint ergo Romanenses sacrificuli, quid aliquando responsuri sint Apostolo, qui omnia sacra ita peragunt, ut neglecta lingua vernacula, & ab omnibus intelligibili, tantum lingua latina utantur, quam nec ipsi saepius sat congrue legere: nedum Auditores intelligere possunt.

Caeterum decisio haec nostra suas patitur & admittit limitationes, quas Apostolus ipse, loco jam citato, satis perspicue exprimit.

Nam 1. si privatus aliqvis domi suæ preces ad DEUM solus fundat, lingua vel Latina, vel Græca, vel Hebraica, vel Gallica, vel alius alicujus sit peritissimus, nihil profectò obstat, qvò minùs preces tali aliqua lingua informet. Nam Apostolus hoc tantùm vult, ut quisqve intelligat ea, quæ ad DEUM loquitur.

Deinde distinguendum inter conventus Ecclesiasticos, qui vel constat ex personis merè idiotis & illiteratis: Ubi sanè nulla aliâ, qvàm solâ vernacula, circa cultum divinum, est utendum. Neqve in unius, aut alterius literati gratiam, hac in parte, diversum observare convenit. Vel constant maximam partem ex literatis, & tùm latinæ, tum aliarum linguarum notitiâ claris: qualis conditio solet esse aularum & Rerumpublicarum celebriorum, cumprimis verò Academiarú, in quibus & preces, & cantiones quasdam Latinas retineri, & in festis cumprimis solennioribus exerceri, nihil prohibet. Nam 1. nullus in universa Scriptura occurrit locus, qui non dico in interpretatione Scripturæ, vel celebratione Sacramentorum: (Hæc enim semper in linguâ ab omnibus intelligibili fieri debet) sed in precibus & cantu linguæ latinæ usum simpliciter, & sic respectu etiam Literatorum prohibeat, de his enim affirmari nequit, quòd non intelligant, quæ vel recitantur, vel cantantur 2. Faciunt hæ Psalmodiæ&cantus figurales Latini ad instituendam juventutem Scholasticam cujus non in Scholis modò, sed & in templis, studia & profectus, uti in capitibus Christianæ religionis, ita in nobilissimâ etiam & verè divina arte Musica, explorari & promoveri possunt, imò verò etiam debent. 3. Sunt hæ ipsæ cantiones Latinæ, quarum usus nostris in Ecclesiis obtinet, quales sunt, Introitus, Kyrie, Graduale, & similes, luculentum & insigne testimonium, quòd DEUS sub densissimis etiam illis tenebris regni Pontificii, aliquam sibi Eclesiaam servaverit, quæ Orthodoxæ Antiquitatis vestigiis insistens, vel in cantionibus illis celebraret maximè illustria DEI beneficia de redemtione generis humani, deqve nostra per Chrtistum gratuitâ justificatione coram DEO, & vel hoc pacto sibi ea applicaret: id quod cumprimis per hymnos, & Collectas, uti vocant, singulis diebus festis & Dominicis destinatas, factum esse, nemo negaverit, nisi qui Solem ipsum in meridie lucere negare ausus fuerit.

Execramur ergò insanam gentis Calvinianæ μωρεσοφίαν, quæ uti cum universo ordine ceremoniarum Ecclesiasticarum, ex Libertate Christiana, salutari consilio introducto, ἄσπονδον gerit πόλεμον: ita cantum etiam Latinum, figuralem & Organicum, simpliciter ex Ecclesia relegare studuit semper, hodieq; studeat, ita ut ex isto hominum genere reperias, qui Conscientia se prohiberi dictitent, quo minus Lutheranorum templa, in quibus sunt organa Musica, saltem ingrediantur.

Frustra autem isti ad autoritatem Apostoli, & quidem primos versus capitis 14. ad priores Corinthios, hac in parte confugiunt. Nam crassa & puerilis committitur Sophisticatio ἑτερο ζητήσεως : dum, quod Apostolus in specie restringit ad Prophetiam, hoc est, interpretationem Scripturæ: id illi ad genus univerfum omnium eorum, quæ in Ecclesia fiunt, accommodant: & indefinitè ad quemlibet cœtum Ecclesiasticum detorquent. Sanè quoad Scripturæ interpretationem, illam linguâ vernaculâ, & omnibus ex æquo intelligibili in quolibet Ecclesiæ cœtu fieri debere, ultrò concedimus. Quod ipsum de Sacramentorum etiam celebratione, contra Pontificiorum insaniam, omninò statuimus. Verùm inde ad quasvis preces, quasvis etiam canciones, quemvis etiam cœtum, non valet consequentia. Hinc linguæ peregrinæ usum non simpliciter ex Ecclesiâ exterminat Apostolus: sed tantùm secundum quid, nempè in Comparatione ad Prophetiam sive interpretationem Scripturæ: uti cumprimis patet ex versu 6. Deinde idem Apostolus versu 7. & 8. commendationem subjicit satis illustrem Musicæ tùm figuralis, tùm instrumentalis in Ecclesiâ retinendæ: Quemadmodum, inquiens, non satis est, inflare tibiam, aut incerto digitorum strepitu citharam pulsare: sed harmonicè & secundum artem id fiat necesum est: ita qui loquitur in Ecclesia, sed ita, ut intelligi non posit, is aerem verberat, & barbarus haberi debet. Qualia encomia utriusque Musicæ alibi quoque in Scripturis continentur: ut Num. 10. 2. & 3. ubi ad ipsius DEI institutum tubis argenteis signum dari debuerit, quando populus ad tabernaculum Domini confluere debebat. Sic in dicendis DEO laudibus, & celebrandis beneficiis ejus, juxta dispositionem Mosis, Exod. 15. v. 1. & 20. populus DEI utebatur Musicâ tùm instrumentali, tùm vocali. Quod ipsum de Davide & Asapho tùm ex Psalmis, tùm ex 1. Paral. 23. vers. 5. & 25. 1. satis luculenter patet. Unde David vult laudari DEUM in sono tubæ, in psalterio & cythara, in tympano & choro, in chordis & organo, in cymbalis benè sonantibus, in cymbalis jubilationis, Psal. 150. Præterea Scriptura testis est, peculiarem quandam, & arcanam quasi vim obtinere utramque Musicam, in recreandis hominum mentibus, & propulsando spiritu melancholico, qui pater est omnis tristitiæ. 1. Sam. 16. v. 16. & 23. 2. Reg. 3. v. 15. Eccles. 32. v. 7. & 8. Tandem cum in altera vita præcipuum beatorum munus sit futurum, ut cum universâ militiâ cœlesti subinde DEO accinant illud τρισάγιον: Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Dominus DEUS Zabaoth. Esa. 6. haud malè inde colligitur, quôd hymni & cantus in laudem DEI, & voce, & instrumentis Musicis instituti, sint certum quasi quôddam præludium æternæ illius & cœlestis harmoniæ; ad quam cum desiderio meritô adspiramus omnes. Facesat ergò tetricus ille Calvinianorum spiritus, cui gratior accidit vel mugitus bonum, vel latratus canum, quàm concentus harmonicus in laudem DEI, sive publice, sive privatim institutus.

Sed objicit nobis idem ille Spiritus, 1. Cor. non semper respondere cantui : sed saepiuscule dari sine mente sonum. Sed Accidentis haec Sophistica. Removeatur ergò vitium hoc, & excutiatur veternus, tum rectè habebit cantus, & correspondebit ori. Quid, quòd stante hac ratione, omnis prorsus cantus, etiam vernaculâ linguâ conceptus, imò preces quoque, linguâ usitatissimâ, & omnibus intelligibili recitatae, penitùs abrogandae essent: quibus singulis, ex vitio Auditorum ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ obtingere solet. Hic ergò locum habet illud πολυθρήλλητον, quod Calviniani semper in ore ferunt:

Non vox : sed votum : non chordula Musica : sed cor: Non clamans, sed amans cantat in aure DEI.

Deinde objiciunt autoritatem S. Patrum, cumprimis B. Hieronymi, qui in Commentario ad c. 5. Epistolae ad Ephesios scripserit : Canere, & psallere, & laudare Dominum magis animo, quàm voce debemus. Sed crassa committitur ἄγνοια ἐλέγχου. Non enim dicit August. quòd voce planè non debeamus laudare Dominum : sed quòd magis animo, quam voce id fieri debeat: sic innuens, veram laudem DOMINI non consistere in solâ vocis cantione: sed cumprimis in devotione animi, quae ad vocem externam accedere debeat. Quod ipsum & nos statuimus. Quams. in sententia in D. Augustinus praeclarè scripsit lib. 10. Confess. cap. 33. Cùm fluctuor inter periculum voluptatis, & experimentum salubritatis, magis adducor, cantandi consuetudinem approbare in Ecclesia, ut per oblectamenta aurium, infirmior animus in affectum pietatis assurgat.

Tandem objiciunt, Cantum figuralem & Organicumin Ecclesia apostolica non fuisse usitatum.

Respondemus, quòd licèt hoc à nobis negari non possit, neque tamen interim quicquam decedat nostrae sententiae. Alia enim est ratio Ecclesiae demùm plantandae, alia Ecclesiae jam plantatae. Illa quoad ceremonias ad temporis statum, & populi conditionem se accommodare necesse habuit. Haec verò jam in Statum Libertatis suae plenè quasi afferta, secundum praeceptum Apostoli 1. Cor. 14. ult. ordinare potest in ceremoniis, quae faciunt ad τάξιν καὶ εὐσχημοσύνην. Deinde licèt usus Musicae figuralis & Organicae Apostolorum aetatem non attingat: antiquissimú tamen eum esse satis constat. Refert Marianus Scotus, sub annum Domini 756 Organica instrumenta, prius in Occidente nunquam visa, à Constantino Copronymo, in Franciam Pipino Regi missa esse. Unde eorum in Oriente antiquiorem fuisse usum, promptum est colligere.

Sed haec hoc loco de precibus & cantionibus latinis dixisse sufficiat.


### Question VII. For whom prayer is to be made?

The Apostle defines this question in 1 Timothy 2, verses 1 and 2: 'I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.' The Apostle teaches, of course, that one must pray for all men: by the word 'men,' inculcating in us the fellowship of our kind; but by the term of universality, excluding no one with respect to sex, age, rank, fortune, condition, or religion, so that the Apostle seems to have wished to insinuate to us in this place a work that is plainly singular and most proper to Christians. Yet this very universality has its own declaration added, and a kind of specification, as it were: namely, that one must pray even for Kings, and for any who are set in authority. By this designation are understood both Emperors and Monarchs, as well as dynasts and toparchs, and whatever nobles are established in magistracy and power of any kind. And indeed, the Apostle wished to add this declaration or specification with a certain definite purpose, namely, lest any Christian, on account of the Gentile religion which all Magistrates at that time professed, should think that the benefit of prayers ought to be denied to that political order, as being Gentile. For this very reason he recounts the benefits which, from prayers poured out for the Magistrate, however impious and infidel he may be, can redound to the Church: namely, 1. The tranquility of a peaceful life. 2. Civil honesty of morals. 3. A tolerable exercise of worship and religion.

This Apostolic decision distinguishes, or rather separates, the Christian religion and faith from the worship of all other peoples; indeed, it establishes a clear distinction among those who profess the name of Christ and carry it on their lips. The Jews certainly conceive prayers only for their own people, while cursing all other peoples. The Turks, Tartars, and peoples of other regions do the same. Thus, although the Papists call themselves Christians and are so proud of this title that they boast they alone are Catholics, the very practice of the Roman Church evidently demonstrates that they do not rise to this Apostolic property of the Christian faith; because they place no small part of divine worship in cursing or anathematizing the greatest part of the human race, and consequently in condemning and persecuting even a magistrate of a different religion. Making a divorce from these, true Christians conceive prayers for all men, not only for the reason which the Blessed Ambrose expresses in Book 1 of the Hexaemeron: 'If,' he says, 'you pray only for yourself, you will pray alone for yourself; but if you pray for all, all will pray for you.' But also because the Apostle, in verse 3, asserts in express words that this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior.

Various questions are moved in this place, which deserve more accurate observation. And first, indeed, it is asked: If prayers ought to be conceived by Christians for all men, and thus even for infidels and our enemies, what should we pray for them?

We rightly form the answer, however, if we weigh partly the sayings and partly the examples of the Scriptures that pertain to this. The sum comes to this: one must pray for the infidels and enemies of the Church, not that God may approve, help, or promote their impious counsels and endeavors, or confirm the impiety of their worship—for this would fight diametrically against the second petition of the Lord's Prayer, 'Thy kingdom come,' not the kingdom of Satan or of the World—but that GOD, having mercy on them, may lead them to the kingdom of His Son through true conversion, and may endow and illuminate them with true faith; and since salvation has been provided for each and all men, and GOD Himself seriously protests that He does not want the death of the sinner, but wants all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, that He may take care to derive the rivulets of this His mercy to them also, if they are going to show themselves docile and convertible. And this is what the Savior commanded, Matthew 5, verse 44. 'Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same? And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the Gentiles so?' Thus Abraham prayed for the Sodomites, Genesis 18; for Abimelech, Genesis 20. Thus Moses did not hesitate to pour out prayers to GOD for the impious King and persecutor of the Israelite people, Pharaoh: Exodus 9, verses 28 and 33. Thus Jeremiah commands the people to pray for the peace of the impious city, because in its peace consists the peace of the people: Jeremiah 29:7. Thus the Savior and Stephen [prayed] for their executioners.

Some testimonies of Scripture are objected in this place, such as that David throughout the Psalms imprecates eternal destruction upon the enemies and persecutors of the Church, and testifies that he hates them with a perfect hatred, Psalm 139:21 and 22; that GOD Himself prohibits Jeremiah from praying for the impious people, saying: 'Therefore pray not thou for this people, neither lift up cry nor prayer for them, neither make intercession to me: for I will not hear thee,' Jeremiah 7, verse 16; that likewise in 1 John 5:16, prayer is forbidden for those who sin unto death; that finally John writes in his 2nd epistle, verses 10 & 11: If anyone comes to you, and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, nor say Ave to him: For he who says to him, Ave, shares in his evil works. And indeed that one should pray for infidels and enemies of the Church: although the duties of humanity ought not to be denied to them, as Thomas taught in 2. Secundæ quæst. 25. and Durandus in l. 3. sent. dist. 30. q. 1. Hence in Canon law, Can. Qui communicaverit: 11. quæst. 3. it is cautioned that if any layman prays for an excommunicated person and a heretic, such a person himself should be judged as one; but if a priest does this, he should be deposed.

But it is most rightly answered that an ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχου [ignorance of refutation] and a sophistication ἀπὸ τοῦ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς [from the particular to the absolute] are committed in the cited passages of Scripture and examples. For David does not treat of the enemies and persecutors of the Church in any way whatsoever, and indeed considered with respect to us: but insofar as they pursue GOD himself with hatred. Whence David does not say: I hate with a perfect hatred those who hate ME, but those who hate YOU: and I pined away over YOUR enemies. One must therefore distinguish between our enemies and the enemies of GOD: It is fitting to love the former, and to assist them with our prayers for their conversion and salvation. But to hate the latter: lest we appear to approve in any way of their blasphemies and insults cast against GOD with a cursed mouth. The former kind of men regards the persons themselves in themselves: but the latter does not primarily concern the persons: but the impiety, blasphemies, and crimes which are directed against GOD, even though we also are attacked by them in their own way and respect. For it is the faith and the Gospel which they tear apart with insults, not ours, but GOD'S: Therefore in this way, they are called enemies of GOD κατ' ἐξοχήν [preeminently], and they ought to be commended to GOD in our prayers no more than the insults and blasphemies themselves.

The other passage, Jerem. 7:16, is to be understood κατὰ τί [in a certain respect] and according to what. For God does not simply disapprove and forbid the Prophet's zeal in praying for the people: but only for the condition of the present state and time. Because God had decreed by a just judgment to punish the unconquerable stubbornness of his people, and the execution of the decree was already, as they say, at the door, God warns the Prophet to cease praying any longer for a people for whom no hope of amendment remains: and therefore to cease in vain to avert the punishments already impending, because He is unwilling to hear his prayers any longer. And not only does the whole coherence of the text evidently confirm this answer: but GOD himself explains this prohibition thus: Jerem. 14:11 & 16. Do not pray for this people FOR GOOD: For I will consume them with the sword, pestilence, and famine.

In this very sense, GOD also did not want the Prophet Ezekiel to pray for the elders of the people, chap. 20.

Thirdly, the passage in 1 John 5:16 deals specifically with those who sin against the Holy Spirit, who, with a set purpose, turn away from the means of salvation, despise them, expose them to mockery, trample the merit of Christ underfoot, and crucify him again for themselves, deny the truth they have acknowledged against the testimony of their own heart and conscience, hate it, and persecute it: certainly it would be no more lawful to pray for these than it ought to be considered pious to pray to GOD that He receive someone into grace without Christ, or rather against Christ and his Gospel. From this singular case, therefore, the consequence does not hold for the universal genus of infidels.

Finally, regarding the other command of John, in the 2nd Epistle verses 10, 11, etc., it is to be understood as that, namely, concerning fraternal society and conversation with heretics and false teachers: but not concerning the duties of humanity or civil society, or even the debt of prayers by which we are bound to them: But outside these limits, and indeed regarding the fraternity and peace of religion to be entered into with heretics and pseudo-teachers, the love of enemies does not extend. For here that passage of 2 Corinthians 6:14 & seqq. has place: Do not be yoked together with unbelievers: For what fellowship has Christ with Belial? or light with darkness? or righteousness with iniquity? etc.

Let the profanity of the Scholastics therefore be gone: as also that Canon of Pontifical law. For taught by the word of GOD, we establish that one must pray for any of our enemies and persecutors, indeed even for the excommunicated and heretics, as far as their persons are concerned: with James 5:19 & 20 also agreeing: My brethren, if any of you wanders from the truth, and someone converts him: he ought to know that he who turns a sinner from his error shall save his soul from death, and shall cover a multitude of sins.

Latin:

QUæstionem hanc definit Apostolus in 1. Tim. 2. v. 1. & 2. Hortor ante omnia, ut fiant deprecationes, preces, intercessiones, gratiarum actiones pro omnibus hominibus, pro regibus & omnibus in eminentia constitutis, ut pacatam & tranquillam vitam agamus, in omni pietate & honestate. Docet nimirum Apostolus, orandum esse pro omnibus hominibus: Hominum vocabulo, societatem generis nostri nobis inculcans: Universalitatis autem termino, quemvis sexus, ætatis, ordinis, fortunæ conditionis, religionis cujuscúq; respectu excludes, ita ut planè singulare, & Christianorum maxime proprium opus nobis insinuare Apostolus hoc loco voluisse videatur. Habet verò hæc ipsa Universalitas adjectam suam δήλωσιν, & quandam quasi specificationem: Orandum scilicet esse pro Regibus etiam, & quibusvis in eminentia constitutis. Quâ notatione intelliguntur tùm Imperatores & Monarchæ; tùm dynastæ & toparchæ, qviqve in magistratu & potestate quacunqve constituti sunt proceres. Et sanè certo quodam consilio δήλωσιν sive specificationem hanc adjicere voluit Apostolus, ne videlicet Christianorum aliquis, ob religionem Ethnicam, quam Magistratus omnes tùm profitebantur, existimaret, Precum beneficium Ordini isti Politico, tanquam Ethnico, denegandum esse. Quam ipsam ob causam commoda recenset, quæ ex precibus pro Magistratu, quantumvis impio & infideli fusis, ad Ecclesiam redundare possunt: nempè 1. Vitæ pacatæ tranquillitas. 2. Civilis morum honestas. 3. Cultus & religionis tolerabile exercitium.

Decisio hæc Apostolica distinguit, imò separat Religionem & fidem Christianam, ab omnium aliorum populorum cultu: quin inter eos, qui Christi nomen profitentur, inqve ore ferunt, luculentum discrimen constituit. Judæi certè pro suâ duntaxat gente preces concipiunt, reliquos populos devovendo omnes. Id ipsum Turcæ, Tartari, aliarumqve regionum populi factitant. Sic, licèt Pontificii Christianos se nominent, & de hoc titulo ita superbiant, ut se solos Catholicos glorientur: ipsa tamen praxis Ecclesiæ Romanæ evidenter demonstrat, ipsos ad hanc Apostolicam Christianæ fidei proprietatem non assurgere: propterea quòd in devovenda sive anathematizanda parte generis humani maxima, adeoqve magistratu etiam diversæ religionis damnando persequendoqve partem cultus divini non minimam collocant. Ab his divortium facientes veri Christiani pro omnibus hominibus preces concipiunt, non ob eam tantùm causam, quam exprimit B. Ambrosius lib. 1. Hexametri: Si, inquiens, pro te tantum rogas solus pro te rogabu: Sin autem pro omnibus rogas, omnes pro te rogabunt. Verùm etiam, quia Apostolus vers. 3. disertis verbis asserit; Bonum & gradum hoc esse coram Salvatore nostro Deo.

Variæ hoc loco moventur quæstiones, quæ observationem accuratiorem merentur. Ac primùm quidem quæritur. Si preces concipi debeant à Christianus pro omnibus hominibus, & sic pro infidelibus etiam, ac inimicis nostris: Quidnam illis precari debeamus?

Responsionem autem rectè informamus, si partim dicta, partim exempla Scripturarum huc facientia, expendamus. Summa huc redit: Orandum esse pro infidelibus & hostibus Ecclesiæ, non ut Deus impia ipsorum consilia & conatus approbet, juvet, promoveat: aut impietatem cultus ipsorum confirmet: Hoc enim è diametro pugnaret cum secunda petitione Orationis Dominicæ, Adveniat regnum Tuum, non regnum Satanæ aut Mundi: sed ut DEUS ipsorum misertus, ad regnum Filii sui per veram Conversionem eos adducat, verâ fide donet & illuminet, & cùm salus parta sit singulis & universis hominibus, & ipse DEUS seriò protestetur, se nolle mortem peccatoris, sed velle omnes salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis pervenire: ut hujus suæ misericordiæ rivulos ad ipsos quoqve, si dociles & convertibiles se præbituri sint, derivari curet. Et hoc est, quod Servator præcepit, Matth. 5. v. 44. Diligite inimicos vestros, benefacite his, qui oderunt vos, & orate pro persequentibus, & calumniantibus vos: ut sitis Filii Patris vestri, qui in cælis est, qui Solem suum oriri facit super bonos & malos, & injustos: Si enim diligitis eos, qui vos diligitis eos, qui nos diligunt, quam mercedem habebitis? nonnè & publicani hoc faciunt? Et si salutaveritis fratres vestros tantùm, quid ampliùs facitis, nonnè & Ethnici hoc faciunt? Sic Abraham oravit pro Sodomitis Gen. 18. pro Abimelech Gen. 20. Sic Moses non dubitavit preces ad DEUM fundere, pro Rege impio, & persecutore populi Israelitici, Pharaone: Exod. 9. v. 28. & 33. Sic Jeremias jubet orare populum pro pace civitatis impiæ: eò quòd in pace illius consistat pax populi: Jerem. 29, 7. Sic Servator & Stephanus pro interfectoribus suis.

Objiciuntur hoc loco nonnulla Scripturæ testimonia, ut qvod David passim in Psalmis hostibus & persecutoribus Ecclesiæ æternum exitium imprecatur, & perfecto odio se eos odisse attestatur, Psal. 139, 21. & 22 qvòd DEUS ipse prohibeat, ne Jeremias oret pro populo impio: Noli, inquiens, orare pro populo hoc, nec assumas pro eis laudem & orationem, & non obsistas mihi: quia non exaudiam te. Jerem. 7. v. 16. quòd item 1. Joh. 5. v. 16. prohibetur oratio pro iis, qui peccant ad mortem. : quòd denique Johannes in epistola 2. versu 10. & 11. scribit : Si quis venit ad vos, & hanc doctrinam non adfert, ne recipite eum domum, nec Ave ei dicite : Qui enim dicit ei, Ave, communicat operibus ejus malis. Et profectò ex perverso locorum istorum sensu, orta est doctrina Scholasticorum, negantium pro infidelibus & hostibus Ecclesiæ esse orandum : licet humanitatis officia illis negari non debeant, uti docuit Thomas in 2. Secundæ quæst. 25. & Durandus in l. 3. sent. dist. 30. q. 1. Hinc in jure Canonico, Can. Qui communicaverit : 11. quæst. 3. cautum est, ut si Laicus aliquis oret pro excommunicato & hæretico, talis & ipse censeatur si verò id fecerit Sacerdos, deponatur.

Sed rectissimè respondetur, committi ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχε, & Sophisticationem ἀπὸ τῶ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς, in citatis Scripturæ locis & exemplis. Nam David non agit de hostibus & persecutoribus Ecclesiæ, quovis modo, & quidem ratione nostri consideratis : sed quatenus DEUM ipsum odio profequuntur. Unde David non dicit : Perfecto odio odi eos, qui oderunt ME, sed qui oderunt TE: & super inimicos TUOS tabescebam. Distinguendum ergò inter inimicos nostros, & inimicos DEI: Illos amare, & precibus nostris ad conversionem & salutem ipsorum juvare convenit. Hos verò odisse : ne blasphemias & convitia ipsorum in DEUM maledico ore projecta, ullo pacto probare videamus. Prius illud genus hominum personas ipsas in se respicit : Posteriùs verò hoc non primò personas : sed impietatem, blasphemias & scelera concernit : quæ in DEUM feruntur, licet nos quoqve suo modo ac respectu, illis petamur. Est enim fides & Evangelium, quôd convitiis illi proscindunt, non nostrum, sed DEI : Ergò hoc pacto, inimici etiam DEI κατ' ἐξοχὶν dicuntur, & precibus nostris DEO haud magis, atq; convitia & blasphemiæ ipsæ commendari debent.

Alter locus Jerem. 7. v. 16. κτ' τὶ & secundum quid est accipiendus. Non enim DEus simpliciter improbat & prohibet studium Prophetæ orandi pro populo : sed tantùm pro conditione præsentis status & temporis. Quia enim justo judicio DEus inexpugnabilem populi sui contumaciam punire decreverat, & executio decreti jam præ foribus, quod dicitur, erat, monet DEus Prophetam, ut cesset orare ampliùs pro populo, de quo nulla emendationis spes sit reliqua : ac proinde frustrà desinat avertere pœnas jam ingruentes, eò quòd nolit ampliùs exaudire preces ipsius. Et responsionem hanc non modò tota textus συνέπεια evidenter confirmat : sed & DEUS ipse prohibitionem hanc sic explicat : Jerem. 14. v. 11. & 16. Noli orare pro populo isto IN BONUM: Quoniam gladio, peste, ac fame consumam eos.

Quo ipso sensu noluit etiam DEUS orare Prophetam Jezechielem pro senioribus populi, cap. 20.

Tertiò Locus in 1. Johan. 5. v. 16. agit in specie de peccantibus in Spiritum Sanctum, qui cum media salutis destinato consilio aversentur, contemnant, ludibrio exponant, meritum Christi pedibus conculcent, eundemq́; denuò sibi ipsi crucifigant, veritatem agnitam contra proprium cordis & conscientiæ testimonium abnegent, oderint, persequantur: certè haud magis licitum fuerit pro his orare, atque pium censeri debet, orare DEUM, ut aliquem sine Christo, imò contra Christum, & ejus Evangelium, in gratiam recipiat. Ab hac ergò singulari specie, ad genus universum infidelium, non valet consequentia.

Tandem quoad præceptum alterum Johannis, in 2. Epistola vers. 10. 11. &c. id illud est intelligendum, nempe de fraternâ societate & conversatione cum hæreticis & falsis doctoribus: non verò vel de humanitatis officiis vel de civili societate, vel etiam de debito precum, quo ipsis obstricti sumus: Verùm extra hos limites, & quidem ad fraternitatem & pacem religionis, cum hæreticis & pseudodoctoribus ineundam, dilectio inimicorum se non diffundit. Hic enim locum habet illud 2. Corinth. 6. v. 14 & seqq. Nolite jugum ducere cum infidelibus: Quæ enim est societas Christo cum Belial? luci cum tenebris? justitiæ cum iniquitate? &c.

Faceslat ergò Scholasticorum prophanitas: ut & Canon illa juris Pontificii. Verbo enim DEI edocti, pro quibusvis hostibus & persecutoribus nostris, imò pro excommunicatis etiam & hæreticis, qvoad personas ipsorum, orandum esse statuimus: adstipulante etiam Jac. c. 5. v. 19. & 20. Fratres mei, si quis vestrum aberraverit à veritate, & converterit eum quispiam: scire debet, qui averterit peccatorem ab errore suo, quòd salvaturus sit animam ejus à morte, & obtecturus multitudinem peccatorum


### Question VII. For whom prayer is to be made? (continued)

Thus even public and solemn Excommunication does not take away the zeal of prayers toward the excommunicated: but at least that public fellowship which flourishes in the temple among Christians, both regarding the sacraments themselves and regarding public prayers.

Furthermore, it is asked: Is it lawful to pray against some, and to imprecate evils upon them? Which question can be resolved generally at the beginning by distinguishing partly between the object, and partly between the manner in which one can pray against some.

The object either concerns persons: or the things, pursuits, endeavors, and counsels of the impious. In the former respect, we establish that one must pray for the impious: in the latter, against the impious. Hence there emerges also a twofold manner of praying against someone: The one is when we pray that God may either confound the ungodly in their wicked counsels, or, if there remains absolutely no hope of their amendment for the better, that they may be utterly destroyed. And we do not doubt in the least that this manner of praying against the ungodly is lawful and permitted, because it seeks and concerns the amendment and salvation of enemies rather than their destruction. In this manner David prayed against his enemies and persecutors, 2 Sam. 15. v. 31: Look upon, O LORD, the counsel of Ahithophel. Thus the Apostles prayed, Acts 4. v. 29: Look upon, O LORD, their threatenings, and grant unto thy servants that with all boldness they may speak thy word, &c. The other manner of praying against some is when we pray simply against our enemies and persecutors, that God may destroy them and cast them down into the abyss of hell. This manner of praying, so simply, nakedly, and absolutely seeking the destruction of anyone, hardly has a place among Christians, except when prayers are poured out against the Devil, of whom there can be no hope of salvation. But that we should pray in such an absolute and unconditional manner against any human being, however much an enemy and adversary to us, we determine to be illicit and unpermitted. 1. Because such a mode of praying conflicts with Christian Charity, which commands us to love even our enemies, and those who persecute us and slander us, and to wish them well and do them good. Matt. 5. 44. 2. Because by this means we cut off all hope of their amendment: a thing which conflicts with the judgments of GOD, which, just as they are unsearchable, so they can recall those enemies of ours to the way beyond all our hope and expectation: a thing which is evident from the example of Saul, the persecutor of the nascent Church of the Christians. Acts 9. 1. & seqq. 3. This inordinate zeal deprives enemies of that means by which they could be led to the acknowledgment of the truth. For true faith can obtain for the infidel also conversion to GOD and faith: therefore this manner of praying is deservedly rejected in our Churches: and prayer is made for our enemies, that GOD may grant them conversion and acknowledgment of their sins: Unsern Feinden/Verfolgern/vnd Lästerern vergebē/vnd sie bekehre/ as the formal words of our Litany have it.

nations: do not have mercy on any who work iniquity: And ver. 12. Scatter them by your mighty works, and bring them down, O Lord my protector: And ver. 15. and following. They shall suffer hunger, they shall howl like dogs, they shall run about in the city, and they shall wander to seek bread, and they shall murmur if they are not satisfied. Likewise when Jeremiah chap. 18. v. 19. and following prays against his enemies, saying: Attend O LORD to me, and hear the voice of my adversaries: Shall evil be rendered for good, because they have dug a pit for my soul? Remember that I stood in your sight, that I might speak good for them, and turn away your indignation from them. Therefore deliver up their children to famine, and pour them out by the hands of the sword: let their wives be bereaved of their children, and widows: and let their men be put to death: let their young men be slain by the sword in battle: let a cry be heard from their houses, when thou shalt bring a troop suddenly upon them; for they have digged a pit to take me, and hid snares for my feet. Yet thou, O LORD, knowest all their counsel against me to death: forgive not their iniquity, neither blot out their sin from thy sight.

Thus the Apostle prays against Alexander the coppersmith, saying: Alexander, he says, did me much evil, the LORD will reward him according to his works, of whom be thou ware also, 2 Tim. 4. 14. When, I say, we read such things in the Scriptures, it is to be noted that the surface of the letter is not to be pressed: for in this way these prayers and similar ones would not be entirely free from all fault: which it is hardly permissible to think concerning such great Prophets: but the intent and sense, or the mind of the Prophets, ought to be regarded, which suggests a triple understanding. For 1, they were seeking not so much their own honor and dignity as that of GOD Himself, whose ministers and legates they were: and therefore they were handing over the unassailable contumacy and malice of their enemies to be avenged by GOD. Therefore this hatred was not properly of persons; but of the Cause: (just as above concerning the prayer of David, Psalm 139. v. 21. 22. We have shown that they did not desire the perdition of the person himself considered in himself, but rather the dissipation and confusion of the pursuits and counsels by which they wished to harm the Church and the Saints; a thing which does not conflict with Christian charity, because such a prayer seeks and promotes not the eternal destruction of the enemies, but rather their correction.

Furthermore, these prayers, inasmuch as they proceeded from the Prophets, also partake of a Prophetic sense: and as Augustine rightly determined in book 1 of his *De Sermone Domini in monte*, they are not those of persons wishing or imprecating, but of those foretelling what will eventually happen to those impious ones. Nor does the nature and mood of the Optative stand in the way, since the ἐναλλαγὴ of tense and the permutation of moods is most customary for the Prophets.

If, therefore, there occur in the Holy Scriptures examples of Saints who prayed absolutely and simply against their enemies: as when David prays in Psalm 5, verses 10 and 11, "There is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain; their throat is an open sepulchre; they deal deceitfully with their tongues; judge them, O GOD," or as the property of the Hebrew text sounds, האשימם, that is, "destroy and condemn them; let them fall by their own counsels; cast them out in the multitude of their transgressions, for they have rebelled against thee, O LORD." And Psalm 59, verse 6, "Awake to visit all"

Thirdly, carried away also by a singular zeal and heroic spirit for the assertion of divine justice, they broke out into prayers of this kind, not principally with the end that they might seek the condemnation of the impious, but that they might desire that examples and testimonies of divine justice might at last publicly exist, by which others might be deterred from similar impiety and contumacy. Since this zeal was proper to the Prophets, and so very pure, and simply separated from carnal affection, it can scarcely fall to any pious person today; certainly it will not be permitted to imitate these prayers of the Prophets, burning with some singular zeal, rashly. Nor, however, is this zeal to be judged to have fought in any way with the legitimate worship of God. For God is also worshipped when He is acknowledged and invoked as a just judge and as the author of all scourges and punishments, by which He can restrain the contumacious and headstrong and bring them into order: provided that such zeal be alien from all carnal affection and the desire for private vengeance. To which opinion Augustine also argues in his commentary on Psalm 78, Vol. 8, and finally concludes that even the pious sometimes rejoice at the eternal perdition of the impious, and in this part sin nothing against Christian charity, in that they rejoice and are glad, not properly at the perdition of the impious, but partly at the justice of God most justly revealed against the impious, and partly at the desired liberation of the Church from such cancers. Thus, therefore (Augustine finally infers), let the enemy be loved so that the justice of God, which punishes, does not displease; and let the justice which punishes be so pleasing that one rejoices not at his evil, but at the good judge. The pious, however, rejoice in the just judge: 1. Because they love God Himself and wish nothing to be diminished from His justice; 2. Because they also love the enemy, whom they rejoice to see corrected by divine vengeance; 3. Because they love their neighbor, whom they desire to be more and more confirmed in the pursuit of piety by the punishments and examples of others; 4. Because they love themselves, and, rendered more cautious by the danger and harm of others, they learn to walk forthwith in the fear and ways of the Lord and to amend their errors: Just as Augustine discourses quite prolixly on these four causes in the place already cited; and from Augustine, Thomas on that passage of the Apocalypse, 'Avenge, O Lord, the blood of Thy saints,' etc. he constructs two modes of praying against enemies: of which one seeks the vengeance of enemies from God out of a depraved and malicious affection and a desire for private vengeance: which mode is simply prohibited in sacred things; but the other [seeks it] out of a zeal for justice and according to the will of God, so that, namely, either the curable may be saved, or the incurable may be judged and justly condemned. Which mode, if it proceeds from a true love of God and neighbor, is not rejected. See more in Thomas, 2nd of the second part, question 83, article 8.

Thirdly, it is asked in this place: Since according to the admonition of the Apostle one must pray for all men, must one also pray for the departed or the dead?

We answer, however, in the negative: and we maintain that no help for establishing funeral rites for the departed can be elicited from the words of the Apostle: For 1. Those who have finished their life have already ceased to be in the census and society of men, and having become citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, and liberated from all human infirmity, they cannot be transferred to a better state. 2. The Apostle wishes prayers to be made for all men in this life for no other reason more than because of the calamities to which mortals are subject. But those who have already departed to the triumphant Church are clearly immune from these. 3. A most false hypothesis underlies the affirmative of the Romanists, and that a double one: One, that there is a purgatorial fire in which at last the souls even of the pious are fully and perfectly purified: The other, that these very souls can be helped by the prayers of men still surviving, especially through funeral rites and vigils for the dead, that purgatorial punishments can be mitigated, and at last they can be liberated from them more quickly and transmitted into heaven. Than which two figments scarcely anything more vain or more like an old woman's tale can be thought up: so that the voice of Bellarmine can bring us to astonishment, asserting that it is pious and religious to pray even for those dead of whom it is uncertain whether they are in heaven or in hell. Vol. 1, General Controversy 1, book 1, chapter 15, letter D. To which assertion we oppose this general syllogism:

Whatever is not of faith is sin. But the invocation of GOD for the dead is done without faith. Therefore. The major is self-evident, from chapter 14, last verse, of Romans. The minor is confirmed thus: Whatever is done from faith, it is necessary that it look to the express Word of GOD, whether of command, or of promise, or of both together, as a foundation. For faith is of the nature of correlatives: whose correlative is the express word. But the invocation for the dead has no word at all, either of command or of promise, expressed in sacred things. Therefore it cannot be done from faith.

Furthermore, the whole Scripture knows no more than two classes of the departed: One of those who departed hence in the true faith of Christ: The other, who went away in incredulity: Scripture does not hand over the former to be purged at last by any infernal fire: But from the first moment of death, it places them in the heaven of the blessed: Thus the Savior Himself confirming with religious attestation and a double oath, as it were: John 5, v. 24: 'Amen, amen I say to you, he who hears My Word, and believes Him who sent Me, has eternal life, and DOES NOT COME INTO JUDGMENT: but PASSES THROUGH DEATH INTO LIFE.' But the latter it consigns not just for a time, but for all eternity to the eternal punishment of the underworld: John 3, v. 18 & 36: 'He who does not believe, is ALREADY judged, and will not see life, but the wrath of GOD REMAINS upon him.' Therefore our prayers can help neither side in the least, but rather they contract the guilt of a most atrocious sin, in that they attempt to change, with an audacity more than rash, the immutable rule of divine justice in the Word

Latin:

Sic Excommunicatio etiam publica & solennis, non tollit studium precum erga excommunicatos: sed publicum saltem illud consortium, quod in templo viget inter Christianos, tum quoad sacra ipsa, tum quoad preces publicas.

Porrò quæritur: An liceat orare contra aliquos, iisdemq; male imprecari? Quæ quæstio initiò generaliter expediri potest, distinguendo partim inter objectum, partim inter modum, quo contra aliquos orari potest.

Objectum vel concernit personas: vel res, studia, conatus, & consilia impiorum. Priore respectu pro impiis: posteriore contra impios orandum esse statuimus. HincEmergit etiam geminus precandi modus contra aliquem: Unus est, quando oramus, ut Deus impios in pravis suis consiliis vel confundat, vel si spes de emendatione ipsorum in melius nulla planè supersit, prorsus disperdantur. Et hunc modum orandi contra impios licitum & concessum esse, neutiquam dubitamus, propterea quod magis emendationem, & salutem, quàm exitium hostium quærit & concernit. Quo modo oravit David contra inimicos & persecutores suos, 2. Sam. 15. v. 31. Respice DOMINE consilium Achitophelis. Sic orarunt Apostoli Act. 4. v. 29. Respice DOMINE in minas eorum, & da servis tuis cum omni fiducia loqui verbum tuum, &c. Alter modus orandi contra aliquos est, quando simpliciter contra hostes & persecutores nostros oramus, ut Deus illos perdat, & ad inferorum barathrum præcipitet. Qui modus orandi, ita simpliciter, nudè & absolutè interitum alicujus quærens, vix locum habet apud Christianos, nisi quando contra Diabolum, de quo nulla salutis spes esse potest, preces funduntur. Verùm ut contra hominem aliquem, quantumvis nobis hostem & adversarium sic absolutè & sine conditione oremus, illicitum & inconcessum esse statuimus. 1. Quia talis orandi modus pugnat cum Charitate Christiana, quæ etiam hostes nostros, & persequentes nos, & calumniantes nos, diligere, ijsdemque bene velle & facere jubet. Matth. 5. 44. 2. Quia hoc pacto spem omnem emendationis ipsis præcidimus: id quod pugnat cum judicijs DEI, quæ uti impervestigabilia sunt, ita hostes illos nostros, præter omnem nostram spem & expectationem in viam revocare possunt: id quod patet exemplo Sauli persecutoris Ecclesiæ novellæ Christianorum. Act. 9. 1. & seqq. 3. Privat zelus iste inordinatus, hostes eo medio, per quod ad agnitionem veritatis perduci possent. Potest enim vera fides infidelibus quoq; impetrare conversionem ad DEUM & fidem: Proinde modus iste orandi nostris in Ecclesiis meritò reijcitur: & pro hostibus nostris oratur, ut DEUS illis conversionem & agnitionem peccatorum impertiat: Unsern Feinden/Verfolgern/vnd Lästerern vergebē/vnd sie bekehre/ prout habent verba Litaniæ nostræ formalia.

gentes: non miserearis ullis, qui operantur iniquitatem: Et vers. 12. Disperge illos in virtute tua, & depone eos protector meus Domine: Et vers. 15. & seqq. Famem patientur, ululent ut canes, circumcursitent in civitate, & vagentur ad quærendum panem, & non saturati murmurabunt. Quando item Jeremias cap. 18. v. 19. & seqq. contra inimicos suos orat, dicens: Attende DOMINE ad me, & audi vocem adversariorum meorum: Numquid reddetur pro bono malum, quia foderunt foveam animæ meæ? Recordare, quòd steterim in conspectu tuo, ut loquerer pro eis bonum, & averterem indignationem tuam ab eis. Propterea da filios eorum in famem, & deduc eos in manus gladii: fiant uxores eorum absq; liberis, & viduæ: & viri earum interficiantur morte: juvenes eorum confodiantur gladio in prælio: audiatur clamor de domibus eorum, quando adduces exercitus super eos repente; quia foderunt foveam, ut caperent me, & laqueos absconderunt pedibus meis. Tu autem DOMINE scis omne consilium eorum adversus me ad mortem: Ne propitieris iniquitati eorum, & peccatum earum à facie tuâ ne deleatur.

Sic Apostolus orat contra Alexandrum fabrum ærarium: Alexander, inquiens, multa mala mihi ostendit, reddat ipsi DOMINUS secundum opera ejus, quem & devita, 2. Tim. 4. 14. Quando inquam in Sacris talia legimus, notandum quòd non superficies literæ sit urgenda: hoc enim pacto orationes hæ & consimiles non planè omni vitio carerent: id quod de tantis Prophetis cogitare vix licet: sed Advota & sensus, sive mens Prophetarum spectari debeat, quæ triplicem innuit intellectum. Nam 1 non càm suam, quàm DEI ipsius, cujus ministri & legati erant, honorem & dignitatem quærebant: ac proinde inexpugnabilem hostium contumaciam, & malitiam DEO vindicandam tradebant. Odium ergò hoc non erat propriè personarum; sed Causæ: (quemadmodum supra de precatione Davidis, Psalm. 139. v. 21. 22. Ostendimus, ita ut non personę ipsius in se consideratę perditionem: sed studiorum potiùs & consiliorum, quibus Ecclesiæ & Sanctis nocere cupiebant, dissipationem & confusionem exoptarent: id quod cum charitate Christiana non pugnat, propterea quod non æternum hostium exitium: sed ipsorum potiùs correctionem talis precatio quærit & promovet.

Deinde Orationes hæ, quippe à Prophetis profectæ, sensum etiam Propheticum sortiuntur: & ut Augustinus lib. 1. de Serm. Dom in monte, rectè statuit, non sunt vel optantium, vel imprecantium, sed prænunciantium, quid aliquando cum impiis illis futurum sit. Neque obstat modi Optativi natura, & affectio: Siquidem ἐναλλαγὴ temporis & permutatio modorum Prophetis est ulitatissima.

Quod si ergò occurrunt in Sacris exempla Sanctorum, qui absolutè & simpliciter contra hostes suos precati sunt: ut quando David orat. Psalm. 5. v. 10. & 11. In Ore eorum non est veritas: Cor eorum vanum est: Sepulchrum patens est guttur eorum, linguis suis dolose agunt, Judica illos DEUS, vel ut Hebræi textus proprietàs sonat האשימם hoc est, disperde & condemna eos, decidant à cogitationibus eorum, secundum multitudinem impietatum expelle eos, quoniam irritaverunt te DOMINE. Et Psalm. 59. v. 6. Intende ad visitandas omnes

Tertiò singulari etiam Zelo, & Spiritu heroico pro assertione justitiæ divinæ abrepti, in hujusmodi orationes eruperunt, non eo principaliter fine, quòd quærerent condemnationem impiorum: sed quòd optarent, vel tandem justitiæ divinæ exempla & testimonia publicè extare, quibus cæteri à consimili impietate & contumaciâ absterrerentur. Qui Zelus cùm Prophetarum fuerit proprius, & usque adeò purus, & ab affectu carnali simpliciter segregatus, vix in pium quemque hodie cadat; certè has Prophetarum orationes, singulari aliquo zelo ferventes, non temerè imitari licebit. Neque tamen propterea zelus iste cum legitimo Dei cultu ullatenus pugnasse judicandus est. Colitur enim etiam Deus, cum agnoscitur & invocatur ut justus judex & ut autor omnium flagellorum & pœnarum, quibus contumaces & præfractos compescere, & in ordinem redigere potest: modò talis Zelus alienus sit, ab omni affectu carnali, & vindictæ privatæ cupiditate. Quam in sententiam Augustinus quoque disputat in enarratione Psalm. 78. Tom. 8. & tandem concludit, quòd etiam pii aliquando lætentur de æterna perditione impiorum: & hac in parte nihil peccent contra charitatem Christianam, eò quòd gaudeant & lætentur, non propriè de perditione impiorum: sed partim de justitiâ Dei adversus impios, justissimè patefacta: partim de optatâ liberatione Ecclesiæ ab ejusmodi carcinomatis. Sic ergò (infert tandem Augustinus) inimicus diligatur, ut non displiceat Dei justitia, quæ punitur: & sic placeat justitia, quæ punitur, ut non de malo ejus, sed de bono judice gaudeatur. Gaudent autem pii de justo judice, 1. Quia Deum ipsum diligunt, & de ipsius justitiâ nihil diminutum volunt, 2. quia diligunt etiam inimicum, quem per divinam vindictam corrigi lætantur, 3. quia diligunt proximum, quem aliorum pœnis & exemplis, in studio pietatis, magis magisque confirmari optant, 4. quia diligunt seipsos, & alieno periculo & damno cautiores redditi, subinde in timore & viis Domini ambulare, & errata emendare discunt: Quemadmodum de quatuor istis causis prolixè satis differit Augustinus, loco jam citato: Et ex Augustino Thomas in illud Apocalypseos, Vindica Domine sanguinem Sanctorum tuorum, &c. duos extruit modos orandi contra inimicos: quorum unus vindictam hostium à Deo petat ex affectu pravo & malitioso, privatæque vindictæ cupido: Qui modus in sacris simpliciter sit prohibitus: alter verò ex zelo justitiæ, & secundum voluntatem Dei, ut scilicet vel curabiles serventur, vel incurabiles judicentur, justeque damnentur. Qui modus, si ex verâ dilectione Dei & proximi proveniat, non rejicitur. Vide plura apud Thomam 2. secundæ quæst. 83. art. 8.

Tertiò quæritur hoc loco: Cùm secundum admonitionem Apostoli pro omnibus hominibus sit orandum: anne pro defunctis quoque sive mortuis sit orandum?

Respondemus autem Negativè: neque ex verbis Apostoli quicquam subsidii, pro exequiis defunctorum stabiliendis, elici posse, statuimus: Nam 1. Qui vitâ functi sunt, in hominum censu & societate jam esse desierunt, & cives facti cœlestis Hierosolymæ, omnique humanâ infirmitate liberati, in statum meliorem transferri nequeunt. 2. Preces hac in vitâ non aliam ob causam magis, quam propter calamitates, quibus mortales sunt obnoxii, pro omnibus hominibus fieri vult Apostolus. Atqui ab his immunes planè sunt, qui ad triumphantem Ecclesiam jam excesserunt. 3. Subest falsissima hypothesis sub affirmativâ Romanensium, eaque gemina: : Una, quod sit ignis purgatorius, in quo demùm plenè & perfectè purificentur animæ etiam piorum: Altera, quòd hæ ipsæ animæ per preces hominum adhuc superstitum, cum primis per exequias & vigilias defunctorum, adjuvari, pœnæ purgatoriales mitigari, & tandem ex illis citius liberari, inque cœlum transmitti possint. Quo utroque figmento vix quicquam vanius, aut anile magis dici excogitativè potest: ita ut stuporem nobis inferre possit, vox Bellarmini afferentis, Pium & religiosum esse, orare pro iis etiam mortuis, quos incertum est, an in cœlo, vel in gehennâ sint. Tom. 1. Controv. generali 1. lib. 1. cap. 15. lit. D. Cui assertioni opponimus hunc Syllogismum generalem:

Quicquid non sit ex fide, peccatum est. Atqui invocatio DEI pro mortuis fit sine fide. Ergo. Major est αὐτόπιστος, ex cap. 14. ult. Rom. Minor sic confirmatur. Quicquid fit ex fide, illud expressum DEI Verbum sive mandati, sive promissionis, sive utriusque simul, ceu fundamenti loco respiciat, necesse est. Fides enim est ex naturâ Correlatorum: Cujus correlatum est expressum verbum. Atqui invocatio pro mortuis nullum prorsus verbum sive mandati, sive promissionis in sacris habet expressum. Ergò ex fide fieri nequit.

Porrò Scriptura universa non plures, quàm duas novit classes defunctorum: Unam eorum, qui in verâ fide Christi hinc discesserunt: Alteram, qui in incredulitate abierunt: Illos non demùm purgandos igni cuipiam infernali tradit Scriptura: Sed à mortis primo momento, in cœlum beatorum collocat: Sic religiosâ attestatione, & gemino quasi juramento confirmante ipso Servatore: Johan. 5. v. 24. Amen, amen dico vobis, qui Verbum meum audit, & credit ei, qui misit me, habet vitam æternam, & IN JUDICIUM NON VENIT: sed TRANSIT PER MORTEM IN VITAM. Hòs verò non ad tempus saltem, sed in omnem æternitatem mancipat æterno inferorum supplicio: Johan. 3. v. 18. & 36. Qui non erit, JAM judicatus est, & non videbit vitam, sed ira DEI MANET super illum. Neutros ergò preces nostræ vel tantillum juvare possunt, sed atrocissimi potiùs peccati reatum contrahunt, eò quòd immutabilem justitiæ divinæ regulam in Verbo cla-


### Whether one should pray for the dead

most clearly revealed. This is relevant to that passage of Ecclesiastes 11:3: If the tree fall, whether toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there it shall be. Which passage Jerome, Bernard, and other Fathers have explained with great consensus regarding the immutability of the condition of the soul after death.

But the Esauvites scrape together some passages from the Scriptures, about which a few words must be said. The primary one is that in 2 Maccabees 12:43, Judas Maccabeus is read to have offered a sacrifice for the dead. But I reply that this 1st book, being apocryphal and supposititious by the consensus of the whole Church, can in no way prejudice the authority of the Canonical Scriptures, which know not even a jot about the funeral rites of the deceased. Whence the blessed Jerome also judged that these books could be read for the edification of the people, but not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas: for which reason, in the Council of Laodicea also, chapter 59, or the last, the books of the Maccabees were struck from the census and number of the Canonical Scriptures. What of the fact that the author of this second book himself vehemently doubts its faith and authority, when in chapter 2, verse 24, he confesses that he compiled the history from the five volumes of Jason of Cyrene: and in the last chapter, verse 39, he asks for pardon if he has not attained what he wished. Both of which are simply abhorrent to the style of the Holy Spirit and the authority of the Canonical books. And although Bellarmine objects to this first response of ours with the example of the Evangelist Luke, who himself also expressly confesses that he borrowed the history written by him from others: and yet the Canonical authority of Luke's history was not denied for that reason: the response is nevertheless ready and far more evident, that in both cases a great disparity presents itself. For Luke at the same time clearly testifies that he borrowed the history from those who themselves also had the testimony of the indwelling Holy Spirit.

Then he solemnly attests that he had thoroughly attained all things that pertained to the history concerning Christ. Luke 1:2, 3, and 4. But the author of the history of the Maccabees, as far as the second book is concerned, patched his work together from a clearly Gentile writer: then he himself doubts the truth of all the histories. Whence a judgment can be made concerning the fig-tree and more-than-straw-like Esauvitic exception. But to the matter.

In the second place, therefore, regarding the very deed of Judas Maccabeus, some things in it offer themselves as worthy of praise and imitation: but some things as worthy of reproach. For it is worthy of praise: 1. that he acknowledges the just judgment of God in those who were killed, namely that they were slain in battle because they had stolen and hidden under their tunics the anathemas or votive offerings from the idolatrous temple that had been at Jamnia. 2. that, having turned to prayers with his men, he prays that the whole army might not be destroyed on account of the committed sin. 3. that he exhorts the people, warned by the tragic example of their companions, to beware for themselves against similar or other sins. 4. that he thought well and religiously about the Resurrection. On the contrary, however, it is most worthy of reproach that Judas sent twelve thousand drachmas (for the Romanists count so many from the faulty Vulgate version: although the Greek text has only two thousand, κατασκευάσαντες εἰς ἀργυρῖς δραχμὰς δισχιλίας) to Jerusalem, so that a sacrifice might be offered for the sin committed for the salvation of the slain. For in the whole Mosaic law one cannot find even a single syllable about any sacrifice for the dead: thus in the entire Scripture no command, no promise, no formula or idea of any prayer for the deceased presents itself. This deed of Judas, therefore, even if it happened exactly as it is narrated, cannot fabricate any new article against the Canonical Scriptures. What of the fact that it also fights diametrically against the funeral rites of the Romanists. For Judas took care to offer a sacrifice for the dead only once, if indeed he took care. But the Romanists, not content with one oblation, repeat the funeral rites again and again, and join the seventh day to the first: to the seventh they add the thirtieth: to these they finally add the anniversary, with the goal that they might milk almost the entire inheritance of the deceased from the simpler folk, and from there make inestimable profit. Finally, it is evident from this whole history that Judas was more concerned about the army still surviving, lest it too be cut off in the fury of the Lord, than about the soldiers who were killed. He therefore took care for a sacrifice to be offered not for the salvation of the dead, but for the salvation of those still living. As this deed has its foundation in the law of Moses, so the Gentile writer Jason errs enormously, who dreams that it was done for the sake of the dead: which is even more clearly evident from the fact that the same history is described also in 1 Maccabees 5:57 and following, where, however, no trace of this sacrifice exists at all.

SECONDLY, a passage is objected from Tobit 4:14: Set thy bread and thy wine upon the burial of a just man: and do not eat and drink thereof with sinners.

I reply that a gross ignorance of the elenchus is being committed, which in the present argument clearly has no force. For not even a jot is held in this passage about prayers or intercessions for the deceased: but this whole admonition looks only to the care of the surviving poor, which was done at the tombs of the recently deceased. For it was placed in the custom and habit of the ancients of that time, that after the funeral rites of friends they celebrated feasts: and from there sent food and bread to the tombs of the deceased, and that for the use of the poor, who were accustomed to gather there. Which custom, if all superstition is absent, had nothing of vice in itself: but it contributes nothing at all of help to prayers for the deceased to be freed from purgatory.

THIRDLY, the Esavvites object with the examples of the Saints, of whom mention is made in the Canonical history. For 1 Sam. 31, or the last chapter, verse 13, it is read that the citizens in Jabesh-Gilead, having heard of the death of Saul, fasted for seven days. And 2 Sam. 1, 11 and 12, it is written that David wept and fasted for Saul and Jonathan, and others killed in battle. And chapter 3, 32 and 35, for Abner, who was stabbed by Joab.

But how weak these arguments are, even Bellarmine himself acknowledged, writing with a conscience too cauterized, lib. 1 de purgatorio cap. 3. Col. 1784. Although the mourning, weeping, and fasting of David and others for the slain seem to have been done as a sign of grief and sadness: yet it is CREDIBLE that they were done chiefly to help the souls of the deceased. But we refute this Credible with a non-Credible, indeed with a manifest crime of falsehood. For from the entire history of David, and his Psalms, not even one point can be brought forward which confirms, even probably in appearance, that he believed the souls of the deceased could be freed from hell by the prayers of the survivors, or at least that their punishments could be mitigated: indeed, it is clearly evident that he observed the exact opposite practice, from 2 Sam. 12, 14 up to verse 24. For while the boy was still sick, born from the adultery committed with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, David prayed to the LORD for the little one, and fasted, prostrate on the ground, nor did he wish to taste anything of food or drink before the little one had met his day: Which having died, it is not read that he conceived any further prayers for freeing him from the limbo of infants: but the text holds thus: for the infant while he was still living, I fasted and wept: for I was saying: Who knows, if perhaps the LORD may give him to me and the boy may live? But now because he is dead, why should I fast any longer? Shall I be able to call him back to life? I shall go rather to him (to the limbo of infants, from which the elders are excluded?) but he will not return to me.

These things being so, we respond to the produced examples, that the weeping, mourning, and fasting of the saints were nothing other than signs of grief and sadness, conceived as much from the tragic death of the enemy Saul as from the premature death of his friends Jonathan and Abner. Which cause of his mourning David himself defined, thus addressing the remaining courtiers, 2 Sam. 3, 38 and 39. Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen today in Israel? But I am still tender, and just now anointed King. Which same thing must be determined entirely concerning the mourning of the citizens in Jabesh-Gilead.

FOURTHLY, they object with the authority of the Holy Fathers, who approved of prayers for the dead. But it is answered in a few words, that it is not obscure to us that Epiphanius against the Arians, haeres. 75, Tertullian de corona militis, and elsewhere, Augustine lib. 9 Confess. chaps. 12 and 13. Likewise in the book de cura pro mortuis, if indeed that book acknowledges Augustine as its author: Likewise Serm. 34 de verbis Apostoli: Arnobius lib. 4 adversus gentes near the end: and many others wonderfully commended prayers for the deceased: but it is also certain that the Fathers were not sufficiently consistent with themselves in this part: which is evident even from the fact that among the same Fathers one may read testimonies not less weighty in the clearly contrary opinion: as when Augustine writes in Epist. 80 to Hesychius: In whatever state his own last day finds each man, in that the last day of the world will comprehend him: Since as each one dies on this day, so will he be judged on that day.

Likewise in Tractate 49 on John: Each one sleeps with his own cause, and will rise with his own cause.

Which same thing he repeats in lib. 2 quaest. Evangel. cap. 38. And Serm. 15 de Sanctis.

If the Esavvites have so reconciled this dissonance, or rather manifest contradiction, in the writings of the Fathers regarding the present question, that no scruple of doubt remains, then at last we shall grant that the consensus of the Fathers stands on their side. A certain theologian rightly notes in this place: that it has happened to those Fathers, as we see it happening today also to learned men, that they sometimes look in their writing to the received opinion and custom of their own times; but sometimes they treat the same matter more accurately according to the norm of the Holy Scriptures, without regard for Catholic opinion and custom, and thus it happens that they speak of it in different ways. And this has happened to them in this cause as well. Where they speak of it according to the Scriptures, they say such things as by no means support the opinion and received custom concerning the making of sacrifice and prayers for the dead: but where they accommodate themselves to custom without consulting the Scriptures, they say those things which our adversaries bring forward against us.

But what sensible person does not see how different that subtlety in disputation is (as Cicero warns somewhere) when the truth itself is being refined, from when the discourse is adapted to common opinion? And how much more faith is to be placed in those things which concern our faith, piety, and salvation, in a doctrine conformed to the Holy Scriptures, than in opinions received without the Scriptures? Indeed, as much as there is a difference between truth and common opinion, and as much as truth is to be held more certainly than opinion: so much is there a difference between those things which are said about the state of the dead according to the Scriptures, and those things which are said about sacrifices and prayers to be made for the dead according to common opinion, and so much are the former to be preferred to the latter. Thus he.

FINALLY, they object the inveterate custom of the Church of praying and sacrificing for the dead. But this argument also is easily refuted. For 1. no custom, however ancient, makes an article of the Christian faith, or provides a defense for an error, unless its foundation is expressed in the sacred writings either by way of command or by way of promise. Furthermore, although it may be ancient, it is not the most ancient, nor does it reach back to the age of the Apostles: but it had its origin a long time later, partly from Gentilism, and partly from a certain natural affection toward the dead: and it was retained in the Church by a certain good zeal of some Bishops, although that zeal was not κατ᾽ ἐπίγνωσιν according to knowledge, and therefore it does not obtain the force of a Rule. Rom. 10. It is pleasing, however, at this point to hear Polydore Vergil, book 6, chapter 9, page 443 in my edition, discoursing thus on the origin of funeral rites: That today the annual funeral rites of the dead are performed on the day after the Kalends of November, Odilo was the author, as rumor has it, and Peter Damian testifies. That man, the prefect of the Cluniac monks, when in Sicily, during the papacy of John XVIII, Roman Pontiff, he frequently heard groans and cries around Mount Etna, which are made there continuously, as Trogus testifies, partly from the roaring of the boiling heat of the sea, and partly from the eruption of the Etnean fire, where a sharper wind presses through the vents of the caverns; he thought that demons were lamenting because, through the prayers and sacrifices of Christians, the souls of the dead were being freed from those torments: for it is a constant opinion of the common people that at Mount Etna, where a perpetual fire has burned for so many centuries, or at the underworld, an entrance lies open, or that the souls of the guilty are expiated by a fiery abyss. Therefore, he immediately arranged with his monks that after they had sacrificed on the Kalends of November in honor of all the saints, they should likewise perform funeral rites on the following day for all who had been deprived of life. This institution, as being full of piety, the Fathers eventually received. That year was about the one thousand and second of human salvation.

And after a few words. Among the Gentiles, annual parentalia were performed long ago, that is, a sacrifice every year in honor of the dead: which (besides Tully in the first Philippic, and in the oration for Flaccus) Macrobius and Cato report, writing thus, that Laurentia was honored with the honor of the annual parentation. For there were Parentalia, rites and feasts, which were celebrated at the funeral and at the tomb of parents and relatives by sons and kinsmen, whose author

is said to have been Aeneas, who by that pact was the FIRST OF ALL to honor his parent Anchises, worshiped him with supplications, and consecrated the memory of his name, just as Virgil describes in book 5 of the Aeneid. Thus we observe that very institution for the salvation of the dead. Whence it seems to have come about entirely that the idea of celebrating the annual obsequies of the dead came into Odilo's mind for this religion.

Thus far Polydore Vergil, who in the same book 6, chapter 10, discourses at greater length on this matter, and shows how the nine-day and seven-day sacrifices for the dead were propagated to the Church of GOD from the custom of the Gentiles. This origin and authority of this cult we willingly and entirely leave to the Romanists: but we congratulate our own Churches that they have no commerce with that Gentile superstition and blindness. And this is the one thing worthy of note in this place.

Next, the custom of the Ancient Church had a far different scope and end proposed for itself than what the Roman Church urges today. That this may be evidently clear: let us hear Dionysius discoursing on this matter in his book on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 7, in this manner: The holy assembly being gathered, the Pontiff, if he be a Priest, begins the Prayer to God, and the thanksgiving. The Pontiff and the holy choir sing adapted Psalms. The ministers recite to us the promises made concerning the resurrection from the sacred utterances. Then the Archdeacon, and the principal Minister, excludes only the Catechumens from the doors of the temple, and celebrates the saints who have already piously died. He follows the one who has recently departed with equal panegyric and praise: he exhorts all to pray for a joyful consummation for themselves in Christ. The venerable prelate approaching, performs the most sacred prayer over the one resting. After the Prayer, the Pontiff greets the deceased: And after him, likewise, all who are present. Over the greeted saint he pours oil. Soon the body is placed in an honorable place with other holy bodies.

This is the summary of the whole seventh chapter of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy of Dionysius. Whence it is clear that those prayers held at the tombs of the saints were not satisfactions for the sins of the dead, and for their liberation from purgatory, nor for the mitigation of punishments and infernal torments: but were public eulogies of the piously deceased, and applications of the divine promises concerning the Resurrection of the flesh: exhortations of the survivors to the pursuit of piety: and finally, declarations of Christian sympathy and mourning, which is conceived from the death of friends as well as of any pious persons. For he would be a beast, not a man, who would not be affected by the state and condition of mortality, from which not even the holiest are exempt, which is most miserable. And the Apology of the Augsburg Confession asserts that such prayers for the dead are not prohibited in our Churches: and Blessed Luther in the Greater Confession.

And although in the progress of time sacrifices were added: yet those were not propitiatory sacrifices for the sins, punishments, and faults of the departed: but only sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving, by which thanks were partly given to GOD for the preservation of the Church and the ministry of the pious: and partly the mighty works and merits of the departed Saints were celebrated. And Cyprian treats of these sacrifices, lib. 4, epist. 5, showing how the Church was accustomed to offer sacrifices for the martyrs Laurence, Ignatius, and the rest: the sayings of very many Fathers, both Greek and Latin, also treat of this, produced in great number by Bellarmine, lib. 1, de Purgatorio, cap. 6, so that in their citation a perpetual fallacy of non-cause as cause is committed, and a shameful confusion of most diverse ends.

Away, therefore, with the blasphemous prayers of the Romanists for the dead, which are execrable by the very sound of the words: as when they cry: Deliver, O LORD, the souls of all the faithful departed from the punishments of hell, and from the deep pit, deliver them from the mouth of the lion, lest hell swallow them up, lest they fall into darkness. The Savior certainly refutes this impiety with full mouth, Luke 23:43, saying to the thief: TODAY you will be with me in Paradise: the book of Wisdom, ch. 3:1, refutes it: The souls of the just are in the hand of GOD, and the torment of death SHALL NOT TOUCH them, but they are in PEACE: The Apostle refutes it, 2 Cor. 5:10: Everyone shall report according to what he did in the body: And Gal. 6:5. Everyone shall bear his own burden: For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap: Justin the Philosopher and Martyr refutes it: After the soul, he says, is shaken off, there is immediately a distinction of the good and the bad: For they are led by Angels to places that are worthy of them: The souls of the good indeed to Paradise: But those of the wicked to the places of the underworld: Finally, the blessed Jerome refutes it, saying: Submerged in the tempest of death, like a log, wherever you fall, there you will remain forever, whether the final time finds you rigid and fierce, or clement and merciful.

But enough and more on this question in this place: What things deserve observation specifically concerning the Papal Purgatory will be handled below in the Article concerning hell.

Latin:

rissimè patefactam, ausu plus quàm temerario immutare conantur. Pertinet huc illud Ecclesiastæ 11, 3. Si ceciderit lignum sive ad austrum, sive ad aquilonem, ubicunq́; ceciderit, ibi erit. Quem locum Hieronymus, Bernhardus, & alii Patres magno consensu, de immutabilitate conditionis animæ post mortem exposuerunt.

Sed ex Scripturis nonnulla loca corradunt Esavvitæ, de quibus paucis agendum. Primarium est, quòd 2. Macchab. 12, 43. Judas Macchabæus legitur obtulisse sacrificiũ pro mortuis. Sed respondeo 1. librum istum, quippe totius Ecclesiæ consensu apocryphum & supposititium, nihil quicquam posse præjudicare autoritati Scripturarum Canonicarum, quæ de exequiis defunctorum ne γρῦ quidem noverunt. Unde B. etiam Hieronymus legi libros hosce posse censuit ad ædificationem plebis, non verò ad autoritatem Ecclesiasticorum dogmatum confirmandam: Quâ de causâ in Concilio etiam Laodicensi, cap. 59. sive ultimo, libri Macchabæorum ex censu numeroq́; Canonicarum Scripturarum sunt dispuncti. Quid quòd ipse autor libri hujus secundi, de fide & autoritate ejus vehementer dubitat, quando c. 2, 24. fatetur, se historiam contexuisse ex quinque voluminibus Jasonis Cyrenæi: & cap. ult. vers. 39. veniam deprecatur, si non assecutus sit, quod voluerit.
