This religion of the heathens ought indeed to have struck shame, or rather to have stirred a prick of conscience, in the Anabaptists, partly without the Libertines, and partly in the Papist Doctors: the former of whom, not only by doctrine and impiety, but also by the external force of arms and manifest sedition, attempted to remove every civil Magistrate, both elsewhere and most especially at Münster in Westphalia, 80 years ago: the latter, however, under the privilege of I know not what sanctity and liberty, simply exempt the entire order of Clerics and Nuns from the obedience due to the civil Magistrate by divine law.

To the fury of all these, rather than to their error, our author PHILIP expressly opposed the treatment of this Article. It is completed in three main parts: the first of which, having premised certain general matters concerning the doctrine or the necessity and use of this Article, argues against the Anabaptists that the Political Order is from GOD, and that political offices are good things pleasing to GOD. The second provides certain rules useful and necessary for rightly asserting the peace and observance due to the Magistrate. The third and last briefly discusses civil contracts; and it warns that equity must always be regarded in them.

And such indeed is the Philippean Treatise, in itself sufficiently plain, accurate, and Orthodox, not needing a fuller explanation. We therefore, having regard for the present time as well as for the controversial questions coming under discussion today, establish four chapters for the future Treatise.

THE FIRST will examine the very nature and proper affection of the Political Order from the Holy Scriptures, and will briefly refute the errors pertaining to this of both the Anabaptists and the Papists: in particular, however, it will treat that controversy which is moved today against our Churches primarily by Bellarmine and the Jesuitical race: namely, whether the Right of both swords, as they say, that is, both secular and spiritual jurisdiction, belongs to the one Ecclesiastical order by divine law? Or, as the status of this Controversy is informed by others: Does the Roman Pontiff have any Right and Empire over Kings, Princes, and secular Magistrates by divine law? Where we will build the negative upon firm foundations of the Scriptures, and will solidly refute the contrary arguments of Bellarmine.

The second chapter will explain both in general the doctrine of the Church concerning the office of the Magistrate, and in particular the more difficult questions, partly theoretical, partly practical, which are raised in this place: such as these eight:

1. Can the Political Magistrate compel subjects to embrace his own Religion?

2. Can he with a good conscience permit the αὐτονομίαν or liberty of religion?

3. Should he, and how should he, take action against heretics?

4. Can the civil Magistrate so entirely arrogate to himself the calling and dismissal of Ministers of the Church, as a kind of Political Royal prerogative, that, excluding the other two orders, namely the Ecclesiastical and the common people, he has the power at his pleasure either to call or to dismiss Ministers of the Church?

5. Does the same Magistrate have the right and power to forbid Ministers of the Church from publicly, in a sermon or from the pulpit, specifically criticizing and refuting Papists, or Calvinists, or other heretics and Schismatics?

6. Can a Christian Magistrate tolerate Jews in his Republic, and grant them the power to practice usury upon his subjects?

7. Is it lawful for the Magistrate to seize the goods and resources of subjects at his pleasure, or to plunder them with other exactions?

8. Is it lawful for the Magistrate to wage war for the sole cause of asserting religion?

And the treatment of the Second Chapter will consist of these and similar questions, if any others occur.

The third will discuss the duty of subjects, and whether they are bound to render absolute obedience to the Magistrate, superior to every exception?

The fourth and last will give judgment concerning civil contracts, partly in general, partly in particular concerning the Contract of loan: whether it should be called by the name and definition of Usury; whether it can be practiced among Christians with a good and uninjured conscience; or whether indeed, as impious, illicit, and in Scripture prohibited, and simply disapproved by Blessed Luther, it ought to be abrogated and removed from the Christian Commonwealth?

Latin:

OIKONOMIA Tractationis.

MAgistratus politici nomen & officium in honore semper, & ubique locorum fuit habitum, non in Christianorum tantum, sed ipsorum quoque Gentilium Republica. Aristoteles certe Principem νόμον ἔμψυχον legem animatam: Homerus ποιμένα λαω̃ν pastorem populorum: Plato σωτη̃ρα, φύ- λακα, καὶ ἐπίκουρον, Salvatorem, custodem, opitulatorem: Theseus apud Euripidem εὐεργέ- την καὶ φίλον μέγαν, benefactorem, & amicum magnum appellare non dubitavit.

Quæ sane Ethnicorum religio Anabaptistis partim sine Libertinis, partim vero Doctoribus Pontificiis, pudorem incutere, imo potius Conscientiæ stimulum concitare debebat: quorum illi non doctrina saltem impietate: sed externa etiam armorum vi, & seditione manifesta, Magistratum civilem omnem, tum alibi, tum potissimum Monasterii VVestphaliæ, ante annos 80. e medio tollere conati sunt: Hi vero, sub nescio cujus Sanctitatis & libertatis privilegio, ab obedientia, Magistratui civili jure divino debita, universum Clericorum, & Monialium ordinem, simpliciter eximunt.

Quorum omnium furori potius, quam errori, Autor noster PHILIPPUS Articuli hujus Tractationem ex professo opposuit. Absolvitur vero ea tribus potissimum partibus: quarum Prima præmissis quibusdam generalibus, de doctrina, sive Articuli hujus necessitate & usu, contra Anabaptistas disputat, Ordinem Politicum esse a DEO, & officia politica, esse res bonas DEO placentes. Altera certas tradit regulas, ad pacem & observantiam Magistratui debitam, rite asserendam utiles & necessarias. Tertia & postrema de contractibus civilibus breviter disserit: inq; illis æquitatem semper spectandam esse monet.

Et talis quidem est Tractatio Philippea, per se satis plana, accurata, & Orthodoxa, explicatione uberiore non indigens. Nos ergo præsentis temporis, ut & quæstionum controversarum hodie potissimum sub disquisitionem venientium habita ratione, quatenus tuor constituimus futuræ Tractationis capita.

PRIMVM naturam ipsam & affectionem propriam Ordinis Politici ex Scripturis Sacris expendet, & tùm Anabaptistarum, tùm Pontificiorum errores huc pertinentes breviter refutabit: in Specie autem eam pertractabit controversiam, quæ à Bellarmino potissimùm, & gente Esavviticâ hodiè nostris movetur Ecclesiis: An videlicet uni ordini Ecclesiastico, Jus utriusque gladii, uti loquuntur, hoc est, jurisdictio & secularis & spiritualis jure divino competat? Vel, uti ab aliis status hujus Controversiæ informatur: An Pontifex Romanus, in Reges, Principes, & Magistratus seculares, Jus aliquod & Imperium, jure divino habeat? Ubi negativam firmis Scripturarum fundamentis superstruemus, & Bellarmini argumenta contraria solidè refutabimus.

CAPUT alterum expediet tum in genere doctrinam Ecclesiæ de officio Magistratus: tùm in specie quæstiones difficiliores, partim theoreticas, partim practicas, quæ hoc loco moventur: quales sunt hæ octo:

1. An Magistratus Politicus subditos ad suam amplexandam Religionem cogere possit?

2. An bonâ Conscientiâ Religionis αὐτονομίαν sive libertatem permittere possit?

3. An & quomodo in hæreticos animadvertere debeat?

4. An Magistratus civilis, Vocationem, & dimissionem Ministrorum Ecclesiæ, tanquam Regale quoddam Politicum, ita sibi in solidum arrogare possit, ut exclusis reliquis duobus ordinibus, Ecclesiastico nimirum, & plebeio, pro lubitu potestatem habeat, vel vocandi, vel dimittendi Ministros Ecclesiæ?

5. An idem Magistratus jus & potestatem habeat interdicendi Ministris Ecclesiæ: Ne publicè pro concione sive suggestu, vel Pontificios, vel Calvinianos, vel alios hæreticos & Schismaticos nominatim perstringant & refutent?

6. An Magistratus Christianus suâ in Repub. Judæos ferre, iisdemque usuras in subditos exercendi potestatem facere possit?

7. An Magistratui licitum sit Subditorum bona & facultates pro lubitu ad se rapere, vel aliis exactionibus illos expilare?

8. An solius Religionis asserendæ causâ bellum gerere Magistratui liceat?

Et his quidem ac consimilibus, si quæ occurrent, quæstionibus aliis, constabit Secundi Capitis Tractatio.

Tertium disseret de officio subditorum, & nùm absolutam, omníque exceptione majorem obedientiam Magistratui præstare teneantur?

Quartum & postremum de Contractibus civilibus, partim in genere, partim in specie de Contractu mutuationis feret sententiam: Nùm ille sub Usurarum nomen definitionemque vocari: num inter Christianos bonâ & illæsâ conscientiâ exerceri; an verò tanquam impius, illicitus in Scripturis prohibitus, & à B. LUTHERO simpliciter improbatus, abrogari, & tolli è Repub. Christianorum debeat?


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Proper Quasi-affection of the Political Magistracy

In order that the nature of the civil Magistrate may be rightly investigated, the causes constituting any thing must be weighed. And at the beginning, indeed, as regards the efficient cause, or the origin of the political order, it depends not only on the Law of Nature, but also on the express Ordination of God, and consequently on divine law. For although, with Nature as a guide, men have progressed to such a degree of prudence that they have set wiser and more robust men over the rest of the multitude as Leaders and Rulers, imitating cranes and little bees in this respect, which by instinct of nature have their Leaders and, with ranks arranged, keep watch by night; and therefore some contend, not falsely or wrongly, that the Political Magistrate is of natural law: yet it can by no means be denied that it also draws its origin from GOD himself and divine ordination.

The truth of the statement is evident first from the most evident testimonies of the Scriptures. Certainly, Genesis 9:6, political power is read to be founded in express words, with Jehovah himself so ordaining: Whosoever shall shed human blood, his blood shall be shed. And Deut. 16:18, Thou shalt appoint judges and magistrates in all thy gates, etc. Hence Scripture attributes all his authority, fortune, and success entirely to GOD alone: Psalm 144:10, GOD gives salvation to kings. 2 Chronicles 19:6, See what you do: for you do not exercise the judgment of man, but of GOD. Proverbs 8:15 and 16, By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree just things: by me Princes rule, and the powerful decree justice. Daniel 2:21, It is GOD who transfers kingdoms and establishes them: who gives wisdom to the wise, etc. Romans 13:1. Let every soul be subject to the power of the Magistrate: For there is no power but from GOD: Therefore he who resists it, resists the ordination of GOD.

Then our assertion is evident even from the fact that Scripture adorns the Political Magistrate with such praises as clearly confirm his divine origin. For because of that vicarious work which they perform for GOD on earth, it calls Kings and princes GODS; Exod. 22:28, Psalm 82:1. It calls them Angels of GOD: 2 Sam. 14:17 and chap. 19:27. It calls them Saviors: Judg. 3:9, Nehem. 9:27. It calls them nursing fathers of the Church: Isa. 49:23. It calls them ministers of GOD, the ordination of GOD, avengers for wrath: Rom. 13:4.

Thirdly, the authority and holiness of those Kings and princes, whom the Sacred history of both Testaments mentions, confirms our thesis: and it declares that they were called by God himself, partly immediately, partly mediately, to the helms of governing the Republic.

Finally, experience itself bears witness concerning the divine ordination of Empires, Kingdoms, and all Magistrates. For as our author also speaks, it is manifest that atrocious crimes are divinely punished by manifest corporal punishments: according to that Matthew 26:52, He who shall have taken the sword, shall perish by the sword: and Isa. 33:1, Woe to you who plunder, for you shall be plundered in turn, etc.

Such is the force and evidence of these arguments, that we do not hesitate to assert that the Magistrates and polities of the Heathens themselves have always been, and are today, from GOD, and are ruled and preserved by his nod and will: so much so that M. Tullius wrote not wrongly: That there has been no great man without divine inspiration: And Plato, 4th of Laws: This discourse truly says that for whatever cities not GOD, but some mortal holds the command, there is no escape from evils or labors for them: etc.

The question is raised at this point, whether a Magistrate who is impious and Tyrannical is also from GOD? Where some depart into diverse opinions: some defending a simple negative: others fighting for the affirmative, but too loosely and generally. We therefore maintain that the question is most correctly explained by employing a twofold distinction.

For at the beginning one must properly distinguish between the Thing itself, namely the Magistrate, or political power considered in itself, which is from GOD: and between the abuse of the thing, namely Tyranny, impiety, and the malice of men established in the Magistracy, which is not from GOD, but from the Devil, and the depraved will of men.

Furthermore, Tyranny itself is also considered in two ways in the scriptures: the one, by reason of fault: the other, by reason of punishment. By reason of Fault, God is so far from being the author or approver of Tyranny, that He rather forbids it, pursues it with hatred, and finally punishes it: by the example of Pharaoh king of Egypt, Exod. 14, 28. Jeroboam: 1 Kings 13, 34. Both Herods: Matt. 2, 19. Acts 12, 25. By reason of punishment, however, Tyranny is entirely from GOD: according to that universal prophetic axiom: Amos 3, 6. Is there evil in a city, which the LORD has not done? For GOD, offended by the malice and ingratitude of the people, grants power to Tyrants, so that they may pay the penalty, who were unwilling to obey pious Magistrates: Hos. 13, 11. I gave you a king in my anger.

In what sense David also calls the tyrant and persecutor Saul the Lord's Anointed, 1 Sam. 24:7, certainly not approving of his tyrannical cruelty, but acknowledging God's ordination in him. In this very sense, Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar are also called in the sacred writings the rod and staff of God's fury, nay, the servants of God, Isa. 10:5, Jer. 25:9. It is evident from this what is the best method of shaking off the yoke of tyrants and asserting ourselves into our former liberty: namely, that we should patiently bear the punishments we have deserved by our own stubbornness and ingratitude, pray to God with pious prayers, and finally, with our whole hearts, through serious repentance, turn to God who strikes us, and await His help in true humility. Far be it, therefore, especially from Christians, that in such a case they should attempt anything through sedition or any rebellion; for by this means, so far from a remedy being prepared for the evil, heavier punishments are rather drawn upon us.

And such indeed is the efficient cause of the political magistrate. There follows the material cause from which he proceeds, which is given as none other than the very body of men. For God did not wish angels, but men, to preside over men as rulers and leaders; yet not just any men, but those who excelled the rest not so much in age or seniority as in piety, prudence, and the use and experience of affairs, and also in authority. For thus God Himself said to Moses, Exod. 18:21, Deut. 1:12: Provide out of all the people wise men, and such as fear God, in whom there is truth, and who hate avarice, and constitute from them tribunes, and centurions, and fifty-men, and decurions, who may judge the people at all times; but whatever is more serious, let them refer to you, and let them judge only the lesser matters.

The manner of choosing such persons varies according to the diversity of times and peoples. Among the people of God, judges, kings, and princes were sometimes constituted immediately by God Himself, as Othniel, Saul, David; sometimes mediately, with the suffrage and consent of the people intervening. Thus today, almost every province and nation has its peculiar laws and statutes by which one must abide in electing a magistrate. However, these two modes are most common, that one is raised to the possession of a kingdom either by election, or by hereditary right, or even by the right of war; concerning which, as well as other similar modes, we permit politicians and jurists to dispute. It suffices for us that the matter or subject of the civil magistrate is men, and that by the authority and command of God Himself.

The formal cause of the political magistrate is considered in two ways: either regarding the diverse forms of governments, or regarding the manner or medium which the magistrate is accustomed to use in administering the republic. Regarding the former form, three species of governments are commonly established by politicians: namely, monarchical, democratic, and aristocratic. Monarchical is when one presides and moderates all things by just and equitable laws, for the public good and the consent and will of the subjects. Opposed to this is tyranny, in which, contrary to the laws of the republic and against the will of the subjects, one man dominates, directing all things to his own advantage. Democratic is a regime in which the power is in the hands of the whole people, yet with the faculty and condition of each individual preserved. This mostly degenerates into a conspiracy, that is, a mutual collusion, bending justice and laws at will, and finally into manifest conspiracy and sedition. Aristocratic is when the sum of affairs is in the hands of the nobles in a praiseworthy manner. Opposed to this is oligarchy, where a few of the richer and more powerful preside over the republic, caring more for private than for public advantage.

Moreover, the schools of politicians deal expressly with these forms of government, while theologians do not disapprove of them, provided they contain themselves within the bounds defined by divine and human laws. If this is done, then the dignity of kings or monarchs, the power of the nobles, and the legitimate liberty of the people will stand; the republic itself will last for a very long time without disturbances; and the Church will be in the best state.

The latter form of the civil magistrate looks to the medium which he is accustomed to use, or rather ought to use, in administering the republic. These, however, are the laws, whether civil or municipal, and peculiar to any kingdom or province; if these do not conflict with the Word of God, they should by no means be repudiated. For if it is lawful to act as a magistrate by divine right, then by the nature of a correlate it would also be lawful, according to the condition and quality of times, men, and places, to enact laws and strictly observe them. Nor can we approve of the moroseness of certain Calvinists who repudiate the laws of the Roman Emperors, comprised in the civil law—not indeed all of them simply, but some—because they do not agree with the Mosaic ones. Some write that Franciscus Junius was of this opinion. But they ought to have remembered that those Mosaic forensic laws pertained only to the magistrate and polity of the Israelite people; which is clearly evident from the fact that this condition was expressly added to their promulgation: And you shall observe these my precepts in your families and kindreds. Since this condition has expired today under the New Testament, the Mosaic forensic law is certainly not of immutable or perpetual right, but rather was abrogated with the Israelite polity itself. Therefore, it is free for Christians, having omitted and neglected the Mosaic ones, unless insofar as they agree with the law of nature and the precepts of the Decalogue, to enact and

Latin:

UT Natura Magistratûs civilis ritè investigetur, Causæ rem quamlibet constituentes, expendendæ veniunt. Ac initio quidem quoad Causam efficientem, sive Originem ordinis Politici, dependet ea non modò à Jure Naturæ: sed & ab expressa Dei Ordinatione, & consequenter à jure divino. Etsi enim Naturâ duce, Homines eò prudentiæ sunt progressi, ut sapientiores & robustiores reliquæ multitudini, tanquam Duces & Rectores præficerent: grues & apiculas hac in parte imitati, quæ naturæ instinctu suos habent Ductores, & dispositis ordinibus noctu excubias agunt: ac proinde Magistratum Politicum Juris naturalis esse, haud falsò, aut malè quidam contendunt: negari tamen nullâ ratione potest, ab ipso etiam DEO, & divinâ ordinatione, illum suam trahere originem.

Dicti veritas patet primùm ex Scripturarum testimoniis, longè evidentissimis. Certè Genes. 9, 6. potestas politica disertis verbis fundata legitur: sic ordinante ipso Jehovah: Quicunque effuderit sanguinem humanum, fundetur sanguis illius. Et Deut. 16, 18. Judices & magistratus constitues in omnibus portis tuis, &c. Hinc omnem ejus autoritatem, fortunam, successum, soli DEO Scriptura in solidum acceptum refert: Psal. 144, 10. DEUS dat salutem regibus. 2. Paralip. 19, 6. Videte quid faciatis: non enim hominis exercetis judicium, sed DEI. Proverb. 8, 15. & 16. Per me reges regnant, & legumlatores justa decernunt: per me Principes imperant, & potentes decernunt justitiam. Daniel. 2, 21. DEUS est, qui transfert regna, & constituit: qui dat sapientiam sapientibus &c. Rom. 13, 1. Omnis anima potestati Magistratus sit subdita: Non enim est potestas nisi à DEO: Itaque qui ei resistit, DEI ordinationi resistit.

Deinde patet assertio nostra vel inde etiam, quòd Scriptura ejusmodi elogiis ornat Magistratum Politicum, quæ divinam ejus originem luculenter confirmant. Nam ob vicariam illam, quam in terris DEO præstant operam, Reges & principes nominat DEOS; Exod. 22. 28. Psal. 82. 1. nominat Angelos D E I: 2. Sam. 14, 17. & cap. 19, 27. nominat Salvatores: Judic. 3, 9. Nehem. 9. 27. nominat nutritios Ecclesiae: Efa. 49, 23. nominat DEI ministros, DEI ordinationem, vindices in iram: Rom. 13, 4.

Tertio confirmat thesin nostram autoritas & sanctitas eorum Regum & principum, quorum Sacra historia utriusque Testamenti meminit: eosq; a Deo ipso partim immediate, partim mediate ad Reipub. regendae gubernacula, vocatos fuisse perhibet.

Tandem experientia ipsa testimonium fert de divina Imperiorum, Regnorum, omniumq; Magistratuum ordinatione. Nam ut autor etiam noster loquitur, manifestum est, atrocia scelera manifestis corporalibus suppliciis divinitus puniri: secundum illud Matth. 26, 52. Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit: & Efa. 33, 1. Vae qui praedaris, nam vicissim spoliaberis, &c.

Horum sane argumentorum ea est vis & evidentia, ut non dubitemus asserere, ipsorum quoque Ethnicorum Magistratus & politias, ratione Generis fuisse semper, hodieq; esse a DEO, ejusq; nutu, & arbitrio regi & conservari: adeo, ut haud male scripserit M. Tullius: Nullum fuisse virum magnum sine afflatu divino: Et Plato 4. de legibus: Vere dicit hic sermo, quod quarumcunque civitatum non DEUS, sed mortalis quispiam tenet imperium, iis neque malorum, neq; laborum sit effugium: &c.

Quaeritur hoc loco, an Magistratus etiam impius & Tyrannicus sit a DEO? Ubi in diversas sententias nonnulli abeunt: quibusdam simplicem negativam defendentibus: aliis pro affirmativa, sed nimis laxe & generaliter pugnantibus. Statuimus ergo quaestionem rectissime explicari, gemina adhibita distinctione.

Nam initio probe distinguendum inter Rem ipsam, nempe Magistratum, sive potestatem politicam in se consideratam, quae a DEO est: & inter abusum rei, nempe Tyrannidem, impietatem & malitiam hominum in Magistratu constitutorum, quae non est a DEO, sed a Diabolo, & prava hominum voluntate.

Deinde vero ipsa quoque Tyrannis duobus modis in sacris consideratur: uno quidem ratione culpae: altero, ratione poenae. Ratione Culpae, Deus adeo non est autor aut approbator Tyrannidis, ut potius eam prohibeat, odio prosequatur, & tandem puniat: exemplo Pharaonis regis Aegypti, Exod. 14, 28. Jeroboami: 1. Reg. 13, 34. Herodis utriusque: Matth. 2, 19. Actor. 12. 25. Ratione poenae vero, Tyrannis omnino a DEO est: secundum universale illud axioma propheticum: Amos, 3, 6. Non est malum in civitate, quod non fecerit DOMINUS. DEUS enim offensus populi malitia & ingratitudine, imperium Tyrannis concedit, ut poenas luant, qui piis Magistratibus parere noluerunt: Hos. 13, 11. dedit tibi regem in furore meo.

Quo sensu David quoque Tyrannum & persecutorem Saulem nominat Unctum DOMINI. 1. Sam. 24, 7. non certè approbans tyrannicam ejus sævitiem: sed DEI ordinationem in ipso agnoscens. Quo ipso etiam sensu Sennacherib & Nebucadnezar appellantur in sacris virga & baculus furoris Dei, imò Servi DEI. Esa. 10, 5. Jerem. 25, 9. Patet hinc, quænam optima sit ratio excutiendi Tyrannorum jugum, nosq; in pristinam asserendi libertatem: nimirùm, ut quas nostra pervicacia & ingratitudine pœnas meruimus, etiam patienter feramus, piis ad Deum precibus deprecemur, totis denique animis per seriam pœnitentiam convertamur ad DEUM percutientem, ipsiusq; auxilium in verâ humilitate expectemus. Absit ergò à Christianis præsertim, ut tali casu quicquam per seditionem aut rebellionem aliquam tentent: Nam hoc pacto usque adeò non malo medicina parabitur, ut graviores potiùs pœnæ attrahantur.

Et talis quidem est Causa Efficiens Magistratus Politici: Sequitur Causa Materialis, ex qua ille provenit: quæ nulla datur alia, quàm ipsa Hominum Universitas. Neque enim DEUS Angelos, sed Homines hominibus, tanquàm Rectores & Ductores præesse voluit: non tamen Homines quosvis, sed eos, qui cæteris non ætate magis, sive senio, quàm pietate, prudentia, rerum usu & experientiâ, autoritate etiam præstarent. Sic enim DEUS ipse ad Mosen, Exod. 18, 21. Deut. 1, 12. Provide de omni plebe viros sapientes, & timentes DEUM, in quibus sit veritas, & qui oderint avaritiam, & constitue ex eis tribunos, & centuriones, & quinquagenarios, & decanos, qui judicent populum omni tempore: quicquid autem gravius fuerit, referant ad te, & ipsi minora tantùm judicent.

Modus eligendi tales personas secundum diversitatem temporum & populorum variat. In populo DEI interdum constituebantur Judices, Reges, & Principes ab ipso DEO immediatè, ut Athniel, Saul, David: interdum mediatè, accedente suffragio & consensu populi. Sic hodiè singulæ fermè provinciæ & nationes, peculiaria habent jura & statuta, quibus in eligendo Magistratu stari debet. Duo autem isti modi sunt usitatissimi, ut vel Electione, vel jure hæreditario, vel jure etiam Belli, ad regni possessionem aliquis evehatur: de quibus, ut & consimilibus modis aliis, disputare permittimus Politicos, & Jureconsultos: Nobis sufficit Materiam, sive subjectum Magistratus Civilis esse Homines: idq; DEI ipsius autoritate & mandato.

Formalis causa Magistratus Politici, duobus modis consideratur: Vel quoad diversas gubernationum formas: vel quoad modum, sive medium, quo in administranda Repub. Magistratus uti solet. Quoad priorem formam, tres vulgò à Politicis constituuntur, Gubernationum species: Monarchica nimirùm, Democratica & Aristocratica. Monarchica est, quando unus præest, & justis, æquisque legibus omnia moderatur, ad bonum publicum, & subditorum consensum ac voluntatem. Huic opposita est Tyrannis, in quâ contra leges Reipub. ac præter voluntatem subditorum, Unus dominatur, ad proprium commodum omnia conferens. Democratica est regimen, in quo imperium est penes universum populum, servatâ tamen uniuscujusque facultate & conditione. Hæc plærumque degenerat in σύστρεμμα, hoc est, collusionem mutuam, jus, legesq́; pro arbitrio flectentem, & tandem in manifestam conspirationem ac seditionem. Aristocratica est, quando rerum summa est penes optimates laudabiliter. Huic opposita est oligarchia, ubi pauci ex ditioribus & potentioribus Reipub. præsunt, privatum magis, quàm publicum curantes commodum.

Cæterùm de his Gubernationum formis, Politicorum Scholæ ex professo agunt, Theologis interim eas non improbantibus, si modò intra metas legibus divinis & humanis definitas se contineant. Quod si fiat, tum & regibus sive Monarchis sua dignitas, & Optimatibus sua potentia, & populo legitima libertas constabit: Respub. ipsa sine motibus durabit diutissimè: Ecclesia verò rectissimè habebit.

Posterior Magistratus Civilis forma respicit medium, quo ille in administrandâ Repub. uti solet, imò debet. Hoc autem sunt leges sive civiles illæ, sive municipales, & regno ac provinciæ cuilibet peculiares: quæ si Verbo DEI non repugnent, repudiari minimè debent. Nam si fas est, jure divino agere Magistratum; utique ex naturâ correlati fas etiam fuerit, pro conditione & qualitate temporum, hominum, locorum, ferre leges, easq́; strictè observare. Neque probare possumus Calvinizantium quorundam morositatem, qui Romanorum Imperatorum leges, jure civili comprehensas, non quidem simpliciter omnes, aliquas tamen repudiant, ideò, quòd cùm Mosaicis non consentiant. Quâ in sententiâ Franciscum Junium fuisse aliqui scribunt. Verùm meminisse debebant, leges illas Mosaicas forenses, tantùm ad Israelitici populi Magistratum, & politiam pertinuisse: id quod vel inde luculenter patet, quòd promulgationi istarum disertè addita fuit hæc conditio; Et observabitis hæc præcepta mea in familiis, & cognationibus vestris. Hæc conditio cum hodiè sub novo Testamento expirârit, utique Lex forensis Mosaica etiam non juris est immoti vel perpetui: sed potiùs cum ipsâ politiâ Israeliticâ abrogata. Liberum proinde est Christianis, omissis & neglectis Mosaicis, nisi quatenus illæ cum lege naturæ, & cum præceptis Decalogi conveniunt, peculiares, & ad sui fori, suorumque temporum mores accommodatas leges pro-


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Proper Quasi-affection of the Political Magistracy: Final cause of the political magistrate

promulgate peculiar laws accommodated to the customs of their own forum and their own times, and according to them exercise law and judgment. Whence Christ himself, and the Apostle are read to have used Roman law: Matt. 17, 24. Acts 16, 37, and chap. 22, 25.

Moreover, the execution of this means is done by the use of the sword against those who have offended against the laws: and that by divine right. For he does not bear the sword in vain: but is the minister of GOD; an avenger for wrath to him who does evil. Rom. 13, 4. Which formal cause constitutes the specific difference between civil power, and paternal and Ecclesiastical power: since the right of the sword belongs to neither, as will be expressly disputed toward the end of this chapter concerning Ecclesiastical power against Bellarmine.

The final cause of the Political Order regards its office, which, as the Apostle defines, 1 Tim. 2, 2, ought always to be referred to three main heads, by reason of the end: 1. is, The tranquility of a peaceful life: 2. The civil honesty of morals: 3. The tolerable and legitimate exercise of Worship and Religion. But in what way the civil Magistrate may duly attain this triple end: the digression of the second chapter will expressly show.

ANTITHESIS

These things having been thus established concerning the nature of the Political Magistrate, the impiety of certain Gentiles, such as Julian, Celsus, Porphyry, and the like, is to be detested, who judged that Christians were to be exterminated even for this reason, that the doctrine of the Gospel would utterly remove and abolish every Political Magistrate and all human judgments. Whose calumnies Origen expressly refuted in the eight books written against Celsus: Volume 4 of his Works: Cyril of Alexandria in the 10 books published against Julian: Volume 3 of his Works. Likewise Nazianzen, in his published oration Στηλιτευτικῇ against the same: Euseb. book 6, chap. 19, and 36. Socrates book 1, chap. 9.

But more intolerable is the fury, rather than error, of the Anabaptists, being men professing the name and doctrine of Christ, who desire the political magistrate to be utterly overturned and removed: contending that he had a place only in the Old Testament: but in the New, the condition of the Church is far different: and therefore that no Christian can in good conscience hold the office of magistrate: nor is there even need for judgments, but it is permitted to the people to abrogate every magistrate, in whatever way that may be done: and as Peter Kelficensis wrote, as witnessed by Possevin in his Examination of the Picard sect: that in the Republic one must not flee to profane Magistrates for one's own defense, nor are thieves or robbers to be cast into chains, or punished: nor are tributes to be paid by Christians, nor are services to be rendered to the Lord: finally, that all civil laws of Emperors, Kings, Provinces, and Cities are simply to be condemned.

The arguments with which they fought, and fight today, are chiefly these:

1. The law is not laid down for the just: 1 Tim. 1, 9, since the pious and regenerate do their duty of their own accord. Therefore there is no need for Magistrates, nor for civil laws.

2. Vengeance is clearly prohibited by GOD himself: according to that of Romans 12, 19. Vengeance is mine, and I will repay: And Matt. 5, 39. Do not resist evil. And the political magistrate administers no other office than that by which vengeance is exercised. Therefore.

3. Whoever arrogates dominion over others to himself, he recalls Gentilism into the Church: by the witness of the Savior himself: The Kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship, and they that exercise authority are called benefactors: Luke 22, 25. But the political magistrate arrogates and exercises dominion over others: Therefore he recalls Gentilism into the Church of GOD, against the command of the Savior.

4. Whatever was permitted only to the imperfect: that has been abrogated in the Church of the perfect through Christ. Now, indeed, GOD promised the Jews, on account of their imperfection, to possess certain faculties and to exercise political offices: just as John the Baptist also permitted the publicans and soldiers, being imperfect, only to exercise civil contracts and to earn wages in war. Therefore, among Christians, being perfect, all these things have been abrogated through Christ.

5. If the political Magistrate were from GOD, certainly he himself would not for the most part be defiled by manifest crimes: nor would so many confusions of all things exist: nor would the wicked so often escape their deserved punishments. But these vices can always and everywhere be seen in the political Magistrate. Therefore, the political Magistrate is not from GOD.

But these arguments are not of such weight or moment that they could in any way obscure, much less abolish, the authority of the political Magistrate: which will easily appear from a brief refutation of each. For first, it fails shamefully by the fallacy of the figure of speech. For it is not held in the Greek: δικαίῳ νόμος οὐ κεῖται, a law is not given, or has been given, to the just: but, νόμος οὐ κεῖται, the law does not lie. Now, indeed, these two forms of speaking differ greatly in meaning and emphasis. For the former denotes the promulgation of the law, from which the Apostle does not exempt the just. Certainly, in Paradise itself, GOD gave a law to Adam, although most just, to be observed holily. The latter phrase, which the Apostle uses, denotes those proper offices of the law, such as: to accuse, to terrify, to condemn. In which sense, indeed, to the just νόμος οὐ κεῖται, the law does not lie, that is, pressing like an intolerable yoke, or constraining by fear of punishment, like a schoolmaster. To which opinion Augustine writes excellently in book 3 against the two letters of the Pelagians, chapter 4: Who is so impious, he writes, who would say that he does not keep the moral precepts of the law because he is a Christian, and is not under the law, but established under grace? Assuredly, that law of GOD, not only to that people then, but even now, no one would doubt that it is necessary for us for the right ordering of life: But there is a great distance between when those constituted under the law do this out of legal compulsion, and when those constituted under grace do this out of love. We conclude, therefore, that the Apostle is speaking not of every use of the law, but of the pedagogical use, which has no place in the Church of the reborn. Regarding which matter, see the sixth Article of the Book of Concord.

The second argument fails by the fallacy παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For both the precept of the Savior and that of the Apostle deal with the evil of injuries and with private vengeance: and just as it shows that the former must be borne patiently and that our enemy must even be loved, so it shows that the latter in no way pertains to private Christians. But the reason is different when the question is no longer about the evil of injuries, which has a place among private individuals, but about the evil of manifest wickedness and the desecration of life and morals. Here, certainly, it is most clearly evident from the Scriptures produced above that the political Magistrate retains his office and that vengeance according to divine laws pertains to him. This collection is therefore most vicious, which partly plays basely upon the equivocation of words, and partly proceeds from the information of private men to the public office of the civil Magistrate with a childish πλεονεξίᾳ of terms.

The third argument lays snares for the truth with a double Sophistication: The former is παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For the discourse of the Savior in Luke ch. 22, 25 is not indefinitely to all Christians, as if all political dominion should simply be alien to them: but it shows that it is only to the Apostles, whose office ought to be occupied in teaching and ministering, and not in any external dominion or preeminence. Now, however, the consequence from the office of the Apostles to the office of the political Magistrate does not hold exclusively. The latter Sophistication is παρὰ τὸ χῆμα τῆς λέξεως. For this phrase, The Kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship, does not have the sense as if political dominion could and should not have a place among Christians as well as among the Gentiles: But it involves only the condition and respect of the Time. For at that time the political Magistrate flourished only among the Gentiles, until the Church of the New Testament was established, and Christians also, having shaken off the yoke of the Gentiles, performed political offices. What is more, the Savior did not always express this notation, but those whom He here called Kings of the Gentiles: a little later, as also in Matt. 20, 25, He simply calls τὺς μεγάλυς, καὶ ἐξυσιάζοντας, the magnates, and those exercising power. It is evident, therefore, that the Savior, by this phrase, Kings of the Gentiles, looked not so much to the persons of men as to the state of His Church.

The fourth argument labors under several petitions of the principle, indeed manifest vanities and falsehoods, than is evident from the terms. In the Major premise, 1. a definition of the perfect is missing, whose eulogy, if the Anabaptists disparage it in the faithful of the Old Testament, as also in those who heard John the Baptist as a teaching Preceptor: they render their error more atrocious with notable impiety and sacrilege. 2. A manifest ψεῦδος is committed against Scripture when the sermons of Christ and the Baptist are opposed ἀντιφατικῶς: or it is feigned that the doctrine of John the Baptist was antiquated by Christ. For if John was the forerunner of the LORD, if he had to prepare the way for Him, if he was the Prophet of the Most High, and gave knowledge of salvation to His people, which is in the remission of sins: certainly no one would affirm that his doctrine was contrary to the doctrine of Christ the Savior, unless he has lost common sense along with all shame. In the Minor premise it is simply false. 1. That GOD, because of some imperfection proper to the Old Testament, granted to the Israelite people the power of exercising political government. 2. That because of the same imperfection, John the Baptist permitted publicans and soldiers the use of civil contracts and wars.

The fifth and last plays vainly with the childish Sophism τῷ συμβεβηκότι. But just as in any other matters a vicious accident does not remove the thing itself: for otherwise the Heaven and the elements themselves would have to be removed from the midst: So neither the vices of persons constituted in the Magistracy, nor the ἀταξία of the government itself, can or ought to corrupt or overturn the good ordinance of GOD, namely the political magistracy itself.

Succeeding the Anabaptists in the class of those who err are the Doctors and Pontifical Monks, indeed the Roman Pontiff himself; with the whole order of Clerics, who, although they wish to seem to think and speak honorably enough of the Political Magistrate in words, in reality, however, undermine, overturn, and trample it underfoot. The practice of the Roman Church, which is accustomed to be adorned and disguised with these excellent little flowers and Emblems, gives assurance to this assertion of ours.

1. The preeminence of the Roman Pontiff is greater than any other creature, being free and absolute from any coercive rule, extending itself to celestial, terrestrial, and infernal things: as Ant. Florentinus holds; and Baldus in the proemium of the decretals.

2. Just as the Moon receives light from the Sun: so the Imperial or Caesarean dignity derives its splendor from the Papal radiance: as Innocent III did not hesitate to write to the Emperor of Constantinople.

3. The Pope renders neither obedience nor reverence to any mortal at all: but the Emperor rises slightly for the kissing of the foot: as may be read in book 3 of the Ceremonies of the Roman Curia.

4. The Pope has the power, even without a Council, to depose an Emperor; a fact which Gregory II fulfilled ipso facto, who deposed Leo III, the Constantinopolitan Emperor: Zacharias, who deposed Childeric, King of France: Leo III, who deposed the Constantinopolitan empire. snatched away: Innocent III, who removed Otto IV; Innocent IV, who removed Frederick II; Clement VI, who removed Louis IV from the Imperial seat.

Nor does the Pontiff wish only himself, but also the entire order of Bishops and Papal Clerics, to be exempt from all jurisdiction of the political Magistrate: this is testified to by the writings of both Bellarmine and others against the King of England, recently published on this matter with a sufficiently bloody pen and style. And from this arose that remarkable practice of the Jesuits, offering a most secure asylum for every wickedness and perfidy. For in express words they claim that privilege for their order, that they are not even bound to render an oath of fidelity to Kings or Princes in whose dominion they live, much less to pay tributes or bear public burdens,

What of the fact that they have not feared to write that Papal Clerics, even if they stir up sedition against the King or any other Magistrate, are not held by the crime of high treason: for the reason that a Cleric is not a subject of the King. Hence it is that the Pontiff takes away from the political Magistrate all care of the first table, that is, of religion and the Church, and very often absolves subjects from the Oath by which they are bound and obligated to the Magistrate by divine law, in ecclesiastical matters, and indeed even in civil ones.

Let him who is of sound mind now judge whether this is not to subvert the order of the civil Magistrate entirely? Indeed, let him judge what the Roman Pope, with his Bishops and Clerics, will one day answer to Christ, the most just judge of mortals, who through the Apostle wished this authentic decree to be promulgated, Rom. 13, 1: Let every soul be subject to the power of the Magistrate. Where indeed the note of universality excepts no one, of whatever lot or condition he may be, from this subjection due to the civil Magistrate: much less does it exempt him by some singular privilege, or render him immune. Whence Chrysostom rightly infers upon this passage: Even if you are an Apostle, if an Evangelist, if a Prophet, or whoever you may finally be, be subject to the supereminent powers: For this subjection does not subvert piety. And the Apostle does not simply say, Let every soul obey the Magistrate: but, let it be subject.

The Jesuits do indeed object at this point with various Donations, Rights, privileges, and Immunities, by which the Roman see, and especially the Papal dignity, is raised above every political Magistrate and is simply exempt from all superior jurisdiction.

But first, these are all fabulous. For 1. those diplomas of Donations were for the most part fabricated by flatterers of the Roman see: 2. some were sought by evil arts and deceit: 3. some were extorted by manifest force: just as was demonstrated by us elsewhere. Furthermore, Kings and Princes could by no right confer such privileges upon the Pontifical See: because it is manifestly contrary to the divine ordination, which wills that the ecclesiastical and political order should differ from each other in matter or subjects, and in form, and in end, and it generates destructive disorder or Confusion. Finally, CHRIST himself, whose vicar on earth the Roman Pope splendidly lies that he is, is nowhere read to have sought or affected any such immunity or exemption: But, although he was constituted by GOD the Father as the head of the whole Church and Universal Doctor, he nevertheless wished to be born under the empire of Augustus, and to be a tributary to him while still constituted as if in his mother's womb, and at the first sight of this light: and so that he might not seem the author of any scandal or confusion, he did not at all refuse to pay the tax for himself and Peter, Matt. 17, 24. From which subjection, since the Roman Pope wishes himself and his Clergy to be simply exempt, it is most manifestly clear even from that, that he is not the vicar of CHRIST, but of him who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called GOD, or is worshipped; he who is the man of sin, and the son of perdition, the very Antichrist himself, 2 Thess. 2, 3 and 4.

But the Romanists also foster another error at this point, much more atrocious than the former, while they not only exempt the Pope, the Bishops, and the entire Roman Clergy from all jurisdiction of the civil Magistrate by their own wicked daring: But they do not hesitate to assign to them, and especially to their Pontiff, an empire that is plainly infinite, absolute, and as they say, pure and mixed, as much in secular and civil matters as in ecclesiastical: such as the Pontiff himself did not shudder to usurp for himself, especially in previous centuries. Whence those remarkable eulogies concerning the twofold power of the Pontiff were born.

1. The power of the Pope is absolute, and he has it as he wishes: Franc. de Ripa.

2. The Pope can do everything against the law, above the law, and outside the law. Phil. Decius.

3. The Pope's power extends itself to all things celestial, terrestrial, and infernal. Antoninus of Florence.

4. The Pope received the right of both swords from Christ, and the Empire itself depends upon the Church: Panormitanus.

And lest by chance anyone might think that such horrendous paradoxes were once scattered only by Papists and sycophantic Canonists: it is worth observing that modern Jesuits, under various wrappings of words and phrases, hold the same impiety today and strive to defend it. For thus Bellarmine, book 5, on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 1, page 1055 in my edition: The Pontiff as Pontiff does not indeed have any temporal power directly and immediately, but only spiritual; nevertheless, by reason of the spiritual monarchy, he has at least indirectly a certain power, and that the highest, in temporal matters. And Bellarmine asserts this opinion to be the common one among Catholic theologians: which he explains in the same book, chapter 6, in these words: The Pontiff as Pontiff, even if he does not have any merely temporal power,

Latin:

mulgare, & secundum eas jus judiciumque exercere. Unde Christus ipse, & Apostolus Romano jure usi leguntur: Matth. 17, 24. Act. 16, 37, & cap. 22, 25.

Cæterùm medii hujus executio fit usu gladii in eos, qui contra leges deliquerunt: idque jure divino. Neque enim sine causâ gladium gestat: sed DEI minister est; vindex in iram ei, qui malè agit. Rom. 13, 4. Quæ formalis causa differentiam specificam constituit inter potestatem civilem, & potestatem patriam ac Ecclesiasticam: Siquidem neutri jus gladii competit, uti sub finem hujus capitis de Ecclesiasticâ potestate contra Bellarminum ex professo disputabitur.

Finalis causa Ordinis Politici respicit ejusdem officium, quod definiente Apostolo, 1. Tim. 2, 2. ad tria potissimùm capita, ratione finis, semper referri debet: 1. est, Vitæ pacatæ tranquillitas: 2. Civilis morum honestas: 3. Cultus & Religionis tolerabile & legitimum exercitium. Quo verò pacto triplicem istum finem Magistratus civilis ritè assequi possit: capitis secundi diexodus ex professo ostendet.

ΑΝΤΙΘΕΣΙΣ

His de naturâ Magistratus Politici ita constitutis, detestanda est Gentilium quorundam, ut Juliani, Celsi, Porphyrii & similium impietas, qui Christianos vel hoc etiam nomine exterminandos censuerunt, quòd doctrina Evangelii omnem prorsus Magistratum Politicum, omniaque judicia humana tolleret & aboleret. Quorum calumnias ex professo refutarunt Origines libris octo contra Celsum scriptis: Tomo 4. Operum: Cyrillus Alexandrinus editis libris 10. contra Julianum: Tomo 3. Operum. Nazianzenus item, publicatâ Oratione στηλιτευτικῇ contrà eundem: Euseb. lib. 6. cap. 19, & 36. Socrates lib. 1. cap. 9.

Intolerabilior autem est furor potiùs, quàm error Anabaptistarum, quippe hominum Christi nomen & doctrinam profitentium, qui Magistratum politicum funditùs eversum & sublatum cupiunt: contendentes, eum in Veteri tantùm Testamento locum habuesse: in Novo autem longè aliam esse rationem Ecclesiæ: ac proinde Christianum neminem bonâ conscientia fungi posse magistratu: neque judiciis etiam opus esse, sed licere populo abrogare omnem magistratum, quacunque etiam id fiat ratione: & ut Petrus Kelficensis, teste Possevino in Examine sectæ Pikardicæ scripsit: in Repub. non esse ad profanos Magistratus, ob sui defensionem confugiendũ, nec fures nec latrones in vincula conjiciendos, aut plectendos esse: nec tributa à Christianis pendenda, neq; operas Domino esse præstandas: leges denique civiles omnes Imperatorum, Regum, Provinciarum, & Civitatum simpliciter esse damnandas.

Argumenta, quibus pugnabant, hodieque pugnant, præcipua sunt isthæc:

1. Justo non est lex posita: 1. Tim. 1. 9. siquidem pij & renati ultrò faciunt officium. Ergo nec Magistratibus, nec legibus civilibus opus est.

2. Vindicta est à DEO ipso planè prohibita:secundum illud Romanor. 12, 19. Mihi vindictam, & ego retribuam: Et Matth. 5, 39. Ne resistatis malo. Atque Magistratus politicus nullum aliud administrat officium, quàm quo vindicta exercetur. Ergò.

3. Quicunque dominium in alios sibi arrogat, ille Gentilismum in Ecclesiam revocat: teste ipso Servatore: Reges Gentium dominantur, & qui potestatem exercent, benefici vocantur: Luc. 22, 25. Atqui Magistratus politicus Dominium sibi in alios arrogat & exercet: Ergo Gentilismum in Ecclesiam DEI, contrà præceptum Servatoris revocat.

4. Quicquid imperfectis tantùm est permissum: illud in Ecclesia perfectorum per Christum est abrogatum. Jam verò DEUS Judæis propter imperfectionem ipsorum promisit possidere certas facultates & politica exercere officia: quemadmodum etiam Johannes Baptista, publicanis & militibus, quippe imperfectis permisit tantùm exercere contractus civiles, & stipendia in bello mereri. Ergo apud Christianos quippe perfectos, hæc omnia per Christum sunt abrogata.

5. Si Magistratus politicus esset à DEO, utiq; neq; ipse plerumq; sceleribus esset manifestis mis conspurcatus: neq; tot rerum omnium confusiones existerent: neq; scelerati pœnas promeritas toties effugerent. Atqui hæc vitia omnia in Magistratu politico semper & ubique cernere licet. Ergo Magistratus politicus non est à DEO.

Verùm non tanti ponderis aut momenti hæc sunt argumenta, ut Magistratus politici autoritatem quovis modo obscurare, nedùm tollere possint: id quod ex brevi singulorum refutatione facilè elucescer. Nam primùm turpiter fallit Sophismate figuræ dictionis. Neque enim in Græco habetur: δικαίῳ νόμος & τίθεται Justo non datur, vel data est lex: sed, νόμος & κεῖται Lex non jacet. Jam verò duæ hæ loquendi formulæ, significatione & emphasi plurimùm differunt. Prior enim legis promulgationem notat, à quâ justos non eximit Apostolus. Certè in ipso Paradiso DEUS Adamo, quamvis justissimo legem tulit sanctè observandam. Posterior phrasis, quâ Apostolus utitur, notat propria illa legis officia, qualia sunt: accusare, terrere, damnare. Quo sanè sensu justo νόμος & κεῖται. Lex nõ jacet, premens scilicet tanquam jugum intolerabile, vel cohorrens metu pœnæ, sicut pædagogus. Quam in sententiam præclarè Augustinus lib. 3. contra duas epistolas Pelagii cap. 4. Quis tam impius est, scribit, qui dicat, ideò se moralia legis non custodire præcepta, quia Christianus sit, nec sub lege, sed sub gratiâ constitutus? Profectò illam DEI legem, non solùm illi tunc populo, verùm etiam nunc nobis ad vitam recte instituendam, necessariam esse nemo dubitaverit: Sed magna distantia est, quando hoc faciunt sub lege constituti ex coactione legali, & quando sub gratia constituti hoc faciunt per dilectionem. Concludimus ergo, quod Apostolus non de omni usu legis, sed de pædagogico saltem loquatur, qui in Ecclesia renatorum locum non habet. Qua de re videatur Articulus sextus libri Concordiæ.

Alterum argumentum fallit Sophismate παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς Utrumque enim & Servatoris, & Apostoli præceptum agit de malo injuriarum, deq; vindicta privata : Er uti illud patienter ferendum, inimicum etiam nostrum diligendum: ita hanc privatis Christianis minimè competere, ostendit. Diversa verò ratio est, quando non ampliùs de malo injuriarum, quod inter privatos locum habet: sed de malo manifestæ improbitatis, & conscelerationis vitæ morumque est quæstio. Hic certè Magistratui politico suum officium constare, & vindictam secundum leges divinas competere, ex Scripturis suprà productis luculentissimè constat. Vitiosissima ergò hæc est collectio, quæ partim sub æquivocatione vocabulorum turpiter ludit, partim verò ex informatione privatorum hominum, ad publicum Magistratus civilis officium, puerili terminorum πλεονεξίᾳ procedit.

Tertium argumentum geminâ Sophisticatione veritati struit insidias : Prior est παρὰ τὸ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Est enim Servatori apud Lucam cap. 22, 25. sermo non indefinite ad omnes Christianos, quasi simpliciter omne dominium politicum ab ipsis debeat esse alienum: sed tantùm ad Apostolos, quorum officium, in docendo & ministrando, non verò in externo aliquo dominatu, sive præeminentia, occupatum esse debere, ostendit. Jam verò ab officio Apostolorum, ad officium Magistratus politici exclusivè non valet consequentia. Posterior Sophisticatio est παρὰ τὸ χῆμα τῆς λέξεως Phrasis enim hæc, Reges Gentium dominantur, non istum habet sensum, quasi dominatus politicus tantùm inter Gentes, non item inter Christianos locum habere possit & debeat: Sed Temporis saltem conditionem & respectum involvit. Siquidem illo tempore Magistratus politicus non nisi inter gentes florebat, donec constituta Novi Testamenti Ecclesia, Christiani quoque, excusso gentilium jugo, officia politica obierunt. Quid quòd Servator hanc notationem non semper expressit, sed quos hic nominavit Reges Gentium: paulò post, ut & Matth. 20, 25. simpliciter appellat τὺς μεγάλυς, καὶ ἐξυσιάζοντας, magnates, & potestatem exercentes. Constat proinde, Servatorem hac phrasi, Reges Gentium, non tàm ad personas hominum, quàm ad Ecclesiæ suæ statum respexisse.

Quartum argumentum pluribus laborat petitionibus principii, imò manifestis vanitatibus, & falsitatibus, quam constat terminis. In Majore 1. desideratur definitio perfectorum, quorum elogium, si Anabaptistæ fidelibus Veteris Testamenti; ut & illis, qui Johannem Baptistam Præceptorem docentem au diverunt, derogant: næ insigni impietate & sacrilegio errorem suum atrociorem reddunt. 2. Manifestum ψεῦδος in Scripturam committitur, quando Conciones Christi, & Baptistæ ἀντιφατικῶς opponuntur: vel fingitur à Christo doctrina Johannis B. fuisse antiquata Si enim Johannes præcursor fuit DOMINI, si viam ipsi præparare debuit, si Propheta altissimi fuit, deditq; notitiam salutis populo ejus, quæ est in remissione peccatorum: certè doctrinam ipsius, Christi Servatoris doctrinæ fuisse contrariam, nemo affirmaverit, nisi qui sensum communem cum omni pudore perdidit. In Minore simpliciter falsum est. 1. DEUM propter imperfectionem aliquam Veteris Testamenti propriam concessisse populo Israëlitico politici regiminis exercendi potestatem. 2. propter eandem imperfectionem Johannem Baptistam publicanis & militibus usum contractuum civilium, & bellorum permifisse.

Quintum & postremum puerili Sophismate τῷ συμβεβηκότι inaniter ludit. Queadmodum verò in rebus quibusvis aliis accidens vitiosum non tollit rem ipsam: aliàs enim Cœlum & elementa ipsa è medio removenda forent: Ita neque personarum in Magistratu constitutorum vitia; neque ipfius regiminis ἀταξία, bonam DEI ordinationem, nempe magistratum ipsum politicum corrumpere aut evertere vel potest, vel debet.

Anabaptistis succedunt in classe errantium Doctores ac Monachi Pontificii, imò Pontifex ipse Romanus; cum universo Clericorum ordine, qui licet verbis satis honorificè de Magistratu Politico sentire, & loqui videri vult, reipsâ tamen eundem subruit, evertit, & pedibus conculcat, Assertioni huic nostræ fidem facit praxis Ecclesiæ Romanæ, quæ egregiis hisce flosculis & Emblematus exornari, & fucari consuevit.

1. Pontificis Romani praeminentia major est omni aliâ creaturâ, quippe libera & absoluta ab omni regulâ coërcente, extendens se ad cœlestia, terrestria, infernalia: ut habet Ant. Florentinus: & Baldus in proœmio decretalium.

2. Sicut Luna recipit lumen à Sole: ita Imperialis sive Cæsarea dignitas à splendore Papali fulgorem suum sortitur: ut Innocentius III. ad Imp. Constantinopolitanum scribere non dubitavit.

3. Papa nulli omninò mortalium vel obedientiam, vel reverentiam præstat: sed Imperator ad osculum pedis aliquantulum affurgit: uti legere licet in lib. 3. Ceremoniarum Curiæ Romanæ.

4. Papa potestatem habet, etiam sine Concilio, deponere Imperatorem; id quod ipso facto explevit Gregorius II. qui Leonem III. Imperatorem Constantinopolitanum: Zacharias, qui Childericum regem Franciæ: Leo III. qui Constantinopolitanis imperium eripuit: Innocentius III. qui Ottonem IV. Innocentius IV. qui Fridericum II. Clemens VI. qui Ludovicum IV. de sede Imperatoria deturbavit.

Neque solus Pontifex se tantùm, sed & universum Episcoporum & Clericorum Papalium ordinem, ab omni jurisdictione Magistratus politici vult esse exemtum: id quod testantur scripta tùm Bellarmini, tùm aliorum contra Regem Angliæ, hac de re cruento satis calamo & stylo nuper edita. Et hinc ortum traxit praxis illa egregia Esavvitarum, omni consceleratione, & perfidia tutissimum asylum præbens. Nam disertis verbis ordini suo id privilegium vendicant, ut ne illi quidem Regibus, aut Principibus, in quorum ditione vivût, fidelitatis iuramentum præstare, nedum tributa pendere, vel publica ferre onera teneantur,

Quid? quòd scribere non sunt veriti, Clericos Papales, si maxime contra Regem, aut aliũ Magistratum seditionẽ moveant, non teneri crimine læsæ majestatis: propterea quòd Clericus non sit subditus Regis. Hinc est, quod Pontifex Magistratus politico omnem curam primæ tabulæ, hoc est, religionis & Ecclesiæ adimit, & subditos à Juramento, quo Magistratui jure divino sunt devincti & obligati, in rebus Ecclesiasticis, imò & civilibus sæpissimè absolvit.

Judicet jam, qui sanæ mentis est, an hoc non sit Ordinem Magistratus civilis penitùs subvertere? Imò judicet, quid aliquando Papa Romanus, cum suis Episcopis & Clericis responsurus sit Christo justissimo mortalium judici, qui per Apostolum hanc authenticam promulgari voluit, Rom. 13, 1. Omnis anima potestati Magistratus sit subdita. Ubi sanè Universalitatis nota neminem, cujuscunque sit sortis aut conditionis, ab hac subjectione Magistratui civili debita, excipit: nedum singulari aliquo privilegio ab eâ eximit, aut immunem præstat. Unde rectè Chrysostomus super hunc locum infert: Etiamsi ergo Apostolus sis, si Evangelista, si Propheta, sive quisquis tandem fueris, potestatibus supereminentibus sis subditus: Neq; enim pietatem subvertit ista subjectio, Et non simpliciter dicit Apostolus, Omnis anima Magistratui obediat: sed, subdita sit.

Obvertunt quidem hoc loco Esavvitæ, varias Donationes, Jura, privilegia, Immunitates, quibus sedes Romana, & cumprimis Papalis dignitas, super omnem Magistratum politicum evecta, & ab omni superiori Jurisdictione simpliciter sit exemta.

Sed primùm fabulosa hæc sunt omnia. Nam 1. diplomata illa Donationum, maximam partem ab adulatoribus sedis Romanæ sunt conficta: 2. nonnulla malis artibus & dolo quæsita: 3. quædam per vim manifestam extorta: quemadmodum alibi à nobis demonstratum fuit. Deinde Reges & Principes nullo jure potuerunt ejusmodi privilegia in Sedem Pontificiam conferre: propterea quod divinæ ordinationi, quæ Ecclesiasticum, & Politicum ordinem & materiâ sive subjectis, & formâ, & fine à se mutuô discre= pare vult, manifestè contrariatur, & exitio= sam ἀταξίαν sive Confusionem gignit. Tandem CHRISTUS ipse, cujus vicari= um in terris Papa Romanus se splendidè mentitur, nuspiam talem aliquam immuni tatem, sive exemptionem, vel quæsivisse, vel affectasse legitur: Sed, licet totius Ecclesiæ caput & Doctor Universalis à DEO Patre es= set constitutus, tamen sub imperio Augusti na= sci, eidemq; tributarius quasi in ipso matris ute= ro adhuc constitutus, inq; primo lucis hujus aspectu fieri voluit: & ne ullius vel scanda= li, vel confusionis autor videri posset, Cen= sum pro se, & Petro dependere minimè de= trectavit, Matth. 17, 24. A quâ subjectione cüm se, suumque Clerum simpliciter exem= tum velit Papa Romanus, vel inde manife= stissimè liquet, non CHRISTI, sed illius vica= rium ipsum esse, qui se opponit & effert su= pra omne, quod DEUS est, aut dicitur: in ô qui est homo peccati, & filius perditionis, ipsissimus nimirûm Antichristus 2. Thess. 2, 3. & 4.

Sed alterum etiam errorem, priore mul= tô atrociorem, hoc loco fovent Romanen= ses, dum non modò Papam, Episcopos, & Cle= rum Romanum universum, ab omni Jurisdictio= ne Magistratûs civilis, ausu proprio & nefa= rio eximunt: Sed iifdem, & potissimûm Pontifici suo, infinitum planè, absolutum, & uti loquuntur, merum ac mixtum imperi= um, tam in secularibus & civilibus rebus, quàm in ecclesiasticis, assignare non dubi= tant: quale etiam Pontifex ipse, superiori= bus potissimûm seculis sibi usurpare non ex= horruit. Unde nata sunt egregia illa, de u= traque Pontificis potestate, elogia.

Et ne forte quis olim tantùm à Pontifi= ciis, & adulatoribus Canonistis ejusmodi horrenda paradoxa sparsa fuisse existimet: observationem meretur, quòd moderni Esa= vvitæ, sub variis verborum & phrasium in= volucris, eandem impietatem hodieque te= nent, ac defendere student. Sic enim Bellar= minus lib. 5. de Rom. Pontif. cap. 1. pag. mi= hi. 1055. Et hanc sen= tentiam asserit Bellarminus esse Catholicorum Theologorum communem: Quam eodem in libro, cap. 6. his verbis explicat: Pontifex ut Pontifex, etsi non habeat ullam merè temporalé potestatem,


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Proper Quasi-affection of the Political Magistracy: That the Political and Ecclesiastical are two separate powers

yet he has, in relation to the spiritual good, supreme power to dispose of the temporal affairs of all Christians: page: 1062 for me, letter D. And a little later: Ecclesiastical and political power seem indeed to be distinct powers: and yet one is subordinate to the other, since the end of the one is by its nature referred to the end of the other. The political has for its end temporal peace: the ecclesiastical, eternal salvation. They are sometimes found separated, as once in the time of the Apostles: sometimes joined, as now. But when they are joined, they form one body, and therefore they ought to be connected, and the inferior subject and subordinate to the superior. Thus, the spiritual does not mix itself in temporal business, but lets all things proceed as they were before they were joined, provided they do not hinder the spiritual end, or are not necessary for attaining it. But if any such thing should happen, the spiritual power can and ought to coerce the temporal by every reason and way that seems necessary for that purpose. Book 5, On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 6, page 1063 for me, letters A and D; 1064, letter A.

This doctrine of the Esauvites is insidious and entirely designed for deception. For in words they wish to appear to distinguish accurately between ecclesiastical power and civil or secular power: but in reality they confuse both, and claim the power over secular matters entirely for the Pope and the Roman Bishops: that is, as our blessed Luther was accustomed to speak, they establish CæsaroPapism.

Furthermore, in order that this whole controversy may be more solidly defined and settled, three things must be performed by us: 1. That we show that political or secular power is so separated and sequestered from ecclesiastical power by divine law itself that both can never belong to any one order. 2. That we examine more accurately the Esauvite conditions and limitations by which they attempt to palliate and disguise the power of the Roman Pontiff in secular matters, and demonstrate more clearly what tyranny they hide in this place. 3. That we respond solidly to the arguments of the same Bellarmine, by which he wished to fight for this very power of the Pope in temporal matters.

Regarding the first: Each government, both ecclesiastical and political, is considered in two ways: Either simply and absolutely, from its own causes, by which each consists and is completed in itself: Or concretely, that is, by reason of the subject or the person of the magistrate sustaining it. The former consideration regards causes partly internal, partly external. The internal are matter and form. Now regarding the matter, Bellarmine himself admitting it, ecclesiastical power is concerned with internal, spiritual goods, directed solely to the soul of the sinful man, and reaching to eternal salvation. But secular power is concerned with the goods of the body and fortune, with the external honesty of life and morals, and with praiseworthy discipline.

Regarding the form, ecclesiastical government consists of the preaching of the word, the administration of the sacraments, and the legitimate use of the keys of the kingdom of heaven. The very instruction of the Apostles, prescribed by Christ the Savior, proves this: Mark

16:15. Matt. 28:19. Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Apostle infers a general aphorism, 2 Cor. 10:4, saying: The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through GOD, for the destruction of strongholds, etc. But political or secular government consists of civil laws and the use of the external sword: Rom. 13:4. The magistrate does not bear the sword in vain: for he is the minister of GOD, an avenger in wrath to him who has done evil. And this form is so peculiar and proper to political government that Christ himself simply forbade the use of the external sword both to Peter and consequently to all his successors, with this added threat: He who takes the sword shall perish by the sword: Therefore put your sword back into its place. Matt. 26:52.

The external causes are the efficient and the final. Therefore, ecclesiastical government, regarding the efficient cause in the New Testament, is from Christ, its primary and sole founder, according to that, John 20:21: As the Father has sent me, so I also send you. But political government, although, as shown above, it also has GOD as its author: yet it depends simultaneously on the Law of Nature, or as Christ speaks, on the law of Nations. Luke 22:25: The kings of the nations exercise lordship. The evidence of this difference is such that one may irrefragably conclude from it that the Roman Pontiff arrogates to himself political or secular jurisdiction not by divine law, but at least by human, and only by human, law. Regarding the final cause, ecclesiastical government looks to that end which the matter itself, about which it is solely occupied, produces of itself, namely spiritual justice, peace of conscience with GOD, and the eternal salvation of souls. Rom. 14:17. The kingdom of GOD is justice, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. John 18:36: My kingdom is not of this world: If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now my kingdom is not from here.

Which single assertion of the Savior ought to repress the rash usurpation of the worldly kingdom in the Roman Pontiff, if only he wishes to be and to appear to be the vicar of Christ on earth. For neither is the servant above his Master: nor should any vicar or legate take upon himself more authority or power than the Lord or Prince himself usurped: unless he wishes to appear a meddler and a busybody. Political government, by reason of the final cause, looks to civil justice, the honesty of external morals, and the peace and tranquility of this life, as the Apostle defines it, 1 Tim. 2:2: We must pray for kings, and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a quiet life under them, in all piety and honesty.

And this indeed is the former comparison of Ecclesiastical government with Political. Now if those things which differ in their causes, differ in their very definition, they certainly can be no more subordinate, these two governments, or can it belong to one individual, and the Roman Pontiff can be said to be the Archangel Gabriel, or Michael: since they are different in their entire genus; unless perhaps in the Pontiff Nature has erred, and has produced some horrible monster, that is, neither a man, nor a pure Angel: but an incarnate Devil.

The subsequent consideration of both governments, which theologians call concretive, regards the Subject itself, about which it is asked: Namely, whether both can fall into one Subject, or a pure Man, whoever he may be? Where we determine that one must answer through a distinction of times and of present necessity. For in the ancient Church of the Israelites, these two governments were for some time not incompatible: so that those who were the leaders of Religion and the Church obtained political leadership. An example can be Melchizedek, who was both King of Salem and Priest of the most high, Gen. 14, 18. Likewise Moses, who not only judged the people in secular matters, Exod. 18, 13, but also at the same time as Priest burned incense of spices upon the golden altar, Exod. 40, 25. Likewise Eli, who is read to have been both Priest and judge of the people, 1 Sam. 7, 10, and chap. 4, 18. But this coupling of both governments in one individual had to last at least for a time. For GOD himself, by special sanctioned laws, willed them to be so distinct, nay separated, by reason of the subjects, that it was a crime for both Priests and kings to arrogate to themselves the right and authority of both governments. For thus the divine authentic texts held: Num. 18, 7. You (Aaron) and your sons keep your priesthood: and all things which pertain to the worship of the altar, and are within the veil, shall be administered by the Priests: if any stranger approaches, he shall be killed. And 2 Chron. 26, 18. The Priests address King Uzziah, wishing to burn incense upon the altar of incense, thus: It is not your office, Uzziah, to offer sacrifice to the LORD: but that of the Priests, that is, the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to such ministry: Go out of the Sanctuary: lest you have despised: this will not be reckoned to you for glory by the LORD your GOD. When King Uzziah had refused to obey this warning, he was struck with leprosy in his face, so that he was forced to dwell and live separated from the company of men for his whole life, verses 19, 20, 21. Although indeed this very ordinance of GOD is read to have been abrogated by the Maccabees in the progress of time, or at least less strictly observed: yet it is rightly determined that that was a matter of fact, not of right, and perhaps of necessity. Nor does the consequence hold from there to the state of the Church of the New Testament. For the Savior, having undertaken the reformation of His Church, willed these two governments to be distinct in subjects, and incompatible in one individual: with these laws promulgated, Luke 22, 25. The Kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors: But you shall not be so. And 2 Tim. 2, 4. No man that warreth (for GOD) entangleth himself with the affairs of this life.

This very thing is evident from the practice of Christ and the Apostles; for He, being requested for the division of an inheritance between two brothers, simply removing this office from Himself, said, Man, who made me a judge, or a divider over you? Luke 12, 13. But these men refused to put their sickle into the political harvest to such an extent that they did not even want to be occupied with the distribution of alms. Acts 6, 2.

And this indeed is the first member of our refutation, to the weakening of which Bellarmino opposes himself, with great, but vain effort.

And at the beginning, indeed, he retorts to that saying of Christ, Luke 22, 25, in this manner: The LORD, he says, here only institutes mere ecclesiastical princes, and teaches that they, as they are such, ought to preside over subjects, not in the manner of kings, but in the manner of fathers and pastors. But it does not follow from this that one and the same person cannot be Bishop and Prince. Then, the LORD in these words does not forbid to Bishops a dominion such as can be that of pious Kings and Princes: but such as is that of kings who do not know GOD, who are tyrants rather than kings. Which is evident from the propriety of the Greek words: For Matthew chap. 20, 25 (Mark likewise 10, 42) does not say, κυριεύουσιν αὐτῶν; that is, they exercise dominion simply: but κατακυριεύουσιν, that is, they exercise dominion violently. Just as 1 Pet. 5, 3. It is held, Not as being lords over God's heritage, μηδ' ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων.

Latin:

tamen habet in ordine ad bonum Spirituale summam potestatem disponendi de temporalibus rebus omnium Christianorum: pag: mihi 1062. lit. D. Et paulò pòst : Potestas Ecclesiastica, & politica videntur quidem distinctæ esse potestates: & ta men una alteri est subordinata, quoniam finis unius ad finem alterius naturâ suâ refertur. Politica pro fine habet temporalem pacem : Ecclesiastica salutem æternam. Inveniuntur quandoque separatæ, ut olim tempore Apostolorum: quandoque conjunctæ, ut nunc. Quando autem sunt conjunctæ, unum corpus efficiunt, ideoq; debent esse connexæ, & inferior superiori subjecta, & subordinata. Itaq; Spiritualis se non miscet temporalibus negociis, sed sinit omnia procedere, sicut antequàm essent conjunctæ, dummodò non obsint fini Spirituali, aut non sint necessaria ad eum consequendum. Si autem tale quid accidat, Spiritualis potestas potest & debet coercere temporalem omni ratione, ac via, quæ ad id necessaria esse videtur. lib. 5. de Rom. Pont. cap 6. pag. mihi 1063. lit. A. & D. 1064. lit. A.

Insidiosa hæc est Esauvitarum, & ad decipiendum tota comparata doctrina. Nam verbis videri volunt, potestatem Ecclesiasticam à civili sive seculari accuratè distinguere: Verùm reipsa utramque confundunt, & rerum secularium potestatem, Pontifici, & Episcopis Romanis in solidum vendicant: hoc est, ut B. Lutherus noster loqui consuevit, καισαροπαπίαν CæsaroPapismum stabiliunt.

Cæterùm tota hæc controversia ut solidiùs definiatur, & dirimatur, tria nobis præstanda sunt: 1. ut ostendamus, potestatem Politicam sive secularem ab Ecclesiastica ita esse jure ipso divino separatam, & sequestratam, ut uni alicui ordini utraq; nunquàm possit competere. 2. Vt conditiones, & limitationes Esauviticas, quibus Potestatem Pontificis Romani in secularibus palliare, & fucare conantur, accuratiùs examinemus, & quam tyrannidem hoc loco occultent, dilucidiùs commonstremus. 3. Ut ad ejusdem Bellarmini argumenta, quibus pro hac ipsâ potestate Papæ in temporalibus pugnare voluit, solidè respondeamus.

Quoad primum: Consideratur utrumque regimen, & Ecclesiasticum, & Politicum duobus modis: Vel simpliciter & absolute, ex causis propriis, quibus utrumque per se constat & absolvitur: Vel Concretivè, sive ratione Subjecti, aut personæ Magistratus sustinentis. Prior consideratio respicit causas partim internas, partim externas. Internæ sunt, Materia & Forma. Jam quoad materiam, fatente ipso Bellarmino, potestas Ecclesiastica versatur circa bona interna, Spiritualia, ad animam hominis peccatoris unicè directa, & ad salutem æternam pertingentia. Potestas autem secularis versatur circa bona Corporis & Fortunæ, circa externam vitæ, morumq; honestatem, & disciplinam laudabilem.

Quoad Formam, Gubernatio Ecclesiastica constat prædicatione verbi, administratione Sacramentorum, & legitimo usu clavium regni cælorum. Evincit hoc ipsa instructio Apostolorum, à Christo Salvatore præscripta: Marc.

16,15. Matth.28,19. Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, & filii, & Spiritus Sancti. Hinc Apostolus generalem infert Aphorismum, 2. Cor. 10,4. Arma, inquiens, militiæ nostræ, non sunt carnalia, sed potentia DEO, ad destructionem munitionum &c. Gubernatio verò politica, sive secularis, constat legibus civilibus, & usu gladii externi: Rom. 13,4. Magistratus non sine causâ gestat gladium: DEI enim minister est, vindex in iram ei, qui malum egerit. Et hæc forma usque adeò peculiaris & propria est Regimini politico, ut Christus ipse usum gladii externi & Petro, & consequenter omnibus ipsius successoribus simpliciter interdixerit, hac adjectâ comminatione, Qui gladium sumserit, gladio peribit: Converte ergo gladium in locum suum. Matth. 26, 52.

Causæ externæ sunt Efficiens & finalis. Regimen ergo Ecclesiasticum, quoad causam efficientem in Novo Testamento est à Christo, primario & unico ejus fundatore, juxta illud, Johan. 20, 21. Sicut misit me Pater, ita & ego mitto vos. Regimen Politicum verò, etsi, uti suprà ostensum, DEUM quoque auctorem habet: tamen à Jure Naturæ, vel uti Christus loquitur, à jure Gentium simul dependet. Luc. 22, 25. Reges gentium dominantur. Cujus differentiæ ea est evidentia, ut irrefragabiliter inde colligere liceat, Pontificem Romanum non jure divino, sed humano saltem, & modò humano, arrogare sibi jurisdictionem politicam sive secularem. Quoad Causam finalem, Regimen Ecclesiasticum finem spectat eum, quem Materia ipsa, circa quam unicè est occupatum, de se gignit, nempe justitiam spiritualem, Pacem Conscientiæ cum DEO, & salutem animarum æternam. Rom. 14, 17. Regnum DEI est justitia, & pax, & gaudium in Spiritu Sancto. Joh. 18, 36.
