Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo: Si ex hoc mundo esset regnum meum, ministri mei utiq; decertarent, ne traderer Judæis: nunc autem regnum meum non est hinc.

Quæ vel una assertio Servatoris temerariam usurpationem regni mundani in Pontifice Romano reprimere debebat, si modò Christi vicarius in terris esse, & videri velit. Neque enim servus supra Dominum: neque vicarius aut legatus aliquis, plus sibi autoritatis aut potestatis sumere debet, quàm Dominus aut Princeps ipse usurpavit: nisi ardelio & πολυπραγμων videri velit. Regimen Politicum ratione causæ finalis spectat, Iustitiam civilem, Honestatem morum externam, pacem & tranquillitatem vitæ hujus, sic definiente Apostolo, 1. Tim. 2, 2. Orandum pro regibus, & omnibus in eminentia constitutis, ut quietam vitam agamus sub ipsis, in omni pietate, & honestate.

Et hæc quidem prior est regiminis Ecclesiastici cum Politico collatio. Jam si ea, quæ causis differunt, ipsâ definitione differunt, utique haud magis subordinata esse possunt, duo hæc regimina, vel uni individuo competere, atque Pontifex Romanus dici potest esse Archangelus Gabriel, aut Michael: quippe toto genere differentia; nisi fortè in Pontifice Natura aberravit, & monstrum aliquod horrendum, hoc est, neque hominem, neq; Angelum purum: sed incarnatum Diabolum produxit.

Posterior Consideratio utriusque Regiminis, quam Concretivam Theologi appellant, respicit Subjectum ipsum, de quo quæritur: An videlicet utrumque in unum aliquod Subjectum, sive Hominem purum, quicunque ille sit, cadere possit? Ubi per distinctionem temporum & necessitatis præsentis respondendum esse statuimus. Nam in veteri Israëlitarum Ecclesiâ, duo isthæc regimina aliquandiu non erant incompatibilia: ita ut principatum politicum obtinerent ii, qui Religionis, & Ecclesiæ erant antistites. Exemplo potest esse Melchisedech, qui & Rex Salem erat, & Sacerdos altissimi, Genes. 14, 18. Item Moses, qui non modò judicavit populum in secularibus, Exod. 18, 13. sed & simul ut Sacerdos adolevit super altari aureo incensum aromatum. Exod. 40, 25. Item Heli, qui & Sacerdos, & judex populi fuisse legitur, 1. Sam. 7, 10. & cap. 4, 18. Sed ad tempus saltem durare debuit hæc utriusque regiminis in uno individuo copulatio. Nam DEUS ipse peculiaribus sancitis legibus, ea ita ratione subjectorum distincta, imò separata esse voluit, ut nefas esset & Sacerdotibus & regibus, utriusque regiminis jus autoritatemque sibi arrogare. Sic enim divina habebat authentica: Numer. 18, 7. Tu (Aaron) & filii tui custodite sacerdotium vestrum: & omnia, quæ ad cultum altaris pertinent, & intra velum sunt, per Sacerdotes administrabuntur: si quis extraneus accesserit, occidetur. Et 2. Paralip. 26, 18. Sacerdotes Regem Oziam sive Usiam, volentem adolere incensum super altare thymiamatis, sic alloquuntur: Non est tui officii Ozia, ut sacrificium facias DOMINO: sed Sacerdotum, hoc est, filiorum Aaron, qui consecrati sunt ad hujusmodi ministerium: Egredere de Sanctuario: ne contemseris: non reputabitur tibi hoc in gloriam à DOMINO DEO tuo. Cui monitioni cùm Rex Ozias parere recusasset, percussus est leprâ in facie, ut ab hominum consortio separatus habitare & vivere cogeretur per omnem vitam, versu 19, 20, 21. Quanquam verò hæc ipsa DEI ordinatio, progressu temporis à Macchabæis abrogata, vel certè minùs strictè observata fuisse legitur: facti tamen illud, non juris, & fortè necessitatis fuisse, rectè statuitur. Neque inde ad statum Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti valet Consequentia. Nam Servator susceptâ Ecclesiæ suæ reformatione, duo hæc regimina subjectis distincta, & uni individuo incompatibilia esse voluit: his promulgatis legibus, Luc. 22, 25. Reges Gentium dominantur, & Magistratus benefici appellantur: Vos autem non sic. Et 2. Tim. 2, 4. Nemo militans (DEO) implicat se negociis secularibus.

Patet hoc ipsum ex praxi Christi & Apostolorum; Ille enim requisitus ad divisionem hæreditatis inter duos fratres, hoc officium simpliciter à se removens, Homo, inquit, quis me constituit judicem, aut divisorem inter vos? Luc. 12, 13. Hi verò falcem suam in messen politicam immittere usque adeò recusarunt, ut ne quidem Eleemosynarum dispensationi vacare vellent. Actor. 6, 2.

Et hoc quidem primum est refutationis nostræ membrum, cui enervando opposit se Bellarminus, magno quidem, sed irrito conatu.

Ac initiò quidem ad illud Christi, Luc. 22, 25. hunc in modum regerit: DOMINUS primùm, inquit, hic solùm instituit meros principes Ecclesiasticos, ac docet, debere eos, ut tales sunt, præesse subditis, non more regum, sed more patrum & pastorum. Non autem sequitur hinc, non posse unum & eundem esse Episcopum & Principem. Deinde, DOMINUS his verbis non prohibet Episcopis dominatum, qualis esse potest Regum, & Principum piorum: sed qualis est regum ignorantium DEUM, qui tyranni potiùs sunt, quàm reges. Id quòd patet ex Græcorum verborum proprietate: Nam Matthæus cap. 20, 25. (Marcus item 10, 42.) non ait, κυριεύουσιν αὐτῶν; id est, dominantur simpliciter: sed κατακυριεύουσιν, id est, violenter dominantur. Sicut 1. Pet. 5. 3. Non dominantes in cleris habetur, μηδ' ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Proper Quasi-affection of the Political Magistracy: That the Political and Ecclesiastical are two separate powers (continued)

I answer that this Esauvitic exception, compared to the words of Christ, Luke 22, 25, collapses of its own accord and vanishes into smoke. For 1. ἄγνοια ἐλέγχου (ignorance of the refutation) is detected to be quite gross. The disciples certainly were not affecting any violent dominion, or κατακυριότητα: but they were contending at least about who of them seemed to be the greatest: as is evident from verse 24. Now Christ answers appositely, commanding that they should establish that all dominion is most alien to them: having sought the argument from the diversity of the Subject: as if He were saying: The Kings of the Gentiles or seculars exercise dominion, and exert power. But you are not such, but the nature of your office is occupied in teaching. Therefore, no dominion over others belongs to you either. Now if the Esauvitic exception concerning at least violent, or tyrannical forbidden dominion were to stand, the Speech of Christ would turn out clearly ἀσύστατον (inconsistent) and incongruous, since He would be answering something other than what was in question or Controversy: ἄτοπον (absurd).

Then this opposition is vicious, when the Esauvite asserts; that the LORD willed here to institute mere ecclesiastical princes, so that they might preside over subjects, not in the manner of kings, but in the manner of fathers and pastors. As if political kings and princes ought not to preside in the manner of fathers and pastors! But in the manner of Tyrants. Why then are they saluted as fathers of the country, and ποιμένες λαῶν (shepherds of the people)? Is this not to convert all political power into tyranny? 3. Thirdly, a shameful petitio principii occurs in that he concludes: 1. That the Apostles ought to preside in the manner of fathers and pastors: and that Christ wills this. 2. Hence it does not follow that one and the same person cannot be both Bishop and Prince. For both, as has already been shown, are κρινόμενον [in dispute], and not yet proven from the text. Added to this, in the fourth place, is the Sophistry of the figure of speech in the phrase, 'to preside in the manner of fathers and pastors': which we grant entirely belongs to the Apostles and all Doctors of the Church. But it is one thing to preside; another to command; another to be a Doctor of the Church; another to be a Prince or Monarch of the Church: which two the Savior wills to be so separated that they cannot belong to the Apostles at the same time, as the texts most clearly show.

Fifthly, the response of the Esauite overturns itself: For if the Apostles ought to preside not in the manner of kings, but in the manner of fathers and pastors: Therefore, royal power or dominion, and consequently any political power whatsoever, is denied and forbidden to them. Nor is there any reason for him to seek support for his error from the Greek word κατακυριεύειν. For 1. Luke has the simple verb κυριεύειν: which he immediately explains by ἐξουσιάζειν, and Mark renders by ἄρχειν, in such a way that ἄρχειν and κατακυριεύειν are equivalent for him. 2. The preposition κατὰ, added to the verb κυριεύειν, does not always denote evil, vicious, or tyrannical rule: but it is also taken in a good sense: as when Adam was constituted by GOD as Lord of the earth, the Septuagint Greeks rendered it, κατακυριεῦσαι τῆς γῆς, Genesis 1:28. With these things thus established, we conclude that the Savior forbids the Apostles not the mode of the thing, but the thing itself—that is, not a tyrannical or at least violent mode of political rule, but all worldly rule whatsoever. And even if Christ's words were to be taken most strongly regarding this mode of ruling, the thing itself speaks, that no rule has ever existed in the world more violent or tyrannical than that which the Roman Pontiff has exercised, and still exercises today where he is still held in any esteem, over Emperors, Kings, and Princes with force and arms for some past centuries. Therefore, even if there were any truth in the Esauite's argument, it would have no weight at all for confirming the dominion of the Roman Pontiff, but would rather utterly overturn it.

But the Esauite objects, and from the subsequent verse 26 urges the Greek word ὁ ἡγούμενος. For thus Christ says to the Apostles: ὁ ἡγούμενος, ὡς ὁ διακονῶν: He who presides, or who leads, let him be as he who serves: Therefore, some one person was designated by Christ as a leader or Prince, who should command the other Apostles.

But this argument also fails: 1. By the sophism παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως [based on the figure of speech]. For the phrase, ἡγούμενον εἶναι, does not denote τὸν ἄρχοντα or a worldly Prince, as in

Mark the Savior designated secular Princes with this word: But it denotes any Leader and President, which fits Ministers and Doctors of the word very well, since it is their duty to lead and show the way to others both by doctrine and by example: but not to exercise dominion over others by an external sword. Thus the Epistle to the Hebrews calls Ministers of the Word τὰς ἡγεμένους: 'Remember τῶν ἡγεμένων ὑμῶν, your leaders, who spoke to you the Word of GOD; whose faith imitate,' etc. Heb. 13:7.

Furthermore, this verse 26 also does not so much approve that fictitious primacy or worldly dominion of the Roman Pontiff and Bishops, as it rather utterly undermines and overturns it. For when the Apostles were contending among themselves, who of them could be seen as the greatest? The Savior answers: 'You shall not be so, but he who is greatest, or, as verse 24 implies, he who wishes to be seen as the greatest among you, let him be as he who is the least: and he who leads, let him be as he who serves.' Which words certainly assign no Monarchical rule to Peter, nor any primacy to the other Apostles: but uniquely commend humility and the zeal for serving: to which He also wished to invite them by His own example: saying, 'I am among you as he who serves: and I covenant for you a kingdom, just as my Father has covenanted for me,' verses 27 and 29.

But the Esauite proceeds to that passage of Christ, refusing to be a judge of the division of an inheritance, Luke 12:13, as well as to the act of the Apostles, who removed the distribution of alms from themselves, Acts 6:2, and answers: In both places, Pontiffs and Princes are admonished not to be so occupied with minute and base duties that they are forced to omit greater ones, book 5 de Pont. cap. 10, p. 1079 C.

But I answer that the Esauite is trifling, not disputing. For this very thing, which he takes as confessed and indubitable, is in question and controversy. 1. That Christ and the Apostles, by this act of theirs, wished to instruct Princes and Pontiffs regarding which objects of secular things and actions they ought to be most occupied with. 2. That Christ and the Apostles wished by this pact to distinguish between actions of one kind, namely greater and lesser political ones: when they rather wished to separate Genus from genus, that is, political actions from ecclesiastical actions, since they differ in their very Genus, and to show that both kinds of actions are clearly incompatible for one and the same Individual.

Thirdly and lastly, he objects against that passage, 2 Tim. 2:4, 'No one serving (GOD) entangles himself in secular cares': in the same place, page 1080 C in my edition. I deny that secular business in this place is called Political rule, but rather the care of providing for one's livelihood, and consequently negotiations, merchandise, and the like. For it is in Greek, τὰ βίε πραγματείας, that is, the businesses of life or livelihood.

I answer, that a gross ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχε is committed, and indeed in two ways. For 1. although the Apostle mentions only one species of secular business: yet under it he understands all the rest, which indeed can be taken care of outside of one's own vocation. There is no reason, therefore, for the Jesuit to hesitate in that one instance regarding the providing of a livelihood.

Furthermore, the scope and intention of the Apostle, as is manifestly clear from the entire context of this passage, turns on this alone: that he distinguishes most accurately between secular business and the duties of the Episcopal office, and shows that they are not to be confounded with one another. The comparison brought forward from those who serve as soldiers proves this. For just as they undertake no care for conducting secular business other than that which the reason and condition of military vocation demands, so it also befits Bishops to conduct no business other than that which the condition of an Ecclesiastical vocation or Evangelical Ministry admits. But this must be occupied solely with the propagation and defense of the kingdom and doctrine of Christ through the preaching of the Word and the administration of the Sacraments. Therefore, they ought in no way to be entangled in the conducting of secular business. Finally, what I ask is the reason that the same Bellarmine, as if forgetting this explanation of his of the Apostolic saying, in his disputation on the celibacy of priests, argues against us from this very passage thus: No one serving as a soldier to GOD (Note, here he himself adds the word 'GOD', which elsewhere in the present disputation, and in the passage cited a little before, he wishes to be struck out) entangles himself in secular business: therefore, neither in marriage. If this method of arguing ought to proceed regarding the prohibition of the marriage of priests, why should it not also proceed regarding the remaining secular business in which Bishops, by reason of lordship, ought not to be entangled? Thus, therefore, a liar must have a good memory.

And thus indeed we have dispatched the first part of this controversy.

The SECOND part of the present controversy is occupied with showing what kind of theology regarding the power of the Roman Pontiff the Jesuits hold and defend today. Bellarmine establishes a triple power of the Roman Pontiff and Bishops: one he calls of Order, the second of interior Jurisdiction, the third of exterior Jurisdiction. The same Bellarmine defines the first by the power of consecrating and administering the Sacraments; the second by the power of ruling the Christian people in the interior forum of conscience; the third by jurisdiction over the same people in the exterior or secular forum. Bellarmine, lib. 5 de Pont. c. 22. But the question here is not properly about those first two powers, but only about the third: Whether, and by what right, does the Roman Pontiff exercise secular power? Regarding the unfolding of which question our Jesuit holds the wolf by the ears, and although he is convinced in his conscience that such power in secular matters does not belong to the Pontiff and Bishops either by divine right or even by human right—if indeed you consider the legitimate usurpation of this right—yet by a double fabricated distinction, he strives to cast a certain cataract before the eyes of the simpler reader and to palliate that secular dominion of the Pontiff.

Latin:

Respondeo exceptionem hanc Esavviticam, collatam ad verba Christi, Luc. 22, 25. sua sponte corruere, & in fumum evanescere. Nam 1. ἄγνοια ἐλέγχου satis crassa deprehenditur. Discipuli certè non affectabant violentum aliquod dominium, sive κατακυριότητα: sed contendebant saltem, quis eorum videretur esse maximus: uti patet ex versu 24. Jam appositè respondet Christus, jubens, ut omnem dominatum à se statuant debere esse alienissimum: petito argumento à diversitate Subjecti: quasi dicat: Reges Gentium um sive seculares dominantur, & potestatem exercent. Vos autem tales non estis, sed muneris vestri ratio in docendo est occupata. Ergo vobis etiam nullus competit dominatus in alios. Jam si exceptio Esavvitica de violento saltem, sive tyrannico interdicto dominio deberet subsistere, ἀσύστατον planè, & inconcinnè evaderet Oratio Christi, quippe qui ad aliud responderet, quàm quod esset in quæstione sive Controversia: ἄτοπον.

Deinde vitiosa est hæc oppositio, quandò Esavvita asserit; DOMINUM voluisse hic instituere meros principes Ecclesiasticos, ut præsint subditis, non more regum, sed more patrum & pastorum. Quasi verò reges & principes politici non præesse debeant more patrum & pastorum! sed more Tyrannorum. Cur ergo patres patriæ, & ποιμένες λαῶν salutantur? Annon hoc est omnem potestatem politicam convertere in tyrannidem? 3. Tertio turpis petitio principii occurrit in eo, quòd colligit, 1. Apostolos præesse debere more patrum & pastorum: & hoc velle Christum. 2. Hinc non sequi, non posse unum & eundem esse simul Episcopum & Principem. Nam utrumque, ut jam ostensum est, κρινόμενον, & ex textu nondum probatum. Accedit quarto loco, Sophisticatio figuræ dictionis in phrasi, præesse more patrum & pastorum: id quod Apostolis, & omnibus Ecclesiæ Doctoribus competere omninò largimur. Aliud verò jam est præsidere; aliud imperare; aliud esse Doctorem Ecclesiæ: aliud esse Principem aut Monarcham Ecclesiæ: quæ duo ita vult esse separata Servator, ut Apostolis simul competere non possint, vt textus manifestissimi.

Quinto evertit semetipsam responsio Esavvitæ: Si enim Apostoli debent præesse non more regum, sed more patrum & pastorum: Ergo potestas sive dominium regium, & per consequens politicum quodvis, ipsis est negatum & interdictum. Neque est, ut ex verbo Græco κατακυριεύειν errori patrocinium quærat. Nam 1. Lucas habet verbum simplex κυριεύειν: quod exponit statim per ἐξουσιάζειν, & Marcus reddit per ἄρχειν, ita, ut ἄρχειν & κατακυριεύειν ipsi sint æquipollentia. 2. Præpositio κατὰ, addita verbo κυριεύειν, non semper malum, vitiosum, aut tyrannicum notat imperium: sed in bonam etiam partem accipitur: ut quando Adamus constitutus à DEO fuit Dominus terræ, reddiderunt Græci Septuaginta, κατακυριεῦσαι τῆς γῆς, Genes. 1, 28. Quibus ita constitutis colligimus, Servatorem non modum rei, sed rem ipsam, hoc est, non imperii politici modum tyrannicum, aut violentum saltem, sed omne omninò imperium mundanum Apostolis interdicere. Et si maximè de modo hoc imperandi Verba Christi acciperentur, res ipsa tamen loquitur, nullum unquàm magis violentum aut tyrannicum in mundo extitisse imperium, quàm quod Pontifex Romanus superioribus aliquot seculis, in Imperatores, Reges, Principes, vi armisq́; exercuit, hodieque exercet, ubi quidem in aliquo adhuc est pretio. Proinde si maximè argumento Esavvitico aliqua constaret veritas, pro confirmando tamen dominatu Pontificis Romani, nihil quicquam momenti obtineret, quin funditus potius illum everteret.

Sed excipit Esavvita, & ex subsequente versu 26. urget vocabulum Græcum ὁ ἡγούμενος. Sic enim Christus ad Apostolos: ὁ ἡγούμενος, ὡς ὁ διακονῶν: Qui præest, sive qui antecedit, sit sicut qui ministrat: Ergo unus aliquis à Christo designatus fuit dux aut Princeps, qui reliquis Apostolis imperaret.

Sed fallit hoc quoque argumentum 1. Sophismate παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως. Nam phrasis, ἡγούμενον εἶναι, non notat τὸν ἄρχοντα sive Principem mundanum, sicut apud

Marcum hoc vocabulo Principes seculares indigitavit Servator: Sed notat quemlibet Ducem, & Præsidem, id quod Ministris & Doctoribus verbi optimè convenit, quippè quorum est præire, & viam monstrare aliis tùm doctrinâ, tùm exemplo: non verò gladio externo dominium exercere in alios. Sic Epistola ad Hebræos Ministros Verbi nominat τὰς ἡγεμένυς: Memores estote τῶν ἡγεμένων ὑμῶν, præpositorum vestrorum, qui locuti sunt vobis Verbum DEI; quorum imitamini fidem, &c. Hebr. 13. 7.

Deinde hic quoque versus 26. tantum non approbat fictitium illum primatum, sive dominatum mundanum Pontificis Romani, & Episcoporum: ut eum potiùs funditùs subruat, & evertat. Cùm enim contenderent invicem Apostoli, quisnám ipsorum videri posset maximus? Respondet Servator: Vos non ita estote, sed qui maximus est, vel, ut versus 24. innuit, qui videri vult esse maximus inter vos sit sicut qui minimꝰ est: & qui antecedit, sit sicut qui ministrat. Quæ sanè verba nullum prorsus regimen Monarchicum vel Petro, vel primatum aliquem reliquis Apostolis adsignant: sed humilitatem, & ministrandi studium unicè commendant: ad quod suo etiam exemplo invitare illos voluit: Ego, inquiens, sum inter vos, ut qui ministrat: Ego verò pacifcor vobis regnum, prout pactus est mihi Pater meus, versu 27. & 29.

Sed pergit Esavvita ad illud Christi, nolentis esse judex familiæ herciscundæ Luc. 12, 13. ut & ad factum Apostolorum, distributionem Eleemosynarum à se amolientium, Actor. 6, 2. & respondet: In utroque loco admoneri Pontifices & Principes, ne minutis & vilibus officiis ita occupentur, ut omittere cogantur majora, lib. 5. de Pont. cap. 10. p. 1079. C.

Sed respondeo, nugari, non disputare Esavvitam. Hoc ipsum enim, quod ipse pro confesso & indubitato sumit, est in quæstione & controversia. 1. Christum & Apostolos suo hoc facto voluisse instruere Principes & Pontifices, circa quæ potissimùm objecta rerum & actionum secularium occupati esse debeant. 2. Christum & Apostolos voluisse hoc pacto distinguere inter unius generis actiones, politicas nimirùm majores & minores: cùm potiùs Genus à genere, hoc est, actiones politicas, ab actionibus Ecclesiasticis, quippe Genere ipso differentes separare, & uni eidemq́ue Individuo utrumque actionum genus planè incompetibile esse, ostendere voluerint.

Tertiò & postremò excipit contra illud, 2. Tim. 2, 4. Nemo militans (DEO) implicat se curis secularibus: eodem loco pag. mihi 1080. C. Negotia secularia hoc loco non vocari regimen Politicum, sed curam parandi victus, & proinde negotiationes, & mercimonia, & similia. Est enim Græcè, τὰ βίε πραγματείας, id est, negociis vitæ sive victus.

Respondeo, committi crassam ἄγνοιαν ἐλέγχε, & quidem dupliciter. Nam 1. licèt Apostolus speciem unam tantùm, negociorum secularium exprimat: tamen sub ea intelligit reliquas omnes, quæ quidem extra cujusque vocationem curari possunt. Non est ergò, ut in unâ illâ specie, de parando victu, hæreat Esavvita.

Deinde verò Scopus & intentio Apostoli, uti ex integrâ loci hujus συνεπείᾳ manifestè liquet, in eo solo vertitur, ut accuratissimè inter negocia secularia, & inter officia muneris Episcopalis distinguat: neque ea invicem confundenda esse, ostendat. Evincit hoc allata similitudo à militantibus. Quemadmodum enim hi curam nullam suscipiunt de negociis tractandis secularibus aliis, præter ea, quæ vocationis militaris ratio & conditio exigit. Sic Episcopos etiam decet non nisi ea tractare negocia, quæ vocationis Ecclesiasticæ, sive Ministerii Evangelici Conditio admittit. Atqui hæc unicè in eo occupata esse debet, ut regnum & doctrina Christi propagetur & defendatur, per prædicationem Verbi, & administrationem Sacramentorum. Ergò negociis secularibus tractandis implicari nullo modo debent. Tandem, quid quæso causæ est, quòd idem Bellarminus hujus suæ explicationis dicti Apostolici quasi oblitus, in disputatione de cœlibatu Sacerdotum, ex hoc ipso loco adversum nos sic arguit: Nemo militans DEO (Nota, hîc ipsemet adjicit vocabulum (DEO) quòd aliàs in præsente disputatione, & loco paulò ante citato, expunctum vult) implicat se negociis secularibus: Ergò nec nuptiis: Si hæc argumentandi ratio procedere debeat, quoad prohibitionem conjugii Sacerdotum: quidnî procedat etiam quoad reliqua negocia secularia, quibus Episcopi ratione dominii implicari non debeant. Sic ergò Mendacem oportet esse memorem.

Et sic quidem primum Controversiæ hujus membrum expedivimus.

ALTERUM præsentis Controversiæ membrum in eo est occupatum, ut ostendat, quamnam Theologiam de potestate Pontificis Romani teneant, ac defendant hodie Esavvitæ. Constituit autem Bellarminus triplicem & Pontificis, & Episcoporum Romanensium potestatem: Unam vocat Ordinis: alteram Jurisdictionis interioris: tertiam Jurisdictionis exterioris. Primam definit idem Bellarminus per potestatem Sacramenta conficiendi, & administrandi: alteram per potestatem regendi populum Christianum in foro interiori conscientiæ: tertiam per Jurisdictionem in eundem populum in soro exteriori, sive seculari. Bellarmin. lib. 5. de Pont. c. 22. Verùm de duabus illis primis potestatibus, hoc loco propriè non est quæstio, sed tantùm de tertiâ, Utrum, & quo jure Pontifex Romanus exerceat potestatem secularem? Circa quam quæstionem evolvendam Esavvita noster lupum tenet auribus, & quanquam in conscientiâ est convictus, talem potestatem in secularibus Pontifici & Episcopis neque jure divino, neque jure etiam humano, si quidem legitimam juris hujus usurpationem consideres, competere: tamen duplici conficta distinctione, Lectori simpliciori γλαύκωμα quoddam objicere, & dominatum illum Pontificis secularem palliare studet.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Proper Quasi-affection of the Political Magistracy: That the Political and Ecclesiastical are two separate powers (continued)

For first he writes that the Pontiff as Pontiff does not indeed have any temporal power directly and immediately, but yet, by reason of a spiritual Monarchy, he has supreme power in temporal matters indirectly, insofar as political power is subject and subordinate to the Ecclesiastical. lib. 5 de Pont. c. 1 & cap. 6.

But this novel Jesuitical distinction initially rejects and removes the old doctrine of the Romanists, which asserted that jurisdiction in Ecclesiastical and political matters belonged to the Pontiff and Bishops by divine right, as erroneous. Certainly, Pope Nicholas, citing Gratian, dist. 22, Can. Omnes, brought forth this opinion: Christ, to whom all power was given in heaven and on earth, committed the rights of the earthly and at the same time the heavenly Empire to Blessed Peter, the key-bearer of eternal life. And Pope Boniface, in the extravagant chapter Unam Sanctam, de Majoritate et Obedientia, elicits from those words of the Apostles, Luke 22:38, 'Behold, here are two swords,' and that Christ did not say, 'It is too much,' but 'It is enough,' that the Pontiff ought to exercise two swords, spiritual and political, on earth. But this assertion is too trifling, exploded even by the sounder Papists themselves, since they have rightly perceived that: 1. Nowhere were the keys of the kingdoms of this world given by Christ to the Apostles, but only the keys of the kingdom of heaven. 2. The Apostles, and thus Peter also, never obtained the power of Empire and temporal jurisdiction either by hereditary succession, or by title of election, or by right of war, or by special gift; nor could they propagate it to successor Pontiffs, according to that most true rule in this very matter: What one does not have, one cannot transfer to another. 3. The consequence from the exaltation and dominion of the human nature of Christ to the Roman Pontiff is invalid, because it was never said to any of the Angels, let alone men: 'Sit at my right hand.' Heb. 1:13. 4. The consequence taken from the two swords of the Apostles is ridiculous, especially since the Savior immediately forbade the use of the external sword to Peter and the rest of the Apostles, Matt. 26:52. Therefore, although the Jesuitical distinction departs from this Old Pontifical Theology, yet it too is nothing other than mere and empty babbling or begging the question. For it assumes as certain and indubitable that the Roman Pontiff indirectly possesses supreme power in temporal matters, which is nevertheless most uncertain and highly controversial, because, as they themselves teach, the Scriptures neither directly nor indirectly grant that both jurisdictions, or ecclesiastical and temporal power, belong to any man, whether an individual, or whether he be an Apostle, or a Pontiff, or a Bishop: whatever respect of diversity or deception may be employed.

The other distinction, by which Bellarmine tries to deceive the reader, is likewise trifling, and begs the question, when he contends that secular power is subordinate to ecclesiastical power, so that the Roman Pontiff, not indeed as Pontiff, but as a spiritual Monarch, has supreme power even in temporal matters. For this very thing is the κρινόμενον [point in dispute], which he himself assumes as certain. And it has already been demonstrated above from the Scriptures that the administration of secular power belongs neither to the Pontiff, nor to any Bishop, not only insofar as he is a Pontiff or Bishop, but in no way or respect whatsoever: nor is there any order under the Sun by which, under the category of power, secular jurisdiction is subordinate to ecclesiastical. As long, therefore, as he does not sufficiently prove this subordination, and indeed by reason of power in temporal matters, for so long he acts the Sophist, and brings forth an empty noise of words, not the things themselves.

What an utterly empty noise of words and most trifling trifling it is, when in the same chapter 6 of book 5 de Pont. he writes: The Pope, as Pope, cannot ordinarily depose temporal Princes, even for a just cause, in the way in which he deposes Bishops, that is, as an Ordinary Judge: nevertheless, he can change kingdoms, and take away from one and confer upon another, as a supreme spiritual Prince: if that be necessary for the salvation of souls. Thus, as regards Laws, the Pope, as Pope, cannot ordinarily establish a civil law, or confirm or invalidate the laws of Princes, because he himself is not the political Prince of the Church: nevertheless, he can do all those things if any civil Law is necessary for the salvation of souls, and yet Kings do not wish to establish it: or if another is harmful to the salvation of souls, and yet Kings do not wish to abrogate it. Thus, as regards judgments, the Pope, as Pope, cannot ordinarily judge concerning temporal matters: But nevertheless, in a case where it is necessary for the salvation of souls, the Pontiff can assume even temporal judgments, when, of course, there is no one who can judge: as when two supreme kings contend, or when those who can and ought to judge do not wish to pass sentence. Thus far Bellarmine.

This is the Lerna and sink of all evils and confusions that have ever arisen in Church and State. For if you ask, Why has the Pope taken upon himself the power of dispensing in temporal punishments, so that from this dispensation there has been no exception for incest, not adultery, not homicide, not parricide, not Simony, not poisoning, not bestiality, not perjury, not similar crimes and outrages? The Esauite will answer: Because the Pontiff is a spiritual Monarch, and has temporal power subject to him, and therefore he can invalidate the civil laws of Princes, because it seems necessary for the salvation of souls. Thus if you ask: By what right has the Roman Pontiff raged so greatly with violent excommunications, proscriptions, arms, and wars against Emperors, Kings, Princes, and any secular powers whatsoever? By what right, likewise, has he stripped them of their empire, kingdoms, and principalities, and bestowed them upon others? The Esauite will answer: because he is the supreme spiritual Prince: because all temporal power is subject to him, because it seemed necessary for the salvation of souls.

Speaking summarily, whatever does not please the Roman Curia, whatever does not kiss and approve its idolomania: whatever, finally, in any way resists Pontifical laws and traditions, even in secular matters, that the Pope, as resisting the Spiritual Monarchy and adverse to the salvation of souls, changes, abrogates, excommunicates, proscribes, and deems must be vindicated for himself by force and arms at his own whim and pleasure. And this was that brazen wall which sustained and preserved the Pontifical kingdom in previous centuries: and in rebuilding which the Pontiff, with his entire Pontifical cohort, labors strenuously today, but in vain (by the grace of GOD).

And indeed, in order that we may utterly undermine and overturn this fortress or acropolis, as it were, of Pontifical dominion: we shall first attack it with firm and immovable arguments: but afterwards we shall accurately examine and crush the weapons with which Bellarmine fights to defend his opinion.

Regarding the first: We oppose to Bellarmine at the beginning this Dilemma: by which Bellarmine himself in book 5 de Pont. Rom. cap. 3. pag. 1056. lit. B. skillfully refutes the opinion of the Canonists, who contend that Kings and Emperors have whatever power they possess, whether supreme or of execution, from the Pope, in this manner: Either the Pope can in some way, whether directly, or indirectly, or as Pope, or as supreme Spiritual Prince, or as ordinary or extraordinary judge, change kingdoms, and take away from one and confer upon another: or he cannot: If he can: Therefore he is in some way, whether directly, or indirectly, or ordinarily, or extraordinarily, greater and more powerful than GOD himself, because what GOD granted to the Emperor, Kings, and Princes, he himself takes away and confers upon another: which is prodigiously absurd. Since he who is lesser or equal cannot change or take away what has been granted by a greater or equal. What of the fact that even a legate or vicar of someone, without the express mandate of his Lord, ought not to assume more authority and power for himself than the will of the Lord permits? If he cannot: Therefore it is false, and contrary to the Scriptures, what the Esauite says, that the Pope has supreme power to dispose indirectly of the temporal affairs of Christians, to change kingdoms, to abrogate imperial laws, and to depose Emperors and Kings from their throne, and to substitute others in their place.

The second argument, which we oppose to Bellarmine in this place, we again formulate in his own words from the same book and chapter, in this manner: If the matter were as Bellarmine defines it, it would certainly be evident either from the Scriptures or from the undoubted tradition of the Apostles. But from the Scriptures it is not permitted to gather more than that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to the Pontiff: of the keys of the kingdom of the earth no mention is made: Thus the adversaries produce no Apostolic tradition. Therefore the matter is not as Bellarmine defines it. Nor is it for him to object that there is no need here for either Scriptures or Apostolic tradition, if indeed jurisdiction in temporal matters pertains to the Pope only indirectly, and by a certain quasi-consequence, as to the supreme spiritual Prince and supreme Pastor of souls. For we ask that proof of this assertion also be given, either from the Scriptures or from the certain and undoubted tradition of the Apostles. And even if it were confessed on our part as well that the Pope is the supreme and universal pastor of all Christians—a thing which we nevertheless deny—it would still not follow that a necessary and inseparable adjunct of that pastoral care is power and dominion over the temporal affairs and business of Christians: otherwise, certainly, the Savior and the Apostles would not have wrapped it in such deep silence.

Thirdly, we oppose to Bellarmine that axiom, most true in political as well as sacred matters: Whatever is not directly permitted to anyone by GOD: that can neither be done nor undertaken indirectly, or by any consequence or dependence, nor ought it to be. The reason for this axiom is such that no Jesuit will infringe it by any artifice: Namely: Whatever is prohibited by GOD: that cannot be permitted by any other law or respect. Therefore, if the Pope, as Pope, has no temporal jurisdiction over Christians directly and by divine law—a thing which Bellarmine is forced to admit even against his will—then certainly he will not obtain it indirectly, nor by any other law, unless the Jesuit wishes to establish that human law can derogate from divine law or prejudice it in any way: a thing which is manifestly impious and blasphemous.

Latin:

Primum enim scribit, Pontificem ut Pontificem, non habere quidem directè & immediatè ullam potestatem temporalem: sed tamen ratione spiritualis Monarchiæ, habere indirectè summam potestatem in temporalibus, quatenus nimirum potestas politica Ecclesiasticæ est subjecta, & subordinata. lib. 5. de Pont. c. 1. & cap. 6.

Verùm distinctio hæc novella Esavvitica initiò veterem Romanensium doctrinam, quæ Pontifici & Episcopis, jure divino Jurisdictionem in rebus Ecclesiasticis, & politicis competere asseruit, ceu erroneam rejicit & tollit. Certè Nicolaus Papa, citante Gratiano, dist. 22. Can. Omnes, hanc tulit sententiam: Christus, cui data fuit omnis potestas in cælo & in terra, B. Petro, æternæ vitæ clavigero, terreni simul, & cælestis Imperii jura commisit. Et Bonifacius P. in extravagante cap. Unam Sanctam, de Majoritate & Obedientia: ex verbis illis Apostolorum, Luc. 22, 38. Ecce duo gladii hîc; & quod Christus non dixit, Nimis est: sed satis est, elicit, Pontificem duos gladios, spiritualem & politicum debere in terris exercere. Verùm nugatoria nimis hæc est assertio, ab ipsis quoque sanioribus Pontificiis explosa, quippe qui probè animadverterunt. 1. Nuspiam Apostolicis claves regnorum hujus seculi, sed tantùm claves regni cælorum esse à Christo datas. 2. Apostolos, & sic Petrum quoque Imperii & Jurisdictionis temporalis potestatem, neque ex successione hæreditaria, neque electionis titulo, neque jure belli, neque dono speciali unquàm obtinuisse; neq; in successores Pontifices propagare potuisse, secundum verissimam illam, hoc quidem in negotio regulam: Quod quis non habet, non potest transferre in alium. 3. Ab exaltatione & dominio humanæ Christi naturæ, ad Pontificem Romanum non valere consequentiam: proptereà quòd nulli Angelorum, nedum hominum dictum unquàm fuit: Sede à dextris meis. Hebr. 1, 13. 4. Ridiculam esse consequentiam ex duobus Apostolorum gladiis petitam, præsertim cùm Servator statim usum externi gladii Petro, & reliquis Apostolis interdixerit, Matth. 26, 25. Ab hac ergò Veteri Theologia Pontificia licet discedat Esavvitica distinctio, tamen ea quoque nihil est aliud, quàm mera & inanis ἀδολεσχία sive principii petitio. Pontifici enim Romano indirectè competere potestatem summam in temporalibus, pro certo & indubitato sumit, quod tamen est incertissimum, maximéq; controversum: propterea quòd sic ipsis docentibus Scripturis neque directè, neque indirectè ulli homini, sive individuo, sive sit Apostolus, sive Pontifex, sive Episcopus, competit utraque jurisdictio, sive potestas Ecclesiastica, & temporalis: quicunque etiam diversitatis respectus aut fucus adhibeatur.

Altera distinctio, quâ Bellarminus lectori fucum facere conatur, itidem nugatur, petitque principium, ut quando contendit, Potestatem secularem esse subordinatam potestati Ecclesiasticæ, ita ut Pontifex Romanus, non quidem ut Pontifex, sed ut Spiritualis Monarcha habeat summam potestatem etiam in temporalibus. Hoc ipsum enim est κρινόμενον, quod ipse pro certo sumit. Et jam suprà ex Scripturis demonstratum, neque in Pontificem, neque in Episcopum quenquam, non tantum quatenus est Pontifex, aut Episcopus; sed nullo prorsus modo aut respectu competere secularis potestatis administrationem: neque ullum sub Sole esse ordinem, quo sub ratione potestatis, Jurisdictio secularis, Ecclesiasticæ sit subordinata. Quamdiu ergò subordinationem hanc, & quidem ratione potestatis in temporalibus, non sufficienter probat, tamdiu agit Sophistam, & inanem verborum strepitum, non res ipsas profert.

Qualis inanis prorsus verborum strepitus, & nugacissima nugatio est, quando eod. cap. 6. libri 5. de Pont. scribit: Non potest Papa, ut Papa, ordinarie temporales Principes deponere, etiam justa de causâ, eo modo, quo deponit Episcopos, id est, tanquam Ordinarius Judex: tamen potest mutare regna, & uni auferre, atque alteri conferre, tanquam summus Princeps spiritualis: si id necessarium sit ad animarum salutem. Sic quantum ad Leges, non potest Papa, ut Papa, ordinarie condere legem civilem, vel confirmare, aut infirmare leges Principum, quia non est ipse Princeps Ecclesiæ politicus: tamen potest omnia illa facere, si aliqua Lex civilis sit necessaria ad animarum salutem, & tamen Reges eam non velint condere: aut si alia sit noxia animarum saluti, & tamen Reges eam non velint abrogare. Sic quantum ad judicia, non potest Papa, ut Papa, ordinariè judicare de rebus temporalibus: At nihilominus in casu, quo id animarum saluti necessarium est, potest Pontifex assumere etiam temporalia judicia, quando nimirum non est ullus, qui possit judicare: ut cum duo reges supremi contendunt, vel quando qui possunt, & debent judicare, non volunt sententiam ferre. Hactenus Bellarminus.

Lerna hæc est & sentina omnium malorum & confusionum, in Ecclesiâ & Politiâ unquam exortarum. Si enim quæras, Cur Papa potestatem dispensandi in pœnis temporalibus sibi sumserit, ita ut ab hac dispensatione non fuerit exceptus incestus, non adulterium, non homicidium, non parricidium, non Simonia, non veneficium, non bestialitas, non perjurium, non similia scelera & flagitia? Respondebit Elavvita: Quia Pontifex est spiritualis Monarcha, & habet sibi subjectam potestatem temporalem, ac proptereà potest infirmare leges civiles Principum, quia sic videturnecessarium ad animarum salutem. Sic si quæras: Quo jure Pontifex Romanus violentis excommunicationibus, proscriptionibus, armis & bellis tantoperè sævierit in Imperatores, Reges, Principes, & potestates quasvis seculares? Quo item jure eosdem imperio regnis, principatibus exuerit, & alios iisdem donârit? Respondebit Esavvita: quia est summus Princeps spiritualis: quia potestas temporalis omnis huic est subjecta, quia sic necessarium visum fuit ad animarum salutem.

Summatim loquendo, quicquid Curiæ Romanæ non arridet, quicquid Idolomaniam ejus non exosculatur & approbat: quicquid denique ullo pacto legibus & traditionibus Pontificiis, etiam in secularibus repugnat, illud Papa, tanquam Spiritualis Monarchiæ repugnans, & animarum saluti adversum, pro nutu & arbitrio suo mutat, abrogat, excommunicat, proscribit, & vi, armísque sibi vindicandum esse censet. Et hic fuit murus ille aheneus, qui regnum Pontificium superioribus seculis sustinuit & conservavit: & in quo denuò erigendo, strenuè hodieque, sed frustrà (DEI beneficio) laborat Pontifex cum universa cohorte Pontificia.

Et sanè ut hanc quasi arcem sive acropolin dominatus Pontificii funditus subruamus, & evertamus: initiò firmis & immotis argumentis eam oppugnabimus: postmodùm verò arma, quibus Bellarminus pro defendendâ suâ sententiâ pugnat, accuratè excutiemus & conteremus.

Quoad prius: Opponimus initiò Bellarmino hoc Dilemma: quo Bellarminus ipse lib. 5. de Pont. Rom. cap. 3. pag. 1056. lit. B. Canonistarum opinionem, contendentium, Reges & Imperatores, quicquid habent potestatis sive summam executionis, à Papa habere scitè refutat, in hunc modum; Aut potest Papa aliquo modo, sive directè, sive indirectè, sive ut Papa,sive ut summus Princeps Spiritualis, sive ut ordinarius, sive extraordinarius judex, mutare regna, & uni auferre, atque alteri conferre: aut non potest: Si potest: Ergò est aliquo modo, sive directo, sive indirecto, sive ordinario, sive extraordinario, major & potentior ipso DEO, quia quod DEUS Imperatori, Regibus & Principibus concessit, ipse aufert, & in alium confert: id quod prodigiose absurdum. Siquidem minor aut æqualis qui est, non potest mutare, aut auferre, quòd à majore vel æquali est concessum. Quid quòd legatus etiam sive vicarius alicujus, sine expresso Domini mandato, plus sibi autoritatis, potestatisq́; sumere non debet, quàm voluntas Domini permittit. Si non potest: Ergò falsum, & Scripturis adversum, quod Esavvita dicit,Papam habere summam potestatem indirectè disponendi de rebus temporalibus Christianorum, mutandi regna, abrogandi leges imperatorias, & deponendi de solio Imperatores & Reges, aliosq́; in ipsorum locum substituendi.

Alterum Argumentum, quod Bellarmine hoc loco opponimus, rursum ipsius verbis ex eodem libro, & capire informamus, in hunc modum? Sires ita se haberet, prout definit Bellarminus, utique id constaret vel ex Scripturis,vel ex Apostolorum indubitata traditione.atqui ex Scripturu plus non licet colligere, quàm datas Pontifici claves regni cælorum: de clavibus regni terrarum nulla mentio fit: Sic traditionem nullam Apostolicam adversarii proferunt. Ergo res ita se non habet, prout definit Bellarminus.Neque est,ut excipiat ille nulla hic vel Scripturarum, vel Apostolorum traditione opus esse, Siquidem Jurisdictio in temporalibus competat Papæ tan­ tùm indirectè, & per quandam quasi consequentiam, tanquam summœ Principi spirituali, & supremo animarum Pastori. Nam hujus quoque assertionis probationem petimus dari, vel ex Scripturis, vel ex certâ ac indubitatâ Apostolorum traditione. Et si maxime ex nostrâ etiam parte in confesso efset, Papam esse supremum, & universalem omnium Christianorum pastorem: id quod tamen negamus: nullum tamen foret consequens, Curæ illius pastoralis adjunctum necessarium & inseparabile esse, potestatem & dominium in temporalibus Christianorum rebus & negotiis: aliâs certè Servator & Apostoli tàm alto silentio id non involvissent.

Tertiò opponimus Bellarmino axioma illud, tàm in Politicis, quàm sacris longè verissimum: Quicquid directè à DEO alicui non est permissum: illud nec indirectè, sive per ali quam consequentiam aut dependentiam fieri aut su scipi vel potest, vel debet. Cujus axiomatisea est ratio, quam Esavvitąrum nullus ullo ar­ tificio infringet: Nempe: Quicquid à DEO est prohibitum: illud alio jure aut respectu non potest esse permissum. Ergò si Papa, ut Papa, nullam jurisdictionem temporalem inChristianos directè,& jure divino habet:id quod Bellarminus vel invitus fateri cogitur: utique nec indirectè, nec ullo jure alio eam obtinebit, nisi jus humanum divino derogate, aut præjudicare quicquam posse, statuere velit Esavvita: id quod manifestè impium & blasphemum.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Proper Quasi-affection of the Political Magistracy: That the Political and Ecclesiastical are two separate powers (continued)

Fourthly, we oppose to Bellarmine's opinion the practice of the Christian Church, which, ever since the times of the Apostles, over the course of several centuries, had Emperors who were Christians in name and profession, but heretics in religion, cruel in their manner of ruling, and impious in life and morals; as is evident from the history of Constantine, Julian, Valens, Valentinian the Younger, Anastasius, Heraclius, and others. Yet no Roman Pontiff dared to take away their kingdoms, or prescribe laws to them, or summon them to a tribunal. Either, therefore, the Roman Pontiffs then judged that that supreme care of souls did not pertain to them in temporal matters either: or they did not perform their duty. But the Jesuits will not concede this latter point, unless they wish to affirm at the same time that, over the course of so many centuries, various Vicars of Christ and successors of St. Peter, sitting even in the very chair, lacked the Holy Spirit as their guide and governor: and consequently, that the Catholic Church then had a head that was languid, slothful, idle, and useless. Therefore, the former point will be established, namely, that the Pontiffs of those centuries, content with Ecclesiastical jurisdiction, abstained simply and in all respects from temporal dominion, as from a duty and profession alien to them.

The Romanists object: 1. That those were times in which the Pontiffs ought to have been more prepared to undergo martyrdom than to exercise temporal jurisdiction. 2. That it could not have been resisted against those heretics and tyrants then without detriment to the people. But both reasons are worthless, and the former is clearly unworthy of a Christian man, let alone a successor of Peter and a pastor of souls. For has the state of the Church so changed that in our times and the times and centuries of our fathers, the Bishops and prelates of the Roman Church ought to exercise warfare and external dominion over Christians rather than undergo martyrdom? Will the Pontiff thus dare to lie that he is the vicar of Christ and the successor of Peter, and flee from the cross of the former and the sword of the latter? Where then is the Savior's [word], Matt. 10:24-25? The disciple is not above his master, nor the servant above his lord: It is enough for the disciple that he be as his master: and the servant, as his lord. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more them of his household? And verse 38: He that taketh not his cross, and followeth after me, is not worthy of me. Where is that of Peter, ch. 4:13: In that you are partakers of Christ's sufferings, rejoice, that when his glory shall be revealed, you may be glad also with exceeding joy. And verse 17: The time is come that judgment must begin at the house of GOD.

The latter reason, which Bellarmine exaggerates, lib. 5 de Rom. Pont. cap. 7, is manifestly false: for the vigor and power of the Roman Church and the Christian world was as great in the time of those Emperors as it was scarcely ever afterwards: so that it could easily have corrected their vices and exercised dominion, if only the Church had believed this to be its duty, or Christians had believed this to be permitted to it. What is more, histories do not even reveal any will or attempt of the Pontiff in this regard.

I allow that to lie hidden, which the Popes, having no regard for the people, but having exposed many myriads of men to miserable death for the sake of establishing their own impious dominion, have sufficiently betrayed the vanity of this latter reasoning by the very fact. Let William Barclay, J.C., be consulted on this matter in his book on the power of the Pope, chapters 7, 8, 9, 10.

Fifthly and lastly: Every distinction which establishes only a different mode of acquiring some thing, does not remove the thing itself. But the Jesuitical distinction between direct and indirect [jurisdiction] establishes at least a diversity of modes by which jurisdiction in temporal matters can be acquired. Therefore, this distinction does not remove, but establishes; does not limit, but confirms; does not diminish, but increases the jurisdiction of the Pope in temporal matters, considered in itself and by reason of lordship: so that Christian Kings and Princes may appear to be vassals and clients of the Roman Pope: which I prove from the words of Bellarmine thus: The Supreme Pontiff, not indeed as Pope, but as supreme spiritual Prince, can take away a kingdom from someone and confer it upon another, if it be necessary for the salvation of souls. Now, indeed, to pass judgment on this very thing, and to decide whether such a change of kingdoms is necessary for the salvation of souls, pertains to the Pope alone, and pertains in such a way that no one may dare either to call his judgment into doubt or to dispute about it; as the Canon Law holds, Can. Patet: and Can. aliorum: distinct. 9. q. 3. Therefore, it will be placed in the nod and most free will of the Pope to take away a kingdom from whom he wishes, and to confer it upon whom he wishes. Whence it is most manifestly clear that Bellarmine, with his conscience protesting, has been crafty in the present business. For while he wishes to appear to refute the Canonists, who contend that the Pope received from Christ the jurisdiction to be exercised directly over temporal matters in the whole world: he casts only a γλαύκωμα (cataract) before the reader with the mists of his distinctions, and in truth, he says the same thing as the Canonists: that is, he constitutes Kings and Princes as vassals and clients of the Roman Pope, as the supreme and greatest Lord in this age. How impious this is, how contrary to the Scriptures, how contrary to the practice of the ancient Roman Church, we confirm with these four arguments.

I. Such as Christ was in these lands, not indeed by reason of his person, but by reason of his office: such the Roman Pontiff ought to be, if indeed he wishes to be the vicar of Christ, as he boasts himself to be. But Christ not only did not constitute himself a judge of secular Princes, even in the most iniquitous causes, but he subjected himself, so that he allowed himself to be judged by Pilate. Therefore, neither should the Roman Pontiff vaunt himself as superior to secular Princes. The assumption is clear from the fact that Christ not only willingly subjected himself to Pilate to be condemned even to death, so that he might become a victim for the sins of the whole world: but he also asserted in express words that this power and superiority of Pilate was from GOD himself: saying, 'You would have no power against me, unless it had been given to you from above': John 19:11.

II. The Apostle Paul not only appealed himself to Caesar, as a superior judge: Acts 25:10 & 11, but he also laid down this general law, that 'Every soul be subject to the higher powers.' Romans 13:1. Therefore Peter also, and consequently, all his successors (arguing from the Jesuitical hypothesis) the Roman Pontiffs, ought to acknowledge Caesar as a superior judge in temporal matters.

The reason for the consequence is by far the most evident. For 1. no reason can be given from the whole of Scripture which could exempt Peter and his successors from that subjection which Paul established that he owed to the political magistrate. 2. Peter himself laid down this universal authentic [law], to be observed equally by all Christians, as much Clerics as Laics or political persons. 'Be subject to every human ordinance for the LORD'S sake: whether to the King, as the ὑπερέχοντι (superior), or as excelling, or to governors, as sent by him, etc.' 1 Pet. 2:13 & 14. Nor does that fictitious distinction between a heathen and a Christian magistrate have any place here: as if Clerics and Roman Pontiffs ought to have been subject only to the former, but not to the latter, just as Albert Pighius raved in book 5 of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 7. For if heathen magistrates could be, nay, truly were, legitimate judges of the Apostles: much more certainly does this befit Christian Magistrates. For religion does not remove Republics, much less the obedience and subjection owed to any Magistrate in secular matters. It is added that the heathen Magistrate obtained this right, not from gentilism: but from the ordination of GOD, as the Apostle teaches, Romans 13:1. 'There is no power, except from GOD': Therefore this subjection owed to the magistrate depends not on religion, but on the thing itself.

III. If in the Old Testament the Pontiffs were subject to secular kings not only in secular matters, but also if they performed their office badly in the discharge of their Ecclesiastical duty: much more is this to be observed in the New. But the former is true, therefore the latter also. The major is clear from the fact that King Solomon deposed the priest Abiathar, and in his place appointed Zadok; because of the conspiracy entered into with Adonijah and Joab. 1 Kings 1:7 & chapter 2:27 & 35. The reason for the consequence, however, is this, that in the Old Testament there was one high priest appointed by GOD: but in the New, it is not so, but all, however much they are Ecclesiastical, are placed over the Church on an equal condition.

IV. Histories testify that the Roman Emperors, and indeed not those heathen ones, but Christian ones, very often passed judgment on removing Pontiffs from office, on account of vices and secular excesses more than ecclesiastics. Therefore, the power of judging in temporal matters belongs not to the Roman Pontiff but to the Emperor. The antecedent is evident first from the fact that the Emperor Constantine sent Pope Liberius into exile and later recalled him from exile, as being of one mind with the Arians, as Platina testifies in the life of Liberius: that the Emperor Justinian deposed Pope Silverius, who wished to betray the city of Rome to the enemy Goths, and relegated him to the island of Pontia: that King Theodoric cast Pope John I into prison, where he perished from filth, thirst, and starvation: that Otto I deposed John XII (according to Platina, XIII) on account of the defilement of his life and morals, and substituted Leo VIII in his place: that Henry II, the Emperor, as Platina relates, cast Pope Gregory VI from the Pontifical see as a most foul monster, and substituted Clement II.

Furthermore, the truth of the antecedent is also clear from the fact that the Roman Pontiffs themselves submitted to Emperors, as their superiors and Lords, to be judged, to such an extent that the confirmation of an elected Pope depended upon the confirmation of the Emperor, and the latter could render it void: as one may read in Gratian, caus. 2, q. 7, can. Si quis, and dist. 63, c. Adrianus. Hence Pope Leo IV sought judges from the Emperor Louis and promised that he would comply with their sentences: dist. 63, cap. In the Synod: Where one may read these words of the Pontiff: I, Leo, Bishop, servant of the servants of GOD, with the whole clergy and the Roman people, constitute, confirm, corroborate, and by our apostolic authority grant and bestow upon Lord Otto I, King of the Teutons, and his successors of this kingdom of Italy in perpetuity, the power of electing a successor and of ordaining the Pontiff of the supreme Apostolic see, and through this, that archbishops or bishops should receive investiture and consecration from him, whence they ought: except for those whom the Emperor has granted to Pontiffs and archbishops: and that no one henceforth, of whatever dignity or religious standing, shall have the power of electing a patrician or the Pontiff of the supreme Apostolic see, or of ordaining any bishop, without the consent of the Emperor himself (which, however, should be done without any money), and that he himself be patrician and King. But if any bishop is elected by the clergy and people, unless he is approved and invested by the aforementioned King, he shall not be consecrated. If anyone should attempt anything against this rule and Apostolic authority, we decree that he shall be subject to excommunication, and unless he repents, he shall be punished by irrevocable exile or suffer the ultimate penalties.

Latin:

Quartò opponimus sententiæ Bellarmini praxin Ecclesiæ Christianæ, quæ jam inde ab Apostolorum temporibus, aliquot seculorum decursu habuit Imperatores, nomine quidem, & professione Christianos, sed religione hæreticos, imperandi ratione crudeles, vita & moribus impios; uti patet ex historiâ Constantini, Juliani, Valentis, Valentiniani junioris, Anastasii, Heraclii, & aliorum. Quibus tamen nullus Pontificum Romanorum, vel regna adimere, vel leges præscribere, vel sub tribunal vocare ausus fuit. Aut ergò Pontifices Romani tùm supremam illam animarum curam etiam in temporalibus sibi non competere arbitrati sunt: aut officio suo non sunt functi. Atqui posterius hoc non concedent Esavvitæ, nisi affirmare simul velint, tot seculorum decursu, varios Christi, & successores D. Petri, in ipsâ etiam cathedra sedentes, Spiritu Sancto Rectore ac gubernatore caruisse: & per consequens, Ecclesiam Catholicąm tùm habuisse caput languidum, ignavum, otiosum, inutile. Ergò ratum erit illud prius, nempe illorum seculorum Pontifices, Ecclesiasticâ Jurisdictione contentos, à temporali dominio, tanquàm à munere & professione sua alieno simpliciter, & per omnia abstinuisse:

Excipiunt Romanenses. 1. Ea tunc fuisse tempora, quibus ad martyrium potiùs subeundum, quam ad temporalem exercendam jurisdictionem, Pontifices paratiores esse deberent. 2. Sine populi detrimento tùm hæreticis, & tyrannis istis resisti non potuisse. Sed utraque ratio est ficulnea, & prior quidem homine Christiano, nedùm successore Petri, & pastore animarum planè indigna. Annè enim itą Ecclesiæ status est mutatus, ut nostris, & Patrum nostrorum temporibus atque seculis, Episcopi & præsules Ecclesiæ Romanæ, militjam magis, atque externum dominium in Christianos exercere, quàm Martyrium subire debeant? Siccinè vicarium Christi, & successorem Petri se ampliùs Pontifex mentiri, & illius crucem, hujus autem gladium defugere audebit? Ubi ergò Servatoris, Matth: 10.24. 25. Non est discipulus super magistrum, nec servus super dominum suum: Sufficit discipulo, ut sit sicut magister ejus: & servo, sicut dominus ejus. Si Patrem familias vocarunt Beelzebub, quantò magis domesticos ejus? Et versu 38. Qui non accipit crucem suam, & sequitur me, non est me dignus. Ubi illud Petri, cap. 4. 13. In eo, quòd consortes estis afflictionum Christi, gaudete, ut & cum patefiet ejus gloria, gaudeatis exultantes. Et versu 17. Tempus est, ut incipiat judicium à domo DEI.

Posterior ratio, quam Bellarminus exaggerat, lib. 5. de Rom. Pont. cap. 7. manifestè falsa est: Romanæ enim Ecclesiæ, & orbis Christiani vigor, & potentia tanta fuit tempore illorum Imperatorum, quanta vix postea unquam: ut facilè illorum vitia corrigere, & dominatum exercere potuisset, si modò Ecclesia hoc sui esse muneris, vel Christiani hoc sibi permissum esse credidissent. Quid, quòd ne quidem de voluntate, aut conatu aliquo Pontificis hac in parte aliquid historiæ produnt.

Latêre patior id, quod Pontifices nullâ populi habitâ curâ, sed multis hominum myriadibus, pro stabiliendo impio suo dominatu, neci miserabili expositis, vanitatem posterioris hujus rationis ipso facto satis prodiderunt. Videatur autem hac de re Guilielmus Barclaius JC. libro de potestate Papæ. cap. 7. 8. 9. 10.

Quintò & postremò: Omnis distinctio, quæ modum tantùm rei alicujus acquirendæ alium, atq; alium constituit, non tollit rem ipsam. Atqui distinctio Efavistica inter directam, & indirectam, constituit saltem diversitatem modorum, per quos Jurisdictio in temporalibus acquiri possit. Ergò distinctio hæc, Jurisdictionem Pontificis in temporalibus in se & ratione dominii consideratam, non tollit, sed constituit: non limitat, sed confirmat: non minuit, sed auget: ita ut Reges & Principes Christiani, videri possint esse vasalli, & clientes Pontificis Romani: id quod ex verbis Bellarmini sic evinco: Summus Pontifex, non quidem ut Papa, sed ut summus Princeps spiritualis, potest alicui regnum auferre, & alteri conferre, si id necessarium sit ad animarum salutem. Jam verò de hoc ipso ferre judicium, & decernere, utrum talis regnorum mutatio sit necessaria ad animarum salutem, pertinet ad solum Pontificem, & ita quidem pertinet, ut ejus judicium vel in dubium vocare, vel de eo disputare nemo ausit; uti habet Jus Canonicum, Can. Patet: & Can, aliorum: distinct. 9. q. 3. Ergò in nutu & arbitrio liberrimo Pontificis erit positum, auferre regnum, cui velit, & alteri conferre cui velit. Unde manifestissimè patet, Bellarminum, reclamante conscientiâ in præsenti negotio versutum esse. Nam dum videri vult Canonistas refutare, qui Papam directè Jurisdictionem temporalem in toto terrarum orbe exercendam à Christo accepisse contendunt: ille objectis distinctionum nebulis Lectori tantùm γλαύκωμα objicit, & in rei veritate, idem dicit, quod Canonistæ: hoc est Reges & Principes constituit vasallos, & Clientes Pontificis Romani, tanquàm Domini in hoc seculo supremi & maximi. Quòd quàm impium, quàm Scripturis adversum, quàm praxi Veteri Ecclesiæ Romanæ contrarium sit, quatuor his argumentis confirmamus.

I. Qualis fuit Christus in his terris, non quidem ratione personæ, sed ratione officii: talem oportet Pontificem Romanum esse, si modò, qualem se gloriatur, Christi vicarius esse velit. Atqui Christus non modò se non judicem Principum secularium, etiam in causis iniquissimis, constituit, sed se ex subjecit, itaut à Pilato se judicari permiserit. Ergò nec Pontifex Romanus superiorem se Principibus secularibus venditare debet. Assumptio patet indè, quòd Christus non modò ut victima fieret pro peccatis totius mundi lubens se ad mortem usque condemnandum Pilato subjecit: sed & hanc Pilati potestatem, & superioritatem à DEO ipso esse, disertis verbis asseruit: Non haberes, inquiens, potestatem adversus me ullam, nisi hoc datum tibi esset desupet: Johan. 19, 11.

II. Apostolus Paulus non modò ipse ad Cæsarem, tanquam judicem superiorem appellavit: Actor. 25,10. & 11. sed & generalem hanc tulit legem, ut Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit. Roman. 13. 1. Ergò Petrus quoque, & per consequens, Omnes ipsius successores (ex hypothesi Esavvitica arguendo) Pontifices Romani, Cæsarem, ut superiorem judicem, in temporalibus agnoscere debent.

Ratio Consequentiæ militat longè evidentissima. Nam 1. nulla ex universâ Scriptura dari potest ratio, quæ Petrum, & successores ejus subjectione eâ eximere possit, quam Paulus magistratui politico se debere statuit. 2. Petrus ipse hanc universalem tulit authenticam, omnibus Christianis, tàm Clericis, quâm Laicis sive Politicis ex æquo observandam. Subjecti estote humanæ ordinationi propter DOMINUM: sive Regi, tanquam ὑπερέχοντι superiori, sive præcellenti, sive ducibus, tanquam ab eo missis&c. 1 Pet. 2, 13 & 14. Neque locum hîc habet fictitia illa distinctio inter Magistratum Ethnicum & Christianum: quasi illis tantùm, non verò his subjecti esse debuerint Clerici ac Pontifices Romani, quemadmodum Albertus Pighius deliravit lib. 5 hierarch. Ecclesiast. cap 7. Nam si Ethnici magistratus potuerunt esse, imò verè fuerunt judices legitimi Apostolorum: multò certè magis hoc competit Magistratibus Christianis. Religio enim non tollit Respublicas, nedum obedientiam, & subjectionem, Magistratui cuilibet in secularibus debitam. Accedit, quod Ethnicus Magistratus hoc jus obtinuit, non ex gentilismo: sed ex DEI ordinatione, sic docente Apostolo, Roman. 13. 1. Non est potestas, nisi à DEO: Ergò Subjectio hæc magistratui debita dependet non à religione, sed ex re ipsâ.

III. Si in Veteri Testamento Pontifices non in secularibus modò: sed & si in obeundo munere Ecclesiastico malè suo functi sunt officio, subjecti fuerunt regibus secularibus: multò magis in Novo id observandum. A' qui prius verum, Ergò & posterius. Major patet inde, quòd Salomon Rex deposuit Sacerdotem Abiathar, inque locum ejus constituit Sadochum; propter conspirationem initam cum Adonia & Joabo. 1. Reg. 1, 7. & cap. 2, 27. & 35. Ratio autem consecutionis est hæc, quòd in Vetere Testamento unus fuit summus Pontifex á DEO constitutus: in Novo autem non item, sed omnes quantumvis Ecclesiastici, æquali conditione Ecclesiæ præfecti.

IV. Testantur historiæ, Imperatores Romanos, & quidem non Ethnicos illos, sed Christianos, sæpiusculè sententiam tulisse de Pontificibus ab officio removendis, ob vitia & excessus seculares magis, quàm Ecclesiasticos. Ergò non Pontifici Romano sed imperatori competit potestas judicandi de rebus temporalibus. Antecedens patet primùm inde, quòd Constantiuus Imp. Liberium Pontificem in exilium misit, eundemque postmodùm ab exilio revocavit, tanquam Arianis ὁμόψηφον, teste Platina in vitâ Liberij: quòd Justinianus Imp. Silverium Pontificem, volentem urbem Romam Gotthis hostibus prodere, Pontificatu dejecit, inque insulam Pontiam relegavit: quòd Theodoricus Rex, Johannem I. Pontificem in carcerem conjecit, ubi pedore, siti, & inediâ periit: quòd Ottho I. Johannem XII. (secundum Platinam XIII.) ob vitæ, morumq́; confcelerationem deposuit, inque ejus locum Leonem VIII. substituit: quòd Henricus II. Imp. referente Platinâ, Gregorium VI. Pontificem, tanquàm teterrimum monstrum, sede Pontificiali excussit, & Clementem II. substituit.

Deinde Antecedentis veritas liquet etiam hinc, quòd Pontifices Romani ipsi Imperatoribus, tanquam superioribus & Dominis suis sese subjecerunt judicandos, itaquidem, ut confirmatio electi Papæ penderet à Confirmatione Imperatoris, & hic eam irritam facere posset: ut legere licet apud Gratianum, caus. 2. q. 7. can. Si quis, & dist. 63. c. Adrianus. Hinc Leo IV. Pontifex petiit à Ludovico Imp. Judices, & eorum sententiæ se obtemperaturum compromittit: dist. 63. cap. In Synodo: Ubi hæc Pontificis verba legere licet: Ego Leo, Episcopus, servus servorum DEI, cum toto clero, ac Romano populo constituimus, & confirmamus, & corroboramus, & per nostram apostolicam autoritatem concedimus atque largimur Domino Otthoni primo regi Teutonicorum, ejusq; successoribq hujus regni Italiæ in perpetuum, facultatem eligendi successorem, atque summæ sedis Apostolicæ, Pontificem ordinandi, ac per hoc archiepiscopos, seu episcopos, ut ipsi ab eo investituram accipiant, & consecrationem, unde debent: exceptis his, quos Imperator Pontificibus, & ar chiepiscopis concessit: & ut nemo deinceps, cujusque dignitatis vel religiositatis eligendi vel patricium, vel Pontificem summæ sedis Apostolicæ, aut quemcunq; episcopum ordinandi habeat facultatem, absque consensu ipsius Imperatoris, (quod tamen fiat absque omni pecunia) & ut ipse sit patritius, & Rex. Quod si à clero & populo quis eligatur episcopus, nisi à suprà dicto Rege laudetur, & investiatur, non consecretur. Si quis contra hanc regulam, & Apostolicam autoritatem aliquid moliatur, hunc excommu nicationi subjacere decernimus, & nisi resipuerit, irrevocabili exilio puniri, vel ultimis suppliciis afficit.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Proper Quasi-affection of the Political Magistracy: That the Political and Ecclesiastical are two separate powers (continued)

However, these things being thus settled, one thing remains in this contest: by what arguments Bellarmine strives to maintain his thesis. Let us now examine this in the third place. Indeed, all the things which he brings forward and argues in this part can be referred to these two hypotheses: THE PRIOR is: That the Pope has temporal power or jurisdiction indirectly. THE LATTER: That it does not conflict with the word of GOD for one man to be an Ecclesiastical and Political Prince at the same time.

He confirms the prior hypothesis at the beginning with this argument: Civil power is subject to spiritual power when both parts are of the same Christian Republic. Therefore, the spiritual Prince can command temporal princes and dispose of temporal matters in order to a spiritual good. For every superior can command his inferior.

He wishes to prove the antecedent with three reasons.

1. Because the temporal end is subordinated to the spiritual end, since temporal happiness is not absolutely the ultimate end, and therefore it ought to be referred to eternal happiness: Now, faculties are subordinated just as ends are subordinated, as Aristotle testifies, lib. 1, Ethic. cap. 1.

2. Because Kings and Pontiffs, Clerics and Laity, do not make two Republics, but one: that is, one Church.

3. Because if temporal administration hinders the spiritual good, in the judgment of all, the temporal Prince is bound to change that mode of administration, even with the detriment of the temporal good. Therefore, this very thing is a sign that temporal power is subject to spiritual, lib. 5, de Roman. Pontif. cap. 7.

I ANSWER: The antecedent of the argument suffers from the fallacy ἀπὸ τõ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. For civil power is subject to spiritual power not simply, but only in a certain respect, namely regarding the objects of spiritual matters: and regarding ecclesiastical government, which is exercised in spiritual matters not by any external jurisdiction, which might consist of war and arms: but by the sword of the Holy Spirit, with all gentleness and meekness, by admonishing, correcting, informing, as long as some hope of amendment remains: but by excommunicating, when the Holy Spirit is contumaciously resisted. Where this at the same time deserves observation, that civil power is indeed subject to the exercise of this spiritual power, as it has now been defined, but not insofar as it is administered by ministers: but insofar as it is the power of GOD: to whom all things are subject in heaven and on earth: and insofar as GOD himself through the voice of the Church keeps even Kings and Princes in the duty of piety: so indeed, that civil power is subject to spiritual power primarily to GOD: but secondarily to the Church κατ' ἄλλο καὶ κατά τι: since the Church in this part does not obtain authoritative power, or ἀνυπεύθυνον: but only ministerial, which for so long binds to obedience all citizens of the Church, insofar as it performs the embassy of GOD rightly, and according to the express Word of GOD: in exactly the same way that a herald, or some envoy sent by an Emperor, mandates or commands something to the Princes or Estates of the Empire, not by his own authority, but by another's, and not to his own, but to another's command. Where, however, no one is so alienated from all reason as to conclude from that, that the Princes and Estates of the Empire are subject to that herald or envoy. Thus, therefore, that Esauvitic axiom: Every superior can command his inferior; is true with respect to GOD himself, but not with respect to the Pontiff or the Church, which, even in spiritual matters, disposes all things not by its own authority, but by GOD's.

Next, the Esauvitic consequent is too narrow, while it is an inference for establishing the dominion of the Roman Pontiff alone in temporal matters: a thing which, however, the reason and nature of the Antecedent does not allow: For not only the Pontiff exercises spiritual power, but any pastor and minister of the Church, to whom the power of teaching, administering the Sacraments, and the use of the keys is granted just as it is to the Pontiff. Therefore, it would follow from the Esauvitic Antecedent that every Pastor or minister of the Church has jurisdiction in disposing of temporal matters.

Thirdly, that hypothesis upon which the Esauvita first built this argument is simply false; namely, that civil power is subject to spiritual power when both parts are of the same Christian Republic. For this communion does not confuse jurisdictions; but leaves to each estate its own office intact, and occupied about its own proper object: so that in the Christian Republic, political or secular persons are subject to Ecclesiastical persons (but in a qualified sense, as has already been shown) in spiritual matters: Again, Ecclesiastical persons are subject to secular ones in temporal affairs. Each, therefore, recognizes and venerates the other in its own order and proper function: and each exercises its own function according to its own laws: and by legitimate means: the Ecclesiastical, indeed, by spiritual weapons: the Political, however, by external and corporal weapons.

Finally, regarding a fuller refutation of this argument, it must also be observed that in this dispute one must accurately distinguish between spiritual and Ecclesiastical power. For although spiritual power is also and is called Ecclesiastical, insofar as it is administered in the Church and by Ecclesiastical persons: yet, speaking properly, spiritual power is only that which consists in the preaching of the Word, in the dispensation of the Sacraments, in the use of the keys: which belongs equally to all legitimately called ministers of the Church: so that it has no privilege or prerogative, or

the Pontiff, or the Bishop, or any other Doctor or Prelate of the Church. Ecclesiastical power, however, speaking properly, is that which exercises some external Jurisdiction in matters concerning the state and convenience of the Church, as well as the external discipline of the hearers: and it is occupied partly with Ecclesiastical ceremonies and rites to be performed aptly and decently: partly with matrimonial causes and judgments: partly with the privileges and immunities of Ecclesiastical persons: and finally, partly with the calling and dismissal of Ministers of the Church. Therefore, as far as spiritual power is concerned, it belongs entirely to those who legitimately preside over the Ecclesiastical Ministry: and by reason of the matter about which it is concerned, and the end which it uniquely regards, it is more excellent than all temporal power, so that the latter is bound to obey the former entirely.

As for Ecclesiastical power, however, it belongs to the whole Church, and thus to all three hierarchical orders: Ecclesiastical, Political, and Oecumenical. Whence the Electors, Princes, and Evangelical estates generally exercise this power through Ecclesiastical Consistories, which consist of Ecclesiastical and Political persons. And here, Ecclesiastical persons are bound to obey the Political just as the Political are bound to obey the Ecclesiastical, that is: both must administer justice and pronounce sentence according to Ecclesiastical laws and constitutions. When, therefore, the Roman Pontiff also seizes and arrogates this right to himself alone, what does he do other than, as an ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος (meddler in others' affairs), invade another's office and act the Tyrant in the Church.

But to respond likewise to the three Esauvitic reasons: The first is manifestly false: For temporal power, insofar as it is such and is so called, does not regard that ultimate end, namely eternal happiness, but only temporal happiness, the increase of the public good, and the honesty and tranquility of life: as the Apostle teaches, 1 Tim. 2:2, who therefore commands to pray for Kings, and all who are in high positions, that under their rule we may lead a tranquil and peaceful life, in all piety and honesty. Therefore, this subordination of ends, by reason of both powers being exercised by one Pontiff and the Roman Church, expires completely. Next, although those who are established in the Magistracy do regard that ultimate end, namely eternal life: they do not, however, regard it insofar as they are Magistrates: but insofar as they are Christians: and therefore they constitute the end of their actions and Political counsels as only temporal, namely that which follows the action as an effect: not that which resides only in the intellect.

The second reason collapses by its own futility: For although the members in a body constitute one subject: it is nevertheless false that one depends upon the other: will the right arm therefore hang either from the arm, or from the left foot, or even from the right foot: or will the head hang from the belly and the lower abdomen. This error is therefore corrected in this manner: Just as individual and universal members in the human body coalesce through a certain excellent harmony and concord into one natural body: so in the mystical body of Christ, which is the Church, all its members ought to agree, of whatever dignity, or office, or condition they may be.
