Now, indeed, just as in the human body, the members do not perform their operations confusedly, but each one obtains and exercises its own peculiar action, distinct from the action of another member: So in the Church, let each member perform the duties proper to its profession: let politicians contain themselves within the limits of temporal affairs: but let ecclesiastics, content with spiritual offices, not go beyond their limits, nor in any way undertake the administration of temporal things. If this is done, then an excellent harmony and concord will intervene among all the members in turn.

It is expressed by the Word. How great, therefore, is the difference in temporal matters between the Emperor himself commanding or forbidding something: and a herald, or official, the interpreter of that command: just as great is the difference between GOD himself, instructing us about his will in the written word: and Spiritual or Ecclesiastical persons, as interpreters of the divine will: so that the Prince is bound to change a perverse mode of administering: not because of any Dominion of the Pope, which belongs to him in no way in temporal matters: but because of the obedience which, as a Christian, he is bound to render to GOD, as the supreme Emperor.

Latin:

Cæterùm his ita expeditis, unum illud hoc in certamine superest, ut quibusnam argumentis Bellarminus thesin suam obtinere studeat. Tertio jam loco dispiciamus. Possunt verò universa ea, quæ hac in parte profert, & disputat, ad duas hasce referri hypotheses: PRIOR est: Papam habere potestatem sive Jurisdictionem temporalem indirecte. POSTERIOR: Non pugnare cum verbo DEI, ut unus homo sit Princeps Ecclesiasticus & Politicus simul.

Priorem hypothesin initio hoc confirmat argumento: Potestas civilis subjecta est potestati spirituali, quando utraq; pars est ejusdem Reipub. Christianæ. Ergò potest Princeps spiritualis imperare principibus temporalibus, & disponere de temporalibus rebus in ordine ad bonum spirituale. Omnis n. superior imperare potest suo inferiori.

Antecedens tribus rationibus vult evincere.

1. Quia finis temporalis subordinatur fini spirituali, dùm nimirùm felicitas temporalis non est absolutè ultimus finis, & ideò referri debet in felicitatem æternam: Jam verò ita subordinantur facultates, uti subordinantur fines, teste Aristot. lib. 1. Ethic. cap. 1.

2. Quia Reges & Pontifices, Clerici & Laici, non faciunt duas Respublicas, sed unam: id est, unam Ecclesiam.

3. Quia si temporalis administratio impedit spirituale bonum, omnium judicio tenetur Princeps temporalis mutare illum modum administrandi, etiam cum detrimento temporalis boni. Ergò hoc ipsum est signum, temporalem potestatem esse subjectam spirituali, lib, 5. de Roman. Pontif. cap. 7.

RESPONDEO: Antecedens argumenti laborat Sophismate ἀπὸ τõ πῆ καὶ ἁπλῶς. Potestas enim civilis subjecta est potestati spirituali non simpliciter, sed tantùm secundum quid, nempè quoad objecta rerum spiritualium: & quoad regimen Ecclesiasticum, quod in spiritualibus exercetur non externâ aliquâ jurisdictione, quæ constet bello & armis: sed gladio Spiritus Sancti, cum omni lenitate, & mansuetudine, monendo, corrigendo, informando, quamdiu quidem spes aliqua emendationis supcrest: excommunicando verò, quando Spiritui Sancto contumaciter repugnatur. Ubi illud observationem simul meretur, Potestatis hujus spiritualis exercitio, prout illud jam definitum est, subjacere quidem potestatem civilem, sed non quatenus illa à ministris administratur: sed quatenus illa DEI est potestas: cui omnia subjacent in cælis, & in terra: & quatenus DEUS ipse per vocem Ecclesiæ, etiam Reges & Principes in officio pietatis continet: ita quidem, ut DEO πρώτως: Ecclesiæ verò δευτέρως κατ' ἄλλο καὶ κατά τι: potestas civilis, spirituali sit subjecta: siquidem Ecclesia hac in parte non obtinet potestatem autoritativam, sive ἀνυπεύθυνον: sed tantùm ministerialem quæ tantisper obligat ad obedientiam oinnes Ecclesiæ cives, quatenus DEI legatione rectè, & secundum expressum DEI Verbum fungitur: eôdem planè modo, quo præco, sive fecialis aliquis ab Imperatore missus non suâ, sed alienâ autoritate, non ad suum, sed alienum imperium, mandat aut præcipit aliquid Principibus aut Ordinibus Imperii. Ubi tamen nemo ita ab omni ratione est alienus, ut inde colligat, Principes & Ordines Imperii subjectos esse præconi, sive feciali illi. Sic ergò axioma illud Esavviticum: Omnis superior imperare potest suo inferiori; verum est respectu ipsius DEI, non verò respectu Pontificis vel Ecclesiæ, quæ in spiritualibus etiam non suâ, sed DEI autoritate omnia disponit.

Deinde consequens Esavviticum nimis est angustum, dum pro solo Pontificis Romani stabiliendo dominatu in temporalibus sit illatio: id quod tamen Antecedentis ratio, & natura non patitur: Nam Spiritualem potestatem exercet non solus Pontifex, sed quivis Ecclesiæ pastor & minister, cui æquè potestas docendi, administrandi Sacramenta, ut & usus clavium est concessus atque Pontifici. Ergò sequeretur ex Antecedenti Esavvitico, quemlibet Pastorem, aut ministrum Ecclesiæ habere jurisdictionem in temporalibus rebus disponendis.

Tertiò hypothesis illa, cui primùm hoc argumentum superstruxit Esavvita, simpliciter falsa est; quòd nimirùm tum potestas civilis subjecta sit spirituali potestati, quando utraq; pars est ejusdem Reipub. Christianæ. Nam communio hæc non confundit jurisdictiones; sed cuilibet statui suum relinquit officium integrum, & circà proprium suum objectum occupatum: ita ut in Repub. Christianâ, politici sive seculares subsint Ecclesiasticis personis (sed secundum quid, uti jam ostensum) in spiritualibus: Rursum, Ecclesiastici subsint secularibus, in negotiis temporalibus. Utraque ergò alteram in suo ordine, & munere proprio recognoscit, & veneratur: & suam functionem utraque secundum suas leges exercet: & per media legitima: Ecclesiastici quidem, armis spiritualibus: Politici verò armis externis & corporalibus.

Tandem circà pleniorem hujus argumenti refutationem observandum & illud, quòd hac in disputatione inter spiritualem, & Ecclesiasticam potestatem accuratè est distinguendum. Etsi enim spiritualis potestas etiam est ac dicitur Ecclesiastica, quatenus in Ecclesia & ab Ecclesiasticis personis administratur: tamen propriè loquendo spiritualis potestas est tantum, quæ consistit in prædicatione Verbi, in dispensatione Sacramentorum, in usu clavium: quæ omnibus Ecclesiæ ministris legitimè vocatis ex æquo competit: ita ut nihil privilegii vel prærogativæ habeat, vel

Pontifex, vel Episcopus, aut quivis alius Ecclesiæ Doctor sive Antistes. Ecclesiastica verò potestas propriè loquendo, est ea, quæ externam aliquam Iurisdictionem, in negotiis, Ecclesiæ statum & commodum, ut & externam Auditorum disciplinam concernentibus, exercet: & versatur partim circa ceremonias & ritus Ecclesiasticos, aptè & decenter peragendos: partim circa causas & judicia matrimonialia: partim circa privilegia & immunitates personarum Ecclesiasticarum: partim denique circa vocationem & dimissionem Ministrorum Ecclesiæ. Quantum ergò ad spiritualem potestatem attinet, ea in solidum debetur iis, qui Ministerio Ecclesiastico legitimè præsunt: & ratione materiæ circa quam, & finis, quem unicè respicit, excellentior est omni potestate temporali, ita ut hæc illi omninò obedire teneatur.

Quantum verò ad potestatem Ecclesiasticam, ea toti Ecclesiæ, & sic omnibus tribus ordinibus hierarchicis, Ecclesiastico, Politico, Oecumenico competit. Unde Electores, Principes, & status Evangelici, hanc potestatem plerumque exercent per Consistoria Ecclesiastica, quæ constant ex personis Ecclesiasticis & Politicis. Et hîc tam Ecclesiastici Politicis, quàm Politici Ecclesiasticis obedire tenentur, hoc est; utrique secundum leges & constitutiones Ecclesiasticas jus dicere, & sententiam pronunciare debent. Quando ergò Pontifex Romanus hoc quoq; jus sibi soli rapit & arrogat, quid facit aliud, quàm quod ut ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος officium alienum invadit, & Tyrannum in Ecclesia agit.

Sed ut ad tres rationes Esavviticas itidem respondeamus: Prima manifestè falsa est: Nam potestas temporalis, quatenus ea talis est ac dicitur, non respicit finem illum ultimum, felicitatem nimirùm æternam, sed tantùm felicitatem temporalem, incrementum boni publici, & vitæ honestatem ac tranquillitatem: sic docente Apostolo, 1. Tim. 2, 2. qui ideò jubet orare pro Regibus, & omnibus, qui in sublimitate sunt, ut sub ipsoru Imperio, vitam tranquillam ac pacatā agere queamus, in omni pietate & honestate. Ergò hæc subordinatio finiū, ratione utriusq; potestatis, uni Pontifici & Ecclesiæ Romanæ exercendæ, penitus expirat. Deinde quanquam qui in Magistratu sunt constituti; respiciunt finem etiam illum ultimum, vitam nimirùm æternam: eum tamen non respiciunt, quatenus sunt Magistratus: sed quatenus sunt Christiani: ac proinde actionum etiam suarum & consiliorum Politicorū finem tantùm constituunt temporalem, eum videlicet qui actionem tanquam effectus sequitur: non qui in intellectu tantùm versatur.

Altera ratio, propriâ suâ futilitate concidit: Etsi enim membra in corpore unū constituant subjectū: falsū tamen est, quòd unum dependeat ab altero: siccine ergò brachium dextrum, pendebit vel à brachio, vel à pede sinistro, vel etiam à pede dextro:vel caput dependebit à ventre & aqualiculo. Corrigitur ergo error iste in hunc modum:Quemadmodum membra singula & universa in corpore humano coalescunt per egregiam quandam harmoniam & concordiam in unum corpus naturale : ita in corpore Christi mystico, quod est Ecclesia, convenire debent omnia ejus membra, cujuscunq; sint vel dignitatis, vel officii aut conditionis. Jam verò quemadmodum in corpore humano, membra non confusè suas operationes edunt, sed quodlibet suam peculiarem actionem, ab alterius membrì actione distinctam obtinet, & exercet: Ita in Ecclesia quodlibet membrum suæ profeffionis propria officia expediat : politici intra limites temporalium negociorum se contineant: Ecclesiastici verò spiritualibus officiis contenti, limites suos non egrediantur, nec temporalium rerum administrationem ullo pacto suscipiant. Hoc si fiat, tunc egregia harmonia & concordia omnibus in vicem membris intercedet.

Verbo est expressa. Quantu ergò discriminis est in temporalibus inter Imperatore ipsu aliquid mandatē aut prohibentē: & inter præconem, sive facialē, interpretem illius mandati: tantum etiam est discriminis inter DEUM ipsum, de voluntate sua in verbo scripto nos erudientem: & inter Spirituales sive Ecclesiasticas personas, tanquam voluntatis divinæ interpretes: ita ut Princeps mutare teneatur perversum administrandi modum: non propter Dominium aliquod Pontificis, quod ipsi in temporalibus nullum competit: sed propter obedientiam, quam ut ChristianusDEO, tanquã summo Imperatori præstare tenetur.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Proper Quasi-affection of the Political Magistracy: That the Political and Ecclesiastical are two separate powers (continued)

THE OTHER argument of Bellarmine is as follows: The Ecclesiastical Republic ought to be perfect: and sufficient unto itself in order to its end. Therefore it ought to have all power for attaining its end. But for the spiritual end, the power of using and disposing of temporal things is necessary: because otherwise evil Princes could with impunity foster heretics, and overturn Religion. Therefore it also has this power.

Furthermore, as regards the connection, by reason of which one is said to depend on the other: neither is that firm enough. For even if in the human body members depend on each other by natural or bodily contact: yet in the Church such a connection has no place: since the members do not cohere to them by bodily contact, but by contact of virtue, which is finally perfected in a spiritual coalition with Christ the head. Now if in the human body those things which depend on others are not therefore said to be subject to them: so if temporal things should even greatly depend on spiritual things, according to contact of virtue: yet this dependence does not regard the proper nature of temporal things and actions, according to which they do not depend on Spiritual things: but it only regards that common nature, insofar as political persons are at the same time members of the Church. Therefore no subjection of temporal power, considered in itself, can be proven from this. Otherwise this argumentation could be inverted in this manner: Spiritual things depend on temporal things: both as regards the persons themselves, who are men just as much as politicians: and as regards the mode of administration, which by reason of preaching and the Sacraments, consists of external, visible, and bodily actions. Therefore will Spiritual power be subject to temporal power? I think the Esauite will answer in the negative, and will distinguish between common and proper dependence. Therefore, let him remember that this very distinction can also have a place on the other side.

I ANSWER: the argument fails by the Sophism of a vicious consequence: and of begging the question. For although it is required for the perfection of the Church that it resist heretics, and not permit them the power of spreading freely and with impunity: it does not immediately follow that this must be done through temporal Jurisdiction: of which the Church can bring forward no command: but other means are granted, which is occupied in admonishing, rebuking, and refuting heretics and their supporters: and indeed in the spirit of Charity and meekness. Now when the Esauite substitutes temporal Jurisdiction in the place of those means defined in the sacred writings: he immediately begs the Question, and assumes as confessed what is in controversy. Then the Sophism of a vicious definition of a perfect Church occurs. For the Church, in order to be perfect in this world, does not require the external extirpation of heretics, which is done by means of the secular arm: but it only requires the pure preaching of the word, the legitimate administration of the Sacraments: and the right use of the keys. Where these things are rightly ordered in the Church, it has aspired to its perfection, but that perfection which ought to be hoped for and expected here on earth.

For absolute perfection of the Church is sought in vain by Esauites and Anabaptists in this world: since it is like a rose among thorns, as the Song of Songs chapter 2.1 has it. And according to the Apostle, It is necessary that there be heresies in the Church: 1 Cor. 11. 19. So that, as Christ testifies, only the fourth part of the seed of the divine Word finds good soil: and tares will always be in the midst of the wheat. Matt. 12.8 and 25. But if the Esauites are so very solicitous about the perfection of the Church, certainly they will be able to seek and find it nowhere, than in the head alone, which is not the Pope, but Christ the Savior alone and only. Eph. 1. 22 and 23. Col. 2. 18. Who alone also [has] jurisdiction, and final

The third reason fails by the Sophism of 'in a certain respect', for a temporal Prince, if his administration hinders the spiritual good, is bound to change that mode of administering, even with the detriment of the temporal good: but he is bound, not to the command of the Pope, or of the Roman Bishop, or of any other cleric: but only to the command of GOD, whose will in passing sentence against heretics and the defenders of the same; according to the good pleasure of His will, either through the temporal Magistrate or on the last day and in the universal judgment, He will rightly administer. And what, I ask, should be determined concerning the primitive Apostolic Church, certainly by far the most perfect of all: which to such an extent never arrogated or usurped any temporal Jurisdiction for itself: that it rather offered its own neck to be tortured by both heretics and tyrants. Finally, the very practice of the Roman Church argues the vanity of this argument: For if it pertains to the perfection of the Roman Church to prohibit heretics through temporal Jurisdiction, lest they spread in the Church: It is asked, Why then does the Pontiff permit Jews, the sworn enemies of Christ and the Gospel, to spread freely in the midst of Rome and the Roman Church, and to rage against Christ and Christians? Why does he not exercise temporal Jurisdiction here, as he strives to exercise against the Lutherans? Or are the Lutherans perhaps worse than the Jews?

THE THIRD argument of Bellarmine is as follows: It is not permitted for Christians to tolerate an infidel or heretical King, if he attempts to draw his subjects to his heresy or infidelity. But to judge whether a King is drawing [them] to heresy or not pertains to the Pontiff, to whom the care of Religion is committed. Therefore, it is for the Pontiff to judge whether a King is to be deposed or not to be deposed.

I ANSWER, the argument fails by the Sophism παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον (of the non-consequent). For although it is not permitted for Christians to connive at the heresy of their Kings and heretics: yet it does not immediately follow, Therefore they ought to exercise some temporal Jurisdiction over them and depose them by external force. For there are other means and weapons, namely Spiritual ones, by which they ought to resist heresies and heretics: concerning which [I spoke] in the refutation of the previous argument. If nothing is achieved by these Spiritual weapons, certainly it will be permitted neither to Christian subjects nor to the Pontiff to depose them from their seat by force and external sword: but it would be their duty to tolerate such infidel and heretical Kings patiently, to pour out prayers to GOD for their conversion, and to commit the outcome to GOD: by the example of the primitive Apostolic Church: and the one immediately following, which deposed neither Valens, nor Constantius, nor Julian, nor Anastasius, nor other heretical and Apostate Emperors, not because strength was lacking to them, but because it judged that such violent deposition did not belong to it. Which truly Christian practice the Church of GOD has always followed, indeed the Roman one also, up to the times of Gregory III, the Roman Pontiff, who was the first to dare to depose Emperor Leo III and Constantine, and to deprive them of the kingdom of Italy, because they refused to worship idols. In which part the opinion of Gregory I, the Great, Pope, is memorable, who writes thus in book 7, epistle 1, to Salvianus, or Sabinianus, concerning the Arian Lombards: If I, their servant, had wished to involve myself in the death of the Lombards, today the race of the Lombards would have neither King, nor Duke, nor counts, and would be divided in total confusion: but because I fear GOD, I am afraid to involve myself in the death of any man. And Ambrose prays, Against Auxentius: My weapons against the Goths and their soldiers are my tears: such are the defenses of priests: otherwise I neither ought nor can resist. The minor [premise] of the argument is likewise false. For judgment concerning doctrine and heresy does not so belong to the pontiff alone, that any priest, or indeed any Christian man, is not bound to perform this care: as has been demonstrated elsewhere. The reasons and testimonies of Scripture, by which the Jesuit strives to confirm his argument, are so far from militating [for him] that they rather render his cause worse. For 1. it is indeed true that the Israelite people were prohibited from choosing a king other than from among their brothers, lest the people be drawn into Idolatry: yet it does not follow from that, Therefore it will be permitted for the Christian people also to depose an infidel King, or to strip him of his kingdom: but only this follows: Therefore the Christian people, in choosing Kings and princes, or in constituting any Magistrates, ought to devote effort so that they do not choose an infidel or heretic, but a pious and Orthodox [one]. Now, however, from the voluntary election of some King, the process does not hold to the deposition of that King who obtains the principate by hereditary right and succession of nature, not finally obtained from the consent of the people. For it is one thing to choose a King or prince, which is a matter of the freest will: but it is another thing to have a King or Prince by hereditary succession: which binds subjects to obedience in all things that can be done with a safe conscience, even if something contrary to civil laws and equity is commanded. For it is so far from the case that either ecclesiastics or the remaining subjects can, with a safe conscience and obligation, enter into counsels through some sedition about deposing such Kings, that they [ought] rather [to act] according to that Petrine [passage], 1 Peter 2:18, 19.

Subjects ought to be with all fear to their masters, not only to the good and gentle: but also to the σκολιοῖς (crooked), that is, the perverse or morose: Because this finds favor, if anyone for conscience toward GOD endures sorrows, suffering unjustly.

The other proof taken from 1 Cor. 6:1 & 6, clearly does nothing to the point. For the Apostle does not permit the Corinthians to depose impious and infidel Judges: But he only disapproves of the fact that under such infidel Judges, they, being believers, were litigating, and indeed brother with brother: and he persuades them that they should rather, when mutual disputes arise, choose arbitrators among themselves as Judges, and acquiesce in the opinion and judgment of these: meanwhile permitting infidel judges to settle and judge the causes and disputes of infidels as well.

Latin:

ALTERAM argumentum Bellarmini sic habet: Respub. Ecclesiastica debet esse perfecta: & sibi sufficiens in ordine ad suum finem. Ergo debet habere omnem potestatem ad suum finem conse quendum. Sed necessaria est ad finem spiritualem potestas utendi & disponendi de temporalibus rebus: quia alioqui possent mali Principes impunè fovere hæreticos, & evertere Religionem. Ergo & hanc habet potestatem.

Porrò quoad connexum, ratione cujus unum ab alio dependere dicitur:neque id firmum satis est. Nam etsi in corpore humano membra à se mutuo dependeant contactu naturali sive corporali : tamen in Ecclesia talis connexus locum non habet: siquidem membra illis non cohærent contactu corporali, sed contactu virtutis, qui tandem in spiritualem coalitionem cum Christo capite perficitur. Jam si in corpore humano ea, quæ ab aliis pendent, non propterea illis dicuntur esse subjecta: sic si maximè temporalia pendeant à spiritualibus, secundum contactum virtutis: tamen hæc dependentia non respicit propriam temporalium rerum & actionum rationem, secundùm quam à Spiritualibus non dependent: sed tantùm respicit communem illam rationem, quatenus personæ politicæ simul sunt membra Ecclesiæ. Ergo nulla hinc temporalis potestatis, in se consideratæ, subjectio evinci potest. Alioquin inverti posset hæc argumentatio in hunc modum: Res spirituales pendent à temporalibus: tam quoad personas ipsas, qui sunt homines æque ac politici: tum quoad modum administrationis, quæ ratione prædicationis, & Sacramentorum, constat actionibus externis, visibilibus & corporalibus. Ergo Spiritualis potestas subjecta erit, temporali potestati? Negate opinor respondebitEsavvita, & distinguet inter dependentiam communem & propriam. Ergo hanc ipsam distinctionem ex altera etiam parte locum habere posse, meminerit.

RESPONDEO: fallit argumentum Sophismate vitiosi consequentis : & petitionis principii. Nam licèt ad perfectionem Ecclesiæ requiratur, ut resistat hæreticis, iisq; liberè & impunè grassandi potestatem non permittat: non tamen statim est consequens, fieri hoc debere, per Jurisdictionem temporalem:cujus mandatum nullum proferre potest Ecclesia: sed media alia sunt concessa, quæ in monendis, reprehendēdis, refutandis hæreticis, & horum propugnatoribus est occupata: & quidem in spiritu Charitatis & mansuetudinis. Jam quando Esawita in locum istorum mediorum in sacris definitorum, substituit Jurisdictionem temporalem: statim petit Principium, & pro confesso sumit, quod est in controversia. Deinde occurrit Sophisma vitiosæ definitionis perfectæ Ecclesiæ. Ecclesia enim ut sit perfecta hoc in mundo, non requirit externam hæreticorum extirpationem, quæ fiat mediante brachio seculari: sed tantùm requirit puram verbi prædicationē, legitimam Sacramentorum administrationem: rectum usum clavium. Hæc ubi in Ecclesia rectè se habeat,illa ad perfectionem suam adspiravit, sed perfectionem eam, quæ hîcce in terris sperari & expectari debet.

Absoluta enim perfectioEcclesiæ frustra ab Esavitis & Anabaptistis hoc in mundo quæritur: siquidem ea est tanquam rosa inter spinas, ut habet Canticum Canticorum cap. 2.1. Et secundum Apostolum, Oportet, ut hæreses sint in Ecclesia: 1. Cor. 11. 19. Ita ut teste Christo, quarta demum pars seminis Verbi divini, bonam terram inveniat: & Zizania semper sint futura in medio tritici. Matth. 12.8. & 25. Quod si autem Esawitæ usque adeo solliciti sunt de perfectione Ecclesiæ, certè nullibi eam quærere & invenire poterunt, quàm in solo capite, quod non est Pontifex, sed solus atq; unus Christus Servator. Eph. 1. 22. & 23. Coloß. 2. 18. Qui solus etiam Jurisdictionem, & finalem

Tertia ratio fallit Sophismate secundum quid, Princeps enim temporalis, si administratio ipsius impediat bonum spirituale, tenetur mutare modum illum administrandi, etiam cum detrimento temporalis boni: sed tenetur, non ad Imperium Pontificis, aut Episcopi Romani, vel alius alicujus clerici: sed tantum ad Imperium DEI, cujus voluntas in sententiam in haereticos, & eorundem propugnatores; pro beneplacito voluntatis suae, vel per Magistratum temporalem, vel in die novissimo & judicio universali, recte administra bir. Et quid quaeso statuendum fuerit, de Apostolicâ primitiva Ecclesiâ, certè longè omnium perfectissima: quae usque adeò nullam Jurisdictionem temporale unquam sibi vel arrogavit, vel usurpavit: ut potiùs cervicem & haereticis & tyrannis excarnificandam praebuerit. Tandem ipsa praxis Ecclesiae Romanae vanitatem hujus argumenti arguit: Si enim ad perfectionem Ecclesiae Romanae pertinet, per Jurisdietionem temporalem prohibere haereticos, ne grassentur in Ecclesia: Quaeritur, Cur ergo Pontifex Judaeos, juratos Christi & Evan gelij hostes, in mediâ Româ, & Romanâ Ecclesiâ, liberè grassari, & contra Christum & Christianos favire permittat? Cur hic non exerceat Jurisdietionem temporalem, quàm in Lutheranos exercere satagit? aut nùm fortè Lutherani Judaei sunt deteriores?

TERTIUM argumentum Bellarmini sic habet: Non licet Christianis tolerare Regem infidelem aut haereticum, si ille conetur pertrahere subditos ad suam haeresin aut infidelitatem. Atqui judicare, an Rex pertrahat ad haeresin, nec ne, pertinet ad Pontificem, cui est commissa cura Religionis. Ergo Pontifici est judicare, Regem esse deponendum, vel non deponendum.

RESPONDEO fallit argumentum Sophismate παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἑπόμενον. Etsi enim Christianis non licet connivere ad haeresin suorũ Regum & haereticorum: tamen non statim est consequens, Ergo Jurisdietionem aliquam temporalem in illos exercere, & externa vi eos deponere debent. Sunt enim alia media & arma, Spiritualia nimirùm, quibus haeresibus & haereticis resistere debeant: de quibus in refutatione argumenti praecedentis proximi. His armis Spiritualibus si nihil proficiatur, certè neque Christianis subditis, neque Pontifici licebit, vi & gladio externo illos de sede deponere: sed ipsorum fuerit, tales & infideles Reges, & haereticos patienter tolerare, pro ipsorum conversione preces ad DEUM fundere, & eventum DEO committere: exemplo pri mitivae Ecclesiae Apostolicae: & insequentis proximae, quae neque Valentem, neque Constantium, neque Julianum, neque Anastasium neq; alios Imperatores haereticos & Apostatas, deposuit, non quod vires ipsi defuerint, sed quia talem violentam depositionem sibi non competere censuit. Quam verè Christianam praxin semper secuta est Ecclesia DEI, imò Romana quoque usque ad tempora Gregorij III. Pontificis Romani, qui primus Leonem III. Imperatorem Constantinum, ideò, quòd idola colere detrectaret, deponere, & regno Italiae privare ausus fuit. Qua in parte memorabilis est sententia Gregorij I. Magni, Papae, qui lib. 7. epist. 1. ad Salvianum, sive Sabinianum, de Longobardis Arianis sic scribit: Si ego servus eorũ in morte Longobardorum me miscere voluissem, hodiè Longobardorum gens nec Regem, nec Ducem, nec comites haberet, atq; in summa confusione esset divisa: sed quia DEUM timeo, in mortem cujlibet hominis, memin stere formido. Et Ambrosius orat, Contra Auxentium: Arma mea adversus Gotthos & ipsorum milites, sunt lachrymæ meæ: talia sunt munimenta sacerdotum: aliter nec debeo, nec possum resistere. Minor argumenti itidem falsa est. Tam enim soli pontifici non competit judicium de doctrina & hæresi, ut hanc curam Sacerdotu imo Christianorum hominum quilibet, præstare teneatur: ut alibi demonstratum. Rationes & Scripturæ testimonia, quibus argumentum suum confirmare nititur Esavvita, tam non militant, ut potiùs causam ipsius deteriorem reddant. Nam 1. verum quidem est, quod populus Israeliticus prohibitus sit, alium, quàm ex fratrib9 suis eligere regem, ne forte ad Jdololatriam pertrahatur populus: inde tamen non est consequens, Ergo licebit etiam populo Christiano Regem infidelem deponere, sive regno exuere: sed illud tantùm sequitur: Ergò populus Christianus in eligendis Regibus & principibus, sive constituendis Magistratibus quib9libet operam dare debet, ut non infidelem, aut hæreticum, sed pium & Orthodoxu eligat. Jam verò ab electione Regis alicujus voluntariâ, non valet processus ad depositionem illius Regis, qui jure hæreditario & successione naturæ principatum obtinet, non demum ex consensu populi impetrat. Nam aliud est eligere Regem aut principem, id quod liberrimæ voluntatis est: aliud verò habere Regem aut Principem ex successione hæreditaria: id quod ad obedientiam obligat subditos, in omnibus quæ salvâ conscientiâ fieri possunt, si maximè legibus civilibus & æquitati adversum quid præcipiatur. Tantùm enim abest, ut vel Ecclesiastici, vel reliqui subditi per seditionem quandam, de deponendis ejusmodi Regibus consilia inire, salvâ conscientiâ & obligatione possint, ut potiùs secundum illud Petrinum. 1. cap. 2. 18. 19.

Subditi esse debeant cum omni timore Dominis, non solùm bonis & æquis: sed & σκολιοῖς hoc est pravis sive morosis: Quia hoc cedit in gratiam, si quis propter conscientiam DEI suffert molestias, injustè afflictus.

Altera probatio ex 1. Cor. 6. 1. & 6. petita, planè nihil ad rem facit. Neque enim Apostolus permittit Corinthiis, ut Judices impios & infideles deponant: Sed illud tantum improbat, quòd sub ejusmodi Judicibus infidelibus, ipsi quippe fideles litigabant, & quidem frater cum fratre: & suadet, ut ipsi potiùs emergentibus dissidiis mutuis, inter seipsos arbitros tanquam Judices eligant, & in istorum sententiâ ac judicio acquiescant: permittentes interim infideles judices, infidelium etiam causas & dissidia dirimere ac dijudicare.


### Chapter I. On the Nature and Proper Quasi-affection of the Political Magistracy: That the Political and Ecclesiastical are two separate powers (continued)

The third and final proof likewise wanders off the path: For in 1 Cor. 7:13 & 15, the Apostle intends nothing other than that if a believer does not wish to cohabit with an unbelieving spouse, they may depart from them without prejudice to the faith. But what has this to do with the deposition of an unbelieving or heretical Magistrate, which, at Bellarmine's urging, ought to be undertaken by faithful and Orthodox subjects? Nothing at all. Only this much can be elicited from it, that subjects can, without detriment to the faith, depart from an infidel and heretical King and Prince (though eternal equals), and migrate elsewhere: a thing which none of us denies. There is therefore in this proof a πλεονεξία of the consequent.

Bellarmino's fourth argument is as follows: When Kings and Princes come to the Church to become Christians, they are received with an express or tacit pact that they will subject their scepters to Christ: and will promise that they will keep and defend the faith for Christ, even under penalty of losing their kingdom: Therefore, when they become heretics, or are harmful to religion, they can be judged by the Church, and even deposed from their principate: and no injury will be done to them if they are deposed.

I RESPOND; The argument fails by a perpetual Sophistication ὠχῇ & un' ἐκεί- νον. For 1. it collects a Universal from a particular: those princes who were elected and confirmed under the express condition of asserting the Orthodox faith, but afterwards fall away from the faith, can be deposed: Therefore all infidel and heretical Kings can and ought to be deposed: a thing which has no place in those who aspired to the kingdom not by the election and will of the people, but by right of hereditary succession: in whom such a condition does not always apply. 2. It does not follow: Such Kings are to be deposed: Therefore they are to be deposed by the Church or the Pope: For a third party is given: namely, they can be deposed by the very orders of the whole Kingdom, to whom the King obligated himself and took an oath. 3. From a judgment concerning heresy, there is no process given for execution against heretics. To judge indeed concerning the heresy and Apostasy of a King and Prince is an Ecclesiastical act, and pertains to the Church: Execution, however, is a civil act, which the Church by no right can or ought to arrogate or usurp to itself: But it pertains to the political orders. 4. The whole reason of the Consequence expires when Bellarmino argues thus: A King or some Prince submits his scepters to Christ: Therefore he is subject to the Roman Pontiff in temporal matters: But only that follows: Therefore the judgment concerning the infidelity or apostasy of the King pertains to Christ: which He is accustomed to exercise Himself, partly through the Church, partly through the Political Magistrate, distinctly and in diverse ways, without any confusion of dominions. Finally, the consequence from the Church to the Pope is not valid: For the Church consists of all the orders: The Pope acts as one and constitutes a Sacrificer: What therefore can pertain to the Church is not immediately to be assigned to the Pope.

which, so that he may distribute suitable food to each. Therefore the supreme Pontiff has this triple power.

I RESPOND, the argument proceeds, and the whole is easily conceded, if it is understood concerning the pastoral care which pertains to the Pope, Bishops, and Ecclesiastical persons according to the scriptures. But when Bellarmino distorts it to establish temporal jurisdiction: he commits a shameful πλεονεξία of the consequent. Furthermore, if the argument is taken concerning the supreme Pontiff, who is Christ alone: there is no controversy remaining: but if concerning the Roman Pontiff: we deny the whole: since he is neither the supreme Pontiff himself, nor can any man have such power as Bellarmino imagines. 3. Peter, who was commanded to feed the sheep, fed them indeed, but only with the uncorrupted Word of GOD: according to that form which he himself prescribed both for himself and for all fellow-presbyters and Bishops, in this fashion: Feed the flock of the LORD, which is committed to you, not by constraint, but willingly: not for the sake of filthy lucre, but from the heart: not as being Lords over the clergy, but as being examples to the flock. 1 Pet. 5, 2 & 3. What therefore Peter neither had, much less ever usurped regarding the pastoral care of the sheep, namely secular power, that certainly by no right can or ought the Roman Pontiff (but a spurious and fictitious one) to arrogate to himself. 4. Every pastor cares only for his own sheep, not those of another. Therefore the Roman Pontiff is an ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος, when he nefariously arrogates to himself without a calling the care of all the sheep of Christ dispersed throughout the whole Christian world. 5. To care for and feed the sheep of Christ, and to defend them against wolves, nowhere in the Scriptures signifies the same as to depose Kings, and to strip them of their Kingdom, even if they should turn out to be wolves or heretics: or kids or goats, that is, be infamous for the impiety and wickedness of their lives and morals. 6. Since pastoral care of the sheep of Christ also pertains to the Political Magistrate, according to that Prophetic saying: Kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and queens thy nursing mothers: it would follow, either according to the logic of Bellarmino, that Ecclesiastical Jurisdiction in Spiritual matters also pertains to the Political Magistrate, which is manifestly false: or that that pastoral care ought to contain itself within the boundaries of temporal jurisdiction: just as conversely the pastoral care committed to the Church also ought to contain itself within the limits of spiritual power: and neither to desire nor to invade temporal Jurisdiction by any pact: so that all confusion may be avoided between these two orders, which GOD Himself willed to be distinct both by their objects and by their very different mode of government.

Bellarmino's fifth and final argument is as follows: It was said to Peter: feed my sheep: John: last chapter, verse 16. Therefore all faculty which is necessary for a pastor to protect the flock was given to him. But a triple power is necessary for a pastor: One concerning wolves, so that he may ward them off by every means he can: another concerning rams, so that if at any time they harm the flock with their horns, he may be able to shut them up: the third concerning the sheep. And thus far indeed we have examined the former hypothesis of Bellarmino, and that most principal one: There remains the other, by which he attempts to prove that it does not conflict with the Word of GOD for one man to be an Ecclesiastical and Political prince at the same time. For the sake of confirming this hypothesis, he contends at the beginning that in the Old Testament there occur examples of Saints who were both Kings and Judges, and Priests at the same time. Then he strives to defend it with four arguments, the FIRST of which is this. Ecclesiastical and Political power are not contrary, but both are good, both from GOD, both praiseworthy. THE SECOND: peace and war are more diverse than temporal and spiritual goods: Yet one and the same King presides over both the Senate and the army: the gowned and the armed. Therefore, much more will one be able to preside over temporal and spiritual matters. THE THIRD: One King can govern most diverse kingdoms, which have different customs, rites, laws, and habits. Therefore, one Bishop will also be able to rule one Bishopric, and one principality, etc. THE FOURTH: The patrons of the Church, Constantine the Great, Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, earned singular praise from the Church because they donated temporal principalities to Bishops, book 5, on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 9.

But the response to each of these is easy. For in the beginning, those examples of the Old Testament are specific, and of fact rather than of Law: also of present necessity rather than of divine command: Now, since the Church of the New Testament has been so reformed that both powers taken together cannot belong to one individual, Bellarmine strives in vain to trouble us with such examples, as has also been shown above.

Regarding those four arguments; THE FIRST overturns itself: For if both powers can belong to the Pope because they are not contrary: then by the same reasoning, both powers must be granted to the Emperor as well, and to other Princes and political Magistrates. There is added the fallacy of the non-cause as the cause: For these two powers cannot belong to one individual not because one is good and the other bad, or as if they were contrary and distrusted one another: but because they are diverse in their very genus, and the objects of things, about which each power is concerned, by the ordination of GOD, require a peculiar and distinct Ruler or governor.

THE SECOND argument wanders clearly off the mark, and labors partly with the vanity of the consequence, and partly with a false hypothesis. The vanity of the consequence is evident from the fact that there is a huge dissimilarity between peace and war: and between spiritual and corporal power: The administration of war and peace can belong to one individual because both are contained under the same genus of temporal things, and are not prohibited by GOD. Yet the incompatibility of both powers, by the ordination of GOD, especially under the New Testament, depends solely on that. The false hypothesis arises from the fact that Bellarmine, not attending to the ordination of GOD, falsely persuades himself that these two regimes are incompatible for one individual only because they are contrary in their very genus: whereas we should rather attend to: not what the difference is between things differing in genus, but what divine Law might permit.

THE THIRD argument is overturned from the foundations by the same weights of arguments by which the second has already been destroyed and overturned.

THE FOURTH and last argument fails with the sophism of the vicious Consequent. For it is not immediately a Consequent: The donations of Emperors made to the Church earned praise from the Church, Or, the intention itself of the Emperors was good. Therefore the Roman Church has power in temporal matters even over the Emperors, Kings, and princes of this age themselves. For those Emperors could never have dreamed of this end, even in a fever: but they sought only the propagation of the Church, and its more liberal conservation and sustenance. But that the outcome did not correspond to these plans of theirs, that is a matter of accident. Furthermore, the condition of those donations is such that both the Emperors exceeded the limit with this excessive munificence: and the Roman prelates sinned gravely, while they accepted some temporal dominion, even if offered and donated voluntarily by the Emperors, and wickedly usurped it afterwards to the ruin of the Church.

Finally, most of the diplomas of those Donations are fictitious and supposititious, as we have recently demonstrated expressly and at length in our Action against the Jesuit Gretser. For the sake of brevity, we refer students of theology to that work. From this, however, the decision of that question becomes clear: whether by human law (since it cannot have it by divine law) jurisdiction belongs to the Pope and Bishops, both in ecclesiastical and in political matters. For since Bellarmine himself in this place appeals to these Donations of the Emperors as the primary foundation of both papal powers, it is rightly concluded from this that the Pope and Bishops do indeed have the administration of temporal things by human law, namely by the law of Donation, but altogether illegitimately.

For neither ought the Emperors to have assigned such power to ecclesiastical persons, nor could they even by Law: nor was it permitted for these to accept what was donated and offered, much less to exercise it. Insofar, therefore, as the Pope and Bishops possess such external dominion by human, but illegitimate, Law: to that extent they cease to be what they were, namely Bishops: and turn into secular Lords: and that all the more, the more they abstain from every Episcopal duty, which in preaching, and dispensing the Sacraments, and the right use of the keys, according to the ordination of Christ, ought to be solely occupied. Which opinion Bernard held many centuries before, thus discoursing on the temporal dominion of the Clergy to Pope Eugenius, Vol. 2, fol. 1316. Grant that you claim these for yourself by any other reason: yet not by Apostolic Law.

For neither could Peter give you what he did not have. What he had he gave, solicitude over the Churches. Was it dominion? Hear him himself (1 Pet. 5:2): Not lording it, he says, over the clergy, but being made a pattern to the flock. Go then you, and dare to usurp for yourself either a lording apostleship, or an Apostolic lordship. You are clearly prohibited from either one. If you wish to have both at the same time, you will lose both. This is the Apostolic pattern: Lording is forbidden, ministering is enjoined. Your power is in crimes, not in possessions. Since it was for the former, not for the latter, that you received the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Which dignity seems greater to you, dismissing sins or dividing estates? There is no comparison. These lowest and earthly things have their own judges, the Kings and Princes of the earth. Why do you invade foreign boundaries? You have been made superior, but to what end? Not to lord it, I suppose. We therefore, that we may think much of you, shall we think that a ministry was imposed, not a lordship given? Learn that you have need of a hoe, not a scepter, that you may do the work of a Prophet: etc.

Latin:

Tertia & postrema probatio itidem extra oleas vagatur: Nam 1. Cor. 7. 13. & 15. nihil aliud vult Apostolus, quàm si fidelis infideli conjugi cohabitare nolit, quòd possit ab ea discedere sine detrimento fidei. Sed quid hoc ad depositionem infidelis aut hæretici Magistratus, quæ à subditis fidelibus & Orthodoxis, suadente Bellarmino, suscipi debeat? Nihil prorsus. Illud tantùm inde elici potest, quòd subditi sine detrimento fidei à Rege & Principe infideli & hæretico (æternis tamen paribus) discedere, & aliò migrare possint: id quod nemo nostrum negat. Est ergò in hac probatione πλεονεξία consequentis.

Quartum Bellarmini argumentum sic habet: Quando Reges & Principes ad Ecclesiam veniunt, ut Christiani fiant, recipiuntur cum pacto expresso vel tacito, ut sceptra sua subjiciant Christo: & polliceantur, se Christo fidem servaturos & defensuros, etiam sub pæna regni perdendi: Ergo quando fiunt hæretici, aut religioni obsunt, possunt ab Ecclesia judicari, & etiam deponi à principatu: nec ulla eis injuria fiet, si deponantur.

RESPONDEO; Fallit argumentum perpetuâ Sophisticatione ὠχῇ & un' ἐκείνον. Nam 1. antecedens ex particulari colligit Universale: illi principes qui sub expressâ fidei Orthodoxæ asserendæ conditione sunt electi & confirmati, postmodum verò à fide deficiunt, possunt deponi: Ergo omnes Reges infideles & hæretici possunt & debent deponi: id quod locum non habet in iis, qui non electione & voluntate populi, sed jure successionis hæreditariæ ad regnum adspirarunt: in quibus talis conditio non semper militat. 2. Non sequitur: Tales Reges sunt deponendi: Ergo ab Ecclesia Pontifice sunt deponendi: Datur enim tertium: nempe ab ipsis totius Regni ordinibus, quibus sese Rex obligavit, & jusjurandum præstitit, deponi potest. 3. A judicio de hæresi, ad executionem contra hæreticos non datur processus. Judicare quidem de hæresi, & Apostasia Regis & Principis, est actus Ecclesiasticus, & pertinet ad Ecclesiam: Executio autem est actus civilis, quem Ecclesia nullo jure sibi arrogare aut usurpare vel potest vel debet: Sed ad ordi nes politicos pertinet. 4. Omnis ratio Consequentiæ expirat, quando Bellarminus sic arguit: Rex aut Princeps aliquis sceptra sua submittit Christo: Ergo Pontifici Romano in temporalibus subjacet: Sed illud tantùm sequitur: Ergo Christo competit judicium de Regis infidelitate aut apostasia: quàm ipse, partim per Ecclesiam, partim per Magistratum Politicum distinctè & diversimodè, sine ulla dominiorum confusione exercere solet. Tandem ab Ecclesia ad Pontificem non valet consequentia: Ecclesia enim constat ex omnibus ordinibus: Pontifex unum agit & constituit Sacrificulum: Quod ergo Ecclesiæ competere potest, non statim Pontifici est adsignandum.

quas, ut singulis tribuat convenientia pabula. Ergo hanc triplicem potestatem habet summus Pontifex.

RESPONDEO, procedit argumentum, & facilè totum conceditur, si de cura pastorali, quæ Pontifici, Episcopis, & Ecclesiasticis personis, secundum scripturas competit, intelligatur. Quando verò Bellarminus illud ad astruendam temporalem jurisdictionem detorquet: turpem committit πλεονεξίαν consequentis. Deinde si de summo Pontifice, qui est solus Christus, argumentum accipiatur: nulla est reliqua controversia: sin de Pontifice Romano: negamus totum: siquidem nec summus ipse est Pontifex, nec potestatem talem, qualem fingit Bellarminus, ullus homo habere potest. 3. Petrus qui jussus fuit pascere oves, pavit utique eas, sed non nisi Verbo DEI incorrupto:secunduti eam formam, quam ipsemet & sibi ipsi, & omnibus compresbyteris & Episcopis præscripsit, in hanc faciem: Pascite gregem DOMINI, qui vobis commissus est, non coactè, sed libenter: non turpis lucri gratia, sed ex animo: non ut Dominantes cleru, sed ut fitis exemplaria gregis. 1. Pet. 5, 2. & 3. Quod ergo Petrus nec habuit, nedum circa curam pastoralem ovium nunquam usurpavit, secularem videlicet potestatem, eam certè jure nullo successori ipsius Pontifex Romanus (sed spurius & fictitius) sibi arrogare vel potest, vel debet. 4. Quisquæ pastor suas tantùm non alienas curat oves. Ergo Pontifex Romanus est ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος, quando omnium ovium Christi, per totum orbem Christianum dispersarum, curam sine vocatione sibi nefariè arrogat. 5. Curare & pascere oves Christi, & defendere contra lupos, nuspiam in Scripturis idem significat, ac deponere Reges, & Regno eos exuere, si maxime evadant vel lupi vel hæretici: vel hitci sive hædi, hoc est, vitæ morumque impietate & consceleratione sint infames. 6. Cum Magistratui Politico competat etiam cura pastoralis ovium Christi, secundum illud Propheticum: Reges erunt nutritii tui, & reginæ nutrices tuæ: consequens fuerit, aut secundum logicam Bellarmini, Magistratui Politico competere etiam Jurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam in Spiritualibus, id quod manifestè falsum: aut curam illam pastoralem debere se continere intra crepidines jurisdictionis temporalis: sicut vicissim cura pastoralis Ecclesiæ commissa continere se etiam decet, intra limites potestatis spiritualis: neque &, temporalem Jurisdictionem ullo pacto vel appetere, vel invadere: ut sic omnis confusio evitetur inter duos istos ordines, quos DEUS ipse, & objectis & modo gubernationis diversissimo voluit esse distinctos.

Quintum & postremum Bellarmini argumentum sic habet: Petro dictum est: pasce oves meas: Johan: ultimo, vers. 16. Ergo data est illi facultas omnis, quæ est pastori neceffaria ad gregem tuendū. Atqui pastori necessaria est potestas triplex: Una circa lupos, ut eos arceat omni ratione, quâ poterit: altera circa arietes, ut si quando cornibus lædat gregem, possit eos recludere: tertia circa oves reliEt hactenus quidem priorem hypothe sin Bellarmini, eamq; maximè principalem, examinavimus: Superest altera, qua probare conatur, Non pugnare cum Verbo DEI, ut unus homo sit princeps Ecclesiasticus & Politicus simul. Hujus hypotheseos confirmandæ gratiâ, initio contendit, quod in Vetere Testamento occurrant exempla Sanctorum, qui & Reges atq; Judices, & Sacerdotes simul fuerunt. Deinde quatuor rationibus eam propugnare studet, quarum PRIMA hæc est. Potestas Ecclesiastica & Politica non sunt contrariæ, sed utraque bona, utraque à DEO, utraque laudabilis. ALTERA: pax & bellum magis sunt diversa, quàm bona temporalia & Spiritualia: Atqui unus & idem Rex præest, & Senatui & exercitui: togatis & armatis. Ergo multò magis poterit unus præesse in temporalibus & Spiritualibus. TERTIA: Rex unus diversissima regna potest gubernare, quæ diversos mores, ritus, leges, consuetudines habent. Ergo unus etiam Episcopus poterit regere unum Episcopatum, & unum principatum &c. QUARTA: Patroni Ecclesiæ, Constantinus M. Carolus, M. Ludovicus pius, singularem laudem meruerunt ab Ecclesia, quòd temporales principatus Episcopis donaverunt, lib. 5. de Rom. Pont. cap. 9.

Sed facilis est ad singula isthæc responsio. Nam initiò exempla illa Veteris Testamenti sunt propria, & facti magis, quàm Juris: præsentis etiam magis necessitatis, quàm mandati divini: Jam cùm Ecclesia Novi Testamenti ita sit reformata, ut utraque potestas concrecivè accepta, uni individuo non possit competere, frustra omninò ejusmodi Exemplis molestus nobis esse studet Bellarminus, uti supra quoq; ostensum.

Quoad quatuor illas rationes; PRIMA seipsam evertit: Nam si ideò Pontifici potest utraque potestas competere, quia non sunt contrariæ: utique Imperatori quoque eâdem ratione, ut & Principibus & Magistratibus aliis Politicis, utraque potestas erit concedenda. Accedit Sophisticatio τοῦ μὴ ἀιτίου ὡς ἀιτίου: Non enim ideò potestates hæ duæ uni individuo non possunt competere, quasi una sit bona, altera mala, aut quasi contrariè disfideant à se invicem: sed quia ipso genere sunt diversæ, & objecta rerum, circa quas quælibet potestas versatur, ex ordinatione DEI, peculiarem etiam & distinctum Rectorem sive gubernatorem requirunt.

ALTERA ratio planè extra oleas vagatur, & partim consequentiæ vanitate, partim falsâ hypothesi laborat. Consequentiæ vanitas indè elucescit, quia ingens est dissimilitudo inter pacem & bellum: & inter potestatem spiritualem & corporalem: Belli & pacis administratio uni individuo ideò competere potest, quia sub eodem genere, rerum temporalium, utraq; continetur, neque à DEO est prohibita. Atqui utriusque potestatis incompatibilitas, ex DEI ordinatione, sub Novo præsertim Testamento unicè dependet. Falsa hypothesis inde oritur, quòd Bellarminus non attentâ ordinatione DEI, falsò sibi persuadet, ideò tantùm duo hæc regimina esse uni individuo incompatibilia, quia genere ipso sint contraria: cum potius nos attendamus: non quid rerum genere differentium differentiâ, sed quid Jus divinum possit permittere.

TERTIA ratio iisdem argumentorum ponderibus funditùs evertitur, quibus jam secunda est diruta & eversa.

QUARTA & postrema ratio fallit Sophismate vitiosi Consequentis. Neq; enim statim est Consequens: Donationes Imperatorum factæ Ecclesiæ, laudem promeruerunt ab Ecclesiâ, Vel, intentio ipsa Imperatorum fuit bona. Ergo Ecclesia Romana habet potestatem in temporalibus etiam supra ipsos Imperatores, Reges & principes hujus seculi. Hunc enim finem, nunquam vel per febrim somniare potuerunt Imperatores illi: sed propagationem tantùm Ecclesiæ, & liberaliorem ejusdem conservationem sustentationemq; quæsiverunt. Quod verò eventus hisce ipsorum consiliis non respondit, illud accidentis est. Deindè verò Donationum istarum ea est conditio, ut & imperatores nimiâ hac munificentiâ modum excesserint: & præsules Romani graviter peccarint, dùm temporale aliquod dominium, etiam ab Imperatoribus ultrò oblatum & donatum acceptarunt, & improbè postmodum in perniciem Ecclesiæ usurparunt.

Tandem pleraq; Donationum istarum diplomata sunt fictitia & supposititia, quemadmodum nuper in Actione nostrâ adversus Gretserum Esauvitam, ex professo & prolixè demonstravimus. Quò brevitatis studio, Theologiæ studiosos ablegatos volumus. Patet autem hinc decisio illius Quæstionis: An Jure humano (quia divino habere non potest) Pontifici & Episcopis, tum in rebus Ecclesiasticis, tum in politicis competat Jurisdictio. Quia enim Bellarmin9 hoc loco ipse provocat ad Donationes hasce Imperatorum, tanquam ad fundationem primam utriusq; potestatis Pontificiæ; rectè quidem inde colligitur, quòd Pontifex & Episcopi Jure quidem humano, nempe Jure Donationis habeant rerum temporalium administrationem: verùm prorsus illegitimè.

Nam neque Imperatoribus talem potestatem Ecclesiasticis personis adsignare debuit, vel Jure etiam potuit: neque his donatam & oblatam acceptare, nedum exercere licuit. Quatenus ergò Jure quidem humano, sed illegitimo, Pontifex ac Episcopi tale dominium externum possident: eatenus desinunt esse quod fuerunt, nempe Episcopi: & evadunt Domini seculares: idq; eò magis, quò magis ab omni officio Episcopali abstinent, quod in concionando, & dispensandu Sacramentis, & recto usu clavium, secundum ordinationem Christi, unicè debet esse occupatum. Quam sententiam ante secula benè multa tulit Bernhardus, sic de Clericorum dominio temporali disserens ad Eugenium Pontificem Romanum, Tom. 2. fol. 1316. Esto, ut aliâ quacunq; ratione hæc tibi vindices: non tamen Jure Apostolico.

Neque enim Petrus dare tibi, quod non habuit, potuit. Quod habuit dedit, follicitudinem super Ecclesias. Numquid dominationem? Audi ipsum (1. Petr. 5, 2. ( Non dominantes, ait, in clero, sed forma facti gregis. I ergo tu, & tibi usurpare aude aut dominans apostolatum: aut Apostolicus Dominatum. Plane ab alterutro prohiberis. Si utrumque simul habere voles, perdes utrumque. Forma Apostolica haec est, Dominatio interdicitur, indicitur ministratio. In criminibus non in possessionibus vestra est potestas. Quoniam propter illa, non propter has accepistis claves regni cœlorum. Quænam tibi videtur major dignitas, dimittendi peccata, an prædia dividendi? nulla comparatio. Habent hæc infima & terrena, suos judices, Reges & Principes terræ. Quid fines alienos invadis? Factus es superior sed ad quid? Non ad dominandum opinor. Nos igitur, ut multum sentiamus de vobis, impositum senserimus ministerium, non dominium datum? Disce sarculo tibi opus esse, non sceptro, ut opus facias Prophetæ: &c.


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate

The Apostle expressed the office of the Political Magistrate in a brief, yet sufficiently accurate definition, Rom. 13:1, 3, 4. Every (Political) Magistrate, he says, is a minister of GOD, and indeed ordained by GOD himself, and equipped with the sword and public authority, an avenger for wrath to him who has done what is evil: but he is approved for the praise of those who have done what is good. From this emerges the twofold office of the Political Magistrate, according to the two tables of the decalogue.

For first, regarding the former table, he ought to be a minister of GOD, to serve Him principally, and to take diligent care in their own place and manner of those things which make for the promotion of His honor and true worship. David also discusses this office, Ps. 2:10 and following: Be instructed, O kings, who judge the earth; Serve the LORD in fear, and exult to Him with trembling: Kiss the son, lest the LORD be angry, and you perish from the just way. The latter office of the Political Magistrate, regarding the latter table of the Decalogue, looks to external or civil Justice, in bodily matters, and that both in peace and in war or military affairs: the end and principal scope of both of which is public peace and tranquility: the safety of citizens: and the liberty of the fatherland: for the praise and benefit of the good: and the punishment of the bad, as our definition holds. With respect to both of these offices, two columns of the Republic are commonly established: RELIGION, and JUSTICE. The former takes care of what is owed to GOD: the latter of what is owed to the fatherland and subjects, rightly, in order, and according to the laws.

And hence that common principle and Symbol of the Great: FOR ALTARS AND HEARTHS.

Furthermore, in executing this office of his, the Magistrate uses three means above all

Political: namely, by Laws: by Judgment: by the execution of judgment. Regarding Laws, they ought from the beginning to consent with the Law of Nature and the will of GOD. For since the Magistrate is a minister of GOD, he ought to decree or determine nothing that is adverse to His will. GOD has indeed revealed this will of His in the law partly moral or Decalogue, and partly forensic or Judicial: in both of which, with admirable brevity, He has encompassed individual and universal things; which make for the laudable and salutary government both of the whole Republic and of individual citizens. For although some laws seem to pertain only to the Republic of the Jews, according to the condition of those times and of the promised land; yet these very ones also show those fountains of Judgments to which all true νομοθεσία (legislation) can be conveniently directed and accurately examined: so that one could not falsely name even the Decalogue alone as the fountain of all other laws. For from the laws of the first table concerning the true worship of GOD, flowed all those things which Minos, Solon, Lycurgus, Charondas, Zaleucus, Numa, the Roman Decemvirs, and other Lawgivers handed down concerning the worship of their own Gods, although most corruptly: Which likewise Christian Emperors established concerning this matter. Hence in the Justinian Code arose titles and laws, concerning the H. Trinity, and the catholic faith: concerning sacrosanct Churches: concerning Bishops and clerics, concerning heretics, concerning apostates, concerning blasphemies, concerning oaths. Now as regards the precepts of the second table, they contain under their scope both things and persons, and the kinds and differences of actions. For by the first precept of the second table are shown in order the distinctions of persons, and after the manner of the law of Nature is commanded piety; and honor towards parents, and those who are in the place of parents; towards Princes, Magistrates, tutors, preceptors, ministers of the Church: as likewise the duties of masters, servants, patrons, clients, freedmen. From this first precept of the second table, therefore, have been sought: those things which in civil law have been handed down concerning the right of persons, concerning the status of men, concerning the duties of Magistrates, concerning the duty of a president, proconsul, etc. Likewise concerning the acknowledging of children, concerning adoptions; concerning tutelages, concerning the works of freedmen, concerning servants, concerning those who are of their own or another's right, concerning manumissions and similar things; all of which, pertaining to this source of honoring parents, command that account be taken of discipline and obedience and of the calling of each one.

The second precept of the second table is prohibitory concerning not killing: Whence have proceeded civil Laws concerning homicides, concerning parricides; concerning assassins, concerning punishments, concerning inquiries, concerning injuries, concerning retaliation, concerning the Aquilian law, and other laws and constitutions of this kind.

To this precept in excellent order is subjoined the prohibition of Adultery: from which edict have been born laws concerning adulteries, concerning defilements, concerning incest, concerning betrothals, concerning nuptials and matrimony, concerning divorces.

By the fourth precept of the second table, Theft and the handling of another's property is forbidden, which is done against the will of the Owner: likewise frauds in contracts, and all manner of unjust occupations and possessions of the property of others. And thus, by this commandment, the distinction of property is sanctioned: for when GOD forbids thefts, He wills that individuals should keep their own proper possessions. To this commandment, therefore, pertain those things which are handed down throughout the Civil Law concerning the division of property, the acquiring of ownership of things, the recovery of property, the third and half shares, successions, the petition for an inheritance, the division of an inheritance, testaments, and legacies: as well as those things which are likewise handed down concerning thefts, embezzlement, and sacrileges. Moreover, although actions, just like things, spring from several commandments, those things which are commanded by the fifth commandment concerning avoiding false testimony sufficiently declare that judgments and actions arise from this source: and consequently that those things which are contained in the Civil Law concerning accusations, calumniators, the law of defamation, prevaricators, witnesses, proofs, exceptions, the producing of an instrument, the credibility of instruments, judgments, sentence, and res judicata, and appeals, pertain to this commandment. To the sixth and seventh, namely the last two commandments of the Decalogue, concerning concupiscence, although some refer the actions of the Aquilian law, the Julian law, concerning adulterers, cattle-thieves, a corrupted slave, if a quadruped has caused damage, moved boundaries, the governing of citizens, and indeed the whole of both economy and polity: yet these very things are more freely and correctly referred to the preceding commandments, because the doctrine concerning concupiscence, handed down in these two commandments, is proper to the Church of GOD, inasmuch as it accuses and condemns not so much the misdeeds themselves, designated by the act itself, as the internal concupiscences of the soul, conceived at least in thought or imagination, even if they never break forth into action. Indeed, this comparison of civil laws with the commandments of the Decalogue shows what fanatical, certainly Anabaptistic, spirit rules and moves the Herbornians, who contend that the Mosaic forensic laws are to be simply recalled into use, with the laws of the Emperors abolished, as if these did not agree with the Decalogue, especially regarding the punishments for crimes. But it is rash to seek the abrogation of those laws which agree with the Decalogue in their very foundation: and although they may differ in some circumstances from that form of judgments which was prescribed to the Jews in the forensic law: it is to be noted, however, that that very form, inasmuch as it was not expressed in the Decalogue or moral law, was accidental, and was bound by GOD Himself only to the Israelite people. It is enough, therefore, if the substance of the laws defined in the Decalogue is kept safe and sound: that is, if political laws are pious, honest, and salutary, and congruent with the moral law, which is the perpetual rule of the divine will concerning the things and actions of men, and consequently with natural law or equity. If the laws of any Republic are such, although they may differ from the Mosaic forensic laws regarding the types of punishments and the external form of judgment, they are to be borne and used, and not abrogated: nor are those Mosaic ones to be recalled into use. For just as

GOD Himself did not will that all people, and thus the Christian also, be bound by this forensic form of the Israelite Republic: so He also permitted the Christian Magistrate of the New Testament the freedom, according to the condition of the time, the people, and the Church, as well as the diversity of other circumstances, to constitute a certain form of judgments, and indeed one different from the Israelite, provided that the foundation and the very substance of the divine will expressed in the Decalogue is in no part violated or changed. Let the most learned Treatise of Hadrianus Junius, 'De politia Mosis observatione', Tom. 1. Operum, Col. 1473 et seqq., be consulted on this matter.

The other medium, which the Magistrate uses in performing his duty, is Judgment. For since there is no use for laws unless they are directed to that end for whose sake they were enacted: namely, that the honor of GOD may be promoted, the pious affected with rewards, and the impious with punishments: therefore there is need of Judgment, in which, according to the laws, sentence may be passed concerning individual matters contributing to this end. But what process, what form of judgments is best, and what is primarily to be observed: the civil laws show this in general, while provincial and municipal laws show it in particular: concerning which we also determine that the schools and books of politicians and jurists are to be consulted: inculcating at least this one authentic rule, to be well observed, from Moses to individual and all judges: Hear the causes of your brethren, and judge justly between a man and his brother, and between his stranger: You shall not respect the face in judgment: you shall hear the small as well as the great: nor shall you fear any man: nor shall you accept the person of anyone, because it is the judgment of GOD. Deut. 1. 13, 16, 17. And that other one of King Jehoshaphat: See what you do, for you do not exercise the judgment of man, but of GOD: and whatever you shall judge, it will redound upon you: Let the fear of the Lord be with you: and do all things with diligence: for there is no iniquity with the LORD our GOD, nor acceptance of persons, nor desire of gifts. 2 Paral. 19, 6 and 7.

The third and last medium, which the Magistrate uses in performing his duty, is the Execution of Judgment. For there is not the slightest profit in judging, unless the matter judged is brought into action, or handed over for execution. This, however, consists in the defense of the good and the punishment of the bad: where, on this side, excessive severity, and on that side, excessive indulgence, must be accurately guarded against. For just as excessive severity eventually degenerates into cruelty, so that the punishment more often anticipates the just and legitimate investigation of the committed crime, or establishes a harsher punishment than the nature of the committed offense demands: so excessive indulgence diminishes, loosens, and removes the authority of the Magistrate and the bonds of the laws: and it is most hateful to GOD, as is evident from the example of the preposterous clemency of Saul toward King Agag: 1 Samuel 15, 9. To this execution of judgment also pertains the undertaking of wars against enemies, if the glory of GOD, the safety of the Republic, and the security of the citizens so demand, and the enemies cannot be kept in check by other legitimate means. Where, however, all rashness must be carefully avoided, which rushes to arms as if with a blind impulse. For here that saying holds true: It becomes a wise man to try everything with counsel before arms.

But let these things said regarding the duty of the Political Magistrate concerning the second table of the Decalogue suffice: since they pertain more to the political than to the theological forum. That question seems to us more important and more necessary to explain, which is agitated concerning the duty of the civil Magistrate regarding the first table of the Decalogue: Namely, what and what kind of care belongs to him regarding asserting, preserving, and propagating Religion: concerning which it pleases us to discourse first in general: and then indeed in particular.

Latin:

OFficium Magistratus Politici, brevi quidem, sed satis accurata definitione expressit Apostolus, Rom 3. 1. 3. 4. Omnis, inquiens, Magistratus (Politicus) est minister DEI, & quidem a DEO ipso ordinatus, gladioque, & publica autoritate instructus, ultor ad iram ei, qui quod malum est, fecerit: approbatur vero in laudem eorum, qui quod bonum est, fecerint. Emergit hinc geminum Magistratus Politici officium, secundum duas decalogi tabulas.

Primum enim, quoad priorem tabulam, minister DEI esse debet, ipsi principaliter servire, & quæ ad ejus honorem, cultumque verum promovendum faciunt, suo loco ac modo sedulò curare. Quo de officio disserit etiam David, Psal. 2, 10. & seqq. Erudimini reges, qui judicatis terram; Servite DOMINO in timore, & exultate ei cum tremore: Osculamini filium, ne irascatur DOMINUS, & pereatis de via justa. Posterius Magistratus Politici officium, quoad posteriorem Decalogi tabulam, respicit Justitiam externam sive civilem, in rebus corporalibus. eamque tum togatam, tum bellicam sive militarem: cujus utriusque finis & scopus principalis est, pax & tranquillitas publica: Salus civium: & libertas patriæ: in laudem & commodum bonorum: & pœnam malorum, uti nostra habet definitio. Respectu utriusque hujus officii, duæ vulgo constituuntur Reipublicæ columnæ: RELIGIO, & JUSTITIA. Illa quod DEO: hæc quod patriæ & subditis debetur, recte, ordine, & secundum leges curat.

Et hinc vulgatum illud principium & Magnatum Symbolum: PRO ARIS & FOCIS.

Cæterum in expediundo suo hoc officio, tribus potissimum mediis utitur Magistratus

Politicus: nempe, Legibus: Judicio: Judicii executione. Quoad Leges, debent ex initio cum Lege Naturæ, & DEI voluntate consentire. Cum enim Magistratus DEI sit Minister, nihil statuere aut decernere debet, quod hujus voluntati sit adversum. Hanc verò voluntatem suam patefecit DEUS in lege partim morali sive Decalogo, partim forensi sive Judiciali: qua utráque admirabili brevitate, singula & universa est complexus; quæ tùm ad totius Reipublicæ, tùm ad singulorum civium gubernationem laudabilem & salutarem faciunt. Etsi enim leges nonnullæ, ad solum Judæorum Rempublicam, pro temporum illorum, & terræ promissæ conditione, pertinere videntur; tamen hæ ipsæ quoque monstrant eos Judiciorum fontes, ad quos omnis vera νομοθεσία commodè dirigi, & accuratè examinari queat: ita ut vel solum Decalogum fontem omnium aliarum legum, haud falsò quis nominare possit. Ex legibus enim primæ tabulæ de vero DEI cultu, omnia ea fluxerunt, quæ Minos, Solon, Lycurgus, Charondas, Zaleucus, Numa, Decemviri Romani, aliíque Legislatores de suorum Deorum cultu, licèt corruptissima, tradiderunt: Quæ item Imperatores Christiani hac de re constituerunt. Hinc in Codice Justinianeo ortæ sunt tituli & leges, de S. Trinitate, & fide catholica: de sacrosanctis Ecclesiis: de Episcopis & clericis, de hæreticis, de apostatis, de blasphemiis, de juramentu. Jam quoad præcepta secundæ tabulæ, continent ea sub suo ambitu & rerum & personarum, & actionum genera & differentias. Nam primo secundæ tabulæ præcepto monstrantur ordine personarum discrimina, & ad modum legis Naturæ præcipitur pietas; & honor erga parentes, & eos qui parentum loco sunt; erga Principes, Magistratus, tutores, præceptores, ministros Ecclesiæ: quæ item dominorum, servorum, patronorum, clientum, libertorum officia. Ex hoc ergo primo præcepto secundæ tabulæ, petita sunt: quæ de jure personarum, de statu hominum, de officiis Magistratuum, de officio præsidis, proconsulis &c. Item de liberis agnoscendis, de adoptionibus; de tutelis, de operis libertorum, de servis, de his, qui sunt sui vel alieni juris, de manumissionibus & similibus, in jure civili tradita sunt; quæ omnia ad hunc fontem de parentibus honorandis pertinentia, disciplinæ & obedientiæ ac vocationis cujusque rationem habendam præcipiunt.

Alterum secundæ tabulæ præceptum prohibitorium est de non occidendo: Unde profectæ sunt Leges civiles de homicidiis, de parricidiis; de sicariis, de pœnis, de quæstionibus, de injuriis, de talione, de lege Aquilia, & hujus generis leges & constitutiones aliæ.

Huic præcepto optimo ordine subjungitur Adulterii prohibitio: ex quo edicto leges de adulteriis, de stupris, de incestu, de sponsalibus, de nuptiis & matrimonio, de divortiis natæ sunt.

Quarto secundæ tabulæ præcepto, Furtum & alienæ rei contrectatio, interdicitur, quæ fit invito Domino: item fraudes in contractibus, omnisq́; generis injustæ occupationes possessionesq́; alienarum rerum. Atque ita hoc præcepto, Rerum distinctio sancitur: Nam cùm furta prohibet DEUS, singulos vult suas res proprias tenere. Ad hoc igitur præceptum pertinent, quæ de rerum divisione, de acquirendo rerum dominio, de rei vindicatione, triente & semisse, de successionibus, de petitione hæreditatis, familiæ herciscundæ, de testamentis, de legatis: quæ item de furtis, de peculatu, de sacrilegiis passim traduntur in Jure civili. Actiones autem etsi sparsim sicut & res è pluribus præceptis scaturiunt, ea tamen quæ præcepto quinto de falso testimonio vitando præcipiuntur, satis declarant, ex hoc fonte Judicia, actionesq́; oriri: ac proinde ad hoc præceptum pertinere, quæ de accusationibus, de calumniatoribus, de lege dissamari, de prævaricatoribus, de testibus, de probationibus, de exceptionibus, de edendo instrumento, de fide instrumentorum, de Judiciis, de sententiâ & re judicata, de appellationibus, in Jure civili leges continentur. Ad sextum & septimum, postrema nimirùm duo Decalogi præcepta, de concupiscentia, tametsi aliqui referunt actiones legis Aquiliæ, legis Juliæ, de adulteris, de Abigeis, de servo corrupto, si quadrupes pauperiem fecerit, termini moti, civium regendorum, totamq́; adeò & œconomiam & politiam: tamen hæc ipsa ad superiora præcepta liberiùs rectiùsque referuntur, proptereà quòd doctrina de concupiscentia, duobus hisce præceptis tradita, est Ecclesiæ DEI propria, quippe quæ non tam ipsa malefacta, opere ipso designata, quàm internas animi concupiscentias, cogitatione saltem vel imaginatione conceptas, in actum licet nunquam erumpentes, accusat, & damnat. Monstrat verò hæc legum civilium cum præceptis Decalogi collatio, quis Spiritus fanaticus, certè Anabaptisticus, regat & moveat Herbornenses, qui contendunt, leges; Mosaicas forenses in usum simpliciter revocandas esse, antiquatis legibus Imperatorum, quasi hæ cum Decalogo, præsertim quoad pœnas delictorum non conveniant. Sed temerarium est, abrogationem earum legum quærere, quæ in fundamento ipso cum Decalogo conveniunt: & quamvis in circumstantiis nonnullis discrepent ab ea forma Judiciorum, quæ in lege forensi Judæis præscripta fuit: notandum tamen illam ipsam formam, quippe in Decalogo, sive lege morali non expressam, fuisse accidentis, & ab ipso DEO ad populum tantùm Israëliticum alligatam. Satis ergo est, si substantia legum in Decalogo definita, sarta tecta retineatur: hoc est, si leges politicæ sint piæ, honestæ, salutares, cum lege morali, quæ est perpetua voluntatis divinæ circa res & actiones hominum regula, & consequenter cum Jure sive æquitate naturali congruentes. Tales si sint leges alicujus Reipub. licet quoad pœnarum genera, & externam Judicii formam, à Mosaicis forensibus discrepent, ferendæ & usurpandæ sunt, neque abrogandæ: aut Mosaicæ illæ in usum revocandæ. Quemadmodum enim

DEus ipse noluit forensi hac Reipub. Israeliticæ forma, omnem populum, & sic Christianum quoque obligari: ita liberum etiam permisit Christiano Magistratui Novi Testamenti, pro conditione temporis, populi, Ecclesiæ, ut & pro diversitate aliarum circumstantiarum, certam judiciorum formam constituere, & quidem ab Israëliticâ diversam, modò fundamentum & substantia ipsa voluntatis divinæ in Decalogo expressæ, nulla ex parte violetur aut mutetur. Videatur hac de re eruditissimus Tractatus Hadriani Junii de politia Mosis observatione Tom. 1. Operum. Col. 1473. & seqq.

Alterum medium, quo Magistratus in suo obeundo munere utitur, est Judicium. Cum enim nullus legum usus sit, nisi ad finem eum dirigantur, cujus gratiâ eæ sunt latæ: nimirum ut DEI honor promoveatur, piis præmiis, impii pœnis afficiantur: ideò Judicio, opus est, in quo secundum leges, de singulis ad finem hunc facientibus, feratur sententia. Quis autem processus, quæ forma judiciorum sit optima, quæque cumprimis observanda: illud partim leges civiles generatim: partim verò Jura provincialia & municipalia, in specie ostendunt: de quibus etiam politicorum & ICtorum scholas & libros consulendos esse statuimus: Unam saltem hanc authenticam probè observandam, ex Mose singulis & universis Judicibus inculcantes: Audite causas fratrum vestrorum, & judicate justè inter virum & fratrem ejus, & inter peregrinum ejus: Non recipietis faciem in judicio: tàm parvum, quam magnum audietis: neq; timebitis ab ullo viro: neq; accipietis personam cujusquam, quia DEI Judicium est. Deut. 1. 13, 16, 17. Et illam alteram Regis Josaphati: Videte, quid faciatis, non enim hominis exercetis judicium, sed DEI: & quodcunq; judicaveritis, in vos redundabit: Sit timor Domini vobiscum: & cum diligentia cuncta facite: non enim est apud DOMINUM DEUM nostrum iniquitas, nec personarum acceptio, nec cupiditas munerum 2. Paral. 19, 6. & 7.

Tertium & postremum medium, quo Magistratus in suo peragendo munere utitur, est Judicii Executio. Neque enim judicando vel tantillum proficitur, nisi res judicata in actum deducatur, sive executione tradatur. Hæc verò consistit, in defensioni bonorum, & pœna malorum: Ubi ex hac quidem parte, nimia severitas; ex illa verò, nimia indulgentia accuratè caveri debet.
