Quemadmodum enim nimia severitas, tandem in crudelitatem degenerat, ut pœna sæpius vel admissi sceleris justam legitimamque cognitionem antevertat: vel duriorem pœnam statuat, quàm admissi flagitii ratio postulat: Ita nimia indulgentia autoritatem Magistratus, & legum vincula minuit, solvit, tollit: Deoque vel maximè est exosa, uti patet exemplo præposteræ clementiæ Saulus in Regem Agagum: 1. Samuel. 15, 9. Pertinet ad hanc Judicii executionem etiam Bellorum susceptio contra hostes, si ita DEI gloria, Reipub. salus, & civium incolumitas exigat, neque aliis mediis legitimis, hostes in officio contineri possint. Ubi tamen probè cavenda est Temeritas omnis, quæ cæco quasi impetu ad arma prosilit. Hic enim locum habet illud: Omnia consilio priùs, quàm armis experiri sapientem decet.

Sed hæc de officio Magistratus Politici quoad secundam Decalogi tabulam, dicta sufficiant: quippe ad politicum magis, quàm Theologicum forum pertinentia. Potior & explicatu magis necessaria ea nobis videtur quæstio, quæ de officio Magistratus civilis circa primam Decalogi tabulam, agitatur: Quæ nimirum & qualis cura ipsi competat circa Religionem asserendam, conservandam, propagandam: de qua primùm in genere: Deinde verò in specie disserere placet.


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: I. on the Office of the Political Magistrate concerning Religion, in general

Just as the third commandment of the Decalogue binds all men to the Sanctification of the Sabbath: so it demands from the Political Magistrate above all, that he devote effort diligently, and by his authority as well as by laws bring it about, that pure Religion be preserved: that the exercises of piety flourish rightly in temples and schools: that all things in temples be done and conducted in order and decently: that finally the Sabbath be rightly sanctified by the whole Church, that is, that the worship of GOD be performed by the Ministers and all the Auditors, as is fitting. Now that observation deserves mention in general, that Political Magistrates, for no other reason more than this, are named in the Scriptures as Nursing Fathers and nursing mothers of the Church: Isaiah 49:23. Servants and ministers of GOD, the LORD'S anointed, than because GOD uses even their work for the preservation of His Church and religion. Certainly they cannot be so named on account of political administration: otherwise these distinguished titles would belong also to impious and infidel Magistrates: nor even on account of the profession of the Christian Religion: since they have that in common with all auditors and citizens of the Church, who nevertheless are not distinguished by these illustrious titles in the Scriptures. Thus we nowhere read in the Scriptures that either the Jewish Kings were ever rebuked by the Prophets, or Emperors or Magistrates by the Church, because they took up the care of Religion: But rather we see them praised, because they proclaimed councils when heretics were spreading: because they purged temples from heresies, propagated religion, and asserted it safe and sound by solemnly promulgated laws, as is most clearly evident from the Justinian Code. And although a purer Religion ought to be a care and concern to every Christian, yet this care is too general and common; nor does it rise to that special and principal care which the Political Magistrate, by reason of the power divinely granted, is bound to perform singularly and according to certain and distinct duties concerning Religion, by the very command of GOD. To which opinion Augustine writes excellently in his explanation of the second Psalm: How then do Kings serve the LORD in fear, unless by prohibiting and punishing with religious severity those things which are against the commands of the LORD? For he serves in one way because he is a man: in another way, because he is also a King. Because he is a man, he serves Him by living faithfully: but because he is also a King, he serves Him by enacting laws that command what is just and prohibit the contrary, with appropriate vigor. As Hezekiah served, by destroying the groves and temples of idols, and those high places which had been built against the commands of GOD. As Josiah served, by doing such things himself. As the King of the Ninevites served, by compelling the whole city to appease the LORD. As Darius served, by giving Daniel the power to break the idol, and by casting his enemies to the lions. As Nebuchadnezzar served, of whom we have already spoken, by prohibiting all those placed in his kingdom from blaspheming GOD, by a terrible law. In this, therefore, kings serve the LORD, in so far as they are kings, when they do those things to serve Him which they cannot do unless they are kings. And what need is there of many words, when the Gentiles themselves, destitute of the true knowledge of the true GOD, judged that the care of their religion belonged to their princes.

It pertains here that GOD wills the Magistrate to be the guardian of both tables, that he should always have the volume of the law in his hands, and that he should take notice of idolaters and blasphemers, false Prophets and seducers, just as much as of Murderers and adulterers. For why, I ask, did the Athenians condemn Socrates? Because they did not want to permit a new religion, concerning the worship of only one GOD, as Socrates wanted, to be introduced. Why likewise did Tiberius not want to refer Christ into the number of the Gods, unless the consent of the Roman Senate was added? Because, indeed, he had learned, even from the light of nature, that this care pertained to him.

Moreover, if we consider more accurately both the sacred Scriptures and the examples of Christian Emperors, Kings, and Princes, it is permitted to gather that various and distinct duties of the Political Magistrate concerning Religion can be established: which, however, can be reduced to two general kinds as it were: of which one directly regards the things themselves pertaining to the business of Religion; the other indeed regards men or subjects.

Regarding the first kind, the duty of the Magistrate at the beginning is, seriously and with all zeal to provide that in the provinces subject to him, pure Religion may be set forth from the fountains of Israel according to the analogy of faith: that errors, schisms, heresies, and corruptions may be soundly refuted and, as far as possible, removed from the midst: and thus the glory of GOD, the purity of Religion, and the welfare of the Church may be promoted: after the example of Joshua, Samuel, David, Hezekiah, and others.

Then he shall take care that not only ordinary and, as it were, weekly meetings of the Ministers of the Word are instituted, but also annual or even semi-annual visitations, for the express purpose that the life and morals of the hearers, more atrocious vices, the labors of the Ministers themselves, the discipline and ecclesiastical εὐταξία (good order) as a whole, and finally corruptions creeping in secretly in doctrine, may be judged more accurately: after the example of Moses, Exod. 32, 20; King Asa, 1 Kings 15, 12 & 13; King Jehu, 2 Kings 10, 25 & 26; Hezekiah, 2 Kings 18, 4 & 5; Josiah, 2 Kings 23, 4, 5 & 6; Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 19, 4, 8 & 9.

Thirdly, he shall set over the Church pure and orthodox Doctors, whose piety and sincerity are openly established: after the example of King Jehoiada, 2 Chron. 23, 18; Hezekiah, 2 Chron. 29, 10, 11; Josiah, 2 Chron. 36, throughout the whole chapter.

Fourthly, he shall take care that Ecclesiastical goods, bequeathed by ancestors for pious uses, are administered rightly and by faithful men: and that from them the ministers of the Church and schools, the poor, and especially those who seem apt to handle letters and studies, are sustained, and that sacred buildings are kept in good repair: after the example of Pharaoh, Gen. 47, 5 & 6; David, 1 Chron. 92, 2; Hiram, 1 Kings 5, 10; Solomon, 1 Kings 8, 64; Cyrus, Ezra 1, 67; Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel 1, 3 & 4. Especially King Joash, who, noticing that the sacred money was not being administered by the Priests in very good faith, took the care of this matter upon himself, 2 Kings 12, 6 & seqq. The same care regarding the public buildings of temples and schools is read to have been taken by Solomon, 1 Kings 5, 4 & 5 and ch. 6, 2; Josiah, 2 Kings 22, 3, 4 & 5; Cyrus, 2 Chron. 36, 22; Darius, Ezra 6, 2 & 3.

Finally, he shall remove and utterly take away idols and all those things by which the people impiously abuse themselves toward Idolatry and superstition, after the example of Moses crushing the golden calf fashioned by Aaron to be worshipped in the place of GOD: Exod. 32, 20. Likewise after the example of King Hezekiah breaking in pieces the bronze serpent, the high places, and the idolatrous statues, 2 Kings 18, 4. And thus indeed stands the duty of the political Magistrate in general regarding Religion, or the true worship of the true GOD: as far as things pertaining to the business of Religion are concerned. Now, however, if the Magistrate's duty is weighed a little more specially, and indeed regarding men or the subjects themselves, many questions occur, difficult to explain both in theory and in practice: concerning which, without prejudice to the sounder wishes and opinions of others, we shall show what seems to us to be the case.

what

Latin:

QUemadmodum omnes homines ad Sanctificationem Sabbati, tertium Decalogi præceptum obstringit: ita à Magistratu cumprimis Politico exigit, operam ille det sedulò, & sua tùm autoritate, tùm legibus efficiat, ut pura Religio conservetur: ut pietatis exercitia in templis scholisque ritè floreant: ut omnia in templis ordinè & decenter fiant & gerantur: ut denique ab universa Ecclesia Sabbatum rectè sanctificetur, hoc est, cultus DEI ex parte Ministrorum, & Auditorum omnium, prout decet, peragatur. Jam illud observationem in genere meretur, quod Magistratus Politici, nullam aliam magis ob causam, in Scripturis nominantur Nutritii, & reginæ nutrices Ecclesiæ: Esaiæ: 49, 23. Servi & ministri DEI, uncti DEI, quàm quod ipsorum etiam opera DEUS utitur, ad Ecclesiæ & religionis suæ conservationem. Certè propter administrationem politicam sic nominari non possunt: aliàs insignia isthæc elogia competerent etiam impiis, & infidelibus Magistratibus: neque etiam propter professionem Religionis Christianæ: quippe quam cum omnibus auditoribus & civibus Ecclesiæ communem habent, qui tamen his præclaris elogiis in Scripturis non insigniuntur. Sic nuspiam in Scripturis legimus, vel Reges Judaicos à Prophetis, vel ab Ecclesia Imperatores aut Magistratus eos unquam fuisse reprehensos, quòd curam susceperunt Religionis: Quin potiùs laudari videmus eos, quòd grassantibus hæreticis concilia indixerunt: quòd templa ab hæresibus repurgarunt, Religionem propagarunt, eamque legibus solemniter promulgatis, sartam tectam asseruerunt, uti ex Codice Justinianeo clarissimè patet. Et quanquam cuilibet Christiano purior Religio curæ cordiq; esse debet; hæc tamen cura nimis est generalis & communis; neque ad eam assurgit specialem & principalem curam, quam Magistratus Politicus ratione potestatis, divinitus concessæ, singulariter & secundum certa ac distincta officia, circa Religionem, ex ipsius DEI mandato, præstare tenetur. Quam in sententiam præclarè scribit Augustinus in explicatione Psalmi secundi: Quomodo ergo Reges serviunt DOMINO in timore, nisi ea quæ contra jussa DOMINI sunt, religiosa severitate prohibendo atque plectendo ? Aliter enim servit, quia homo est: aliter, quia etiam Rex est. Quia homo est, ei servit vivendo fideliter: Quia verò etiam Rex est, servit ei, leges justa præcipientes, & contraria prohibentes, conveniente vigore sanci endo. Sicut servivit Ezechias, lucos & templa idolorum, & illa excelsa, quæ contra DEI præcepta fuerant constructa, destruendo. Sicut servivit Josias, talia & ipse faciendo. Sicut servivit Rex Ninivitarum, universam civitatem ad placandum DOMINUM compellendo. Sicut servivit Darius, idolum frangendum in potestatem Danieli dando, & inimicos ejus leonibus ingerendo. Sicut servivit Nebuchodonosor, de quo jam diximus, omnes in suo regno positos, à blasphemando DEO, lege terribili prohibendo. In hoc ergo DOMINO serviunt reges, in quantum sunt reges, cum ea faciunt ad serviendum illi, quæ non possunt facere nisi reges. Et quid multis opus est, cum Gentiles ipsi, vera veri DEI agnitione destituti, principibus suis curam Religionis suæ competere judicarint.

Pertinet huc quod DE us Magistratum vult esse custodem utriusque tabulæ, ut volumen legis semper habeat in manibus suis, & ut tam in idololatras atque blasphemos, falsos Prophetas atque seductores, quàm in Homicidas atque adulteros animadvertat. Cur enim quæso Athenienses damnarunt Socratem? Quia nolebant permittere, ut nova Religio, de uno tantùm DEO colendo, uti Socrates volebat, inveheretur. Cur item Tiberius noluit Christum referre in numerum Deorum, nisi accederet consensus Senatus Romani? Quia nimirùm hanc curam ad ipsum pertinere, vel ex lumine naturæ didicerat.

Cæterùm si & Scripturas sacras, & exempla Christianorum Imperatorum, Regum, atque Principum accuratiùs consideremus, varia atque distincta Magistratus Politici officia, circa Religionem constitui posse, colligere licet: quæ tamen ad duo summa quasi genera revocari possunt: quorum unum res ipsas ad Religionis negocium pertinentes; alterum verò homines sive subditos directè respicit.

Quoad primum genus, officium Magistratus initiò est, seriò atque omni studioprovidere, ut in provinciis sibi subjectis, pura Religio ex fontibus Israëlis secundum analogiam fidei proponatur: errores, schismata, hæreses & corruptelæ solidè & refutentur, & quantum fieri potest, è medio tollantur: & sic gloria DEI: Religionis puritas: Ecclesiæ salus promoveatur: exemplo Josuæ, Samuelis, Davidis, Ezechiæ & aliorum.

Deinde curabit, ut non modò conventus Ecclesiæ ordinarii & quasi hebdomadarii inter Ministros Verbi, sed & anniversariæ vel semestrales etiam visitationes instituantur, eo potissimùm fine, ut de Auditorum vita & moribus, de vitiis atrocioribus, de ipsorum etiam Ministrorum laboribus, de disciplina & εὐταξίᾳ Ecclesiastica universa, & tandem de corruptelis in doctrina clanculùm irrepentibus, accuratiùs judicari queat: exemplo Mosis: Exod. 32, 20. regis Asæ, 1. Reg. 15, 12. & 13. regis Jehu, 2. Reg. 10, 25. & 26. Ezechiæ, 2. Reg. 18, 4. & 5. Josiæ, 2. Reg. 23, 4. 5. & 6. Josaphati, 2. Paral. 19, 4. 8. & 9.

Tertiò, præficiet Ecclesiæ puros & orthodoxos Doctores, de quorum & pietate, & sinceritate palàm constet: exemplo regis Jojadæ, 2. Paral. 23, 18. Ezechiæ, 2. Par. 29, 10. 11. Josiæ, 2. Paral. 36. per totum caput.

Quartò, Bona Ecclesiastica, inque pios usus à majoribus legata, rectè, & per viros fideles administrari: indeque Ecclesiæ scholarumque ministros, pauperes, & eos cumprimis, qui ad literas & studia tractanda apta esse videntur, sustentari, ut & ædificia sacra, sarta tecta conservari, curabit: exemplo Pharaonis, Genes. 47, 5. & 6. Davidis, 1. Paral. 92, 2. Hirami, 1. Reg. 5, 10. Salomonis, 1. Reg. 8, 64. Cyri, Esdræ 1, 67. Nebucadnezaris, Daniel. 1, 3. & 4. Imprimis Regis Joas, qui animadvertens pecuniam sacram à Sacerdotibus fide haud usque adeò bona administrari, ipsemet rei hujus curam suscepit, 2. Reg. 12, 6. & seqq. Quam ipsam curam circa ædificia publica templorum & scholarum gessisse leguntur, Salomon, 1. Reg. 5, 4. 5. & cap. 6, 2. Josias, 2. Reg. 22, 3. 4. & 5. Cyrus, 2. Paral. 36, 22. Darius, Esdræ 6, 2. & 3.

Tandem idola & omnia ea, quibus populus ad Idololatriam & superstitionem impiè abutitur, amovebit, & penitùs tollet, exemplo Mosis comminuentis vitulum aureum ab Aarone DEI loco colendum, conflatum: Exod. 32, 20. Exemplo item Regis Ezechiæ conterentis serpentem æneum, excelsa & statuas idololatricas, 2. Reg. 18, 4. Et sic quidem se habet officium Magistratus politici in genere circa Religionem, sive verum veri DEI cultum: quoad res ad Religionis negocium pertinentes. Jam verò si paulò specialius, & quidem quoad homines sive subditos ipsos, Magistratus officium pensitetur, multæ occurrunt quæstiones, quà theoriam, quà praxin, explicatu difficiliores: de quibus, salvis sanioribus aliorum votis atque sententiis, quid nobis videatur, ostendemus.

qùid


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: On the Office of the Political Magistrate Specifically considered with regard to subjects

QUESTION I.

Latin:

QUÆSTIO I.


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: Whether a Christian Political Magistrate can & ought to force his subjects to embrace the true Religion?

Regarding the decision of this question, it does not seem one and the same to all. And although in the time of Augustine a sharp question was raised on this matter, yet such a decision of his can scarcely be elicited from the responses of Augustine, which could satisfy the conscience in every part and satisfy the solid removal of all doubts occurring in this place. The heretical Donatists at that time certainly denied simply that anyone could or should be compelled by the Magistrate to embrace the true Religion: but rather that it should be permitted that each one believe what he wishes, and worship God according to his own whim and judgment. Whence it happened that Petilianus, the primary champion of the Donatists, in publicly written letters, complained gravely that he and his associates in Religion were being compelled by force by the Emperors to the Catholic faith. To this Augustine replies: We do not persecute you, except in the way that truth persecutes falsehood: Vol. 7, book 2, against the letters of Petilianus, Chapter 82. My column 135. This is what Augustine means, that no injury is done to the Donatists by this persecution, because by this means their salvation is sought. When Petilianus objected (chapter 83), Far be it, far be it from our conscience that we should compel anyone to our faith: Augustine replied: No one is indeed to be compelled to the faith against their will, but through the severity, and indeed through the mercy of GOD, perfidy is accustomed to be chastised by the scourges of tribulations. Is it the case that, because the best morals are chosen by the freedom of the will, therefore the worst morals are not punished by the integrity of the law? But yet, discipline that avenges evil living is preposterous, unless when the preceding doctrine of good living is despised. If, therefore, any laws have been established against you, you are not compelled to do good by them: but you are prohibited from doing evil. For no one can do good unless they have chosen it, unless they have loved it, which is in the free will: however, the fear of punishments, even if it does not yet have the delight of a good conscience, at least restrains evil desire within the confines of thought. Those, however, who established the opposing laws, by which your audacity might be suppressed, are they not those of whom the Apostle says: And because they do not bear the sword in vain, for they are ministers of GOD, avengers in wrath to him who does evil.

And a little later: Whom do you fear, either the laws themselves, or the envy, or are you unequal to resisting, I do not say against so many men, but against so many Catholic nations, even boasting of gentleness, because you compel no one to your side. In this way also the kite, when it could not snatch the chicks from the frightened [mother], calls itself a dove. For where you could and did not do it? Whence you show that you would do more if you could.

And ch. 84, Petilianus objecting: Our Lord Christ says: No one comes to me, unless the Father has drawn him. Why therefore do you not permit everyone to follow free will, since the LORD GOD himself gave free will to men, yet showing the way of Justice, lest anyone perhaps perish in ignorance. Augustine answers among other things: Just as it can happen that those whom GOD has left in free will, he nevertheless draws to the Son: so it can happen that those things which are admonished by the coercions of the laws do not take away free will.

The sum of this whole discussion is this, that Augustine holds and defends the affirmative against Petilianus; namely, that it is lawful for the Magistrate to compel subjects by external force and punishments to embrace the true faith or Religion: for three reasons especially: 1. because such force and coercion results in the salvation of those who err. 2. because it prohibits and restrains the evil desires of those in error. 3. because it does not take away free will, but admonishes and excites it, so that it may pass from evil to good, from error to truth.

He also strives to defend this same affirmative at length, Epist. 48 to Vincentius, asserting in express words that he indeed had previously approved the opinion of the Donatists, that no one should be compelled to the Catholic faith by external force or punishments; but afterwards, confirmed partly by the oracles of the sacred scriptures, partly by experience, he had learned that one must think and act otherwise: because by edict and punishments, and the fear of them, many cities, and among these also Hippo, his fatherland, had been brought to the Catholic faith. And this same opinion of Augustine is held by Hieronymus Zanchius, lib. 1 de Imaginibus cap. 15, moved by the following reasons:

1. Because the Magistrate is instructed by God for this reason, that he may restrain not only those who transgress the second, but also those who transgress the first table: that he may promote true religion, having overthrown errors and idolatries, as far as it can be done by him.

2. Because all authority, as much to Magistrates as to pastors, is given by GOD, not that they may use it for destruction, but for edification: Rom. 13. 4. If therefore a pious Magistrate sees that nothing can be an impediment, but that the use of his sword results in the glory of GOD, and in the good of the Church: he ought in no way to omit it.

3. Because God teaches by his own example that this is to be done: for he compels his elect, if words of admonition and correction do not suffice, to recede from evil by stripes, and to turn themselves

to good. And in the parable of the supper he said concerning some: Compel them to enter, Luke 14. 23.

4. Good parents do the same toward their children, and teachers toward their students, who cannot be taught by simple admonitions. To this point tends that saying: He who spares the rod, hates his son. True love, therefore, demands that you use the rod when there is need.

Furthermore, that we may explain more clearly what our view is, we must first carefully examine what properly comes into controversy in this place, and what does not. The question is not: Whether a Christian Magistrate is appointed by GOD as guardian of both tables, and consequently whether he ought to take care of those things which pertain to the first table, namely the worship of GOD and religion, as well as those which are proper to the second table? For on this point, we also hold the affirmative against the Papists. Nor is it in controversy: Whether a Christian Magistrate ought to diligently take care that in his principality or kingdom, the true Religion is defended against any heretics whatsoever, publicly and privately, according to the Word of GOD and the analogy of faith? For here too we hold the affirmative in all respects, and for this very reason we judge those Republics, provinces, kingdoms, and empires blessed, whose Emperors, Kings, and Princes are so led by the Spirit of God that they hold nothing more important or ancient than the assertion and propagation of the purer Religion: so that they themselves understand what makes for the peace and salvation of Israel: so that, finally, they may also, by legitimate means, remove each and every obstacle which seems able to delay or inhibit the course of sound doctrine: by the example of that Constantine the Great, who, having convened the Nicene Synod, saw to it that the heresy of Arius was condemned: by the example of both Theodosiuses, Marcian, and other Emperors who, having convened Synods, repressed the heresies that had arisen.

Finally, the question is not raised in this place concerning any Magistrate whatsoever, and thus not concerning an impious or heretical one. For whatever care is undertaken for the propagation of an impious religion or heresy, that is illicit, impious, and hateful to God, both with respect to the Magistrate himself and the subjects. But the Question is only concerning a Christian Magistrate κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν so called, that is, concerning an orthodox Magistrate; Whether, if by chance he has subjects addicted to a diverse and heretical Religion, he can and ought to compel them to his own Religion? To define this question, which is highly controversial in our century and, because of the diversity of opinions, more difficult to explain, more accurately: certain Hypotheses and Distinctions must be observed: which being observed, the Decision of this question will emerge of its own accord, both plain and clear.

As for the Hypotheses, we provide primarily two. The PRIOR is this: the true and orthodox Religion claims this as its own unique property, that it was neither introduced into the world by external arms or violent arguments and aids, nor extended, nor propagated down to our own times: but it was scattered and disseminated solely by the preaching of the Word, through the mediation of the power of the Holy Spirit, among all nations, throughout the whole world, without any clatter of arms or use of the external sword. Alcoran, certainly, was disseminated at the beginning by arms throughout the entire Orient, and was preserved down to this our own age by the protection of arms: just as Mahomet himself did not hesitate to boast: That he was sent not in the power of miracles, but of the sword. Thus, ecclesiastical history records quite at length how the Arian heresy persecuted the orthodox Church of Christ, and by external force, especially with certain Emperors acting as auxiliaries, occupied not only the Orient, but almost the entire Christian world. Thus, it is more than sufficiently well known, without need of laborious proof, how the Pontifical religion invaded almost the entire West by external machinations, arts, frauds, and persecutions, and infected almost every single part of the European world. Thus, Sleidan’s history clearly records how the Anabaptist scum sought to establish their religion initially through the Westphalia by external arms, and subsequently to propagate it. That the Calvinists also seek and attempt the incrustation and propagation of their own dogmas by these very same means, efforts, and external machinations, cannot be obscure to him who weighs a little more deeply the matters managed here and there concerning religion, and indeed against the Lutherans: so that if their strength corresponded to their will and designs, perhaps more, or certainly no less danger and persecution would be to be feared and expected by us from the Calvinist race than from the Pontificals. Therefore, this first hypothesis shows that the true or orthodox Religion, which is the very faith of the Apostles, abhors all such coercion of those who err as is done by arms and external force.

Latin:

CIrca decisionem hujus quæstionis non unum idemque videtur omnibus. Et quanquam tempore Augu stini acris hac de re mota fuit quæstio: talis tamen ejus decisio ex responsionibus Augustini vix elici posse videtur, quæ conscientiam ex omni parte placare, & dubiis omnibus hocloco occurrentibus solide tollendis satisfacere possit. Donatistæ hæretici illo certe tempore simpliciter negabant, a Magistratu quempiam ad veram amplexandam Religionem cogi posse aut debere: sed permittendam potius esse, ut quisq; credat, quod velit, & Deum pro suo nutu ac arbitrio colat. Unde factum, ut Pætilianus Donatistarum primarius hyperaspites, lite ris publice scriptis, graviter conquereretur, se cum suis in Religione sociis, ab Imperatoribus ad fidem Catholicam vi cogi. His respondet Augustinus: Non persequimur vos, nisi quemadmodum veritas persequitur falsitatem: Tom. 7. lib. 2. contra epistolas Pætiliani, Cap. 82. Col. mihi 135. Id nimirum vult Augustinus, Nullam Donatistis fieri injuriam hac persecutione, propterea quod hoc pacto salus ipsorum quæratur. Excipiente Pætiliano (cap. 83.) Absit, absit a nostra conscientia, ut ad nostram fidem aliquem compellamus: respondit Augustinus: Ad fidem quidem nullus est cogendus invitus, sed per severitatem, imo & per misericordiam DEI, tribulationum flagellis solet perfidia castigari. Numquid, quia mores optimi libertate voluntatis eliguntur, ideo mores pessimi non legis integritate puniuntur? Sed tamen male vivendi ultrix disciplina præpostera est, nisi cum præcedens bene vivendi doctrina contemnitur. Si quæ igitur adversus vos leges constitutæ sunt, non eis benefacere cogimini: sed malefacere prohibemini. Nam benefacere nemo potest nisi elegerit, nisi amaverit, quod est in libera voluntate: timor autem pænarum etsi nondum habet delectationem bonæ conscientiæ, saltem intra claustra cogitationis coërcet malam cupiditatem. Qui tamen adversas leges constituerunt, quibus ves stra comprimatur audacia, nonne hi, de quibus dicit ApoAnlu, Et Quia non sine causa gladium portant, ministri enim DEI sunt, vindices in iram ei, qui male agit.

&do Et post pauca: Quis nos vel ipsas leges, vel invidiam formidatis, vel ad resistendum impares estu, non dico adversus tot homines, sed adversus tot gentes Catholicas, etiam de mansuetudine gloriantes, quod ad vestram partem neminem cogitis. Isto modo & milvus, cum pullos rapere territo non potuit, columbum se nominat. Ubi enim potuistu & non fecisti? Unde oftenditis, quod plura faceretis, si possetis.

Et c. 84. objiciente Pætiliano: Dicit Dominus noster Christus: Nemo venit ad me, nisi quem Pater attraxerit. Cur ergo vos non liberum arbitrium unumquemq; sequi permittitis, cum ipse DOMINUS DEUS liberum arbitrium dederit hominibus, viam tamen Justitie ostendens, ne quis forsitan nescius deperiret. Respondet inter reliqua Augustinus: Sicut fieri potest, ut quos DEUS in libero dimisit arbitrio, attrahat tamen ad Filium: sic fieri potest, ut ea quæ legum coërcitionibus admonentur, non auferant liberum arbitrium.

Summa totius disputationis hujus hæc est, quòd Augustinus contra Petilianum Affirmativam tenet ac defendit; Licere nimirùm Magistratui vi externa & pœnis cogere subditos ad veram amplexandam fidem sive Religionem: tribus potissimum de causis: 1. quia talis vis & coactio cedat in salutem errantium. 2. quia prohibeat & coërceat malas cupiditates errorum. 3. quia non tollat liberum arbitrium, sed admoneat & excitet illud, ut à malo ad bonum, ab errore ad veritatem transeat.

Quam ipsam affirmativam prolixè etiam defendere studet, Epist. 48. ad Vincentium, disertis verbis asserens, se quidem anteà Donatistarum approbasse sententiã, neminem externa vi, sive pœnis ad fidem Catholicam esse cogendum; sed postmodum partim sacrarum literarũ oraculis, partim experientia confirmatum didicisse, aliter esse sentiendum & faciendum: eò quod edictu & pœnis, & istarum metu, multæ civitates, & inter has quoq; Hippona patria ad Catholicam fidem sit perducta. Et hanc quidem eandem sententiam Augustini tenet Hieronymus Zanchius, lib. 1. de Imaginibus cap. 15. sequentibus motus rationibus:

1. Quia Magistratus à Deo ideò instructus est gladio, ut non solum compescat, qui secundam, sed etiam qui primam tabulam transgrediuntur: ut veram religionem promoveat, profligatis erroribus & idololatriis, quoad ejus fieri potest omnibus.

2. Quia autoritas omnis, tàm Magistratibus, quàm pastoribus datur à DEO, non ut ad destructionem, sed ad ædificationem illa utantur: Rom. 13. 4. Si ergo videat pius Magistratus, nihil impedimento esse posse, quin usus sui gladij cedat in gloriam DEI, & in bonum Ecclesiæ: nullo modo omittere illum debet.

3. Quia Deus suo exemplo idem docet, esse faciendum: is enim electos suos, si verba admonitionis, correctionisq; non sufficiant, verberibus cogit à malo recedere, & ad bonum

se convertere. Et in parabola cœnæ de quibusdam dixit: Cogite istos intrare, Luc. 14. 23.

4. Faciunt idem boni parentes erga suos liberos, & præceptores erga discipulos, qui simplicibus admonitionibus doceri non possunt. Quo spectat illud: Qui parcit virgæ, odit filium. Amor igitur verus exigit, ut utaris virgâ, cum opus est.

Cæterùm, ut quid nobis videatur, dilucidiùs aperiamus, initiò probè dispiciendum, quid propriè hoc loco in controversiam veniat, quid non? Non autem de eo quæritur: An Magistratus Christianus, custos à DEO sit constitutus utriusq; tabulæ, ac proinde tàm eas quæ ad primam tabulam, cultum nimirum DEI, & religionem pertinent, quàm quæ secundæ tabulæ propriæ sunt, curare debeat? Nam de eo ex nostra etiam parte Affirmativam tenemus contra Pontificios. Neque etiam de eo controversitur: An MagistratusChristianus diligenter curare debeat, ut in suo principatu aut regno, vera Religi contra quosvis hæreticos, publicè privatimq; ex Verbo DEI secundum analogiam fidei defendatur? Nam & hic Affirmativam per omnia tenemus, & vel hoc ipso nomine beatas judicamus eas Respublicas, provincias, regna, imperia, quorum Imperatores, Reges & Principes, Spiritu Dei ita ducuntur, ut nihil prius aut antiquius habeant, purioris Religionis assertione & propagatione: ut ipsi intelligant, quæ faciant ad pacem & salutem Israelis: ut denique possint etiam mediis legitimis tollere impedimenta singula & universa, quæ cursum sanæ doctrinæ, vel remorari, vel inhibere posse videntur: exemplo Constantini illius Magni, qui convocatâ Synodo Nicena, Arij hærefin damnari curavit: exemplo Theodosij utriusq;, Martiani aliorumq; Impp. qui convocatis Synodis exortas hæreses represserunt.

Tandem quæstio etiam hoc loco non movetur, de quovis Magistrato, & sic de impio quoque & hæretico. Quæcunq; enim Religionis impiæ, sive hæreseos propagandæ cura suscipitur, illa tàm Magistratus ipsius, quàm subditorum respectu est illicita, impia & Deo exosa. Sed Quæstio est tantùm de Magistratu Christiano κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν sic dicto, hoc est, de Magistratu orthodoxo; An u. si fortè subditos habeat diversæ & hæreticæ Religioni addictos, eos ad suam Religionem cogere possit & debeat? Hanc quæstionem, nostro hoc seculo valde controversam, & propter sententiarum diversitatem, explicatu difficiliorem, aut accuratiùs definiamus: observandæ sunt certæ quædam Hypotheses, & Distinctiones: Quibus observatis, Decisio quæstionis hujus & plana & perspicua ultro emerget.

Quoad Hypotheses, damus potissimùm duas. PRIOR est hæc: vera & orthodoxa Religio hoc sibi soli proprium vendicat, quòd armis externis sive violentis rationibus & adminiculis, neq; in orbem est introducta, neqs dilatata, neque ad nostra usque tempora propagata: sed sola prædicatione Verbi, mediante virtute Spiritus Sancti, in omnes gentes, per vniversum terrarum orbem, sine ullo armorum strepitu, aut gladii externi usu, sparsa & disseminata fuit. Hoc elogio destituuntur omnes omnium aliorum populorum, tam infidelium, quam fidelium religiones. Alcorani certè Turcici barbaries, armis in totum Orientem disseminata initiò, & ad hanc nostram usque ætatem armorum præsidiis conservata fuit: quemadmodum Mahomet ipse gloriari non dubitavit: Se missum esse non in virtute miraculorum, sed gladii. Sic Ariana hæresis, quomodo persecuta sit orthodoxam Christi Ecclesiam, & externa vi, præsertim Imperatoribus quibusdam succenturiantibus, non Orientem modò, sed universum penè orbem Christianum occupârit, prolixè satis commemorat historia Ecclesiastica. Sic Pontificia religio, quomodo externis machinis, artibus, fraudibus, persecutionibus, totum penè occidentem invaserit, & reliquas orbis Europæi partes fermè singulas & universas infecerit, notius est, quam ut operosa probatione opus sit. Sic quomodo fex Anabaptistica, armis externis Religionem suam per Westphaliam initiò fundare, & postmodum propagare studuerit, Sleidani historia luculenter commemorat. Quibus ipsis medijs, studijs, moliminibus externis, Calvinianos suorum quoq; dogmatum incrustationem, propagationemq; quærere & tentare, haud obscurum potest esse illi, qui res circa Religionem & quidem contra Lutheranos passim gestas, paulo altius expendit: ita, ut si vires ipsorum voluntati & consiliis responderent, plus fortassè vel certè, nihil minus periculi & persecutionis à gente Calviniana, quam à Pontificiis, nobis metuendum & expectandum esset. Prima ergò hæc hypothesis ostendit, veram sive orthodoxam Religionem, quæ est ipsa Apostolorum fides, ab omni tali coactione errantium abhorrere, quæ fiat armis & vi externa.


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: Whether a Christian Political Magistrate can & ought to force his subjects to embrace the true Religion? (continued)

THE LATTER Hypothesis is: every violent coercion to faith excludes the proper office of the Holy Spirit. For because the internal conversion of hearts, assent to doctrine, and faith belong to Him alone: and He Himself works these effects only through the Word preached and heard: certainly such violent coercion not only cannot have a place in moving men to embrace the true faith, but will rather produce the contrary effect, and render men more obstinate. What is more, such violent and bloody coercion can even impel men to approve of impiety and heresy itself. Therefore, it cannot be a suitable means for propagating the orthodox faith: Tertullian also supporting this to Scapula, in these words: It is not of religion to compel religion, which ought to be undertaken spontaneously, not by force, since even sacrifices are requested from a willing mind.

Regarding the distinctions, three likewise are to be well observed: and indeed two on the part of the predicate: the third on the part of the subject. The former on the part of the predicate rests on the word to compel: which Augustine and other interpreters understand simply of any coercion whatsoever, in whatever way it may be done. Now, it is indeed true that this term is ἄγραφος, and occurs in the Scriptures, and indeed in definitive terms: as Luke 14:23, where the Holy Spirit, discoursing concerning the calling of the Gentiles to the Kingdom of Christ, reports that the King preparing that great supper said to his servant: Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in ἀνάγκασον εἰσελθεῖν, that my house may be filled. But because Scripture is to be explained by Scripture, and such are the predicates, as also the attributes, as are permitted by the subjects: we conclude evidently and plainly irrefutably that the word of coercion in this place cannot or ought not in any way be taken concerning some external force of arms: For 1. the Savior’s discourse in this place is not with the political Magistrate, but with the Apostles, and consequently with the Ministers of the Church: to whom, as the use of the external sword is clearly not granted at all, so from there nothing can or ought to be concluded directly regarding the office of the Political Magistrate concerning the care of Religion.

Then the means of this coercion are defined by Christ Himself as none other than that which consists in the assiduous invitation to that great supper, that is, in the preaching of the Word, and especially in the inculcation of legal threats. Weighing which means, the Apostle says in 2 Cor. 10:4: The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through GOD for the subversion of strongholds. It would therefore be rash to wish to elicit from there some violent and external coercion.

Finally, the word to compel in the scriptures, and indeed regarding this or equivalent questions, nowhere denotes some violent force or coercion to embrace some faith, as in Galatians 2:14: Why do you compel the Gentiles ἀναγκάζεις to Judaize? where certainly the Apostle does not argue that Peter used some violent coercion by which he forced the Gentiles to embrace the Jewish faith: but he notes Peter’s conduct, by which he could entice the Gentiles to Judaism. Thus, in Galatians 6:12, the Apostle writes: Whoever wishes to please in the flesh, these compel you to be circumcised: that is, they try to persuade you that you should be circumcised: just as the Apostle explains himself in the verse immediately following, rendering the word to compel by the word to wish: they wish, he says, for you to be circumcised, so that they may boast of your flesh. Thus, the disciples at Emmaus compelled Christ to stay overnight with them, that is, they assiduously requested it: Luke 24:29. With these things thus weighed, a manifest equivocation emerges in the word to compel, which either regards the object of coercion, which, just as it is twofold, so it also admits a twofold and diverse mode of compelling. For either coercion is directed toward embracing some faith, as if a Magistrate, under penalty of death, should warn and command that none of his subjects follow and profess any faith and religion other than the Lutheran. Or it is directed toward those external means through which the Holy Spirit is accustomed to work faith in men: as when a Magistrate, by public edict, under penalty of imprisonment or a pecuniary fine, commands that none of his subjects withdraw themselves from the hearing of the divine Word, but that they frequently attend sermons, and perceive what is preached, at least with their external ears, and with due modesty and attention.

That former coercion is by no means granted to the Magistrate: as it 1. has neither example nor command in the Scriptures. 2. It compels consciences to believe that of which they determine the contrary in their hearts. Whence such faith is nothing other than mere hypocrisy and a tyranny of consciences clearly intolerable, which at length degenerates into the saddest apostasy or despair. 3. It is blasphemous against the office of the Holy Spirit: For if faith can be imparted to men by the Magistrate through edicts, through prisons, threats, blows, and punishments, certainly the Holy Spirit, and indeed He alone, will no longer be the one who moves, who opens the hearts of men through the preached Word, and who alone grants and works faith unto salvation. 4. Such coercion is a mark proper to the Antichrist and to heretics, as was shown above in the first hypothesis. From this, therefore, a pious and orthodox Magistrate ought to beware no less than from the very impiety of the Antichrist, which is utterly execrable.

Moreover, the latter coercion is not only granted to a pious Magistrate, but is also commanded in the sacred writings, so that, namely, not only by words, not only by laws and edicts, but also by external punishments and bodily force, and even under penalty of banishment, he may compel his subjects to the hearing of the Word. For he owes this care to GOD, who appointed him guardian of both tables and nursing father of the Church: he owes it to his subjects, whose salvation he is bound to seek and promote equally with his own: he owes it to himself, so that he may one day be able to render an account of the administration of his office to the most just Judge of mortals.

On this account, the pious King in Judah, Jehoshaphat, is commended in the sacred writings, who sent priests into the cities of Judah to teach the true worship of GOD and to instruct the people, 2 Chron. 17:7 et seqq. And Josiah, King of Judah, who, having gathered the whole people, from the least to the greatest, caused the volume of the law to be read publicly, with an edict published that the whole people should keep the precepts of GOD, and the testimonies and ceremonies, with all their heart and with all their soul, 2 Kings 23:1 et seqq. And to this pertains that indefinite assertion of the Apostle, saying The magistrate does not bear the sword in vain: for he is an avenger for wrath to him who has done what is evil. Rom. 13. 4. Just as, therefore, he ought to take care that the Ecclesiastical order diligently performs its duty: so he will also restrain the people within the bounds of piety, and will compel them by edicts and threats to the hearing of the Word, the communion of prayer, the use of the Sacrament, to Catechetical exercises, and other exercises of that kind: but he will severely punish those who are delinquent with the rigor of published laws. And such coercion does not bring force to consciences, like that former one: but it is merely a bridle of the locomotive, so that one may not, according to his own pleasure, stubbornly neglect or spurn the means of receiving the faith.

Nor is there any reason for someone to object, if the Magistrate ought to compel subjects by force to hear the Word: Therefore he ought also to compel them to the use of the Sacraments. For there is a great difference in this place. Because the hearing of the Word is, by the ordinance of GOD, the medium through which true faith is finally conferred: but the Sacraments are seals of the Righteousness of faith: Therefore the Hearing of the Word ought to precede. Furthermore, because the testing of oneself is required for the use of the Sacraments: certainly one ought not to be admitted to, much less compelled to, the participation of the Sacrament, unless he can test himself, whether he is in the faith:

The third distinction rests on the subject, or on the term subjects, who can be divided into various and clearly different classes. For at the beginning there is a group of subjects such that it entirely professes and embraces the true and orthodox Religion. This group ought to be fostered more, and kept in the study of piety by benevolence and rewards, rather than be impelled to the worship of GOD and the exercises of the Christian faith by more severe edicts. But there is no question about these in this place.

But then, among the number of Subjects, there are often quite a few who are addicted to a false religion, such as the Papist or Calvinist: so that they abhor not a little from the purer Church and the truer Religion: not indeed by any set purpose, much less from a habit of heresy: but thus persuaded by heretics, deceived mostly by ignorance and false opinion. Just as, therefore, such people are not to be held as heretics, since they are not stubbornly fighting against recognized truth: but as Augustine speaks, in the book on the utility of believing, deluded by heretics with a certain imagination of truth and piety, they assent to their error, not indeed by obstinacy of mind, but by a certain simplicity of heart and facility, or levity and rashness of believing: So the orthodox Magistrate ought not to compel them by any external violence to the abjuration of errors: For this would be to lord it over consciences, and to command a faith not yet recognized: that which is proper to Tyrants: but he will diligently take care that such people are more rightly informed about the heads of the purer Religion by the Ministers of the Church: that the preconceived errors are removed from them: And all the doubts which they harbor in their mind are solidly refuted. Here, therefore, having been thus weakened and admonished, he will either repent and abjure the error, or he will slip into manifest heresy. If that happens; the matter is in the ford: but if this: then the Magistrate will observe in coercing them that method which we will show more accurately in the third question is to be observed concerning heretics.

Thirdly, there sometimes creep into the assembly of Christians those who do not harbor some simple heresy, but are manifestly blasphemers against the Most Holy Trinity: denying and tearing apart with dire insults either the Unity of the divine essence, as the Tritheists: or the distinction of persons, as the Sabellians, Samosatenians, and in the previous century Michael Servetus, a Spaniard by nation, a physician by profession, who was burned at Geneva for execrable blasphemies, in the year of Christ 1553, on the 17th of October: or the divinity of the Son of GOD, and the Holy Spirit, as the Arians, Photinians, and today especially those who follow Socinus and Ostorodt: or finally, there are those who do not shrink from blaspheming both the most sacred name of GOD and all sacred things with dire execrations. If such people do not wish to leave room for frequent admonitions and instruction, and to yield to the shown truth: but stubbornly continue to blaspheme GOD himself, that the Magistrate can punish them with arms and external force, with proscriptions, prison, the sword, and remove them from the fellowship of Christians according to the gravity of the blasphemy, there is absolutely no doubt! Nor can the Magistrate be said in this way to compel anyone to the faith by arms: Since it is not their error or heresy, but stubborn blasphemy against GOD, and profligate impiety that is thus coerced and punished, according to that most severe command of GOD, Levit. 24. 13. Bring the blasphemer outside the camp, and let all who heard him lay their hands upon his head, and let the whole people overwhelm him with stones: And you shall speak to the children of Israel: A man who has cursed his GOD shall bear his sin: and he who has blasphemed the name of the LORD, let him die by death: The whole multitude of the people shall overwhelm him with stones, whether he be a citizen or a stranger. He who has blasphemed the name of the LORD, let him die by death. Nebuchadnezzar also promulgated such an edict, Daniel 3. 96. By me this decree is set, that every people, tribe and language, which shall have spoken blasphemy against the GOD of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, shall perish, and his house shall be laid waste. For which very reason GOD added this threat to the second precept of the Decalogue: Jehovah will not hold him guiltless who has taken his name in vain.

Nor is there any reason for anyone to object that these laws bound only the Israelite people to obedience. For just as the moral law is the perpetual norm and rule of the divine will, to which the Christian Magistrate is bound to conform all his actions, counsels, judgments, and decrees: so he ought entirely to follow and observe the threatening of the second commandment, and its fuller explanation in Leviticus, in punishing those who are manifestly blasphemous.

Next, those forensic laws must be considered in two ways. One: insofar as they are laws prescribed to one certain people. The other: insofar as they are doctrine, by which it is shown what is agreeable to the divine will, consistent with the law of nature, and finally useful and salutary to the Republic. In the former way, the laws concerning the killing of blasphemers do not bind Christians so precisely and strictly as they did the Jews. For the latter were bound to subject any blasphemer whatsoever—without weighing the quality of the deed or the variety of circumstances, and without first issuing one or two special warnings—to capital punishment, and indeed to a certain kind of death: as is clear from the example of that man who, in Leviticus 24, was stoned for blasphemy.

revealed by the scriptures of the Prophets and Apostles, they fashion others for themselves, or believe those fashioned by others to be true G O D S, and having neglected and denied the true G O D, they adore, invoke, and pursue them with divine worship. Such idolatry was committed by Aaron with the Israelite people, when the golden calf was cast: concerning which the people said: These are your Gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt: And Aaron himself caused it to be proclaimed by a herald: Tomorrow is a solemnity of the L O R D: to whom finally the people offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.

By this act the people so offended God that He thought of utterly cutting them off, had not Moses stood in the way and appeased the wrath of the L O R D, with three thousand Israelites killed in one day, Exodus 32, throughout the whole chapter. Such worship of Idols G O D most severely prohibited, Exodus 20, v. 3, 4, and 5. You shall have no strange Gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor the likeness of those things which are either in heaven above, or in the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth: you shall not adore them, nor worship them. For this sin G O D defined a capital punishment, Exodus 22, v. 20. He who sacrifices to Gods, other than to God alone, let him be killed: and indeed with execration or anathema: which the Hebrew word Hharàm indicates, which signifies not simple killing, but execration and anathema. The Holy Spirit Himself indeed hints at what He wishes to be understood by an Idol: not, namely, any simulacrum or image whatsoever, but that which is set forth for worship and adoration. The very name of the word also proves this nomenclature: as it has its name from εἰδώλου and λατρεύειν. Idolatry, therefore, is properly the worship of a simulacrum, which is either held for God, or is believed to represent G O D, and is consequently religiously adored, and trust is placed in it. Whence it follows that that simulacrum or image which is erected and placed either in public sacred places or in private houses, for the sole purpose that they may be a sign and monument of some deed performed, cannot or ought not to be called an Idol. The Sacramentarians therefore betray a singular ignorance joined with enormous malice, who do not hesitate to be troublesome to Lutheran and truly Orthodox Princes, because they do not do their duty in rooting out and demolishing images as Idols. But we do not need such monitors in this part; rather, we ourselves are the authors and persuaders to our Princes and Magistrates that they should cast Idolaters out of their dominions, and if their obstinacy requires it, that they should afflict them with bodily punishment, indeed even capital punishment: having followed in this part the example of King Asa, who under penalty of death most severely prohibited the worship of Idols: indeed, he even deprived his grandmother Maacah of her dignity and power as Queen, because she had made a horrible Idol in a grove: 1 Kings 15, v. 13. 2 Chronicles 15, v. 16, and Elijah, 1 Kings 18, v. 40.

From this rigor of the law we have been freed in the New Testament through Christ: but in such a way that the substance of the law remains intact, and the Magistrate with a clear conscience ought to take action against blasphemers: meanwhile, however, it may also be lawful, according to the quality of the offense, either to exacerbate or to mitigate the punishments: or to subject the source to civil or capital punishment. For although every blasphemy, as much in remiss degrees as in more intense ones, offends that infinite and highest Good, which is God Himself, yet both by reason of the person so sinning and with respect to the Church, it obtains a great disparity of guilt and punishment. For he sins more gravely who is a blasphemer against G O D by set purpose and deliberate malice, than he who does so out of ignorance. He sins more gravely who blasphemes God pertinaciously and obstinately, than he who is carried away by a more vehement motion of the affections and especially of anger: but, having been warned, is led to some repentance. Thus he sins more gravely who offends many, and especially the simpler ones, not yet sufficiently confirmed in the profession of Evangelical truth, with his blasphemies. Thus, finally, he sins more gravely who vomits forth blasphemies publicly and as it were in the very theater of the Church, than he who does so privately. As therefore the law of nature teaches that, according to the quality of the offenses, the punishments also are not of one kind: some civil, some capital: So it appears sufficiently manifest that those heretics who, knowingly and willingly, directly, pertinaciously, and with damage to the Church and the eternal destruction of many, are blasphemers against the Sacrosanct and adorable Trinity—such as are especially in this our century the more recent Photinians, or Arians, or Antitrinitarians—are to be subjected to capital punishment by the Political Magistrate: but other heretics, not likewise: as we shall demonstrate in the third question. Which reason for diversity the Old Testament did not admit concerning this kind of offense: which is to be well observed against certain Aristarchs of our time.

Fourthly: into the number and society of subjects, Idolaters very often intrude themselves, those called such κατ' ἐξοχήν, namely those who, besides the true and one G O D, in the scriptures

Finally, it happens very often that, either by the right of war or by some other reason, Turks and other infidel peoples come into our power, and thus are to be held in the census and number of subjects. It is asked, therefore, whether it is to be permitted to them to exercise their worship either publicly or privately?

But the answer is simply in the negative: For since the worship of these people is nothing other than manifest idolatry and abomination before God, the magistrate would certainly implicate himself in a most grave guilt: nay, he would also create no small danger to the salvation and religion of his subjects if he were to permit such a thing. Therefore, he shall coerce men of this kind so that they find it necessary to attend the worship of Christians, especially to hear sermons: nay, if they continue contumaciously to be blasphemous against God and His Son, and have left no room for any sounder admonitions, he shall even punish them with the penalty of death.

Latin:

POSTERIOR Hypothesis est: omnis violenta coactio ad fidem excludit officium Spiritus Sancti proprium. Quia enim huic soli competit interna cordium conversio, assensus doctrinæ & fides: & hæc effecta ipse etiam tantùm per Verbum prædicatum & auditum operatur: utique violenta hujusmodi coactio tam non locum habere potest, in permovendis hominibus ad veram amplexandam fidem, ut potius contrarium effectum fortietur, & homines reddat obstinatiores. Quid quòd talis violenta & sanguinaria coactio, ad ipsam quoque impietatem & hæresin approbandam, homines impellere potest. Ergo conveniens medium propagandæ fidei orthodoxæ ea esse nequit: Suffragante etiam Tertulliano ad Scapulam, his verbis: Non est Religionis, religionem cogere, quæ spontè suscipi debet, non vt, cum & hostia ab animo libenti expostu lentur.

Quoad distinctiones, tres itidem probè observandæ: & duæ quidem ex parte prædicati: tertia ex parte subjecti. Prior ex parte prædicati in cogendi verbo hæret: quod Augustinus, & alii interpretes simpliciter de quavis coactione, quocunque id fiat modo, intelligunt. Jam verum quidem est, quod terminus iste sit ἄγραφος, & in Scripturis occurrat, & quidem in terminis terminantibus: ut Luc. 14. 23. ubi de vocatione gentium ad Regnum Christi differens Spiritus Sanctus, Regem parantem cœ nam illam magnam, ad servum suum dixisse refert: Vade ad vias, & sepes, & coge ingredi ἀνάγκασον εἰσελθεῖν, ut impleatur domus mea. Verùm quia Scriptura per Scripturam explicanda & talia sunt prædicata, ut & attributa, qualia permittuntur à subjectis: evidenter & planè irrefragabiliter colligimus, coactionis vocabulum hoc loco de externa aliqua armorum vi, nullo modo posse aut debere accipi: Nam 1. non cum Magistratu politico, sed cum Apostolis, & consequenter cum Ministris Ecclesiæ, hoc loco sermo est Servatori: quibus uti gladij externi usus planè nullus est concessus: ita inde ad officium Magistratus Politici circa curam Religionis, nihil directè colligi vel potest, vel debet.

Deinde media coactionis hujus, à Christo ipso sunt definita nulla alia, quàm quæ in assidua invitatione ad cœnam illam magnam, hoc est, in prædicatione Verbi, & cumprimis inculcatione comminationum legalium, consistit. Quæ media expendens Apostolus 2. Cor. 10. 4. Arma inquit militiæ nostræ non sunt carnalia, sed potentia DEO ad subversionem munitionum. Temerarium ergo fuerit, violentam aliquam & externam coactionem inde velle elicere.

Tandem verbum cogendi in scripturis, & quidem quoad hanc, vel æquipollentes quæstiones, nuspiam notat violentam aliquam vim, sive coactionem ad fidem aliquam amplexandam, ut Galat. 2. 14. Cur gentes cogis ἀναγκάζεις Judaizare? ubi certè Apostolus Petrum non arguit violentæ alicujus coactionis, quâ Gentes ad Judaicum amplexandam fidem impulerit: sed conversationem Petri notat, quâ Gentiles ad Judaismum allicere potuit. Sic Gal. 6. 12. scribit Apostolus: Quicunq; volunt placere in carne, hi cogunt vos circumcidi: hoc est, conantur vobis persuadere, ut circumcidamini: quemadmodum Apostolus versu statim subsequente proximo semetipsum explicat, verbum cogendi reddens per verbum volendi: volunt, inquiens, vos circumcidi, ut de carne vestra glorientur. Sic discipuli Emauntici coëgerunt Christum secum pernoctate, hoc est, assiduè id efflagitarunt: Luc. 24. 29. Quibus ita expensis emergit manifesta æquivocatio in verbo cogendi: quod vel violentiam spicit coactionis objectum, quod uti geminum est, ita geminum etiam ac diversum cogendi modum admittit. Vel enim coactio fit ad fidem aliquam amplexandam, ut si Magistratus sub capitis periculo caveat & præcipiat, ne quis subditorum aliam, quàm Lutheranam fidem ac Religionem sequatur & profiteatur. Vel fit ad media illa externa, per quæ Spiritus Sanctus fidem in hominibus operari solet: Ut quandoMagistratus publico edicto, sub pœna carceris, vel mulcta pecuniaria mandat, ne quis subditorum ab auditu Verbi divini se subducat: sed concionibus frequenter intersint, & quid prædicetur, externis saltem auribus, debitaque cum modestia & attentione percipiant.

Prior illa coactio Magistratui nullo pacto est concessa: ut quæ 1. in Scripturis nullum habet vel exemplum, vel mandatum. 2. Conscientias cogit credere id, cujus diversum in corde statuunt. Unde talis fides nihil est aliud, quàm mera hypocrisis, & conscientiarum tyrannis planè intolerabilis, quæ tandem in tristissimam vel apostasiam, vel desperationem degenerat. 3. Blasphema est in officium Spiritus Sancti: Quod si enim edictis, si carceribus, minis, plagis, pœnis, fides hominibus impertiri potest à Magistratu: certè Spiritus Sanctus, & quidem solus non amplius erit is, qui movet, qui aperit per Verbum prædicatum corda hominum, quiq; solus fidem donat & operatur ad salutem. 4. Talis coactio est propria Antichristi, & hæreticorum nota, uti suprà hypothesi prima fuit ostensum. Ab hac ergo sibi haud minus cavere debet Magistratus pius & orthodoxus, quàm ab ipsa Antichristi impietate prorsus execrabili.

Cæterùm posterior coactio Magistratui pio non modò concessa, sed & mandata est in sacris, ut nimirum non verbis modò, non tantum legibus & edictis: sed & pœnis externis & vi corporali, imò sub pœna etiam Relegationis, ad auditum verbi cogat subditos. Hanc enim curam debet DEO, qui ipsum constituit custode utriusque tabulæ, & nutria tium Ecclesiæ: debet subditis, quorum salutem æquè ac propriam quærere & promovere tenetur: debet sibi ipsi, ut aliquando justissimo mortalium Judici, rationes administratui sui officij reddere possit.

Hoc nomine commendatur in sacris Rex pius in Juda, Josaphat, qui misit Sacerdotes in civitates Juda, ut docerent verum DEI cultum, & erudirent populum 2. Paral. 17.7. & seqq. Et Josias Rex Juda, qui convocato universo populo, à parvo usque ad magnum volumen legis publicè legi curavit, edicto publicato, ut universus populus custodiret præcepta DEI, & testimonia & ceremonias, toto corde, totaq; anima. 2. Reg. 23. 1. & seqq. Et huc pertinet indefinita illa assertio Apostoli, dicēMagistratus non frustra gestat gladium: est enim ultor ad iram ei, qui quod malum est, fecerit. Rom. 13. 4. Quemadmodum ergo curam agere debet, ut ordo Ecclesiasticus suum officium diligenter faciat: ita populum quoque intra cancellos pietatis coercebit, & ad auditum Verbi, orationis communicationem, Sacramenti usum, ad exercitia Cathechetica, & id genus exercitia alia, edictis & minis compellet: in delinquentes autem rigore legum publicatarum severe animadvertet. Et talis coactio non vim adfert conscientiis, sicut prior illa: sed est frenum modo locomotivæ, ut ne pro lubitu fidei percipiendæ media contumaciter negligat aut aspernetur.

Neque est ut objiciat aliquis, si Magistratus vi cogere debet subditos ad audiendum Verbum: Ergo cogere etiam debet ad usum Sacramentorum. Nam magna hoc loco est diversitas. Quia enim auditus Verbi ex ordinatione DEI est medium, per quod demum confertur vera fides: Sacramenta v. sunt sigilla Justitiæ fidei: Ergo Auditus Verbi præcedere debet. Deinde quia ad Sacramentorum usum requiritur probatio sui ipsius: utique ad Sacramenti participationem non admitti, nedum cogi debet, nisi qui seipsum probare potest, utrum sit in fide:

Tertia distinctio hæret in subjecto, sive in voce subditorum, qui in varias ac diversas planè classes dividi possunt. Nam initiò datur subditorum cœtus talis, qui ex toto veram & orthodoxam Religionem profitetur, & amplectitur. Hic foveri magis, & benevolentia ac præmiis in studio pietatis contineri, quàm severioribus edictis ad cultum DEI, & exercitia Christianæ fidei impelli debet. Verùm de his hoc loco est quæstio nulla.

Deinde verò ex Subditorum numero sunt sæpius benè multi, falsæ religioni addicti, ut Pontificiæ aut Calvinianæ: ita ut à puriore Ecclesiâ & veriore Religione haud parum abhorreant: non quidem destinato aliquo consilio, nedum ex habitu hæreseos: sed sic persuasi ab hæreticis, inscitiâ potissimùm & falsa opinatione decepti. Quemadmodum ergò tales pro hæreticis non sunt habendi, quippe non pertinaciter contra veritatem agnitam pugnantes: sed ut Augustinus loquitur, lib. de utilitate credendi, imaginatione quadam veritatis & pietatis ab hæreticis illusi, assentiuntur eorum errori, non animi quidem obstinatione, sed quadam cordis simplicitate & facilitate, sive levitate temeritateque credendi: Ita Magistratus orthodoxus nulla violentia externa ipsos ad errorum abjurationem cogere debet: Hoc enim esset dominari conscientiis, & imperare fidem nondum agnitam: id quod Tyrannorum est proprium: sed sedulò curabit, ut tales per Ministros Ecclesiæ de capitibus Religionis purioris rectius informentur: errores præconcepti illis eximantur: Et dubia quæ in animo fovent omnia, solidè refutentur. Hic ergo sic infirmatus & admonitus, vel resipiscet, & errorem abjiciet, vel ad manifestam hæresin prolabetur. Si illud eveniat; res in vado est: sin hoc: tùm Magistratus in illis coërcendis eam observabit rationem, quam circa hæreticos observandam esse, quæstione tertiâ accuratiùs ostendemus.

Tertiò irrepunt interdum in cœtum Christianorum, qui non simplicem aliquam fovent hæresin, sed manifestè sunt blasphemi in Sacrosanctam Trinitatem: negantes & diris convitiis proscindentes vel Unitatem essentiæ divinæ, ut Tritheitæ: vel distinctionem personarum, ut Sabelliani, Samosateniani, & superiore seculo Michael Servetus, natione Hispanus, professione Medicus, qui ob execrandas blasphemias Genevæ exustus fuit, Anno Christi 1553. die 17. Octobr. vel divinitatem Filii DEI, & Spiritus Sancti, ut Ariani, Photiniani, & hodie cumprimis, qui Socinum & Ostorrodum sequuntur: vel deniq; sunt, qui diris execrationibus & sacratissimum DEI nomen & sacra omnia blasphemare non exhorrescunt. Tales si admonitionibus crebris & institutioni nolint locum relinquere, & ostensæ veritati cedere: sed pertinaciter DEUM ipsum blasphemare pergant, quin Magistratus armis & externa vi in eos animadvertere, proscriptionibus, carcere, gladio pro gravitate blasphemiæ eosdem è consortio Christianorum tollere possit, nullum! prorsus est dubium. Neque hoc pacto Magistratus quenquam armis ad fidem cogere dici potest: Siquidem non error ipsorum sive hæresis, sed pertinax in DEUM blasphemia, & profligata impietas sic coërcetur, & punitur, secundum severissimum illud DEI mandatum Levit. 24. 13. Educ blasphemum extra castra, & ponant omnes qui audierunt, manus suas super caput ejus, & lapidibus eum obruat universus populus: Et ad filios Israelis loqueris: Homo, qui maledixerit DEO suo, portabit peccatum suum: & qui blasphemaverit nomen DOMINI, morte moriatur: Lapidibus eum opprimet omnis multitudo populi, sive ille civis, sive peregrinus fuerit. Qui blasphemaverit nomen DOMINI morte moriatur. Edictum tale promulgavit etiam Nebuchodonosor, Daniel 3. 96. A me positum est hoc decretum, ut omnis populus, tribus & lingua, quæcunq; locuta fuerit blasphemiam contrà DEUM Sidrach, Misach & Abed Nego, dispereat, & domus ejus vastetur. Quam ipsam ob causam DEUS præcepto Decalogi secundo hanc adjecit comminationem: non insontem habebit Jehovah eum, qui assumserit nomen suum in vanu.

Neq; est ut aliquis excipiat, leges hasce populum tantùm Israeliticum ad obedientiam obligasse. Nam uti lex moralis est perpetua norma & regula voluntatis divinæ, ad quam omnes suas actiones, consilia, judicia, decreta, Magistratus Christianus exigere tenetur: ita præcepti secundi comminationem, & uberiorem ejus in Levitico explicationem, in puniendis manifestè blasphemis, omninò sequi & observare debet.

Deinde leges illæ forenses duobus modis considerari debent. Uno: quatenus sunt leges, uni certo populo præscriptæ: Altero: quatenus sunt doctrina, quâ quid voluntati divinæ congruum, legi naturæ consentaneum, Reipublicæ denique utile & salutare esse queat, ostenditur. Priore modo, leges de blasphemis occidendis, non ità præcisè & strictè Christianos obligant, prout Judæos. Hi enim blasphemum quemvis, non expensâ qualitate facti, vel circumstantiarum varietate, non præmissâ unâ aut alterâ speciali præmonitione, capitali supplicio, & quidem certo mortis genere afficere tenebantur: ut patet exemplo illius, qui Levit. 24. ob blasphemiam lapidibus obruebatur.

pturis Prophetarum & Apostolorum patefactum, alios sibi fingunt, vel ab aliis fictos credunt esse veros D E O S, eosque neglecto, & abnegato vero D E O adorant, invocant, & divino cultu prosequuntur. Qualem idololatriam commisit Aaron cum populo Israelitico, conflato vitulo aureo: de quo populus: Hi sunt Dii tui Israel, qui te eduxerunt de terra Ægypti: Et Aaron ipse per præconem edici curavit: Cras solennitas DOMINI est: cui deniq; populus obtulit holocausta & hostias pacificas.

Quo facto Deum ita offendit populus, ut de eo penitùs excindendo cogitaret, nisi obstitisset Moses, & placasset iram DOMINI, interfectis uno die tribus millibus Israelitarum Exod. 32. per caput integrum. Talem Idolorum cultum severissime prohibuit D E U S, Exod. 20. v. 3. 4. & 5. Non habebis Deos alienos coram me. Non facies tibi sculptile, neque imaginem eorum, quæ vel sunt in cælo sursum, vel in terra deorsum, vel in aquis sub terra: non adorabis ea, neque coles. Peccato huic D E U S definivit pœnam capitalem, Exod. 22. v. 20. Qui sacrificârit Diis, præterquàm soli Deo, occidatur: & quidem cum execratione sive anathemate: Id quod verbum Hebræum Hharàm indicat, quod non simplicem occisionem, sed execrationem & anathema significat. Innuit verò Spiritus Sanctus ipse, quid per Idolum velit intellectum: non videlicet quodcunque simulachrum sive imaginem, sed eani quæ prostat ad cultum & adorationem. Quod ipsum vocabuli etiam nomen clatura comprobat: ut quod nomen habet ἀπὸ τῶ εἰδώλꙋ καὶ λατρεύειν. Idololatria ergò propriè est cultus simulachri, quod vel pro Deo habetur, vel D E V M repræsentare creditur, ac proinde religiosè adoratur, & fiducia in eo collocatur. Unde consequens est. Idolum nominari non posse vel debere illud simulachrum sive imaginem, quæ vel in locis sacris publicis, vel in ædibus privatis erigitur & collocatur, eo tantùm fine, ut sint signum & monumentum rei alicujus gestæ. Inscitiam ergò singularem cum enormi malitiâ conjunctam produnt Sacramentarii, qui Lutheranis & verè Orthodoxis Principibus molesti esse non dubitant, eò quod in exturpandis & demoliendis imaginibus tanquam Idolis, officium non faciant. Sed ipsis monitoribus hac in parte non indigemus, quin nos ipsi autores suasoresq; sumus nostris Principibo & Magistratibus, ut Idololatras suis è ditionibus ejiciant, & si ipsorum obstinatio id requirat, pœnâ etiam corporis afflictivâ, imò capitali afficiant: secuti hac in parte exemplum regis Asæ, qui sub pœna capitis Idolorum cultum severissimè prohibuit: quin aviam etiam suâ Mahacam dignitate & potestate Augustæ privavit, eò quòd fecisset horrendum Idolum, priapicum luco: Reg. 5. v. 3. 2. Paral. 15. v. 13. & Elia, 1. Reg. 18. v. 40.

Ab hoc rigore legis nos in Novo Testamento per Christum liberati sumus: sed ita ut substantiu legis maneat integra, & Magistratus salvâ conscientiâ in blasphemos animadvertere debeat: interim verò licitum etiam sit, pro qualitate delicti, pœnas vel exasperare, vel mitigare: vel civili, vel capitali pœna fontem afficere. Quanquam enim omnis blasphemia, tam in gradibus remissis, quàm intensioribus, offendit infinitum illud & summum Bonum, quod est Deus ipse, tamen tum ratione personæ sic delinquentis: tùm respectu Ecclesiæ, magnam imparitatem reatus & pœnæ obtinet. Gravius enim peccat, qui blasphemus est in DEUM ex proæresi, ex destinata malitia, quàm qui ex ignorantia. Graviùs sic peccat, qui pertinaciter & obstinatè, quàm qui vehementiore affectuum & cumprimis iracundiæ motu abreptus, blasphemat Deum: sed monitus pœnitudine aliqua ducitur. Sic gravius peccat, qui multos & cumprimis simpliciores, nondumq́ve circâ veritatis Evangelicæ professionem satis confirmatos, suis blasphemiis offendit. Sic denique graviùs peccat, qui publicè & in ipso quasi Ecclesiæ theatro, quàm qui privatim, blasphemias evomit. Quemadmodum ergo jus naturæ docet, pro qualitate delictorum, pœnas quoque non unius esse generis: quasdam civiles, quasdam capitales: Ita satis manifestè apparet, illos hæreticos, qui scientes volentes, directè, pertinaciter & cum damno Ecclesiæ, plurimorumq́; æterno exitio blasphemi sunt in Sacrosanctam & adorandam Trinitatem, quales cumprimis hoc nostro seculo sunt, recentiores Photiniani, sive Arriani aut Antitrinitarii: eos à Magistratu Politico capitali supplicio esse afficiendos: Alios verò hæreticos, non item: uti quæstione tertia demonstrabimus. Quam diversitatis rationem Vetus Testamentum, circa hoc delicti genus non admittebat: Id quod contra quosdam nostri temporis Aristarchos probè observandum.

Quartò: in subditorum numerum & societatem sæpissimè sese ingerunt Idololatræ, καἳ ἐξοχὼν sic dicti, illi nimirùm, qui præter verum & unum D E U M, in scripturis

Tandem sæpissimè accidit, ut vel jure belli, vel aliâ quapiam ratione veniant in potestatem nostram Turcæ, alijque populi infideles, & sic censu numeroque subditorum habendi sint. Quæritur ergo, an istis permittendum ut cultum suum vel publicè vel privatim exerceant?

Respondetur autem simpliciter Negatè: Quia enim cultus istorum nihil aliud est, quàm manifesta Idololatria & abominatio coràm DEO, utiq; gravissimo reatu sese implicaret Magistratus: quin & subditorum saluti & religioni periculum haud exiguum crearet, si tale quid permitteret. Proinde ejusmodi homines sic coercebit, ut Christianorum cultui, concionibus præsertim audiendis interesse necesse habeant: quin imò si blasphemi in DEUM, & Filium ipsius esse contumaciter perrexerint, neque ullis sanioribus monitis locum reliquerit, capitis etiam supplicio ipsos afficiet.


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: Question II. Whether a Christian and orthodox magistrate can permit to his subjects diversity of religion, that is, the liberty of several…

Can a Christian and Orthodox magistrate permit to his subjects the autonomy of religion, that is, the liberty of several religions dissenting among themselves?

This question, formulated in such a general way, does not produce one certain meaning, but several and diverse ones, which, however, can be conveniently reduced to two principal states. The former is: Can a mixture of religions, or what is the same, a Mixed Religion, have a place in the true Church of God?

There are indeed found some politicians, among whom that fictitious and masked person, the jurist Antonius Benbellona de Godentijs, wished to show himself a man in that untimely, or rather impious and untimely, gathering for princes, printed at Zerbst in the year 1602, who is entirely occupied in persuading princes that a mixture of Lutheranism and Calvinism can stand together without any loss of truth, and that power can, and indeed must, be permitted to both the Calvinist and Lutheran religions to be freely professed and exercised, without prejudice to the honor and worship of God. He pretends, above all, the public tranquility among those Churches which have made a divorce from the Roman Pontiff, and a conjunction of forces by which all the pride and tyranny of the Romanists can be easily repressed and beaten back. Others are found who, being very wise in their own homes, from the mutual dissensions of theologians, especially if there are those who dare to publicly criticize Calvinist reformations,

and dare to measure them by the standard of the scriptures, seem to foresee for themselves I know not what coming storms and changes of kingdoms and empires: and therefore, by wondrous arts, or rather by tortuous and clearly serpentine windings, they strive to reconcile these diverse religions, which dissent on their very foundation, by some specious reasoning. To whose opinion we can in no way subscribe, nor ought we. For, to pass over in silence at the beginning that contrary practice of the Calvinist people, which, where it holds power, it observes so diligently and strenuously that, with the exercise of the Lutheran religion extirpated and utterly destroyed, only Calvinism prevails: so far are they from permitting public liberty to both: that certainly deserves the greatest observation in this place, that such a mixture and confusion of either two or more religions dissenting among themselves is abominable to God and in many ways destructive to the Orthodox Church. For just as there is one Lord, one God and Father of all; so there is only one faith and true Religion in number: and therefore also several dissenting religions cannot please God. Which is the reason why He Himself in His law, by some similitudes, most severely forbade such a mixture of religions to His people, commanding them not to mix the species of animals and seeds: not to plow with an ox and an ass together: not to wear a garment woven from linen and wool.

By which he did not principally intend to forbid that external mixture of things: But to show this above all, that he abominates a mixed religion, and requires a faith segregated from all false opinions: since, as the Apostle testifies, a little leaven leavens the whole lump and renders it useless. And although these similitudes, as regards the letter and πρώτως, do not pertain to the Church of the New Testament: yet as regards the mystical sense, which God intended to be noted under these wrappings, and thus δευτέρως they altogether bind Christians of the New Testament: that they should not mix seeds, that is, that they should not mix with that spiritual seed, which is the word of God, the seeds of tares, or of false religions, in the field of God, which is the Church. Whence Calvin not ineptly gathers that these Mosaic precepts, as they condemn all adventitious corruptions, are appendices of the first commandment of the Decalogue, concerning not having strange Gods, besides the one and only God.

And Conrad Pellican, a writer of no mean reputation, a Sacramentarian, upon the passage of Exodus, says thus among other things: The field is not to be sown with mixed seed, it seems to be allegorical, against hypocrisy in words and deeds, and any iniquity whatsoever. Just as also concerning the garment woven of mixed material, of wool and linen, that false doctrine is not to be mixed with true, that a secular life is not to be sold under a religious habit.
