In sum, it condemns all hypocrisy and falsity, the Word of truth and the Law of the Lord. fol. 146 in my copy.

That the Calvinist religion directly attacks the very foundation of the faith, and is therefore false and heretical, has been invincibly demonstrated elsewhere. Far be it, therefore, that we should allow ourselves to be persuaded of such a Samaritanism compounded of true and false religion: concerning which Ecclesiasticus ch. 50, v. 27: Two nations I hate, and the third is more than all the rest abominable, the Samaritans, the Philistines, and the foolish people of Sichem. The principal cause of which hatred was that notable craftiness and deceit of the Samaritans, who (as the Calvinists are wont to do today) were so slippery that, when the affairs of the Jews were flowing at their beck and call, they wished to appear as Jews: but when the same were agitated by the wind and storm of adverse fortune, they would associate themselves with the Gentiles.

Moreover, we seek the immovable construction of this decision of ours from the mouth of two witnesses who are above all exception: the former of whom is the most celebrated prophet of the Old Testament, Elijah, who thus addresses the people joining the Baalitic cult with the true worship of GOD: How long do you halt between two sides, or as the Hebrew סעפים implies, between two branches, as it were, or two opinions? If Jehovah is God, follow him: but if Baal, follow him. He argues that the people are of the highest inconstancy, showing them unworthy of the Jewish profession, to be in doubt concerning the business of faith and salvation: a thing which is diametrically opposed to the very nature of GOD.

The latter witness in the New Testament is the Son of GOD himself, who sharply rebukes the Angel or Bishop of the Church of Laodicea for such negligence in religion, saying: I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor fervent: I would thou wert cold or fervent: but because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will begin to vomit thee out of my mouth. Apoc. 3, v. 15 & 16. This sharp threat is worthy to be weighed more deeply on account of the babblings of some who hold diverse opinions. For the Son of God rebukes lukewarmness or tepidity, χλιαρότητα, in the Laodiceans as a vice unworthy of the Church of the New Testament: and he describes it by the removal of two extremes: namely, of fervor and coldness, ζέσεως καὶ ψυχρότητος: so that by fervor he denotes the Zeal with which the cause of divine worship and religion is conducted. But by the cold he understands the atheist or the Epicurean man, who is touched by no care at all for religion and divine worship. He places the lukewarm in the middle order, therefore, as one who partakes of both opposites, showing himself to be double-handed, and a companion of many religions, accommodating himself to this one when things are going well; but in a time of adversity, accommodating himself to the other religion, and thus, courting the favor of men more than of GOD, he is bent toward every part or breath of the wind.

But let the wiseacres of our century remember what judgment the Son of GOD himself passes concerning this mixture of diverse religions, and its authors

and approvers: Because thou art lukewarm, he says, I will vomit thee out of my mouth: implying that for such double-handed and neutral people no other judgment is to be expected than that which is argued by that natural effect of lukewarm water, which is wont to be the cause of vomiting: so, says the Son of GOD, these will be vomited out of my mouth, that is, out of most just indignation I shall cast them away forever. Which is one thing.

Then let those politicians also observe that which, by the testimony of the Savior, the lukewarm man: that is, he who bends himself to two diverse religions, is worse than the cold, that is, the manifest impious. The reason is this:

1. That the cold or ἄθεος [godless] person openly professes what he is, and in the business of religion especially, does not display one thing in speech and appearance while suppressing another locked in his heart. There is hardly any other vice more abominable to GOD than this.

2. The cold or impious person is not always such by set purpose, but more often by a defect of nature or education; meanwhile, having been taught better things, he can be curable. Lukewarmness, however, or neutrality in religion is an evil or vice contracted by the inclination of the mind and by deliberate counsel, and is therefore more incurable.

3. The cold or impious person suffers from one simple vice: namely, impiety or infidelity. But in the lukewarm man, two contrary vices concur: namely, the simulation of piety and true faith, and communion with heretics. Just as physicians maintain that the cure of contrary diseases is most difficult, so in a man who is lukewarm regarding religion, the healing is of the greatest labor: so much so that the Son of God wishes him to be plainly cold. And the Son of God undoubtedly looked to this as well, asserting that publicans and harlots, men who are plainly ἀθέους [godless] or impious, would go before the Pharisees and priests, that sink of lukewarm men, into the kingdom of God.

Finally, those war counselors will also observe that fervent men, who use a certain singular zeal regarding the assertion of religion, please God: as those who in this passage are expressly opposed to both the cold and the lukewarm, they can be an example: Phinehas, Num. 25; Elijah, 1 Kings 18; and Paul after his conversion. For the Spirit of God is a fiery thing (so to speak), and a heavenly force always burning, never lukewarm or sluggish in the souls of those whom it imbues. In which very fervor, however, there are more excellent and more remiss degrees, according to how that divine Spirit exerts its power in each one.

Let the Sacramentarians therefore see with what face the fervor of the blessed Luther in reforming

The Church, and especially also to be purged from the Zwinglian leaven, as he accuses it of being too harsh, impetuous, φιλόνεικον, and contentious. Those men certainly betray that they do not yet have the genius of Luther known and perceived, and therefore they pass a judgment upon it that is clearly untimely

Latin:

An Magistrat9 Christianus & Orthodoxus Religionis αὐτονομίαν, hoc est, plurium ac invicem dissidentium Religionum libertatem, subditis permittere possit?

QUæstio hæc ita generaliter informata, non unum aliquem certum parit sensum: sed complures ac diversos: qui tamen ad duos status principales commodè revocari possunt. Prior est: An Religionum mixtura, vel quod idem est, Religio Mixta, in vera Dei Ecclesia locum habere possit?

Reperiuntur quidem nonnulli politici, inter quos virum se præbere voluit fictitius ille atque personatus tabula Antonius Benbellona de Godentijs JCtius, intempestivo illo suo, veriùs impio atque in tempestivo suscitabulo pro principibus, Servestæ ANNO 1602. impresso, qui in eo totus est, ut persuadeat viris principibus, mixturam Lutheranismi & Calvinismi, sine ulla veritatis jacturâ simul stare posse, & tàm Calvinanæ quàm Lutheranæ religioni, liberè profitendæ & exercendæ potestatem salvo DEI honore atque cultu permitti posse, imò debere. Prætendit autem iste cumprimis tranquillitatem publicam inter eas Ecclesias, quæ â Pontifice Romano divortium fecerunt: & conjunctionem virium, quâ omnis Romanensium fastus & tyrannis facilè reprimi & retundi possit. Reperiuntur alii, qui domi suæ apprimè sapientes, ex mutuis Theologorum dissensionibus, præsertim si sint, qui Calvinianas reformationes publicè reprehendere,

& ad scripturarum amussim exigere ausint, nescio quas venturas tempestates, regnorum & imperiorum mutationes, sibi prospicere videntur: ac proinde miris artibus, vel tortuosis potiùs & planè serpentinis flexibus, diversas hasce, & toto fundamento dissidentes religiones, fucatâ quadam ratione conciliare student. Quorum sententiæ subscribere nullo modo vel possumus vel debemus. Nam, ut initiò silentio involvamus cōtrariam illam gentis Calvinianæ praxin, quam, ubi rerum potitur, ita sedulò & strenuè observat, ut extirpato, ac penitùs profligato Lutheranæ religionis exercitio, Solus Calvinismus obtineat: tantum abest, ut utriq; libertatem publicam permittant: Illud certè observationem hoc loco maximè meretur, quòd talis vel duarum, vel plurium religionum invicem disfidentium, mixtura atque confusio, Deo est abominabilis, & Ecclesiæ Orthodoxæ multis modis exitiosa. Quemadmodum enim unus est Dominus, Unus Deus & Pater omnium; ita una tantùm numero est fides ac Religio vera: ac proinde etiam plures dissidentes Religiones Deo placere non possunt. Quæ causa est, quòd ipsemet in lege sua aliquot similitudinibus ejusmodi religionum mixturam populo suo severissimè interdixit, præcipiens ei, ne species animatium & seminum miscerent: ne in bove & asino simul ararent: ne stestem gerent ex lino & lana contextam.

Quibus non principaliter externam illam mixturam rerum prohibere voluit: Sed id potissimùm ostendere, quòd mixtam religionem abominetur, & fidem ab omnibus falsis opinionibus segregatam requirat: siquidem teste Apostolo, paululum fermenti totam massam fermentat & inutilem reddit. Et quanquam hæ similitudines, quoad literam & πρώτως ad Ecclesiam Novi Testamenti non spectant: tamen quoad sensum mysticum, quem Deus sub istis involucris notatum voluit, & sic δευτέρως Christianos Novi Testamenti omninò obligant: ne semina misceant, hoc est, cum Spirituali illo semine, quòd est verbum Dei, misceant semina Zizaniorum, sive falsarum religionum, in agro Dei, qui est Ecclesia. Unde haud ineptè colligit Calvinus, præcepta hæc Mosaica, ut quæ omnes adventitias corruptelas damnant, primi præcepti Decalogi, de non habendis Diis alienis, præter unum & solum Deum, esse appendices.

Et Conradus Pellicanus scriptor haud ignobilis Sacramentarius supra locum Exodi sic inter reliqua: Agrum non mixtim serendum, allegoricum videtur esse, contra hypocrisin in verbis & factis, & iniquitatem quamcunq;. Sicut & de veste mixtim contexta, ex lana & lino, doctrinam falsam, veræ non miscendam, vitam secularem religioso habitu non venditandam. In summa omnem damnat hypocrisin & falsitatem, Verbum veritatis & Lex Domini. fol. mihi 146.

Jam Religionem Calvinianam directè impugnare ipsum fundamentum fidei, ac proinde esse falsam & hæreticam, alibi invictè demonstratum. Absit ergo, ut talem nobis Samaritanismum ex vera & falsa religione conflatum nobis persuaderi patiamur: De quo Ecclesiasticus cap. 50. v. 27. Duos populos odi, & tertium plus quàm omnes reliquos abominor, Samaritanos, Philistæos & stolidum populum Sichym. Cujus odii causa principalis erat insignis illa Samaritanorum calliditas & vafricies, qui (pro ut hodiè Calviniani factitare solent) adeò lubrici erant, ut rebus Judæorum ad nutum fluentibus, Judæi videri vellent: iisdem verò adversæ fortunæ vento ac turbine agitatis, Gentibus se adsociarent.

Decisionis autem hujus nostræ immotam κατασκευὴν petimus ex ore duorum testium omni exceptione majorum: quorum prior est Veteris Testamenti Propheta celeberrimus Elias, qui populum conjungentem cum vero DEI cultu Baaliticum, sic compellat: Quousq́; tandem claudicatis in duas partes vel ut Hebræum סעפים innuit, in duos quasi ramos, sive in duas cogitationes? si Jehovah est Deus, sequimini eum: si verò Baal, sequimini ipsum. Summæ nimirùm inconstantiæ arguit populum, indignum professione judaica ostendens, de negotio fidei & salutis ambigere: id quod cum ipsa natura DEI è diametro pugnet.

Posterior testis in Novo Testamento est, ipse filius DEI, qui Angelum sive Episcopum Ecclesiæ Laodicensis, ob talem in Religione oscitantiam, acriter reprehendit: Scio, inquiens, opera tua, quia neq́;ue frigidus es, neq́; fervidus: utinam frigidus esses, aut fervidus: sed quoniam tepidus es, & nec frigidus, nec calidus, incipiam te evomere ex ore meo. Apoc. 3. v. 15. & 16. Digna autem est acris hæc comminatio, quæ propter nonnullorum diversorū sentientium φλυαρίας altiùs expendatur. Reprehendit nimìrum Filius Dei in Laodicensibus Tepidrtatem sive Teporem χλιαρότητα; tanquàm vitium Ecclesiâ Novi Testamenti indignum: idque describit remotione duorum extremōrum: Fervoris scilicet & frigiditatis, ζέσεως καὶ ψυχρότητος: ita ut per fervorem notet Zelum, quo cultus divini, & religionis causa agitur. Per frigidum verò intelligat ἄθεον sive hominem Epicureum, qui nulla planè religionis & cultus divini curâ tangitur. In medio ergo ordine Tepidum collocat, ut qui de utroq́ve contrario communicet, ἀμφιδέξιον, & plurium religionum socium se exhibens, rebus benè habentibus, huic; tempore autem adversitatis, alteri religioni se accommodet, & sic hominum magis, quàm DEI favorem aucupans, in omnem venti partem sive flatum flectatur.

Meminerint autem sapientuli nostri seculi, quamnam Ἐπίκρισιν de hac religionum diversarum mixtione, ejusdemq́ve autoribus

& approbatoribus, ipse Filius DEI ferat sententiam: Quia tepidus es, inquit, evomam te ex ore meo: innuens, ejusmodi ambidextris & neutralibus non aliud esse expectandum judicium, quàm quòd arguit naturalis ille effectus aquæ tepidæ, quæ vomitionis causa esse solet: ita inquit Filius DEI, evomentur isti ex ore meo, hoc est, ex indignatione justissima in æternum ipsos abjiciam. Quod unum est.

Deinde observent Politici illi & istud, quod teste Servatore homo tepidus: hoc est, ad duas diversas religiones se inflectens, deterior sit frigido, hoc est, manifestè impio. Ratio est hæc:

1. Quòd frigidus sive ἄθεος palàm profitetur, qualis sit, non aliud in Religionis præsertim negocio, ore & specie præse fert, aliud corde clausum premit. Quo vitio vix ullum aliud DEO abominabilius.

2. Frigidus sive impius non semper de果tinato consilio, sed naturæ sæpius vel educationis vitio talis est, interim de melioribus edoctus potest esse sanabilis. Tepiditas autem sive Neutralitas in Religione est malum sive vitium inductione animi, consilioque deliberato contractum, ac proinde insanabilius.

3. Frigidus sive impius uno simplici laborat vitio: nempe impietate sive infidelitate. In homine verò tepido duo concurrunt vitia contraria, nempe pietatis & fidei veræ simulatio, & cum hæreticis communicatio. Quemadmodù verò Medici perhibent morborum contrariorum curationem esse difficilimam: ita in homine circa Religionem tepido, maximi laboris est sanatio: ita ut Filius Dei optet talem planè esse frigidum. Et huc respexit sine dubio etiam Filius Dei, asserens publicanos & meretrices, homines planè ἀθέους sive impios, præcessuros in regno Dei Pharisæorum & Sacerdotum, hominum tepidorum colluviem.

Tandem observabunt & illud belli isti consiliarii, homines fervidos, qui circa religionis assertionem singulari quodam zelo utuntur, placere Deo: ut qui hoc loco & frigidis & tepidis disertè opponuntur, Exemplo esse possunt Phineas: Num. 25. Elias: 1. Reg. 18. & Paulus post conversionem. Ignea enim (ut sic loquar) res est Spiritus Dei, & vis cœlestis semper flagrans, nunquam tepens, aut torpens in animis eorum, quos imbuit. In quo ipso tamen fervore gradus excellentiores & remissiores esse, prout quidem in uno quoque vim suam divinus ille Spiritus exerit.

Viderint proinde Sacramentarii, quâ fronte fervorem B. Lutheri in reformanda

Ecclesia, & cumprimis etiam à Zwingliano fermento repurganda, ut nimis acrem, incitatum, φιλόνεικον & contentiosum criminâ- tur. Produnt certè isti se genium Lutheri nondum habere cognitum & perspectum, ac proinde intempestivum planè de eò ferre judiciũ


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: Question II. Whether a Christian and orthodox magistrate can permit to his subjects diversity of religion, that is, the liberty of several… (continued)

Luther did not plead a private cause: nor yet one common to many, when he began the work of reformation, but a singular one. Nor did that fervor proceed from a private agitation of the affections: but was infused by the inspiration of the divine deity, and governed by the same: so that it can neither be judged nor ought to be judged by such unjust and rash censors. Let them also see with what conscience they can accuse before princes, and denounce as torches and trumpets of sedition, those theologians who refuse to consent to the impious fraternities, reconciliations, and confederations of the Calvinists.

But let these things suffice to have discussed concerning the former state of the proposed question, for the Negative of our Churches: which if they seem too harsh to the adverse party, I ask that they consult what Johannes Wolphius, a Sacramentarian writer, noted in the commentary of Peter Martyr, on chapter 17, book 2 of Kings, fol. 348. b.: and perhaps the effervescence of bile will soften: especially if they more accurately weigh the example of the Pseudo-Apostles produced by the Author. For just as the Calvinists today repeatedly rattle on that they agree with us on the foundation of salvation: so neither did the Pseudo-Apostles want Christ and his Gospel eliminated, but they contended that circumcision at least ought still to be observed. But for this time, enough on this matter.

The latter state of the proposed question is this: Whether in some certain case of necessity arising, a Magistrate or Prince, some Christian, can for a time at least—I do not say approve, for this would be impious and apostatic—but at least tolerate with a good conscience the exercise of several and dissenting Religions: until a mutual consensus can be entered into between the dissenting parties: Or whether it is more advisable that he pursue and excise the dissenting subjects by force and arms? Such a case arose in the previous century under the empire of the Emperor D. FERDINAND: especially around the year of the Lord 1552, when it began to be debated: Whether it is more advisable that, for the sake of asserting the safety of the Roman Empire and of all the orders within it, both private and public, the Emperor should permit the Lutherans the free power of exercising their Religion: or whether, with the ruin of the Empire itself, he should extirpate them by war and arms and remove them from the midst? Such a case also can arise in some Principality, as when subjects depart into diverse and contrary Religions, and

cannot be recalled to the way by laws and edicts: likewise if some Prince, whether by right of war, or by right of fief, or by right of inheritance and succession, or by other legitimate means and ways, acquires new provinces and subjects addicted to a diverse and false religion: but these would sooner pour out their life and blood than make a loss of their ancestral and paternal religion: It is asked: Whether it is more advisable, and less hateful to God: Whether for some time, the toleration of diverse Religions in one Principality: or rather the excision of all dissenters, and the overturning of the whole Kingdom, or Principality, or Republic?

Although the decision of this question does not lack singular difficulty on either side: yet, relying on the protection of the Holy Scriptures, against the Romanists, we answer in the affirmative: That an Emperor or Prince, or any other Christian Magistrate, in such a state, can, with an uninjured conscience, permit to his subjects for a time the exercise of diverse Religions: especially if the safety of the Empire and the Republic cannot otherwise be asserted and kept safe and sound. Where, however, we establish that at the beginning a twofold caution must be used. The former is: that in such a state of affairs, the Emperor or Prince, or any other Magistrate, should publicly protest in express words that he is convinced in his heart and conscience that there is only one true faith and religion, comprehended in the writings of the Prophets and Apostles, and hitherto asserted by him with all his might, and to be asserted until the last breath of life: and that he does not in any way either now approve or will ever approve the remaining dissenting opinions: but for the sake of avoiding more serious harm and danger, he will for some time tolerate and permit that any part of the dissenters may perform the exercise of their religion, until, with all hindrances and obstacles removed, some consensus concerning Religion may be entered into among all the provincials. The latter caution is that, during such a state of confusion, the Christian and truly pious Prince should steer and govern the helm of the Republic, like some skilled shipmaster. For just as he, when diverse and contrary winds have arisen and waves are contending among themselves, now spreads the sails, now contracts them, so that the ship may hold its course correctly and according to the cynosure amidst the waves and whirlwinds of storms, and finally arrives at the port safe and unharmed. So the prince, agitated by the diverse storms of Religions, will sometimes contract the sails, that is, he will inhibit, as much as can be done without the overturning of the Republic, the course of heterodox and heretical persons who are about to break out too much into violence: Meanwhile, however, as far as it can be done while the purer Religion remains safe, he will allow them to use and enjoy a freer air but in such a way that he always looks to the Cynosure of the divine Word, and takes care that those erring out of simplicity and ignorance, as well as those seduced by others, are instructed with gentleness as if they were teachable: but as for the unteachable, the rebellious, the refractory, and the contumaciously erring, while such a state continues, he shall so restrain and check them with laws and edicts that they cannot run riot at will and infect the Lord's sheepfold: nay, he may even remove the seditious and disturbers of the public peace from the midst, as perjurers and oath-breakers, even by capital punishment: so that thus the ship of the Church, amidst these storms, may be able to continue the course of the Gospel unharmed and unblemished, and at length arrive at the most desired port of eternal tranquility.

Furthermore, we seek the reasons and arguments for this affirmative position of ours partly from the examples of pious Kings and Princes, who, in such an emerging state, maintained a practice already defined, not without the singular approval of GOD: and partly from reasons consistent with the analogy of faith:

1. DAVID, certainly a King after the heart and will of GOD, is read to have ruled not only over the Jews, who were of one mind with him in the true Religion, but also over the Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites, and Syrians of Damascus, peoples of the most diverse Religions, brought under his power by the right of war: and to have permitted to these same peoples, who loathed the Jewish Religion worse than a dog or a snake, the free exercise of their own religion: lest by excessive rigor he should utterly destroy the obedience and loyalty of the peoples in political matters, as well as the peace of the Jewish Church: but he is read to have permitted this in such a way that he meanwhile took care that the worship of the true GOD was so conducted that daily, from those very infidel peoples, many would pass over to the Jewish Church and become proselytes. Concerning which matter, see 2 Sam. 8:1 ff., indeed the whole history of David in the 2nd book of Samuel and the 1st book of Chronicles.

2. King Nebuchadnezzar, the first Monarch of the Babylonian kingdom, is read to have reigned from the river of the land of the Philistines to the border of Egypt: but because he could not force all those peoples to the worship of the God of Daniel, he certainly permitted to each the power of exercising their own religion: content solely with this, that by public edicts and proposed capital punishments he took care that no one in all those kingdoms and provinces should blaspheme the true God: saying, 'By me this decree is made, that every people, tribe, and language, which shall speak blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, shall perish, and his house shall be laid waste.' Daniel 3:96.

3. Cyrus, the first Monarch of the Persians, permitted the Jews to both restore the temple at Jerusalem and freely practice their own Religion. He did not, however, prohibit the remaining peoples from holding a faith meanwhile most diverse from the religion of the Jews: since violent coercion to embrace one faith and religion could not take place without the most immediate destruction of the kingdom. Ezra 1:2, etc.

4. King Darius of the Persians also held this permission of the Jewish religion to be valid: so that, although Artaxerxes, circumvented by the counsels of certain courtiers, had given a mandate to suppress the studies and efforts of the Jews (Ezra 4:21), Darius nevertheless, perceiving that it could not be done without enormous danger and loss to the kingdom, wished to confirm that permission of Cyrus, even with the enemies of the Jews protesting: with this added threat: 'Whoever shall change this sanction, let a beam be taken from his house, and let it be erected, and let him be fastened upon it, and let his house be made a public dunghill.' Ezra 6:6 & 11. What of the fact that the same Darius, having afterwards turned to the God of Israel, found it necessary to permit freedom of Religion to his subjects for the same reason: content with the example of Nebuchadnezzar, he decreed by public edict that none of his subjects should despise or treat with ignominy the God of Israel: according to this law: 'Peace be to you: it is constituted and decreed by me that in all my Empire and Kingdom, all shall tremble and fear the God of Daniel.' Daniel 6:26. The principal reasons upon which we rely are these:

1. Because no one can or ought to be forced to embrace a certain Faith: since no mortal has any right over the conscience of another, as was shown in question 1. Nor is it for anyone to object that this coercion proceeds from true knowledge, which indubitably establishes and knows that the Religion to which the subjects are being forced is true and salvific: for as the Apostle teaches in 1 Cor. 8:7, for the excuse of an act, right knowledge is not sufficient: but it is further required that regard also be had for the conscience and knowledge of others. If this is not done, certainly, just as an abuse of knowledge and liberty is admitted, so the conscience of others is gravely injured, by which a grave guilt is also contracted. Since by this very act those who sin in this way testify that they have greater regard for their own knowledge and will than for the divine reason. Looking to which, Maximilian II, Emperor, truly Augustus, being incited by some to destroy the Lutherans with force and arms even to the point of extermination, is read to have replied: 'No sin is graver than the desire to dominate consciences: for they attempt to oppose God who wish to dominate consciences in the cause of Religion.' Crat. in Orat. fun.

Latin:

Non privatam causam egit Lutherus: neq; adhuc multis communem, quando opus reformationis inchoavit, sed singularem. Neque fervor iste à privata affectuum concitatione profectus: sed divini numinis afflatu inditus, & ab eodem gubernatus fuit: ut ab iniquis & temerariis ejusmodi censoribus judicari neque possit neque debeat. Viderint etiam, quâ conscientia apud viros principes accusare, & tanquam faces & tubas seditionum proscindere possint eos Theologos, qui impias Calvinianorum fraternitates, conciliationes, confœderationes consentire nolũt.

Sed sufficiant hæc de priore quæstionis propositæ statu, pro Ecclesiarum nostrarum Negativâ disseruisse: quæ si adversæ parti duriora videntur, consulant quæso quæ Johannes Wolphius scriptor Sacramentarius, in commentario Petri Martyris, ad cap. 17. lib. 2. Regum, fol. 348. b. annotavit: & fortè bilis effervescentia mitescet: præsertim si exemplum PseudoApostolorum ab Autore productum accuratiùs expenderint. Quemadmodum enim Calviniani hodie subinde crepant se in fundamento salutis nobiscum consentire: ita neque Pseudo-Apostoli Christum, ejusq́; Evangelium eliminatum volebant, sed circumcisionem saltem adhuc observandam esse contendebant. Verùm hac vice, hac de re satis.

POSTERIOR propositæ quæstionis status iste: An certo aliquo emer gente neceßitis casu, plurium & dißidentium Religionum exercitium, Magistratus sive Princeps, aliquis Christianus, ad tempus saltem non dico probare: hoc enim impium & apostaticum foret: sed tolerare saltem bonâ conscientiâ possit: usq́; dum mutuus consensus inter partes dißidentes iniri possit: An verù consultiùs sit, ut vi & armis dissentientes subditos persequatur & excindat? Talis casus emersit superiore seculo proximo sub imperio D. FERDINANDI Cæsaris: cumprimis circo annum Domini 1552. ubi disputari ceptum fuit: An consultius sit, ut ad asserendam Imperii Romani, omniumque in eo ordinum salutem privatam & publicam, Imperator Lutheranis permittat liberam suæ exercendæ Religionis potestatem: an verù cum ruina ipsius Imperii, bello & armis eos extirpet & è medio tollat? Qualis casus etiam in Principatu aliquo emergere potest, ut quando subditi in diversas & contrarias Religiones abeunt, &

legibus atq; edictis errantes in viam revocari nequeunt : item si Princeps aliquis, vel jure belli, vel jure feudi, vel hereditatis & successionis jure, vel mediis modisq; aliis legitimis, novas acquirat provincias, & subditos diversæ & falsæ religioni addictos : Hi verò vitam citiùs atque sanguinem profundere, quàm avitæ & paternæ religionis jacturam facere velint : Quæritur : Utrum sit consultiùs, Deoq; minus exosum: Num ad tempus aliquod, Religionum diversarum, in uno Principatu tolerantia : an verò omnium dissentientium excisio, & totius sive Regni, sive Principatus, sive Reipub. eversio?

Quæstionis hujus decisio licet ex utraq; parte, difficultate singulari non careat : tamen Scripturarum Sacrarum freti præsidio, contra Romanenses, affirmatè respondemus : Posse Imperatorem vel Principem, vel alium quempiam Magistratum Christianum, tali statu, illæsâ conscientiâ, subditis ad tempus diversarum Religionum exercitium permittere : præsertim si salus Imperii & Reipub. aliter asseri, & sarta tecta conservari nequeat. Ubi tamen initiò geminâ cautione utendum esse statuimus. Prior est : ut tali rerum statu, Imperator vel Princeps, vel quivis Magistratus alius, disertis verbis publicè protestetur, se in corde & conscientiâ suâ convictum esse, unā tantùm esse veram fidem ac religionem, scriptis Prophetarum & Apostolorum comprehensam, & à se hactenus pro virili assertam, & ad extremum usq; vitę halitum asserendam: neq; se reliquas dissentientes opiniones ullo pacto vel jam approbare, vel approbaturum unquàm : sed gravioris damni & periculi, evitandi gratiâ ad tempus aliquod toleraturū, & permissurum, ut quælibet dissidentium pars, suæ religionis exercitium obire possit, usq; dum remotis omnibus remoris & obstaculis, inter provinciales omnes consensus aliquis de Religione ineatur. Posterior cautio est, ut durante tali confusionis statu, Princeps Christianus & verè pius, clavum Reipub. regat & gubernet, instar periti alicujus naucleri. Quemadmodum enim iste, diversis & contrariis ventis obortis, & fluctibus inter se certantibus, vela jam pandit, jam contrahit, quò navis medios inter procellarum fluctus & turbines, cursum rectè & secundum cynosuram teneat, tandemque ad portum salva & incolumis appellat. Ita princeps diversis Religionum agitatis procellis, interdum vela contrahet, hoc est, heterodoxis & hæreticis in nervum nimiùm erupturis liberiùs grassandi cursum, paululùm, quantum sine eversione Reipub. fieri potest, inhibebit: Interea verò, quoad salvâ puriore Religione id fieri queat, liberore aura ipsos uti frui permittet : sed ita , ut semper ad Cynosuram Verbi divini respiciat , & ex simplicitate ac ignorantia errantes , ut & seductos ab aliis, tanquam dociles cum lenitate, institui curet: Indociles verò , rebelles, refractarios & contumaciter errantes , tali durante statu sic legibus & edictis coerceat & compescat, ut pro lubitu grassari & ovile Domini inficere nequeant : quin seditiosos , & pacis publicæ turbatores , tanquam perjuros & fædifragos, vel capitis etiam supplicio è medio tollat : ut sic navis Ecclesiæ,inter medios istos turbines, cursum Evangelii illæsum illibatumq; continuare , & tandem ad portum æternæ tranquillitatis desideratissimum appellere queat.

Cæterùm rationes & argumenta Affirmativæ hujus nostræ petimus partim ab exemplis piorum Regum & Principum , qui tali emergente statu praxin jam definitam , non sine singulari DEI approbatione tenuerunt : partim verò à rationibus analogiæ fidei consentaneis:

1. DAVID certè Rex secundum cor & voluntatem DEI, non Judæis modò , in Religione vera sibi ὁμοψηφοις : sed & Philistæis, Moabitis, Ammonitis, Syris Damasci, diversissimarum Religionum populis , in potestatem jure belli redactis , imperasse : iisdemq; Judaicam Religionem , cane & angue pejus aversantibus, liberum suæ religionis exercitium permifisse legitur: ne nimio rigore,populorúm obedientiam fidemque in Politicis, ut & pacem Ecclesiæ Judaicæ penitùs perderet: sed hoc ita permifisse legitur, ut cultum interim veri DEI ita peragi curaret, ut indies ex illis ipsis populis infidelibus , plurimi ad Ecclesiam Judaicam transirent, & proselyti fieren-. Qua de re videatur 2. Sam. 8. v. 1. seqq. imò tota Davidis historia , in lib. 2. Samuelis, & lib. 1. Paralipomenon.

2. Rex Nabuchodonosor Monarcha primus regni Babylonici regnasse legitur à flumine terræ Philistæorum usque ad terminũ Ægypti : sed quia universos istos populos ad cultum DEI Danielis adigere non posset, permisit utique singulis suæ religionis exercendæ potestatem : eo unicè contentus , quòd publicis edictis & pœnis capitalibus propositis cavit, ne quis in omnibus illis regnis atq; provinciis,verum Deum blasphemaret: A me, inquiens , hoc decretum esto , ut omnis populus tribus & lingua , quæcunq; locuta fuerit blasphemiam contra Deum Sidrach , Misach, & Abednago, dispereat , & domus ejus vastetur. Daniel. 3. v. 96.

3. Cyrus primus Persarum Monarcha , Judæis permisit , ut Hierosolymis & templũ restaurarent, & Religionis suæ exercitium liberè tractarent. Reliquos autem populos à Judæorum interim religione diversissimam fidem tenere , non prohibuit : siquidem violentò lenta ad unam amplexandam fidem atq; religionem coactio, sine præsentissimo regni exitio locum habere non poterat. Esdræ 1. v. 2. &c.

4. Quam religionis Judaicæ permissionem ratam etiam habuit Darius Rex Persarum: ut, licèt Artaxerxes aulicorum quorundam Consiliis circumventus, de supprimendis Judæorum studiis & conatibus mandatum dedisset: Esdræ 4. v. 21. Darius tamen, animadvertens sine enormi periculo & damno regni fieri non posse, permissionem illam Cyri, reclamantibus etiam Judæorum hostibus, confirmare voluit: hac adjecta comminatione: Quicunq; hanc mutaverit sanctionem, tollatur lignum de domo ipsius, & erigatur, & configatur in eo, domus autem ejus pub icetur. Esdræ 6 v 6. & 11. Quid? quod idem Darius, ad Deum Israëlis postmodum conversus, libertatem Religionis suis subditis, eandem ob causam permittere necesse habuit: Exemplo Nebucadnezaris contentus, publico edicto sancivisse, ne quis subditorum Deum Israëlis contemneret, aut ignominia afficeret: secundum hanc legem: Pax vobis: à me constitutum & decretum, ut in universo Imperio & Regno meo, omnes tremiscant, & metuant Deum Danielis, Danielis 6. v. 26. Rationes, quibus nitimur præcipuæ sunt hæ:

1. Quia ad Fidem certam amplexandam nemo cogi vel potest vel debet: si quidem nemo mortalium jus aliquid habet in alterius conscientiam: uti quæst. 1. ostensum. Neque est, ut aliquis objiciat, Coactionem hanc provenire ex verâ scientiâ, quæ indubitatò statuat, & sciat, Religionem, ad quam coguntur subditi, esse veram ac salvificam: Nam docente Apostolo 1. Cor. 8. v. 7. ad excusationem facti, non sufficit Justa scientia: sed id insuper requiritur, ut conscientiæ & scientiæ aliorum etiam habeatur Ratio. Quod si non fiat, certè uti abusus scientiæ & liberalitatis admittitur: ita aliis conscientia graviter læditur, quo gravis etiam reatus contrahitur. Siquidem hoc ipso testatum faciunt, qui sic peccant, se suæ scientiæ atque voluntatis majorem, quam divinæ rationem habere. Quo respiciens Maximilianus II. Imperator verè Augustus, incitatus à nonnullis, ut Lutheranos vi armisque ad internecionem usque deleret, respondisse legitur Nullum peccatum gravius est, quàm conscientiis dominari velle: Deo enim se opponere conantur, qui conscientiis in causa Religionis dominari volunt. Crat. in Orat. fun.


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: Question II. Whether a Christian and orthodox magistrate can permit to his subjects diversity of religion, that is, the liberty of several… (continued)

2. Because the peace of Religion, in such an emerging case of necessity, is that very means through which God himself is accustomed to preserve profane or civil peace for the benefit of his Church, so that, according to that word of the Apostle, 1 Tim. 2:2, we may lead a peaceful and tranquil life under the rule of Princes in all piety and modesty. The examples of those kingdoms, which we have just mentioned from the Scriptures, confirm this. The same was confirmed by that golden peace of Religion, which, established in the Roman Empire by the force of the Transaction of Passau, so associated men of most diverse Religions that they nourished one another in sweetest peace and concord for many years now; nor was it lawful for anyone to break or violate in any way the conditions of this peace, in which the entire safety of the Roman Empire uniquely consisted. And what if by this very pact those prophecies of the Prophets had been fulfilled, by which, under the New Testament, the singular pacification of the Kingdom of Christ is described from the doctrine of the Gospel. Isa. 2. v. 4. They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks, nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more. And chap. 11. vers. 6. & 7. Then the wolf shall dwell with the lamb: and the leopard shall lie down with the kid: the calf and the lion and the sheep shall dwell together, and a little child shall lead them. And chap. 65. vers. 25. They shall not hurt, nor destroy in all my holy mountain, says the LORD. Mich. 4. vers. 4. & 5. And then a man shall sit under his vine, and under his fig tree, and there was none to make them afraid: for the mouth of the LORD of hosts has spoken it: For all peoples will walk every one in the name of his GOD: But we will walk in the name of the LORD our GOD forever and ever.

3. Because God himself permits many and most diverse Religions in the world for this reason, that the purer Religion may be propagated all the more conveniently: and that the wheat may not be plucked up with the tares out of excessive zeal: until the most absolute segregation of the just and the impious is made by the angels on the last day. In exactly the same way, if the peace of the Church cannot always be asserted intact, unless some liberty is sometimes granted even to a false religion: certainly the Political Magistrate does not sin if, in such a case, he permits it until all subjects, or at least the greatest part of them, coalesce under the unity of faith and Spirit, through the mediation of divine grace. If he finally attains this end, he will certainly rejoice greatly for himself, he will congratulate the Church of GOD, and he will give thanks to GOD for this singular success. But if not, and the stubbornness of some is so great that they cannot be recalled to the way of truth: he will bear it patiently, and will commend the whole matter and outcome to GOD with pious prayers: but in such a way that he himself meanwhile strenuously and ceaselessly does his duty, striving to lead those wandering from the true religion to the pure worship of GOD through frequent and fatherly admonitions, through ministers of the Word, through assemblies and Synods or colloquies, and through right instruction: but he should not force them to the faith by arms, nor utterly extirpate the contumacious: but leave the judgment in this part to GOD. If a pious Emperor or Prince does this, then he ought to be considered to have rightly taken care of both tables, and also to have had regard for both kinds of peace.

Furthermore, this decision of ours is not to be extended outside of such cases of necessity. For where in any Kingdom or Duchy, it is agreed between the Prince himself and the Provincial Estates concerning the one true and saving Religion to be asserted; and truly, by the secret craftiness of certain ill-disposed persons, whether Theologians or Politicians, false Doctors creep in, who strive to sow their darnel and tares in the field of the Church by night, that is, secretly and with almost no one noticing: in this case, certainly, it is the duty of the Prince to take away from such persons all liberty of teaching, and if they are unwilling to revoke their errors, to remove them from their place, and to banish them to those peoples among whom those errors are held in some esteem: as was shown more fully above in the first question.

The Sacramentarians are in an uproar at this point, and they accuse our Princes of a new persecution and Tyranny, and our Orthodox Theologians of cruelty, because these are the authors who incite them to rage against the Calvinists with prisons, fines, and exiles, and to strip them of their dignities and offices, just as that masked man named above, Benbellona, exaggerates it in his den in a wonderful manner.

But these are crocodile tears, that is, clearly feigned and simulated. For let them show whose body or life has ever been harmed by our people solely for the sake of religion. They will not show or name even a single individual. There are indeed some Calvinists who have been put to death by our Princes: but not because they were Calvinists, but because they were seditious, perjured, perfidious, and had gone about with a traitorous mind to overthrow the Princes together with their Principalities and all their subjects.

Furthermore, it is not a matter of persecution but of duty: not of tyranny but of law, whatever our people sometimes decree against Calvinist Doctors. They enter the Church at the beginning, covered in sheep's clothing, promising even under oath the candor and ὁμοδοξίαν of Religion: soon, having assumed the fox's skin, they seek an opportunity by which they might infect the simple sheep with Sacramentarian poison without the Magistrate knowing: Having obtained this, they put on the wolf's skin, and they rage in the Church at will, feigning and refeigning new laws one after another, until, supported by some external arm, extorted in any way whatsoever, they disturb, despise, and overturn everything: and they keep neither sacred nor political faith honestly enough toward their Magistrate or the Republic.

& the Churches approve. Shall a truly Christian Magistrate therefore permit such license to run riot with impunity to those people? Certainly nothing of the sort. The Apostle certainly, Tit. 3. v. 10, wishes a heretical man to be avoided after one or two admonitions: If, however, he is to be avoided, it is certainly incumbent upon the Magistrate to remove such people from the place and to eject them from his territories, so that they may be avoided. Thus the same Apostle, Galat. 5. v. 12, imprecating excision upon such pseudo-Doctors: I would, he says, that they were cut off who trouble you. If, however, they are to be cut off, they certainly ought not to enjoy communion with the rest of the faithful. Thirdly, the Princes of the Protestants, having given their faith to the Emperor, protested openly that they had never granted, nor would ever grant, a place to the Sacramentarians in their territories: on the 22nd of Sept. A. C. 1530. Fourthly, public offices or duties, dignities, honors, privileges, and stipends, which are taken away from Calvinist Doctors, are not their own property, but are public goods. Therefore, in such a case, the Prince will be taking away nothing of their own or private property, but is reclaiming for himself what is his own.

But they say, this very method is coercive: since now religion is no longer left free to anyone. But it is correctly answered in the negative. For if such fanatics are removed from a place, they are certainly not compelled to embrace another faith: but it is left free to them to profess their religion freely elsewhere. Therefore, that which is not permitted to them in one place is defined too ignorantly and petulantly as coercion to the faith.

Others object partly that: Everything coerced is displeasing to GOD, and partly that Rom. 14. v. 5: Let every man abound in his own sense: But neither prejudices our cause and opinion in the least. For that former reason must be accepted with a grain of salt and a certain moderation. For if that holds simply, how does the householder, having sent his servants to the roads and hedges, command men to be compelled to enter, so that his house may be filled, Luke 14. v. 23? Therefore, a distinction must first be made, partly of men, partly of religions. For if they are outside the boundaries of the Church of Christ, that is, if they are clearly infidel men: the Christian religion is indeed to be preached to them: but it is not to be forced upon them by violence, external coercion, or punishments, which the Spaniards did in India and the provinces of the new world, following and betraying the Spirit of Antichrist. For here that saying of Tertullian to Scapula holds: It is not of religion to compel religion, which ought to be undertaken of one's own accord, not by force: Likewise that saying of Epiphanius: οὐκ ἐπαναγκὲς ἡ ϑεοσέβεια, ἀλλ’ ἐκ προαιρέσεως ἡ δικαιοσύνη: Religion does not admit of coercion: but that which is right is accepted by spontaneous motion.

And in these terms of the question, that which Constantine said to Athanasius is praised: I wish to do violence to no one, nor to compel anyone to the faith, but only to exhort: and to leave the judgment to GOD. Thus it is reported of Constantine: Tripart. lib. 7. c. 4. That he permitted everyone to believe and worship God as he wished, thinking that he would accomplish more by this leniency and mildness than by harsher edicts. But in the very bosom of the Church, where the name has once been given to the Christian religion and profession: if heresies of any kind are permitted to run riot and wander promiscuously and impiously, it is certain that the state of the Church is utterly ruined. Here the Emperor Jovinian is wrongly praised by Themistius, who permitted the religion of every heretic to be free.

Then, under this reasoning, it is also to be noted that liberty in religion is not immediately opposed to coercion. For there is a third thing intermediate between these two, namely, that heresies should not be permitted to wander. For by this being done, although the sails of that liberty are not spread wide: yet no coercion will be made to embrace an adverse religion.

The meaning of the Apostolic saying is far different, and the opinion most diverse. For he does not approve of a πανσπερμίαν of religions, which fights against the express Word of GOD: You shall not do every man that which seems right to himself, Deut. 12. v. 8. But what I command you, keep, Deut. 4. v. 2. But the Apostle forbids that anything be done with a feigned or wavering mind: and he commands that all things be done according to conscience and from a firm reason of the divine word.

Finally, what else does that Calvinist [argument] for the liberty of Religion provide, than that by this pact it partakes of the heresy of the Rhetorians, who taught that everyone would be saved in his own religion: and who, as Augustine speaks, de haeres. cap. 72, contended with wonderful vanity that all heretics walk rightly and speak the truth: Which Augustine pronounces to be so absurd that it seems in a way incredible to relate. See the Lampetians, who likewise urged the liberty of Religion in Damascenus. What impiety that of Francesco Pucci was, having proceeded from this fountainhead of error, is more than sufficiently known to all.

They also object to that saying of Christ: Matth 13. v. 30, let both grow until the harvest. But a gross ἄγνοια ἐλέγχꙋ is committed. For this law was laid down not for the Magistrate, but especially for the ministers.

Furthermore, be it so, that it extends even to the Magistrate: yet it is to be accepted only in a certain respect: namely, that they may not rage against the bodies and lives of those who scatter tares in the field of the LORD. But if all severity against heretics were simply forbidden to the Magistrate, then the care of the first table would not pertain to them at all, as it consists chiefly in this, that with all false dogmas extirpated, the one true Religion may prevail.

Finally, they object with the examples of Christian Emperors, Nerva, Hadrian, Pius, Commodus, Alexander Severus, Constantine, both Theodosiuses, Valentinian, and others, who permitted everyone to believe and worship God as they wished, and did not wish to use force against anyone for the sake of faith.

I respond that there is a huge difference in the examples: For those Emperors had a matter and business with Gentiles who had not yet perceived any taste of the Christian religion at all. Therefore, to force these to the Christian faith by edicts, or threats, or punishments would have been clearly ill-advised, since they were to be taught before they were to be terrified. For to terrify and not to teach, especially those who had never yet been involved in the Church, is a certain wicked domination over consciences, as Augustine judges, Epist. 45. That the Arians were tolerated by the Emperor Theodosius, we do not deny: but that was done when this heresy had spread immensely and had occupied almost the entire Christian world: nor could it be suppressed by any power. Therefore, that was a matter of impotence and present necessity rather than of will and design.

Next, what the Calvinists assert about the more recent Christian Emperors is false. Theodosius and Valentinian certainly passed a law against the Arians and Manichaeans, Cod. lib. 1. tit. 5 l. Ariani, likewise another law was promulgated against the Nestorians: Ibid. l. Damnato. Thus the Emperors Valentinian and Marcian promulgated a law against the Apollinarists and Eutychians: Ibid. l. Quicunq;. By these laws, heretics are ordered to be driven from cities, it is commanded that no place be left for them, in which injury is done even to the elements themselves: it is decreed that their books are to be publicly burned: they are prohibited from building churches and monasteries, from holding secret meetings and conventicles, from aspiring to military service, from disputing about heretical error: finally, unless they cease to resist public laws and to spread their heresies, they are ordered to be handed over even to punishments.

Moreover, since this complaint is today quite solemn and customary for the Sacramentarian race, and they strive to gain ill-will for our Churches from this alone: it would be worth the effort to weigh a little more accurately whether they seriously seek some such freedom of religion, and promise peace to our Churches and Confession without pretense and deceit? So that this may be plain to all, the truth must be extracted from the very principles of religion. There are, however, three things above all by which the Church in the matter of religion can be asserted as safe and sound, either uniquely or especially, and be preserved in a harbor of tranquility against any waves and storms.

THE FIRST is a Norm of certain doctrine, taken uniquely from the Sacred Scriptures, to which, as an infallible Cynosure of truth, any dogmas can, and indeed must, be judged.

THE SECOND: Freedom of the Ecclesiastical office, no less regarding refutation than teaching. THE THIRD: that the truth be asserted not only by a living voice but also by writings. The Sacramentarians thoroughly undermine and tear down that first one; for they have never agreed among themselves about any Symbolic norm, nor do they agree today: so that they have publicly written that the Augsburg Confession, the most august symbol of our Churches, must be thoroughly eliminated as a torch by which all of Gaul would be set on fire if it were received: as Calvin in his Letters: Others have explicitly affirmed that it can only be subscribed to if a convenient interpretation is admitted, as Beza: Others have not feared to affirm that the Augsburg Confession and the Zwinglian one are one and the same, and that both do not differ in sense: as Ambrosius Wolssius: Others have contended that the Tetrapolitan Confession, or that of the four cities, written by Bucer in the year 1530, is the symbol of the Calvinist Churches: as Johannes Sturmius and Wolssius: Others have determined that this very Confession is lacking, mutilated, and not in every part consonant with the truth and the analogy of faith: as Bucer himself, who did not hesitate to write books of Retractions against it: Others have simply refused in the past to profess themselves associates of the Augsburg Confession: as Zwingli himself: Others seek protection under a changed and adulterated Confession: openly rejecting that former one as if it were a successor to Papal impiety: as most of the modern Calvinists: Others finally lie splendidly that both editions agree in sense in all things: as Benbellona. Thus, therefore, to this very day the Calvinists are uncertain about some certain norm of doctrine, or at least what they hide in their mind, they do not dare to profess publicly. With what face, therefore, with what conscience, do they demand from Princes who are entirely addicted to the Augsburg Confession that the free exercise of their own religion be permitted to them: indeed, they write that it is owed to them by a certain right as if by imperial authority; while they shamelessly and against their conscience pretend and lie that they are associates of the same Confession.

That other protection of true religion, namely the freedom of the Ecclesiastical office, especially regarding refutation, they snatch away from our Churches and Theologians by whatever means they can: so much so that they even provide by public decrees that it is not lawful for any of ours to publish anything about sacred matters to the public, unless it has first been approved by them, even by the political Sacramentarian wolves. To this institution they are accustomed to pretend the advantage of partly reducing quarrels among Theologians; partly of rescuing the best authors from the shadows: so that not even the Princes themselves (whose goodness this race of men most wickedly abuses for the most part) can smell that peace is not being sought for purer religion by this pact, but rather ambushes are being laid: not that disputes are diminished, but that the weapons of defense are taken away, stripped of which the Lutherans would be rendered as prey to the whim of their Sacramentarian enemies: and this asylum of religion granted to the Sacramentarians would turn into a snare, servitude, and eternal ruin for our own. And this is what they wish to have wrung from Orthodox Princes by such great complaints, lamentations, and sighs, rather than requested: against which the Lutheran orders and all who desire both the increase of the purer Religion and the royal rights of the Church of Christ to be kept safe and sound will guard themselves no less than they would against the Trojan horse.

THE THIRD safeguard for exercising the purer Religion is the assertion of the truth, which is done as much by public writings as by the living voice. The Calvinist Spirit does not fear to snatch both of these from our Church: to put shackles on the ministry itself: that is, to fit a halter upon the Holy Spirit Himself: For to this end those Mandates, clearly treacherous to the Truth and the more sincere Religion, are accustomed to be published by the Calvinists where they strive to fix their seat and eject the Lutherans, by which, under the threat of the most severe punishments, silence is commanded to the Ministers, lest they be induced to call the Sacramentarian wolf, which is hostilely invading the fold of the LORD, by its own name while speaking from the pulpit. Now if a more favorable outcome should respond to those wicked attempts, one may soon see, nay, even touch with one's hands, what kind of religious liberty they have demanded from our Princes, not one that grants the power to profess the Lutheran faith freely: but one that quickly dispatches everything by hand, force, command, prison, fine, and exile, expels the Lutherans from their seats, and finally casts out and proscribes Luther himself along with his Religion. This is that beautiful asylum of the Calvinist Religion, which, where it finds a place and plants a firmer foot, soon begins to rage and act insanely, and permits the Lutheran Religion a safe and free exercise only to the extent that it would rather disturb both political and ecclesiastical figures—whom they know to have achieved something thus far in preserving and restoring the purity of doctrine, or whom they suspect might be able to achieve something hereafter—from their dignities and offices, or at least terrify them with threats, circumvent them with snares, and hem them in with dangers, so that they may either crush and cast them out when they wish; or, if not cast out and crushed, at least wear them down and finish them off with anxieties. The sighs of the Electoral Palatinate bear witness to this: the bloody tears of Upper Hesse, the exiles, captivities, and pressures of many Orthodox: which show more clearly than the midday sun what practice the Calvinists seek and conceal under the artifice and clearly Sinonian counsel of the asylum of Religion.

Latin:

2. Quia pax Religionis, tali emergente necessitatis casu, est illud ipsum medium per quod Deus ipse pacem prophanam sive civilem, in emolumentum suæ Ecclesiæ conservare consuevit, ut secundum illud Apostoli, 1. Timoth. 2. v. 2. vitam pacatam & tranquillam, sub Principum Imperio agere queamus in omni pietate & modestia. Comprobant hoc illorum regnorum exempla, quorũ ex sacris modò mentionem fecimus. Comprobavit idem pax illa Religionis aurea, quæ vigore Transactionis passaviensis imperio Romano constituta, diversissimarũ Religionũ homines ita consociavit, ut suavissimâ pacê ac concordiâ annis jam benè multis invicê alerent: neq; fas cuiquam esset, conditiones pacis hujus, in qua salus Imperii Romani tota unicè consistebat, quoquo modo rumpere aut violare. Et quid si hoc ipso pacto impleta fuissent illa vaticinia Prophetarum, quibus sub Novo Testamento, ex doctrina Evangelii singularis pacatio Regni Christi describitur. Esa. 2. v. 4. Conflabunt gladios suos in vomeres, & lanceas suas in falces, non levabit gens contra gentem gladium, non exercebuntur ultrà ad prælium. Et cap. 11. vers. 6. & 7. Tunc habitabit lupus cum agno: & pardus cum hædo accubabit: vitulus & leo & ovis simul morabuntur, & puer parvulus minabit eos. Et cap. 65. vers. 25. Non nocebunt, neque occident in omni monte sancto meo, dicit DOMINUS. Mich. 4. vers. 4. & 5. Et sedet tunc vir subtus vineam suam, & subtus ficum suum, & non erat qui deterreat: quia os DOMINI exercituum locutum est: Quia omnes populi ambulabunt unusquisq; in nomine DEI sui: Nos autem ambulabimus in nomine Domini DEI nostri eternum & ultrà.

3. Quia Deus ipse ideò plures in mundo & diversissimas Religiones permittit, ut purior Religio tantò commodius propagari possit: neque ex vehementiore zelo, triticum cum zizaniis evellatur: usque dum in die novissimo ab angelis fiat justorum & impiorum absolutissima segregatio. Eundem planè in modum, si pax Ecclesiæ farta tecta asseri non semper possit, nisi ut interdum falsę etiam religioni aliqua concedatur libertas: utique non peccat Magistratus Politicus, si tali casu, & eo usque id permittat, usque dum omnes subditi, vel certè maxima eorum pars, sub unitatem fidei & Spiritus, divinâ mediante gratiâ coalescat. Quem finem si tandem assequatur, utique sibi plurimum gaudebit, Ecclesiæ DEI gratulabitur, DEO verò pro singulari hoc successu aget gratias. Sin minus, sed tanta sit quorundam pervicacia, ut in viam veritatis revocari non possint: patienter illud feret, rem & eventum omnem DEO piis precibus commendabit: sed ita ut ipse interim strenuè & indefinenter suum faciat officium, aberrantes à verâ religione, crebris & paternis admonitionibus, per ministros Verbi, per conventus & Synodos sive colloquia, & recta institutione ad purum DEI cultum, adducere studeat : non autem armis ad fidem cogat, aut contumaces funditus extirpet : sed DEO hac in parte judicium relinquat. Hoc si fecerit pius Imperator sive Princeps, tum utriusque tabulae curam, utriusque etiam pacis rationem recte habuisse, censeri debet.

Caeterum haec decisio nostra, extra ejusmodi casus necessitatis non est extendanda. Nam ubi in Regno sive Ducatu aliquo, inter Principem ipsum, & Ordines provincialium, de una vera & salvifica Religione asserenda convenit; & vero clam male feriatorum quorundam sive Theologorum, sive Politicorum astutia irrepunt falsi Doctores, qui in agrum Ecclesiae noctu, hoc est, clam & nemine ferme animadvertente, eorum lolia atque zizania spargere satagunt: hoc certe casu Principis officium est, talibus omnem docendi libertatem adimere, etsi errores revocare nolint, loco movere, & ad eos ablegare populos, apud quos errores illi in aliquo sunt pretio : prout supra quaestione prima fusius ostensum.

Tumultuantur hoc loco Sacramentarii, & tum Principes nostros novae persecutionis & Tyrannidis, tum Theologos Orthodoxos, crudelitatis insimulant, eo quod hi autores sint illis, ut in Calvinianos carceribus, mulctis, exiliis saeviant, dignitatibus & officiis suis exuant, quemadmodum personatus ille supra nominatus Benbellona in suo suscitabulo mirum in modum id exaggerat.

Sed Crocodili hae sunt lachrymae, hoc est, fictae plane & simulatae. Monstrent enim in cujus corpus aut vitam, unquam a nostris, religionis tantum causa fuerit saevitum. Ne unicum quidem monstrabunt aut nominabunt individuum. Sunt quidem Calvinianorum aliqui a nostris Principibus capite plexi : sed non quia Calviniani, sed quia seditiosi, perjuri, perfidi erant, & proditorio animo Principes una cum Principatibus & subditis universis, eversum iverant.

Deinde vero, non persecutionis sed officii : non tyrannidis sed juris est, quicquid in Doctores Calvinianos interdum a nostris statuunt. Intrant illi initio in Ecclesiam, ovilla veste tecti, Religionis candorem & ὁμοδοξίαν etiam jurato promittentes: mox vulpina assumta, occasionem quaerunt, qua oves simplices veneno Sacramentario inscio Magistratu inficere possit: Hac potiti lupinam induunt, & in Ecclesia grassantur pro lubitu, fingentes ac refingentes leges subinde novas, donec brachio aliquo externo, quovis modo extorto suffulti, omnia turbant, dispiciunt, evertunt: & neque sacram, neque politicam fidem satis ingenue suo Magistratui, Reipub.

& Ecclesiæ probant. Siccine ergò istis sic impune grassandi licentiam permittet Magistratus verè Christianus? Nihil certè minus, Apostolus certè, Tit. 3. v. 10. Hæreticum hominem post unam atque alteram admonitionem vitari vult: Si autem vitandus: utique Magistratui incumbit, tales loco movere, suisq; ditionibus ejicere, ut vitari possint. Sic idem Apostolus Galat. 5. v. 12. abscisionem imprecatus ejusmodi pseudo-Doctoribus: Utinam, inquiens, abscindantur, qui perturbant vos. Si autem abscindendi sunt, utique communi cum reliquis fidelibus communione frui non debent. Tertiò, Principes protestantium, data imperatori fide, protestati sunt palàm, se Sacramentariis locum in suis ditionibus nunquàm concessisse, neque concessuros nuquã: die 22. Sept. A. C. 1530. Quartò, officia sive munera publica, dignitates, honores, privilegia, stipendia, quæ eripiuntur Calvinianis Doctoribus, non sunt ipsorum propria, sed sunt bona publica. Ergo tali casu nihil proprii aut privati ipsis Princeps erit, sed quod suum est sibi rursus vendicat.

Sed inquiunt, hic ipse modus est coactivus: siquidem jam non amplius libera cuivis relinquitur Religio. Rectè autem respondetur negatè. Nam si tales fanatici loco moveantur, utiq; non coguntur ad amplexandam fidem aliam: sed liberum ipsis relinquitur, alibi locorum, liberè suam profitendi religionem. Quod ergo uno in loco illis non permittitur illud per coactionem ad fidem, inscitè nimis & petulantes definitur.

Objiciunt alii partim illud: Omne coactũ displicere DEO partim verò illud Rom. 14. v. 5. Unusquisq; in suo sensu abundet: Sed neutrum nostræ causæ & sententiæ quicquam præjudicat. Nam prior illa ratio cum grano salis & certo moderamine est accipienda. Si enim simpliciter valet illa, quomodo paterfamiliàs emissis servis ad vias & sepes, cogi ad ingressum jubet homines, ut impleatur domus sua. Luc. 14. v. 23? Est ergò primùm distinctio facienda, partim hominum, partim religionum. Si enim extra pomeria Ecclesiæ Christi, hoc est, si infideles planè sint homines: religio Christiana ipsis quidem prædicanda: non autem vi, coactione externa, aut suppliciis obtrudenda est, quod in India, & novi orbis provinciis Hispani factitarunt, Antichristi secuti & prodentes Spiritum. Hic enim valet Tertulliani illud ad Scapulam: Non est religionis, cogere religionem, quæ sponte suscipi debet, non vi: Item Epiphanii illud: οὐκ ἐπαναγκὲς ἡ ϑεοσέβεια, ἀλλ’ ἐκ προαιρέσεως ἡ δικαιοσύνη: non admittit coactionem Religio: sed spontaneo motu acceptatur, quod rectum est.

Et in his quæstionis terminis laudatur, quod Constantinus ad Athanasium: Nemini volo vim facere, aut ad fidem cogere. sed tantum adhortari: Judicium autem DEO relinquere. Sic de Constantino refertur: Tripart. lib. 7. c. 4. Quod unumquemq́; credere ac Deum colere, sicut vellet, permiserit, existimans plus se hac lenitate & mansuetudine effecturum, quàm acerbioribus edictis. In gremio autem ipso Ecclesiae, ubi religioni & professioni Christianae nomen semel datum est: si promiscue & impie grassari vagarique haereses quaelibet permittantur, certum est, Ecclesiae statum prorsus pessundari. Hic perperam a Themistio laudatur Jovinianus Imp. qui liberam esse cujusque haeretici religionem permisit.

Deinde sub ista ratione illud etiam est notandum, libertatem in religione, coactioni non immediate esse oppositam. Est enim Tertium quiddam intermedium inter duo ista, nempe ut haereses vagari non permittantur. Hoc enim facto, quamvis libertati isti sua non pateant vela: tamen ad religionem adversam amplectandam nulla fiet coactio.

Dicti Apostolici longe alia est mens, & sententia diversissima. Neque enim probat Religionum πανσπερμίαν, quae cum expresso DEI Verbo pugnat: Non facietis singuli, quod vobis rectum videbitur. Deut. 12. v. 8. Sed qua ego praecipio vobis, custodite. Deut. 4. v. 2. Sed ne ficto aut fluctuante animo quicquam fiat, prohibet Apostolus: utque pro conscientia, & ex firma verbi divini ratione agantur omnia, praecipit.

Tandem quid aliud praestat Calviniana illa pro Religionis libertate, quam quod hoc pacto participat de haeresi Rhetorianorum, qui in sua quemque religione salvum fore docuerunt: quique ut Augustinus loquitur, de haeres. cap. 72. mirabili vanitate contenderunt, omnes haereticos recte ambulare & vera dicere: Quod ita absurdum esse pronunciat Augustinus, ut relatu incredibile quodammodo esse videatur. Videatur de Lampetianis libertatem Religionis itidem urgentibus apud Damascenum. Quae impietas fuerit Francisci Puccii, ex hac erroris scaturigine profecta, plus satis notum est omnibus.

Objiciunt etiam illud Christi: Matth 13. v. 30. sinite utraq; crescere ad messem. Sed crassa committitur ἄγνοια ἐλέγχꙋ. Nam non Magistratui: sed ministris praecipue haec lex lata est.

Deinde esto, ad Magistratum etiam illa extendatur: tamen secundum quid tantum accipienda: nempe ne in corpora & vitam eorum, qui Zizania in agrum DOMINI spargunt, saeviant. Quod si simpliciter omnis severitas in haereticos Magistratui esset interdicta: neq́; primae tabulae cura quicquam ad ipsos pertineret, ut quae in eo praecipue consistit, ut extirpatis omnibus falsis dogmatibus una vera Religio obtineat.

Tandem objiciunt exempla Imperatorum Christianorum, Nervæ, Hadriani, Pii, Commodi, Alexandri Severi, Constantini utriusq; Theodosii, Valentiniani, & aliorum, qui unumquemq; credere, ac Deum colere, sicut vellet, permiserunt, nec fidei causa vim cuiquam facere voluerunt.

Respondeo ingentem esse diversitatem in exemplis: Nam Imperatoribus istis, res atque negocium fuit, cum Gentilibus, qui nullum adhuc prorsus Religionis Christianæ gustum perceperant. Hos ergò vel edictis, vel minis, vel pœnis ad fidem Christianam cogere, planè inconsultum fuerat, quippè qui docendi priùs quàm terrendi. Terrere enim & non docere, præcipuè nunquam adhuc in Ecclesia versatos, improba quædam in Conscientias est dominatio, judice Augustino, Epist. 45. Sic Arianos à Theodosio Imp. toleratos fuisse, non imus inficias: sed factum id, cum hæresis hæc in immensum dilatata, totum penè orbem Christianum occupasset: neq; ullâ potentiâ reprimi posset. Impotentiæ ergò & necessitatis præsentis magis, quàm voluntatis & consilii istud fuit.

Deinde falsum est, quod de recentioribus Impp. Christianis asserunt Calviniani. Theodosi9 certè & Valentinianus legem tulerunt contra Arianos & Manichæos, Cod. lib. 1. tit. 5 l. Ariani, item aliâ lex promulgata contra Nestorianos: Ibid. l. Damnato. Sic Valentianus & Martianus Impp. legem promulgârunt contra Apollinaristas & Eutychianos: Ibid. l. Quicunq;. Quibus legibus de civitatibus pelli jubentur hæretici, nihil loci ipsis relinquendú esse præcipitur, in quo ipsis etiam eleinentis fiat injuria: libros istorum publicè comburendos esse statuitur: Ecclesias & monasteria construere, parasynaxes & conventicula agere, ad militiam adspirare, de hæretico errore disputare prohibentur: deniqve nisi reluctari legibus publicis, & spargere hæreses suas desinant, suppliciis etiam tradi jubentur.

Cæterùm cùm hæc querela genti Sacramentariæ hodiè admodum sit solennis, & usitata, & ex ea vel sola, nostris Ecclesiis invidiam se conciliare studeant: operæ pretium fuerit, paulò accuratiùs expendere, utrum seriò talem aliquam Religionis libertatem expetant, & pacem nostris quoqve Ecclesiis, & Confessioni, sine fuco & dolo polliceantur? Quod ut planum fiat omnibus, ex ipsis Religionis Principiis, veritas eruenda fuerit. Tria autem sunt potissimum, quibus Ecclesia in Religionis negocio, vel unicè vel maximè potest sarta tecta asseri, inqve tranquillitatis portu conservari adversus quosvis fluctus atque turbines.

PRIMUM, est Norma doctrinæ certæ, ex scripturis Sacris unicè petita, ad quam velut infallibilem veritatis Cynosuram dogmata quævis judicari queant, imò debeant.

ALTERUM: Libertas muneris Ecclesiastici, non minùs circa ἔλεγχον quàm διδασκαλίαν. TERTIVM: ut non viva tantùm voce: sed & scriptionibus veritas asseratur. Primum illud Sacramentarii penitùs subruunt & convellunt; Nam de norma aliqua Symbolica, usque adeò ipsis invicem nunquam convenit, neque hodiè convenit : ut Augustanam, potiùs Confessionem, Ecclesiarum nostrarum Symbolum augustissimum, tanquam faoem, quâ universa Gallia si ea recipiatur, conflagratura sit, penitùs eliminandam esse, publicè scriptitârint: ut Calvinus in Epistolis: Alii, non nisi commodâ admissâ interpretatione subscribi illi posse, disertè affirmârint, ut Beza: Alii Confessionem Augustanam cum Zwinglianâ unam eandemque esse, nec sensu discrepare utramque, affirmare non sint veriti : ut Ambrosius Wolssius: Alii Confessionem Tetrapolitanam sive quatuor civitatum, anno 30. supra sesquimillesimum à B圧ero scriptam, Ecclesiarum Calvinianarum Symbolum esse contenderint: ut Johannes Sturmius, & Wolssius: Alii Confessionem hanc ipsam, mancam mutilam, neque ex omni parte veritati & analogiæ fidei consonam esse statuerint:ut Buccerus ipse, qui Retractationum libros in eam scribere non dubitavit: Alii Confessionis Augustanæ socios se profiteri, simpliciter olim recusarint: ut Zwinglius ipse: Alii sub mutana & adulterata Confessione quærant præsidium: priorem illam tanquam impietati Pontificiæ succenturiantem palàm rejicientes: ut plærique modernorum Calvinianorum: Alii denique utramque editionem sensu per omnia convenire, splendidè mentiantur: ut Benbellona. Sic ergo in hunc usque diem de certa aliqua Doctrinæ norma sunt incerti Calviniani, vel certè quod in animo occultant, publicè profiteri non audent. Quâ igitur fronte, quâ Conscientiâ, à Principibus Confessioni Augustanæ ex asse addictis, liberum suæ Religionis profitendæ exercitium sibi permitti postulant: imò satis pro Imperio jure quasi quodam id sibi debere scriptitant; ejusdem Confessionis socios se impudenter & contra Conscientiam simulantes & mentientes.

ALTERVM illud veræ Religionis præsidium, Libertatem nimirùm muneris Ecclesiastici, quoad ἔλεγχον imprimis, nostris Ecclesiis & Theologis, quibus possunt modis eripiunt: adeò ut publicis etiam decretis caveant, ne cuiquam ex nostris fas sit, de rebus sacris in publicum quicquam emittere, nisi vel ab ipsis priùs lupis etiam politicis Sacramentariis approbatum. Huic instituto prætexere solent commodum partim rixarum inter Theologos minuendarum; partim autorum optimorum ex tenebris vindicandorum: ut ne ipsi etiam Principes (quorum bonitate plerumque sex hæc hominum pessimè abutitur) olfacere possint, non hoc pacto Religioni puriori pacem quæri, sed insidias strui: non lites minui, sed defensionis arma adimi, quibus exuti Lutherani, hostium Sacramentariorum libidini præda pro arbitrio redderentur: & hæc religionis ἀσυλουσία Sacramentariis concessa, nostræ evaderet in laqueum, servitutem & ruinam sempiternam. Et hoc est, quod tantis querelis, lamentationibus & suspiriis, ab Orthodoxis Principibus expressum magis quàm exoratum volunt: à quo sibi haud magis, atque ab equo Trojano sibi cavebunt, ordines Lutherani quique, quotquot quidem & purioris Religionis incrementum & Ecclesiæ Christi regalia sarta tecta esse cupiunt.

TERTIUM purioris Religionis exercendæ præsidium est, veritatis assertio, tam quæ scriptionibus publicis, quàm quæ viva voce fiat. Utrumque hoc Spiritus Calvinianus Ecclesiæ nostræ eripere: ministerio ipsi compedes injicere: hoc est, ipsi Spiritui Sancto capistrum aptare non verentur: Hoc enim fine Mandata illa, Veritatis Religionisq; sincerioris planè proditoria à Calvinianis, ubi sedem figere, Lutheranos verò ejicere satagunt, publicari consueverunt, quibus sub comminatione gravissimarum pœnarum silentium imperatur Ministris, ne lupum Sacramentarium, ovile DOMINI hostiliter invadentem, proprio nomine, pro suggestu verba facientes, appellare in animum inducant. Jam si improbis istis Conatibus eventus optior respondeat, mox videre, imò manibus palpare licet, qualem illi Religionis libertatem à nostris Principibus efflagitârint, non quæ Lutheranæ liberè profitendæ potestatem indulgeat: sed quæ manu, vi, imperio, carcere, mulcta, exilio omnia raptim expediat, Lutheranos sedibus suis expellat, Lutherum denique ipsum cum Religione prorsus ejiciat & proscribat. Hæc est bella illa Religionis Calvinianæ ἀσυλουσία, quæ ubi locum invenit, & pedem tutiorem figit, mox furere & insanire incipit, & tantum non Lutheranæ Religioni salvum liberumq; permittit exercitium, ut potius & politicos & Ecclesiasticos, quos in conservanda restaurandaque doctrinæ puritate, vel hactenus aliquid præstitisse noverunt, vel deinceps etiam præstare posse suspicantur, eos vel ocyus dignitatibus atq; officiis suis deturbent, vel ita saltem minis territent, insidiis circumveniant, periculis concludant, ut aut elidere ipsos atque excutere, cùm velint, possint; aut non excussos atque elisos maximè, curis tamen emacient & conficiant. Testantur hoc Palatinatus Electoralis suspiria: Hassiæ superioris sanguinolentæ lachrymæ plurimorum Orthodoxorum exilia, captivitates, pressuræ: quæ quam praxin Calviniani sub Religionis ἀσυλουσία artificio & consilio planè Sinonio quærant & occulteat, sole meridiano clariùs oftendunt.


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: Question III. Whether and how a Christian Magistrate ought to take action against heretics?

IN ORDER that the decision of this question may be duly carried out, some distinctions must be premised, which can bring light to this whole Controversy. And at the beginning, it must be well observed that by a heretic is not understood just any Schismatic or erring person. For it is human to err: and the field of the Church always has tares sown among the wheat: since even among the Doctors themselves, or the hearers, there are always those who build hay, wood, and stubble upon the foundation, 1 Cor. 3:12. But such a man is understood who, having professed the Christian faith, directly corrupts, depraves, or denies some head or article of the Christian faith or Religion: and even when warned, nay, even convicted, nonetheless obstinately continues to maintain and defend the error he has conceived.

Then one must accurately distinguish between a Heretic and a manifest blasphemer: and again, between him who knowingly and willingly, with a set plan and purpose, scatters errors and tears apart God and all sacred things with dire and execrable blasphemies: and him who does this unknowingly, and not with set malice or plan: but sins through error and simplicity of mind, and weakness of judgment, fascinated by Satan and enticed by his instruments, so that he cannot recognize his errors.

Finally, one must also distinguish between a Heretic as a Heretic: and a heretic insofar as he is at the same time a rebel and seditious.

With those three distinctions, or hypotheses, presupposed, we also respond distinctly to the proposed Ζήτημα. For initially, regarding the manifestly blasphemous, who, knowingly and willingly, and even after being warned several times, yet obstinately and contumaciously vomit forth dire blasphemies against God and the Orthodox religion: we have already proven above in question 1 from the Scriptures that the Christian Magistrate ought to take action with the sword even against such persons: as those who, spontaneously and with fickle impiety, defecting from GOD to the Devil, petulantly repel all grace of GOD from themselves: so that no hope can remain for their amendment. Hence God himself commanded that such a one be put to death and removed from the society of the Christian people: Levit. 24. v. 15. & 16.

Furthermore, regarding heretics properly so called, even if they are not blasphemers in this most extreme degree: but besides heresy, they stir up rebellion, movements, and seditions against the Orthodox Magistrate and his public edicts, move factions in the Church, sow quarrels and contentions among the hearers of the Word, and lay snares for the purer religion: then I maintain entirely that such persons, according to the quality of the offense, can and ought to be punished either by stripes, or by prison, or by fines, or even by the sword: relying on those precepts and statutes of the Scriptures by which such punishments for the seditious have been established by God Himself: by the example of Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and their household, who, being seditious against Aaron, had rushed forward to the tabernacle with their censers for the sake of offering incense: but they were so punished by God that, with fire stirred up by divine power from the censers and blazing forth, and seizing their own bodies, they necessarily perished by a miserable death. Num. 16, through almost the whole chapter.
