His ita constitutis, manifestum est, Adversarios Sectariorum nomina aversantes in insidiis latére. Vident enim, si obtineant, ut diversa hæc diversarum confessionum nomina, ex Ecclesia DEI proscribantur, facilè fieri posse, ut sub æquivoco, & generali Christianorum titulo, quamlibet Ecclesiam invadere, & sub venerando hoc pallio virus suum liberè, & nemine animadvertente spargere possint. Et hic latet anguis in herba, à cordatis & Orthodoxis Theologis meritò proterendus, & conculcandus.

Objiciunt verba B. LUTHERI, ex Tom. 1. Witteb. fol. 7. Es sind etliche / so sie ein Blat oder zwey gelesen oder eine Predigt gehoͤrt / rips raps ausserswischen / vnd nichts mehr thun / dann vberfahren / vnd versprechen die andern mit jhrem Wesen. Sie thuns darumb / das sie gut Lutherisch wollen gesehen seyn. Nicht also du Narr / hoͤr / vnd las dir sagen / zum ersten bitte ich / man wolle meines Nahmens geschweigen / vnd sich nicht Lutherisch sondern Christen heissen. Was ist LVTHER? Ist doch die Lehr nicht mein. Wie keme ich armer stinckender Madensack dazu / das man die Kinder Christi solte mit meinem heiloson Nahmen nennen? Lasset vns tilgen die parteyische Nahmen / vnd Christen heissen. Verùm locus iste, & sententia B. LUTHERI nihil quicquàm nobis officit, neque tantillùm juvat Adversarios. Distinguit enim ipse LUTHERUS inter Personam & Doctrinam: eosque reprehendit, qui neglectâ doctrina Lutheri, nomen saltem ejus externum venerantur,inque ore ferunt. Quemadmodum hodie Calvinianorum nonnulli, sibi Lutheranorum nomen & elogium verè competere, reclamante conscientia gloriantur, cùm ne γρῦ quidem cum doctrina LUTHERI commune habeant. Deinde vim manifestam verbis Lutheri inferunt, dum partim truncata, partim in alienum sensum detorta recitant. Finis & scopus B. LUTHERO unicus est propositus iste, ut ostendat; 1. Fundamentum fidei nemini mortalium: sed soli CHRISTO esse superstructum: Quare statim subjicit: Ich bin/vnd wil keines Meister seyn. 2. Solis externis illis denominationibus doctrinam Evangelij propagari non posse:Sic enim verba LUTHERI integrè posita cohærent: Tom. 2. Germ. Wit. mihi pag. 4. Es sind etliche/so sie ein Blat oder zwey gelesen / oder ein Predigt gehört/rips raps ausserwischen/vnnd nichts mehr thun/denn vberfahren / vnd versprechen die andern mit ihren wesen/ als die nicht Evangelisch seyn/ vnangesehen/ das zuweilen schlechte einfëltige Leute sind/die wol die Warheit lernëten/so man sie ihnen sagete: das hab ich auch niemand gelehret/vnd S. Paulus hat es hart verbotten. Sie thuns nur darumb/ das sie wollen etwas newes wissen/ gut Lutherisch gesehen seyn. Aber sie misbrauchen des H. Evangelij zu jhrem Muthwillen / darmit wirstu das Evangelium nimmermehr in die Hergen treiben/ du wirst sie viel mehr abschrecken/vnd müst ein schwere Antwort geben/das du sie also von der Warheit getries ben hast. Nicht also du Narr/ Höre &c. 3. Sermo est LUTHERO ad eos, qui in doctrina ac fide erant ὁμόψηφοι. Quare subjicit: Nicht also liebe Freunde/ lasset vns tilgen die Parteysche Namen/ vnd Christen heissen/des Lehre wir has ben. Quam sententiam LUTHERI uti ex asse approbamus: ita inde nulla ratione evinci posse statuimus, quòd illis, qui veri Christiani sunt, haud licitum sit,se suasque Ecclesias, certa denominatione à confessione ipsa petita (durch gewissen Confessional Nahmen) à Pontificiorum, Calvinianorum, Arianorum, aliorum Sectariorum hæreticis confessionibus palàm discernere ac segregare. Sic ergo Calviniani in citando LUTHERO fallunt & falluntur, perpetuis Sophisticationibus Ignorationis Elenchi, à dicto secundum quid: & vitiosæ divisionis.


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: Question VI. Whether a Christian magistrate, with a safe conscience, may tolerate Jews in his commonwealth, and grant to them the power of…

Can a Christian Magistrate in his Republic tolerate Jews with a safe conscience, and grant them the power of exercising usury upon his subjects?

Regarding this question the Calvinists hold the Affirmative. For thus Zanchus Tom. 4. of his Works: lib. 1. on the Fourth commandment: Col. 795 for me. A pious Prince can with a good conscience permit Jews to dwell in his dominion, and to behave and trade civilly with his faithful: provided he takes care that the faithful do not contract marriages with the Jews, or communicate in their religion and rites, or even cultivate close friendship, and behave familiarly. And Col. 796. Pious Princes can permit Jews the Synagogues which they have: provided they are content with the reading of the Bibles, and prayers conceived from the holy scriptures, and do not in any way blaspheme Christ, or traduce his Church. Which same sentiment is also held by Amandus Polanus Tom. 2. of his Syntagma: lib. 10. cap. 65. Col. 971 for me. But the Roman Pontiff is accustomed to tolerate Jews throughout all Italy, and in the city of Rome itself, and grants them the power, with money intervening, to vomit forth horrible blasphemies against Jesus of Nazareth in their synagogues with impunity: when on the contrary he pursues with sword and flames those who preach JESUS CHRIST and place all their trust for eternal salvation in him alone and one.

We simply abhor the deed of the Roman Pontiff: so we do not resist the Affirmative of the Calvinists too stubbornly, if it is circumscribed by certain limits or conditions. Now the principal conditions are these:

1. That they simply abstain from all blasphemy against JESUS OF NAZARETH, and his Holy Gospel, as also against all Christians: and that they promise this to the Magistrate under oath, and under penalty of death.

2. That they do not disturb the public peace in any way, but be bound by oath to maintain civil society.

3. That in contracts and negotiations they be obligated either to the Imperial civil laws, or to the municipal laws of any kingdom, province

Latin:

An Magistratus Christianus sua in Repub. Iudæos salvâ conscientiâ ferre, ijsdemque usuras in subditos exercendi potestatem facere possit?

Circa hanc quæstionem Calviniani Affirmativam tenent. Sic enim Zanchus Tom. 4. Operum: lib. 1. in Quartum præceptum: Col. mihi 795. Posest pius Princeps bonâ conscientiâ permittere Judæos in suâ habitare ditione, & civiter cum suis fidelibus versari & negotiari: modo caveat, ne fideles cũ Judæis aut connubia côtrahant, aut in religione illorumǫ ritibus communicent, aut etiam arctam amicitiam colant, familiariterǫ versentur. Et Col. 796. Possunt pij Principes Judæis Synagogas, quas habent, permittere: modò contenti sint lectione Bibliorum, & precibus è sacru literis conceptis,nec ullâ ratione Christum blasphement, ejusve Ecclesiam traducant. Quam eahdem sententiam tenet etiam Amandus Polanus Tom. 2. Syntagmatis: lib. 10. cap. 65. Col. mihi 971. Sed Pontifex Romanus Judæos per totam Italiam, & in ipsa etiam urbe Româ ferre solet, & pecuniæ intervenit potestatem largitur eu impunè in Synagogis suis horrendas in Jesum Nazarenum blasphemias evomendi: cùm econtra eos qui JESUM CHRISTUM prædinant & in illo solo atque uno omnem fiduciam æternæ salutis collocant, ferro flammisǫ persequatur.

Nos uri Pontificis Romani factum simpliciter abominamur: ita Calvinianorum Af firmativæ, si certis ea limitibus sive conditionibus circumscribatur, morosius haud reluctamur. Conditiones autem præcipuæ sunt hæ:

1. Ut simpliciter ab omni blasphemia in JESUM NAZARENUM, & Sanctum ejus Evangelium, ut & Christianos omnes abstineant: idque juratô, & sub pœnâ capitis Magistratui promittant.

2. Ne pacem publicam ullo pacto turbent, sed ad civilem tuendam societatem juramento sint adstricti.

3. Ut in contractibus & negociationibus sint obligati vel ad leges civiles Imperatorias, vel ad municipales cuilibet regno, provin-


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: Question VII. The decision of this question properly belongs to the schools of jurists, to whom we also in this place readily cast our vote…

own, and proper to the Republic: otherwise they are to be punished as thieves and usurers.

4. That they do not lend money at interest to fellow citizens of humbler fortune.

5. And lastly: That they do not in any way draw anyone away from Christianity to impiety and Jewish blasphemies. If a Christian Magistrate wishes to tolerate Jews in his Republic under these laws and conditions, and can keep them in line so that they do not in any way overstep, then we certainly determine that he does not sin at all. And to arrive at this opinion, the following reasons move us.

1. Because blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in: and so all Israel should be saved: Rom. 11. 25. Since, therefore, according to this prophecy of the Apostle, there is still to be, before the end of the world, a clear conversion of the Jewish people to Christ: they are certainly not to be insulted; but neither should every opportunity by which they might be led to the recognition of Christ be simply cut off.

2. Because, as the Apostle indicates, it is very profitable to have before one's eyes from time to time the example of divine severity, which did not spare the natural branches because of their unbelief. Rom. 11. 20. For if GOD did not spare them, see that He does not also not spare you; who were grafted in contrary to nature into the good olive tree. vers. 21. & 24.

3. By the laws of pious Emperors it has always been permitted to tolerate Jews in a Christian Republic, but under those conditions of which we have spoken. C. lib. 1. tit. 12. de Judæis & cælicolis. And C. de Judæis l. 10. Judæos. To this also pertains the law of the Emperors Honorius and Theodosius: Let the governors of the provinces prohibit (the Jews) from mixing the sign of their faith in their places: but let them retain their rites without contempt for the Christian religion: they will undoubtedly lose what has been permitted thus far, unless they refrain from illicit acts. The same is permitted in Canon Law Extra, lib. 6. de Judæis & Sarracenis.

Finally, Orthodox Antiquity is also clearly ὁμόψηφος [of one mind] with us in this part: as can be seen especially in Augustine, lib. 4. de Civit. DEI, and lib. 18. Likewise on Psalm 58.

But this also must be added in this place: that it is the duty of a Christian Prince and Magistrate to strive diligently that the Jews not only abstain from all blasphemy and extortion of Christians: but also that they be instructed concerning the heads of the Christian religion. In which part coercion has a place, not indeed coercion to embrace the Christian faith not yet known: but coercion to hear the Word of GOD, to frequent the sacred assemblies of Christians. In which matter many princes sin gravely today, who, when they tolerate Jews among Christians, are more solicitous about their own tributes and pensions than about their salvation. Least of all is the avarice of those Princes and Magistrates to be approved, who, when they cannot seize the goods and faculties of their subjects for themselves through unjust usury, permit that to be done through the Jews.

And for these reasons, and also under these conditions, we determine that Jews can be tolerated in a Christian Republic. Meanwhile, however, we judge that Republic or province to be happier which is entirely immune and free from this kind of people. For the Jews will no sooner abstain from blasphemies against Christ, as well as from the usury and plundering of Christians, than the Leopard changes his spots, and the Ethiopian his skin.

Latin:

ciæ, ac Reipub. proprias: aliàs tanquam fures & usurarij plectendi.

4. Ne tenuioris fortunæ concivibus pecuniam in usuras elocent.

5. & postremò: Ne quenquam à Christianismo ad impietatem & blasphemias Judaicas quovis modo abstrahant. His legibus & conditionibus si Magistratus Christianus Judæos in sua Repub. ferre velit, eosdemque in officio, ne ullatenus exorbitent, continere possit: tùm sanè ipsum minimè peccare statuimus. Et ut in hanc sententiam descendamus movent nos sequentes rationes.

1. Quia cæcitas ex parte contigit Israeli, donec plenitudo Gentium intraret: & sic omnis Israel salvus fieret: Rom. 11. 25. Cùm ergo secundum hoc vaticinium Apostoli, futura adhuc sit ante finem mundi luculenta populi Judaici ad Christum conversio: utique ipsis non modò non insultandum: sed nec omnis omninò occasio, quâ ad Christi agnitionem adduci queant, simpliciter præcidenda.

2. Quia indice Apostolo plurimùm prodest subinde in conspectu habere exemplum severitatis divinæ, quæ naturalibus ramis propter incredulitatem eorum non pepercit. Rom. 11. 20. Si enim DEUS his non pepercit, vide ne quando etiam tibi non parcat; qui præter naturam insitus es in bonam oleam. vers. 21. & 24.

3. Legibus piorum Impp. semper licuit ferre Judæos in Repub. Christiana, sed sub illis, de quibus diximus, conditionibus. C. lib. 1. tit. 12. de Judæis & cælicolis. Et C. de Judæis l. 10. Judæos. Huc pertinet etiam lex Honorij, & Theodosij Impp. Provinciarum rectores prohibeant, ne (Judæi) locis suis fides suæ signum immisceant: sed ritus suos citra contemtum Christianæ religionis retineant: amissuri sine dubio permissa hactenus, nisi ab illicitis temperaverint. Idem permittitur in Jure Canonico Extra, lib. 6. de Judæis & Sarracenis.

Tandem Orthodoxa Antiquitas hac etiam in parte nobis planè est ὁμόψηφος: uti cumprimis videre est apud Augustinum, lib. 4. de Civit. DEI, & lib. 18. Item in Psalmum. 58.

Est verò illud quoque hoc loco addendum: Principis & Magistratus Christiani officium esse, operam dare sedulò, ut non modò Judæi ab omni blasphemiâ, & exactione Christianorum abstineant: sed & ut circa capita religionis Christianæ informentur. Quâ in parte coactio locum habet, non quidem coactio ad fidem Christianam nondũ cognitam amplexandam: sed coactio ad audiendũ Verbum DEI, ad frequentandos Christanorum cœtus sacros. Quâ in re hodiè à plerisque principibus graviter peccatur, qui quando Judæos inter Christianos tolerant, magis de ipsorum tributis & pensionibus, quam salute sunt solliciti. Minimè omnium eorum Principum & Magistratuum probanda est avaritia, qui cum Subditorum bona & facultates,iniquis usuris ad se rapere non possunt: id per Judæos fieri permittunt.

Et his quidem de causis, his etiam conditionibus Judæos in Repub. Christiana tolerari posse statuimus. Interim verò beatiorem judicamus eam Rempub. sive provinciam, quæ ab hoc hominum genere planè est immunis & libera. Haud enim citius Judæi à blasphemiis in Christum, ut & ab usuris & expilationibus Christianorum abstinebunt, quàm Pardus mutârit maculas, & Æthiops cutem.


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: Question VII Is it lawful for a Magistrate to seize the goods and faculties of his subjects for himself at will: or to plunder them by other exactions?

Question VII.

Is it lawful for a Magistrate to seize the goods and faculties of his subjects for himself at will: or to plunder them by other exactions?

The decision of this question pertains properly to the Schools of the Jurisconsults, to whom we also in this place easily add our own vote in the Negative. There is one thing which can move some scruple for theologians in this part: Namely, how that description of Royal Right, which exists in 1 Sam. 8:11 and following, can be reconciled with our Negative regarding the proposed question. This will be the right of the king who is to reign over you: He will take your sons, and set them for himself in his chariots, and his horsemen, and they shall run before his chariot. He will also set for himself captains of thousands, and captains of fifties, and to plow his plowing, and to reap his harvest, and to make his weapons of war, and the instruments of his chariots. Furthermore, he will take your daughters for perfumers, and cooks, and bakers. Moreover, he will take your fields, and your vineyards, and your best olive groves, and will give them to his servants: And he will take the tithes of your seeds, and of your vineyards, and will give them to his eunuchs and to his servants: And he will take your menservants, and your maidservants, and your best young men, and your donkeys, to do his work: He will take the tithes of your flocks, and you shall be his servants.

Samuel, or rather GOD himself through Samuel, defines four axioms of royal right. FIRST, that he has a right over the sons and daughters of his subjects, and can employ them for any service at his own discretion. SECOND, that he has a right to claim for himself the houses, fields, vineyards, and other goods of his subjects. THIRD, that he has a right to exact tithes from his subjects for the support of his ministers: besides those tithes which they were bound by divine law to pay to the Levites. FOURTH and last: That he has a right over the menservants and maidservants of his subjects, to compel them to carry out his own business, even if it is done with great inconvenience and loss to the subjects. The question is therefore raised among theologians: Whether a Christian King or Magistrate can and ought to arrogate and usurp any such right over his subjects, just as it is defined by GOD in this place?

But the answer is in the negative, for those reasons which we shall note in order a little later. Nor does the passage produced to the contrary stand in the way. For 1. if the coherence of the whole history is weighed more accurately, it is clear that the royal right described by Samuel is not what it ought to have been according to the institution of GOD in Deut. 17:16 and following: but rather what it would be as a result of abuse and vicious accident, and indeed as a punishment for the people, who were stubbornly demanding a change of the Republic, and contrary to the will of GOD.

Certainly GOD, in the place already cited, so circumscribes the royal right with his own certain laws that he can or ought in no way to arrogate or claim for himself any such absolute right over the goods, faculties, servants, and children of his subjects.

THE FIRST law is: Do not multiply horses, for this excess requires great expense, and is accustomed to be the cause of the most heavy burdens which are imposed upon subjects.

THE SECOND: That he may not, out of zeal and lust for dominating and propagating the borders of his kingdom, return to Egypt: and that he may not have commerce with impious and profane nations, and especially with the Egyptians.

THE THIRD: That he may not have many wives, lest they turn his heart away from what is right.

THE FOURTH: That he may not accumulate much silver and gold: since this cannot be done without rapine and violent exactions from his subjects.

THE FIFTH: That he may receive a copy of the second law, that is, of Deuteronomy, in which the chief chapters of the divine law are repeated anew, transcribed from the Priests and Levites: and that he may read in it, not once only, but throughout the whole course of his life: that he may learn to fear GOD, and to keep his precepts: and that, puffed up by pride and arrogance, he may not despise and oppress his brothers.

And such indeed ought to be the Royal Right, according to the prescription and will of GOD. But that which Samuel defines is not a Royal, but a Tyrannical Right: called Royal because kings, having for the most part abused their power, degenerate into Tyrants: who administer all things according to their own lust, and, having neglected the public good, care for and promote primarily their own private interest: and therefore they impiously usurp for themselves de facto an absolute right over the goods, faculties, and families of their subjects: just as Samuel graphically describes it. The sense, therefore, of the whole passage in Samuel is not definitive, but partly prophetic, partly comminatory.

For since the Israelite people stubbornly ask for a King after the manner of other nations, and are unwilling to live content with the government established by GOD himself, Samuel predicts, by the just judgment of GOD, that they would receive Tyrants in place of true Kings: which the entire history of the Kings of Israel and Judah abundantly testifies to have happened (if only you except David, Solomon, Hezekiah, Jehoshaphat, Josiah, and a few others).

Therefore, no strength or weight can be sought from this for defining royal right over the goods of subjects: especially since it is clear from the history of King Ahab how greatly the unjust occupation and violent possession of Naboth's vineyard displeased GOD: concerning which GOD spoke thus through Elijah to King Ahab: Hast thou killed, and also taken possession? Thus saith Jehovah: in the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, shall dogs lick thy blood also. 1 Kings ch. 21. 16. & 19.

Moreover, the reasons confirming our negative regarding the proposed question are chiefly these:

1. Because such a Right conflicts with the law of GOD, defined above from Deuteronomy. For although those laws concerning Royal Right pertained properly to the Kings of Israel: yet by reason of their kind, in respect of which they share with the moral law or Decalogue, they oblige all Christian Kings and Princes to their observance.

2. Because this is a precept not only of Divine, but also of Natural Law: Thou shalt not steal. Now the people possess certain things as their own, by divine and human law: As soon as the Magistrate invades and occupies these by unjust force, he immediately commits theft, and involves himself in the guilt of the Seventh commandment.

3. Because the judgment is the same for similar cases: Therefore, just as it is not permitted for a Magistrate, although he holds the right of the sword over criminals, to rage against the bodies and lives of subjects—otherwise he incurs the guilt of the Fifth commandment before GOD: So, although the Magistrate

He can in good conscience exact taxes and assessments established by law: yet over the remaining assets and families of the subjects, absolute right does not belong to him at all.

4. Because such tyranny is everywhere in the Scriptures most severely both forbidden and reproved by GOD.

Isa. 3. 14. GOD will enter into judgment with the princes of the people: For you have despoiled the vineyard, and the plunder of the poor is in your house: Why do you crush my people, and grind the faces of the poor, says the LORD of hosts.

Ezek. 19. 3. The King became a lion: and he learned to catch prey, and to devour man.

And chap. 22. 27. Princes in the midst of the people are like wolves tearing the prey: to shed blood, and to destroy souls, for the sake of greed, and to pursue gain.

5. And lastly: Because such tyranny generally incites the people to move toward sedition against the Magistrate: Where although the people may sin gravely: the Magistrate himself nevertheless deserves no excuse, and if it happens that he is cast out of the kingdom, he can impute it to no one but himself: so that even in such a case, the action is indeed unjust, but the suffering is just.

Latin:

Quæstio VII.

An Magistratui licitum sit, subditorum bona & facultates pro lubitu ad se rapere: vel aliis exactionibus illos expilare?

PErtinet quæstionis hujus decisio propriè ad Scholas Jurisconsultorum, quibus nos etiam hoc loco nostrum calculum in Negantem facilè adjicimus. Unum est, quod Theologis hac in parte scrupulum aliquem movere potest: Quomodo nimirùm cum Negativâ nostrâ circa propositam quæstionem conciliari possit, illa Juris Regij descriptio, quæ extat 1. Sam. 8. 11. & seqq. Hoc erit Jus Regis,qui regnaturus est super vos: Filios vestros tollet, & ponet sibi in curribus suis, & equitibus suis, & current ante currum ejus. Ponet quoque sibi tribunos, & quinquagenarios, & ad arandum arationem suam, & ad metendam messem suam, & ad faciendam vasa bellica sua,& instrumenta curruum suorum. Filias præterea vestras tollet pro unguentariis, & coquariis, & panificis. Agros insuper vestros, & vineas vestras, & oliveta vestra optima accipiet, dabitque servis suis: Et de seminibus vestris, & vineis vestris capiet decimas, & dabit eunuchis suis atque servis suis: Servosque vestros, & ancillas vestras, juvenesque vestros optimos, & asinos vestros tollet, ut faciat opus suum: De pecoribus vestris decimas accipiet, & eritis ei servi.

Quatuor nimirùm Juris Regij axiomata definit Samuel, vel DEUS potiùs ipse per Samuelem. PRIMUM, quòd jus habeat in filios filiasque subditorum, eosque pro suo arbitratu ad quodvis ministerium adhibere possit. ALTERUM, quòd jus habeat, vindicandi sibi domos, agros, vineas & reliqua subditorum bona. TERTIUM, Quòd jus habeat exigendi à subditis decimas in sustentationem ministrorum: præter illas decimas, quas lege divinâ Levitis solvere tenebantur. QUARTUM & postremum: Quòd jus habeat in servos & ancillas subditorum, adigendi eos ad sua expedienda negocia, licet id fiat cum magno incommodo & damno subditorum. Quæstio ergo movetur inter Theologos: Num Rex sive Magistratus Christianus tale aliquod jus in subditos sibi arrogare, & usurpare possit & debeat, prout quidem illud à DEO hoc loco definitum?

Sed respondetur negatè, ob eas causas, quas paulò post ordine notabimus. Neque obstat locus in contrarium jam productus. Nam 1. si totius historiæ cohærentia accuratiùs expendatur, patet, describi à Samuelè Jus regium non quale illud ex DEI Institutione Deuter. 17, 16 & seqq. esse debebat: sed potius quale illud ex abusu & accidente vitioso, & quidem in pœnam populi, mutationem Reipub. contumaciùs, & præter DEI voluntatem exigentis, futurum erat.

Certè DEUS loco jam citato Jus regium certis suis legibus ita circumscribit, ut tale aliquod absolutum Jus in bona, facultates, famulos, & liberos subditorum arrogare, sive vindicare sibi nullo modo possit aut debeat.

PRIMA lex est: Ne multiplices equos, Excessus enim iste & sumtus magnos requirit, & onerum gravissimorum, quæ subditis imponuntur, causa esse solet.

ALTERA: Ne studio & libidine dominandi, propagandique regni fines, redeat in Ægyptum: & cum impijs, & prophanis gentibus, & maxime cum Ægyptijs commercium habeat.

TERTIA: ne multas uxores habeat, ne à recto deflectant Cor ejus.

QUARTA: ne cumulet multum argentis & auri: Siquidem hoc sine rapinis, & violentis exactionibus subditorum fieri nequeat.

QUINTA: Ut exemplar secundæ legis, hoc est, Deuteronomij, in quo præcipua capita legis divinæ denuò repetita sunt, descriptum accipiat à Sacerdotibus & Levitis: ing; eo legat, non semel tantùm, sed toto vitæ cursu: ut discat timere DEUM, & servare præcepta ejus: neq; fastu & superbia elatus fratres suos despiciat, & opprimat.

Et tale quidem debet esse Jus Regium, ex præscripto & voluntate DEI. Illud verò, quod Samuel definit, non Regium, sed Tyrannicum Jus est : ideo Regium nominatum, quia plerumque reges potestate sua abusi in Tyrannos degenerant : qui omnia pro libidine administrant, & publico posthabito commodo, privatum potissimum curant, & promovent : ac proinde Jus sibi absolutum in subditorum bona, & facultates, & familias sibi de facto impie usurpant : prout Samuel illud graphice describit. Sensus ergo totius loci apud Samuelem non est definitivus, sed propheticus partim, partim comminatorius.

Quandoquidem enim populus Israeliticus, Regem more aliarum gentium contumaciter a DEO petat, neque regimine a DEO ipso constituto contentus vivere velit, prædicit Samuel, justo DEI judicio fore, ut Tyrannos loco Regum verorum accipiant : id quod etiam factum esse, universa Regum Israeliticorum, & Judaicorum historia abunde testatur ( si modò Davidem, Salomonem, Ezechiam, Josaphatum, Josiam, & paucos alios excipias.

Nihil ergo hinc roboris aut momenti ad definiendum jus regium in subditorum bona petere licet : præsertim cùm ex historia Regis Achabi constet, quantoperè DEO displicuerit injusta occupatio & violenta possessio vineæ Nabothi : de qua sic DEUS per Eliam ad regem Achab : Nonne occidisti, & insuper possedisti? Sic dicit Jehovah : in loco, in quo linxerunt canes sanguinem Naboth, lingent canes sanguinem etiam tuum. lib. 1. Reg. cap. 21. 16. & 19.

Cæterum rationes confirmantes negativam nostram circa propositam quæstionem, præcipuæ sunt hæ :

1. Quia tale Jus pugnat cum lege DEI, supra ex Deuteronomio definita. Etsi enim leges illæ de Jure Regio, propriè ad Reges Israeliticos spectabant : ratione generis tamen respectu cujus cum lege morali sive Decalogo participant, omnes Christianos Reges & Principes ad sui observationem obligant.

2. Quia non divini tantùm, sed & Naturalis Juris hoc est præceptum : Non furtum facies. Habet autem populus res aliquas proprias, jure divino & humano : Quas simul ac Magistratus per vim injustam invadit, & occupat, statim furtum committit, & Septimi præcepti reatu se implicat.

3. Quia de similibus idem est judicium : Quemadmodum ergo Magistratui, licet jus gladij obtineat in fontes, tamen in corpora & vitam subditorum sævire minimè concessum est: aliàs Quinti præcepti reatum coram DEO contrahit : Ita licet Magistratus

tributa & census legibus constitutos exigere bona conscientia potest: tamen in reliquas Subditorum facultates & familias, Jus absolutummi nime competit.

4. Quia talis Tyrannis a DEO passim in Scripturis severissime & prohibetur, & reprehenditur.

Esa. 3. 14. DEUS judicium faciet contra principes populi: Vos enim spoliastis vineam, & rapina pauperis est in domo vestra: Quare atteritis populum meum, & facies pauperum commolitis, dicit DOMINUS exercituum.

Ezech. 19. 3. Rex Leo factus est: & didicit capere prædam, hominemq́; comedere.

Et cap. 22. 27. Principes in medio populi tanquam lupi rapientes prædam: ad effundendum sanguinem, & ad perdendos homines, ad avaritiam, & sectanda lucra.

5. & postrema: Quia talis Tyrannis plerumque populum ad seditionem contra Magistratum movendam concitat: Ubi licet populus graviter peccet: Magistratus tamen ipse quoque excusationem nullam meretur, & si regno ipsum ejici contingat, nemini alij, quàm sibi ipsi id imputare possit: ita ut tali etiam casu, Actio sit quidem in justa, Passio vero justa.


### Chapter II. On the Office of the Political Magistrate: Question VIII. and Final. Whether one may wage war for the mere assertion of Religion alone?

Is it lawful to wage war for the sole purpose of asserting religion?

The decision of this question can and ought to be sought for the greatest part from those things which we have discussed at length in the article concerning the Cross and Calamities, and concerning the Covenants of Christians. In this place, it is pleasing to reduce the whole matter into a sort of summary. True religion, therefore, is either to be propagated or to be defended against enemies. Propagation by arms and war has never been sought or obtained since the origin of the Church: but this consists in and is acquired by the preaching of the Word alone: where all force and effect is owed entirely to the Holy Spirit. Far be it, therefore, from Christians to think that pure religion can be propagated by force and arms, or to move war on this account: the outcome of which will certainly follow as far more sad. And although it happens not rarely that Christians, having defeated and subjugated the impious, Gentiles, and idolaters, have gained control of affairs, and consequently, having extirpated the false worship of GOD, have restored the true, and propagated the kingdom of GOD: that, however, is a matter of accident, and no rule can be constructed from it: especially since those wars were not undertaken directly for the sake of religion, but for other political causes, and on our part defensively. Such are the wars which the Christian world is accustomed to move against the Turk: Where if victory favors us, nothing prevents us, once Mohammedanism is overthrown, from taking care that the Church be gathered for Christ through the sincere preaching of the Word.

Regarding the defense of religion, even if the Savior rules in the midst of his enemies, and knows how to powerfully repress the enemies of his kingdom: indeed he is accustomed to defend the Church with the very same arms with which he propagates it: yet the office of the Magistrate requires that, as the guardian of the first table, he repel all unjust force by which either tyrants, or even heretics, go about overturning and assaulting the purer religion and the true worship of GOD: according to that common saying: One must fight for altars and hearths. And this war is merely defensive, concerning which Augustine writes in Epistle 105 to Boniface: When you put on your armor, consider that that strength is a gift of GOD, and resolve within yourself not to misuse that gift against GOD: nay, rather act so that you fight for his laws and name. Thus the leaders and kings of the people of GOD fought for the defense of Israelite worship against the Philistines and other enemies, who were persecuting the people of GOD and the divine religion with unjust force: Thus the Maccabees fought against Antiochus Epiphanes: Thus Constantine the Great, Theodosius the Great, and other Christian Emperors fought against the Gentiles. But because the outcome of war is uncertain, it is to be noted that one must not judge the certainty and truth of religion from the event of war or victory. For it happens more often that victory is on the side of heretics and idolaters. Therefore, the confidence of defense also must be placed solely in the nod and will of GOD, who more often permits the Orthodox to be defeated by enemies, lest, having become too insolent, they ascribe the defense of the Gospel to their own powers.

Latin:

An solius Religionis asserendæ causa, bellum gerere liceat?

Decisio hujus Quæstionis maximam partem peti potest & debet ex iis, quæ in articulo de Cruce & Calamitatibus, de Fœderibus Christianorum prolixè disseruim9. Hoc loco rem omnem in compendium quasi quoddam redigere placet. Religio ergò vera vel est propaganda, vel contra hostes defendenda. Propagatio armis & bello nunquàm ab origine Ecclesiæ vel quæsita, vel impetrata: sed sola prædicatione Verbi hæc constat, & acquiritur: Ubi vis, & effectus omnis, Spiritui Sancto in solidum debetur. Absit ergò à Christianis, ut puram Religionem, vi armisque propagari posse existiment, vel hoc pacto bellum moveant: cujus eventus certè sequetur longè tristissimus. Et quanquam haud rarò accidit, ut Christiani devictis subjugatisque impiis, Ethnicis, & Idololatriis, rerum potiti sint, ac proinde extirpato falso DEI cultu, verum instaurarint, regnumque DEI propagarint: illud tamen Accidentis est, neque regula inde extrui potest: præsertim cùm bella illa, non directè Religionis causâ, sed ob causas alias politicas, & ex nostra parte defensivè sint suscepta. Qualia bella ho stes dic Orbis Christianus contra Turcam movere solet: Ubi si Victoria nobis faveat, nihil prohibet, quò minus profligato Machometismo, Ecclesiam Christo, per sinceram prædicationem Verbi colligi curemus.

Quoad defensionem Religionis, et si Servator dominatur in medio inimicorum suorum, Regníque sui hostes potenter reprimere novit: quin iisdem planè armis Ecclesiam defendere solet, quibus eam propagat: Officium tamen Magistratús requirit, ut tanquam custos primæ tabulæ, omnem injustam vim propulset, qua vel Tyranni, vel Hæretici etiam, puriorem Religionem, & verum DEI cultum eversum, expugnatumque eunt: secundum vulgatum illud: Pugnandum pro aris & focis. Et hoc bellum merè est defensivum de quo Augustinus Epist. 105. ad Bonifacium: Cùm arma induis, cogitato, DEI donum esse robur illud, & statue apud te, ne adversus DEUM eo munere abuteris: imò id age, ut pugnes pro ejus legibus ac nomine. Sic Duces & Reges populi DEI pro defendendo cultu Israëlitico pugnarunt contra Philistæos & alios hostes, populum DEI, ac religionem divinam injustâ vi persequentes: Sic pugnarunt Maccabæi adversus Antiochum Epiphanem: Sic Constantinus Magnus, Theodosius Magnus, alijŕ́ Christiani Imperatores adversus Gentiles. Cæterùm quia anceps est alea belli, notandum, de Religionis certitudine & veritate non esse judicandum ex belli eventu, vel victoria. Sæpiùs enim accidit, ut Victoria sit penes hæreticos, & Idololotras. Ergo fiduciá etiam defensionis non in bello ipso, ejusque eventu, sed in DEI nutu atque arbitrio unicè collocanda est, qui sæpiùs Orthodoxos ab hostibus vinci permittit, ne insolentiores redditi, suis viribus Evangelij defensionem adscribant.


### Chapter Third. Of the Duty of Subjects: and whether they are bound to render absolute Obedience to the Magistrate?

The duty owed by subjects to the political magistrate is expressed by the Apostle by the single word of subjection, Rom. 13. 1. saying, Let every soul be subject to the higher power. And he adds a most evident reason: Because there is no power but from GOD. This decision of the Apostle is, both on the part of the Subject and the Predicate, very pregnant and emphatic. As for the Subject, the Apostle does not say, Every man: but let every soul be subject. The sense of which notation is not that which the Roman Pontiff falsely elicits, as if authority over even the very souls of men were granted to him. For Christ testifies that this belongs to GOD alone, Matt. 10. 28. The safety and destruction of the body indeed [may be] from a human [source]: But asserting that the safety and destruction of the body and soul together depend upon GOD alone. But the Apostle wished that point to be noted, Whatever draws the human spirit: whatever bears the appearance of human form, that must be subject to the superior Magistrate. Where that saying of Chrysostom is celebrated: Even the Priest, even the Prophet and the Monk, nay indeed even the Apostle owes obedience to the Magistrate. Either therefore the Roman Pontiff will render the obedience and subjection due to the political Magistrate, and especially to the Roman Emperor, or he will ingenuously confess that he does not possess a human spirit or soul. Nor is it the case that certain peculiar privileges, by which the Pope with his clergy is exempted from every court or political Jurisdiction, should be brought forward. For of what weight and moment those things are, was shown above in chap. 1.

Regarding the Predicate, the Greek verb ὑποτάσσεσθαι again deserves special emphasis: Which denotes not a simple and absolute subjection, but only ὑποταγὴν, or subordination. The Apostle is indeed looking to the power granted to the Magistrate, not absolute and infinite, but subordinated, and determined to the prescription of divine law, as of a superior, nay, of a supreme Order. Whatever therefore the Law of GOD permits subjects to render to their Magistrate, to that they are obligated. In which number are honor and reverence: prayers, tributes: rents or annual pensions from immovable goods: Taxes on movable goods: external defense even that which is done by arms, but legitimately: finally all kinds and duties of subjection and obedience, which can be rendered with a safe conscience and without violation of divine law. Rom. 13. 6. & 7. But if the Magistrate commands impious things, which cannot be rendered without offense to GOD and conscience: there that Apostolic saying has place, Acts 5. 29. We must obey GOD rather than men. In which sentiment Polycarp is read to have responded to the Proconsul: We Christians have been so instructed, that we render to the powers ordained by GOD the honor which is appropriate, and does not harm us. Euseb. book 4. chap. 1. from the epistle of the Smyrneans. And Justin, Apol. 2. We adore GOD alone: but in other things we serve you gladly, and we profess that you are Kings and Princes of men. Rightly therefore did the Egyptian midwives act, not obeying Pharaoh, who commanded that the Hebrew infants be killed at the very birth: Exod. 1. 15. & 17. So the companions of Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, refuse to comply with the Babylonian King in adoring the Idolatrous statue, and prefer to be cast into the furnace of fire than to obey an impious edict. Daniel 3. 5.

& 12. & following. Thus Peter and the Apostles, ordered not to preach any more about Jesus of Nazareth, respond intrepidly: We must obey GOD rather than men, Acts 5. 29. And this is that which the Savior commanded: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's: And to GOD, the things that are GOD's. Matt. 22. 21.

But a question arises here: If by chance someone embraces a false religion and attempts to compel subjects by force to its approval: Is it lawful for subjects to repel this yoke likewise by external force and the sword? We answer in the negative: For all sedition, undertaken in any way against an ordinary Magistrate, even a Tyrant, is prohibited: according to that saying of Solomon, Prov. 24. 21. Fear the LORD, my son, and the King, and do not join with the seditious. For their destruction will arise suddenly, and who knows the ruin of both? Which general rule the Apostle Peter transfers to the specific case, 1. chap. 2. 18. Subjecting servants to the obedience of masters, not only the good: but also the perverse and the tyrants.

Nor in the whole Scripture does a single place occur, which permits subjects, who are merely subjects (for the question is about these), to resist the Magistrate by force and arms, however impious he may be. Therefore regarding the present question, if the Magistrate wishes to compel subjects by force to a false Religion: they will certainly never consent: but neither will they oppose themselves to the Magistrate with an armed hand: mindful of that threat: He who takes the sword, will perish by the sword: But first, having become suppliants to the Magistrate, they will most humbly ask that the power of asserting and exercising a purer Religion be permitted to them henceforth as well. If by this pact nothing is achieved, but the Magistrate continues to exercise cruelty and tyranny against the confessors of the truth: then not even then will they take up arms, or stir up sedition: but they will follow that counsel of CHRIST: Matt. 10. 23. If they persecute you in one city, flee into another. But, if neither can this be done conveniently because of the cruelty of the Magistrate, that last practice of the Holy Confessors and Martyrs of Jesus must be seized, that we do not hesitate to pour out life and blood for the sake of asserting the truth of the Gospel: sustaining ourselves with the sweetest promises of CHRIST the Savior: Blessed are they who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven: Blessed are you, when they shall revile you, and persecute you for my sake: Rejoice, and be exceeding glad, for your reward is great in heaven: For so they persecuted the Prophets, who were before you: Matt. 5. 10, 11, & 12. And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Matt. 10. 28.

And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name's sake: shall receive a hundredfold, and shall possess eternal life. Matth. 19. 29. And this very thing was the practice of Christ, the Prophets, the Apostles, and the Martyrs of the primitive Church, who were so far from resisting their Magistrates in such a case with force and armed hand, that they rather did not hesitate to meet death with a most ready Spirit, and to seal the heavenly truth with their own blood.

Latin:

OFficium Subditorum Magistratui Politico debitum, Uno Subjectionis vocabulo exprimit Apostolus, Rom, 13. 1. Omnis inquiens, anima potestati supereminenti sit subdita. Et rationem subjicit evidentissimam: Quia non est potestas, nisi à DEO. Est verò decisio hæc Apostoli, ex parte tùm Subjecti, tùm Prædicati, prægnans admodùm & emphatica. Quoad Subjectum, non dicit Apostolus, Omnis homo: sed omnis anima sit subdita. Cujus notationis sensus non est, quem Pontifex Romanus falsò elicit, quasi imperium in ipsas etiamhominum animas sibi sit concessum. Hoc enim soli DEO competere Christus testatur Matth. 10. 28. Corporis quidem salutem atque exitium ab humano : Verùm Corporis atque animæ simul salutem atq; exitium à solo DEO pendere, asserens Sed illud notatum voluit Apostolus, Quicquid Spiritum humanum trahit : quicquid forma humana speciem præ se fert, illud Magistratui superiori debere esse subjectum. Ubi celebratur illud Chrysostomi: Etiam Sacerdos, etiam Propheta atq; Monachus, imò verò etiam Apostolus Magistratui obedientiam debet. Aut ergò Pontifex Romanus Magistratui politico, & cumprimis Imperatori Romano obedientiam & subjectionem debitam præstabit, aut Spiritum, sive animam humanam se non habere, ingenuè fatebitur. Neque est, ut peculiaria quædam privilegia, quibus Papa cum clero suo, ab omni foro sive Jurisdictione politica, sit exemtus, obvertantur. Nam cujus ea sint ponderis & momenti, supra cap. 1. ostensum.

Quoad Prædicatum, rursus emphasin peculiarem meretur verbum Græcum ὑποτάσσεσθαι : Quod non simplicem & absolutam subjectionem, sed tantùm ὑποταγὴν, sive subordinationem notat. Respicit nimirùm Apostolus ad potestatem Magistratui concessam, non absolutam, ac infinitam, sed subordinatam, & ad præscriptum legis divinæ determinatam, tanquam superioris, imò supremi Ordinis. Quicquid ergò Lex DEI permittis, ut subditi præstent suo Magistratui, ad illud sunt obligati. Quo in numero sunt honor & reverentia : preces, tributa: reditus sive pensiones annuæ de bonis immobilibus : Vectigalia de bonis mobilibus : defensio externa etiam quæ fiat armis, sed legitimè : omnia denique subjectionis, & obedientiæ genera, atque officia, quæ salvâ conscientiâ, & sine violatione legis divinæ præstari possunt. Rom. 13. 6. & 7. Cæterùm si impia præcipiat Magistratus, quæ citra offensionem DEI & conscientiæ præstari nequeant: ibi locum habet illud Apostolicum, Actor 5. 29. Oportet DEO magis obedire, quàm hominibus. Quam in sententiam respondisse legitur Polycarpus Proconsul: Nos Christiani sic instituti sumus, ut potestatibus à DEO ordinatis honorem, qui competat, nec obsit nobis, exhibeamus. Euseb. lib. 4. cap. 1. ex epistolâ Smyrnensium. Et justinus Apolog. 2. DEUM solum adoramus : vobis autem in aliis rebus læti servimus, Regesq; vos & Principes hominum esse profitemur. Rectè ergò fecerunt obstetrices Ægyptiacæ, non obsequentes Pharaoni, præcipienti, ut parvuli Hebræorum in ipso partu necentur : Exod. 1. 15. & 17. Ita socij Danielis Sadrach, Mesach, & Abednego, Regi Babylonio morem gerere derrectant, in adorandâ statuâ Idololatrica, & malunt conijci in caminum ignis, quàm impio edicto obedire. Daniel. 3. 5.

& 12. & seqq. Sic Petrus & Apostoli jussi, ne prædicarent ampliùs de Jesu Nazareno, respondent intrepidè: Oportet DEO magis obedire quàm hominibus, Actor. 5. 29. Et hoc est illud, quod Servator præcepit: Date Cæsari, quæ sunt Cæsaris: Et DEO, quæ sunt DEI. Matth. 22. 21.

Sed quæstio hîc oritur: Si fortè Magistratui aliquis falsam amplectatur religionem, & ad ejus approbationem subditos vi cogere tentet: An liceat subditis hoc jugum itidem vi externâ, atque gladio propulsare? Respondemus negatè: Omnis enim seditio, quovis modo contra Magistratum ordinarium, etiam Tyrannum suscepta, est prohibita: secundum illud Salomonis, Proverb. 24. 21. Time DOMINUM, fili mi, & Regem, & ne conjungaris seditiosis. Subitò enim orietur exitium eorum, & ruinam amborum quis novit? Quam regulam generalem D. Apostolus Petrus ad speciem transfert, 1. cap. 2. 28. Servos subjiciens obedientiæ Dominorum, non tantùm bonorum: sed etiam pravorum & tyrannorum.

Neque in universâ Scripturâ unicus occurrit locus, qui subditis, qui merè subditi sunt (de his enim quæstio est) permittat, ut vi & armis resistant Magistratui, quantumvis impio. Ergo quoad præsentem quæstionem, si Magistratus ad falsam Religionem subditos vi cogere velit: nunquam profecto consentient: sed nec armata manu Magistratui se opponent: memores comminationis illius: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit: Sed primùm supplices facti Magistratui, purioris Religionis asserendæ, & exercendæ potestatem sibi deinceps quoque permitti, humilimè rogabunt. Sin hoc pacto nihil proficiatur, sed crudelitatem & tyrannidem in confessores veritatis exercere Magistratus perrexerit: tum ne sic quidem arma capessent, aut seditionem movebunt: sed sequentur consilium illud CHRISTI: Matth. 10. 23. Si persecuti vos fuerint de civitate unâ, fugite in alteram. Verùm, si neque hoc commodè propter sævitiam Magistratus fieri possit, ultima illa arripienda praxis Sanctorum Confessorum & Martyrum Jesu propria, ut pro asserendâ Evangelij veritate vitam, sanguinemque profundere non dubitemus: sustentantes nos dulcissimis promissionibus CHRISTI Servatoris: Beati, qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cælorum: Beati estis, cùm maledixerint vobis, & persecuti vos fuerint propter me: Gaudete, exultate, quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cælis: Sic enim persecuti sunt Prophetas, qui fuerunt ante vos: Matth. 5. 10 11. & 12. Et nolite timere eos, qui corpus occidunt animam autem occidere non possunt. Matth. 10. 28.

Et omnis, qui reliquerit domum, vel fratres, vel sorores, aut patrem, aut matrem, aut uxorem, aut filios, aut agros propter nomen meum: centuplum accipiet, & vitam æternam possidebit. Matth. 19. 29. Et hæc ipsa fuit praxis Christi, Prophetarum, Apostolorum, & primitivæ Ecclesiæ Martyrum, qui tantum abest, ut tali casu, vi & armata manu suis Magistratibus restiterint: ut potius mortem promtissimo Spiritu oppetere, & sanguine suo cœlestem veritatem obsignare, non dubitaverint.


### Chapter Four. and last. On civil contracts: and in particular on the contract of mutuation

Concerning civil contracts: and specifically concerning the contract of loan.

That legitimate Ordinances and civil Contracts, not repugnant to divine and natural law, are lawful, is placed beyond all Controversy in the Schools and Churches of Christians. And the Apostle warns that the manner is to be observed in them only, 1 Cor. 7. 30. Those who buy, should be as though they did not possess: Where under the guise of buying and possession, all the business and contracts of this life are comprehended. Just as therefore the Apostle permits marrying a wife, weeping, and rejoicing: so he does not forbid also buying and possessing goods by means of certain contracts, provided only that the manner be observed in those businesses: that is to say, that those buying should be as though they did not possess: that is, that they should not be occupied with desire or trust in external goods: according to that of David: If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them: which is what usually happens to those who, trusting in perishable goods, think of heavenly things either rarely or never.

Furthermore, in these civil contracts equity must be observed: according to that 1 Thess. 4. 6. That no one should oppress or circumvent his brother in business: because the LORD is the avenger of all these things. Those who sin in this way are first the richer and more powerful, who violently oppress men of humbler fortune: and grow rich from their plunder.

Then those who, through frauds and impostures, covet the goods, resources, and money of their neighbor: and that in any business whatsoever, whether it be a contract of buying or selling, or an exchange of things, or a loan, or a commodatum, or a hiring and letting, or a contract of partnership. If these and similar vices are absent from civil Contracts, then indeed the doctrine of the Gospel permits and approves them entirely. So that on this matter in the Church of GOD there is no doubt at all, much less should an Anabaptist community of goods or an abrogation of civil contracts be established by any pact.

However, two questions occur, about which there is sharp controversy among Theologians: One: concerning the contract of loan, or mutuum: The other concerning the lending of money at interest: Whether this ought to be simply and always free? or whether it is permitted both to ask and to receive something above the principal, that is, as they commonly speak: Is it permitted to receive usury? These questions can be recalled to six main heads, or kinds of things most worthy of explanation: the First of which shows, What a Loan is and what its proper nature and affection is according to divine Law. The Second, What usury properly is. 3. How many kinds of it are there? 4. Whether any species of usury is to be tolerated in the Republic of Christians, and which one, and with respect to what men? 5. What moderation ought to be observed concerning usury? 6. And finally: Did B. LUTHER simply disapprove and condemn all usury?

Latin:

De contractibus civilibus: & in specie de contractu mutuationis.

Legitimas Ordinationes, & Contractus civiles, juri divino & naturali non repugnantes, esse licitos, in Christianorum Scholis atque Ecclesiis extra omnem Controversiam est positum. Et Apostolus modum in illis tantum servari monet, 1. Cor. 7. 30. Qui emunt, sint ut non possidentes: Ubi sub emtionis & possessionis specie, universa vitæ hujus negocia & contractus comprehenduntur. Sicut ergo uxorem ducere, flere, & gaudere permittit Apostolus: ita non prohibet etiam, certis mediantibus contractibus bona emere & possidere: tantum modus in negociis istis observetur: ut nimirum ementes sint tanquam non possidentes: hoc est, æque cupiditate, neque fiducia bonorum externorum occupentur: secundum illud Davidis: Si divitiæ affluant, Cor non opponant: id quod istis usu venire solet, qui bonis caducis confidentes, de cœlestibus vel raro, vel nunquam cogitant.

Deinde in contractibus hisce civilibus observanda est æquitas: secundum illud 1. Thes. 4.6. Ne quis opprimat, aut circumveniat in negocio fratrem suum: quoniam vindex est DOMINUS de his omnibus. Peccant hoc modo primum ditiores, & potentiores, qui tenuioris fortunæ homines violenter opprimunt: & ex illorum expilationibus, ditescunt.

Deinde illi, qui per fraudes, & imposturas, inhiant bonis, facultatibus atque pecuniis proximi sui: idque in negocio quocunq; sive sit contractus emptionis aut venditionis, sive permutatio rerum, sive mutuum, sive commodatio, sive conductio, & locatio, sive contractus societatis. Hæc & consimilia vitia si absint a Contractibus civilibus, tum sane doctrina Evangelij eos omnino permittit, & approbat. Ita ut hac de re in Ecclesia DEI nullum prorsus sit dubium, nedum communio bonorum Anabaptistica: aut contractuum civilium abrogatio ullo pacto statuatur.

Cæterùm duæ occurrunt quæstiones, de quibus inter Theologos acriter controvertitur: Una: de Contractu mutuationis, sive mutui: Altera de Elocatione pecuniarum: Utrum hæc simpliciter & semper gratuita esse debeat? an verò supra sortem aliquid & petere, & accipere, hoc est, uti vulgò loquuntur: An usuras accipere liceat? Quæstiones hæ ad sex summa capita, sive rerum genera explicatu dignissima revocari possunt: quorum Primum ostendat, Quid sit Mutuatio & quæ secundum Jus divinum, propria ejus sit natura & affectio. Alterum Quid propriè sit Usura. 3. Quotuplex ea? 4. An aliqua Usuræ species in Repub. Christianorum sit ferenda, & quænam, & quorum hominum respectu? 5. Quæ moderatio circa usuras observari debeat? 6. & postremò: An B. LUTHERUS simpliciter omnem usuram improbarit, & damnaverit?


### Chapter Four. and last. On civil contracts: A Member About the Contract of Mutuation

Regarding the first member, they commonly define a Loan as a contract in which either money, or grain, or wine, or if anything else necessary for the use of this life is to be consumed, is transferred to another: so that he may return an equivalent. I say equivalent, to distinguish it from a Commodatum, where the same species of the thing lent: and the very same individual must be returned: Whereas in a Loan the Genus is returned, and indeed an equivalent: although not the same individual.

This duty of lending ought to be most highly recommended to all Christians: and it ought not to be denied not only to a brother in need, but not even to our enemy, when he asks such a thing of us. For thus GOD himself commands in Deut. 15. 7. up to verse 12. If one of your brothers, who dwell within the gates of your city, in the land which the LORD your GOD is about to give you, has fallen into poverty: you shall not harden your heart, nor draw back your hand: but you shall open it to the poor, and you shall give a loan, which you have perceived him to need. v. 9. Beware, lest perhaps an impious thought creeps in, and you say in your heart: The seventh year of remission approaches: and you turn your eyes away from your poor brother, unwilling to lend him the loan which he requests, lest he cry out against you to the LORD; and it becomes a sin for you. v. 10. But you shall give to him: nor shall you do anything craftily in relieving his necessities: so that the LORD your GOD may bless you at all times, and in all things to which you have put your hand. v. 11. There will not be lacking poor in the land of your habitation: therefore I command you, that you open your hand to your brother who is needy, and to the poor, who dwells with you in the land. Thus Christ also commands in Matth. 5. 42. He who asks from you, give to him: and to him who wishes to borrow from you, do not refuse: And v. 44. I say to you, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you. Luc. 6. 35. Love your enemies, do good, and lend. This duty of lending is also required by Christian charity itself: which does not permit that we should abound, while our brother is in need: but as a fruit and effect of faith, it exerts itself, both through the duty of lending and through other offices of charity.

Furthermore, this duty of lending must be simply gratuitous: and nothing beyond the principal should be sought: but it should suffice if an equivalent is returned at some time without any exaction or acceptance of either profit or gift. For thus the Savior commands: Luc. 6. 35. Lend, hoping for nothing thereby. And this is the proper mark distinguishing the children of GOD from the children of this world: according to that saying of the Savior: If you do this, your reward shall be great: and you shall be the children of the Most High.

Finally, because the duty of lending pertains to commutative justice, which requires equity on both sides, both of the one giving the loan and of the one receiving it: certainly not only must he who gives the loan do so without any deceit and fraud: but also he who receives the loan is bound in good faith to return the equivalent at the defined time: and indeed likewise without any deceit and fraud. For he is wicked who borrows and does not repay, as David judges, Psalm 37. 21. Against which class of men Sirach inveighs heavily in chapter 29. 4. and following. Saying, Many have esteemed a loan as a discovery (Luther rightly translates: many think it is found, what he borrows) and have caused labor to those who helped them. Until he receives, he kisses his hands, and in the money of his neighbor he will humble his voice, and in the time of repayment he will prolong the time, and will return words of sloth, and will complain of the time. But if he is able to give, he will scarcely bring half, and will count it as a discovery: Luther: And counts it for them as a gain. But if he cannot give, he has deprived the lender of his money: And here he has acquired for himself an enemy with his own money: And he returns curses and insults for grace. Many, therefore, give a loan with difficulty, not from an evil mind: but because they fear lest they be defrauded. But do not desert your brother in necessity, but rather add this alms, that you leave the time of repayment to him. Lose money for the sake of your brother, and do not hide it under a stone to your own destruction.

Therefore, they betray a fanatical spirit who dream that the duty of lending ought to be so gratuitous toward all that an equivalent is not recovered. Certainly, such a command appears nowhere in the entire Scripture. For in this, lending differs from alms, that the latter seeks neither the principal nor anything beyond the principal: Lending, however, as a legitimate contract, binds the borrower to return the equivalent at a just time entirely: but it is merely gratuitous in that it demands nothing at all beyond the principal or the thing lent. And indeed, even in the Old Testament, although it was not permitted to demand the payment of a loan in any seventh year: yet for that reason the ledgers of receipts and expenses were not deleted. For Moses commands not to give away the loan, but not to demand it back in the seventh year.

And how, I ask, would anything be lent if it were never to return to its owner? Therefore, Moses demands no other remission of a loan in the seventh year from the Jews than that they should refrain from demanding debts, and allow a respite to their brother, because there was no produce in that year, and therefore it would be entirely inconvenient, indeed impossible, for the poor to provide payment.

Thus the Savior, Luc. 6. 35, does not wish that we should never again hope for or demand back from a brother every loan given to any brother whatsoever: But that we should not hope for or accept anything beyond the principal for the sake of profit. Otherwise, not only would all ownership of goods be abolished in a short time: but also every occasion and ability to exercise Christian charity toward one's neighbor would quickly expire entirely: so that no one would retain anything of their own from which they could lend to others and do good. Such a confusion of things neither Christ nor the Apostles ever taught. Meanwhile, we do not deny that the Savior's saying, Luc. 6. 35, Lend, hoping for nothing thereby, if it is applied to brothers who are fully poor, namely those who, reduced to extreme poverty, are unable to pay or restore, admits the meaning that the thing lent is no longer hoped for or demanded back. And in this case, we maintain that the nature of a loan properly so called expires, and that from a loan it becomes either a gift or an alms.

Moreover, since these words of the Savior are extended too widely, and are snatched up by some as if among Christians every loan must simply be gratuitous, and even regarding the letting out of money no compensatory interest could have a place in the Church of GOD: it will be worth the effort to have the genuine and native meaning of these words known and understood. I prefer, however, to follow the opinion of other most approved Theologians on this matter: rather than to stand by my own private judgment or opinion.

…Thus, however, B. Hunnius discourses excellently concerning these words of the Savior in his commentary on 2 Cor. 8: If we examine the saying of Christ more deeply, it will be evident from the context that it does nothing to establish the opinion of those who pronounce the contract of the lending of money, under the power of recovery, at under certain conditions, which are defined by the laws, they pronounce that the initiation (which perhaps is less appropriately noted by the term loan) is illicit. Let us see the very words of the Savior, which in Luke are as follows: If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what thanks is it to you? For even sinners lend to sinners, to receive equal amounts. But rather love your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing therefrom. Matthew describes the same sermon of Christ, but repeated a little further back, in this manner: If anyone shall strike your right cheek, turn to him the other also: And to him who wishes to drag you into court, and take your tunic, permit him also your cloak. And whoever shall force you to go one mile, go with him two: give to him who asks of you, and do not turn away from him who wishes to borrow. These words of the Evangelists, when looked into deeply, clearly show that the opinion of Christ concerning a loan is not to be taken simply, but comparatively. And the indivisible connection of the mentioned members proves this sense: that, just as Christ in the preceding members teaches by comparison which of two things is more excellent: namely, that it is better to turn the other cheek also to the one striking, than to strike back: and it is better that one, along with the tunic, should also make a loss of the cloak, than that one should contend hatefully and with the loss of goods before a judge over the taken tunic. And that it is more prudent that one should go two miles for the sake of a neighbor, and thus perform the duty, than that one should refuse the request of one mile: So in like manner he suggests that the understanding of this member also, which is about a loan, is to be taken not absolutely, but comparatively, in this very sense; that it is more excellent in common life to lend to the poor in such a way that you not only receive nothing above the principal: but that you would rather risk the principal itself, if the situation so requires, than that you should completely deprive a brother, in need of your assistance, of this duty of lending. For Christ did not deal here with a loan in which the same things are returned or even demanded, or as the Evangelist says, τὰ ἴσα, but in which, because of the indigence of the neighbor, not even the restitution of the principal can be certainly hoped for: and therefore the principal itself is finally remitted, either in whole or in part. That this is the genuine explanation is most clearly taught by the antithesis in Luke, where it is demonstrated that that duty of a loan, in which τὰ ἴσα are hoped for and received, is also practiced by tax collectors and by sinners, who themselves also lend so that they may receive equal amounts. Christians, however, ought to be more perfect, and rather not even demand equal amounts in a loan given, than to close their heart to a needy brother: if indeed he, having the intention of restoring, cannot however repay due to poverty. This antithesis, expressly placed in the words of Christ, would not stand if the little word INDE were to be referred only to usury, and not also to the principal itself: and the sense of the words is entirely too tight to allow any crack for covering. For he says: What thanks is it to you, if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive: but he speaks manifestly about the very sum lent. And he tightens this opinion more closely, which follows: For sinners

and they lend to sinners, so that they may receive equal amounts: and yet they have nothing before GOD therefrom, either of commendation or of reward, however much they do not receive more, but only equal amounts: but that Christians ought willingly in such a case, even with some loss, to assist a struggling brother. This interpretation was also approved by Charles Dumoulin, and the Theological Faculty of the Academy of Tübingen, in the censure upon the Ratisbon controversy concerning Usury. From these things, therefore, thus weighed and explained, we conclude undoubtedly that that saying of the Savior ought not to be extended indiscriminately to any persons whatsoever, nor to any sums of money whatsoever.

However, it well deserves observation in this place how inept are the disputants who gather from this saying of Christ as follows: The Savior wishes that a loan should be given even to those who cannot restore τὰ ἴσα: Therefore, it is not to be lent to those who can restore τὰ ἴσα: nay, our money is to be let out only to those from whom we can neither hope for nor receive any compensation at all. The whole of that text in Luke most evidently refutes this inept method of gathering. For Christ says there also: Love those who do not love you. Is it therefore a consequence that we should not love those who do love us? The same: If you do good to those who also do good to you, what thanks is it to you (namely, before GOD): Would it therefore be a consequence that one should not do good to those who can do good to us in return? I do not think anyone would be so foolish as to wish to argue thus from the words of Christ. We therefore correct this stupidity, rather than error, in this manner: Christ wishes that we should not only love those, and not only do good to those, who love us in return and can do good to us: but also our enemies, and those from whom it is not permitted to hope for any benefit. So also the Savior wishes a loan to be given to the poor, and to hope for or receive nothing in return from them: so that meanwhile he does not prohibit us from giving a loan also to the rich, who can repay τὰ ἴσα: and therefore he does not prohibit, if these rich people return equal for equal, that we should receive that. For just as it is of charity and humanity to gratify with our services even friends and the rich when they have need: So in turn it is of equity that they, when they can, should return equal for equal. Which law of equity Christ never and nowhere disapproved, or removed from the midst. Thus there is no reason for the consequence, nor can it be proven by any reason from the words of Christ what those little fools gather: Our money is to be let out to the poor, without any hope of compensation: Therefore our money either ought not to be let out to the rich at all, or with this condition, that if they should enrich their affairs wonderfully with our money, and without any loss to us beyond the principal, they could give something by way of compensation, yet we should receive nothing from them: not only not on account of the duty of lending, which we ourselves acknowledge should always be free, we grant willingly: but not indeed for other reasons, which in this place come under consideration: concerning which we shall treat expressly in the fourth member. Which inept method of disputing, we judge worthy not of any laborious refutation, but rather of an explosion.

Nor does our blessed LUTHER differ from this explanation, in his Sermon on Usury, published in the year 1519: where among other things he writes thus: Christ wills that we should lend, not only to friends, the rich, and those to whom we are inclined, who may in turn lend or do good to us in this or in another matter. But also to those who are not able, or not willing to do the same, such as the needy and enemies. And after a few words: But whoever lends, he expects the same thing back that he lends. And if he were to expect nothing, as they understand it, then it would be given, and not lent. Since it is so trivial that one lends to another who may be friendly, rich, or otherwise useful to him in the same way, which even sinners who are not Christians can do, so Christians ought to do more, and lend to those who do not do the same, that is, to the needy and enemies. Tom. 1. Jen. German folio 195b in my copy. Which words translated into Latin sound thus: Christ wills that we should give a loan not only to friends, the rich, and those toward whom we are well-disposed; who can either give the same or something else as a loan to us in return; and can do good to us. But also to those; who cannot, nor wish to do this; such as the needy, and enemies. And after a few words: He who gives a loan; he expects in return that very thing which he gave as a loan: and if he did not expect that; then he would not have given a loan, but would have given it purely as a gift. But since such lending is so common; that even sinners, who are not Christians, are able to perform it: it is fitting indeed for Christians to perform more in this regard, and to give a loan even to those who cannot repay; that is, to the needy, and enemies. And Tom. 7. Jen. German folio 397 in my copy, in the Admonition to pastors; concerning preaching against usury, published in the year 1540: the same LUTHER discourses thus concerning a loan; or lending: To lend is called that, when I do for someone with my money, goods, or equipment so that he may use them, as long as he has need, or I can and will; and he returns the same to me at his time, as good as I have lent it to him, as one neighbor lends money or the value of money to another, for which I should take nothing. Which words translated into Latin have it thus: To give a loan is, when I hand over my money, goods, and furniture to someone to be used for as long as he has need of them, or I can and am willing to do without them: And he himself restores the same to me at his time, in that quality, in which I gave it to him as a loan: Just as a neighbor gives a loan of money and other things to another, but in such a way that he ought to receive nothing above the principal.

And thus in this part between us, and blessed LUTHER, there is a unanimous consensus concerning the duty of lending, that it must indeed be free, and that it is not permitted to either hope for or receive anything beyond the principal, or the thing given as a loan: Nay rather, if a brother or neighbor is reduced to extreme poverty, and can no longer repay the principal, that we should bear his loss without murmuring: as Jehovah himself commands, Deut. 15, 7. & 8. If there be with you any poor man of your brothers, within any of your gates, in your land, which Jehovah your GOD will give to you: do not harden your heart, nor close your hand against your poor brother: But liberally open your hand to him, and liberally lend to him, as much as is sufficient for his need, that which he lacks.

Latin:

QUoad primùm membrum, Mutuationem vulgò definiunt, quod sit contractus, in quo aut pecunia, aut frumentum, aut vinum, aut si quid aliud ad usum vitæ hujus necessarium, consumendum est, transfertur ad alium: ita ut is reddat æquivalens. Æquivalens dico, ad differentiam Commodati, Ubi eadem rei commodatæ species: & idem planè individuum reddi debet: Cùm in Mutuatione reddatur Genus, & quidem æquivalens: licèt non idem individuum.

Officium hoc mutuationis omnibus Christianis debet esse commendatissimum: idque non modò non fratri egenti, sed ne quidem inimico nostro, tale quid à nobis petenti, negari debet. Sic enim mandat DEUS ipse Deut. 15. 7. usque ad versum 12. Si unus de fratribus tuis, qui morantur intra portas civitatis tuæ, in terra, quam DOMINUS DEUS tuus daturus est tibi, ad paupertatem devenerit: non obdurabis Cor tuum, nec contrahes manum: sed aperies eam pauperi, & dabis mutuum, quo ipsum indigere perspexeris. v. 9. Cave, ne fortè subrepat impia cogitatio, & dicas in corde tuo: Appropinquat septimus annus remissionis: & avertas oculos tuos à paupere fratre tuo, nolens ei, quod postulat mutuum commodare, ne clamet contra te ad DOMINUM; & fiat tibi in peccatum. v. 10. Sed dabis ei: nec ages quippiam callidè in ejus necessitatibus sublevandis: ut benedicat tibi DOMINUS DEUS tuus in omni tempore, & in cunctis, ad quæ manum miseris. v. 11. Non deerunt pauperes in terrâ habitationis tuæ: idcircò ego præcipio tibi, ut aperias manum fratri tuo egeno, & pauperi, qui tecum versatur in terra. Sic mnadat Christus etiam Matth. 5 42. Qui petit à te, da ei: & volenti mutuare à te, ne detrectes: Et v. 44. Ego dico vobis, Diligite inimicos vestros, benefacite his, qui oderunt vos. Luc. 6. 35. Diligite inimicos vestros, benefacite, & mutuum date. Exigit hoc mutuationis officium ipsa quoque charitas Christiana : quæ non permittit, ut nos abundemus : frater autem noster egeat : sed tanquam fructus, & effectus fidei sese exerit, tùm per mutuationis, tùm per alia charitatis officia.

Deindè verò hoc Mutuationis officium debet simpliciter esse gratuitum : neque ultra sortem aliquid petendum : sed sufficiat, si aliquando reddatur æquivalens sine ullâ vel lucri, vel doni exactione, aut acceptatione. Sic enim mandat Servator: Luc. 6. 35. Mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes. Et hæc est propria nota, discernens filios DEI, à filiis hujus seculi: secundum illud Servatoris : Hoc si feceritis, merces vestra erit multa : & vos eritis filij Altissimi.

Tandem, quia Mutuationis officium pertinet ad Justitiam commutativam, quæ æquitatem ex utraque parte, tum mutuum dantis tum accipientis exigit : utique non modò is, qui mutuum dat, absque dolo, & fraude omni dare debet : sed & is, qui mutuum accepit, bonâ fide definito tempore, æquivalens reddere tenetur : & quidem itidem sine omni dolo, & fraude. Improbus enim est, qui mutuò accipit, & non reddit, judice Davide, Psal. 37. 21. In quod genus hominum graviter invehitur Syracides cap. 29. 4. & seqq. Multi, inquiens, quasi inventionem æstimaverunt mutuũ (Lutherus rectè vertit: mancher meinet es sey gefunden/ wz er borget) & præstiterunt laborem his, qui adjuverunt se. Donec accipiat deosculatur manus ejus, & in pecuniis proximi humiliabit vocem, & in tempore redditionis protrahet tempus, & reddet verbum pigritiæ, & tempus causabitur. Si autem potuerit dare, vix afferet dimidium, & computabit illud quasi inventionem : Lutherus: Vnd rechnets jenen für einen gewin zu. Si autem non possit dare, privavit mutuò dantem pecuniis suis: Et hic sua sibi ipsi pecunia acquisivit hostem : Et ille reddit maledicta, & convitia, pro gratiâ. Multi igitur ægrè mutuum dant, non malo animo: sed quia metuit, ne defraudetur. Sed ne desere fratrem in necessitate, quin hanc adjice eleemosynam, ut tempus redditionis ipsi relinquas. Perde pecuniam propter fratrem, & non abscondas eam sub lapide in perditionem.

Spiritum ergo fanaticum produnt illi, qui Mutuationis officium ita gratuitum erga omnes esse debere somniant, ut non reperatur æquivalens. Certè tale mandatum nuspiam in universa Scriptura occurrit. In hoc enim mutuatio differt ab Eleemosyna quòd hæc neque sortem, neque aliquid ultra sortem repetit: Mutuatio autem tanquam legitimus contractus, mutuo accipientem ad reddendum justo tempore aequivalens, omnino obligat: In eo autem est mere gratuitum, quod nihil quicquam ultra sortem, vel rem mutuatam exigit. Et profecto in Veteri etiam testamento, licet quovis anno septimo, solutionem mutui exigere non liceret: tamen propterea tabulae accepti & expensi non erant deletae. Moses enim mutuum non donare, sed non reposcere praecipit anno septimo.

Et quomodo quaeso mutuo daretur, quod nunquam ad Dominum suum rediret? Proinde non aliam remissionem mutui anno septimo a Judaeis exigit Moses, quam ut abstineant ab exigendis debitis, & inducias permittant fratri, eo quod anni illius nullus esset proventus, ac proinde pauperibus solutionem praestare prorsus incommodum, imo impossibile accideret.

Sic Servator Luc. 6. 35. non vult, ut omne mutuum fratri cuicunque datum, nunquam amplius speremus, aut repetamus a fratre: Sed ut ne aliquid ultra sortem, lucri gratia speremus, & accipiamus. Alias non modo proprietas bonorum omnis exiguo tempore tolleretur: sed & omnis exercendae charitatis Christianae erga proximum occasio & facultas, cito tota expiraret: ut nemo quicquam retineret proprium, ex quo aliis mutuum dare, & benefacere posset. Qualem rerum confusionem, neque Christus, neque Apostoli uspiam tradiderunt. Interim non negamus, Servatoris dictum Luc. 6. 35. Mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes, si ad fratres plene pauperes accommodetur, eos nimirum, qui ad extremam paupertatem redacti, neque solvendo, aut restituendo esse possunt, eum admittere sensum, ut neque res mutuo data amplius speretur, aut repetatur. Et hoc casu Naturam mutui proprie sic dicti expirare, & ex mutuo fieri vel donationem, vel eleemosynam statuimus.

Caeterum cum verba haec Servatoris nimis late extendantur, & a nonnullis eo raptantur, ac si inter Christianos omne mutuum simpliciter debeat esse gratuitum, neque etiam circa elocationem pecuniarum usura compensatoria ulla in Ecclesia DEI locum habere possit: operae pretium fuerit, verborum istorum genuinam & nativam sententiam habere cognitam & perspectam. Malo autem aliorum probatissimorum Theologorum hac de re sequi sententiam: quam meo stare privato judicio aut arbitrio.

Sic autem de verbis hisce Servatoris B. Hunnius in suo commentario ad 2.
