Cor. 8. praeclare differit: Si penitius examinemus dictum Christi, patebit ex contextu, nihil illud facere ad eorum opinionem stabiliendam, qui contractum elocationis pecuniarum, sub repetendi potestate, certis certis conditionibus, quæ legibus definitæ sunt, initu (qui fortè minùs commodè notatur appellatione mutui) illicitum esse pronunciant. Verba Servatoris ipsa videamus, quæ apud Lucam sic habent: Si mutuũ dederitis, his à quibus speratis vos recepturos, quæ gratia est vobis? Siquidem & peccatores peccatoribus dant mutuum, ut paria accipiant. Quin imò diligite inimicos vestros, & benefacite, & mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes. Matthæus eandem concionem Christi describit, sed paulò altiùs repetitam, in hunc modum: Si quis impegerit alapam in dexteram tuam maxillam, obverte illi & alteram: Et ei, qui te velit in jus trahere, & tunicam tuam tollere, permitte illi & pallium. Et qui te adegerit ad militare unum, ito cum illo duo: petenti abs te dato, & cupientem mutuum accipere, ne averseru. Hæc Evangelistarum verba penitùs introspecta, palam ostendunt, sententiam Christi de Mutuo, non simpliciter accipiendam sed comparatè. Et evincit indivisa membrorum commemoratorum connexio hunc sensum: ut, quemadmodum Christus in antecedentibus membris per comparationem docet, utrum utro sit præstabilius: nimirùm satius esse alteram quoque maxillam obvertere percutienti, quàm repercutere: & præstare, ut quis unà cum tunicâ, pallij quoque jacturam faciat, quàm ut super ablatâ tunicâ odiosè, & cum dispendio rerum coram judicio contendat. Et consultiùs esse, ut quis in gratiam proximi duo miliaria vadat, & sic officium condupt cet, quàm ut petitionem unius miliarij recuset: Sic pari modo hujus quoque membri, quod de mutuo est, intelligentiam, non absolutè, sed comparatè, capiendam esse, subinduat, hoc omnino sensu; præstabilius esse pauperibus in communi vitâ, sic dare mutuum, ut non modò nihil supra sortem accipias: sed de sorte ipsa quoque, si res ita ferat, periclitari malis, quàm ut fratrem, subsidi j tui indigum, hoc mutuitionis officio planè destituas. Christus enim hîc non egit de mutuo, in quo redduntur, vel etiam exiguntur eadem, seu ut Evangelista loquitur, τὰ ἴσα, sed in quo, propter indigentiam proximi, ne quidem restitutio sortis certò sperari potest: atque ideò sors ipsa tandem remittitur et vel ex toto, vel ex parte. Genuinam hanc esse explicationem, clarissimè docet antithesis apud Lucam, ubi demonstratur, illud officiũ mutui, in quo sperantur & recipiuntur τὰ ἴσα, exerceri quoque à publicanis, & à peccatoribus, qui & ipsi mutuum dant, ut recipiant paria. Christianos autem debere esse perfectiores, & potiùs, ne paria quidem efflagitare in dato mutuo, quàm ut Cor suum claudant egenti fratri: si nimirùm is habens animum restituendi, reddere tamen per egestatem nequeat. Hæc antithesis in verbis Christi expressè posita non subsisteret, si vocula INDE, ad solam usuram, & non etiam ad sortem ipsam referenda foret: & omninò elisior est verborum sensus, quàm ut ad tegendum ulla rima pateat. Dicit enim: Quæ gratia vobis est, si mutuũ dederitis his, à quibus speratis vos recepturos: sed de ipsâ summâ mutuò creditâ manifestè loquitur. Et hanc sententiam arctiùs astringit, quod sequitur: Nam peccatores

& peccatoribus dant mutuum, ut recipiant paria: nec tamen quicquam apud DEUM habent inde vel commendationis, vel præmii, quantumvis non plura, sed paria duntaxat recipiant: Christianos verò libenter in tali casu, etiam cum aliquo dispendio, laboranti fratri subvenire debere. Hanc interpretationem approbavit etiam Carolus Molinæus, & Facultas Theologica Academiæ Tubingensis, in censurâ super controversia Ratisponensi de Usuris. Ex his ergo ita perpensis & explicatis concludimus indubitanter, dictum istud Servatoris, nec ad quaslibet personas indiscretè, nec ad quasvis pecuniarum summas extendi oportere.

Observationem autem hoc loco probè meretur, quàm inepti sint disputatores, qui ex hoc dicto Christi sic colligunt: Servator vult, ut illis etiam detur mutuum, qui τὰ ἴσα restituere non possunt: Ergò illis non est mutuò dandum, qui τὰ ἴσα restituere possunt: imo illis etiam tantum nostra elocanda pecunia, à quibus nihil quicquam Compensations vel sperare, vel accipere possumus. Quam ineptam colligendi rationem tòtus ille textus apud Lucam evidentissimè refellit. Dicit enim ibi quoque Christus: Diligite eos, qui vos non diligunt. Ergonè consequens est, ut non diligamus eos, qui nos diligunt? Idem: Si benefeceritis illis, qui vobis quoque benefaciunt, quæ vobis est gratia (scilicet apud DEUM:) Ergone consequens fuerit, non esse benefaciendum illis, qui nobis vicissim benefacere possunt? Haud opinor quisquam ita bardus fuerit, qui ex verbis Christi sic arguere velit. Corrigimus ergò stuporem istum magis, quàm errorem in hunc modum: Vult Christus, ut non tantùm diligamus eos, & non tantùm benefaciamus illis, qui nos vicissim diligunt, nobisque benefacere possunt: sed & inimicos nostros, & eos, à qui bus beneficij nihil sperare liceat. Sic etiam Servator vult, mutuum dari pauperibus, ab ijsquè nihil vicissim sperare aut accipere: ut interim non prohibeat, quin mutuum demus etiam divitibus, qui τὰ ἴσα rependere possunt: ac proinde non prohibet, si isti divites par pari referant, quin illud accipiamus. Sicut enim charitatis & humanitatis est, amicis etiam, & divitibus, cùm opus habent, nostris officijs gratificari: Jta vicissim æquitatis est, ut illi, cùm possunt, par pari referant. Quam æquitatis legem Christus nunquàm & nuspiam improbavit, vel è medio sustulit. Sic nulla est ratio consequentiæ, neque ex verbis Christi ullâ ratione evinci potest, quod ineptuli illi colligunt: Pecunia nostra elocanda est pauperibus, sine ullâ Compensationis spe: Ergo divitibus nostra pecunia vel planè elocari non debet, vel cum hac conditione, ut si maximè nostrâ pecuniâ illi mirificè res suas locupletent, & sine ullo damno nobis ultra sortem, compensationis loco, aliquid dare possint, tamen nihil ab ipsis accipiamus: non modò non propter mutuationis officiū, id quod nos ipsi gratuitum semper esse debere, ultrò concedimus: sed ne quidem propter causas alias, quæ hoc loco sub considerationem veniunt: de quibus membro quarto ex professo agemus. Quam ineptam disputandi rationem, nullâ operosâ refutatione, sed explosione potiùs dignam judicamus.

Neque ab hac explicatione abhorret B. LUTHERUS noster, in Sermone de Usura, anno 1519. publicato: ubi inter alia sic scribit: Christus wil/ daß wir Leihen sollen/ nicht allein den Freunden/ Reichen/ vnnd da wir geneigt hin sind/ die vns wider mögen in dem oder in einem andern Leihen oder wolthun. Sondern auch denen/ die dasselb nicht vermögen/ oder nicht wollen/ als den Dürfftigen vnd Feinden. Et post pauca: Wer aber leihet/ der gewartet je wider dasselbige/ das er Leihet. Vnd solt er nichts gewarten/ wie sie es verstehen/ so were es gegeben/ vnnd nicht geliehen. Dieweil es denn so gering ist/ dz ein r dem andern leihet/ der jhm freundlich/ Reich/ oder sonst im gleichen wider nützlich seyn mag/ das auch die Sünder/ die nit Christen seyn/ dasselb thun/ so sollen die Christen mehr thun/ vñ denen leihen die dasselbe nicht thun/ das ist den Dürfftigen vnd Feinden. Tom. 1. Jen. Germ. fol. mihi 195. b. Quæ verba Latinè versa sic sonant: Vult Christus, ut mutuum demus non tantùm amicis, divitibus, & in quos benè affecti sumus; qui vel idem, vel aliud nobis mutuum vicissim dare; nobisq; benefacere possunt. Sed etiam iis; qui hoc non possunt, nec volunt; ut egenis, & inimicis. Et post pauca: Qui mutuum dat; ille idipsum, quòd mutuò dedit, vicissim expectat: & nisi id expectaret; tum non mutuum dedisset, sed purè donasset. Quoniam verò talis mutuatio ita vilis est; ut eam peccatores etiam, qui Christiani non sunt, præstare valeant: decet utiq; Christianos plus hac in parte præstare, & illis etiam mutuum dare, qui reddere nequeunt; hoc est, egenis, & inimicis. Et Tom. 7. Jen. Germ. fol. mihi 397. in Commonefactione ad pastores; contra usuras concionandi, anno 1540. edita: sic idem LUTHERUS de mutuo; sive mutuatione disserit: Leihen heisst das/ wann ich jemād mein Gelt/ Gut/ oder Gerete thu daß ers brauche/ wie lange jhm Noth ist/ oder ich kan vnd wil/ vñ sic er mir dasselbe zu seiner Zeit wiedergebe/so gut/ als ichs jhme habe geliehen/wie ein Nachbar dem andern Geld / oder Geldes wert leihet/dafür ich nichts nemen solt Quæ verba latinè versa sic habent: Mutuum dare est, quando alicui meam pecuniam, bona & supellectilem eò usq; usurpandam trado, quamdiu illis opus habet, vel ego illis carere possum & volo: Et ipse idem suo tempore mihi restituat, in eâ bonitate, quâ ego ipsi mutuò dedi: Quemadmodum vicinus alteri pecuniam, & res alias dat mutuò, sed ita ut nihil supra sortem accipere debeat.

Et sic hac in parte inter nos, & B. LUTHERUM, de mutuationis officio unanimis est consensus, quòd nimirùm illud debeat esse gratuitum, & ultra sortem, sive rem mutuò datam, nihil vel sperare, vel accipere liceat: Quin imô si frater vel proximus ad extremam egestatem redactus, nec sortem ampliùs reddere possit, ut sine murmuratione ejus jacturam faciamus: sic præcipiente ipso Jehovah, Deut. 15, 7. & 8. Si fuerit apud te egenus quispiam è fratribus tuis, intra aliquam è portis tuis, in terrâ tuâ, quam Iehovah DEUS tuus dabit tibi: ne obfirmato animum tuum, neque obcludito manum tuam adversus fratrem tuum egenum: Sed liberaliter aperito manum tuam ei, & liberaliter mutuato ei, quantùm satis est indigentiæ ejus, id cujus indiget.


### Chapter Four. and last. On civil contracts: II. On Usuries: What By Reason of etymology

USury is said by the Latins to be from using, and properly signifies the same as use. Whence, the usury of light, of life, of money is said to be granted to him, to whom it is granted to use light, life, money. Thus Tully in the Tusculans: Nature has given the usury of life, as of money, with no day set: What is it therefore, that you complain of, if he asks it back when he wishes, for you had received it on that condition? And in this general and grammatical sense, to give money at usury, is nothing other than to grant the use of money: that is, to let out money to someone for a time, without any addition of either profit or gift to the principal.

But by forensic custom, the name of Usury is taken for the price of use, or for the reward of usury, that is, for that which is paid for the sake of usury, or use. Whence in this sense it is defined by the Jurists that Usury is an addition lawfully owed to the principal, or quantity. But in this very signification the word Usury is sometimes taken broadly, sometimes strictly. Broadly, for every increase of the principal, consisting in quantity, from whatever cause even other than from money given as a loan: as when a buyer [withholds] the price after delivery has been made; or when a father-in-law [withholds] a dowry from a son-in-law; or when a guardian retains the money of a ward: and the buyer, father-in-law, or guardian is said to have usury, on account of the fact that the seller, son-in-law, or ward lacked the use of the money owed. And concerning this looser sense of usury, there is no question properly in this place. But strictly it is accepted for that which is added beyond the principal in a loan, and that in two ways: either properly, for that which is exacted solely beyond the duty of lending, without another just cause; and it is called Fœnus, Wucher: or less properly for that which is accepted in a loan beyond the principal, not on account of the duty of lending, which ought to be gratuitous, but on account of another just cause; such as that either the one giving the loan suffers loss from the fact that he must lack his money, or the one receiving the loan makes a profit and increases and amplifies his wealth from our money. And in this latter stricter signification the word usury is accepted in the present discussion, so that whatever is accepted on account of the use of money granted to another, that is and is called usury. In itself, therefore, and by reason of its origin, the word usury is accepted in a good sense; although today it has a bad reputation: but beyond the usage of the Latin language, and only accidentally, as will be made clear. And although Aristotle in book 5 of the Ethics and book 1 of the Politics, chapter 7, accepts the word usury almost always in a bad sense, establishing that it is most unjust and against nature if money begets money: yet to what extent this is true and ought to be conceded, the following digression will show more fully and accurately.

Among the Hebrews, usury is called partly Nesech נשֶׁךְ, that is, a bite, because it bites the lender like a serpent and exhausts all his resources: but partly Tarbith תַּרְבִּית, that is, multiplication, because the resources of him who gives a loan and receives interest are multiplied.

Among the Greeks it is called τόκος, that is, offspring: to which the Latin Fœnus seems to correspond, as if it were a fetus: because interest is born like offspring from the principal, either in a legitimate or illegitimate way, just as other children are legitimate, others spurious. But jurists distinguish interest from usury: whence most recent writers establish two species of usury: namely, interest and usury. But because canonists almost only call interest usury, naming the other species of usury, of which we shall speak soon, interest rather than usury: hence that definition of usury drew its origin, that it is a profit exacted above the principal, solely on account of the duty of lending. And that such usury is impious and illicit is clear and evident in itself from those things which we discussed a little earlier concerning the gratuitous duty of lending. Wherefore theologians rightly establish that usury, condemned by the law of God, is a profit which is exacted and accepted above the principal with the loss of the debtor, on account of loaned money. But let these things suffice in general concerning the notation of the word usury. Its division follows.

Latin:

USura Latinis dicta est ab utendo, & propriè idem, quòd usus significat. Unde, Lucis, vitæ, pecuniæ usura ei concedi dicitur, cut luce, vitâ, pecuniâ uti conceditur. Sic Tullius in Tuscul: Natura dedit usuram vitæ, tanquam pecuniæ, nullâ præstitutâ die: Quid est igitur, quod querare, si repetit cum vult, ea enim conditione acceperas? Et hoc sensu generali ac Grammaticô, dare pecuniam ad usuram, nihil est aliud, quàm concedere usum pecuniæ: hoc est, elocare alicui ad tempus pecuniam, sine omni accessione vel lucri, vel doni ad sortem.

Verùm consuetudine forensi, accipitur nomen Usuræ, pro usus pretio, sive pro mercede usuræ, hoc est, pro eo, quod usuræ, sive usus causâ præstatur. Unde hoc sensu à JCtis definitur Usura, quòd sit ad sortem, sive quantitatem legitimè debita accessio. Sed in hac ipsâ significatione vocabulum Usuræ interdum late, interdum strictè accipitur, Latè, pro omni augmento sortis, in quantitate consistentis, ex quacunque causâ etiam aliâ, quàm ex mutuo datæ pecuniæ: ut cùm emtor pretium post traditionem factam: vel cùm socer generi dotem, vel cùm tutor pupilli pecuniam retinet : & usuram habere dicitur emtor, socer, tutor, propter id, quod venditor, gener vel pupillus debitæ pecuniæ usu caruit. Et de hoc laxiore sensu Usuræ, hoc loco propriè non est quæstio. Strictè verò accipitur pro eo, quod accedit ultra sortem in mutuo, idq́; dupliciter, vel propriè, pro eo, quòd tantùm præter mutuationis officium, sine aliâ justâ causâ exigitur: & dicitur Fœnus Wucher: vel minùs propriè pro eo, quod in mutuo ultra sortem accipitur, non propter mutuationis officium, quod esse debet gratuitum: sed propter aliam justam causam; ut quòd vel dans mutuum, damnum patitur ex eo, quòd pecunia sua carere oportet: vel accipiens mutuum lucrum facit, & ex nostra pecunia divitias auget, & amplificat. Et in hac postrema strictiore significatione vocabulum Usura in præsenti disputatione accipitur, ita ut quicquid propter pecuniæ usum alteri concessum, accipitur, illud Usura sit, & dicatur. In se ergo, & ratione originis, Usura vocabulum in bonam partem accipitur; quanquam hodiè malè illud audiat: sed præter usum linguæ Latinæ, & tantùm per accidens, uti patebit. Et quanquam Aristoteles lib. 5. Ethicorum & lib. 1. Politicorum, cap. 7. Usuræ vocabulum in malam partem fermè semper accipit, iniquissimum, & contra naturam esse statuens, si numus numum pariat: tamen quatenus hoc verum sit, & concedi debeat, insequens diexodus pleniùs & accuratiùs ostendet.

Hebræis Usura dicitur partim Nesech נשֶׁךְ hoc est, Morsus, propterea quòd instar serpentis mutuantem mordeat, ejusque facultates omnes exhauriat: partim veró Tarbith תַּרְבִּית hoc est, multiplicatio, quia ejus qui mutuum dat, & fœnus accipit, facultates multiplicantur.

Græcis dicitur τόκος, hoc est, partus: Cui respondere videtur Latinum Fœnus, quasi fœtus: quòd fœnus tanquàm soboles nascatur ex sorte, vel modo legitimo, vel illegitimo, quemadmodum liberi alii sunt legitimi, alii spurii. Sed distinguunt JCti fœnus ab Usura: unde recentiores plærique duas usuræ species constituunt: Fœnus nimirùm, & Usuram. Quia verò Canonistæ ferme solum fœnus vocant usuram: Cæteras usuræ species, de quibus mox dicemus, Interesse potiùs, quàm usuras nominantes: hinc illa Usuræ definitio traxit originem, quod sit lucrum supra sortem exactum, tantummodo propter officium mutuationis. Et talem usuram impiam & illicitam esse, liquidò, & perse constat, ex iis, quæ de mutuationis of ficio gratuito paulò antè disseruimus. Quare rectè Theologi statuunt, Usuram lege DEI damnatam, esse lucrum, quod supra sortem cum damno debitoris, propter mutuam pecuniam exigitur, & accipitur. Sed de Notatione vocabuli Vsuræ hæc in genere sufficiant. Sequitur eju divisio.


### Chapter Four. and last. On civil contracts: III. Into fourfold becomes usura, or which are its species

Various distinctions of usury offer themselves among the Doctors. Some theologians, looking to the propriety of the Hebrew speech, divide usury into biting and non-biting. They define biting as that which occurs with the loss of the debtor: non-biting as that which occurs without his loss and inconvenience: or, as others define it: that which is a part of the profit, which is received by the creditor above the principal, without the loss of the debtor, from the profit made through the loaned money. They contend that the former is illicit, the latter licit. Again, they divide biting usury into simple and conjunct, or multiplying, called by others usury of usury: which was infamous even by the judgment of the Gentiles. Jurists divide simple usury into terrestrial and nautical: concerning which their schools also should be consulted. We follow that received distinction of the Doctors, by which they divide usury into three species: namely, lucrative, compensatory, and punitory.

Lucrative is that which, contrary to the nature of a loan, exacts profit from the sole duty of lending.

Compensatory is that which is called such, which, from the profit that the debtor receives from our money, pays the creditor a just and legitimate interest, without any loss to the debtor.

Punitory is that which is inflicted, not on account of the profit of the debtor, but on account of the delay of the one not paying, as a penalty, either by law or by the creditor.

Concerning these, therefore, the question now is: Which of these three species is licit, which illicit: and if one of them is licit, to what extent it is such: which the fourth member will now explain.

VI. Whether any usury is lawful, and to what extent.

We determine that the first kind of usury, namely lucrative or biting, exacted for the mere service of a loan, is simply condemned in the scriptures, and therefore is by no means to be tolerated in a Christian commonwealth, for the following reasons:

1. Because it conflicts with the nature of a loan: which ought always to be gratuitous, and to demand nothing beyond the principal; indeed, from a poor and needy brother, one ought not even to hope for or demand back the principal itself: as was demonstrated in the first member from the words of Christ, Luke 6:35, 'Lend, hoping for nothing thereby.'

2. Because it is expressly prohibited and condemned in the sacred scriptures: As: Exod. 22, 25. If you lend money to my people, to the poor among you who is with you: do not be to him as a usurer, nor shall you impose upon him Nescheb, a biting usury. Levit. 25, 35. 36. 37. When your brother has become impoverished and his hand has faltered with you, and you have received him as a stranger and a sojourner, and he has lived with you: do not take Nescheb, a biting usury, from him, and increase זַרְבִּיחַ וְנֶשֶׁךְ but fear your GOD, so that your brother may live with you: you shall not give him your money בְּנֶשֶׁךְ וּבְמַרְבִּית at a biting usury, and you shall not give your fruits for increase. Deut. 23, 9. & 20. Do not give at a biting usury לֹא תַשִׁיךְ to your brother, usury of money, usury of food, usury of anything that is given for usury: to a foreigner you may give at usury: but to your brother you shall not give at usury, Lo Taschich: so that Jehovah your GOD may bless you &c. Psal. 15, 1. & 5. He shall dwell in the tabernacle of the Lord, who has not given his money at a biting usury, לֹא נָתַן בְּנֶשֶׁךְ. Ezech. 18 8. He who has not given at a biting usury, and has not received increase or interest: בְּנֶשֶׁךְ לֹא יִתֵּן וְתַרְבִּית לֹא יִקָּח he shall live. And verse 13. He who gives at a biting usury, and receives increase or interest, shall he live? He shall not live.

And indeed, the whole context or coherence of the entire text of this eighteenth chapter of Ezekiel clearly shows that it expressly deals with a poor and impoverished brother: For mention is expressly made of the hungry, the naked, the needy, and the poor. And especially verse 17 removes all doubt, which reads as follows: He is just; and he shall live, who withdraws his hand from injury to the poor, and does not take usury or interest. Therefore, those who understand every class of men, even the richer and those abounding in wealth, to be meant in this place do an injury to this text, so that they contend that simply nothing at all is to be received from anyone beyond the principal. What is more, from usury that is biting and from increase prohibited in the sacred scriptures, the consequence does not hold to a just and legitimate compensation resting on certain equity and laws, and a shameful fallacy of four terms is committed. As would be shown a little later.

3. Because it manifestly fights against Christian Charity, and against the law of Nature, confirmed by Christ himself: Luke 6. 31. Whatever you want men to do to you, do also to them. To which corresponds that common rule: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to another. Just as, therefore, you would not want money lent to you to be demanded back from you with your loss and ruin: so you also should not hope for, much less demand, any profit or advantage from a loan beyond the principal. And looking to this, M. Tullius in book 3 of his Offices truly wrote: To take away from another, and for a man to increase his own advantage by the disadvantage of another man, is more against nature than Death. And Aristotle in book 1 of his Politics, chapter 7. Usurious acquisition is most against Nature: because money is sterile, and cannot beget money: namely, if it is alone, and by itself, or lies shut up in a chest, or is spent on necessary things: But when by the benefit of money I buy goods, lands, estates; that in this case human industry can make a profit from money, although bare money does not make other money, no one will deny, unless he is not entirely of sound mind. But these things are said in a subtle manner.

4. Because such usury has been disapproved and prohibited by the laws of all Emperors, even Heathen ones: and this mode of acquiring property has always been rejected and disapproved by the law of Nations and civil law as illicit and dishonest.

5. Because it is in itself iniquitous to demand profit from a loan from a debtor who himself receives no profit or gain from the loan, but is more often forced to feel a loss.

Latin:

VAriæ sese offerunt apud Doctores Usurarum distinctiones. Theologi nonnulli respicientes ad proprietatem sermonis Hebræi, Vsuram dividunt in Mordentem, & in non Mordentem. Mordentem definiunt, quæ fiat cum damno debitoris: Non mordentem, quæ fiat sine ejusdem damno, & incommodo: Vel, ut alii definiunt: quæ sit pars lucri, quæ supra sortem, sine damno debitoris, ex lucro per tuam mutuatam pecuniam facto, à Creditore percipitur. Hanc licitam, illam illicitam esse contendunt. Rursum Vsuram mordentem dividunt in Simplicem, & in Conjunctam, sive multiplicantem ab aliis Vsuram Vsurarum dictam: quæ etiam Gentilium judicio infamis erat. Simplicem JCti dividunt in terrestrem, & Nauticam: de quibus Scholæ etiam ipsorum consulantur. Nos sequimur receptam illam Doctorum distinctionem, quà Vsuram in tres species dividunt: nempe in Lucratoriam, Compensatoriam, & Punitoriam.

LVCRATORIA est, quæ ex solo mutuationis officio, contra naturam mutui, lucrum exigit.

COMPENSATORIA est, & dicitur, quæ ex lucro, quod debitor ex nostrâ pecuniâ percipit, justum ac legitimum interesse, sine ullo ejusdamno, Creditori persolvit.

PVNITORIA est, quæ non propter lucrum debitoris, sed propter moram non solventis, pro pœnâ, vel à lege, vel à Creditore infligitur.

De his ergo jam quæstio est: Quænam ex tribus istis speciebus, sit licita, quæ illicita: & si una earum est licita, quatenus talis sit: id quod Quartum jam membrum expediet.

VI. An Vsura aliqua sit licita, & quatenus.

PRimam Vsurarum speciem, nempe Lucratoriam sive Mordentem, pro solo Mutuatio nis officio exactam, in sacris simpliciter damnatam, ac proinde in Repub. Christianorum minimè ferendam esse statuimus: propter sequentes rationes:

1. Quia pugnat cum natura Mutui: quod semper esse gratuitum, & ultra sortem nihil exigere: imò à fratre paupere & egeno, ne quidem Sortem ipsam sperare aut repetere debet: uti membro 1. ex verbis Christi, Luc. 6, 35. Mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes, demonstratum.

2. Quia in sacris expressè prohibita, & damnata est: Ut: Exod. 22, 25. Si pecuniam dederis mutuam populo meo, pauperi ipsi, qui est tecum: ne esto ei tanquam foenerator, nec impones ei Nescheb usuram mordentem. Levit. 25, 35. 36. 37. Cùm attenuatus fuerit frater tuus, & mutaverit manus ejus tecum, & susceperis eum quasi advenam & peregrinum, & vixerit tecum: ne accipias Nescheb Usuram mordentem ab eo, & multiplicationem זַרְבִּיחַ וְנֶשֶׁךְ sed time DEUM tuum, ut vivere possit frater tuus apud te: pecuniam tuā non dabis ei בְּנֶשֶׁךְ וּבְמַרְבִּית ad usuram mordentem, & in multiplicationem non dabis fructus tuos. Deut. 23, 9. & 20. Ne dato in usuram mordentem לֹא תַשִׁיךְ fratri tuo, Usuram pecuniae, usuram cibi, usuram ullius rei, quae in usuram datur: Extraneo dabis in usuram: fratri autem tuo ne dato in usuram, Lo Taschich: ut benedicat tibi Jehovāh DEUS tuus &c. Psal. 15, 1. & 5. Is habitabit in tabernaculo Domini, qui pecuniam suam non dedit ad usuram mordentem, לֹא נָתַן בְּנֶשֶׁךְ. Ezech. 18 8. Qui in usuram mordentem non dederit, & multiplicationē, sive foenus non acceperit: בְּנֶשֶׁךְ לֹא יִתֵּן וְתַרְבִּית לֹא יִקָּח ille vivet. Et versu 13. Qui dat in usuram mordentem, & multiplicationem, sive foenus accipit, hicnè vivet? Non vivet.

Et sanè caput hoc decimum octavum Jezechielis ex professo agere de fratre paupere, & attenuato, totius textus συνέπεια sive cohaerentia luculenter ostendit: Expressa enim fit mentio esurientium, nudorum, egenorum, & pauperum. Et cumprimis versus 17. dubium omne tollit, qui sic habet: Is est justus; & vivet, qui à paupero injuriā retrahit manum suam, & usuram aut foenus non accipit. Proinde textui huic injuriam faciunt, qui omne genus hominum, etiam ditiores, & opibus abundantes hoc loco intelligunt, ita ut simpliciter nihil quicquam à quoquam ultra sortem accipiendum esse contendant. Quid quòd ab usurâ mordente, & à Multiplicatione in sacris prohibita, ad justam & legitimam compensationem, certâ aequitate & legibus nitentem, non valet consequentia, & turpis ἀσυλλογία quatuor terminorum committitur. Uti paulò pòst ostenderetur.

3. Quià manifestè pugnat cum Charitate Christianâ, & cum lege Naturae, ab ipso Christo confirmata: Luc. 6. 31. Quaecunque vultis, ut faciant vobis homines, & vos facite illis. Cui respondet vulgata illa regula: Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri non feceris. Quemadmodum ergò nolis mutuum tibi datum, à te cum damno, & exitio tuo repeti: ità tu quoque ex mutuo lucrum aut commodum aliquod ultra sortem, ne sperato, nedum exigito. Et huc respiciens M. Tullius lib. 3. offic. verè scripsit: Detrahere alteri, & hominem hominu incommodo suum augere commodum, magis est contra naturam, quàm Mors. Et Aristoteles lib. 1. Pol. cap. 7. Usuraria acquisitio est maximè contra Naturam: quia nummus sterilis est, & non potest gignere nummum: nempè si solus sit, & per se, vel in cistâ clausus haereat, vel in res necessarias insumatur: Sed quando beneficio nummorum emo merces, fundos, praedia; quin hoc casu industria humana ex nummo possit facere lucrum, licet nudus nummus nummum alium non faciat, nemo negaverit, nisi qui mentis non per omnia compos est. Sed haec ὠχρθινικῶς.

4. Quia talis usura omnium Imperatorum etiam Ethnicorum legibus improbata & prohibita est: & modus iste acquirendi dominii, jure Gentium ac civili semper tanquam illicitus, & inhonestus fuit rejectus & improbatus.

5. Quia per se iniquum est, exigere lucrum ex mutuo à debitore, qui ipse lucrum aut quaestum nullum ex mutuo percipit, sed damnum saepius sentire cogitur.


### Chapter Four. and last. On civil contracts: II. The Compensatory species of Usury

II. The Compensatory species of Usury.

The Doctors name the other species of Usury Compensatory, concerning which there is also the greatest controversy among Theologians and Politicians: and because the word Usury, on account of the abuse of the thing, is for the most part taken in a bad sense: this species deserved to be called Compensation and Interest rather than Usury. Although if a grammarian obtains the sense and use of this word: we also, regarding this species, do not shrink from it in the least. But this Compensation, or Compensatory Usury, is nothing other than a legitimate contract, resting on equity and laws, concerning a just and certain annual payment, which the debtor is bound to pay, not on account of the duty of lending but on account of the profit and advantage which he receives from our money, and can pay without loss. That this usury or compensation is lawful, and in no way disapproved or condemned in the sacred scriptures, can be demonstrated invincibly and clearly.

At the beginning, however, a distinction must be premised between the different classes of men who can come under consideration in this place: and concerning whom one must pronounce in different ways in this question. There are, however, three classes of men who can seek money from us under a contract of legitimate compensation. They are, in the beginning, the Poor, who by inevitable necessity of poverty have been reduced to extreme destitution, and although they promise the return of the principal and the payment of the due compensation, they are nevertheless able to perform neither.

There are then others who are not entirely poor, but in order to be able to conduct their business and promote their convenience, they need the help of others for a time, and are able to restore what they have received at some point.

Finally, there are those who hold ample possessions and are concerned about increasing them, and consequently make convenience and profit from our money.

Regarding the first class of men, that falls neither under the contract of loan nor under compensatory usury, but according to the precepts of God, it ought to be helped by purely gratuitous beneficence, that is, alms: Deut. 15:11. There will not be wanting poor in the land of your habitation; therefore I command you to open your hand to your needy and poor brother who dwells with you in the land. And verse 4. There shall be no beggar or needy person among you.

Regarding the second class of men, who indeed have some resources, yet they are not so great that they suffice for them to buy or do something that might be of use to them, and consequently they have need of another's help: neither do these fall under compensatory usury, nor even alms, but they are to be helped by a loan: in such a way, indeed, that a certain profit above the principal is not exacted from them, nor is the principal itself demanded back with their loss and inconvenience, but time is granted to them until they can restore what was either given as a loan or lent for use, regarding the harm.

Regarding the third class of men, that falls under the present discussion concerning compensatory usury, and it will soon be demonstrated that a legitimate profit, or interest, as they say, can be sought and received from them with a clear conscience.

But there is also another distinction to be observed, concerning persons who can place their money with the wealthier in the hope of profit and convenience, or rather are compelled by a kind of necessity. For there are those whose entire patrimony is placed in money, and who, either because of bodily infirmity, such as widows, orphans, the infirm, and the sick, or because of their life's function, such as students of the arts and letters, doctors of schools, ministers of the Republic and the Church, cannot exercise their money in any honest and licit gain, whether of agriculture, or of livestock, or of any craft, or of trade, or of any other business, and whose money is not so great that it suffices for their support if they always deduct something from its sum and add nothing to it. That it is licit for these to agree to participate in some certain sum from the profit with others, and to seek and receive some compensation, the following reasons prove most evidently.

1. Because such compensation, which is made without loss and detriment to the debtor, is nowhere prohibited by God. For each and every statement of Scripture that is brought forward to the contrary deals with Neschech or biting usury, and with Tarbith, that is, the multiplication of usury, namely when usury is extorted for the mere service of lending, and that being unpaid, it begets new usury. Furthermore, Jehovah speaks of the poor among His people who were receiving money or something else to relieve their necessities, as is evident from Exodus 22:25, Leviticus 25:35, which an ocular demonstration of the Biblical texts irrefragably proves. And they betray remarkable ignorance who attempt to twist the Hebrew Neschech, which, as all theologians and grammarians attest, denotes only biting usury, which is exacted with damage to one's neighbor, to any usury whatsoever, and indeed to compensatory usury, which does not bite and occurs without damage to one's neighbor. For disparate species have disparate properties. Therefore, just as usury with Neschech is prohibited by divine law, so usury without Neschech is not prohibited, but is lawful and permitted by the same law. The argument from the contrary holds.

2. Because it is in agreement with the law of nature: which prohibits only that we should not do to others what we would not wish to be done to ourselves: that is, that we should not inflict damage upon our neighbor. Therefore, because this compensation, or interest, is provided without damage to one's neighbor, it is certainly consistent with the law of nature.

3. Because it is nothing other than the restitution of emerging damage and ceasing profit, as far as the creditor is concerned. For he himself could have applied his money to other uses and therefrom made a profit or perceived some advantage. Now, indeed, if another uses his money and increases his own affairs from it, the creditor would certainly be deprived of the fruit and use of his own money if he perceived no advantage from the debtor's profit: a thing which would be most unworthy and contrary and opposed to all law, both divine and human.

4. Because such compensation, strictly speaking, is not profit exacted above the principal for the mere service of lending, but is only the price or valuation of the use of the consumed principal with damage to the creditor. The reason is: because the debtor seeks and receives money from the creditor not out of indigence, but so that through it he may acquire greater wealth and possessions and be able to grow richer and richer.

In which case, indeed, the authentic apostolic text, 2 Cor. 8:13, has place, which establishes that the duties of charity are to be performed to one's neighbor in such a way that there is not for others indeed relaxation: but for us ourselves, distress or affliction.

we are free: thus it is not necessary that this law be observed in all things and in the same way: nevertheless, in what matter equity consists, and indeed according to Divine Law, can thence easily be gathered: namely 1. that it is lawful to buy and sell all those things which can come into a contract of buying and selling. 2. that this very contract ought to be so based on the Law of equity, that it is a loss or detriment to neither the buyer nor the seller. That this same thing must be observed concerning the Contract of selling and buying regarding money, no one will deny, unless he be one who dares to despoil it of the Law of equity too rashly and impudently.

5. Because the Gospel does not abolish polities. Just as, therefore, a Christian can, and indeed ought to, observe with a good and uninjured conscience the equitable and, to human society, most necessary and salutary Ordinances or political Constitutions concerning marriages, burials, Testaments, inheritances, successions, the acquiring of ownership of things, thefts, adulteries, weights and measures, purchases and sales, and other civil contracts of that kind: So nothing at all stands in the way of a Christian being able and bound to observe, with a safe conscience, the most equitable Constitutions of Emperors, and those legitimately confirmed in the Recesses of the Empire, concerning Usury: for common necessity has extorted them. For unless this Contract holds its place, certainly in a small space of time, the Church will be despoiled of its revenues, the Ministers of the Word and of Schools of their Stipends: the Poor of public alms: orphans of necessary sustenance: Students of public Stipends and subsidies: the old and infirm of their resources, Hospitals and Orphanages of their revenues: and it will be necessary that the whole civil society perish. Since, therefore, Scripture itself has commended the disposition concerning civil contracts to be moderated by the civil Magistrate according to the proportion of time, persons, places, and other circumstances: certainly all Christians whatsoever are bound to obey constitutions published in this part according to equity: according to the Precept of the Apostle, Rom. 13.1. Let every soul be subject to the supereminent powers: For there is no power, except from GOD: And whoever resists the powers, resists the ordinance of GOD: But those who resist, acquire for themselves damnation.

7. Because charity is ordered, and begins from itself, and persuades that you have greater regard for those whom GOD and Nature have more closely joined to you, namely your spouse, children, and whole family: than for others. Now, that you may have care for these, and rightly provide for their conveniences: you will certainly place your money in such a way that fruit and some convenience can redound from it to you and yours. And this very thing the Apostle commands, 1 Tim. 5.8. If anyone does not have care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.

8. Because Charity ought to be reciprocal. Therefore, he who has made great profit from my money, ought to pursue me with such an affection of charity that he makes me a participant in that profit. For I am in this part, above all others, his neighbor. Moved by these and other similar reasons, we undoubtedly determine that it is lawful to bargain for profit above the principal, and to both seek and receive compensation for damage emerging and profit ceasing: not only in immovable goods: such as fields, vineyards, and the like: but also in money. For even if that is sterile by itself, and produces nothing from itself: yet by use it is by no means sterile: but generates rich gain, as is detected from negotiation, that is, buying and selling.

6. Because the judgment is the same concerning similar things. Now indeed the Law of GOD nowhere abolishes the contract of buying and selling: but rather shows what the will of GOD is concerning these very contracts. For example, Levit. 25.13. and following, such a precept is held concerning the year of Jubilee: In the year of jubilee all shall return to their possessions, when you sell something to your citizen, or buy from him, do not sadden your brother: but according to the number of years of the Jubilee you shall buy from him, and according to the calculation of the fruits he shall sell to you: The more years that remain after the Jubilee, the more the price will increase: and the less time you count, the less the purchase will cost: for he will sell you the time of the fruits etc. The LORD shows, indeed, what the ratio of contracts ought to be in the buying and selling of fields, houses, etc. so that indeed it may be done under the condition of redemption: And that neither the buyer nor the seller may be burdened, but there may be a just proportion on both sides, and the price of the sale may be estimated according to the multitude of the produce, as also of the years. Although indeed, as from other ceremonies of the Mosaic Polity

But it is asked in this place. What is to be thought concerning purchased censuses and annual revenues of this kind, whether they ought to be called Usurious [Wucherische Kauff vnd Contract]. But the answer is easy from what has already been said through a distinction. If censuses and revenues of this kind have been purchased either from those who cannot pay and settle them without damage and inconvenience: or the contract has been entered into against public laws: then indeed that Usurer is deservedly judged impious and illicit. But if censuses and revenues of this kind have been purchased from those who have a place in the third class of men, and purchased according to laws legitimately constituted and approved by the Magistrate: then indeed they cannot be called Usurers, just as today that word has a bad reputation and is taken in a worse sense: but they are more rightly called compensatory and remuneratory.

It is further asked: What is to be determined concerning that contract of purchase, very common today, when a certain sum of money is bought from another for a certain annual pension defined and conceded by the laws, as if someone buys one hundred florins by paying five florins every year: but on the condition that the ownership of the one hundred florins passes completely from the buyer, or the one lending the money, and it is not permitted for him ever to demand it back: but for the seller, who pays that annual pension, it is intact, at any time, to restore the sum, as they call it, the capital, and to recall that annual pension of his to himself? Which kind of contract is German, and is called: A redeemable interest.

I answer: Although such contracts are not a pure purchase, and differ from a true purchase in certain circumstances: if, however, the price of the pension in them is fair, we certainly ought not on this account to cast snares upon consciences: but to approve them as lawful and honest. Especially since they have been confirmed by the calculation of the Emperors and the Roman Empire: nor can such purchases or contracts be changed without a universal change of the entire public state.

But the question is more difficult: What is to be judged concerning those contracts where the buyer, or Creditor, who lends a certain sum of money, and for it buys a certain annual pension from another, reserves for himself the power of renouncing the purchase and demanding back the principal or the sum lent?

Some respond that such a contract is vicious, as being in conflict with Christian charity. But what they say, they do not prove. For such a contract can also be so arranged that it nowhere exceeds the measure of Christian charity. It is certainly of Christian charity that one helps a brother with his money in such a way that he can make his own profit from it and increase his own household property. Where both the reason of equity, and the law of nature, and the love of neighbor, and the rule of Christ, Matt. 7, 12, warn and command that he not only duly pay the legitimate annual pension: but also, after that space of years has passed which is expressed in the contract, restore the principal itself. For various cases can occur in which the Creditor then may have need of that money, either in the placing of children, or in buying some land, or for another necessary matter. Where it would truly be of the highest iniquity if we were forced to be without our money to our own loss and inconvenience. Which same reason also militates in that case if the Creditor does not express and define a certain number of years in the contract: but in general reserves this power to himself, upon some urgent necessity, of demanding back the principal itself: but in such a way that the Debtor is not forced to provide the payment or restoration of the principal abruptly and immediately: but a just time, and at least a half-year, is granted to him. Where the Debtor can also reserve this same power for himself, so that either after a certain number of years has elapsed, or if he no longer has need of the money, he can restore the principal to the creditor, and not be forced to retain it any longer to his own inconvenience.

Which reciprocity is certainly entirely consonant with the law of nature, and equity, and Christian charity: so that they betray either notable ignorance or a clearly inordinate zeal who do not hesitate in this case to cast snares upon the consciences of men without cause, and to bring danger upon themselves. But enough and more than enough concerning Compensatory Usury.

Latin:

II. Usurae species Compensatoria.

Alteram Usurae Speciem nominant Doctores Compensatoriam, de quâ etiam potissimùm inter Theologos & Politicos controvertitur: & quia Usurae vocabulum propter abusum rei, plerumque in malam partem accipitur: Species haec Compensatio magis & Interesse, quàm Usura dici meruit. Quanquam si Grammaticus vocabuli hujus sensus & usus obtineat: nos etiam quoad hanc speciem, ab eo minimè abhorremus. Est verò haec Compensatio, sive Usura Compensatoria nihil aliud, quàm contractus legitimus, aequitate, & legibus nitens, de Justa ac certâ pensione annuâ, quam debitor solvere tenetur, non propter mutuationis officium sed propter lucrum & commodum, quod ex nostrâ pecunia ille percipit, & sine damno exolvere potest. Hanc usuram sive compensationem esse licitam, & in sacris minimè improbatam aut damnatam, invictè, & ad oculum demonstrari potest.

Initio autem praemittenda distinctio inter diversa hominum genera, qui hoc loco sub considerationem venire possunt: & de quibus diversimodè hac in quaestione pronunciari debet. Tria autem dantur hominum genera, qui pecuniam à nobis sub contractu compensationis legitimae petere possunt. Sunt initio Pauperes, qui inevitabili Paupertatis necessitate ad extremam egestatem sunt redacti, & licet redditionem sortis, & solutionem debitæ compensationis promittant: tamen neutrum præstare possunt.

Sunt deinde alii, qui non prorsus pauperes sunt, sed ut rem suam facere, & commodum promovere queant, ad tempus alieno auxilio indigent, & acceptum aliquando restituere possunt.

Sunt denique, qui amplas possessiones tenent, deque illis amplificandis sunt solliciti, ac proinde ex pecuniâ nostrâ commodum, & lucrum faciunt.

Quoad primum genus hominum, illud neque sub contractum mutui : neque sub Usuram compensatoriam cadit : sed secundum DEI præcepta, purè gratuitâ beneficentiâ, hoc est, eleemosyna juvari debet: Deut. 15, 11. Non deerunt pauperes in terrâ habitationis tuæ: idcirco præcipio, ut aperias manum tuam fratri egeno & pauperi, qui tecum versatur in terra. Et versu 4. Omnino mendicus & indigens non erit inter vos.

Quoad alterum genus hominum, qui quidem habent aliquas facultates, tantæ tamen non sunt, ut sufficiant ipsis ad aliquid emendum, aut faciendum, quod ex usu illosum sit, ac proinde alieno opus habent auxilio: neque hi sub usuram compensatoriam cadunt: neque etiam eleemosyna: sed mutuo juvandi sunt: ita quidem, ut non exigatur ab illis lucrum quoddam, supra sortem: nec sors ipsa reposcatur, cum ipsorum dispendio, & incommodo: sed tempus ipsis concedatur, usque dum circa noxam, quod vel mutuò datum, vel commodatum est, possint restituere.

Quoad tertium genus hominum, illud sub præsentem disputationem de Usurâ Compensatoriâ cadit: & ab his legitimum lucrum, sive interesse, uti loquuntur, salvâ conscientiâ, peti & accipi posse, mox demonstrabitur.

Sed est & altera distinctio observanda, de personis, quæ pecuniam suam ditioribus, sub spe lucri, & commodi elocare possunt, imò necessitate quasi quâdam adiguntur. Sunt enim quorum omne patrimonium in pecunia est positum: quique vel propter Corporum imbecillitatem, ut viduæ, pupilli, infirmi & ægri: vel propter vitæ functionem, ut Studiosi artium & literarum: Scholarum Doctores: Ministri Reipub. & Ecclesiæ, non possunt pecuniam suam honesto aliquo & licito quæstu exercere, sive agriculturæ, sive rei pecuariæ, sive aliquo opificio, sive mercatura, sive ullâ aliâ negociatione: & quorum pecunia non est tanta, ut alendis illis sufficiat, si de summâ ejus semper aliquid detrahant, & nihil ei adjiciant. His licitum esse de certâ aliquâ summâ ex lucro participandâ cum aliis pacisci, & compensationem aliquam petere & accipere, sequentes rationes evidentissimè probatum faciunt.

1. Quia talis Compensatio, quæ fiat sine damno & detrimento debitoris nuspiam à DEO est prohibita. Singula enim & universa scripturæ dicta, quæ in contrarium proferuntur, agunt de Neschech sive Usura mordente, & de Tarbith, hoc est, multiplicatione usuræ, quando videlicet usura ob solum mutuationis officium extorta, ea verò non persoluta, novam parit usuram : Deinde loquitur Jehovah de pauperibus in populo suo, qui pecuniam aut aliquid aliud accipiebant ad suas necessitates sublevandas: uti patet ex Exodi 22, 25. Levit. 25, 35. id quod ocularis demonstratio textuum Biblicorum irrefragabiliter evincit. Et insignem inscitiam produnt, qui Hebræum Neschech, quod, attestantibus omnibus Theologis, & Grammaticis notat tantùm Usuram mordentem, quæ cum damno proximi exigitur, ad quamvis usuram, & quidem Compensatoriam, quæ non mordet, & fit sine damno proximi, detorquere conantur. Disparatæ enim species, disparatas etiam affectiones. Quemadmodum ergo usura cum Nesech jure divino est prohibita: Ita Usura sine Neschech non est prohibita, sed eodem jure licita & concessa. Valet argumentum à contrario.

2. Quia congruit cum lege Naturæ: ut quæ id tantùm prohibet, ne faciamus aliis, quod nobis fieri nolimus: hoc est, ne damnum inferamus proximo. Ergo, quia Compensatio hæc, sive Interesse, præstatur sine damno proximi: utique Legi Naturæ est consentanea.

3. Quia nihil est, quàm restitutio damni emergentis, & lucri cessantis, quoad Creditorem. Potuisset enim ipse pecuniam suam alios in usus conferte, & indè lucrum facere, sive commodum aliquod percipere. Jam verò si alius pecuniâ illius utatur, & ex eâ res suas augeat, utique creditor propriæ suæ pecuniæ fructu & usu privaretur: si ex lucro debitoris nullum commodum perciperet: id quod longè indignissimum, Juri omni & divino, & humano foret adversum & contrarium.

4. Quia talis Compensatio, propriè loquendo, non est lucrum supra sortem exactum, propter solum mutuationis officium: sed tantùm est precium, sive æstimatio usus sortis consumtæ cum damno creditoris. Ratio est. Quia debitor pecuniam à Creditore petit & accipit non ex indigentiâ? sed ut per eam majores opes & possessiones acquirere, & magis magisq́; ditescere possit.

Quo sanè casu locum habet authentica Apostolica, 2. Cor. 8, 13. quæ officia Charitatis ita proximo præstanda esse statuit, ut ne aliis quidem sit relaxatio: nobis ipsis verò angustia sive afflictio.

liberi sumus: ita nec hanc legem per omnia eodemq́; modo observari necessum est: tamen quâ in re æquitas consistat, & quidem secundum Jus divinum, inde facilè potest colligi: nempè 1. licere emere & vendere ea omnia, quæ in emtionis & venditionis contractum venire possunt. 2. hunc ipsum contractum æquitatis Jure ita niti debere, ut ille neque emtori, neque venditori damno aut detrimento sit. Quod ipsum de Contractu venditionis & emtionis circa pecuniam, observandum esse, nemo negaverit, nisi qui illum æquitatis Jure nimis temerè, & impudenter spoliare ausit.

5. Quia Evangelium non abolet politias. Quemadmodum ergò Christianus bonâ & illæsâ conscientiâ, æquas, & societáti humanæ perquàm necessarias ac salutares Ordinationes, sive Constitutiones politicas, de matrimoniis, de sepulturis, de Testamentis, de hæreditatibus, de successionibus, de acquirendo rerum dominio, de furtis, de adulteriis, de ponderibus & mensuris, de emtionibus & venditionibus, deq́; id genus contractibus civilibus aliis, observare potest, imò debet: Ita nihil prorsus obstat, quò minùs Christianus iisdem salvâ conscientiâ, æquissimas Constitutiones Imperatorum: inq; Recessibus Imperii legitimè confirmatas, de Vsuris, observare possit, & debeat: quippe quas communis necessitas extorsit. Nisi enim Contractus iste locum obtineat, exiguo certè temporis spatio, Ecclesia suis reditibus, Ministri Verbi & Scholarum suis Stipendiis: Pauperes eleemosynis publicis: pupilli sustentatione necessaria: Studiosi Stipendiis & subsidiis publicis: senes & infirmi suis facultatibus, Xenodochia, & Orphanotrophia suis reditibus, spoliabuntur: totaque civilis societas dispereat necessum erit. Cùm ergò Scriptura ipsa dispositionem circa contracto civiles pro ratione temporis, personarum, locorum, aliarumq; circumstantiarum moderandam, Magistratui civili commendârit: utique omnes omninò Christiani constitutionibus, hac in parte secundum æquitatem publicatis, obtemperare tenentur: secundum Præceptum Apostoli, Rom.13.1. Omnis anima potestatibus supereminentibus sit subdita: Non enim est potestas, nisi à DEO: Et quicunq; resistit potestatibus, DEI ordinationi resistit: Qui autem resistunt, ipsi sibi damnationem acquirunt.

7. Quia charitas est ordinata, & à semetipsâ incipit, & suadet, ut potiorem rationem habeas eorum, quos DEUS & Natura tibi arctiùs conjunxerunt nempè conjugis, liberorum, & familiæ universæ: quàm aliorum. Jam horum ut curam habeas, ipsorumq; commoditatibus rectè prospicias: utique pecuniam tuam ita elocabis, ut inde fructus, & commodum aliquod ad te, tuosq; redundare possit. Et hoc ipsum præcipit Apostolus, 1 Tim. 5,8. Siquis suorum, & maximè domesticorum curam non habet, fidem abnegavit, & infideli est deterior.

8. Quia Charitas debet esse reciproca. Ergò qui ex mea pecuniâ magnum fecit lucrum, eò charitatis affectu me prosequi debet, ut illius lucri me faciat participem. Sum enim hac in parte, præ aliis omnibus, ipsius proximus. His & consimilibus rationibus aliis moti, indubitatò statuimus, licere de lucro supra sortem pacisci, & compensationem damni emergentis, & lucri cessantis, & petere, & accipere: non tantùm in bonis immobilibus: ut agris, vineis, & similibus: sed etiam in pecunia. Nam etsi illa per se stelis sit, nihild; ex se producat: usu tamen minimè est sterilis: sed uberem quæstum gignit, ut ex negociatione, hoc est, emtione & venditione deprehenditur.

6. Quia de similibus idem est judicium. Jam verò Lex DEI contractum emtionis & venditionis nuspiam tollit: sed potius ostendit, quæ circa hos ipsos contractus DEI sit voluntas. Exempli gratia, Levit. 25, 13. & seqq. de anno Jubilæo tale habetur præceptum: Anno jubilæo redibunt omnes ad possessiones suas, quando vendes aliquid civi tuo, vel emes ab eo, ne contristes fratrem tuum: sed juxta numerum annorum Jubilæi emes ab eo, & juxtà supputationem frugum vendet tibi: Quantò plures anni remanserint post Jubilæum, tantò crescet & pretium: & quantò minus temporu numeraveris, tantò minoris, & emtio constabit: tempus enim frugum vendet tibi &c. Ostendit nimirùm DOMINUS, quæ ratio contractuum esse debeat in emtione, & venditione agrorum, domorum &c. ut nimirùm id fiat sub conditione redemtionis: Et ne vel emtor, vel venditor gravetur, sed justa utrinque sit proportio, & secundum proventuum, ut & annorum multitudinem, pretium venditionis æstimetur. Quanquam verò, uti ab aliis Politiæ Mosaicæ ceremoniis

Sed quæritur hoc loco. Quid de huiusmodi emtu censibus, & reditibus annuis sit sentiendum, An Vsurarii Wucherische Kauff vnd Contract dici debeant. Sed facilis est ex jam dictis responsio per distinctionem. Si ejusmodi census & reditus emti sunt, vel ab illis, qui citra damnum & incommodum pendere, & solvere eos non possunt: vel contra leges publicas contractus est initus : tùm sanè Vsurarius ille, impius & illicitus meritò censetur. Si verò ejusmodi census & reditus emti sint ab illis, qui in tertio genere hominum locum habent, & emti secundum leges à Magistratu legitimè constitutas & approbatas: tùm sanè Vsurarii dici nequeunt, prout quidem hodiè vocabulum istud malè audit, & in deteriorem partem accipitur: sed rectiùs compensatorii, & remuneratorii appellantur.

Quæritur porrò: Quid statuendum sit de illo contractu Emtionis, hodie usitatissimo, quando certa pecuniæ summa ab alio emitur, pro certâ & legibus definita ac concessâ pensione annuâ, ut si quis centum florenos emat, singulis annis quinque florenis pendendo: sed ea conditione, ut dominium centum florenorum ab emtore, sive pecuniam elocante, planè transeat, neque illi liceat unquam reposcere: venditori autem, qui pensionem illam annuam solvit, integrum sit, quovis tempore, summam uti vocant capitalem restituere, suamq́; illam pensionem annuam ad se revocare? Qualis contractus Germanis est, ac dicitur: Ein widerkaufflicher Zins.

Respondeo: Quanquam tales contractus non sunt pura emtio, & quibusdam circumstantiis à verâ emtione differunt: si tamen in illis pretium pensionis sit æqvum, certè non debemo hoc nomine laqueos conscientiis injicere: sed tanquam licitos, & honestos approbare. præsertim cùm Imperatorum, & Romani Imperii calculo sint confirmati: neque sine universali mutatione totius status publici, tales sive emtiones, sive contractus possint mutari.

Sed difficilior est quæstio: Quid de illis contractibus sit judicandum, ubi emtor, sive Creditor, qui certam pecuniæ summam elocat, & per eam certam pensionem annuam ab alio emit, potestatem sibi reservat, renunciandi emtioni, & repetendi sortem sive summam elocatam?

Respondent nonnulli, talem contractum esse vitiosum, quippe cum charitate Christianâ pugnantem. Verùm quod dicunt isti, non probant. Potest enim talis etjam contractus ita esse comparatus, ut Charitatis Christianæ, modum nuspiam excedat. Certè Charitatis Christianæ est, quod sua pecuniâ quis fratrem ita juvat, ut ex eâ commodum suum facere, suamq́; rem familiarem augere possit. Ubi & æquitatis ratio, & lex naturæ, & dilectio proximi, & regula Christi, Matth. 7, 12. monent & præcipiunt, ut non modò pensionem annuam legitimam ritè solvat: sed &, exacto illo annorum spatio, quod in contractu expressum est, sortem ipsam restituat. Possunt enim varii incidere casus, quibus Creditor tùm, vel in elocatione liberorum, vel in emendo fundo aliquo, vel aliam ad rem necessariam pecuniâ illâ opus habeat. Ubi profectò summæ iniquitatis foret, si cum nostro damno & incommodo pecuniâ nostrâ carere cogamur. Quæ ipsa ratio etiam militat eo casu, si Creditor non certum annorum numerum in contractu exprimat, & definiat: sed in genere, sibi hanc potestatem reservet, urgente necessitate aliquâ, sortem ipsam reposcendi: sed ita, ut solutionem, vel restitutionem sortis, Debitor non ex abrupte, & incontinenti præstare cogatur: sed justum ipsi tempus, & ad minimum semestre concedatur. Ubi hanc ipsam quoque potestatem Debitor sibi reservare potest, ut vel certo annorum numero decurso, vel si pecunia non ampliùs opus habet, fortem creditori restituere possit, nec eam diutiùs cum suo incommodo retinere cogatur.

Quæ certè reciprocatio & legi naturæ, & æquitati, & Charitati Christianæ omninò est consona: ita ut vel insignem ruditatem, vel Zelum planè inordinatum prodant, qui hoc casu conscientias hominum sine causâ laqueos injicere, & sibi ipsi periculum accersere non dubitant. Sed de Usurâ Compensatoriâ plus satis.


### Chapter Four. and last. On civil contracts: III. Species of Usury, Punitive

III. Species of Usury, Punitive.

Punitive Usury is that which, on account of delay in paying, is imposed by the Magistrate according to the laws as a penalty. For there are those who, led by either malice or avarice, do not pay just and legitimate pensions, even though they could do so without loss and the ruin of their own affairs. Here, if the Magistrate commands payment in such a way that the Debtor is forced to pay something more beyond the defined and customary pension to the Creditor for the loss which he perceived from that, because the money was not paid on the just day: he certainly does not sin. Because this is of equity, and restrains the malice of the debtor. But if, indeed, the Debtor is oppressed by some adverse misfortune and cannot provide the pension, then punitive usury has no place to such an extent that in such a case the Creditor ought rather to remit the whole pension: as the fifth member of our treatise will now explain.

Latin:

III. Usuræ Species, Punitoria.

USura Punitoria est, quæ ob moram non solventu,propæna,à Magistratu secundum leges imponitur. Sunt enim, qui sive malitiâ, sive avaritiâ inducti, pensiones justas ac legitimas, licet sine damno, & rerum suarum jacturâ possint, non exolvunt. Hic si Magistratus solutionem ita imperet, ut Creditori pro damno, quod inde percepit, quia non justo die pecunia soluta fuit, ultra definitam & consuetam pensionem aliquid ampliùs solvere cogatur: certè non peccat. Quia hoc æquitatis est, & malitiam debitoris coèrcet. Quod si verò adverso aliquo infortunio Debitor oppressus, pensionem præstare nequeat, tùm usura punitoria usque adeò locum non habet, ut potius tali casu Creditor pensionem totam remittere debeat: ut: Quintum Tractationis nostræ membrum jam expediet.


### Chapter Four. and last. On civil contracts: V. Member. What moderation concerning Usuries ought to be observed?

This moderation partly respects the price which is to be counted in place of the annual pension: but partly respects the persons of the Creditors, who are accustomed to lend their money to the rich.

As to the FORMER, the Emperor Justinian in the Code regarding Usury permitted, in maritime contracts, the stipulation of one percent interest, that is, for every hundred florins, one per month: Das ist/das Jahr 12. gülden von hundert: by which agreement in the hundredth month the principal is equaled by the interest. Thus, therefore, in every eighth year, and one added month, the principal is equaled by the interest. In other lawful business dealings, two-thirds of one percent, that is, for every hundred, eight florins per year. For illustrious and noble persons, however, in any contract, not above one-third of one percent: that is, for every hundred florins, four florins per year. But for the common people, one-half of one percent, that is, six florins per year. And this indeed was the rule of those times. In our century, in the Roman Empire, the custom has prevailed that, with due moderation applied, four or five florins per hundred are received for each year. And this custom was confirmed in the Imperial Diets held in the year 1530 at Augsburg, and in the year 1576 at Regensburg: specifically, however, by the Electors of Saxony in the provincial constitutions published in the year 1550. and 1656: as also approved in the Torgau rescript, the Torgau Edict of the year 1583, in these words especially: Experience shows that when there is no certainty regarding interest, as to how far it is permitted, usurious and dangerous contracts have crept in for that very reason, in that many hold it to be the same whether they take much or little, and therefore attempt all sorts of ways to gloss over it; whereas, if the same were set at a certain measure, everyone would have knowledge of what they are to hold to, and those who exceed such could be brought to punishment all the sooner, etc.

we, by which we have demonstrated above that compensatory usury is lawful.

With regard to persons, certain rules and conditions must be observed by those lending their money to others for a certain compensation: which, however, can be referred primarily to the end and the outcome. With regard to the end, equity and charity ought always to be looked to in contracts of this kind: the former on the part of the debtor, the latter on the part of the creditor. For just as the giver ought to be moved by charity to lend money, so the receiver ought to be moved by equity and honesty to acknowledge the benefit, as if naturally obligated to an ἀντίδοσιν (recompense).

With regard to the outcome: If the debtor has enriched his affairs with our money, it is a matter of equity that he share a part of the profit or gain with the creditor. Again: if the debtor, by some adverse chance, such as fire, storm, plundering of goods, and similar misfortunes, has been reduced to such poverty that he scarcely has wherewith to repay the principal, let alone pay anything more beyond the principal, then it is a matter of Christian charity that the creditor should rightly consult his own conscience and not urge strict law, but remit the payment either in whole or in part. For just as Christian charity is the mother and queen of all other virtues, so it ought to govern contracts of this kind as well, so that neither party is burdened or oppressed.

Therefore, our highly praiseworthy ancestors moderated such interest payments to five, and permitted that one may give and take five per hundred in interest annually on lent money without danger of any penalty, which has also been held in common use in our lands far beyond human memory, and subsequently also under our government, according to the tenor of our previous land ordinance issued on this matter, and has been kept in use continuously; beyond the prescription which was directed toward such interest, they also gave the chancellery consent, and also ordered and decreed aid for it, etc.

By the most recent law of the Empire, the measure of five percent has likewise been prescribed for annual revenues: and by the recess and decree of the deputies at Speyer promulgated in the year 1600, it was approved throughout the entire Empire in such a way that these five percent take the place of what is interest, if the creditor does not wish to undertake the proof of this. In certain provinces of Germany, however, the Justinian half-percent (semisses) has also been recalled into use.

And that this moderation of the price, or of the payments to be paid annually above the principal, is agreeable to the law of nature, to equity, and to charity, we prove by the same reasons

Latin:

MOderatio hæc partim respicit pretium, quod pensionis annuæ loco est numerandum: partim verò personas Creditorum, qui suas pecunias divitibus elocare solent.

Quoad PRIUS, Justinianus Imp. in Codice de Usuris, permisit in trajectitiis contractibus, stipulari usuram centesimam, hoc est, de centum florenis, in singulos menses Unum: Das ist/das Jahr 12. gülden von hundert: Quo pacto centesimo mense sors ab usurâ æquatur. Sic ergo quovis anno octavo, & uno adjecto mense, sors æquatur ab Usurâ. In aliis licitis negociationibus bessem centesimæ, hoc est, de centum, in annum florenos octo. Illustribus tamen, & nobilibus personis, quolibet contractu, non supra tertiam partem centesimæ: hoc est, de centum florenis, in annum florenos quatuor. Vulgo autem dimidium centesimæ, hoc est, in annum florenos sex. Et hæc quidem illorum temporum fuit ratio. Nostro seculo in Imperio Romano consuetudo obtinuit, ut justa moderatione adhibita, quatuor aut quinque floreni pro centum, in singulos annos accipiantur. Et confirmata est hæc consuetudo in Comitiis Imperialibus, anno 1530. Augustæ: & anno 1576. Ratisbonæ celebratis: in specie autem ab Electoribus Saxoniæ in constitutionibus provincialibus, anno 1550. & 1656. publicatis: ut & in rescripto Torgensi, im Torgawische Ausschreiben anno 1583. approbata, his potissimum verbis: Es gibet die Erfahrung/ wenn man der Zinse halben/ wie weit dieselbe nachgelassen/ keine gewißheit hat/ das fürs nemlichen dahero die wucherlichen vnd gefehrlichen Contracte eingeschlichen/ In dem es ihr viel darfür halten/ es gelde gleich/ ob sie viel oder wenig nehs men/ vnd dahero das zubeschönen/ als lerley wege versuchen/ do hier gegen/ wann dieselbe auff gewisse Maß gerichtet würden/ ein jedes was er sich zuvers halten/ wissenschafft haben/ vnd die jes nigen/ so solches vberschreiten/ desto ehe zur straffe gebracht werden können/ etc.

cimus, quibus Vsuram compensatoriam licitam esse suprà demonstravimus.

Quoad Personas, pecuniam suam aliis pro certa compensatione elocantes, certæ regulæ & conditiones observandæ veniunt: quæ tamen ad finem, & Eventum potissimùm revocari possunt. Quoad finem, spectari semper in ejusmodi contractibus debet Æquitas, & Charitas: illa ex parte Debitoris: hæc ex parte Creditoris. Quemadmodum enim dantem oportet moveri Charitate ad pecuniam elocandam: Ita accipientem moveri oportet æquitate atque honestate ad agnoscendum beneficium, velut ad αντίδοσιν naturaliter obligatum.

Quoad Eventum: Si debitor nostra pecunia res suas locupletavit, æquitatis est, ut partem lucri sive commodi communicet cum creditore. Rursum: si Debitor casu aliquo adverso, ut incendio, tempestate, direptione bonorum, & consimilibus infortuniis, ad eam paupertatem sit redactus, ut vix habeat, unde sortem reponat, nedum ut ultra sortem aliquid amplius solvat: tum Charitatis Christianæ est, ut Creditor suæ conscientiæ rectè consulat, neqs strictum jus urgeat? sed pensionem vel totam, vel ex parte ei remittat. Quemadmodum enim Christiana Charitas omnium aliarum virtutum mater & regina est: Ita Contractus etiam hujusmodi gubernare debet: ut neutra pars prægravetur, aut opprimatur.

Darumb so haben vnsere Hochs löbliche Vorfahren solche Zinsreichung auff fünffe gemessiget vnd darauff nachgelassen/ das man von ausgeliehes nem Gelde Jährlich fünffe vom huns dert Zinse/ ohne gefahr einiger straff/ geben vnd nehmen möge/ welches auch also in vnsern Landen weit vber Mens schen gedencken/ folgents auch bey vns serer Regierung/ nach besage vnserer vorigen hierüber außgegangener Lans des Ordnung/ für vnd für in vblichen Gebrauch gehalte/ vber die Vorschreis bunge/ so auff solchen Zins gerichtet/ auch den Cangeleyen Consens gegeben/ auch Hulffen darauff befohlen/ vnd ans geordnet worden/ &c.

Novissimo jure Imperii itidem annuis reditibus quincuncium modus præscriptus est: & recessu ac decreto deputatorum Spirensi anno 1600. promulgato, in universo Imperio ita comprobatus: ut hæ quincunces succedant in locum ejus, quod Interest, si hujus probationem creditor suscipere nolit. In quibusdam tamen Germaniæ provinciis, etiam Justinianeæ semisses in usum revocatæ sunt.

Et hanc moderationem pretii, sive pensionum, supra sortem quotannis solvendarum legi Naturæ, æquitati, & Charitati proximi consentaneam esse, iisdem rationibus evin-


### Chapter Four. and last. On civil contracts: VI. Whether B. Luther simply disapproved and condemned all usury?

The doctrine concerning usury proposed thus far is in complete agreement with both the Holy Scriptures and the opinions of the Holy Fathers. For although it cannot be denied that the Fathers inveigh against usury most bitterly and most gravely, yet from the entire συνεννοίᾳ (consensus) of their discussion it is most clearly evident that they are not speaking of any usury whatsoever, but specifically of biting or lucrative usury; and in particular, they are arguing against the centesima and sesquicentesima usury, which commonly prevailed at that time, as is evident from the Sermon of St. Basil on Usury. The Council of Nicaea reproves and condemns these very Centesimae, especially in clerics and ecclesiastical persons, by this published canon: Since many clerics, seeking filthy lucre for the sake of avarice, have forgotten the divine precept, which says: He who has not given his money to usury, they, lending at interest, exact the Centesimae. This Holy Council decrees that if anyone is found after this definition to accept usury, or to seek filthy lucre from any such business, or to exact ἡμιόλια (hemiolia), that is, one and a half times the amount, whoever has attempted any such thing for gain shall be deposed from the clergy and held as alien to the ecclesiastical rank. dist. 42. c. Quoniam multi 14 q. 4. c. Quorum.

As for B. LUTHER, we know that he, both in his other writings and indeed especially in his admonition to the Pastors written in the year '40, so moderates his style that he might seem to disapprove of and condemn all usury simply, even compensatory usury, and that which can be provided by the rich without their loss and inconvenience. But if we weigh a little more accurately the moments of the matters and the weight of the arguments upon which B. LUTHER relies, perhaps it will not be difficult to demonstrate to the eye that he is arguing primarily about the duty of lending, which we ourselves concede ought to be free, as well as about lucrative usury, which we likewise simply condemn with B. LUTHER. And such assertions offer themselves in his writings which not obscurely support our doctrine concerning usury, such as these.

I. LUTHER approves in express words of interest concerning emerging loss and ceasing gain, as legitimate: in the Admonition to the Pastors. Tom. 7. Germ. Jen. fol. 399 a & b for me. Where LUTHER added this in the margin: One is obligated to make restitution for the loss that one experiences when one does not keep the day-time, but is tardy with payment. And concerning emerging loss he offers this opinion in the text itself: It is fair, also according to reason and natural law

that you (when I come to harm through your non-compliance) make everything good to me again, both the principal sum and the loss, for I did not lend you the hundred guilders so that I myself, or you, should be ruined by it, but I wanted to help you without my own loss. All this is so clear and bright that, even if all laws and books of jurists were lost, reason would still have to establish it, however weak it might be. Such compensation for loss is called 'Interesse' in the books of the jurists in Latin, and such lending is truly no usury, but a right, praiseworthy, honest service, and a good work shown to one's neighbor, etc.

And after a few words, where he discusses the interest of ceasing gain, he wants the opinions of the jurists to be heard and followed in this part: Such and countless circumstances or accidents of the same kind ought to be reckoned and weighed by the jurists, so that the compensation for loss or 'Interesse' does not become a knave and a usurer.

II. B. Luther explains himself everywhere, that the matter and the discussion for him are against the usury which is accepted from the poor: as is especially evident from Luther's response, which he gives to the exception of compensation and gift: where he makes mention of the poor several times in express words: As on fol. 398 b of the same writing: A gift is not called a right gain, but a thing given and taken voluntarily and for nothing: Yet you adorn it, lie, and call it a gift, when in truth it is a gain and usury, given to you by the needy in his distress.

III. That LUTHER is discussing the duty of lending, and indeed with respect to the poor, he himself confesses in the same place: fol. 399. It seems better advised to me that you, Pastor, refer this question to the jurists, whose oath and office it is to judge and teach in such mortal, perishable, miserable worldly matters; especially where one wants to be clever and sharp against the text, yet provided that you remain firm and stiff on the text, namely, that lending and taking more for it is usury; all laws and jurists will have to confirm this text for you, not only according to the Gospel, but also in their books. This state of the question being well observed, his entire discussion is also solely or at least principally directed against those who wish the duty of lending to be lucrative. And it is especially worthy of note that LUTHER himself protests, when he deals with the duty of lending, that he does not mean a legitimate contract for buying rents or fruits, etc. The words of Luther are as follows: We are not speaking this time of giving or gifting, nor of buying or selling, nor of redeemable interest, but of lending, in which usury carries on almost all its business: whoever lends something and takes something more or something better for it, that is usury, for lending should take back nothing more, but the very same thing that was lent, as the prophets, Christ himself, and the secular laws teach. And in the highest heat of the discussion he says: It is not fitting for us preachers to be idle here, for it concerns our salvation that we boldly rebuke and condemn usury from the pulpit, and state the text diligently and plainly, namely: whoever lends something and takes more or better for it, he is a usurer. fol. 404. Therefore, they pervert the state of the controversy sophistically who are accustomed to distort this admonition of LUTHER simply to the prohibition of all contracts and stipulations which are made according to laws and equity, both in immovable and movable goods: when nevertheless LUTHER himself, by protesting, confirms as it were that he is only discussing the duty of lending.

IV. The discussion of B. LUTHER is concerning illicit and illegitimate usury, as is especially evident from those things which he discourses upon regarding the usury of the Germans concerning the hundredths, two-hundredths, three-hundredths, and other detestable contracts of that kind, ibid. fol. 403.

V. LUTHER permits widows, orphans, the poor, the elderly, and all those who either do not have a fixed residence, or because of health, or age, or sex, or ignorance of some trade, cannot use their money themselves for some business, to lend their money to others for lawful usury. And although B. LUTHER calls such usury by a milder term, usury of necessity, a little necessity-usury: yet it does not follow from that that he established such usury in itself and by itself to be illicit and prohibited. Wherefore he advises in the midst of this that Princes and Jurists, Preachers and Councilors, should think of means of such a kind by which just moderation and equity can be preserved regarding contracts of this kind: fol. 405. Therefore I think, if the Prince of the land were called upon in this matter, and he, with reasonable jurists, preachers, and councilors, would find a tolerable means, [Trierische?] or [autre?] siae, then the conscience could be satisfied.
